Body:
We will resolve and return the nomsNumber on demand for custody endpoint requests rather than storing or precomputing it. The custody API will, at request time, look up the current NOMIS identifier from the canonical source (Prisoner Offender Search as primary, with a fallback to Elite2/NOMIS if necessary). We will not persist the nomsNumber in our domain store; instead we will enrich custody responses dynamically.

To control latency and dependency impact, we will:
- Use a short-lived in-memory cache (e.g., 5–15 minutes TTL) keyed by stable identifiers to reduce repeat lookups.
- Apply strict timeouts, retries with backoff, and a circuit breaker around the lookup. If the lookup fails or exceeds the SLA, we will return the custody payload without nomsNumber and include an explicit null/omitted field, preserving endpoint availability.
- Keep the lookup behind a feature flag to allow gradual rollout and fast disable.
- Instrument request/lookup metrics and logs (hit/miss, latency, failure rates) for operational insight.

This approach avoids data duplication and staleness, ensures the identifier reflects the latest NOMIS state, and limits schema changes to a non-breaking enrichment of the custody response. It also confines external dependency risk with caching and resilience patterns, and remains reversible should we later move to a pre-enrichment or event-driven synchronization model.

## Decision

We will scope services around explicit business capabilities and bounded contexts, not technical layers. Each service will own:
- A single, cohesive domain with clear responsibilities and outcomes
- Its data (separate persistence; no shared databases)
- Its public API and backward-compatible contracts

Service size will be “as small as necessary, as large as sensible”: small enough for a two-pizza team to own end-to-end, large enough to avoid excessive chatty calls or distributed transactions. Cross-cutting concerns (authN/Z, observability, messaging, schema registry) will be provided by platform components, not embedded in services.

Interaction rules:
- Prefer asynchronous, event-driven integration for cross-context flows; use synchronous calls only for request/response needs on the critical path.
- Outbound calls must be resilient (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers); inbound contracts versioned and documented (contract-first).
- No direct database access across services; data sharing via events or APIs.
- Idempotency required for externally visible operations.

Evolution and governance:
- New services require a capability map entry, explicit value, and a written boundary definition (responsibilities, non-goals, owned data, APIs, SLAs).
- Boundary changes follow an RFC with impact analysis and migration plan (including data ownership moves via events).
- Use the strangler pattern for legacy decomposition; avoid premature splitting.

Non-functional scope:
- Each service defines SLOs, scaling characteristics, and compliance requirements; aligns deployment, runtime limits, and on-call ownership accordingly.

Remove support for custom JNDI “lookup-name” and standardize on deterministic names

- Status: Accepted
- Deciders: Lewin Chan, Aaron McGrath
- Date: 2026-01-23

We will deprecate and remove the configurable JNDI lookup-name (e.g., @JndiBindable.lookupName or equivalent configuration fields) across all components. JNDI bindings will instead use a single, deterministic naming strategy derived from the component’s unique identifier and runtime namespace (e.g., <namespace>/<component-type>/<unique-id>). The runtime will provide a JndiNameStrategy to construct names consistently and a compatibility AliasRegistry to map legacy lookup-names to the new canonical name during the deprecation window.

Implementation details:
- Introduce JndiNameStrategy (default: CanonicalNameStrategy) and apply it to all bind/unbind and lookup operations.
- Mark all lookupName properties/annotations as @Deprecated; emit startup warnings when detected and register a temporary alias to the canonical name.
- Add configuration validation to fail fast when multiple components would bind to the same canonical name.
- Provide a migration utility that rewrites configs by removing lookupName and, where necessary, setting/normalizing unique-id to preserve the effective JNDI name.
- Update documentation and examples to reference canonical naming only; remove reliance on container-specific JNDI conventions.

Timeline:
- Deprecated now; alias-based compatibility supported for two minor releases.
- Removal of lookupName fields/annotations and aliasing in the next major release.

This simplifies configuration, eliminates name collisions and environment-specific quirks, and enables predictable, portable JNDI usage.

The backend will run exclusively inside Docker containers for all local development. We will provide a docker-compose configuration with a “dev” profile that orchestrates the API, backing services (e.g., database, cache, message broker), and any required dependencies. The compose stack will:

- Use the same base images as production for parity, with a dev override enabling hot-reload, interactive debugging, and verbose logging.
- Mount source code into the container via bind volumes to support live code reload and rapid iteration.
- Manage service configuration via .env files and compose variables; sensitive values will be injected via a local secrets mechanism where applicable.
- Expose well-known local ports and a shared Docker network for inter-service communication.
- Provide named volumes for persistent state (e.g., database data) across container restarts.
- Include a make/npx/script wrapper to standardize developer workflows (build, up, down, logs, test, migrate, seed).
- Support ARM/AMD via multi-arch images and buildx where needed.

Local non-Docker execution of the backend will not be officially supported. CI will validate the dev compose stack to ensure consistent, reproducible local setups.

We will containerize all application components as OCI-compliant images and deploy them across multiple compute nodes (boxes) orchestrated by Kubernetes. A managed Kubernetes service (e.g., EKS/AKS/GKE) will be preferred; otherwise, a self-managed cluster will be provisioned. Stateless services will run as Deployments; stateful components will use StatefulSets with managed, replicated storage classes. Container images will be built in CI, scanned, tagged immutably, and pushed to a central registry; releases will be applied via Helm charts and GitOps (e.g., Argo CD).

Cluster nodes will be grouped by roles (e.g., system, general workload, stateful), with scheduling and isolation enforced via taints/tolerations, node selectors, and resource quotas. Multi-tenancy and blast-radius reduction will be achieved using namespaces and NetworkPolicies. Traffic will be exposed through an Ingress controller with TLS termination; internal traffic will use ClusterIP services and, where necessary, a service mesh for mTLS and traffic shaping.

Observability will be standardized via centralized logging, metrics, and tracing stacks. Blue/green and canary rollouts will be used for safe changes. Horizontal Pod Autoscaling and cluster autoscaling will provide elastic capacity; PodDisruptionBudgets and readiness/liveness probes will protect availability. Backup/restore and disaster recovery will be defined for stateful workloads.

Persist tide projections in Firebase Firestore as the operational source of truth, with Cloud Storage holding raw model artifacts.

- Data model:
  - Collection stations/{stationId}/projections/{projectionId}
    - projectionId: ISO8601 UTC timestamp (e.g., 2026-02-01T00:00Z)
    - fields: timestamp, heightMeters, type (high|low|intermediate), stationId, source (model name), issuedAt, modelVersion, checksum, expiresAt, createdAt, updatedAt, quality (qc flag)
  - stations/{stationId}/metadata (static station info)
  - stations/{stationId}/indexes/latest (cached latest projection window: start, end, count, updatedAt)
- Storage: Upload raw model outputs and CSV/JSON rollups to Cloud Storage gs://<bucket>/tides/{runId}/..., referenced by storagePath in projections when needed.

- Write strategy:
  - Upsert projections idempotently using checksum; skip if unchanged.
  - Batch writes (500/doc batch) and rate-limit to stay within Firestore quotas.
  - Use server timestamps (FieldValue.serverTimestamp).
  - TTL: set expiresAt and enable Firestore TTL to purge superseded projections.
  - Maintain a run manifest document runs/{runId} summarizing ingestion.

- Access and performance:
  - Composite indexes on (stationId, timestamp asc) for range queries.
  - Cache latest window under stations/{stationId}/indexes/latest for fast UI reads.
  - Paginate by timestamp; avoid large arrays.

- Security and governance:
  - Writes restricted to service accounts; reads public or authenticated per product needs via Firestore Rules.
  - Schema versioning via modelVersion and a top-level schemaVersion field.
  - Backups via Firestore automated backups; retain Cloud Storage artifacts N days.

- Observability:
  - Emit metrics/logs per run; store QC summaries on runs/{runId}.

We will standardize on ES Modules across the codebase and prefer named exports. Application and library source code must use import/export (ESM) and avoid both CommonJS module.exports and export default. Default exports are disallowed except when strictly required by framework APIs (e.g., React.lazy interop), in which case a thin adapter may be used.

For Node.js projects, the package.json will declare "type": "module". Any necessary CommonJS interop will be isolated: legacy or third-party boundaries may use .cjs files, and any CommonJS-facing builds will be produced via the build pipeline (dual-publish using the exports field with ESM as primary and CJS fallbacks when needed). We will not synthesize or rely on a default export in CJS wrappers; named members will be preserved.

Linting and code review will enforce:
- No module.exports/require in new code.
- No export default (except documented interop cases).
- Prefer explicit named exports and re-exports (export { foo } from './foo').

This decision ensures consistent semantics, better static analysis, safer refactors, and cleaner interop while containing CommonJS to well-defined edges.

We will standardize on the ECS-Optimized Amazon Linux 2 (AL2) AMI for all EC2-backed ECS clusters across environments. New and replacement capacity will launch via Auto Scaling Groups using Launch Templates that reference the latest recommended AL2 ECS-Optimized AMI through the SSM public parameter (per-architecture), with controlled rollout via instance refresh and deployment waves.

Scope:
- Applies to all EC2 capacity for ECS; Fargate tasks are unaffected.
- Architectures: x86_64 by default; arm64/Graviton2/3 AL2 AMIs adopted where workloads are compatible to reduce cost and improve performance.

Operational stance:
- Avoid custom AMIs; use vanilla ECS-Optimized AL2 with bootstrap via user data (ECS_CLUSTER, SSM/CloudWatch agents, EBS/RAID config as needed).
- Patch cadence via ASG instance refresh to latest AL2/ECS Agent; emergency pinning possible by locking Launch Template to a specific AMI ID.
- Harden per CIS AL2 where feasible (sshd, auditd, IMDSv2 required, restrictive iptables), with AMI drift detection via SSM.
- Enable ECS Agent/AMI-embedded optimizations (enhanced networking, ephemeral storage tuning, Docker/Containerd defaults as provided by AL2).

Migration:
- Perform rolling replacement from Amazon Linux 1 or non-optimized AMIs cluster-by-cluster, maintaining capacity buffers and draining ECS tasks.
- Validate application images on both x86_64 and arm64 in lower environments prior to production cutover.

Rationale:
- AL2 provides long-term support, improved security baseline, better kernel/container runtime compatibility, and first-class ECS agent integration, reducing maintenance overhead and improving stability and performance.

Rollback:
- Revert Launch Template to prior AMI ID and run ASG instance refresh; retain previous AMI for 2 release cycles.

- Prefer composition over inheritance. Use delegation, strategy, and small collaborating objects to share behavior.
- Keep inheritance hierarchies shallow (max one concrete level below an abstract base). Prohibit deep or cross-cutting hierarchies.
- Use interfaces/protocols for polymorphism. Define capabilities via small, focused contracts; depend on abstractions in public APIs.
- Introduce abstract base classes only to capture stable, domain-relevant invariants with shared behavior that cannot be composed easily. Document extension points explicitly.
- Classes are final/sealed by default. Make a class extensible only when there is a clear and tested extension use case; annotate and document such classes/methods as “extension points”.
- Avoid inheriting from framework base classes in domain entities and value objects. If framework inheritance is required, isolate it in adapters or infrastructure layers.
- Disallow overriding methods that manage state, transactions, or security. Expose hook methods or callbacks instead. Favor the Template Method pattern only when hooks are minimal and well-documented.
- Use mixins/traits/modules only for stateless, orthogonal concerns (e.g., logging helpers). Do not use them to share persistent state or cross-domain behavior.
- Public constructors are minimal; prefer factory functions/builders to control subclass selection without exposing inheritance to callers.
- Testing relies on interface-driven substitution. Avoid partial mocks and stubbing of superclass behavior.
- Backward compatibility: adding new subtypes requires contract tests; removing or reparenting classes is a breaking change and must follow deprecation policy.

We will implement downloadable search results via an Export service supporting synchronous streaming for small results and asynchronous background exports for large ones.

- Formats: CSV (UTF-8, RFC4180), JSON Lines (NDJSON). XLSX may be added later via the same pipeline.
- Request model: clients call POST /exports with the exact search query/filters/sort as used in the UI, plus options: format, selected fields/columns, timezone, CSV delimiter, and maximum rows. The service snapshots the query at request time to ensure consistent results.
- Small exports (≤50k rows or ≤50 MB) stream directly from the search backend to the client with backpressure.
- Large exports run asynchronously via a durable queue and worker(s), reading in pages from the search backend, writing to a temporary object store (e.g., S3) in a single file per export (optionally gzip-compressed). The API returns an export ID to poll status and a time-limited signed URL when complete.
- Limits and safeguards: hard cap 1,000,000 rows and 2 GB per export; server-enforced field allowlist; rate limiting per user/org; one concurrent large export per user; exports expire and are deleted after 72 hours. PII fields are redacted or excluded by default according to data classification.
- Consistency and ordering: stable deterministic ordering (e.g., by sort criteria then _id) to avoid duplicates/omissions across pages; point-in-time search or scroll API to maintain a consistent snapshot.
- Schema handling: column headers use human-friendly labels with stable machine field names in metadata. The export includes a metadata block (separate JSON file or header) with query, timestamp, field schema version, and locale/timezone.
- Observability and audit: each export is logged and auditable (who, when, filters, counts, file location, size). Metrics capture duration, throughput, and failures with alerting.
- Security: exports require authentication and authorization equivalent to interactive search; signed URLs are scoped, single-use where supported, and short-lived.
- UX: “Export” button mirrors current filters and selected columns; progress and completion notifications are shown; users can cancel running exports.

This approach scales, preserves search semantics, and provides safe, user-friendly downloads.

In-depth katas are maintained as a distinct track to avoid mixing fundamentals with deep dives while keeping navigation coherent.

- Location: Each topic may have an in-depth subfolder colocated with its normal katas, e.g.:
  - esX/language/<topic>/in-depth/
  - library/<lib>/<topic>/in-depth/
- Naming: Test files use the normal naming rules plus an “in-depth” qualifier in the directory only (not the filename), e.g. es6/language/promise/in-depth/all-race-edge-cases.js. This keeps filenames readable and the separation structural.
- Metadata: Add tag: [in-depth] and level: advanced in the kata header (or the catalog manifest) to enable filtering in UI and CI pipelines.
- Indexing/UX: In-depth katas are hidden from default/beginner tracks and appear under a dedicated “In-depth” group per topic. Deep links from normal katas (e.g., “see In-depth: Promise.all() internals”) are encouraged.
- Scope: Focus on advanced scenarios (edge cases, performance characteristics, spec nuances, interop, pitfalls). Assume the corresponding “Basics” and “The API” katas are known prerequisites; list them explicitly in prerequisites metadata.
- Structure: Follow the same test formatting conventions as normal katas. Longer descriptions and multi-step setups are allowed where necessary, but keep one primary learning focus per file.
- Coverage policy: A feature gets an in-depth kata only when normal katas cannot cover necessary nuance without harming clarity; avoid duplicating content.
- Versioning: When language versions diverge meaningfully, keep separate in-depth katas per version under their respective trees; otherwise, share via symlinks or catalog aliases.

## Decision

We will standardize on Docker to containerize all application services and supporting tools across development, CI, and production. Each service will include a Dockerfile using multi-stage builds to produce minimal, reproducible images (preferring distroless/alpine where appropriate), with explicit version pinning of base images and dependencies. Local development will use Docker Compose for orchestrating multi-service environments and parity with production dependencies. CI will build, scan (SAST/dependency/image), sign, and push images to our container registry; deployments will pull immutable, semver-tagged images (never latest). Runtime containers will follow security best practices: non-root user, read-only filesystem where feasible, least-privilege capabilities, healthchecks, and minimal exposed ports. Configuration will be injected via environment variables and secrets managers, not baked into images. Caching strategies (builder cache, dependency layers) will optimize build times. Platform orchestration (e.g., Kubernetes or managed container services) will run these images with resource limits and liveness/readiness probes. We will maintain a shared base image and linting conventions to enforce consistency, and deprecate non-containerized run paths except for exceptional cases explicitly approved by architecture.

We will adopt a unified, product-wide Design Guideline that standardizes visual language, interaction patterns, and content style across all user interfaces.

- Foundation: Base the system on Material Design 3 principles, customized with our brand. Establish design tokens (color, typography, spacing, elevation, motion, radius) as the single source of truth and distribute them to code via a token pipeline.
- Components: Maintain a canonical component library in Figma and implement it in code (React + Storybook) as reusable, accessible components. Component APIs, states, and interactions must mirror the Figma specs; deviations require review.
- Accessibility: Comply with WCAG 2.2 AA. Enforce color contrast, focus states, keyboard navigation, ARIA semantics, and motion-reduction preferences. Include accessibility checks in design review, linting, and CI.
- Responsiveness: Define standard breakpoints and a responsive grid. All screens must support mobile, tablet, and desktop layouts unless explicitly exempted.
- Content: Use a concise, inclusive microcopy style guide; standardize terminology, error messaging, date/time formats, and i18n/l10n readiness.
- Theming: Support light and dark themes via tokens; no hard-coded colors or sizes. Support product-level theming without forking components.
- Assets: Standardize iconography set and illustration style. Use SVG for icons with variable stroke/size via tokens.
- Governance: Changes are proposed via RFCs, reviewed by Design System WG (Design, Frontend, Accessibility). Version the guideline and component library semantically; publish a changelog and migration notes.
- Adoption: New features must use the design system. Existing screens are migrated opportunistically. Include linters, automated visual regression tests, and documentation gates in CI.
- Documentation: Host living documentation (Figma, Storybook, usage guidelines, do/don’t examples) and track component maturity and coverage.

We will adopt Axon Framework (v4.x) as the standard CQRS and Event Sourcing framework for JVM-based services, integrated with Spring Boot. Axon will be used to model Aggregates, handle Commands and Events, and orchestrate long-running business processes using Sagas. Events will be immutable, versioned, and serialized with Jackson JSON; command and query payloads will follow the same schema conventions.

We will use Axon Server as the default message router and event store:
- Local/dev: Axon Server SE (containerized).
- Production: Axon Server EE (clustered, with replication and disaster recovery).
Where Axon Server is not permitted, we will use Axon Framework’s JDBC event store on PostgreSQL and Axon’s Kafka extension for distributed messaging; the token store will be PostgreSQL in all cases.

Key standards:
- Aggregates use annotated command handlers; state changes occur only via event sourcing handlers.
- Sagas coordinate cross-aggregate workflows; state is persisted in JPA-backed saga store.
- Snapshotting enabled for large aggregates; thresholds defined per aggregate.
- Event upcasters required for all breaking event schema changes; semantic versioning applied.
- Idempotency enforced for command handlers; duplicate event handling guarded via tokens.
- Tracing and metrics via Micrometer and OpenTelemetry; correlation/causation identifiers propagated.
- Security and multi-tenancy metadata carried in message headers.
- Blue/green and rolling upgrades supported via backward-compatible events and feature flags.

Operational practices:
- Zero-downtime replays executed in shadow pipelines; production replays require approval.
- Backups and retention policies managed at Axon Server/DB level; legal hold supported.
- CI/CD includes contract tests for commands/queries and event-compatibility checks.

This decision standardizes our domain-driven architecture, reduces boilerplate for CQRS/ES, and provides a scalable, observable backbone for distributed workflows.

We will standardise on Terraform as our single tool for provisioning, changing, and documenting all infrastructure. Infrastructure code will live in-repo alongside the application, organised as reusable, versioned modules with clear inputs/outputs and README generated via terraform-docs.

Key practices:
- Pin provider and module versions; commit a locked dependency graph (terraform.lock.hcl).
- Maintain separate state per environment (e.g., dev, staging, prod) using a remote backend with encryption and locking; restrict backend access via IAM and enable state recovery/versioning.
- Enforce change management via PRs: terraform fmt/validate, tflint, and policy/static analysis (e.g., Checkov) run in CI; CI produces a terraform plan for review; applies are gated and environment-scoped (manual approval for protected envs).
- Use consistent tagging/labels (owner, cost-centre, environment, data classification) to enable cost allocation and governance.
- Manage secrets and credentials outside code using the platform secret manager/CI variables; avoid hardcoding or leaking into logs; minimise sensitive values in state and restrict plan/artifact visibility.
- Prefer module composition over copy-paste; publish shared modules for common patterns; import existing resources where practical to avoid destructive drift.
- Document environment topology, module usage, and runbooks in the repo; record breaking changes in CHANGELOG; automate drift detection via scheduled plan.
- Keep ephemeral review environments opt-in and disposable; production changes must be idempotent and reversible (plan reviewed, small blast radius, backups).

## Decision

We will adopt a mixed-method, continuous usability testing strategy across the product lifecycle:
- Conduct formative, moderated remote usability tests during discovery and before major releases, using task-based scenarios on high-fidelity prototypes and staging builds. Sessions will be recorded, think-aloud facilitated, and time-boxed (45–60 min).
- Run lightweight, unmoderated, task-based tests for rapid iteration and A/B comparisons between design alternatives and copy changes.
- Establish recurring benchmark tests (quarterly) using standardized metrics (SUS, task success rate, time-on-task, error rate, CES/NPS) to track usability over time.
- Incorporate accessibility evaluations in every round: WCAG 2.2 AA checks, keyboard navigation, color contrast, and assistive technology spot checks (e.g., screen readers).
- Instrument products to capture behavioral analytics (funnels, drop-offs) and sample session replays to complement qualitative findings.
- Recruit participants from target personas with coverage for key platforms, assistive tech, and language locales; maintain a standing panel for fast turnaround. Offer incentives per market norms.
- Use a standard toolkit: moderated via Zoom/Lookback; unmoderated via UserTesting/Maze; analytics via product telemetry; findings stored in a searchable research repository with tagged insights and video clips.
- Operationalize with templates (screeners, consent, scripts), privacy-compliant data handling, and issue creation workflows linking insights to backlog items with severity and acceptance criteria.
- Cadence: at least one usability activity per sprint; benchmark quarterly; report synthesized insights within 48 hours to inform prioritization.

## Decision

Adopt a folder-based input format as the primary input model. The system will treat the provided path as a directory containing all required sources, configuration, and assets for a single job/run.

- Structure and conventions:
  - Required: manifest.(yaml|yml|json) at the root defining schemaVersion, entry points, processing mode, and explicit file ordering/globs.
  - Recommended subfolders: /src (code), /data (datasets), /assets (aux files), /config (additional configs), README.md for human docs.
  - Deterministic ordering: files are processed in the order declared in manifest; if omitted, lexicographic order by relative path.

- Packaging and transport:
  - CLI: --input-dir PATH.
  - API: accept zipped folder uploads (multipart) or presigned bundle URLs; server will expand to a sandboxed workspace.
  - Local runs may point directly to an on-disk directory.

- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Continue accepting single-file inputs; when a file is provided, wrap it as a virtual folder with a generated default manifest (entry = that file).
  - Mark single-file mode as deprecated and schedule removal in two minor versions; provide an auto-migration helper to emit a minimal manifest.

- Validation and limits:
  - Enforce schema validation on manifest and disallow unknown keys by default.
  - Apply limits on total size, file count, and maximum file size; allow overrides for trusted tenants.
  - Reject symlinks, device files, and paths escaping the root; normalize to POSIX-style relative paths.

- Reproducibility and integrity:
  - Compute and store a content hash (Merkle over files + manifest) for caching and provenance.
  - Ignore VCS and transient files by default (.git, .DS_Store, node_modules unless explicitly included).

- Security and isolation:
  - Expand archives and process folders in a restricted, ephemeral workspace with non-root user, no network by default (configurable), and antivirus scanning when enabled.

- Observability:
  - Log manifest summary, resolved file list, and effective configuration; expose via run metadata.

This decision enables multi-file scenarios, explicit configuration, deterministic runs, and easier transport while maintaining a migration path from single-file inputs.

We will implement the compute layer as AWS Lambda functions. HTTP endpoints will be exposed through Amazon API Gateway; asynchronous and event-driven workloads will be triggered via Amazon EventBridge, SQS, and relevant AWS service events (e.g., S3, DynamoDB Streams). Functions will be stateless, configured via environment variables and AWS Secrets Manager/Parameter Store, and instrumented with CloudWatch logs/metrics and AWS X-Ray for tracing. We will package functions as ZIP artifacts by default; container images will be used only when dependency size or native binaries require it. Latency-sensitive paths will use Provisioned Concurrency; others will use on-demand scaling. IAM roles will follow least privilege, and VPC attachment will be applied only where necessary to reach private resources to avoid cold-start penalties. Deployment will be automated via our IaC toolchain (e.g., Terraform/Serverless Framework) and CI/CD, including staged environments and canary/gradual rollouts. This decision standardizes our runtime on serverless compute to achieve elastic scaling, operational simplicity, and cost efficiency.

We will implement defense-in-depth brute-force protection across all authentication- and identity-sensitive endpoints (/login, /mfa/verify, /password-reset, /token, API key creation/rotation):

- Edge controls: Use the WAF/CDN to apply IP reputation filtering, bot detection, geo/risk rules, and coarse rate limits (e.g., 300 req/5m/IP, burst 50). Automatically challenge (JS/CAPTCHAv3/turnstile) when risk is elevated.
- Application throttling: Implement Redis-backed token-bucket/sliding-window limits keyed by user identifier, IP, and credential pair (username+IP) with jittered exponential backoff. Initial thresholds: 10 failed attempts/5m per user, 50/5m per IP, 200/day per IP, with adaptive tightening on anomaly signals.
- Progressive challenges: After N consecutive failures (e.g., 5), require CAPTCHA and add incremental delay. After M failures (e.g., 10), temporarily suspend authentication for that user identifier for 15–30 minutes, with exponential increases for repeated abuse. Avoid long fixed lockouts to reduce account lockout DoS risk.
- Signal hygiene: Do not disclose account existence or factor validity; return uniform error messages and use constant-time credential comparisons. Log all attempts with correlation IDs; emit security alerts on threshold breaches.
- Allow/deny controls: Maintain allowlists for trusted service IPs/clients with higher but capped limits; enforce per-client/app quotas and HMAC-signed request requirements for machine-to-machine flows.
- Recovery: Throttle password reset and enrollment endpoints similarly; require CAPTCHA/rate limits for OTP delivery. Implement automated WAF blocking for persistent abusive sources.
- Governance: Configure metrics, dashboards, and runbooks; regularly tune thresholds using observed telemetry and red-team findings.

- Adopt a UITestablePage interface (protocol) that every screen (UIViewController/UIView and SwiftUI View via wrapper) must implement to declare and assign accessibilityIdentifiers.
- Each page declares a nested enum/struct Ids providing strongly-typed, namespaced identifiers (e.g., LoginPage.Ids.usernameField).
- Provide a single entry point per page, configureAccessibilityIdentifiers(), invoked from viewDidLoad/body initialization, that assigns identifiers to all interactive and test-relevant elements.
- Disallow ad-hoc string literals for accessibilityIdentifier. All identifiers must come from the page’s Ids namespace or a shared CoreIds where cross-page reuse is intentional.
- Enforce a consistent naming convention: <PageName>.<ElementRole>[.<Variant|State>] (e.g., CheckoutPage.payButton.primary).
- Expose a UITestable registry helper to validate uniqueness (per page) and optionally global collisions in debug builds.
- Align UI tests with a Page Object pattern that consumes the same Ids, eliminating duplication and string drift between app code and tests.
- Require new UI components/pages to implement UITestablePage and provide identifier coverage for all actionable and content elements critical to automation and accessibility.
- For SwiftUI, apply identifiers via .accessibilityIdentifier(Ids.*) and ensure hosting controllers call configureAccessibilityIdentifiers() when bridging UIKit.
- Add CI checks: lint for raw identifier strings, and a lightweight unit test to assert that key elements have non-empty accessibilityIdentifiers.

Adopt an inclusive language policy across source code, configuration, database schemas, APIs, documentation, UI text, logs, and communications. New contributions must use inclusive terms; existing occurrences will be refactored incrementally with care to avoid breaking changes.

- Preferred replacements include:
  - allowlist/blocklist instead of whitelist/blacklist
  - primary/replica or leader/follower instead of master/slave
  - main/default instead of master (branch)
  - parent/child or initiator/responder instead of master/slave roles
  - baseline/basic/smoke check instead of sanity check
  - deprecated/legacy exception instead of grandfathered
  - placeholder/sample/example instead of dummy

- Tooling and enforcement:
  - Add prose linters (e.g., alex) and code linters/plugins (e.g., eslint-plugin-inclusive-language) with repository-specific term lists.
  - Configure pre-commit hooks and CI to fail on violations, with autofix suggestions where possible.
  - Provide a glossary and style guide in CONTRIBUTING.md.

- Migration strategy:
  - For internal identifiers, rename with scripted refactors and database migrations; provide aliases/shims where needed.
  - For public APIs and schemas, introduce new fields/endpoints, deprecate offensive terms, and remove them in the next major version following SemVer. Communicate via changelogs and migration guides.

- Governance:
  - Assign ownership to the Architecture/Docs team for policy updates and exceptions.
  - Require ADRs for contentious terms; default to the most inclusive industry-standard alternative.

## Decision

An “environment” is a named, isolated runtime context that encapsulates infrastructure, configuration, secrets, data, and operational controls under a single change-control boundary and lifecycle. An environment may consist of one or more cloud accounts/projects, networks (e.g., VPCs), clusters, namespaces, and configuration sets that collectively host one or more deployments of the product.

We standardize the following environment types:
- development (dev)
- staging (stage)
- production (prod)
- ephemeral preview (preview-<id>) for short-lived validation

Naming must follow: dev, stage, prod, and preview-<id> for ephemerals. All resources, artifacts, secrets, policies, and data are environment-scoped. Cross-environment access is disallowed except via explicitly approved, versioned interfaces.

Clarifications:
- Environment ≠ region/zone; an environment may span regions but retains one lifecycle and control boundary.
- Environment ≠ tenant/customer; multi-tenancy is within an environment.
- Environment ≠ deployment instance/release; deployments are versions within an environment.
- Feature-branch previews are environments only when provisioned as ephemeral preview-<id>.

Change management and configuration promotion occur between environments (dev → stage → prod), not within. Observability, SLOs/SLAs, access control, and incident processes are defined per environment. Each environment has an accountable owner, budget, and tagging policy to ensure auditable isolation, cost attribution, and reproducible operations.

We will split the codebase into independently versioned Git repositories per architectural layer (e.g., domain, application, infrastructure/adapters, UI), and consume each layer from the main system repository as Git submodules under /layers/<layer-name>. Submodules will be pinned to immutable tags (Semantic Versioning) to ensure reproducible builds. Updates will occur via explicit bump PRs that advance the submodule SHA/tag, with CI checks preventing dirty or detached submodule states.

Development and CI will use a standardized bootstrap script (e.g., make bootstrap) to init/update submodules, and a guard (pre-commit/CI) to ensure submodule pointers are committed. Cross-layer dependencies must remain acyclic and follow the defined direction (application → domain; adapters → domain/application; UI → application). Shared utilities are isolated to a dedicated common submodule to avoid leakages and cycles.

Contribution workflow: propose changes in the layer’s own repo, merge and tag a release, then bump the consumer submodule via a dedicated PR. Breaking changes require a major version and migration notes. We will automate detection of new tags and open bump PRs (e.g., Renovate/bot). Temporary integration work may reference submodule branches, but main must pin to tags before merge.

We will implement Translations 2.0 as a key-based, ICU MessageFormat-driven internationalization system with continuous localization and runtime namespace loading.

- Use opaque, stable message IDs (not English-as-key), namespaced by domain/feature (e.g., checkout.payment.card.expired). Keys live alongside source.
- Author messages in ICU MessageFormat with CLDR plural/select rules. No string concatenation. Variables are explicitly named.
- Store translations per locale and namespace as JSON; build compiles messages to ICU AST for fast runtime formatting.
- Provide a framework-agnostic i18n core with thin adapters (e.g., React, Node, CLI). On the web, use Intl.* for dates/numbers/currency; fall back only where required.
- Locale negotiation follows: explicit URL param/segment > user profile > Accept-Language > app default. Implement hierarchical fallbacks (e.g., pt-BR → pt → en).
- Lazy-load translation bundles per namespace/locale with content-hash versioning, ETags, and CDN caching. Preload core namespaces; defer feature namespaces.
- Enforce content policy: no embedded HTML in messages. For rich text, support tokenized placeholders (e.g., <link>…</link>) mapped to components at render time.
- Support RTL via locale-driven dir switching and logical CSS. Provide bidi isolation in interpolations.
- Tooling: static extraction of message descriptors from source; CI sync with a TMS; pseudolocalization in non-prod; validation to detect missing/unused keys and placeholder mismatches.
- Backwards compatibility: provide a legacy adapter for existing i18n calls and a guided migration path to ICU messages.
- Observability: runtime warnings for missing keys, metrics on coverage and fallback rates, and feature flags to gate rollout per surface.

We will adopt a strict layered architecture to improve modularity, testability, and maintainability. The canonical layers and rules are:
- Presentation (UI/Edge): handles user interaction or inbound adapters (HTTP/CLI/Events). No business logic. Depends only on Application contracts.
- Application (Service/API): orchestrates use cases, transactions, and authorization; coordinates domain operations. Depends on Domain and abstracts Infrastructure via ports.
- Domain (Core): entities, value objects, domain services, policies. Pure, side-effect free; no external dependencies.
- Infrastructure (Adapters): persistence, messaging, file systems, external services. Implements ports defined by Application/Domain.

Dependency direction is inward only: Presentation → Application → Domain; Infrastructure depends on Application/Domain ports. Cross-layer calls must go through the immediate layer; no skipping.

Contracts and data:
- Use DTOs at Presentation/Application boundary; map to Domain types at the edge.
- Define ports (interfaces) in Application/Domain; implement adapters in Infrastructure.
- Domain invariants enforced within Domain; validation at edges for shape, in Domain for rules.

Transactions and consistency:
- Unit of work/transactions initiated in Application layer.
- Outbox/publish-subscribe for cross-service integration.

Cross-cutting concerns:
- Logging, metrics, tracing via middleware/interceptors.
- Security handled at Presentation (authentication) and Application (authorization/policies).

Testing:
- Domain: pure unit tests.
- Application: use port fakes.
- Infrastructure: integration tests for adapters.
- End-to-end for critical flows.

Governance and enforcement:
- Enforce boundaries via module structure, static analysis, and code owners.
- Public APIs at layer boundaries are versioned; backward compatibility honored at the Presentation/Application contract.

Mapping:
- For microservices, each service maintains its own layers.
- For a modular monolith, layers are per module with internal boundaries preserved.

Exceptions require ADRs and approved facades/anti-corruption layers.

Adopt Kubernetes startup, readiness, and liveness probes for all long-running workloads as first-class health contracts.

- Readiness: Gate traffic until the container can serve requests. Prefer HTTP GET /readyz (or gRPC Health Checking) with shallow dependency checks (e.g., DB ping with tight deadline). Must fail fast when critical dependencies are unavailable. Readiness should re-evaluate continuously and reflect backpressure (e.g., queue saturation).

- Liveness: Detect and self-heal unrecoverable process faults only. Prefer HTTP GET /livez (or gRPC health “SERVING”) with minimal logic; do not depend on external systems. Avoid deep dependency checks to prevent cascading restarts. Use only after readiness is consistently passing.

- Startup: Protect slow starters and deferred JIT/migration phases. Use startupProbe to block liveness until the app is initialized; avoid large initialDelaySeconds on liveness/readiness. Once startupProbe succeeds, liveness/readiness take over.

Probe conventions and defaults:
- Endpoints: /livez, /readyz, /healthz (200 OK), non-200 = failure. For gRPC, implement standard health service.
- Timeouts/periods: periodSeconds=10, timeoutSeconds=2–5, successThreshold=1. Initial thresholds per service class:
  - CPU-light web: readiness failureThreshold=3, liveness failureThreshold=3
  - IO-heavy/stateful: readiness failureThreshold=6–9, liveness failureThreshold=5
- startupProbe: periodSeconds=5–10, failureThreshold sized to max cold-start (e.g., 60–120s), no external checks.
- Sidecars: must expose their own probes; if loopback-only, use exec probe (e.g., curl localhost) within the container.
- Avoid exec probes unless loopback is required; prefer HTTP/gRPC. Avoid TCP probes except for legacy services.
- Health handlers must be lightweight (<50ms typical), non-allocating, and resilient under load; include circuit-breaker state in readiness.
- For stateful apps, readiness must reflect leader/replica role and safe-serve conditions.
- Centralize probe configuration via Helm/Kustomize values; all exceptions require ADR and SRE sign-off.
- Observability: export probe result metrics; alert on prolonged NotReady (>5m) and restart storms.

Roll out by service tier, verify with load tests and failure injection, and document service-specific probe semantics in the runbook.

We will use hapi.js as the HTTP server framework for this service. hapi provides strong, secure-by-default primitives (input/output validation with @hapi/joi, built-in auth strategies, robust routing, payload handling, and caching) that reduce our need for custom middleware and third‑party glue. Its plugin-centric architecture cleanly modularizes features (e.g., auth, logging, rate limiting) and encourages consistent configuration over ad‑hoc code, improving maintainability and reuse across services. hapi’s explicit request lifecycle, detailed route options, and server.inject testing utility support high testability and predictable behavior. First-party TypeScript types and async/await ergonomics fit our stack, and the framework’s maturity and governance provide stability for long-lived services. We will target the current hapi LTS-compatible version aligned with our Node.js LTS, pin dependencies, and adopt recommended operational plugins for observability (logging/metrics) and security hardening. This choice favors built-in capabilities and enterprise-friendly defaults over minimal cores (e.g., Express) or performance-first tradeoffs (e.g., Fastify), reflecting our priorities of security, consistency, and maintainability.

## Decision

Adopt and enforce the following Security Architecture Principles across all products, services, and platforms:

- Secure-by-design and default: prefer secure configurations, safe defaults, and minimal attack surface; deny-by-default network and access controls.
- Zero Trust and least privilege: authenticate and authorize every request; centralized identity with SSO, MFA, short-lived credentials, and role-based/scoped access.
- Defense-in-depth: layered controls across identity, data, application, network, and endpoint with compensating safeguards for control failure.
- Data first: classify data; encrypt in transit and at rest with managed keys; minimize data collection/retention; apply privacy-by-design.
- Secure SDLC: integrate threat modeling, security requirements, static/dynamic/container scanning, dependency management, and supply-chain integrity (SBOM, provenance) into CI/CD; block on critical findings.
- Secrets and key management: store secrets only in approved vaults; rotate automatically; never embed in code or images.
- Hardened platforms: immutable, reproducible builds; baseline-hardened images; patch within defined SLAs; least functionality; configuration as code.
- Network segmentation: isolate tiers and tenants; egress controls; API gateways with authenticated, rate-limited, schema-validated interfaces.
- Observability and logging: centralized, tamper-evident logs; privacy-aware telemetry; detection engineering with actionable alerts and runbooks.
- Resilience and recovery: backups, key escrow, tested disaster recovery and incident response; design to fail safely and degrade gracefully.
- Third-party and SaaS governance: assess vendors, enforce contractual security controls, continuous posture monitoring.
- Compliance and risk-based approach: map controls to applicable standards, document residual risk, and continuously improve via metrics and retrospectives.

All new and materially changed systems must demonstrate conformance through architecture reviews, security control catalog mapping, and automated policy checks in CI/CD before promotion to production.

We will adopt Red Hat OpenShift as the primary cloud platform for deploying and operating containerized workloads across environments (on-premises and public cloud). OpenShift will be our default target for new microservices, APIs, batch jobs, and event-driven components that require Kubernetes orchestration, CI/CD integration, and enterprise governance.

Scope:
- Applies to newly built containerized services and platform capabilities (CI/CD, observability, security).
- Does not apply to SaaS solutions or workloads better served by managed PaaS/SaaS (e.g., managed databases) unless integration requires in-cluster components.
- Existing systems remain in place; migration requires separate ADRs.

Rationale:
- Consistent Kubernetes abstraction across hybrid/multi-cloud with enterprise features (RBAC, quotas, policy).
- Built-in operator ecosystem, GitOps (Argo CD), service mesh (Istio), image security (Quay/ACS), and workload security baselines to accelerate compliant delivery.
- Standard developer experience (Source-to-Image, pipelines) and platform automation improves velocity and reduces drift.

Consequences:
- Standardize deployment on OpenShift constructs (Namespaces/Projects, Routes/Ingress, Operators, Pipelines), with Helm/Kustomize for packaging and Argo CD for GitOps.
- Establish a Platform Engineering function to operate clusters, manage Operators, networking, storage classes, secrets management, and cost controls.
- Prefer cloud-managed OpenShift (ROSA, ARO, RHOCP on-prem) where available; choose regions meeting data residency and latency needs.
- Integrations: central identity (SSO/OIDC), centralized logging/metrics/tracing, image registry with signing, vulnerability scanning, policy as code (OPA/Gatekeeper).
- Adopt a reference architecture and golden paths; provide templates and guardrails for teams.
- Training required for developers and SREs; update runbooks and incident processes to OpenShift semantics.
- Non-OpenShift hosting or use of raw cloud-native services that bypass platform guardrails requires an exception ADR with mitigations.

Review:
- Re-evaluate in 12 months for cost, reliability, platform maturity, team adoption, and alignment with product roadmap and cloud vendor offerings.

Adopt TOML (v1.0) as the canonical format for all application configuration files. TOML provides human-friendly syntax, first-class typing (strings, integers, floats, booleans, arrays, datetime), deterministic parsing, and supports comments, making it suitable for both developers and operators. This replaces/avoids YAML for its complexity/ambiguities and JSON for its lack of comments and limited readability for hierarchical config.

All services and tooling in this project will read configuration from config.toml (with optional environment-specific files like config.production.toml that are merged deterministically). Configuration schemas will be defined and validated at startup using language-appropriate TOML parsers and a shared schema/validation layer to ensure type and key correctness.

No other configuration file formats will be accepted in the repository. Where external integrations require different formats, they will be generated from the TOML source of truth during build/deploy. TOML parser libraries selected must be stable, widely used, and support TOML v1.0 features.

## Decision

Adopt modern JavaScript (ES2023+) as the primary implementation language across services and frontends, foregoing TypeScript by default. We will:

- Use ECMAScript modules, strict mode, and target current LTS runtimes/browsers.
- Enforce code quality with ESLint (including rules enforcing no-implicit-any patterns, no-floating promises), Prettier, and commit hooks.
- Use JSDoc annotations and enable checkJs/JS type inference in editors for inline type hints where beneficial, without introducing a TS build step.
- Apply runtime schema validation at trust boundaries (e.g., Zod/Valibot) to ensure data correctness where static types would otherwise guard.
- Maintain clear API contracts via OpenAPI/JSON Schema and generate client/server validators where appropriate.

Adopt Shrine as the standard library for image upload and storage across the application. Use S3-backed storage in production (with SSE-KMS encryption, private ACLs, and delivery via CloudFront signed URLs) and local filesystem storage in development/test. Configure Shrine with the cache/store storages pattern, presigned direct browser uploads to S3, backgrounded promotion and processing via ActiveJob/Sidekiq, and the derivatives plugin for responsive image variants.

Standardize attachment persistence using a JSON column per attachment on the owning record. Enforce validations (content type whitelist, max dimensions, max byte size) and extract/store metadata (width, height, content type, checksum). Perform server-side image processing with libvips (preferred) or ImageMagick, generating web-friendly derivatives (e.g., WebP/AVIF + fallback JPEG/PNG) asynchronously. Integrate malware scanning (e.g., Shrine’s hooks with ClamAV or an AV service) and image safety checks before promotion. Apply lifecycle policies for cache (short-lived) and store (retention per data policy), and versioned buckets with replication/backups as required. For public assets, use CDN caching; for private assets, serve time-limited signed URLs. Document a migration path for any existing attachment libraries and prohibit ad-hoc upload mechanisms.

Decision: Maintain the model→logic layering; do not allow org.jabref.model to depend on org.jabref.logic. Instead, invert dependencies and/or relocate functionality to preserve a clean architecture.

Rationale:
- org.jabref.model defines the domain and must remain free of infrastructure, IO, and application orchestration concerns to prevent cyclic dependencies, ease testing, and enable reuse.
- Allowing model→logic access introduces tight coupling and hampers modularity and future refactoring.

Approach:
- Move pure domain algorithms (deterministic, side-effect-free) currently in logic into org.jabref.model where appropriate.
- For behaviors that the model must “trigger” but that require logic concerns (IO, services, external integrations), define narrow interfaces in org.jabref.model.spi (or org.jabref.spi) that express domain-driven needs. Implement these interfaces in org.jabref.logic and provide them via dependency injection/service loader.
- Use domain events from model to notify logic of changes when pull-based SPI is not suitable.
- Keep shared value types and exceptions in org.jabref.model; avoid model referencing logic types.

Enforcement and Migration:
- Introduce architectural tests (e.g., ArchUnit) to forbid model→logic imports.
- Extract interfaces first, adapt call sites, and relocate pure logic-free code into model incrementally.
- Document SPI contracts and stability guarantees.

Outcome:
- Preserves clear layering, eliminates cycles, improves testability and reuse, and enables logic to evolve independently while still satisfying model’s behavioral needs.

## Decision

Define a single source of truth for all default values in a typed configuration schema embedded in code. Persist only user-overrides; never persist defaults. Configuration is resolved at runtime by a Config Service that deterministically merges layers by precedence:
1) runtime overrides/CLI
2) environment variables/secrets
3) persisted user settings
4) computed defaults from the schema.

Defaults are unlocalized, immutable, and environment-agnostic literals unless explicitly declared as computed defaults. Computed defaults must be pure, side-effect free, and derived only from stable environment facts (e.g., OS, CPU count), and must have a static fallback.

The schema encodes:
- type, constraints, and default (literal or computed)
- “unset” vs “empty” semantics (disallow ambiguous empty strings where meaningful)
- deprecation metadata and migration hints.

Consumers must never duplicate or guess defaults; they request resolved values from the Config Service. Validation occurs after merge; invalid or missing values fall back to schema defaults and emit diagnostics.

Defaults are versioned with the application and change only via code review. When a default changes, a migration step records the new effective default while leaving existing user-overrides intact. Localization occurs only at presentation time; stored defaults and comparisons remain unlocalized.

Telemetry and support tooling may distinguish “defaulted” vs “overridden” values for observability and troubleshooting.

Use a zero-downtime, idempotent “staging-to-production” update pattern:
- Load each ETL run’s output into versioned staging tables (or partitioned storage) with strict schema validation.
- Apply deterministic, idempotent, batched upserts (MERGE) from staging to production tables using business keys, with soft-deletes driven by a complete snapshot flag where applicable.
- Execute within controlled transactions with snapshot/RC isolation to avoid long locks, chunking by key ranges/time to bound impact.
- Guard updates behind a feature flag and a single-flight job lock to prevent concurrent runs; enforce idempotency via run_id/version and checksums.
- Switch over via view/ synonym or partition exchange only after integrity checks (row counts, referential checks, quality thresholds) pass; otherwise, abort and leave production untouched.
- Emit change events (CDC) only after successful commit to downstreams; record lineage and audit (run_id, source, counts, timings).
- Provide retry with backoff on transient failures; on persistent failure, auto-rollback and quarantine bad staging data.
- Monitor with detailed metrics (throughput, latency, lock waits), alerts on drift, and data quality SLOs.
- Secure with least-privilege service principal; encrypt at rest/in transit; redact PII in logs.

This approach ensures consistent, observable, and recoverable updates to the running database without service interruption.

- Adopt a message-broker–backed architecture for TaskManager with RabbitMQ as the transport and a durable datastore (PostgreSQL or Redis) as the source of truth for task metadata and state.
- Implement a distributed TaskManager interface with a pluggable backend; workers are stateless consumers that pull tasks from queues and report heartbeats and results.
- Use at-least-once delivery semantics; require idempotent task handlers keyed by a globally unique TaskId; provide deduplication guards in the datastore.
- Persist task lifecycle (Queued, Running, Completed, Failed, Canceled) with optimistic concurrency and per-task leases; workers acquire a lease before execution and renew via heartbeats to prevent duplicate concurrent processing.
- Route tasks via named queues with optional routing keys for affinity (e.g., shard, tenant, capability). Support delayed/scheduled tasks via broker-delayed messages or a scheduler that enqueues at due time.
- Handle retries with exponential backoff, capped attempts, and dead-letter queues for exhausted or poison tasks; include failure reasons and last-error in metadata.
- Support distributed await by broadcasting terminal state events over RabbitMQ and offering a polling fallback with timeouts to handle missed events.
- Provide cancellation by setting a cancellation flag in the datastore and publishing a cancel event; workers honor cancellation cooperatively at safe checkpoints.
- Enforce visibility timeouts: if a worker fails to renew lease, the task is re-queued; ensure single-consumer processing via exclusive lease tokens.
- Secure with TLS for broker connections, scoped credentials per service, and tenancy-aware routing; encrypt sensitive payloads at rest if stored.
- Expose metrics, tracing, and structured logs; ship a management CLI/API for introspection, requeue, and DLQ operations.

We introduce Release as a first-class concept in sfpowerscripts to make deployments reproducible, traceable, and promotable across environments.

A Release is an immutable manifest of:
- Package coordinates (name, version, checksum) and dependency graph
- Metadata/config toggles (e.g., feature flags), data loads, and post-deploy hooks
- Source commit SHA and build provenance

Identity and immutability:
- Each Release has a unique name and semantic version (e.g., MyProduct-2026.01.0).
- Content is locked in a generated sfp-release.lock.json with checksums.

Persistence and traceability:
- Commit the human-authored sfp-release.yaml (intent) to Git.
- Generate sfp-release.lock.json (resolved, immutable) during CI; publish as pipeline artifact and attach to a VCS tag/GitHub Release.
- Record deployment outcome per org in custom settings (current/last successful Release, timestamp, actor, commit SHA, artifact digests).

CLI and pipeline integration:
- New commands: release:init, release:plan, release:create (lock), release:deploy, release:promote, release:status, release:diff, release:rollback (re-deploy previously locked release).
- Pipelines default to release:create → release:deploy; promotion reuses the same lock across environments.
- Backward compatibility: existing ad-hoc package deploys remain supported; if no Release is specified, current behavior applies with deprecation notice.

Quality and governance:
- Enforce dependency resolution, checksum/integrity validation, org preflight checks, and policy gates (tests, code coverage, approvals).
- Optional signing of the lockfile for tamper-evidence.

Outcome:
- Deterministic rollouts/rollbacks, simplified promotions, and end-to-end provenance linking Git, CI artifacts, and target org state.

We will handle command processing by loading aggregates and reading any required event streams within a single, short-lived database transaction per request. Within this transaction, we will:
- Use a consistent isolation level (PostgreSQL Repeatable Read) to guarantee a stable snapshot across all reads.
- Acquire row-level locks on stream heads where necessary (e.g., SELECT … FOR UPDATE on stream metadata/head) to protect critical invariants that require exclusive access.
- Rebuild aggregates from the events read in this transaction, execute domain logic, and append new events with an expected-version check to enforce optimistic concurrency.
- Persist ancillary writes atomically (e.g., outbox records) before commit.

On expected-version conflicts (concurrent writers), the command handler will reload and retry according to a bounded retry policy. We will not span transactions across multiple databases or brokers; cross-boundary delivery will rely on the outbox pattern rather than distributed transactions.

Read-only queries (CQRS read side) remain outside this rule and use separate, read-only transactions optimized for latency.

Operational constraints:
- Keep transactions minimal (no network I/O, no external service calls) and under tight SLAs to reduce lock contention.
- Avoid reading unrelated streams in the same transaction; only read those required for invariants.
- Provide observability around retries and lock waits to tune contention hotspots.

Adopt a pull-based Continuous Delivery approach (GitOps) for Kubernetes workloads, with Git as the single source of truth and Argo CD as the standard controller.

- Use Argo CD to continuously reconcile desired state from Git (manifests/Helm/Kustomize) to clusters, with auto-sync and prune enabled; detect and alert on drift, and self-heal where appropriate.
- Manage applications via app-of-apps/ApplicationSets for multi-environment and multi-cluster deployments; one repo per environment with clear promotion paths via PRs, tags, or release branches.
- Remove the need for CI to hold cluster credentials; CI only updates Git. Cluster-side controllers pull changes, improving security and auditability.
- Enforce change control through signed pull requests, required reviews, and protected branches; enable SSO-backed RBAC in Argo CD for visibility and safe overrides.
- Handle secrets with a controller-based approach (e.g., External Secrets/Sealed Secrets); never store plaintext secrets in Git.
- Support progressive delivery via Argo Rollouts where needed; standardize health checks and sync waves for safe rollouts and ordering.
- Provide per-team namespaces and Argo CD Projects for multi-tenancy and policy guardrails; define quotas and allowed sources.
- Integrate monitoring and alerting for sync/drift status; record deployments via Git history and Argo CD audit logs.

This standard supersedes push-based CD to clusters except for justified exceptions.

Adopt Elasticsearch as the dedicated full‑text search engine for the product. All user-facing search (free text, faceted filters, relevance ranking, highlighting, suggestions, and aggregations) will be served from Elasticsearch, while the primary database remains the source of truth.

Scope:
- Index core entities (e.g., articles, products, customers) as denormalized documents optimized for search.
- Support language analyzers, stemming, stopwords, synonyms, typo tolerance (fuzziness), and highlighting.
- Provide faceting/aggregations for filters and analytics.

Integration:
- Implement a search service/API that encapsulates query construction, relevance tuning, and index evolution; application code must not query Elasticsearch directly.
- Establish near–real-time indexing via CDC/outbox (e.g., Debezium/Kafka) or event-driven hooks; target end-to-end latency <60s.
- Use bulk indexing and backfills for initial and reindex operations; maintain versioned index aliases for zero-downtime reindexing.

Operations:
- Deploy Elasticsearch 8.x (managed service preferred) with at least a 3‑node cluster, security enabled, snapshots, and monitoring/alerting.
- Apply index lifecycle management (ILM) and retention policies; configure shard/replica counts per index size and query profile.
- Constrain to permissible license/features; avoid vendor-locked features unless approved.

Quality and guardrails:
- Define relevance KPIs and evaluation datasets; maintain synonym/boost configs under version control.
- Accept eventual consistency for search; critical reads write-through fallback is not required.
- Feature-flag search to enable rollback to basic DB queries if needed during rollout.

We will export a single canonical identifier field id for every entity. This id is globally unique, immutable, and opaque; clients must not parse or derive meaning from it and should treat it as a stable token for storage, comparison, and linking. Internal database keys will never be exported.

To aid human workflows and debugging, we will also export a semantic_id that is human-readable and reversible by the backend only. Its canonical shape is <dataset>:<object_type>:<object_local_id>. For provisioned/external items, we will prefix the local part with the provisioner identifier to avoid collisions, yielding <dataset>:<object_type>:<provisioner-id>/<object_local_id>.

We will export a source attribute (qualified namespace/FQCN of the extension/provisioner) for items that are not user-editable, enabling traceability and editability rules in consuming systems.

The backend is solely responsible for generating and resolving both id and semantic_id; clients must use lookup/resolve APIs rather than constructing identifiers. The canonical id will be URL-safe; if encoding is required, we will use Base64 URL-safe encoding internally but only expose the final URL-safe id.

Identifier lifecycle guarantees:
- id is never reassigned or recycled.
- Changes to an entity that do not alter identity retain the same id.
- Re-created entities obtain a new id; mappings from deprecated ids may be provided via a resolution API.

Exports and APIs will include forward-compatible fields (id mandatory, semantic_id and source optional) so future format changes do not break consumers.

We will use Spring Boot (3.x) as the web framework for building and operating the service’s HTTP APIs. Spring Boot provides opinionated auto-configuration, a mature dependency injection model, and production-ready features (Actuator, Micrometer) that reduce boilerplate and accelerate delivery while improving operability.

Scope and conventions:
- Programming platform: Java 17+.
- Web stack: Spring Web MVC for synchronous request/response REST endpoints; consider WebFlux only for specific high-concurrency, IO-bound use cases.
- Packaging and runtime: Executable JAR with embedded Tomcat; container images produced via Paketo buildpacks; readiness/liveness via Actuator.
- API design: Annotation-based controllers, request/response validation with jakarta.validation, JSON serialization with Jackson, error handling via @ControllerAdvice, and OpenAPI documentation via springdoc-openapi.
- Security: Spring Security for authentication/authorization; CSRF as appropriate; method-level security where needed.
- Configuration: Externalized configuration via application properties/yaml, profiles for environment-specific settings, and secret management via environment or vault; optional Spring Cloud Config if centralization is required.
- Observability: Micrometer metrics, health checks, tracing via OpenTelemetry exporters, structured logging (JSON) with correlation IDs.
- Data and integration: Use Spring Data where appropriate; REST clients via WebClient/RestClient; messaging via Spring for the chosen broker if needed.
- Testing: Spring Boot Test, MockMvc/WebTestClient, Testcontainers for integration tests.

Rationale: Strong ecosystem, wide community support, consistent developer experience, and proven operability in production outweigh the learning curve and larger footprint compared to minimalist frameworks. This choice aligns with team skills and long-term maintainability.

We will enforce optimistic concurrency for REST resources using HTTP ETags with If-Match preconditions.

- All successful GET/HEAD responses include a strong ETag representing the current persisted version of the resource.
- All state-changing operations (PUT, PATCH, DELETE) must include If-Match with the client’s last-seen ETag. Requests without If-Match are rejected with 428 Precondition Required. If the ETag does not match the current version, the server returns 412 Precondition Failed and does not apply the change.
- On successful modification, responses include the new ETag (200/204) so clients can continue the edit flow. For 412, the server may include the current representation to help clients resolve conflicts.
- For safe reads and caching, GET may accept If-None-Match and return 304 Not Modified when appropriate. For create semantics, endpoints may accept If-None-Match: * to ensure the resource does not already exist.
- ETags will be strong and derived from a stable version token (e.g., rowversion/etag field) that changes on any persisted representation change. Weak ETags will not be used for concurrency control.
- Bulk operations apply per-entity preconditions; partial success is reported explicitly.
- SDKs/clients will surface ETag automatically and attach If-Match on updates by default, exposing clear conflict handling.
- Non-HTTP channels will map to the same version token to keep concurrency semantics consistent across interfaces.

We will standardize on 1Password Business as the single system for storing and sharing all sensitive credentials (passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, recovery codes, and secure documents). Secrets will be organized into least-privilege vaults segmented by team, environment, and system, with access governed via SSO to our IdP and automated provisioning/deprovisioning via SCIM. MFA (WebAuthn/FIDO2 preferred) and device trust will be enforced.

Operationally:
- CI/CD and runtime systems will consume secrets via 1Password Secrets Automation (Connect) and/or the 1Password CLI; no secrets in source control, config files, or environment defaults.
- Human sharing uses item sharing only within the organization, with short-lived, expiring links; plaintext sharing via chat/email is prohibited.
- A break-glass vault will exist for emergency access, protected by dual control and strict audit; recovery procedures will be documented and tested.

Governance:
- Access reviews occur quarterly; audit logs are monitored and retained per compliance requirements.
- Onboarding grants role-based vault access; offboarding revokes accounts immediately and triggers secret rotation for impacted systems.
- Exports are disallowed except for approved, encrypted, time-bound recovery scenarios.

Migration:
- Inventory existing secrets, import to mapped vaults, validate consumers, then purge legacy stores.

Documentation and runbooks will cover vault taxonomy, request/approval flows, automation patterns, rotation policies, and incident handling. This replaces ad hoc secret sharing methods effective immediately.

We will support multiple labels per item by modeling Label as a first-class entity and implementing a many-to-many relationship between Item and Label.

- Data model: introduce tables Labels(id, key, display_name, normalized_key, …) and ItemLabels(item_id, label_id, position). Enforce uniqueness on (item_id, label_id). Maintain a stable order via the position column.
- Validation: labels are case-insensitive; normalize to normalized_key. Prevent duplicates on an item. Enforce a configurable cap (default 20) on labels per item. Only predefined labels can be applied; label creation is restricted to admins/editors.
- API: expose labels as an array on item resources (GET returns array; POST/PUT accepts array for full replacement; PATCH supports add/remove operations). Querying supports filtering by one or more labels via repeated parameters (e.g., ?label=foo&label=bar) with AND semantics by default.
- Behavior: items may have zero labels. Removing the last label leaves the array empty. Ordering is preserved as supplied by clients when replacing; server will return labels in stored order.
- Indexing/search: add indexes on ItemLabels(label_id, item_id) and Labels(normalized_key) to support fast filtering and autocomplete. Emit search index updates when label sets change.
- Migration: migrate existing single-label fields by creating corresponding Labels and linking via ItemLabels; keep old field read-only during transition and remove after completion.
- Events/audit: publish ItemLabelsChanged events and record audit entries for add/remove/reorder operations.
- Permissions: only authorized roles can modify an item’s labels; label taxonomy management is limited to admins.

Adopt a shared defect abstraction model and service to normalize defect data across teams and tooling. We will define a canonical Defect schema (id, title, description, source system, status, severity, priority, category, root cause, introduced version, detected stage, component, environment, customer impact, SLA, timestamps, assignees, labels, links) with controlled vocabularies for severity, category, and root cause. All product teams will map their issue trackers (Jira, GitHub Issues, Azure Boards) to this schema via maintained adapters, exposing events over a versioned contract (CloudEvent-compliant) to a central ingestion API and Kafka topic.

We will provide:
- SDKs and adapter templates to ease mapping and backfill.
- A policy-as-code validation layer to enforce taxonomy and required fields at ingestion time.
- A privacy filter to strip PII and apply team scoping/tenancy.
- A warehouse model (Star schema) and semantic layer for analytics, DORA/quality metrics, SLO breach detection, and trend analysis.
- BI dashboards and a public metrics API for consumption in scorecards and build status checks.
- Bidirectional links written back to source issues for traceability.

Governance:
- A cross-functional Quality Council owns taxonomy evolution, versioning (SemVer), and deprecation schedules.
- Nonconformant fields are quarantined and reported; rollups exclude unclassified defects by default.
- CI/CD gates: release readiness requires zero Critical/High escaped defects and validated mappings.

Rollout:
- Phase 1: pilot in two products, implement Jira/GitHub adapters, backfill 12 months.
- Phase 2: expand to all teams, enable automated root-cause classification suggestions.
- Phase 3: enable cross-team defect duplication detection and proactive risk alerts.

We standardize repository names as lowercase kebab-case using only a–z, 0–9, and hyphens. No spaces, underscores, emojis, or special characters. Keep names ≤50 chars (hard cap 63 for DNS/tooling).

Canonical pattern:
<org>-<program>-<domain>-<artifact>[-<qualifier>]

Component conventions:
- artifact: one of api, svc, ui, lib, infra, ops, config, data, docs, tooling
- qualifiers (optional): lang (e.g., ts, go, py), runtime (e.g., node, dotnet), purpose (poc, demo, sandbox), status (archived)

Rules:
- Organization prefix aligns with owning org or business unit.
- Program is the portfolio/product line (short mnemonic).
- Domain is the functional area or bounded context.
- Use stable, meaningful terms; avoid abbreviations unless standardized.
- Do not include environment, customer, or region in names except for private configuration repos, which must end with -config and may include -<env> if required by tooling.
- Do not include secrets, PII, or ticket IDs.
- One business capability per repo; avoid catch-all names.
- Repositories intended for reuse must not include solution-specific config; solution-specific config belongs in separate -config repos.
- Experimental work must use -poc or -sandbox and may be archived later with -archived.
- Deprecations must add -archived and be read-only.

Examples:
- orgx-payments-ledger-svc
- orgx-payments-ledger-svc-infra
- orgx-shared-observability-lib-ts
- orgx-retail-pricing-api
- orgx-retail-pricing-config-prod (private)
- orgx-data-pipelines-infra
- orgx-platform-developer-portal-ui

Alignment:
- Package names and container images should mirror the repo base name.
- GitHub topics must include program, domain, and artifact (e.g., program:payments, domain:ledger, type:svc).
- Migrations should rename repos to conform and add redirects where applicable.

All application and platform components will emit structured, JSON logs to stdout/stderr with consistent fields (timestamp, level, service, environment, request_id/correlation_id, span_id/trace_id, user/session anonymized ID, operation, outcome, latency, and context). We will standardize on INFO as the default level in production (DEBUG only in ephemeral/dev) and ERROR-only for high-sensitivity jobs when needed. Sensitive data (secrets, credentials, tokens, PII/PHI) must not be logged; we will implement library-level redaction, allow/deny lists, and pre-shipping scrubbing.

Logs will be centrally aggregated per environment using the platform’s native logging pipeline: agents/sidecars ship stdout logs to the central service (e.g., CloudWatch Logs), with lifecycle-managed retention and archival to object storage (e.g., S3 via Firehose) for long-term compliance and ad-hoc analysis (e.g., Athena). Configuration, dashboards, metric filters, and alerts will be infrastructure-as-code managed.

We will instrument services with OpenTelemetry to correlate logs with traces/metrics via trace_id/span_id, enabling end-to-end request debugging. High-volume event classes will use sampling to control cost while preserving error and security event completeness. Access to logs will be role-based with least privilege and audit trails. Operational policies will define retention by environment, P0/P1 alerting from log-derived metrics, and runbooks for common signatures. This decision establishes a uniform, secure, and observable logging foundation across all services.

Adopt styled-jsx for component-scoped styling. We will co-locate styles with React components using <style jsx>{`...`}</style> blocks to guarantee automatic scoping, avoid class name collisions, and enable SSR/SSG-friendly styles with zero additional runtime CSS tooling. Global styles will be limited to a small, centralized entry (e.g., app shell) using <style jsx global> and a base globals.css. Design tokens (colors, spacing, typography) will be exposed as CSS variables on :root for consistent theming and easy consumption inside styled-jsx blocks.

For shared patterns, we’ll create reusable CSS variables, utility classes (in the global layer), and component-level mixins via template literals. Dynamic styling based on props will use styled-jsx’s dynamic expressions. Where needed, we may enable the styled-jsx PostCSS plugin (e.g., autoprefixer) to ensure cross-browser compatibility; Sass may be considered via the official plugin on a case-by-case basis.
