We will enforce conventions via ESLint (eslint-plugin-styled-jsx) and document patterns for responsive rules and states. In Next.js, we rely on built-in styled-jsx support; in other React builds, we add the Babel plugin.

All runtime configuration will be sourced exclusively from a single TOML configuration file. The application will not read configuration values from environment variables or command-line flags, nor from implicit global defaults beyond the documented schema defaults. The CLI will only accept flags for --config (path to file), --help, and --version; any other attempted configuration via CLI will be rejected.

On startup, the configuration file will be parsed, strictly validated (including unknown-field errors), and materialized into an immutable, typed Config object that is injected into all components. No component may read configuration from process environment or other external sources, and configuration may not be mutated at runtime.

If a value is omitted, only the defaults defined in the configuration schema will apply; there are no hidden or environment-driven fallbacks. Where operational concerns require variability (e.g., differing environments), separate config files or overlays must be provided and selected via --config.

Implement a lightweight HTTP redirect from the legacy /bundle endpoint(s) to the canonical Bundle Service URL instead of proxying requests.

- Issue 307 Temporary Redirect for all methods to preserve method and body semantics; switch to 308 Permanent Redirect after verifying client compatibility.
- Construct Location by preserving full path and query string (Location = <bundle-service-base> + request-uri).
- Require clients to resend authentication to the Bundle Service; both services share the same OAuth2 issuer/scopes to avoid auth friction. No header forwarding is attempted.
- Keep host and scheme stable where possible; if cross-origin, ensure CORS is configured on the Bundle Service to allow redirected requests from browsers.
- Maintain idempotency guarantees and timeouts at the Bundle Service; the redirecting endpoint does no business logic.
- Provide clear deprecation notice and observability: log and meter redirect rates; promote 308 after a stabilization window; remove the legacy endpoint once adoption reaches target thresholds.

Adopt explicit, major-versioned URI namespaces for the public HTTP API, with semantic versioning for the API contract:
- Versioning scheme: /v{major}/… in request paths (e.g. /v1/resources). Only the major version appears in the URI. Minor and patch versions are backward-compatible and do not change the URI.
- Backward compatibility: Minor/patch releases may add fields, endpoints, or query parameters, but never remove or repurpose existing ones. Breaking changes require a new major version and a new URI prefix.
- Media types: Use application/json (or application/problem+json for errors). Do not version via media type or headers. Content negotiation is for format only, not version.
- Default version: No implicit default. Requests without a /v{major} prefix are rejected with a 404 and guidance in the error body.
- Deprecation policy: Support at least two concurrent major versions when feasible. Announce deprecations with Sunset and Deprecation response headers, Link headers to migration guides, changelog entries, and email/portal notifications. Provide a minimum 6-month deprecation window before removal.
- Discovery and documentation: Publish a separate OpenAPI document per major version at /v{major}/openapi.json and a versioned docs site. Embed the full semver (major.minor.patch) in the OpenAPI info.version and return it in an X-API-Version response header.
- Error stability: Error codes and shapes are part of the contract; changes to error schemas are breaking.
- Routing and operations: API gateway/routes dispatch by the first path segment. Observability, rate limits, and quotas are tracked per major version to aid migration monitoring.
- SDKs: Provide version-pinned SDKs/clients per major version and maintain them for the duration of the deprecation window.
- Testing: Backward-compatibility tests enforce that minor/patch changes are non-breaking. Breaking-change checks are required before releasing a new major.

Do not introduce a full service mesh solely for traceability. Instead, standardize on OpenTelemetry (OTel) for end-to-end tracing across services and ingress, with consistent context propagation and a shared OTel Collector deployment per cluster/region. Enforce trace context propagation via platform middleware (ingress/egress gateways and language-specific HTTP/gRPC interceptors) and provide default dashboards and sampling policies. Use gateway-level proxies (e.g., Envoy at ingress) to capture north-south spans and metrics without per-pod sidecars.

Adopt a phased, opt-in model for namespaces that require deeper L7 visibility: allow targeted sidecar injection (Envoy/Linkerd) or node-level ambient data plane only where SLOs, zero-trust mTLS, traffic shaping, or multi-tenancy isolation justify the added complexity and resource cost. Mesh features (mTLS, retries/timeouts, traffic mirroring, policy) may be enabled later if/when requirements extend beyond observability.

Success criteria:
- >95% services emitting traces with correct parent/child relationships.
- Trace context preserved across async boundaries and external calls.
- P50 trace collection overhead <2% CPU and <1% latency.
- Clear SLO dashboards with service dependency graphs.

Reevaluate a cluster-wide mesh if: (a) uniform mTLS and policy-as-code become mandatory, (b) pervasive traffic management is required, or (c) OTel-only approach cannot meet trace coverage/overhead targets.

## Decision

Implement a FetchRepositoryWorker as an AndroidX WorkManager CoroutineWorker to synchronize repository metadata in the background. The worker will be enqueued as UniquePeriodicWork ("repo_sync") with the minimum periodic interval supported by the platform, a flex window for jitter, and exponential backoff for retries. It will also support on-demand OneTimeWork requests ("repo_sync_now") with keep/replace policies.

Constraints:
- Requires network connected; unmetered network is optional and configurable via user settings.
- Respects OS battery optimizations by default (no foreground service unless user triggers manual refresh).

Behavior:
- Inputs include accountId, provider (e.g., GitHub/GitLab), scope (user/org), and optional cursor.
- Uses a RepositoryService (Retrofit) with ETag/If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since for incremental sync; handles 304 Not Modified.
- Paginates through provider APIs until exhausted or budget reached; supports resumption via cursors.
- Upserts repositories into Room within transactions; records sync checkpoints. Deletions are detected through delta endpoints when available, else via tombstoning based on lastSeenAt.
- Handles rate limits (429/403 with rate headers) by scheduling next run at reset time or backing off.
- Distinguishes transient errors (retry) from permanent ones (e.g., 401/403 invalid credentials → mark account as needsReauth and fail without retry).
- Idempotent: safe to re-run without duplicating or corrupting state.
- Exposes progress via setProgress and emits a domain event to refresh UI; surfaces failures via telemetry and user-visible, non-intrusive notifications only on manual refresh.
- Observability includes structured logs, metrics (duration, pages, items, error class), and trace spans.

This worker is the single authority for repository sync and is triggered on login, account change, manual refresh, and network reconnect.

We will manage the monorepo using Yarn Workspaces to model internal package relationships and centralize dependency management. The root package.json will define "workspaces" for all packages, and a single lockfile will be committed at the repo root. Internal dependencies will use the workspace: protocol (e.g., workspace:^, workspace:~ or workspace:*), enabling local linking, predictable versioning, and coordinated builds. Where applicable, TypeScript project references will be used to align build order and incremental builds across packages.

We will use Yarn’s hoisting by default to reduce duplication and install times; nohoist will be applied only when required for tooling compatibility. CI will run yarn install with immutable flags to guarantee reproducible installs, and caching of Yarn’s artifacts will be configured to speed up pipelines. Node and Yarn versions will be pinned via engines and repository configuration to ensure consistent developer and CI environments.

Package scripts will be standardized to leverage yarn workspaces (e.g., yarn workspaces foreach) for linting, testing, building, and releasing. External publishing will remain unchanged for packages that are published; internal-only packages will not be published and will rely exclusively on workspace linking. Migration from ad-hoc linking or file: dependencies will be completed, and lerna usage (if any) will be limited to tasks not covered by Yarn or removed where redundant. This decision provides a durable, low-maintenance foundation for code sharing, reproducible installs, and scalable monorepo workflows.

## Decision

Adopt GNU Make as the single entry point to orchestrate and centralise all project tasks across development and CI/CD. The repository will include a top-level Makefile that defines phony, idempotent targets such as setup, bootstrap, install, deps, lint, fmt, test, coverage, build, run, watch, package, publish, clean, distclean, migrate, seed, start, stop, deploy, and help. Make will wrap language- and tool-specific commands (e.g., npm/yarn/pnpm, pip/poetry, gradle/maven, docker/compose, terraform, kubectl) to provide a consistent interface, reduce cognitive load, and decouple callers from underlying tooling.

We will standardise on POSIX-compatible shell commands and limit GNU-specific features to maintain portability (Linux/macOS). Targets will be parallel-safe where possible and support MAKEFLAGS for -j concurrency. Common variables (e.g., TOOL paths, versions, flags, IMAGE, TAG, REGISTRY, ENV) will be parameterised with sensible defaults and overridable via environment, .env, or Makefile.local. The Makefile will be modularised using include for per-component/task files (e.g., make/docker.mk, make/js.mk), and will generate self-documenting help from target comments.

CI pipelines will invoke make targets exclusively (e.g., make test, make build, make deploy) to ensure reproducibility and to keep pipeline definitions thin. Local developer workflows and documentation will reference the same targets to guarantee consistency across environments.

We adopt “Where Away?” as the official product and marketing name, including the trailing question mark. For technical artifacts and identifiers that do not support punctuation or spaces, we standardize on:
- Repository: where-away (e.g., github.com/org/where-away)
- Packages/modules: whereaway or where_away (language-appropriate, lowercase, no punctuation)
- Binaries/CLIs: whereaway
- NPM/registry packages: @org/whereaway
- Mobile app bundle IDs: com.org.whereaway
- Docker images: org/whereaway
- Environment variables and feature flags: WHEREAWAY_*

Typography and usage guidelines:
- Public name: “Where Away?” with title case and question mark.
- Plain text contexts that disallow punctuation: “Where Away”.
- Abbreviation: “WA?” informally; avoid in customer-facing copy.

Domains and handles:
- Primary domain: whereaway.app (fallback: whereaway.io).
- Social handles: @whereawayapp where possible; avoid punctuation.

Legal and availability:
- Proceed pending trademark clearance for “Where Away?” in target jurisdictions and classes.
- Avoid names that could conflict with existing marks; if clearance fails, revisit.

Internationalization:
- Localized strings should preserve meaning; retain punctuation where culturally appropriate.

Search/SEO:
- Use “Where Away” as primary keyword; support queries with and without the question mark.

Implementation note:
- Do not embed punctuation in code identifiers, URLs, or file paths; apply the mappings above consistently across all systems and documentation.

- Validate HMAC signature, payload schema, and supported eventCode. If validation fails, do not process and respond with HTTP 401/400 (no “[accepted]”), allowing Adyen to retry per their policy and aiding detection of misconfigured senders.
- For valid notifications, persist the notification (transactional outbox) and enqueue for asynchronous processing, then immediately respond with “[accepted]” to Adyen to prevent redundant retries.
- Ensure idempotency using the tuple (pspReference, eventCode, success) as a unique key; ignore duplicates and replays. Maintain processing status (received, processing, succeeded, failed-permanent, dead-lettered).
- Classify errors:
  - Transient (network timeouts, 5xx from commercetools/Adyen, lock/version conflicts): retry with exponential backoff and jitter up to a capped limit.
  - Permanent (business rule violations, missing payment, unsupported eventCode, invalid state transitions): mark as failed-permanent without further retries.
- Handle optimistic concurrency by refetching payment and retrying on version conflicts within transient retry budget.
- Guarantee exactly-once side effects by applying changes within the processing transaction and recording completion before acknowledging success; rely on the idempotency key to avoid double mutation on worker restarts.
- Route exhausted transient retries to a dead-letter queue with full context; emit alerts/metrics (failures, retries, DLQ count, latency).
- Do not acknowledge or mutate on invalid signatures or malformed payloads; log securely with PII redaction.

Adopt a Transformer-based architecture as the core modeling approach for language and sequence tasks. Standardize on a modular design that supports both encoder-only (e.g., BERT/DeBERTa) for understanding tasks and encoder–decoder (e.g., T5) for generative/seq2seq workloads; decoder-only (e.g., GPT) may be used for long-form generation where appropriate. Use subword tokenization (BPE/WordPiece) with consistent vocabulary per domain and multilingual variants when required.

Leverage high-quality pretrained checkpoints as a baseline and apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA/Adapters) to reduce compute and enable rapid iteration. Employ mixed precision (bf16/fp16) training, gradient checkpointing, and distributed training (DDP; tensor/sequence parallelism when needed) for scalability. For inference, standardize export to ONNX/TensorRT or BetterTransformer, enable KV cache, and support quantization (int8/4) where latency/cost targets require it.

Encapsulate model usage behind well-defined ports (serving interfaces) to decouple application logic from model internals; package models as versioned artifacts in a registry with full lineage (data, code, hyperparameters). Implement evaluation gates (unit metrics, task benchmarks, bias/safety checks) and canary rollout before promotion to production. Centralize observability (latency, throughput, token usage, drift, toxicity) and enable feature flags for rapid rollback.

Prefer the Hugging Face ecosystem for tooling (Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT, Optimum) with abstraction to allow swapping vendors/runtimes. Support plugin adapters for retrieval augmentation and tool-use when required. This decision provides state-of-the-art accuracy, flexibility across tasks, and a clear path to scale while maintaining testability, safety, and operational reliability.

Adopt Redux for cross-cutting application state using Redux Toolkit (RTK) to enforce a predictable, unidirectional data flow with minimal boilerplate. Use a single store configured via RTK’s configureStore with default middleware (including Immer for immutable updates and serializable checks), augmented as needed.

Organize state by feature using slice-based modules (createSlice) colocated with UI and domain logic. Keep ephemeral/view-only state in local React state; promote only shared, cross-screen, or cached server data to Redux. Normalize collections with createEntityAdapter and expose memoized selectors via Reselect.

Handle async workflows with RTK’s createAsyncThunk for imperative effects and RTK Query for server-state caching, fetching, invalidation, and automatic revalidation where applicable. Prefer RTK Query for CRUD over HTTP APIs; fall back to thunks for non-request side effects or complex orchestrations.

Integrate with React via react-redux hooks (useSelector/useDispatch), using typed hooks in TypeScript (AppDispatch, RootState). Define selectors as the primary read boundary; avoid selecting entire slices to minimize re-renders. Use Redux DevTools for inspection and time-travel debugging.

Establish a feature-first directory structure:
- src/features/<feature>/{slice.ts, selectors.ts, thunks.ts, api.ts(x), components/}
- src/app/{store.ts, rootReducer.ts, hooks.ts}

Apply strict typing for actions, state, and thunks; enable serializableCheck exceptions only for known non-serializable cases (e.g., RTK Query). Persist only required keys with redux-persist if offline/session continuity is needed.

Testing: unit-test reducers and selectors as pure functions; integration-test thunks/RTK Query with mocked services; smoke-test store configuration.

This pattern standardizes state management, scales with features, improves testability and performance, and reduces boilerplate while aligning with modern Redux best practices.

Adopt a simplified, deterministic function-evaluation model:

- Single-pass, explicit evaluation: Evaluate functions in a dedicated phase after parsing and validation. No implicit or recursive re-evaluation of results.
- Explicit invocation only: Functions execute only within clearly delimited expressions (e.g., ${fn(arg)}). Remove auto-execution in string concatenation or implicit contexts.
- Pure, synchronous functions: Only allow side-effect-free, synchronous functions. Disallow I/O, network, and time-dependent operations during evaluation. Async functions are not supported.
- Fixed evaluation order and scope: Evaluate expressions top-down within a document/module boundary with no cross-document resolution unless explicitly referenced. No mutation of the evaluation context during execution.
- Allowlist-based registry: Expose a minimal, versioned set of built-in functions. Third-party functions must be registered at build time with explicit names and schemas; no dynamic runtime registration.
- Deterministic caching: Memoize function results by normalized arguments within a single evaluation phase to improve performance while preserving determinism.
- Strict error semantics: Fail fast on any evaluation error with precise location and cause; no silent fallbacks. Provide partial output only in diagnostic mode.
- Deprecations: Remove nested interpolation causing multiple passes, context-mutation functions, and implicit environment lookups. Provide a compatibility flag for one release cycle with warnings and an auto-migration guide.
- Observability: Emit structured traces and metrics (count, latency, cache hit rate, failures) per function and document.

Use a small, explicit set of “element components” to standardize semantics, styling, and behavior across the app.

- Introduce primitives: Box (div), Flex, Stack, Grid (layout); Text, Heading, Link (typography); Button; Image; Icon; VisuallyHidden; and Form controls (Label, Input, TextArea, Select, Checkbox, Radio).
- Prefer these components over raw HTML in product code to ensure consistency, theming, and a11y. Exceptions: raw elements allowed for third‑party content or highly specialized semantics not covered by primitives.
- Components are polymorphic: support an “as” prop to render the correct semantic element (e.g., Heading as="h1"), forward refs, and pass through native attributes.
- Bake in sensible default styles with themeable variants/sizes; provide variant="unstyled" (or unstyled prop) as an escape hatch.
- Enforce accessibility by default (e.g., Link handles external/target rel, Button disables on submit as needed, Label ties to control, VisuallyHidden for screen reader text).
- Keep surface area minimal—do not wrap every HTML element; prioritize elements with shared design/behavior. Encourage composition of primitives rather than bespoke wrappers.
- Coexist with global tokens: all styling via design tokens and theme; no global CSS leakage.
- Provide tree‑shakable exports and stable APIs; changes to visual defaults are released as new variants to avoid breaking consumers.

## Decision

- Test libraries as black-box products: prioritize public API behaviors over implementation details; avoid mocking internal structures.
- Use the language’s standard xUnit-style framework for unit tests and parameterized tests, supplemented with property-based testing for API invariants and edge cases.
- Add fuzz testing for inputs to parsers/serializers and other user-controlled boundaries to uncover unexpected behaviors.
- Maintain an executable documentation suite (doctests or runnable examples) to ensure examples remain accurate.
- Establish backward-compatibility checks: enforce semantic versioning with automated API surface/binary compatibility verification during CI; any breaking change must bump the major version and be explicitly documented.
- Run a cross-environment CI matrix (supported OSes, architectures, and runtime/language versions) on every PR and release candidate to ensure portability.
- Enforce minimum coverage thresholds focused on the public API and critical paths; measure branch coverage and track trends, but do not chase 100% when not value-adding.
- Add snapshot/golden tests only for stable, well-defined outputs; revisions to snapshots require explicit review.
- Create regression tests for every reported bug and link them to issue IDs to prevent recurrence.
- Provide a lightweight test harness for downstream integrators (e.g., contract tests or conformance suite) to verify integration with new versions.
- Parallelize tests and use deterministic seeding for property/fuzz tests; persist failing seeds to aid reproducibility.

## Decision

We will manage DLXS configuration as code, externalized from the application binaries, and rendered per environment at deploy time.

- Authoritative configuration will live in a versioned repository as templated YAML files (one base plus environment overlays). A JSON Schema will validate structure and required keys in CI.
- Secrets (e.g., database creds, API keys) will not be stored in Git; they will be sourced at runtime from the environment’s secret manager (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager/SSM Parameter Store or Kubernetes Secrets) and injected as env vars.
- Templating will produce the canonical DLXS runtime artifacts (e.g., dlxs.cfg, coll config, Apache/VHost snippets, OAI-PMH, XPAT index paths). Rendering will be performed by the deploy system (Helm for Kubernetes or docker-compose + envsubst for local) and mounted read-only into the container.
- All mutable paths (cache, logs, index directories) will be configurable and mapped to persistent volumes. Defaults will be defined in the base template; environment overlays may override paths and feature flags.
- Config immutability is enforced per release: a specific git SHA of config is bundled with the image tag or Helm chart version to guarantee repeatable deployments and rollbacks.
- A lightweight “config doctor” command will run at container start to validate connectivity, paths, permissions, and schema conformance; startup will fail fast on violations.
- Hot-reload will be supported where DLXS permits (e.g., SIGHUP for web tier); otherwise, config changes trigger a rolling restart coordinated by the orchestrator.
- Local development uses a .env file and sample non-secret configs; production parity is achieved via the same templates rendered with environment overlays.
- Configuration changes follow code review and are tracked via PRs; a changelog documents breaking changes and required migrations.

We will reference internal packages using the workspace protocol in package.json rather than file:, link:, or pinned versions.

- For internal runtime dependencies, use "workspace:^" (or "workspace:~" if we require patch-level alignment). Use "workspace:*" only for tightly co-versioned packages that must always resolve to exactly the same version.
- For dev-only internal dependencies (tooling, fixtures, test utils), "workspace:*" is acceptable.
- For peerDependencies, declare a normal semver range and add a matching devDependency using "workspace:*" (or "workspace:^") to ensure tests resolve a concrete implementation.
- External dependencies continue to use normal semver ranges.

We will not commit relative paths (file:) or manual version pins between workspace packages. Yarn’s prefer-workspace-packages will be enabled to ensure local linking during development. Our release tooling (e.g., Changesets) will replace workspace: ranges with actual versions at publish time; no package with "private": true will be published.

This policy applies to all packages in the monorepo and will be enforced via repository templates and validation scripts (e.g., lint rules) to prevent regressions.

Adopt JUnit 5 (JUnit Jupiter) as the standard testing framework for all Java components. Include junit-jupiter-api and junit-jupiter-engine as mandatory dependencies; enable execution via Maven Surefire/Failsafe (using the JUnit Platform provider) or Gradle’s test task with useJUnitPlatform(). Where legacy JUnit 4 tests remain, allow the JUnit Vintage engine temporarily to support incremental migration.

Use JUnit 5 features by default: @Test, @ParameterizedTest, @BeforeEach/@AfterEach, @Nested, assumptions, assertThrows, and extension-based test tooling. Prefer clear, behavior-oriented test naming and Given-When-Then structure. Enable parallel test execution where modules are thread-safe to reduce build time.

For mocking and fluent assertions, standardize on Mockito and AssertJ (or Hamcrest where already entrenched). For integration tests, run under JUnit Platform with Failsafe/Gradle integration; support Testcontainers-based tests where applicable. Enforce adoption via shared BOMs/parent POMs or Gradle convention plugins and CI gates.

We will adopt the EFK stack for centralized application logging: Fluent Bit for log collection and forwarding, Elasticsearch for storage and indexing, and Kibana for visualization, exploration, and alerting.

Fluent Bit will run as a DaemonSet/sidecar to collect container stdout/stderr and specified file-based logs, parse JSON logs, enrich with metadata (kubernetes/docker fields, environment, service, version), and forward over TLS to Elasticsearch. We will standardize a common JSON log schema (timestamp, level, service, trace/span IDs, request_id, user/org, message, context) to enable consistent querying and correlation.

Elasticsearch will be deployed as a managed service where available or as a clustered deployment with hot-warm (and optional cold) tiers, index templates, and ILM policies for rollover and retention per environment and data class. We will enable authentication, TLS in transit, role-based access, and index-level permissions. Kibana will be used for dashboards, saved searches, log tailing, correlation with APM/metrics, and alerting (threshold and anomaly-based) routed to on-call channels.

We will maintain separate indices and spaces per environment (prod/stage/dev) and apply sane retention defaults with overrides for compliance workloads. Backpressure and buffering will be handled by Fluent Bit with retry and disk buffering. Resource limits and sampling/drop policies will be configured to protect application performance and control costs. Continuous delivery will provision index templates, ILM, dashboards, and alerts as code.

We will persist normalized time and actor metadata with every domain record and change, rather than relying on filesystem/DB metadata. Each mutable entity will include: created_at, created_by; updated_at, updated_by; and when applicable deleted_at, deleted_by (soft-delete tombstones retained). Timestamps are generated server-side in UTC using ISO-8601 (RFC 3339) and synchronized via NTP. Actor fields store stable internal principal IDs, not names or emails; supplemental context includes actor_type (user/service), request_id/trace_id, and impersonated_by when delegation occurs.

All mutations are captured both inline on the entity and in an append-only audit log/event stream that is immutable and queryable. The audit log records before/after values (or diffs), the operation, correlation IDs, and the originating client/IP where available.

Backfills, migrations, and imports must set historical created_* values when trustworthy; otherwise use imported_at and imported_by=system, preserving source timestamps in provenance fields. API clients cannot set these fields directly; they are populated and enforced at the data layer via DB defaults/triggers or ORM middleware. Reads may expose these fields read-only.

Privacy and compliance: store only principal IDs and necessary context; resolve display names at read time. Access to the audit log is restricted. This approach yields consistent, portable, and verifiable temporal and actor provenance across services and environments.

## Decision

ADR-0002 is canceled and superseded by this decision. Interceptors will be generated via the existing CodeGen pipeline and will no longer be authored or maintained manually.

- Scope: Generate client- and server-side interceptors (e.g., logging, metrics, tracing, auth, retry, circuit-breaker, validation) from service/interface definitions and/or declarative annotations on APIs.
- Mechanism: Integrate interceptor generation into the build-time CodeGen phase (generate-sources). Generated artifacts are not committed to VCS.
- Configuration: Behavior is driven by:
  - Annotations/attributes on services and methods (e.g., @Log, @Trace, @Authorize(role=...), @Retry(...)).
  - Central CodeGen configuration (profiles/presets) for cross-cutting defaults.
- Extensibility: Provide stable extension points without editing generated files:
  - Partial classes/partial methods or composition via interfaces.
  - Protected hooks in abstract base classes with concrete generated subclasses.
  - Strategy/provider registries discoverable via DI.
- Overrides and Opt-out:
  - Fine-grained suppression via @NoGenerate / @SkipInterceptor or CodeGen config.
  - Manual custom interceptors can be registered to replace or compose with generated ones via DI configuration.
- Conventions:
  - Naming: <Service>NameInterceptor, <Service>ClientInterceptor, etc.
  - Package/module: emitted under a dedicated generated namespace/module to avoid collisions.
  - Idempotent generation to ensure deterministic builds.
- Backward compatibility and migration:
  - Existing hand-written interceptors remain supported but are deprecated; a migration guide maps features to annotations/config.
  - Where behavior must be preserved, CodeGen emits shims/adapters to maintain previous wiring until migration completes.
- Quality gates:
  - Generated code includes unit-testable seams; golden-file tests validate templates.
  - CI checks ensure no manual edits to generated files and enforce generation freshness.
- Documentation:
  - Templates and supported annotations are documented with examples; defaults and precedence rules are specified.

We will standardize on the Python “click” package for all command-line argument parsing and command dispatch. A root click.Group will serve as the entry point, with subcommands registered modularly to keep concerns separated and to enable future extension (including optional plugin discovery via Python entry points). We will use click’s type-aware options, validation, prompting, defaults, and rich help generation to provide a consistent UX across commands, and we will enable built-in features such as --help, --version, verbosity flags, colored output, and shell completion.

Argument parsing and CLI presentation will remain thin: parsed and validated parameters will be forwarded to application services, keeping business logic out of the CLI layer. Errors will be surfaced using click’s exceptions for uniform messaging and exit codes. Global options (e.g., --config, --verbose, --quiet) will be defined at the group level and inherited by subcommands.

This choice avoids writing and maintaining custom parsers, accelerates development, and ensures a discoverable, user-friendly interface that can evolve without breaking changes to core logic.

## Decision

We will use react-app-rewired to customize Create React App’s build configuration without ejecting. All webpack/Babel modifications will be centralized in config-overrides.js and applied via react-app-rewired scripts in package.json. We will keep overrides minimal and focused on clear needs (e.g., module aliases, Babel plugins/presets, CSS preprocessors/postcss, bundle analysis, Jest transformers), preferring customize-cra or small, well-maintained rewires to reduce maintenance risk.

We will pin compatible CRA/react-scripts versions and validate overrides on upgrades via CI. Any non-trivial or risky modification must be documented inline in config-overrides.js and in the ADR index, with an explicit rollback path. If required changes exceed what react-app-rewired can support reliably (e.g., major webpack restructuring), we will reassess: either eject with guardrails or migrate to a more flexible toolchain (e.g., Vite/Next) through a planned transition.

This approach enables needed customization while preserving CRA’s zero-config workflow and upgrade path.

## Decision

Adopt a Virtual Platform implemented as a Mediator to decouple producers/consumers from runtime, protocol, and topology concerns. The virtual platform will function as a logical layer that owns cross-cutting mediation (not business logic), providing:

- Contract-first integration via OpenAPI/AsyncAPI and a canonical data model; schema and policy enforcement at ingress/egress.
- Protocol and format mediation (HTTP/gRPC/WebSocket/Kafka/NATS), header/claim propagation, and payload transformation.
- Intelligent routing (content-based, routing-slip/recipient-list), rate limiting, retries, circuit breaking, and backpressure.
- Security mediation with zero-trust defaults (OIDC/OAuth2, mTLS, per-tenant authZ), audit, and PII redaction.
- Observability (trace propagation, metrics, logs, DLQ) and governance (versioning, deprecation, compatibility checks).

Architecture:

- Control plane: contract registry, policy store, configuration, and governance workflow (backed by Postgres/etcd).
- Data plane: stateless mediator gateways and connectors (deployed as an HA cluster) with pluggable adapters and transformations.
- Event-first core using a broker (e.g., Kafka/NATS) plus request/response via API gateway where synchronous calls are required.
- Extensibility via SDKs and FaaS hooks for custom logic; adapters isolate domains from the mediator’s internals.

Constraints:

- The mediator must not embed domain orchestration; it mediates interactions and enforces contracts/policies.
- Blue/green and canary rollouts for contract/policy changes; strict schema evolution rules.
- No single point of failure; horizontal scaling and idempotent processing.

This establishes a consistent, evolvable integration surface while allowing teams to change independently and safely.

## Decision

Adopt IIIF Presentation API 3.0 as the canonical format for describing multi-page image-based objects (e.g., manuscripts, albums) and their canvases, with JSON-LD serialization. Manifests will be generated server-side from our source metadata and image derivatives, and exposed at stable, dereferenceable HTTPS URLs. We will provide:

- Presentation 3.0 Manifests as the default.
- A compatibility endpoint that transforms v3 Manifests to Presentation 2.1 for downstream consumers that have not yet migrated.
- IIIF Image API 3.0 service descriptors on each Canvas, including tiles, sizes, and preferred formats; where backends only support Image API 2.x, we will advertise the best available level and transform URLs accordingly.

Operational choices:

- Generate manifests on demand with deterministic content based on current published metadata and cache them (HTTP/CDN) with ETags and long max-age; purge on relevant content updates. Optionally materialize static manifests at publish time for high-traffic objects.
- Use immutable, versioned manifest URIs (…/manifest/v/{semver or content-hash}) with a stable alias (…/manifest) pointing to the latest; changes that affect client rendering will increment the version.
- Represent structures (Ranges) for table-of-contents, sequences, and reading order; include AnnotationPages for OCR/fulltext (Web Annotations) when available.
- Populate required metadata: label (language map), summary/metadata/requiredStatement, rights/license, provider, thumbnail, navDate where applicable, and seeAlso links to source records.
- For very large sets, expose IIIF Collections that page Manifests; for extremely large works, consider partitioning into multiple Manifests linked via Ranges.
- Validate manifests in CI and on publish against IIIF validators; maintain schema tests to ensure backward compatibility across releases.

## Decision

We will assign canonical, dereferenceable HTTPS URIs to every entity in the Pattern/QC Atlas (patterns, quality criteria, relationships, catalogs, views, annotations). URIs will be stable, globally unique, and resolvable for both humans and machines.

- Scheme and authority: https://atlas.<org-domain>
- Path convention: /{space}/{entity-type}/{stable-id}
  - space: logical namespace (e.g., core, community, org-xyz)
  - entity-type: pattern, quality-criterion, relation, catalog, view, annotation
  - stable-id: immutable UUID-based identifier. A human-readable slug is optional and may 302 redirect to the canonical UUID URI.
  - Example: https://atlas.example.org/core/pattern/8f1d3e5a-...; optional pretty: https://atlas.example.org/core/pattern/hexagonal-architecture → 302 → canonical
- Content negotiation: Accept header selects HTML (text/html) for humans, JSON-LD (application/ld+json) as the primary machine format; additional formats (application/json, text/turtle) may be offered.
- Versioning: immutable snapshots exposed as /{...}/{stable-id}/versions/{semver-or-revn}; the canonical URI resolves to the latest stable release via 303 See Other. Older versions remain resolvable.
- Persistence: URIs are never reassigned. Deprecations return 410 Gone with a link to successors. Merges/splits use 301/303 and owl:sameAs/seeAlso relations in JSON-LD.
- Normalization: lowercase paths; percent-encode reserved characters; no trailing slashes on entity URIs; all redirects are canonicalized.
- Linking: responses embed typed links (Link headers and JSON-LD @id/@type) to enable deep linking across entities and external systems.

This decision enables durable, interoperable linking across the Atlas, documentation, and external tools.

## Decision

- We WILL support partial updates via HTTP PATCH using JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396).
- Clients MUST send Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json; requests with other content types will receive 415 Unsupported Media Type.
- PATCH requests MUST be idempotent; repeating the same patch results in the same resource state.
- Concurrency control: clients MUST include If-Match with the latest ETag for mutable resources; absent/mismatched ETag yields 412 Precondition Failed.
- Response codes:
  - 200 OK with the full updated resource representation (preferred) or 204 No Content if the representation is not returned.
  - 400 Bad Request for malformed JSON or invalid patch structure.
  - 404 Not Found if the target resource does not exist.
  - 409 Conflict when business invariants are violated by concurrent changes beyond ETag handling.
  - 422 Unprocessable Entity for validation errors.
- Semantics:
  - Omitting a field leaves it unchanged; setting a field to null removes/clears it (where nullable).
  - Arrays in merge-patch replace the entire array; we WILL NOT support array element operations via merge-patch.
  - Immutable/system-managed fields (IDs, timestamps, ownership, derived values) MUST be ignored and reported as validation errors if supplied.
  - Nested objects may be partially updated per merge semantics; relationships that require referential integrity checks MUST be validated.
- Security and audit:
  - Authorization MUST be field-aware; only permitted fields may be patched.
  - All PATCH operations MUST be audited with before/after diffs where feasible.
- Scope:
  - PATCH is only allowed on individual resource endpoints; collection endpoints do not support PATCH.
  - We MAY consider application/json-patch+json (RFC 6902) for advanced array operations in the future via explicit opt-in media type.

Adopt an in-process supervision tree with explicit lifecycle management for all long-running subsystems of the light client (synchronizer, verifier, RPC server, peer manager, storage, telemetry). The process is built on Abscissa components for initialization and shutdown ordering, with each component owning one or more Tokio tasks. A single root Supervisor manages task spawning, cancellation, and restart policies.

Key decisions:
- Task model: Tokio runtime with one CancellationToken tree propagated to all children for coordinated, bounded shutdown. All tasks must be idempotent on restart and support graceful shutdown deadlines.
- Restart policy: per-task exponential backoff with jitter and a rolling error budget (e.g., max N restarts per M minutes). On budget exhaustion, escalate to process shutdown with clear error reporting.
- Health model: liveness and readiness probes exported via HTTP (/healthz, /readyz). Readiness gates on verifier and storage availability; liveness tracks Supervisor heartbeat and child task status.
- Error handling: all tasks return typed errors mapped to structured logs and metrics; unexpected panics are caught at the Supervisor boundary, counted against the error budget, and logged with backtraces.
- Observability: structured logging (tracing) with correlation IDs per verification session; Prometheus metrics for task restarts, queue depths, latencies, and verification outcomes; log level dynamically adjustable via SIGHUP.
- Signals: SIGINT/SIGTERM trigger graceful shutdown (cancel → drain → deadline → hard stop); SIGHUP triggers config/log-level reload of safe-to-reload parameters (peers, timeouts) without restarting the process.
- Configuration: restart/backoff parameters, health endpoints, queue sizes, and concurrency are configurable via workflow config/CLI with sane defaults; configuration is validated at startup and on reload.
- Operator UX: consistent subcommands (start, status, check, dump-metrics), machine-readable status output (JSON), and clear remediation guidance in fatal logs.

This design improves reliability and operator ergonomics while minimizing dependencies and aligning with Abscissa’s component lifecycle.

## Decision

We will document architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs), following Michael Nygard’s approach with the MADR template. ADRs will be Markdown files stored versioned in the repository under docs/adr/, one decision per file, sequentially numbered, immutable except via PR.

Each ADR must include: Title, Date, Status (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded), Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered, and References. Cross-links to related ADRs are required when superseding or depending on other decisions.

Process:
- Anyone may propose an ADR via pull request.
- At least one architect/tech lead must review and approve; CODEOWNERS enforce this.
- Status changes occur only through PRs and are recorded with rationale.
- ADRs apply to application, platform, data, security, and operational architecture.

Tooling:
- Use adr-tools (or equivalent) for creation and numbering.
- Enforce markdownlint and link-check in CI.
- Publish/read via repository and optional MkDocs site.

All new significant architectural changes must have an Accepted ADR before implementation.

We will operate a small, curated set of shared ingress controller pools per cluster instead of per-team controllers.

- Run two classes of controllers:
  - shared-system: for platform/system ingress.
  - shared-tenant-N (N≥2): sharded pools for tenant workloads to cap per-controller config size and blast radius.

- Each pool is horizontally scalable (HPA) and backed by its own cloud load balancer. Sharding is by ingressClassName (e.g., shared-tenant-a/b) with a deterministic mapping (e.g., hash of namespace) managed by platform automation.

- Teams must target a provided ingressClassName (shared-tenant-*) and may not deploy their own controllers. Admission policies will enforce allowed ingressClassName values.

- TLS is managed centrally via cert-manager with ClusterIssuers; teams request certificates via standard annotations. Default backend, timeouts, limits, and security policies (WAF/ModSecurity where applicable) are set by the platform.

- Controller configuration is standardized (connection limits, body size, header limits, timeouts, proxy buffers) and tuned for multi-tenant fairness. Per-namespace rate limits and annotations are whitelisted; dangerous overrides are blocked.

- High availability is ensured through multi-replica controllers, PodDisruptionBudgets, topology spread constraints, and autoscaling based on CPU and NGINX connection metrics.

- Migration: existing dedicated/team controllers will be phased out. Teams retarget their Ingress resources to the assigned shared ingressClassName; platform tooling will assist with class assignment and validation. After cutover, dedicated load balancers and controllers will be decommissioned.

## Decision

We will model preferences as a single canonical record per user/subject, with fields classified as:
- Locale-agnostic: stored once (e.g., boolean flags, enum choices, IDs).
- Locale-aware: stored as a map keyed by IETF BCP 47 locale tags (e.g., “en”, “en-GB”, “fr-CA”).

For locale-aware fields, the storage shape is:
- fieldName: { "<localeTag>": <value>, ... }
- A default entry is required under the special key “default”. This acts as the authoritative fallback.

Read resolution follows a deterministic fallback chain:
1) Exact match (e.g., “pt-BR”),
2) Language-only match (e.g., “pt”),
3) “default” entry,
4) System-wide default locale (configurable; initial “en”).

Write semantics:
- Updates may target specific locale keys or the “default”.
- Deleting a locale key never removes “default”.
- Schema validates keys as well-formed BCP 47 tags.

APIs:
- Read endpoints accept an explicit “locale” parameter; if absent, Accept-Language is used; if absent, system default is used.
- Responses include the resolvedLocale indicating which value was served.
- Bulk/list endpoints support locale parameter for consistent resolution across items.

We will not duplicate entire preference records per locale nor per index; a single record avoids drift and simplifies authorization and sync. Presentation-layer translations (labels, help text) remain in i18n catalogs; only user-authored, locale-dependent values are stored in the localized maps.

Data storage will use JSON-capable columns/fields (e.g., PostgreSQL JSONB) or document stores with indexed subkeys on fieldName.<localeTag> for common locales. Migration will add the “default” entry for existing values and initialize resolvedLocale behavior.

## Decision

We will remove the va_profile user model and all related code paths from the application. This includes:
- Eliminating the va_profile table and associated ActiveRecord model, factories, fixtures, validations, and callbacks.
- Removing associations from User (e.g., user.va_profile), related scopes, and any dependent background jobs, workers, or cron tasks.
- Deleting serializers, presenters, and API fields that expose va_profile attributes; public APIs will no longer return va_profile data.
- Removing feature flags, config, and environment variables specific to va_profile.
- Retiring service clients and integration logic that hydrate or sync va_profile data; upstream dependencies will be switched to use the canonical identity source (e.g., IAM/SSO or user_profile) where needed.

A two-step migration will be implemented:
1) Deprecation release: stop reading/writing va_profile, switch all consumers to the replacement source, and add runtime warnings/telemetry to detect residual usage.
2) Removal release: drop database objects, delete code, and remove API fields; publish a changelog with breaking-change notes.

We will provide a 1 sprint deprecation window, with feature flags to temporarily re-enable legacy reads if rollback is required. Comprehensive tests and smoke checks will be updated to validate the new data source and ensure no regressions in authentication, personalization, or audit logging.

## Decision

Adopt Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA v2) as the standard mechanism for autoscaling stateless services.

- Scope: One HPA per Deployment/ReplicaSet for HTTP and worker services that are horizontally scalable. Exclude stateful services, CronJobs, and components with external coordination constraints.
- Metrics: 
  - Default to CPU utilization (target 70–80%) with optional memory utilization when CPU is not representative.
  - Support custom application/business metrics (e.g., RPS, queue depth, latency SLO error rate) via Prometheus Adapter as External/Pods metrics.
- Policies:
  - Per-service configurable min/max replicas; platform defaults: min=2, max=10 (override in app config).
  - Enable scaleDown stabilization window (e.g., 300s) and scaleUp stabilization (e.g., 60s) with explicit policies to prevent thrashing.
  - Use behavior settings for max surge rates (e.g., scaleUp 100%/60s; scaleDown 50%/300s) tuned per workload.
- Preconditions:
  - Require resource requests/limits, readiness/liveness probes, and graceful shutdown hooks.
  - HPAs must target Deployments with rolling updates; ensure PDBs do not block scale.
- Operations:
  - Manage HPA manifests as code with environment-specific overrides.
  - Observe autoscaling via metrics/alerts (replica counts, pending pods, saturation) and validate during load tests.
- Out of scope: Event-driven autoscaling beyond HPA (e.g., KEDA) unless a service mandates queue-length-driven policies; evaluate separately per case.

## Decision

We will standardize metadata across all domain resources via a versioned, extensible schema and a single Metadata Service.

- Representation: JSON documents validated against a canonical JSON Schema (v1), with forward-compatible evolution (additive changes only in minor versions; breaking changes require major version and migration).
- Extensibility: Namespaced custom fields under extensions.{vendor}.{feature} to prevent key collisions. Reserved top-level fields: id, type, schemaVersion, createdAt, createdBy, updatedAt, updatedBy, tags[], labels{key:value}, provenance{source, method, ref}, retention, piiClassification, acl, annotations{}, checksum.
- Storage: Postgres JSONB for authoritative storage; selective GIN indexes on frequently queried paths (e.g., tags, labels, type). Large binary attachments stored in object storage with content-addressed keys (sha256) and metadata linking.
- API: CRUD with optimistic concurrency (ETag/If-Match), partial updates via JSON Patch (RFC 6902), and bulk upsert endpoints. Server-side validation, size limits, and strict schema enforcement. Read APIs support filtering by type, tags, labels, and full-text search on selected fields.
- Immutability & audit: id, createdAt, createdBy immutable; full append-only audit log of changes and diffs. Soft delete with tombstones; optional retention policies per type.
- Security & privacy: Field-level ACLs (read/write) evaluated by the service; PII classification required for sensitive fields; encryption at rest for storage and object blobs; deny unregistered namespaces by default.
- Eventing: Metadata change events (created/updated/deleted) published to the message bus with resource id, type, version, and diff summary for downstream indexing and caches.
- Compatibility: Legacy metadata mapped via an adapter layer and migrated in place to schema v1; unknown fields preserved (round-trip safe).
- Operations: Schema registry with review workflow; linting pre-commit hook; blue/green deploys with shadow validation; SLOs for latency/error rates; metrics and structured logs.

This establishes a consistent, evolvable foundation for metadata while enabling domain-specific extension without fragmentation.

We will implement Imo Messaging as a unified, event-driven messaging platform that supports direct (1:1), group, and topic-based pub/sub communication. Client-to-edge communication will use secure WebSockets for real-time delivery, with APNs/FCM push for background/offline wake-ups. Service-to-service messaging and fan-out will be backed by NATS JetStream for durable streams, per-subject partitioning, and at-least-once delivery; intra-service RPC will use gRPC over HTTP/2.

Delivery semantics are at-least-once with client/server idempotency via deterministic message IDs and de-duplication windows. We guarantee per-conversation ordering by partitioning streams with a conversation key; no global ordering is provided. Messages are persisted with configurable retention (size/time), TTLs, and legal hold capabilities; attachments are stored in object storage with signed URLs.

Security is enforced with TLS everywhere, OAuth 2.0/OIDC for client and service auth, and fine-grained, tenant-scoped authorization. For content confidentiality, we adopt end-to-end encryption using the Signal (Double Ratchet) protocol for 1:1 and group messaging; the server stores only encrypted payloads and minimal metadata required for routing and compliance.

APIs expose a consistent model across direct, group, and pub/sub messaging, with explicit acknowledgment flows, backpressure, and flow control. Presence, typing, and read-receipts are modeled as lightweight events on separate subjects. Observability includes structured logs, trace propagation, per-conversation metrics, and dead-letter streams for poison messages.

This design balances low-latency delivery, durability, scalability, and privacy, while providing clear semantics and a stable foundation for future features (search, moderation, compliance exports).

Adopt a modern, type-safe frontend stack and a feature-first architecture to ensure scalability, testability, and maintainability. We will build the frontend as a React + TypeScript single-page application bootstrapped with Vite. Organize code by domain features (feature-sliced structure): src/app (bootstrap, providers), src/shared (ui, lib, api, styles), src/entities (cross-feature domain models), src/features (user-facing capabilities), and src/pages (route-level composition).

Use React Router for routing. Manage server state with TanStack Query (caching, retries, invalidation) and limit global client state to lightweight local stores (Zustand) or React context when needed. Use a centralized HTTP client with request/response interceptors and typed APIs (OpenAPI-generated or zod for runtime validation).

Adopt Tailwind CSS with a small set of shared, accessible UI primitives; compose design system components in src/shared/ui and document them in Storybook. Enforce accessibility with eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y and Storybook a11y checks. Support i18n via i18next.

Quality and DX: ESLint (typescript, react, import, jsx-a11y) and Prettier for formatting; strict TypeScript settings. Unit tests with Jest + React Testing Library; E2E with Playwright. Visual regression optional via Storybook snapshots. Use pnpm and a workspace to share config packages (eslint, tsconfig, ui). Pre-commit hooks (Husky + lint-staged) run lint/tests; commitlint enforces Conventional Commits.

Build-time env via Vite’s import.meta.env with schema validation; no secrets bundled—use runtime configuration where required. CI enforces type-check, lint, tests, and build. Production bundles are code-split, with performance budgets and analytics via Web Vitals.

## Decision

We will standardize on pytest as the testing framework for all Python codebases. Pytest offers concise, discoverable tests, rich plugin support, and strong community adoption. For mocking, we will use unittest.mock with pytest-mock for ergonomic fixtures. To improve feedback cycles and enforce quality, we will adopt pytest-cov for coverage reporting and pytest-xdist for parallel execution. For asynchronous code, we will use pytest-asyncio. Where appropriate, we will introduce Hypothesis for property-based testing to broaden input coverage. For integration tests that depend on external services (databases, queues, etc.), we will use Testcontainers to provision ephemeral, versioned dependencies in Docker, ensuring reproducible environments in CI and locally. Test structure will follow the AAA (Arrange-Act-Assert) pattern, with fixtures used for shared setup/teardown. Tests will run in CI on every PR with minimum coverage thresholds enforced. This stack balances developer ergonomics, speed, reliability, and maintainability while remaining lightweight and widely supported.

## Decision

Adopt event sourcing as the persistence model for the back-end in domains where strong auditability, temporal queries (state as-of/what-if), long-lived aggregates, and complex business invariants justify it. We will pair ES with CQRS: commands mutate aggregate state by appending immutable, versioned domain events to an append-only event store; read models are built via projections for query performance and integration needs.

Scope:
- Apply ES to core, behavior-rich bounded contexts (e.g., financial, order/state machines, compliance). Non-core, CRUD-centric modules remain on relational CRUD to avoid unnecessary complexity.
- Use snapshots for large aggregates to optimize load times.
- Enforce eventual consistency; critical invariants are enforced within aggregate command handling.

Operational choices:
- Event store is the system of record. Events are immutable and backward compatible; schema evolution managed via event versioning and upcasters/transformers.
- Projections are idempotent and replayable; support rebuilds, reprocessing, and blue/green upgrades.
- Outbox/transactional messaging (or native stream integration) is used to publish integration events reliably to the bus.
- At-least-once delivery is assumed; deduplication keys and optimistic concurrency guards are mandatory.
- Observability includes per-aggregate metrics, dead-letter queues, and replay controls.

Governance:
- Strict event design guidelines (semantic naming, minimal payload, explicit intent), review process for new/changed events, and migration playbooks.
- Data privacy handled via encryption/tokenization and redactable payloads; PII kept out of events when possible.
- Provide fixtures and test tooling for command/event/projection testing.

Exit and adoption strategy:
- Start with one pilot bounded context; iterate on conventions and tooling.
- Maintain compatibility paths to migrate aggregates to/from CRUD where feasible.
- If ES overhead outweighs benefits in a context, default to CRUD with outbox for events.

This balances the advantages of ES (audit trail, traceability, scalability via projections) with pragmatic selective use to manage complexity and cost.

We standardize on a limited, well-supported language set to reduce cognitive and tooling overhead while enabling productivity and performance.

- Backend services: Kotlin (JVM), targeting Java 21 LTS. Build with Gradle. Testing with JUnit5/Kotest. Static analysis via detekt/ktlint.
- Frontend and Node-based tooling: TypeScript (>=5.x) on Node LTS. Package manager pnpm. Testing with Jest/Vitest. Lint/format with ESLint/Prettier.
- Data/ML and glue scripting: Python 3.11 with Poetry. Testing with pytest. Lint/format with ruff/black.
- Infrastructure: Terraform (HCL) for IaC; Bash limited to small, portable scripts. Prefer Dockerfiles over bespoke shell logic.
- Inter-service communication: HTTP/JSON and/or gRPC; language boundaries favor network protocols over in-process FFI.
- Performance-critical components: Prefer Kotlin first; Rust may be used only via isolated services (or WASM) with an approved RFC and dedicated ownership. No ad-hoc native FFI.

Constraints and governance:
- No additional languages in production without an ADR/RFC covering rationale, ecosystem maturity, operational impact, hiring/skill availability, build/test implications, and long-term ownership.
- Each language must have CI pipelines with type-checking, tests, security scanning, linting, and reproducible builds.
- Shared coding standards, version pinning, and dependency policies are mandatory; upgrades follow LTS cadence.
- Documentation and onboarding materials must be provided for any approved exception.

This decision balances developer availability, ecosystem maturity, runtime performance, operational simplicity, and long-term maintainability while constraining polyglot sprawl.

We will standardize event-related method naming by adopting an “on” prefix for any method that represents or handles an event. Examples: onUserCreated, onOrderPlaced, onPaymentFailed, onConnectionClosed.

Scope and rules:
- Apply to domain and integration event handlers, lifecycle callbacks, and public-facing event hooks across services, libraries, and UI layers.
- Do not use “on” for commands, queries, or synchronous business operations (e.g., createUser, getOrder) to avoid ambiguity between actions and reactions.
- Event names should be specific, use PascalCase after the prefix, and reflect the event fact (prefer past tense when reacting to completed facts, e.g., onInvoiceIssued; present/progressive acceptable for streaming signals, e.g., onPriceUpdated).
- Overloaded/context-specific handlers should remain distinct via the event name or scope (e.g., PaymentService.onPaymentCaptured vs BillingSaga.onPaymentCaptured).
- Private helper methods supporting handlers must not use the “on” prefix to keep discoverability for actual event entry points.
- In UI components, props and callbacks that represent events use the same convention (e.g., onSubmit, onChange), aligning with platform norms.
- Apply consistently across languages: TypeScript/JS, Java, Python, etc., using idiomatic casing (e.g., on_user_created in snake_case codebases).

Enforcement:
- Add linting/analysis rules (e.g., ESLint/TS rules, custom Checkstyle/Detekt rules) to flag event decorators/registrations whose methods don’t start with “on”.
- Update templates, generators, and code review checklists to reflect this standard.
- Migrate existing handlers opportunistically or via a low-risk refactor, preserving public API stability with deprecation aliases where necessary.

We will use convention-based auto-discovery and DI-driven registration of message handlers.

- Handlers implement IHandle<TMessage> (commands/events) or are annotated with [MessageHandler(typeof(TMessage))]. On startup, the runtime scans configured assemblies, registers handlers in the DI container, and wires subscriptions for all discovered TMessage types.
- Handler lifetime is per-message scope: a new scope is created for each delivery; handler instances are resolved as scoped (default) to ensure clean unit-of-work and transactional boundaries. Stateless handlers may be registered as singleton only if explicitly marked [SingletonHandler].
- Multiple handlers per event are supported; command messages must have exactly one handler — startup validation fails fast if this constraint is violated. Events may have zero handlers without failing startup.
- Ordering is not guaranteed across handlers or deliveries; handlers must be idempotent. Deduplication and retry policies are applied by infrastructure decorators, not in handler code.
- Discovery can be filtered via configuration (AllowedAssemblies/Namespaces) and attributes [DoNotAutoRegister] to opt-out. Explicit registration is supported for external or dynamically loaded modules.
- Message type to routing-key mapping is provided by a central IMessageConvention (default: Namespace.TypeName -> routing key; versioned via [MessageVersion(x.y)]). Registration validates that routing keys and message contracts are resolvable.
- Cross-cutting concerns (logging, metrics, retries, DLQ, circuit breaking) are applied via decorator chain around IHandle<TMessage>, configured at registration time.
- Health checks expose the set of registered handlers and their bindings; startup fails if subscriptions cannot be established.

This approach minimizes boilerplate, enforces consistency, supports modular growth, and provides predictable lifecycle and observability for all message handlers.

## Decision

We will use Selenium WebDriver as the primary tool for browser-based feature and end‑to‑end (E2E) testing to validate user journeys across supported browsers and platforms.

- Tests will be authored in the service’s primary language to maximize reuse of utilities and tooling.
- We will adopt the Page Object Model (POM) and data-test attributes to create stable, maintainable selectors and reduce test fragility.
- Cross‑browser coverage (Chrome, Firefox, and any mandated browsers) will be executed via Selenium Grid; a Dockerized Grid will be used locally and in CI for reproducibility. Headless mode will be the default in CI.
- Tests will be integrated into the CI/CD pipeline with parallel execution, retries for known flake classes, timeouts, and artifact capture (logs, screenshots, video where supported).
- Business‑readable scenarios may be expressed with Cucumber/Gherkin where it improves shared understanding; otherwise, standard test frameworks will be used.
- External integrations will be exercised against a controlled test environment when feasible; otherwise, contract tests or service stubs will be used to keep E2E scope focused on critical paths.
- Test data will be provisioned via seed scripts or fixtures; environments will be isolated and resettable.
- Results will gate releases for critical paths; non-critical suites may run on a scheduled cadence.

This approach provides broad browser fidelity, aligns with existing ecosystem support, and scales in CI through Grid and parallelization while keeping tests maintainable through POM and disciplined selectors.

We will enable production-representative testing in staging without exposing real user identities or impacting production systems by adopting a masked, subsetted, and periodically refreshed replica of production data.

- Data source and refresh:
  - Create nightly (and on-demand) snapshots from production via a read-only backup/CDC pipeline.
  - Apply transformations in an isolated data-processing job, then load into staging.
  - Maintain a small, configurable rolling window and project-level whitelists to minimize volume and cost.

- De-identification and reduction:
  - Irreversibly mask or tokenize direct identifiers (names, emails, usernames, IPs, phone, addresses, IDs).
  - Generalize or noise sensitive quasi-identifiers (dates, locations) to preserve utility while preventing re-identification.
  - Drop non-essential columns and records; retain only data needed for functional testing.
  - Replace secrets, API tokens, and OAuth identifiers with environment-specific test credentials.
  - For binary assets (images/files), copy only whitelisted subsets; otherwise generate synthetic placeholders.

- Compliance and user rights:
  - Enforce “right to be forgotten” by propagating production deletions into staging on each refresh.
  - Keep per-environment encryption keys; never export masked keys back to production.
  - Maintain audit logs of extraction, masking, loads, and access.

- Isolation and safety:
  - Staging has no write access to production; all third-party integrations use sandbox accounts.
  - Outbound notifications (email/SMS/webhooks) are routed to sinkholes.
  - Access to staging data is least-privilege and time-bound; break-glass requires approval.

- Operations:
  - Automated verification gates ensure masking completeness before load; failure aborts the refresh.
  - Documented opt-out for datasets too sensitive; use synthetic data instead.
  - Regular reviews of masking rules and coverage as schemas evolve.

We will use Elasticsearch 8.x (managed on Elastic Cloud) as the primary search engine for image search, indexing both image metadata and vector embeddings to support hybrid (keyword + semantic) retrieval. Images will be stored in object storage; Elasticsearch will index references (URLs), extracted metadata (EXIF/IPTC/XMP), OCR text (where available), and access control fields.

Key elements:
- Metadata search: map structured fields with appropriate analyzers (e.g., multilingual text, normalizers for tags), faceting/aggregations for filters, and synonyms for common terms.
- Semantic search: store dense_vector embeddings generated externally (e.g., CLIP) for both images and text queries; enable approximate kNN (HNSW) for vector similarity; combine with BM25 via rank_feature/recency boosts for hybrid scoring.
- Ingestion: use pipelines to normalize metadata, run OCR when needed, and enqueue embedding generation; support incremental updates and reindexing for schema evolution.
- Multitenancy and security: index-level tenancy with document-level access filters; include PII-safe fields only; signed URL indirection for asset delivery.
- Operations: use ILM for hot-warm storage, snapshots for DR, and monitoring via Elastic APM/metrics; size clusters based on vector memory requirements; enforce idempotent upserts.
- Relevance tuning: maintain synonym sets, field boosts, and learning-to-rank experiments; provide analytics (click/zero-result dashboards) to drive continuous improvement.

This decision enables scalable, low-latency image retrieval with robust relevance controls while minimizing application complexity.

Adopt Project Lombok to reduce Java boilerplate in the server codebase. Lombok will be used to generate common patterns (getters/setters, constructors, equals/hashCode, toString, builders, and loggers), improving readability and development speed without changing runtime behavior.

Scope and usage guidelines:
- Prefer @Getter/@Setter or @Value for simple value objects; use @Builder for DTO construction and API payloads.
- Use @RequiredArgsConstructor for dependency injection and @Slf4j for logging.
- Avoid @Data on JPA entities; explicitly annotate required methods to prevent persistence-side issues.
- Avoid magic or less explicit features (e.g., @SneakyThrows) unless justified and documented.
- Follow a lightweight style guide documenting allowed annotations and examples.

Tooling and build:
- Add Lombok as compileOnly and annotationProcessor (Gradle/Maven) to ensure no runtime dependency.
- Require IDE annotation processing and Lombok plugin; document setup in CONTRIBUTING.
- Optionally enable delombok in CI for javadoc/source inspection if needed.

Risks and mitigations:
- Tooling friction: mitigated with documented setup and CI checks.
- Debuggability/implicit code: mitigated with restrained use and code review guidelines.
- Lock-in: acceptable; periodically reassess in light of Java records, pattern matching, and IDE generation improvements.

Adoption plan: incremental application to new code and touched classes; no mass refactor required. Revisit the decision annually or upon major Java upgrades.

We will introduce an Agent abstraction to represent and describe each runtime instance of a domain class. Each Agent will own the state and lifecycle of a single instance, expose a message-based API for commands/queries, and provide a standardized describe() operation that returns type, identity, version, status, and a safe state snapshot (with redacted/derived fields as needed). This indirection decouples class definitions from runtime concerns (concurrency, retries, caching, policy enforcement), enabling consistent observability, auditing, and resilience.

Agents will be the sole mutation pathway for their instances; direct field access is disallowed outside construction and internal persistence mapping. Repositories will return Agent handles (e.g., IAgent<T>), and services will interact with Agents asynchronously to ensure thread-safety and backpressure. The describe() payload will be a stable, versioned DTO suitable for APIs, logging, and debugging.

Where the platform supports it, we will leverage native concurrency/actor primitives (e.g., Akka/Orleans/GenServer/Clojure agents); otherwise, we will implement a lightweight mailbox/dispatcher per Agent. Agent creation is centralized via factories to enforce invariants, and Agents will integrate with telemetry (metrics, traces), ACL checks, and snapshots for recovery. This approach standardizes how instances are represented and described at runtime while preserving encapsulation and enabling horizontal scaling.

We will adopt a standardized, automated publishing checklist and pipeline for all Rust crates in the organization to ensure consistency, quality, and repeatability.

- Release automation: Use cargo-release to manage version bumps, changelog generation, git tagging, and publishing. All releases go through CI, not local machines.
- SemVer and MSRV: Adhere to semantic versioning; document and enforce a minimum supported Rust version (MSRV) via CI matrix. Breaking MSRV is a semver-major change.
- Pre-publish gates (CI): 
  - cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy with deny(warnings)
  - cargo test --all-features --all-targets
  - cargo test --no-default-features (when applicable)
  - cargo doc --no-deps -D warnings; docs.rs build via DOCS_RS_FEATURES
  - cargo publish --dry-run and cargo package verification
  - cargo udeps and cargo outdated (informational)
  - Security: cargo deny (licenses, advisories, bans) and cargo audit
- Crate metadata hygiene:
  - Cargo.toml: name, description, version, license OR license-file, repository, homepage, documentation, readme, keywords, categories, include/exclude, rust-version, authors, maintenance status (badges).
  - License: include LICENSE (SPDX-compatible) and ensure dual license if required.
  - README: concise overview, usage, MSRV, feature flags, safety/unsafe usage notes, examples, contribution and security policy links.
  - CHANGELOG: Keep a human-readable changelog following Keep a Changelog; cargo-release updates it.
  - CODEOWNERS/Crate owners set and rotated; ensure multiple maintainers.
- Features and compatibility:
  - Support no_std when feasible behind feature flags; document defaults. Avoid implicit heavy deps in default features.
  - Verify feature combinatorics for coherence (at least minimal and full).
  - Maintain stable public API; use rustdoc cfg_attr to document feature-gated APIs.
- Quality controls:
  - Lints: adopt a shared lint config (e.g., rust-toolchain + clippy.toml); deny missing_docs for public API.
  - Minimal dependency policy; prefer optional features; audit transitive licenses.
  - Reproducible builds: lockfile for workspace, but do not publish with Cargo.lock for libraries.
- Release process:
  - Open a release PR (version bump via cargo-release), pass all gates, tag vX.Y.Z, publish via CI with crate token, push git tag, and create GitHub release notes from CHANGELOG.
  - Post-release: verify crates.io, docs.rs, and yanking policy for regressions.

We will source, store, and serve service/location data for West Hampshire CCG from the CCG’s maintained local dataset as the authoritative source for that geography. The local dataset will take precedence over national datasets where records overlap, with deterministic merge/override rules:

- Precedence: Local records override national records for matching entities (matched by ODS/ODS-like codes, URIs, or agreed composite keys). If no local record exists, we fall back to the national source.
- Scope: Apply to entities whose commissioning/operational footprint is within West Hampshire CCG boundaries (as defined by latest boundary set). Cross‑boundary services retain national data unless explicitly whitelisted by the CCG.
- Ingestion: Implement an automated ETL from the CCG-provided format (CSV/Excel/API), with schema mapping, validation, and normalization to our canonical model. Ingest runs at least weekly (or as frequently as feeds are provided) with idempotent upserts.
- Provenance: Persist source provenance and last-updated timestamps per field; expose provenance in APIs and UIs where applicable.
- Governance: The CCG data owner approves schema changes and provides change notifications. We maintain data quality checks (completeness, geo-coding, contact info) and reject or quarantine invalid records with feedback to the CCG.
- Versioning and Rollback: Keep historical snapshots for audit and rapid rollback.
- Feature flag: Enable/disable local precedence per region via configuration to allow phased rollout and quick disablement.
- Deprecation: Reassess quarterly. If national data meets or exceeds local quality/latency requirements, we may retire the local override after stakeholder approval.

- Status: accepted
- Decision: Adopt Apache Kafka as the central messaging middleware for asynchronous inter-service communication, event streaming, and audit/event sourcing use cases.
- Scope:
  - Publish-subscribe events, change data capture, stream processing, and integration with external systems via connectors.
  - Not intended for request/response RPC, message prioritization, or per-message delay scheduling.
- Rationale:
  - High throughput, horizontal scalability via partitions, and per-key ordering.
  - Durable, replicated log with configurable retention/compaction supporting replay and event sourcing.
  - Mature ecosystem (Kafka Connect, Streams/Flink, Schema Registry) and strong operational tooling.
  - Exactly-once semantics available for producer/stream processing pipelines when required.
- Architectural guidelines:
  - Prefer managed Kafka (e.g., MSK/Confluent Cloud) where possible; otherwise self-host in KRaft mode with ≥3 brokers across AZs.
  - Use Avro/Protobuf with a Schema Registry; enforce compatibility rules (backward by default).
  - Define topic naming conventions, partitioning keys, retention, and compaction policies per use case.
  - Use consumer groups for scale-out; implement idempotent producers and transactional outbox for reliability.
  - Provide dead-letter topics and retry semantics (exponential with jitter); avoid in-function busy looping.
  - Secure with TLS, authN/Z (SASL/OAUTHBEARER), and ACLs; enable quotas.
  - Standardize observability: lag monitoring, broker metrics, end-to-end tracing and lineage.
- Integration:
  - Use Kafka Connect for source/sink integration; prefer managed connectors.
  - Use Kafka Streams or Flink for stateful processing; store state in compacted topics or state stores.
- Consequences:
  - Positive: unified event backbone, replayability, decoupling, strong ecosystem.
  - Negative: operational complexity, careful schema and capacity governance required.

We will make component discovery, configuration, and execution order-independent by default and require any ordering to be explicit, deterministic, and documented.

- Treat collections of extensions, handlers, and config entries as sets; do not derive meaning from declaration/registration order.
