- For cases that require ordering, use explicit priority metadata (e.g., integer priority, weight) and apply a stable sort with clearly defined tie-breakers (component name).
- Validate and reject ambiguous configurations where multiple items share identical priority without a deterministic tie-breaker.
- Model dependencies explicitly (requires/provides) and compute execution order via topological sort; fail fast on cycles.
- Normalize inputs (case, whitespace, aliases) and hash keys to canonical forms to avoid incidental ordering differences across platforms/runtimes.
- Persist and exchange data using stable, canonical serialization (e.g., sorted keys) to ensure reproducible builds and signatures.
- Prohibit iteration over inherently non-deterministic containers; use ordered collections solely when an explicit order is intended.
- Provide composition utilities (set-union/merge with conflict resolution) that are associative and commutative; disallow side effects during discovery/registration.
- Add contract and property tests to assert order independence and reproducibility across runs.
- Document the few places where order matters and require consumers to specify priorities rather than relying on positional configuration.

Adopt a new, CI-built CryptPad flist and make it the default for all environments. The flist will be:
- Built on every tagged release from a reproducible Dockerfile
- Multi-arch (amd64, arm64) with SBOMs and vulnerability scans (e.g., Trivy) enforced in CI
- Content-addressable and immutable (pin by sha256 digest); human-readable tags (latest, stable, vX.Y.Z) updated by release workflow
- Minimal base image with only runtime deps; config via env/volume mounts

Actions:
- Replace references to the legacy flist with the new digest-pinned flist in deployment manifests, docs, and charts
- Archive and deprecate old flists; keep last two stable versions for rollback
- Integrate smoke/functional tests and upgrade tests in CI before publishing tags
- Enable auto-rollback in orchestrations on failed health checks
- Publish release notes with migration steps and config diffs

This reduces cold-start and deployment time, improves security/compliance, and ensures deterministic rollouts with a clear rollback path.

We will not support explicit versioning for HTTP app callbacks (no versioned paths, query parameters, or headers to negotiate callback schema). HTTP callback contracts must be stable and evolve only via backwards-compatible, additive changes. Producers may add optional fields and new event types; consumers must ignore unknown fields.

If a breaking change is unavoidable, we will not change the existing callback contract. Instead, we will introduce a new callback contract as a separate event type and subscription (and, if necessary, a distinct callback endpoint agreed with the consumer). We will operate both contracts in parallel during a defined migration window and deprecate the old contract via a clear EOL schedule.

Schemas for callbacks will be documented (e.g., JSON Schema) and changes tracked in release notes, but schema identifiers will not be used for runtime version selection. Delivery semantics (idempotency keys, retries, signatures) remain consistent across contracts to minimize integration burden.

We will adopt Hive-style, directory-based partitioning in S3, optimized for AWS Glue/Athena and Spark. All datasets will use a consistent folder schema:

s3://<bucket>/<department>/<dataset>/<schema_version>/data_date=YYYY-MM-DD[/<secondary_partition>=value]/part-*.parquet

Key decisions:
- Primary partition: data_date (UTC) derived from the business event date when available; otherwise, ingestion date. This balances query pruning efficiency with manageable partition counts and supports backfills and late-arriving data.
- Optional secondary partition: low-cardinality dimension (e.g., council, geography, source_system) when it yields >5x partition pruning benefits and keeps total partitions per dataset <10k. High-cardinality columns (e.g., user_id) are prohibited as partition keys.
- File format: columnar Parquet with Snappy compression. Target 128–512 MB files per partition; compaction jobs will periodically merge small files.
- Immutability: partitions are append-only; corrections/late data are written to the correct data_date, with manifest-based de-duplication performed downstream. Rewrites occur only via controlled backfill jobs.
- Schema evolution: managed via schema_version in the path and Glue schema updates. Backward-compatible changes are preferred; breaking changes trigger a new schema_version.
- Naming: dataset and column names are snake_case; partition keys are lower_snake_case; values are URL-safe.
- Metadata: each partition includes a _SUCCESS marker and optional _MANIFEST for record counts and file checksums to aid validation and SLAs.
- Governance: new partition keys require a data engineering review; partition evolution must include migration and cost impact assessment.

This strategy provides efficient query pruning, predictable costs, and operational simplicity across departments while remaining compatible with existing AWS analytics services.

We will use a surrogate, non-meaningful, globally unique identifier as the primary key for citizen records.

- Primary key: citizen_id as a UUIDv7, generated application-side (with DB fallback), stored as 16-byte binary (or native UUID where supported), and exposed via APIs as a canonical string.
- Rationale: avoids embedding sensitive or jurisdiction-specific meaning (e.g., SSN, passport), supports cross-jurisdiction data, merges/splits, and is stable, immutable, and globally unique. UUIDv7 provides time-ordered characteristics for index locality and high-ingest performance without central coordination.
- All related tables will reference citizen_id via foreign keys. No cascading deletes; use soft-delete and audit trails to meet regulatory retention.
- External identifiers (e.g., national IDs, passports, tax numbers) are not primary keys. They are modeled in a separate CitizenIdentifier table with fields: citizen_id (FK), type, issuing_country, normalized_value (encrypted at rest), normalized_value_hash (salted/hash for dedup/search), validity_period, verification_status, metadata. Enforce uniqueness via composite unique indexes appropriate to identifier semantics, e.g., (type, issuing_country, normalized_value_hash) globally unique when policy allows, and per-citizen uniqueness otherwise.
- Add unique, nullable natural keys only where legally guaranteed immutable (rare) and always behind the surrogate PK.
- Implement strict normalization/canonicalization routines per identifier type to prevent duplicates. All access to sensitive identifier values goes through a vetted service with KMS-backed encryption and role-based access control.
- For interoperability, maintain optional external_system_id mappings in a bridging table rather than overloading the primary key.
- Partitioning and indexing strategies will prioritize citizen_id (clustered/primary), with secondary indexes on lookup keys (e.g., normalized_value_hash, date_of_birth + name phonetics) as needed.

## Decision

When a preserved object is intentionally removed, we will create an immutable preservation tombstone rather than silently deleting the record.

- Tombstone scope: FileSet-level (and created for each component child where applicable). Deleting a parent work triggers tombstones for all preserved children.
- Storage: Replace the preserved payload at its preservation key with a small, immutable object named identically with an added “.tombstone.json” suffix; remove (or lifecycle-expire) the original payload. For stores that disallow key reuse, the tombstone is written alongside the original key path and the payload is deleted.
- Contents:
  - object_identifier(s) and preservation key
  - checksums (all algorithms) and size of the removed payload
  - deletion_timestamp (UTC, RFC3339)
  - deleted_by (actor/service), deletion_reason (enum + free text)
  - prior_replica_locations and storage_class
  - retention_policy and recovery_policy
  - provenance (request id, job id) and application version
- Immutability: Tombstones are write-once. Any attempt to write a new payload to a tombstoned key is rejected unless an explicit, audited “restore_from_tombstone” process is executed.
- Replication: Tombstones are replicated and verified across all preservation backends; fixity jobs exclude tombstoned keys.
- Discovery/Access: Index a lightweight record for audit/search; access requests for tombstoned objects return 410 Gone with reason metadata.
- Retention: Tombstones are retained indefinitely (no automatic expiry) unless legal/policy mandates removal, in which case a superseding “tombstone-removed” marker is written and audited.

We will adopt Redux for global state management and standardize on Redux Toolkit (RTK) to minimize boilerplate and enforce best practices. State will be organized by feature using RTK slices (createSlice), with TypeScript throughout. Server-derived data will be managed via RTK Query for fetching, caching, invalidation, and lifecycle flags; cross-feature, durable client state (e.g., auth/session, user settings) will live in slices; purely local/ephemeral UI state remains in React component state.

We will:
- Configure the store with configureStore, enabling Redux DevTools and RTK default middleware (including Immer for immutable updates and serializable checks), adding listenerMiddleware for orchestrating side effects and optional redux-logger in development.
- Use createAsyncThunk only where RTK Query is not applicable; otherwise, prefer RTK Query endpoints.
- Normalize collections with createEntityAdapter; expose memoized selectors via Reselect.
- Provide typed hooks (useAppDispatch, useAppSelector) with RootState and AppDispatch.
- Co-locate feature code (slice, selectors, api/endpoints, tests) within feature folders.
- Persist required keys (e.g., auth token, user preferences) via redux-persist with strict serialization and versioned migrations.
- Enforce action purity and reducer determinism; side effects confined to thunks, listeners, or RTK Query.

This decision ensures predictable state flow, better developer experience, and scalable patterns for data fetching, caching, and testing.

## Decision

Adopt tar as the archive container format with Zstandard (zstd) compression as the default (.tar.zst) and implement the Archiver via libarchive to ensure cross-platform, streaming, and metadata-preserving operations. Archives must be deterministic (stable ordering, normalized timestamps/permissions where appropriate), support large files (>4GB), and preserve extended attributes (POSIX perms, symlinks, xattrs) when available. Integrity is ensured by an embedded SHA-256 manifest and whole-archive checksum; optional end-to-end encryption is provided via age (default) with GPG as a configurable alternative.

The Archiver exposes:
- Stream-first APIs (create/extract from streams) for low-memory operation and pipeline composition.
- Parallel compression with tunable compression levels; defaults optimized for balanced speed/ratio.
- Selective include/exclude via glob/path filters and size/type predicates.
- Resume/retry semantics with idempotent outputs (content-based manifest).
- Backward-compatible read support for .zip and .tar.gz; optional .zip export for user-facing portability (e.g., Windows Explorer).

Operationally, the service is packaged as:
- A reusable library (core archiving logic using libarchive + zstd).
- A CLI for batch/CI use with JSON logs and exit codes.
- A minimal HTTP worker for server-side jobs (rate-limited, cancellable).

Security hardening includes path traversal protection, safe extraction to confined roots, and verification-before-extraction by default.

We will use integration events as the primary mechanism for cross-bounded-context and external system communication. Integration events will be derived from domain events but treated as explicit, stable contracts focused on consumer needs (not internal state). We will:

- Publish integration events via the central message broker with at-least-once delivery and consumer idempotency enforced via event IDs and deduplication keys.
- Use the outbox pattern with transactional write + async dispatch to ensure no data loss and avoid dual-write anomalies.
- Adopt a canonical event envelope (CloudEvents-compatible) including: type, version, id, source, subject, timestamp, correlation/causation IDs, partition key, and minimal payload.
- Version events semantically; maintain backward compatibility for minor versions; introduce new types for breaking changes; deprecate old versions via planned sunsets.
- Define event naming and ownership conventions: <boundedContext>.<aggregate>.<eventName>.<version>. Each event has a single producer-owner; consumers subscribe without creating tight coupling.
- Keep payloads minimal and PII-free by default; where necessary, apply field-level encryption and data minimization policies aligned with compliance.
- Provide schema registry-backed contracts and consumer-driven contract tests in CI for compatibility.
- Implement dead-letter queues, retries with exponential backoff, and clear failure handling policies; enable observability with end-to-end tracing (correlation IDs), metrics, and alerting.
- Configure retention and replay to support rebuilding projections and late-joining consumers; document replay safety and side-effect guards.
- Treat integration events as asynchronous notifications, not commands; commands remain point-to-point where needed.
- Document SLAs, ordering guarantees (key-based ordering where required), and disaster recovery expectations per event stream.

We will implement a single, centralized reflection-based test suite to guarantee coverage and correctness of the TOSCA YAML builder. The test will:

- Discover all domain types annotated as TOSCA entities (e.g., NodeType, RelationshipType, CapabilityType, DataType) via reflection.
- For each discovered type, construct a minimal and a populated instance using test factories/builders and defaults.
- Serialize instances to YAML with the TOSCA builder, parse the YAML back to an in-memory model (or normalized Map), and assert structural equivalence (round-trip where possible).
- Validate that every annotated property/field is mapped: the test fails if a public/annotated property has no corresponding YAML output (unless explicitly ignored via an @YamlIgnore or similar annotation).
- Normalize YAML before comparison (key order independent, omit nulls/empties if policy dictates) to avoid brittle string assertions; comparisons are structural.
- Verify spec-conformant naming: annotation-provided property names appear in YAML exactly (snake/camel as mandated), and required fields are present.
- Enforce extensibility: new annotated types/properties automatically fall under test without adding test code.
- Allow explicit suppression lists for known exclusions (with justification) to avoid false positives.
This reflection test becomes a CI gate to prevent regressions, unmapped fields, and spec drift, complementing targeted unit tests and a small set of golden-file fixtures for complex, cross-entity scenarios.

We will not use Springfox. Instead, we will adopt springdoc-openapi to automatically generate OpenAPI 3.x documentation from our Spring (Boot) controllers and model annotations. Springfox is no longer actively maintained and is incompatible with Spring Framework 6 / Spring Boot 3, while springdoc-openapi is actively maintained, supports the latest Spring and Jakarta namespaces, and provides first-class OpenAPI 3 support.

The API specification will be served at /v3/api-docs (JSON) and /swagger-ui/index.html for interactive browsing. We will use io.swagger.v3 annotations where needed to enrich schemas and operations, and configure package/path scanning to include public endpoints and exclude internal/actuator routes. GroupedOpenApi will be used to expose separate docs per API module or version where applicable.

The generated specification will be treated as an artifact: validated in CI (OpenAPI linter/validator), published with build artifacts, and used to drive client/server stubs as needed. Backward compatibility checks will be added to detect breaking changes. For non-Spring services, or where annotation coverage is insufficient, we will complement with explicit OpenAPI configuration beans or static YAML merges to ensure a complete, accurate contract.

Migration from any existing Springfox setup will remove springfox dependencies and annotations, replace them with springdoc-openapi and io.swagger.v3 equivalents, and adjust security schemes (e.g., OAuth2/OpenID) via springdoc configuration.

We will implement the TDR frontend using Next.js (React 18) with TypeScript to provide a scalable, SEO-friendly, and developer-efficient foundation. Next.js will be used for file-based routing, server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), and incremental static regeneration (ISR) to balance performance with dynamic content needs. Styling will be implemented with Tailwind CSS and Radix UI primitives for accessible, composable components without runtime CSS-in-JS overhead. Data fetching and caching will use React Query (TanStack Query) for robust server-state management; minimal client state will be handled via React Context or Zustand where necessary. Forms will be managed with React Hook Form and Zod for type-safe schema validation.

We will adopt a monorepo-friendly structure (with turborepo compatibility) and shared UI/util packages where applicable. API integration will target the BFF endpoints with a typed client generated from OpenAPI/Swagger for end-to-end type safety. Internationalization will use next-intl, and accessibility will be enforced through lint rules and component choices. Testing will include unit/integration tests with Jest (or Vitest if non-Next tooling becomes preferable), React Testing Library for component tests, and Playwright for E2E. Code quality and consistency will be maintained with ESLint (typescript-eslint, jsx-a11y), Prettier, and commit hooks via Husky and lint-staged. CI will run type checks, tests, and build verification for each change.

This stack optimizes developer velocity, performance, and maintainability while aligning with our broader ecosystem standards.

We will not change the Property ID format for the Federated Properties MVP. Property identifiers remain opaque and local to their source repositories (e.g., “P123” without any embedded source/prefix/namespace). We will not add repo prefixes, GUID-like namespaces, or hostnames to the ID string.

To support federation:
- The source repository will be carried as separate metadata (e.g., sourceRepository/baseURI) in APIs and internal models.
- Client-side and server-side resolution will dereference property definitions via configured federation mappings (repoId → endpoint/base URI).
- Storage schemas and on-disk representations remain unchanged; no migrations or redirects are introduced.
- Serializations (JSON, API responses) keep the short ID unchanged and include the source as a distinct field; RDF/IRIs will reflect the source only in the full IRI, not by altering the short ID.
- UI will surface the source repository via labels/badges/tooltips rather than encoding it in the ID.

A follow-up ADR may revisit encoding source in identifiers post-MVP, once interoperability and migration impacts are better understood.

## Decision

Adopt React as the standard framework for all new front-end applications and significant rewrites across the organization.

- Scope: Applies to SPA front-ends and embedded UI modules. Legacy apps may continue as-is; net-new features should favor React unless a documented exception is approved.
- Core stack:
  - TypeScript-first with functional components and Hooks.
  - React Router for client-side routing.
  - Context + custom hooks for local/shared state; adopt Redux Toolkit only when cross-cutting global state or complex workflows justify it.
  - React Query (or equivalent) for server state and caching where applicable.
  - Testing Library + Jest for unit/integration tests; Playwright/Cypress for E2E.
- Architectural practices:
  - Emphasize accessibility (ARIA, focus management) and semantic HTML.
  - Prefer composition over inheritance; co-locate component logic, styles, and tests.
  - Support code-splitting and lazy loading for performance.
  - Establish a shared component library/design system to drive consistency and reuse.
- Tooling/build:
  - Use a maintained React build toolchain with zero/low-config defaults; avoid ejecting where possible. Centralize configuration in templates to ensure consistency.
- Interoperability and longevity:
  - Favor libraries with strong community support and stable APIs to reduce churn.
  - Enable progressive enhancement where feasible; SSR/SSG may be introduced via a React-compatible meta-framework (e.g., Next.js) when SEO or performance requires it.
- Governance:
  - New front-end proposals should default to React; alternatives require an ADR demonstrating clear advantages for the use case.
  - Establish linting, formatting, and performance budgets enforced in CI.

This decision standardizes our UI development on a widely adopted, well-supported ecosystem, improves maintainability and developer velocity, and provides a clear path for scalability and shared tooling.

We will eliminate artifact duplication by adopting a single, content-addressable artifact repository and promotion-by-metadata.

- Use a centralized artifact store per artifact type:
  - Container images: OCI-compliant registry (e.g., ECR/GCR/Artifactory) addressed by digest.
  - Non-container binaries: S3-backed CAS (content-addressable storage) with key = SHA-256 digest.
- Artifacts are immutable and stored once per digest. Uploads perform checksum verification; if the digest exists, the push becomes a no-op and returns the existing reference.
- Environment and release promotion will be represented by metadata only:
  - For OCI: move artifacts across environments by adding/removing tags that reference the same digest.
  - For S3: maintain environment-specific manifests (JSON index) that map logical names/versions to the shared digest object.
- CI/CD will:
  - Produce a single build per commit per platform/arch and compute digests.
  - Publish to the central store by digest; skip rebuilds for identical inputs; block duplicate semantic versions that point to different digests.
  - Promote by updating tags/manifests rather than copying blobs.
- Consumers will pull by digest (preferred) or by tag resolved to a digest. SBOMs, signatures, and provenance are stored alongside the digest to avoid duplicating them.
- Garbage collection is reference-counted: artifacts are retained while referenced by any tag/manifest; lifecycle rules purge unreferenced blobs after a grace period.

This decision creates a single source of truth, prevents redundant copies across environments, and reduces storage and network costs while preserving traceability and immutability.

We will adopt AWS CloudFormation as the authoritative mechanism for provisioning and managing all AWS resources across environments and accounts.

- Author templates in YAML using reusable nested stacks/modules and StackSets for multi-account, multi-region deployments.
- Permit higher-level frameworks (AWS SAM/AWS CDK) only when they synthesize to CloudFormation; the synthesized templates remain the auditable source artifact.
- Enforce Git-based version control with code review, cfn-lint/static checks, and CI/CD pipelines that deploy via Change Sets, with mandatory human approval for production.
- Use stack policies, termination protection, and drift detection; enable automatic rollback on failure and capture stack events/logs for traceability.
- Standardize parameterization and configuration via SSM Parameter Store and AWS Secrets Manager; apply consistent tagging and naming conventions per environment.
- Use least-privilege IAM roles for deployment and StackSet administration, with delegated administration for member accounts.
- Prohibit out-of-band console changes to managed resources; any change must be introduced through template updates.
- Maintain backwards-compatible template evolution with semantic versioning and clear deprecation windows; provide migration paths via stack updates or controlled replacement.

This decision establishes a single, declarative, auditable provisioning path with predictable rollbacks and governance suitable for regulated, multi-account operations.

We will containerize all deployable applications and supporting services using Docker. Each service will have a maintained Dockerfile using multi-stage builds, minimal base images (e.g., distroless or Alpine when appropriate), non-root runtime users, and explicit healthchecks. We will standardize image build conventions (.dockerignore, labels/metadata, reproducible builds) and use docker buildx with cached layers to optimize CI/CD performance and enable multi-architecture builds if required.

For local development, we will use Docker Compose to orchestrate applications and dependencies (databases, queues, mocks), ensuring parity with production configurations where feasible. CI will build, test, scan, and publish images to our container registry with semantic version tags plus immutable digests; images will be signed (e.g., Cosign) and scanned for vulnerabilities on every build.

Runtime targets will be container platforms (e.g., Kubernetes, ECS, ACI) or Docker-compatible hosts; no application will assume host-level dependencies. Secrets will be injected via the runtime (not baked into images). We will provide Make/Task scripts for consistent local and CI workflows (build, test, run, push).

This decision establishes Docker as the packaging and execution boundary for applications, improving environment parity, portability, scalability, and security across the delivery pipeline.

Adopt a dedicated Path Provider Library to centralize all filesystem and URL path resolution. Expose a small API (PathProvider) that returns canonical roots (appData, cache, temp, logs, userHome, projectRoot, runtimeWork, downloads) and helpers (join, resolve, relativize, ensureDir, uniqueFile, sanitizeFilename). Provide platform-specific implementations (POSIX, Windows) behind a common interface, selected via DI at runtime. All paths are normalized, validated, and security-checked (no traversal, no invalid characters, optional symlink resolution), with consistent separators internally and platform-correct output at boundaries. The library supports environment-aware and multi-tenant scoping (env, region, tenant, version) via templated segments and configuration, and can derive paths from environment variables with safe fallbacks. It offers lazy directory creation, optional per-root cleanup policies (TTL for temp/cache), and collision-resistant file naming. It is test-friendly via an in-memory/virtual FS adapter and deterministic fixtures. Direct use of raw File APIs or hardcoded paths is deprecated; consumers must request paths via the provider. The library is published as an internal artifact, versioned semantically, documented with usage patterns, and enforced by static checks/linters in CI to prevent bypassing.

Adopt NetworkManager as the single networking facade across the application and deprecate the Fetchable protocol from production code. All components will obtain networking capabilities via dependency injection of a NetworkManaging interface (lightweight protocol) implemented by NetworkManager to preserve testability and enable mocking. NetworkManager will centralize request building, authentication, retries, timeouts, circuit-breaking, logging/metrics, and response decoding, exposing cancellable, async APIs.

Actions:
- Replace direct Fetchable usages with NetworkManaging where abstraction is required; remove remaining Fetchable conformances.
- Provide a temporary adapter (FetchableAdapter) to bridge legacy code paths, slated for removal after migration.
- Consolidate configuration (base URLs, headers, backoff, cache policy) in NetworkManager; forbid per-call ad-hoc clients.
- Standardize error model and map transport and decoding errors to domain-specific errors in NetworkManager.
- Ensure observability hooks (tracing spans, structured logs, metrics) are emitted only from NetworkManager.

Non-goals: multiple competing HTTP clients, duplicative protocol abstractions, and per-feature networking logic.

This decision reduces duplication, enforces consistent policies, simplifies cross-cutting concerns, and maintains testability via the NetworkManaging interface while eliminating the leaky Fetchable abstraction.

We will specify the tracking consent banner language via a data attribute on the banner root element (e.g., data-consent-lang="de" on <div id="consent-banner">). The component will not auto-detect language; instead, it will read data-consent-lang at initialization. If the attribute is absent, it will fall back to document.documentElement.lang, then to a configurable default (en). Language values must be BCP 47 tags (e.g., en, en-GB, de). If a region-specific variant is unsupported, the component will fall back to the base language (e.g., pt-BR → pt). Unsupported tags trigger a console warning and use the default.

The component will re-render when the attribute changes at runtime; a MutationObserver will watch for data-consent-lang updates. An explicit API (ConsentBanner.setLanguage(tag)) will update the attribute to ensure a single source of truth.

Localization bundles will be lazy-loaded per language and cached in-memory; loading failures will fall back to the default language. No geolocation, UA sniffing, or cookie-based language persistence is performed by default; host pages may persist and reapply the attribute as needed. An optional data-consent-persist-lang="true" flag can enable internal persistence via localStorage.

This approach decouples language selection from document-wide lang, enables SSR and client-only embeds, supports dynamic language switching, and keeps integration simple and explicit.

We will run a time‑boxed spike to evaluate Crux/XTDB as our bitemporal document store for operational and audit needs. The trial will be isolated behind a persistence port/repository interface so we can swap implementations without impacting callers.

Scope and approach:
- Stand up XTDB with embedded RocksDB for developer workflows and Kafka + RocksDB for the trial cluster to assess HA and recovery.
- Implement a thin adapter to map our domain aggregates to XTDB documents, leveraging valid/transaction time for audit trails and correction workflows; keep schema definitions in code with JSON/EDN serialization.
- Use Datalog for read models and reporting; materialize a small number of projections for latency‑sensitive endpoints.
- Maintain Postgres as the system of record during the spike: dual‑write (best‑effort) to XTDB, read primarily from Postgres with opt‑in reads from XTDB for selected endpoints; provide a kill‑switch/feature flag.

Success criteria:
- Functional: expressiveness of queries, correctness of bitemporal history, referential composition across documents.
- Performance: p95 read latency ≤ 75 ms for targeted queries at N concurrent users; write throughput ≥ current baseline with <20% overhead; acceptable index/storage growth over 7 days of production‑like load.
- Operations: smooth local setup, automated backup/restore, node recovery < 5 minutes, observability (metrics/tracing), zero‑data‑loss guarantees aligned with Kafka configs.
- Complexity/risk: manageable operational footprint, clear migration path (backfill and cutover), acceptable learning curve.

Deliverables:
- Prototype service module, repository adapter, and migration/backfill job.
- Load and failure‑mode test results, operational runbook, and a go/no‑go recommendation.
- Rollback plan retaining Postgres‑only path.

If the criteria are met, we will draft a follow‑up ADR to adopt XTDB for targeted workloads and a phased migration plan; otherwise we will decommission the spike with minimal code residue.

We will adopt GitHub Actions as the primary automation platform for CI/CD and operations. All automation will be defined as code in .github/workflows, with actions pinned to specific versions and least-privilege permissions.

Key workflows:
- Pull Request validation: lint, type-check, unit tests, build, security (CodeQL/OSS vulnerability scan), license compliance; required checks for merge.
- Main/develop CI: full test matrix (OS/runtime), integration tests, container build, SBOM generation, image signing, artifact publication.
- Release: tagged semantic releases; changelog generation; package/image publishing; environment-specific deployments (dev/stage/prod) with protected environments and manual approvals for production.
- Scheduled maintenance: dependency updates (Dependabot), vulnerability scans, database migrations dry-runs, flaky-test detection.

Practices and controls:
- Reusable workflows and composite actions to enforce consistency across repos.
- Caching and artifacts (actions/cache, upload-artifact) with defined retention; concurrency groups to prevent overlapping deployments.
- Secrets managed via GitHub Environments and OIDC federation to cloud providers; no long-lived cloud keys stored.
- Branch protections enforce status checks, signed commits, and linear history.
- Self-hosted runners only when required (e.g., GPU/private network); otherwise GitHub-hosted runners; runners isolated per environment and workload.
- Observability via job summaries, annotations, and notifications (e.g., Slack) on failures; metrics exported where available.
- Policy-as-code gates (e.g., Open Policy Agent or repository rules) for compliance.
- Version pinning and automated updates for third-party actions via Dependabot.

This standardizes automation across repositories, improves security, reliability, and developer velocity, and provides a scalable path for future workflows.

We will use a per‑module IoC container with a dedicated composition root in each module, and a lightweight root container that composes modules.

- Each module owns its registrations and lifecycle, exposing a single composition entry point (e.g., ConfigureModule/Install/ModuleDescriptor) that returns service descriptors or performs registrations against a provided DI abstraction.
- The application root builds a root container and composes modules by invoking their composition entry points, creating a child scope per module or merging descriptors, according to the platform’s DI model.
- Cross‑module collaboration happens only through explicit, versioned interfaces/contracts published by the providing module; no module may resolve from another module’s container or from a global service locator.
- Lifetimes:
  - Singleton: module‑local singletons remain isolated; shared cross‑module singletons are registered in the root under shared contracts.
  - Scoped: request/operation scope is created by the root and flowed into modules.
  - Transient: default for stateless components.
- Modules may declare optional dependencies on other modules via contracts; the root wires them if present, otherwise the module must degrade gracefully or provide null/object adapters.
- Dynamic modules/plugins are supported by loading their module descriptor at runtime and creating/discarding a module scope; teardown disposes module resources deterministically.
- Validation: the root performs graph verification at startup (or load time) to detect cycles/missing contracts; modules must provide health checks for critical registrations.
- Testing: each module can be bootstrapped in isolation with an in‑memory container and test doubles for external contracts.
- Observability: common logging/metrics/tracing abstractions are registered at the root and injected into modules via shared contracts.

This structure preserves encapsulation, enables parallel development and testing, supports dynamic composition, and limits blast radius of changes while keeping a clear integration point in the root.

## Decision

Standardize on the Linux GPIO character-device interface (gpiod) as the sole supported backend and deprecate/remove the legacy sysfs GPIO API. All GPIO access will be mediated through a small, versioned abstraction built on libgpiod v2, providing:

- Stable logical pin addressing via chip/line name resolution (with fallback to numbers), plus deterministic remapping through configuration.
- Unified APIs for input, output, pull configuration, edge/event subscription, and debounce, backed by epoll-based event delivery.
- Explicit, immutable direction and capability constraints at open time; attempts to change direction or mode on an incompatible line fail fast.
- Non-root operation via Linux capabilities (CAP_GPIO if available, else CAP_SYS_RAWIO) and udev rules; containers receive access only to the specific /dev/gpiochip nodes they require.
- Feature-gated fallbacks per kernel version, with capability probing at startup; unsupported features (e.g., bias, drive) degrade gracefully and are reported.
- A software “simulated GPIO” backend for testing, CI, and offline development, selectable via configuration.
- Strict time-bound operations with clear documentation that hard real-time bit-banging is out of scope; recommend dedicated MCUs for sub-millisecond jitter requirements.
- Centralized policy enforcement: only the GPIO service/broker talks to /dev/gpiochip; applications and add-ons consume a high-level API (IPC/DBus/Unix socket) with fine-grained authorization per line/event.

We will:
- Reject new contributions using sysfs GPIO and schedule removal of any remaining sysfs paths.
- Provide migration tooling to map legacy pin identifiers to gpiod names.
- Maintain compatibility across kernels supported by our OS matrix, prioritizing upstreamed drivers and avoiding out-of-tree patches.

We will externalize and parameterize all ZOS SAL configuration used by the Identity service. Specifically, Identity will read ZOS SAL connection details (endpoint(s), host/port, protocol/TLS settings, timeouts/retries, client ID, client secret/credential, scope, realm/application ID, and optional routing headers) from environment-driven configuration rather than hard-coded values. Non-secret parameters will be supplied via standard application configuration (e.g., config files, config server, or environment variables), while secrets will be sourced exclusively from the enterprise secrets manager (e.g., Vault/KMS/Secret Manager) and injected at runtime.

The configuration model will support:
- Per-environment and per-tenant overrides (namespaced keys), with sane defaults.
- Backward-compatible defaults that mirror current production values to avoid behavior changes on rollout.
- Configuration validation at startup and health checks for ZOS SAL connectivity.
- Optional dynamic refresh where supported by the runtime (e.g., config server/sidecar), otherwise requiring restart on change.

Deployment artifacts (Helm charts/Terraform) will expose the necessary values, and CI/CD will manage promotion of environment-specific configs. Legacy inline/embedded ZOS SAL settings will be deprecated and removed after a deprecation window, with a migration shim that logs usage of legacy keys. Telemetry will include metrics and structured logs for configuration source, failures, and retry behavior.

We will implement a MultiFrameViewer that renders ordered image frames of a single subject with frame-aware interaction and annotation support.

- Architecture: compose the existing single-image viewer as a reusable frame renderer; add a controller for frame navigation, preloading, and state management. Frames are addressed by index and sourced from subject.locations in order.

- Annotations: all marks/measurements are scoped to a specific frame via a required frame index on each annotation. Switching frames filters the displayed annotations to that frame. Copy/paste of marks between frames is supported explicitly by user action; no implicit carryover.

- Positioning: pan/zoom/rotation state is, by default, reset per frame. A workflow-level configuration can override this to maintain positioning across frames.

- Configuration: expose workflow.configuration.subject_viewer_config for:
  - filter_marks_per_frame: boolean (default true)
  - positioning: "reset" | "maintain" (default "reset")
Defaults apply if configuration is absent.

- Navigation and UX: provide next/previous controls, optional thumbnail strip, and keyboard shortcuts. The viewer displays the current frame index and total count, and supports an accessible focus order and ARIA labels.

- Performance: preload adjacent frames (N=1 on each side by default) with cancellation on rapid navigation. Use memoized transforms and layered canvases/SVG for smooth panning/zooming.

- Error handling: gracefully skip or flag missing/unloadable frames while preserving navigation.

- Extensibility: leave hooks for per-frame metadata overlays (e.g., timestamps) and for task UIs that need frame context.

This establishes consistent, configurable multi-frame behavior across projects while keeping per-subject variability out of workflow-wide settings.

We will standardize our styling toolchain on a PostCSS-based pipeline with component-scoped CSS Modules and design tokens via native CSS variables.

- Authoring model: CSS Modules for all component styles; a small, versioned “tokens.css” and “global.css” for reset/base, theming, and utilities.
- Build pipeline: PostCSS with postcss-import, postcss-nesting (or postcss-nested per bundler compatibility), postcss-custom-media, postcss-calc, and autoprefixer. cssnano enabled only for production. Sourcemaps in development.
- Compatibility: Autoprefixer targets defined via a shared browserslist in package.json; same pipeline used across app, packages, and Storybook.
- Linting/formatting: Stylelint (stylelint-config-standard, stylelint-order, stylelint-prettier) and Prettier as the single formatter. CI enforces stylelint --max-warnings=0 and prettier --check.
- Structure: src/styles/{tokens.css, global.css, mixins/} with components co-locating *.module.css files. No Sass or CSS-in-JS by default; exceptions require ADR approval.
- Theming: Tokens (color, spacing, typography) exposed as CSS custom properties with light/dark themes via root-level variable scopes.
- Performance: Tree-shaken imports, minified CSS in production, deterministic class names; no utility framework (e.g., Tailwind) to avoid lock-in and bundle bloat.
- DX: Type-safe class names via generated .d.ts for CSS Modules in TypeScript projects.

This decision unifies authoring, enforces consistency, supports theming, and minimizes vendor lock-in while keeping the toolchain lightweight and maintainable.

We will standardize on a pragmatic, cloud-first toolchain that optimizes for interoperability, security, and team familiarity:

- Cloud and runtime: AWS as the primary cloud; managed Kubernetes (EKS) as the default compute/orchestration for long-running services; AWS Lambda for event-driven/serverless use cases.
- Infrastructure as Code: Terraform with reusable modules and Terragrunt for environment composition; Kubernetes manifests via Helm; policy enforcement via Open Policy Agent/Conftest.
- Languages and frameworks: TypeScript (Node.js) and Java/Kotlin as primary backend languages; Python for data/ML and scripting; Go for platform tooling. Frontend: TypeScript + React. APIs: REST/JSON with OpenAPI; gRPC optional for internal high-performance calls.
- Data: PostgreSQL as the default relational store; Redis for cache/queues; S3 for object storage; DynamoDB permitted for high-scale key–value workloads with clear justification.
- Messaging and events: AWS SNS/SQS for simple pub/sub and queues; Kafka (managed) for high-throughput streaming.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions with centrally maintained reusable workflows; GitOps for Kubernetes deploys (Argo CD); image builds using standardized hardened base images; artifact storage in GitHub Packages/ECR.
- Security and compliance: OIDC-based SSO (Azure AD/Okta) using OAuth2/OIDC; service-to-service auth via mTLS or AWS IAM where applicable. Secrets in AWS Secrets Manager/SSM Parameter Store with envelope encryption; SOPS for Git-managed secrets. Mandatory SAST/DAST/dependency scanning and container image signing (Sigstore/cosign).
- Observability: OpenTelemetry for traces/metrics/logs; Prometheus + Grafana for metrics; CloudWatch/OpenSearch for logs; Tempo/Jaeger for traces; alerting via Alertmanager and PagerDuty.
- Networking and edge: CloudFront + WAF for public endpoints; API Gateway or Ingress Controller for service routing; private VPC networking by default.
- Documentation and governance: Architecture and ADRs in-repo; templates and guardrails provided via starter repos and linters. Exceptions allowed via lightweight review with time-bounded sunset clauses.

This stack is the default for new services; deviations require documented justification and approval.

We will not publish a separate npm package per component. Instead, we will publish a single top-level package (e.g., @org/component-library) that exposes per-component entry points via subpath exports (e.g., @org/component-library/Button). Each component will reside in its own folder with a private, non-published package.json to define main/module/types, enabling clean resolution for CJS/ESM and TypeScript while avoiding multi-package overhead.

Consumers can either:
- import { Button } from '@org/component-library'
- import Button from '@org/component-library/Button'

We will use the package.json exports field to map stable, supported subpaths and to select the appropriate build (esm/cjs) and types, preserving tree-shaking and enabling per-component consumption without duplicative installations. This approach centralizes versioning and release management, simplifies dependency and peerDependency alignment, reduces CI/CD and publishing complexity, and improves discoverability and DX while still meeting the requirement to import individual components. This aligns with Decisions 6 (module support) and 7 (directory/outputs).

## Decision

Adopt OpenAPI 3.1 as the canonical contract for all externally and internally exposed HTTP APIs. Specifications will be authored in YAML, stored in each service’s repository under /api/openapi.yaml, and treated as the single source of truth in an API-first workflow (spec reviewed and approved before implementation). We standardize on JSON Schema 2020-12 within OpenAPI 3.1 for request/response validation and reusability via components/schemas. Every operation must define request/response bodies, standardized error responses, examples, tags, and security schemes. We will maintain a shared API style guide and lint rules (e.g., Spectral) enforced in CI. Backward compatibility is required for minor/patch releases; breaking changes require a major version and separate path or server URL. We will publish human-friendly docs via Redocly (or ReDoc) and maintain an always-current, browsable catalog. Mocking and contract testing will leverage the spec (e.g., Prism, Dredd/Pact) and code generation for clients/servers will use OpenAPI Generator where appropriate, with generated code kept out of core domain logic. Authentication will be described via standardized security schemes (OAuth2/OIDC, HTTP Bearer) and reusable scopes. Reusable components (schemas, parameters, responses) will be centralized in a shared library for consistency, included via $ref. All specs must pass validation, linting, and example execution in CI before merge.

We will adopt MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) as the standard format for documenting architectural decisions across the project. We will use the latest stable MADR template as the canonical structure for all new ADRs, ensuring each record includes context, decision, status, consequences, and links to related ADRs. We will store ADRs in docs/adr using zero-padded sequential numbering (NNNN-title.md) and maintain a single decision per file. We will manage ADR lifecycle states as proposed, accepted, deprecated, and superseded (with explicit references). We will create ADRs via a repository script/template to ensure consistent headers and metadata, and enforce format and filename conventions via CI checks. We will require ADRs to be authored and reviewed through pull requests, with architectural owners as approvers. We will permit minor editorial fixes without renumbering; substantive changes require a new ADR that supersedes the prior one. We will render ADRs directly from Markdown in the repository and optionally aggregate them into project documentation; the Markdown is the source of truth. We will migrate existing ADRs opportunistically to MADR when they are next edited, preserving history and cross-references.

## Decision
We will maintain a lightweight, version-controlled set of Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for all architecturally significant decisions (affecting structure, quality attributes, interfaces, dependencies, data contracts, security, or runtime topology).

- Each ADR captures: Title, Date, Status (Proposed/Accepted/Superseded/Deprecated), Context, Decision, and Consequences. One decision per ADR.
- ADRs are authored in Markdown and stored in the repository at docs/adr/adr-{NNNN}-{kebab-title}.md, where NNNN is a zero-padded, monotonically increasing number. Numbers are never reused.
- Changes to ADRs follow the standard pull request workflow with peer review. The initial author is responsible for drafting; the owning team or architecture group is responsible for acceptance.
- Reversals or changes create a new ADR that explicitly supersedes the prior one; the old ADR remains in the history, marked as Superseded with a backlink.
- ADRs are required for any change that materially impacts non-functional requirements, cross-team interfaces, persistence schemas, platform/runtime selection, external dependencies, or deployment topology.
- A template will be provided (docs/adr/template.md) and referenced by a repository scaffolding script to streamline creation.
- ADRs will be linked from relevant code (README, module docs) and work items to ensure discoverability.
- Periodic reviews (e.g., quarterly) will validate status accuracy and identify candidates for consolidation or retirement.

This approach creates a durable, navigable decision log that reduces institutional memory risk, improves onboarding, and enables intentional evolution of the architecture.

Chosen Alternative: Use github.com/gorilla/mux as the primary HTTP router.

We will standardize on gorilla/mux for request routing due to its mature API, rich route matching (path variables, regex, methods, hosts, schemes), subrouters for modular route grouping, middleware support, and seamless compatibility with net/http. The team has prior experience with mux, reducing onboarding and implementation time.

Implementation guidelines:
- Import github.com/gorilla/mux and construct a root router with subrouters per bounded context (e.g., /api, /admin) to encapsulate middleware and auth concerns.
- Prefer explicit HTTP method constraints and named routes for clarity and reverse URL generation.
- Use path variables sparingly and validate via regex where appropriate.
- Centralize cross-cutting middleware (logging, recovery, tracing, request ID, auth) at the root; apply feature-specific middleware at subrouters.
- Encapsulate router creation behind an internal interface/factory to allow future substitution with minimal impact.
- Provide table-driven tests using httptest with route registration isolated per test suite.

Risks and mitigations:
- Performance overhead compared to minimal routers (e.g., httprouter) is acceptable for our workload; revisit if profiling indicates a bottleneck.
- Upstream maintenance status will be monitored; the abstraction layer enables migration (e.g., to go-chi/chi) if needed without broad refactors.

This decision establishes a consistent, maintainable routing approach aligned with our current needs and developer expertise.

## Decision
Adopt JUnit 5 (Jupiter) as the standard testing library across all services. Use AssertJ for fluent assertions and Mockito for mocking/stubbing. For HTTP/API testing, use REST Assured. For integration tests involving external services (DBs, message brokers), use Testcontainers. For contract/mocking of external HTTP dependencies, use WireMock. For architecture rules, use ArchUnit.

Rationale:
- JUnit 5 provides modern, extensible testing with parameterized tests, tags, nested tests, and broad IDE/CI support.
- AssertJ offers readable, expressive assertions with rich diagnostics.
- Mockito is widely adopted, flexible, and integrates cleanly with JUnit 5.
- REST Assured simplifies expressive API tests.
- Testcontainers ensures reliable, environment-parity integration tests without bespoke infrastructure.
- WireMock enables deterministic tests for HTTP integrations.
- ArchUnit enforces architectural constraints in code.

Standards:
- New tests MUST use JUnit 5; JUnit 4 is deprecated and not to be introduced in new modules.
- Prefer AssertJ over Hamcrest/JUnit assertions for consistency.
- Use Mockito’s JUnit 5 extension for lifecycle management.
- Prefer Testcontainers over in-memory substitutes when behavior matters (e.g., PostgreSQL over H2).
- Provide a base test module with common test utilities and reusable container setups to reduce duplication.
- Integrate with build (Maven/Gradle) and CI to run unit tests on every push and heavier integration tests on merge/nightly via JUnit tags.

Adopt blue-green deployments for application and database changes to achieve zero/low-downtime, safe rollbacks, and predictable cutovers. For each production release, we provision two stacks: Blue (live) and Green (candidate). Green consists of new application instances and a database prepared via snapshot/restore or replica promotion from Blue. We apply schema changes and backfills to Green offline, verify with smoke tests and shadow traffic, and continuously sync data from Blue to Green using logical replication or change data capture. Cutover is executed by switching traffic at the load balancer/DNS to Green after automated health, migration, and data drift checks pass. Rollback is an instantaneous switch back to Blue.

All schema changes must follow expand/contract principles:
- Expand: additive, backward-compatible changes first (new tables/columns/indexes, nullable or defaulted columns).
- Dual-compatibility: deploy app versions that read/write both shapes; use feature flags for reads/writes to new paths.
- Backfill: run idempotent, throttled jobs to populate new structures.
- Contract: remove old paths/columns only after at least one stable release cycle and metrics confirm no usage.

For large online migrations, use tooling (e.g., pt-osc/gh-ost) and gated rollout with SLO-based monitors. During cutover, either quiesce writes briefly or ensure dual-write and replication lag are within bounds. Automate the workflow in CI/CD, including environment creation, data sync, pre/post checks, and traffic shift. Accept higher infrastructure cost and complexity in exchange for safer database migrations and rapid rollback.
