Adopt TypeScript as the primary language for all new frontend (e.g., React) and Node.js backend services, as well as shared libraries and tooling. Enable strict typing across the codebase (strict, noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, noImplicitThis, noUncheckedIndexedAccess) and prefer explicit return types for public APIs.

Establish a centralized tsconfig base that defines compiler options, path aliases, target/module settings, and JSX/runtime config; projects extend from this base. Use @typescript-eslint with ESLint and Prettier for linting/formatting. Enforce type checking in CI via tsc --noEmit and block merges on type errors.

Support gradual adoption for legacy code by allowing interop with JavaScript (allowJs, checkJs) and migrating module-by-module. For published packages, emit type declarations (declaration: true) and maintain strict public types. Prefer type-safe APIs and utilities over any, and add @types/* packages where needed.

Use tsc for type checking; use project-appropriate bundlers/transpilers (e.g., esbuild/SWC/Babel/Vite) for builds, ensuring source maps and declaration generation are preserved. Avoid ts-node in production; it may be used for local tooling/tests only. For runtime data boundaries (e.g., I/O, APIs), pair TypeScript with runtime validation libraries where appropriate.

Document patterns for common frameworks, module resolution, and testing. Provide editor configs for VS Code and enable incremental builds/Project References for large repos. All new code and significant refactors must be written in TypeScript and adhere to the shared configuration.

We will make Kibana accessible to all service teams via organization SSO, with least-privilege, read-only access by default.

- Authenticate via OIDC (e.g., GitHub/SSO) and authorize through role mappings from team groups to Kibana Spaces (one Space per team).
- Scope data access to indices/namespaces owned by the team (index- and field-level security); no cross-team visibility by default.
- Provide a shared “Platform” Space with generic, non-sensitive cluster/platform dashboards visible to all teams.
- Restrict write/admin capabilities (index management, ingest pipelines, ILM, Dev Tools, Saved Object management beyond team Space) to the Platform team.
- Pre-provision baseline dashboards, visualizations, and alerts per team Space; allow teams to create and manage their own visualizations within their Space.
- Enforce data protection: mask/redact sensitive fields at ingest where feasible; apply field-level security to sensitive attributes that must remain.
- Enable audit logging for logins, role mappings, and saved object changes; review periodically.
- Set rate limits and session timeouts; enforce MFA via SSO policy.
- Provide a documented break-glass process for time-bound, auditable cross-team or elevated access when operationally necessary.
- Maintain automation to create/update Spaces, role mappings, and index patterns on team onboarding/offboarding and namespace changes.

We will standardize production containers across services with the following conventions:

- Build: Multi-stage Dockerfiles with reproducible, deterministic builds. Builder stage uses official language images; runtime stage uses distroless (preferred) or minimal Debian if shell needed. No Alpine for glibc apps unless validated.
- Security: Run as non-root with fixed UID/GID, read-only root filesystem, drop all capabilities unless explicitly required, use tini as init, define USER and explicit WORKDIR. No secrets in images or layers; configuration via environment variables and mounted secrets (KMS/Secret Manager). Enable image SBOM generation and signature/attestation (Sigstore/COSIGN) in CI; block unsigned images. Regular vulnerability scans and pinned base image digests.
- Runtime: Provide HEALTHCHECK, graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handling), and predictable ENTRYPOINT/CMD. Expose ports via ENV. Write logs to stdout/stderr in JSON; no file logs. Support for OpenTelemetry via env. Use OCI labels for versioning, commit, build date, and source URL.
- Build/Release: Use docker buildx for multi-arch (linux/amd64 primary, linux/arm64 optional). Do not use latest tag; tag as app:version, app:git-sha, and app:branch for staging. Immutable images; rollbacks by tag. CI builds images on merge, runs tests, scans, signs, and pushes to the internal registry.
- Orchestration: Optimized for Kubernetes. Provide resource requests/limits guidance, liveness/readiness probes aligned with HEALTHCHECK, and mount-only required volumes (tmpfs for writable paths). Avoid host networking and privileged modes.
- Repo hygiene: Include .dockerignore, cache-friendly layer ordering, and minimal layers. Each service maintains its own Dockerfile at repo root or /deploy/.
- Exceptions require an approved ADR amendment with justification and mitigation.

Each pattern will be implemented and documented using a consistent, self-contained structure to maximize clarity, reusability, and testability.

- Location and naming:
  - patterns/<category>/<PatternName> (e.g., patterns/behavioral/Observer)
  - Package: com.example.patterns.<category>.<patternname>
  - Role-based class names (e.g., Subject, Observer, Strategy, Context) aligned with canonical literature.

- Source layout:
  - src/main/...: implementation classes and minimal public API (interfaces first).
  - src/test/...: unit tests covering roles, interactions, and edge cases.
  - examples/: a runnable example (Main or Demo) showing typical usage.
  - docs/: README.md and UML diagrams.

- Documentation (docs/README.md) follows a fixed template:
  - Intent, Also Known As, Motivation, Applicability
  - Structure (UML), Participants, Collaborations
  - Implementation Notes, Variations, Trade-offs
  - Consequences, Known Uses, References

- Constraints:
  - No cross-pattern runtime dependencies; only shared, stable utilities allowed (e.g., testing helpers).
  - Public API limited to role interfaces and a small bootstrap/facade if needed for examples.
  - Internal classes marked package-private where possible.
  - Consistent exception and logging strategy; no I/O in core unless part of the intent.

- Tooling and quality:
  - Code generation scaffold (via ADR 2) provides boilerplate directories, README template, and example stubs.
  - ArchUnit rules enforce layering, visibility, and package boundaries.
  - CI validates compilation, tests, example execution, and documentation presence (README + UML).

- Versioning and release:
  - Each pattern is a submodule/artifact; semantic versioning applies per module.
  - Backwards compatibility assessed on public interfaces only.

This structure standardizes how patterns are added, understood, tested, and consumed.

## Decision

Adopt Vega-Lite as the standard visualization language for all data visualizations.

- We will represent visualizations as Vega-Lite JSON specifications stored and versioned alongside application code, enabling reproducibility, reviews, and automated testing.
- Vega-Lite will be rendered in web clients using vega-embed. Server-side rendering for static exports (PNG/SVG/PDF) will use headless Vega tooling.
- For advanced cases not expressible in Vega-Lite, we may escalate to raw Vega specifications. Any imperative custom rendering (e.g., D3) requires an explicit exemption and rationale.
- We will provide a thin TypeScript wrapper/utilities for:
  - Schema validation against Vega-Lite’s JSON schema
  - Shared themes, color palettes (WCAG-compliant), and responsive layouts
  - Localization (labels, number/date formats) and i18n
  - Sensible defaults for interactivity (tooltips, selection, zoom) and performance (data transforms server-side when feasible)
- Accessibility is mandatory: ensure color contrast, alternative encodings (patterns/markers), keyboard navigation of interactive elements where supported, and ARIA annotations for embedded charts.
- Telemetry will capture spec usage and rendering performance to guide optimization and deprecation.
- Backward compatibility will be maintained by pinning Vega/Vega-Lite versions and migrating specs through controlled upgrades.
- Documentation will include a gallery of approved chart types, templates, and guidelines for when to use Vega vs. Vega-Lite.

This standardizes on a declarative, portable, and testable grammar of graphics, reduces bespoke chart code, and supports cross-platform rendering and automation.

We will adopt Go Modules and remove the requirement for a standard GOPATH project layout. The repository will build and run outside GOPATH (any filesystem location) using a single go.mod at the repo root. Internal imports remain github.com/transcom/mymove/..., and server and client code continue to coexist at the top-level of the repo. We will deprecate the GOPATH-specific guidance in ADR 0003.

Implications:
- Build and dependency management use Go Modules (go 1.18+), not GOPATH. Makefile and scripts will not set or depend on GOPATH.
- CI/CD will use go mod download and cache the module cache; for reproducible builds we may vendor dependencies via go mod vendor as needed by environments that disallow network access.
- Developer setup: no special checkout path; $GOPATH is not required. go install respects GOBIN if set; otherwise binaries land in the default module-aware location.
- Tooling and codegen will invoke go run/go build in module mode; any tools previously expecting GOPATH will be replaced or run via module-aware mechanisms.
- Documentation and onboarding will be updated to reflect module-based workflows and to remove GOPATH instructions and symlink workarounds.

This decision modernizes the project to idiomatic Go practices, simplifies onboarding, and improves build reproducibility and tooling compatibility.

Adopt a pragmatic, risk-driven testing philosophy centered on fast, reliable feedback and clear ownership:
- Favor the testing pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, minimal end-to-end (E2E) smoke paths that reflect critical user journeys.
- Prioritize determinism and isolation: no network, time, randomness, or global state leaks in unit tests; use fakes and mocks at service boundaries only. Prefer contract tests over deep mocking to validate integrations.
- Test behavior, not implementation details: assert observable outcomes and public interfaces. Avoid brittle UI selectors and internal state peeking.
- Make tests readable and maintainable: single reason to fail, clear Arrange–Act–Assert structure, descriptive names, and living fixtures/factories for data setup.
- Embrace TDD where it adds clarity; otherwise write tests alongside code. All new features require tests; bug fixes include regression tests.
- Strive for meaningful coverage (≥80% statements/branches in core domains) while allowing justified exceptions; measure coverage as a guide, not a goal.
- Keep E2E suite lean and stable: cover happy paths and high-risk flows, run in CI on merge; quarantine flaky tests and fix or remove within SLA.
- Use property-based and boundary tests for critical logic; snapshot/golden tests only for stable, intentional formats.
- Enforce fast feedback loops: unit/integration tests run locally and in pre-merge CI within minutes; nightly jobs can run extended suites.
- Document test intent and conventions; code owners are responsible for test health in their areas.
- Security, performance, and accessibility get dedicated checks where applicable and are treated as first-class test categories.

We standardize URI usage as follows:
- Use HTTPS URIs for resolvable resources (APIs, documents, files) and tag URIs (RFC 4151) for globally unique, stable identifiers of domain entities that may not be resolvable.
- URIs are immutable once issued. Never encode environment (dev/test/prod), session, or volatile state in a URI.
- Structure:
  - HTTPS: https://{domain}/{tenant-or-org}/{bounded-context}/{resource}/{id}[/{subresource}/{id}] with optional query only for filtering/sorting; not for identity.
  - Tag: tag:{authority},{yyyy}:{namespace}/{entity}/{natural-key-or-stable-id} where authority and namespace are registered internally; avoid mutable attributes in identifiers.
- Conventions: lowercase, ASCII only, kebab-case for path segments, percent-encode per RFC 3986, no spaces, max length 2,048 chars.
- Identity rules: prefer natural keys if immutable and unique; otherwise use stable surrogate IDs. Do not include PII or secrets. Avoid sequential IDs when exposed publicly.
- Versioning: if the identity changes due to schema evolution, create a new URI; maintain explicit mappings. Resource representation versions are handled via content negotiation or versioned paths, not by changing entity tag URIs.
- Governance: maintain a registry of authorities, namespaces, and reserved segments; automated validation in CI; collision checks and linting in API gateways and data pipelines.

We will standardize database migrations using Flyway executed via the official Docker image.

- Package: Use a pinned Flyway Docker image; run via make/scripts to ensure reproducible, tooling-free execution.
- Artifacts: Store versioned SQL in repo under db/migration using V{semver|timestamp}__description.sql and repeatable R__*.sql. Keep idempotent, forward-only DDL/DML; no inline destructive changes to hot paths.
- Config: Provide flyway.conf templates per service; pass environment-specific settings via environment variables at runtime. Secrets (URLs, users, passwords) are injected from the platform secret store; no secrets in git.
- Schemas: Each service owns its schema. Flyway manages its schema history table in the target schema. Use baselineOnMigrate=true for onboarding existing databases; disallow outOfOrder except by exception.
- Safety: clean disabled in all environments; production migrations require manual approval. Validate on every run; fail on checksum drift unless explicitly repaired.
- CI/CD: 
  - CI runs flyway validate and info on PRs.
  - Non-prod pipelines run migrate automatically on merge.
  - Production uses the same container/image and migration artifact, gated by approval.
- Rollback: Prefer forward-only migrations; reversals are new corrective migrations. Use flyway repair only to resolve checksum issues after audited approval.
- Operations: Mount migrations read-only into the container. Migration user holds required DDL; application user has least privilege. Capture logs and publish migration reports as build artifacts.
- Conventions: Enforce naming, coding standards, and linting for SQL. Provide utility scripts (e.g., make migrate/validate/info/baseline) for local and pipeline use.

This approach yields deterministic, audited, and environment-agnostic migrations with minimal local setup and consistent execution across CI/CD and production.

We will adopt a predominantly serverless, event-driven backend on AWS to optimize for rapid delivery, scalability, and operational efficiency.

- Compute and APIs: Use AWS Lambda (Node.js/TypeScript) behind Amazon API Gateway (HTTP APIs) for synchronous APIs. For long-running orchestrations, use AWS Step Functions with Lambda tasks.
- Data: Use Amazon DynamoDB as the primary transactional store (single-table design per bounded context) and S3 for object storage. For analytics and reporting, stream changes via DynamoDB Streams to Kinesis Firehose -> S3 -> Athena. Where strong relational semantics are required, use Aurora Serverless v2 (PostgreSQL).
- Messaging and workflows: Use EventBridge as the event bus for domain events, SQS for work queues, and SNS for fan-out notifications.
- Identity and access: Use Amazon Cognito for user auth (OIDC/OAuth2), API Gateway authorizers for service access, and IAM for least-privilege between services. Secrets in AWS Secrets Manager/SSM Parameter Store.
- Observability and reliability: Use CloudWatch metrics/logs/alarms, AWS X-Ray tracing, and structured JSON logging. Enable dead-letter queues, retries, idempotency keys, and exactly-once semantics where feasible.
- Networking and security: Keep Lambdas outside VPC unless private resources are needed; when needed, place in VPC subnets with VPC endpoints. Encrypt all data at rest and in transit.
- Delivery and governance: Provisioned via Infrastructure as Code (Terraform or AWS CDK), with CI/CD (GitHub Actions) for lint, test, deploy. Use environment per stage isolation and feature flags. Apply provisioned concurrency for latency-critical paths and set clear SLOs.
- Constraints: Avoid serverless for workloads requiring persistent connections, heavy CPU/memory for extended durations, or specialized runtimes; use containerized services on Fargate selectively when warranted.

## Decision

Represent all audio positions (timestamps) and durations in integer milliseconds across public APIs, persistence, message payloads, and UI. Use signed 64-bit integers for storage and transport to cover long-running sessions and negative offsets (e.g., preroll). Provide canonical conversion utilities to/from seconds (double) and sample frames (int) given a sample rate, rounding to the nearest millisecond on inbound conversions and preserving integers end-to-end to avoid floating-point drift. Internal DSP modules may operate at sample precision or higher-resolution clocks as needed, but must adapt at module boundaries to the millisecond contract. JSON and protobuf fields will carry millisecond values as integers; database schemas will use BIGINT. UI rendering will format milliseconds as HH:MM:SS.mmm. Any external time inputs finer than 1 ms will be rounded; any ambiguity in rounding policy will be centralized in shared helpers to ensure consistency.

Adopt cluster-internal synthetic monitoring using Prometheus Blackbox Exporter as the standard mechanism to measure uptime of internal services in Compliant Kubernetes.

- Deploy a managed blackbox-exporter per cluster (dedicated namespace), discovered by Prometheus via Probe/ServiceMonitor CRDs (Prometheus Operator).
- Define uptime SLI as the ratio of successful probes over a rolling window (e.g., 28 days). Success criteria:
  - HTTP/HTTPS: 2xx/3xx within latency budget (e.g., <2s), valid TLS where applicable.
  - TCP-only services: successful TCP connect within timeout.
  - gRPC: use grpc_health_probe (CronJob or sidecar) exporting results as metrics, or a blackbox grpc module where available.
- Require every internal service to expose a stable health endpoint (/health or /ready) or a TCP port suitable for probing. Teams must label Services with probe=true and provide target path/port via annotations.
- Probe paths:
  - ClusterIP to validate service and in-cluster networking.
  - Optional: internal Ingress/LoadBalancer to include dataplane and policy layers.
- Security and compliance:
  - Restrict probe namespace RBAC to read Service/Endpoints and write metrics.
  - Enforce NetworkPolicies allowing egress from probes only to labeled Services.
  - Use in-cluster DNS; keep all data in cluster. Support mTLS/service mesh via dedicated probe identities and policies.
- Observability:
  - Record probe_success, probe_duration_seconds, TLS and DNS metrics in Prometheus with per-service labels.
  - Provide standard Grafana dashboards and SLO panels.
  - Configure multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts in Alertmanager aligned to SLOs (e.g., 99.9% monthly).
- Configuration:
  - Default interval 15s, timeout 5s; environment-specific overrides allowed.
  - Targets managed via label selectors and static configs for critical dependencies.
- Ownership: Platform team maintains the probing stack; service teams own probe readiness endpoints and annotations.

We will standardize on “GADR” as the canonical term and acronym for Generalized Architectural Decision Record(s), with the plural “GADRs,” and the expansion “Generalized Architectural Decision Record(s)” on first use. “GADR” distinguishes cross-cutting, multi-repo, or organization-wide architectural decisions from repository-scoped “ADR”s while preserving familiarity.

Naming and conventions:
- Title format: “GADR-####: Concise Decision Title”
- File path: docs/gadr/GADR-####-kebab-title.md
- Front-matter: type: gadr; status: proposed|accepted|rejected|deprecated; supersedes/superseded-by for lineage
- Labels/Badges: use “GADR: proposed/accepted/rejected/deprecated”; repositories should add corresponding labels
- References: link as [GADR-####]; avoid alternative spellings (“gADR”, “General ADR”)
- Glossary: add “GADR — Generalized Architectural Decision Record”

Scope and usage:
- Use a GADR when the decision affects multiple systems, shared platforms, standards, governance, or organization-wide practices.
- Repository-local decisions remain ADRs.
- When a GADR constrains local design, local ADRs should reference the governing GADR.

Backwards compatibility and migration:
- Existing documents remain unchanged; do not rename ADRs retroactively.
- For any prior “generalized ADR” artifacts, add an alias note and cross-link to the new GADR series.
- During transition, documentation and templates will accept type: adr|gadr, but new cross-cutting decisions must use GADR.

Tooling and templates:
- Provide a GADR template aligned with ADR format, plus an added “Adoption/Enforcement” section for organization-wide rollout.
- Update linters, generators, and indexers to recognize docs/gadr and type: gadr.

Implement precomputed rollup summary tables to power dashboards, backed by materialized views or denormalized tables in the analytics warehouse. Aggregations will be computed incrementally on an ingestion watermark (event_time) with a 15-minute freshness SLA, and full backfills will be supported for historical ranges. Tables will be partitioned by date/time and indexed on primary dashboard dimensions (e.g., account, product, region) to optimize filtering and drill-down.

Pipelines will be orchestrated via our existing ELT framework (dbt + scheduler) using idempotent, incremental models (MERGE/UPSERT) with late-arriving data handled via sliding-window reprocessing. Data lineage and tests (row counts, referential integrity, aggregate tolerance thresholds) will be embedded in the pipeline, with monitoring/alerts on staleness and volume anomalies. Rollups will be versioned; schema changes will follow a backward-compatible, contract-first process.

Dashboards will query only the rollup tables (read-only roles), not raw fact tables, with a documented semantic layer mapping metrics to definitions. Critical real-time widgets may fall back to a direct query path for the last N minutes if required, but the default is rollups.

Storage and compute costs are accepted; retention for rollups will mirror underlying facts with periodic VACUUM/OPTIMIZE. Rebuilds will be deterministic and reproducible from source facts. This approach becomes the standard pattern for dashboard performance and metric consistency.

We will migrate the existing AngularJS 1.x application to modern Angular (latest LTS) using an incremental, hybrid approach. A single repository (Nx workspace) will host both codebases. We will bootstrap a hybrid app with @angular/upgrade, enabling Angular and AngularJS to co-exist while we progressively replace AngularJS components, services, and routes.

Key decisions:
- All new features will be built in Angular; AngularJS receives only critical fixes.
- Use Angular Standalone APIs (no NgModules), Angular Router, Signals for local state, and RxJS for async streams; adopt Angular Material/CDK and our design system.
- Enable TypeScript strict mode, ESLint, Prettier, Jest for unit tests, and Cypress for E2E; enforce CI checks (build, test, lint, type).
- Create compatibility adapters: upgrade/downgrade selected services/components to minimize duplicate logic during the transition; maintain shared domain models and APIs.
- Strangler pattern by route and feature: migrate leaf routes first, then shared services, then core shells; remove downgraded bridges as features are ported.
- Stabilize contracts at integration boundaries (HTTP API, analytics, auth) to avoid backend churn.
- Maintain performance parity via Webpack/CLI budgets and source-map-based error monitoring.
- Establish deprecation milestones with a migration backlog and telemetry to track AngularJS usage; remove AngularJS runtime and ngUpgrade once the last dependency is ported.

This approach minimizes risk and downtime, enables continuous delivery during the migration, and positions us on a supported Angular platform with modern tooling and best practices.

We will adopt Ruby on Rails (Rails 7.x on Ruby 3.x) as the primary application framework for the product’s core backend and server-rendered web interface. Rails will be used to implement domain logic, REST/JSON APIs, authentication/authorization, background processing, and admin tooling. We will leverage Rails’ batteries-included stack (Active Record, Active Job, Active Storage, Action Mailer) with PostgreSQL as the primary datastore, Redis for caching and job queues, and Sidekiq for background jobs. For the web UX layer, we will preferentially use Rails’ Hotwire (Turbo + Stimulus) for fast, maintainable interactivity without introducing a SPA framework unless clearly justified.

This decision optimizes for delivery speed, maintainability, and team familiarity, aligns with our monolith-first approach, and leverages the mature Rails ecosystem (gems, conventions, community). It also provides clear paths for security, observability, and scaling (e.g., Puma, horizontal scaling, read replicas, CDN). Future services or serverless components may be integrated where they add clear value, but the default is a cohesive Rails application to minimize complexity and operational overhead.

Adopt GOV.UK Verify as the primary mechanism for claimant identity assurance. Integrate as a Relying Party via SAML 2.0 with the Verify Hub, requesting the minimum attributes necessary to assess eligibility (verified name, date of birth, current address, and persistent identifier). Require Level of Assurance 2 and record verification outcome, timestamp, and persistent identifier; do not persist raw identity attributes beyond the session unless explicitly required and justified.

Implement a structured failure and fallback journey: if a claimant cannot complete Verify or no matching identity providers are available, route to assisted or alternative identity verification (manual/KBA/face-to-face) without blocking the claim. Provide clear consent and privacy notices prior to redirection, and bind the SAML transaction to the claimant session to mitigate replay and mix-up attacks.

Operate separate configurations and signing/encryption keys per environment, consuming hub metadata via automated refresh. Monitor assertion validation, clock skew, and certificate rotation. Log audit events for request/response correlation IDs and verification outcomes only, excluding sensitive attributes.

Build the journey to be resilient and non-capturing: treat Verify as a pluggable identity assurance provider to allow future substitution. Implement health checks and circuit breakers to degrade gracefully if the hub or IdPs are unavailable. Validate performance at peak loads and maintain WCAG-compliant UX for the redirection and return flows.

## Decision

We will not echo command input by default. The terminal already renders interactive keystrokes; duplicating them increases noise and risks leaking sensitive data in logs and transcripts.

- Interactive TTY:
  - Do not echo user keystrokes or stdin back to stdout/stderr.
  - For secret prompts (passwords, tokens, private keys), disable terminal echo entirely and mask pasted content; support paste-guard confirmation for multi-line secrets.
  - Display only prompts, validation messages, and results.

- Non-TTY (piped/redirected input, batch mode):
  - Do not echo stdin.
  - Provide an explicit, opt-in --echo-input (or ECHO_INPUT=1) to mirror stdin to stdout for troubleshooting.
  - Add --tee-input=<file> to write an input transcript to a file; never enabled by default.

- Logging and diagnostics:
  - Never log raw stdin.
  - Redact values for known secret-bearing flags/env vars (e.g., --password, --token, *_SECRET, *_KEY) across all verbosity levels.
  - A --debug-io flag may log input source metadata (TTY/piped/file) but not content.
  - Structured audit events capture command name, version, options schema, and execution result only; no input payloads.

- REPL/shell modes:
  - Start with echo off; provide set echo on/off to toggle.
  - History excludes secret-bearing commands and masked inputs.

- Config precedence:
  - CLI flag overrides env, which overrides config file defaults.
  - In all modes, secret prompts ignore echo/enabled settings and remain non-echoing and redacted.

This policy minimizes accidental disclosure while allowing explicit, auditable mechanisms to capture input when required.

## Decision

Adopt a relational, normalized core data model with strict integrity constraints, augmented by controlled schema-less extensions for flexibility.

- Use a single primary RDBMS as the system of record. Model core entities in 3NF with explicit foreign keys and cascading rules.
- Primary keys: UUID v4 (16-byte) as surrogate keys for all tables; expose stable external IDs when required via dedicated columns or views.
- Concurrency: optimistic locking with a version column on all mutable aggregates.
- Standard columns on all tables: created_at, updated_at (UTC), created_by, updated_by; soft-delete via deleted_at where recovery is required.
- Extensibility: per-entity jsonb attributes column for non-critical, infrequently queried fields; critical/query-heavy fields must be promoted to typed columns via migrations.
- Relationships: many-to-many via explicit join tables; reference/lookup data normalized into dedicated tables with natural keys and unique constraints.
- Multi-tenancy: tenant_id on all multi-tenant tables with composite unique indexes to enforce isolation; row-level security where supported.
- Auditing: append-only change log (audit_events) capturing before/after snapshots and actor context for regulated entities; immutable event IDs with ordered timestamps.
- Naming and conventions: snake_case table/column names; singular table names for aggregates; consistent foreign key naming fk_<child>__<parent>; not-null by default; check constraints for domain rules.
- Indexing: primary, foreign key, and selective functional indexes; partial indexes for soft-deleted data patterns.
- Migrations: forward-only, idempotent, and reversible where feasible; seed scripts for reference data with deterministic keys.
- Data privacy: column-level encryption for sensitive fields; PII tagged and isolated; data retention policies enforced via scheduled jobs.

This model provides strong consistency, evolvability, and operational clarity while supporting product-level agility through controlled schema-less extensions.

We will make CMake the single source of truth for project versioning.

- Define the canonical base version in the top-level CMakeLists.txt using project(MyProj VERSION X.Y.Z).
- If the source tree is a Git checkout, attempt to refine the version at configure time using git describe --tags --dirty --always. When a tag vX.Y.Z is checked out exactly, the version is X.Y.Z. Otherwise, append prerelease/build metadata (e.g., X.Y.Z-rc1+g<sha>, or X.Y.Z+g<sha>-dirty).
- Expose the computed version via cached variables (PROJECT_VERSION, PROJECT_GIT_TAG, PROJECT_GIT_SHA, PROJECT_DIRTY) and generate a version header with configure_file that provides:
  - MYPROJ_VERSION_STRING (full string),
  - MYPROJ_VERSION_MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH,
  - MYPROJ_GIT_SHA and MYPROJ_GIT_DIRTY.
- Embed the version into binaries/libraries (e.g., --version output) and metadata:
  - set_target_properties for SOVERSION = PROJECT_VERSION_MAJOR and VERSION = PROJECT_VERSION,
  - CPack: set CPACK_PACKAGE_VERSION* from PROJECT_VERSION,
  - pkg-config: generate .pc with Version: PROJECT_VERSION,
  - Python/wheels or other bindings derive their version from PROJECT_VERSION.
- Provide a fallback for non-Git source (e.g., release tarballs): use the project() VERSION or an override -DPROJECT_VERSION_OVERRIDE=... without Git metadata.
- CI policy: release builds are produced only from annotated tags vX.Y.Z; CI asserts no -dirty state and publishes artifacts with exact X.Y.Z. Non-tag builds produce prerelease versions.
- Write VERSION.txt at configure time for human reference and to aid downstream packaging.

- Adopt a single-tenant, application-owned relational database for the service to ensure strong consistency, transactional integrity, and clear ownership of schema and data.
- Use PostgreSQL as the primary database engine for its mature feature set, robust indexing, JSON support for semi-structured data, and broad ecosystem/tooling.
- Provision one database instance per environment (dev, test, staging, prod); no cross-application shared schemas. Each environment has isolated credentials and network boundaries.
- Manage schema changes via versioned, repeatable migrations in code (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase) executed as part of CI/CD. Migrations are immutable; rollbacks are handled by forward fixes.
- Enforce least-privilege access with distinct DB roles: app runtime (read/write limited to app schema), migration role (DDL), and read-only role (reporting). No superuser in app runtime.
- Use a dedicated application schema (e.g., app) with UTF-8 encoding and UTC as the canonical timezone. Standardize naming and explicit column defaults; avoid implicit type casts.
- Require connection pooling at the application layer (e.g., HikariCP) with sensible limits per environment; tune statement timeouts and lock timeouts to protect availability.
- Implement automated backups and point-in-time recovery per provider capabilities; verify restores periodically in non-prod. Enable monitoring/alerting on latency, locks, bloat, disk, and replication.
- Support read scalability via optional read replicas for reporting and background jobs; all writes go to the primary. No multi-master writes.
- Store secrets in the platform’s secret manager; rotate credentials regularly. Disallow ad-hoc manual schema changes in production.

We will prioritize integration tests to validate end-to-end behavior across bounded contexts and system boundaries, and use command-level (unit) tests selectively for complex, high-branching domain logic.

- Integration tests will cover critical user journeys, public APIs/HTTP endpoints, CLI entry points, database interactions, and contracts with external services (via test containers or contract tests). They must assert observable outcomes and invariants, not internal implementation.

- Command/unit tests will focus on pure domain and command handlers with non-trivial logic, edge cases, and domain invariants. They will stub external dependencies to keep them fast and deterministic. Trivial pass-through code and simple mappings will not be unit-tested if already exercised by integration tests.

- Coverage targets:
  - Overall: ≥80% line coverage.
  - At least 60% of covered lines should come from integration tests to ensure behavior-centric coverage.
  - Modules containing core domain/command logic should maintain ≥70% line and ≥60% branch coverage via unit tests.
  - No per-file hard gates; focus gates on critical modules and risk-based areas.

- Execution policy:
  - On each PR: run all unit/command tests and a smoke subset of integration tests in CI.
  - On merge/main and nightly: run the full integration suite across supported environments.
  - Flaky tests are quarantined with an issue opened within 24h and must be fixed or removed before the next release.

- Duplicative tests are discouraged: when integration tests sufficiently cover behavior, avoid redundant unit tests. New features must include at least one integration test proving the primary user/system outcome.

- Test data will favor realistic fixtures and seeded databases for integration tests; unit tests will use minimal builders/factories.

This balances confidence in real-world behavior with fast feedback on domain correctness while keeping maintenance overhead manageable.

## Decision

We will execute end-to-end (E2E) tests against ephemeral Kubernetes clusters provisioned per CI run using Kind. Tests will be authored primarily with KUTTL for declarative, resource-centric validation, complemented by targeted Ginkgo/Gomega tests (using client-go) for imperative and timing-sensitive scenarios.

Key elements:
- Cluster lifecycle: Create a fresh Kind cluster per job (optionally per test shard), pre-load container images to speed up runs, and destroy clusters after completion.
- Deployment: Install system dependencies (e.g., ingress, CSI, CRDs), then deploy the application via Helm/Kustomize. Use kubectl wait/health checks for readiness.
- Test structure: Organize tests into KUTTL suites (smoke, functional, upgrade/rollback). Use namespaces for isolation and enable parallel execution by sharding suites across CI workers.
- Data and fixtures: Seed test data via manifests or Jobs. Mock external dependencies using test doubles (e.g., WireMock) or in-cluster services when feasible.
- Assertions: Prefer KUTTL assertions on resources, events, and status conditions; employ Ginkgo tests for workflows requiring client-go interactions, race-prone operations, or protocol-level checks.
- Resilience checks: Include upgrade, rollback, and zero-downtime deployment scenarios; validate probes, pod disruption budgets, and failure recovery.
- Observability: During tests, scrape metrics if needed and capture logs/events. On failure, always collect kubectl get/describe for all resources, pod logs, events, and Kind cluster diagnostics as CI artifacts.
- Performance gates: Run a lightweight smoke suite on every PR; execute the full matrix (including upgrade and chaos scenarios) on main and nightly.
- Determinism: Disable auto-scaling for deterministic tests unless explicitly validated; pin image tags and chart versions; freeze external dependencies via local registry/mocks.
- Runtime and cost: Parallelize suites and reuse pre-built test images; cap cluster size to the minimal node count required for HA scenarios.
- Local dev parity: Provide a make target/devcontainer to run the same Kind/KUTTL/Ginkgo suites locally.

This approach provides fast, reproducible, and observable E2E coverage with minimal infrastructure overhead, while remaining extensible for complex workflows.

We will provide an optional, opinionated Wikibase Bundle alongside the core Wikibase extension to simplify installation and ensure predictable deployments.

- The core Wikibase extension remains minimal and independently releasable.
- The Wikibase Bundle is a meta-package that declares and pins a curated set of companion extensions, services, and default configuration required for a typical Wikibase installation (e.g., Query Service components, recommended integrations).
- The bundle will be versioned in lockstep with Wikibase and the corresponding MediaWiki release branch (REL1_xx), with a machine-readable manifest that pins exact versions of bundled components.
- Installation of the bundle will be a single, documented step (e.g., one entry point that loads all included components and applies safe defaults), while still allowing local overrides.
- Bundled components must meet documented inclusion criteria (maintenance status, security posture, compatibility, and test coverage) and follow a deprecation policy; changes to the bundle composition are treated as notable release changes.
- Release pipelines produce both artifacts: a minimal core package and the bundle, with CI validating cross-component compatibility using the pinned manifest.
- Consumers can opt out of the bundle and assemble bespoke stacks, but the bundle is the recommended path for new deployments and reproducible environments (including container images).

1. Use micro-batch loading as the default approach for large datasets, avoiding per-row writes; leverage native bulk mechanisms (e.g., PostgreSQL COPY, Redshift COPY, BigQuery LOAD/INSERT, Snowflake COPY).
2. Land data in object storage (e.g., S3/GCS) as CSV or Parquet with schema/version metadata and checksums; enforce immutable, timestamped paths for traceability.
3. Load via staging tables/partitions, then perform set-based upserts/merges into target tables to isolate validation and enable atomic swaps.
4. Ensure idempotency using natural or surrogate deduplication keys and checkpointed watermarks; design loads to be safe to re-run.
5. Bound parallelism and batch size by environment-specific limits; default chunk sizes and worker counts are configurable and auto-tuned from historical throughput.
6. Validate and reconcile every batch (row counts, hash totals, key uniqueness, referential integrity); quarantine bad records to a dead-letter area with reason codes.
7. Support schema evolution via versioned contracts and backward-compatible changes; reject incompatible payloads automatically.
8. Orchestrate with a workflow engine (e.g., Airflow) providing retries with exponential backoff, circuit breaking, and alerting; all steps are observable with metrics and structured logs.
9. Schedule heavy loads during off-peak windows; enforce backpressure to protect downstream systems and respect SLAs.
10. Prefer partitioned/incremental loads; for reprocess/backfill, use partition-scoped jobs and data snapshots to allow fast rollback.

We will not use before_action filters to set controller instance variables for use by actions or views. Instead, each action must explicitly obtain its required data (via private helper methods or service objects) and assign only the variables it needs. Cross-cutting concerns in before_action are limited to authentication, authorization, and idempotent request-wide concerns (e.g., locale/timezone), not data loading.

Where repeated resource loading is unavoidable (e.g., finding a record by ID), we will provide a private memoized method (e.g., resource or current_account) that actions call explicitly. Views and partials should access data passed from actions or via presenter/view component props, not rely on controller instance variables implicitly set by filters.

We forbid ordering-dependent filters and magic variables (e.g., @user set in one filter for use in another). Shared preconditions must be expressed as reusable methods or services invoked from actions. Exceptions: Rails/Devise conventions like authenticate_user! are allowed; any data-setting before_action must be justified, side-effect free, and controller-local with explicit naming.

This decision improves readability, testability, and traceability of controller behavior by making dependencies explicit and reduces hidden coupling between filters, actions, and views.

## Decision

Adopt a dedicated, cross-platform Key Pair Utility (KPU) as a small CLI and library to standardize asymmetric key management across services.

- Algorithms:
  - Ed25519 for digital signatures (default).
  - X25519 for key agreement/ECIES-style encryption.
  - RSA-2048/3072 only for legacy interoperability (optional flag).
- Key material:
  - Private keys stored as encrypted PKCS#8; public keys as RFC 8410 (for *25519) or SubjectPublicKeyInfo.
  - On-disk encryption with passphrase using Argon2id (memory-hard KDF) and AES-256-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305.
  - OS CSPRNG for entropy; supports hardware-backed generation when available.
- Integrations:
  - Pluggable backends: filesystem (default), cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault), and HSM via PKCS#11.
  - Support for envelope encryption when using remote KMS.
- Features:
  - Subcommands: generate, list, show, sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt, rotate, revoke, import, export, fingerprint.
  - Deterministic serialization, stable fingerprints (SHA-256 over public key bytes with prefix).
  - Key metadata: algorithm, creation time, expiry, usage (sign/encrypt), key ID, version.
  - Rotation policy support with enforced expiry and grace windows.
  - Non-exportable keys when backed by KMS/HSM.
  - Audit logging of operations (without exposing key material).
- Implementation:
  - Written in Go using crypto/ed25519, x/crypto/curve25519, and x/crypto/argon2; optional OpenSSL engine for RSA compat.
  - Secure defaults, FIPS-compatible mode where required.
- Developer UX:
  - JSON and text output, zero-config secure defaults, environment and config file support.
  - Backward-compatible versioning for key files and metadata.

Adopt a canonical, hierarchical location_path for Easyvista locations and enforce it across UI, API, and data stores:
- Format: forward-slash-delimited segments (e.g., company/region/site/building/floor/room); lowercase, ASCII, URL-safe; no leading/trailing slashes; single slash as separator; no empty segments.
- Authority: segments must be selected from the Location registry (no free text). Each node has a stable UUID; location_path is a derived, immutable string for that node’s current position in the hierarchy.
- Storage: persist both the node UUID (primary key) and its computed location_path string; additionally store the ancestry array (list of ancestor UUIDs) to enable efficient hierarchical queries and indexing. Path is indexed for prefix lookups.
- Validation: reject duplicates, illegal characters, and cycles; enforce max depth and segment length; normalize whitespace and case at ingress.
- Mutations: create/move operations occur only via the Location service. Moves update location_path for the moved node and all descendants in a single transactional operation, preserving node UUIDs and audit trails.
- Backward compatibility: accept legacy paths with mixed case or different separators; normalize on write and expose canonical form on read. Provide one-time migration tooling to transform existing records and rebuild ancestry/indexes.
- API: expose both location_uuid and location_path; provide endpoints/utilities to resolve path→UUID and UUID→path, list children/ancestors, and validate a candidate path before commit. Clients must not construct paths manually.
- Observability: emit audit events on create/move/delete with before/after paths; add metrics on path resolution latency and move breadth.
- Security/authorization: path reads are open per existing ACLs; create/move/delete require elevated permissions validated at the target node and all affected descendants.

This standardization ensures consistent addressing, efficient querying, safe refactoring of the hierarchy, and predictable integration with external systems.

We will standardize user authentication and basic authorization on GitHub OAuth 2.0 using a GitHub OAuth App and the Authorization Code with PKCE flow. Access will be restricted to members of our GitHub organization; org/team membership will be the source of truth for roles, mapped to application roles at login. We will request minimal scopes (user:email, read:org) and avoid write or repo scopes. Tokens will be short‑lived; we will not persist access tokens client‑side. Session management will be server‑side with secure, httpOnly cookies. CSRF protection (state), exact redirect URI whitelisting, and PKCE will be enforced.

For service-to-service GitHub API access and automation, we will use a GitHub App with installation tokens, separate from the user OAuth App. Deprovisioning will be near-real-time via GitHub organization webhooks (membership/teams) to invalidate sessions and update role mappings. Multi-tenant apps will isolate role claims per tenant via GitHub teams naming conventions and an authorization policy layer.

All user-facing components will integrate with a shared Auth service that encapsulates the OAuth dance, team-to-role mapping, and token lifecycle. Where supported, downstream services will trust signed ID/session tokens from this service and perform authorization locally; otherwise they will call back to the Auth service for introspection. Audit logging will capture login, consent, role resolution, and session events.

We will standardize on Amazon SQS as the durable, decoupled work queue for all asynchronous task dispatch and Apache Airflow as the centralized workflow orchestrator and scheduler. Airflow DAGs will own task orchestration, dependencies, SLAs, and retries, while SQS provides scalable buffering, backpressure, and dead-letter handling per task type (with FIFO queues used where strict ordering and exactly-once semantics are required).

Airflow workers will pull or be triggered to consume messages from SQS and execute work via appropriate operators (e.g., ECS/Fargate, KubernetesPod, EMR, Lambda) based on task profile. Retries, exponential backoff, and idempotency will be enforced through Airflow task policies and SQS visibility timeouts, with DLQs for poison messages. All queues will be encrypted (SSE), access will be controlled via IAM with least privilege, and networking will remain private.

We will run Airflow as a managed service (MWAA) where feasible; otherwise, we will host it on ECS/Fargate with autoscaling workers. Observability will use Airflow’s metadata database, task logs in CloudWatch (or S3), metrics/alerts via CloudWatch and PagerDuty, and structured message schemas for traceability. This decision establishes SQS as the ingestion and buffering layer and Airflow as the authoritative execution plane for batch, event-driven, and pipeline workloads.

We will standardize on a primary testing framework per language/runtime to ensure consistency, readability, and ecosystem alignment:

- Python: pytest with pytest-mock (unittest.mock fallback) and Hypothesis for property-based tests.
- JVM (Java/Kotlin): JUnit 5 with Mockito (MockK for Kotlin-specific mocks) and AssertJ for fluent assertions; jqwik for property-based tests.
- JavaScript/TypeScript (Node/browser): Jest with Testing Library (React/Vue/etc.) and MSW for HTTP mocking; fast-check for property-based tests.
- .NET: xUnit with Moq and FluentAssertions.
- Go: built-in testing package with Testify for assertions/mocks.

Guidelines:
- Prefer Given-When-Then structure and descriptive test names for readability.
- Use test doubles via the chosen mocking libraries; avoid global state or network/file system unless explicitly part of the test.
- Enable parallel test execution by default; ensure tests are deterministic and seed any randomness.
- Enforce minimal coverage thresholds (e.g., 80% line/branch) via CI, while prioritizing meaningful tests over coverage gaming.
- Adopt the test pyramid: unit first, then component/contract (e.g., Pact where applicable), with a lean layer of end-to-end tests (e.g., Playwright/Cypress for web).
- Limit BDD/spec frameworks (e.g., Cucumber) to cross-team, business-facing acceptance criteria to avoid overhead in unit tests.
- Snapshot testing is allowed for stable, structured outputs only; avoid for volatile content.

This selection leverages community standards, strong tooling, and fast feedback loops, while keeping flexibility across our polyglot stack.

We will implement the read side using a two-layer architecture optimized for simplicity and performance:

- API/Query layer: Exposes query endpoints and query handlers. Contains input validation, authorization checks, response shaping, pagination/sorting, and caching policies. Query handlers depend only on read abstractions and return DTOs/view models (no domain entities).
- Infrastructure (Read Model) layer: Implements read repositories/gateways using the most efficient access patterns (e.g., raw SQL, database views/materialized views, projections, specialized indexes, search engines). It may use read replicas or denormalized stores and can bypass the ORM where beneficial.

There will be no Domain layer or Application Service layer for reads. The API/Query layer owns orchestration and projection logic, delegating data access to Infrastructure via interfaces. Cross-cutting concerns such as telemetry, caching, and retries are applied at the API boundary and/or infrastructure as appropriate.

Guidelines:
- Favor direct projections to DTOs in queries; avoid mapping to domain models.
- Permit technology-specific optimizations in Infrastructure (e.g., SQL tuning, CQRS read models).
- Support resilience (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers) and caching for hot queries.
- Keep query handlers side-effect free.
- Version read DTOs independently if needed to optimize client payloads.

This approach reduces latency and complexity on the read path while preserving testability through interface-driven design.

Use the HMPPS Elite2 API as the sole integration point for retrieving NOMIS data. Consume its versioned REST endpoints over HTTPS using the standard HMPPS OAuth2/OpenID Connect flow, scoped to least-privilege roles, and rely on Elite2’s domain abstractions, validation, and auditing rather than accessing NOMIS databases or bespoke feeds directly. Implement a dedicated client with resilience patterns (circuit breaker, retries with exponential backoff, and timeouts), support for pagination and filtering, and structured logging with correlation IDs for traceability. Cache read-heavy, slow-changing reference data with short TTLs to reduce load and latency while respecting data freshness and caching directives. Prefer server-side sorting/filters exposed by Elite2 to minimize payloads; where bulk queries are required, batch requests within documented limits. Track API schema via contract tests against the sandbox and pin to a specific API version; monitor usage, rate limits, and error budgets via central observability. All PII handling follows HMPPS security controls, with data minimization enforced in the client and redaction at log boundaries. This approach aligns with platform guidance, reduces coupling to NOMIS internals, and allows future migration to successor HMPPS APIs with minimal change behind the client interface.

We will require aggregates and processes to be stateless handlers. All durable state lives in the event stream (or process inbox/outbox) and is rehydrated by the engine into a scope passed to the handler on each invocation. Handlers must be pure with respect to their inputs: given the current scope and an incoming message, they may derive decisions and emit new events/commands via the scope, but they must not retain or mutate any internal state across invocations.

Concretely:
- Aggregate and process handlers will not hold instance fields that influence behavior across messages; any such needs must be expressed as events and read back via the scope.
- Any per-call ephemeral variables are allowed but must not escape the invocation.
- The public API will expose read-only accessors on scopes for all required decision data and will discourage or prevent mutable handler state (e.g., by construction-time injection only of stateless collaborators).
- Caching or memoization inside handlers is prohibited; cross-invocation caching belongs to dedicated, external, stateless services with explicit lifecycles.
- Engine implementations are responsible for reconstructing the current state snapshot from persisted facts and providing it to handlers; handlers never perform their own I/O or persistence.

This ensures determinism, simplifies concurrency and scaling, enables safe parallelism and hot-reload, and makes behavior auditable and reproducible from the log.

## Decision

Adopt a single, shared NGINX Ingress Controller per Kubernetes cluster, operated as one controller Deployment with multiple replicas behind a single AWS NLB. This controller will be the only supported ingress path for workloads in the cluster.

Operational parameters:
- Default ingressClass: “nginx”; admission policy enforces use of this class and blocks creation of additional ingress controllers.
- ModSecurity/WAF is disabled in-cluster; application-layer protection is provided at the edge (e.g., AWS WAF/CloudFront/ALB WAF) where required.
- Controller replicas autoscaled via HPA on CPU/memory and request rate; pod disruption budget ensures at least N-1 availability during maintenance.
- Resource requests/limits sized to handle peak reloads; tune NGINX settings (worker processes/connections, keepalive, large client header buffers) for high rule counts.
- Sharded config disabled; single config to avoid uneven capacity. Template/config reloads bounded with retry/backoff to prevent thrash.
- Centralized TLS management (wildcard and per-host certs) via cert-manager; HTTP→HTTPS enforced at ingress.
- Observability: SLOs on p50/p95 latency and 5xx error rate; dashboards and alerts on config reload failures, memory, connection saturation, and NLB target health.
- Guardrails: policy blocks modsecurity annotations and external load balancer creation; quotas on number of Ingress/Hosts per namespace to control config size growth.
- Migration: all existing ingresses standardized to class “nginx”; legacy dedicated/shared controllers are decommissioned.

Contingency:
- If capacity or AWS limits are approached, scale replicas and node groups first; only if necessary, introduce a second shared controller as a controlled exception with clear sharding criteria and admission enforcement.

We will split the current monolithic Graphviz DOT diagram into multiple, focused DOT files to lower contribution friction and improve maintainability.

- Scope: one DOT file per bounded context/component/layer (e.g., domain, app, infra), plus optional scenario/flow diagrams. Keep each file under ~200 nodes/edges and focused on a single concern.
- Structure: docs/diagrams/
  - 00-theme/common.inc.dot (shared styles, colors, node/edge defaults)
  - 10-domain/*.dot
  - 20-application/*.dot
  - 30-infrastructure/*.dot
  - 90-views/overview.dot (high-level curated view)
- Conventions:
  - File naming: <order>-<area>-<name>.dot (e.g., 10-domain-orders.dot)
  - Stable IDs: use globally stable node IDs (area_component_name) and human-friendly labels to enable cross-diagram recognition.
  - Styles: all diagrams must include common.inc.dot for consistent theming.
  - Legends: each diagram contains a small legend/subgraph for symbols used.
- Composition:
  - No hard cross-file edges; cross-boundary relations are depicted in dedicated “integration” view files to avoid hidden coupling.
  - A lightweight preprocessor (cpp or m4) includes common.inc.dot; Makefile handles preprocessing and rendering.
- Tooling:
  - Provide make render to generate SVG/PNG for all diagrams under docs/diagrams/dist/.
  - Provide make check to validate Graphviz syntax (dot -Tsvg), fail on warnings, and ensure diagrams are up-to-date (git diff on generated artifacts).
  - Pre-commit hook and CI job run the same checks.
- Documentation:
  - Each diagram has a header comment explaining its purpose, scope, and last reviewer.
  - README with a diagram index links to rendered outputs and explains contribution steps.

This decision enables incremental, parallel contributions, consistent visuals, and predictable builds while keeping complexity manageable.

We will document all significant architectural decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) stored alongside the code in version control. Each ADR will capture context, options considered, the decision with rationale, and consequences. ADRs will follow a lightweight template, be numbered sequentially, and track status (proposed, accepted, rejected, superseded, deprecated).

Process:
- Any contributor may propose an ADR for changes with cross-cutting impact (APIs, data models, runtime topology, security posture, technology choices).
- Discussion occurs asynchronously via pull requests/issues; feedback is incorporated into the ADR prior to acceptance.
- Decisions are made by lazy consensus of maintainers; if unresolved after a defined window, the lead architect adjudicates.
- Only accepted ADRs authorize implementation on the main branch. Rejected ADRs remain for historical context.
- Revisions are captured by superseding ADRs; original records are immutable except for status updates and cross-references.
- ADRs will be linked from code (e.g., README, module docs) where relevant to aid discoverability and onboarding.

Tooling:
- Store ADRs as plain text/Markdown in docs/adr/.
- Provide templates and linting/checks in CI to ensure completeness and status consistency.
- Publish an index and changelog to surface current decisions.

This approach institutionalizes transparent, durable, and reviewable architectural governance while minimizing process overhead.
