Decision

- Default to the Data Access Layer (DAL) for all application data access. The DAL remains the single abstraction boundary, enforcing consistency, security, and portability.
- Permit plain SQL in narrowly defined cases where it materially improves correctness or performance and the DAL cannot reasonably express the operation:
  - Complex, set-based queries (window functions, CTEs, lateral joins) not supported or inefficient via the DAL
  - Bulk operations (batch inserts/updates/deletes), ETL, and backfills
  - Vendor-specific features required for performance or capability (e.g., hints, index usage, JSON/TS vector ops)
  - Aggregation-heavy analytics/reporting read paths
  - Database migrations and maintenance tasks
- Guardrails for plain SQL:
  - Must live behind DAL interfaces/repositories; no ad-hoc SQL in controllers/services.
  - Parameterized queries only; no string concatenation.
  - Include tests (unit + integration) validating correctness and query plans where relevant.
  - Add query documentation: rationale, expected row counts, indexes relied upon, and rollback strategy.
  - Security review for injection, tenant isolation, and PII handling.
  - Performance review for production-sized datasets (EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE captured).
  - Return typed DTOs; no leaking driver-specific types across layers.
  - Prefer read-only unless write is justified; wrap writes in transactions with idempotency where applicable.
- Process:
  - Use DAL first; if insufficient, open a technical note proposing either (a) DAL extension or (b) plain SQL with guardrails.
  - Revisit plain SQL usages quarterly; migrate to DAL if/when support becomes adequate.
- Prohibitions:
  - No plain SQL in feature code without review/approval.
  - No business logic in SQL; keep logic in application code.

We will model Elasticsearch documents as denormalized, immutable snapshots per domain entity, optimized for search and aggregations.

- Indices: one index per entity type with ILM-managed, time-partitioned indices via write aliases (e.g., pr-000001, review-000001). Read via stable aliases (prs, reviews). Templates define mappings/settings.
- Identity: deterministic, externally meaningful IDs.
  - PR: {provider}:{org}/{repo}:pr:{number}
  - Review: {provider}:{org}/{repo}:pr:{number}:review:{id}
- Versioning: upsert with optimistic concurrency control (if_seq_no/if_primary_term). Keep updated_at for last source change and ingested_at for pipeline time; no partial updates across entities.
- Structure:
  - Flat fields with consistent naming; arrays of objects use nested type when cross-field queries are required.
  - Avoid parent-child/join; prefer embedding small related snapshots (author, repo, labels, requested_reviewers).
  - Strings as multi-fields: field.text (text with language-appropriate analyzer) and field.keyword (keyword, normalizer=lowercase).
  - Dates as date; numbers as appropriate numeric types; booleans for flags.
  - Common fields: provider, org, repo, repo_id, pr_number, pr_state, is_merged, author.{id,login}, created_at, updated_at, closed_at, merged_at, labels (nested name,color), files.changed (count), metrics.* (aggregations).
  - Reviews link back via pr_id (keyword) and include reviewer snapshot and state.
- Enrichment: ingest pipelines add normalized fields (lowercased org/repo, triage labels, computed metrics), and sanitize text.
- Deletion: soft delete with is_deleted=true; hard deletes only via retention jobs.
- Query/Routing: custom routing on repo_id to co-locate related docs; avoid deep pagination (use search_after).
- Constraints: target document size < 50KB; cap array lengths where feasible to control heap and query cost.

Decision

Adopt a schema-first, deterministic, and centrally managed code generation process.

- Source of truth: Interface contracts and data models are defined in versioned schemas (OpenAPI/AsyncAPI/Protobuf/GraphQL SDL) stored under /schemas with semantic versioning.
- Tooling: 
  - REST: openapi-generator (typescript-fetch/axios).
  - gRPC: buf + protoc (ts via ts-proto).
  - GraphQL: graphql-code-generator (typescript operations + typed hooks).
  - DB: Prisma (schema.prisma) with generated client.
- Configuration: All generator configs live in /codegen with pinned versions (lockfiles) and hermetic execution via containerized runners (Docker) or toolchain binaries checked via asdf/nvm/pnpm. No network templates at runtime.
- Determinism: Generators run with fixed versions, stable sorting, and reproducible timestamps. All outputs include a DO NOT EDIT header and embed the generator/version.
- Invocation: Single entrypoint task (e.g., pnpm codegen) used locally and in CI. CI enforces cleanliness (fails if git diff after codegen). Codegen runs on schema changes and before release.
- Storage policy: 
  - Libraries/services: Do not commit generated code (build/CI generates).
  - Public SDKs and DB migrations: Commit generated artifacts for consumer convenience and traceability.
- Customization: Prefer configuration and mustache/handlebars templates checked into /codegen/templates over forking generators. Any deviation requires ADR approval.
- Quality gates: Generated outputs must pass ESLint/Prettier/TypeScript checks and unit smoke tests.
- Backward compatibility: Schema changes follow semver with breaking changes gated by review; generators are upgraded via controlled PRs with regeneration and diff review.

## Decision

We will adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document significant technical and architectural decisions.

- Scope: An ADR is required for decisions that affect system boundaries, public APIs/contracts, data models/migrations, cross-cutting concerns (security, observability, performance), critical dependencies, deployment/infra, compliance, SLAs/cost, or team-wide conventions.
- Format: Use a lightweight ADR template (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Alternatives, Consequences, References). Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Superseded (with links).
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository at docs/adr/ as sequentially numbered files (e.g., 0001-title.md). Maintain docs/adr/index.md for traceability.
- Process: The proposer authors the ADR and opens a PR. Reviewers from relevant domains approve. Decisions are merged before implementation; urgent decisions may be recorded retroactively but must be created before release.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (optional) to scaffold and index ADRs. Link ADRs to issue IDs and PRs; reference ADR IDs in code comments and commit messages when relevant.
- Governance: Changes to an ADR require a new ADR that supersedes the prior record; minor clarifications may be amended with editorial PRs.
- Applicability: Mandatory for new services and for major changes to existing services.

Adopt Go Modules as the standard dependency management solution for all Go code in this repository.

- Require Go 1.21+ and commit go.mod and go.sum to source control.
- Use minimal version selection and semantic import versioning; prefer tagged releases. Avoid replace directives except for temporary forks, and document any replaces in ADRs with a plan to remove them.
- Do not commit vendor/ by default. Use -mod=vendor only if a downstream environment mandates vendoring; otherwise rely on the module proxy and checksum db.
- Standard environment:
  - GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct
  - GOSUMDB=sum.golang.org
  - GOPRIVATE=<our private module hosts>
  - GONOSUMDB/GONOPROXY aligned with GOPRIVATE
- CI will enforce reproducibility and hygiene:
  - go mod tidy -compat=1.21 must be clean (no diff)
  - go build ./... and go test ./... must succeed with -mod=readonly
  - Disallow unexpected replaces via a linter/script
- Dependency updates are automated via Renovate/Dependabot on a scheduled cadence; security patches may be fast-tracked. All upgrades require CI to pass and release notes to be reviewed for breaking changes.
- Decommission legacy tools (dep, glide). Remove Gopkg.*/glide.* files and any GOPATH-specific build logic.
- Container builds will run go mod download to prime modules and use checksum verification by default.

This decision standardizes dependency management, improves reproducibility and supply-chain security, and aligns with the Go ecosystem’s current best practices.

## Decision

We will not use a linter (e.g., ESLint/TSLint/Stylelint) in this codebase at this time. Our code quality guardrails will be limited to:
- A formatter (Prettier) for consistent style
- The compiler/runtime/type-checking provided by the language and framework
- Unit/integration tests and code reviews enforced via CI

This avoids the operational overhead of configuring, maintaining, and unblocking lint rules across packages and environments, and reduces friction for contributors while we prioritize delivery speed. We will keep the codebase simple and avoid rule churn, custom plugins, and editor tooling drift.

We will revisit adopting a linter if one or more of the following occurs: rising defect trends attributable to avoidable patterns, onboarding friction that a standard rule set would alleviate, or scaling to multiple teams where consistency and automated guardrails outweigh setup cost. If revisited, we will evaluate a minimal rule set aligned with our formatter to minimize developer burden.

- Use arrays only for ordered collections; use objects/maps for keyed lookups and Sets for uniqueness constraints.
- Arrays must be homogeneous: each array contains a single well-defined item type; mixed-type arrays are disallowed.
- For fixed-size, position-semantic data, use tuples (typed fixed-length arrays) where supported; otherwise define explicit objects.
- Do not rely on array indices as stable identifiers; include item IDs and use them for references and UI keys.
- Treat arrays as immutable in application code: prefer create-new operations (map/filter/concat) over in-place mutation to enable predictable state and memoization.
- Establish maximum lengths per endpoint/field; for large collections use pagination or cursor-based streaming instead of returning unbounded arrays.
- Preserve order semantics end-to-end; if order is not meaningful, return sets or explicitly sort on the server and document the sort key.
- Avoid sparse arrays and undefined holes; represent absent items by omission or explicit nulls only when semantically required and documented.
- For APIs: JSON arrays are the canonical wire format; include total counts and paging cursors alongside array payloads in list responses.
- For storage: prefer normalized relations over embedded large arrays; when embedding, cap size and provide append-only patterns where needed.
- Validation: schema enforce item type, min/max length, and uniqueness when required; reject payloads with extraneous or mixed types.
- Versioning: additive changes append new fields to items; do not change item order semantics or repurpose array positions across versions.

We adopt the Ports and Adapters (Hexagonal) architecture to preserve a clean, technology-agnostic core and make infrastructure replaceable. The domain and application layers will define the business use cases and ports (interfaces). All I/O concerns will be implemented as adapters that depend on these ports.

- Inbound adapters (e.g., REST/gRPC controllers, message consumers, CLI) translate external requests into application services and DTOs. They know nothing about persistence or external systems.
- Application services orchestrate use cases, enforce transactional boundaries, and call domain logic and outbound ports. They expose interfaces that inbound adapters use.
- Domain model remains pure (no framework annotations), encapsulating business rules and entities/value objects. Domain events may be raised here.
- Outbound ports (repositories, external service gateways, message publishers, cache) are defined in the application layer; concrete adapters implement them against specific technologies (SQL/NoSQL, HTTP, Kafka, S3, etc.).
- Composition is done via dependency injection: adapters depend on ports; the core never depends on adapter types. Wiring occurs at the outermost layer.
- Data crossing boundaries uses explicit DTOs/mappers to prevent leakage of transport/persistence concerns into the domain.
- Transaction management lives at the application service boundary; idempotency and retries are handled in adapters or cross-cutting components.
- Testing prioritizes domain/app layers with fast, isolated tests; adapters are tested with integration tests behind the port contracts.

This decision standardizes service structure, enables independent evolution of interfaces and infrastructure, and supports future needs like CQRS and event-driven integrations without contaminating core logic.

## Decision

Provide a dedicated, stable Light Client CLI as a separate binary that exposes the core verification and supervision flows in a scriptable, non-interactive interface.

- Implement with Rust using clap for argument parsing and env_logger/tracing for logging.
- Subcommands:
  - init: bootstrap trust (trusted height/hash, primary RPC, witnesses, chain-id) and write a signed trust store.
  - verify: perform one-off verification to a target height/hash or latest, returning machine-readable JSON and non-zero exit on failure.
  - start: run the supervisor daemon with auto-updates and witness cross-checks; supports systemd-friendly foreground mode.
  - trust: update trust state from an out-of-band source (file, stdin) with optional quorum checks.
  - query: inspect current store (trusted header at height, latest, peers, parameters).
  - config: print or validate effective configuration and defaults.

- Configuration model:
  - Load from a TOML/YAML file, with overrides via environment variables (LIGHTCLIENT_*), and CLI flags taking highest precedence.
  - Explicit, versioned config schema with migration guardrails.

- Output and UX:
  - Default human-readable; --json for stable JSON suitable for automation.
  - Structured error types mapped to deterministic exit codes.
  - No interactive prompts; all inputs via flags/env/stdin.
  - Deterministic behavior in offline mode when given explicit trust and headers.

- State and safety:
  - Store trusted headers and peers in a dedicated data directory with file-locking.
  - Read-only verify mode that does not mutate state unless --commit is set.
  - Require chain-id and trust root; forbid implicit trust.

- Backward compatibility:
  - Deprecate ad-hoc tools; provide shims for legacy flags where feasible.

Adopt managed, versioned database services with explicit engine pinning and controlled upgrades.

- Use cloud-managed offerings that expose engine versions (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis) and pin exact major.minor (and patch where supported) in Infrastructure as Code. Disallow “latest”.
- Maintain identical engine versions across non-prod and prod; provision per-environment instances with the same configuration and extensions.
- Manage schema changes via automated migrations (e.g., Flyway/Liquibase) with backward-compatible, zero-downtime patterns; gate breaking changes behind feature flags and dual-read/write where needed.
- Establish a lifecycle policy: support N and N-1 engine majors, review quarterly against vendor EOL, and plan upgrades ahead of deprecation.
- Execute upgrades via rehearsed playbooks: validate in ephemeral and staging environments, run performance/regression suites, then perform blue/green or replica-based cutovers (e.g., logical replication/pglogical for Postgres; in-place minor with maintenance windows). Ensure fast rollback via snapshots and validated PITR.
- Specify and test extension versions (e.g., PostGIS) alongside engine versions; track a compatibility matrix for drivers, ORMs, extensions, and clients.
- Enforce observability and SLOs during upgrades: health checks, replication lag, error rates, and query plans; freeze schema changes during cutover windows.
- Automate backups, PITR, and encryption at rest/in transit by default; store runbooks and change records for auditability.
- Provide local/dev parity using containers with the pinned versions; block deployments if drift is detected between intended and actual engine versions.

We will define the WikibaseManifest format using OpenAPI 3.1 as the canonical specification. The manifest will be modeled as a Schema Object under components/schemas (root: components.schemas.WikibaseManifest), authored in YAML, and aligned with JSON Schema 2020-12 via OpenAPI 3.1’s native support. We will publish the spec in the repository (versioned with SemVer), generate a bundled JSON/YAML artifact for distribution, and provide example manifests for key variants. Validation will be supported via standard OpenAPI/JSON Schema tooling; CI will lint (Spectral), validate, and ensure backwards-compatibility (e.g., openapi-diff). We will generate derived artifacts as needed (pure JSON Schema, TypeScript types) from the OpenAPI source to keep a single source of truth. Documentation will be published via Redoc/Swagger UI for human readability. Changes to the format require PRs updating the OpenAPI spec, examples, and changelog, with explicit deprecation windows for breaking changes.

We will adopt Jenkins as the primary CI system and standardize on Jenkins Pipeline (declarative) with a Jenkinsfile stored in each repository. A shared Jenkins Library will centralize common steps (checkout, build, test, lint, security scans, packaging, publishing) to ensure consistency and reduce duplication.

Builds will run on ephemeral agents using containerized executors for reproducibility and isolation. Where available, autoscaling agents will be provisioned on demand; otherwise, Docker-based agents will be used on static nodes. Workspace and dependency caches will be leveraged to optimize build times while preserving isolation.

Integration with the VCS will use multibranch pipelines and webhooks to auto-discover branches and PRs, run PR validations, and publish status checks. Artifacts and reports (binaries, SBOMs, test results, coverage, and screenshots) will be archived and/or published to the designated artifact repository and storage.

Credentials and secrets will be managed via Jenkins Credentials with masking; no secrets in source control. Jenkins Configuration as Code (JCasC) will define controllers, folders, RBAC, credentials bindings, and jobs as code for reproducibility and review. Plugins will be minimized, pinned, and vetted; controller and agent images will be version-pinned and regularly updated.

Quality and security gates (SAST/DAST/Dependency scans), code style, and license checks will be enforced in pipelines. Notifications will be sent to Slack/Email. Logs, metrics, and job health will be monitored; backups and disaster recovery procedures will be in place with job/artifact retention policies.

This decision provides a scalable, reproducible, and auditable CI foundation aligned with our governance and delivery needs.

We will standardize on Yarn as the JavaScript/TypeScript package manager across the codebase. We will use Yarn Berry (v3+) managed via Corepack, pinning the Yarn version in the repository (packageManager field) to ensure deterministic and reproducible installs across developers and CI. We will enable Yarn Workspaces to manage multi-package repositories and shared dependencies efficiently. For broad tooling compatibility, we will default to nodeLinker: node-modules (opt-in to Plug’n’Play where explicitly validated). We will commit yarn.lock to source control, require yarn commands in all documentation and scripts, and block npm/pnpm usage via CI and preflight checks. One-off tooling will be executed with yarn dlx. Existing projects using npm package-lock.json will be migrated using yarn import to preserve dependency resolutions. CI will cache the Yarn global cache and leverage zero-installs only where appropriate and approved. This decision provides consistent developer experience, faster installs, and strong monorepo support while retaining compatibility with the wider Node ecosystem.

## Decision

We will include application source code and test suites inside Docker images using a multi-stage build:

- Use a .dockerignore to exclude non-essential files (e.g., .git, node_modules/venv, build artifacts).
- In the builder/test stage:
  - COPY dependency manifests first to leverage layer caching, install dependencies (including dev/test deps).
  - COPY source (src/) and tests (tests/) plus required configs.
  - Run linters and unit/integration tests inside this stage.
- In the final/production stage:
  - COPY only the built artifacts and runtime dependencies from the builder stage.
  - Do not include source maps (optional), tests, or dev dependencies, yielding a minimal image.

For local development:
- Default to bind-mounted volumes (docker-compose) for fast iteration/hot reload.
- Provide a fallback build target that COPYs source/tests when bind mounts are unavailable (e.g., CI, remote dev).

Additional practices:
- Set WORKDIR and non-root user; ensure correct file ownership/permissions after COPY.
- Structure COPY commands to minimize cache invalidation (copy manifests, then src/tests).
- Keep deterministic builds by pinning dependency versions.

This approach enables reproducible CI builds and in-container testing while keeping production images small and secure.

## Decision

We will use JSON Schema as the canonical source of truth for all structured data contracts, including API request/response bodies, domain models, event payloads, and configuration files.

- Standard: Adopt JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 to align with OpenAPI 3.1. If any component still uses earlier OpenAPI versions, we will transpile or constrain features accordingly, but canonical schemas remain Draft 2020-12.
- Organization: Store schemas in a dedicated /schemas directory with stable $id URIs, semantic versioning, and clear ownership. Publish schemas to an internal registry for discovery and reuse.
- Reuse and composition: Maximize reuse with $ref; prefer composition via allOf/oneOf/anyOf where appropriate. Define shared primitives (e.g., pagination, IDs, timestamps) as reusable components.
- Conventions: 
  - additionalProperties: false by default (explicitly opt-in when needed).
  - Use format, pattern, min/max constraints, and enums to make contracts precise and validate early.
  - Provide examples and defaults where meaningful; avoid ambiguous nullable semantics by using type unions.
- Integration: Reference JSON Schemas directly from OpenAPI 3.1 components.schemas to ensure a single contract drives docs, validation, and code generation. Apply the same schemas for eventing (e.g., AsyncAPI) and configuration validation.
- Tooling and enforcement: 
  - Validate all examples and OpenAPI documents against the canonical schemas in CI.
  - Generate server/client models and validators from schemas where possible.
  - Perform backward-compatibility checks (additive-only in minor versions; breaking changes require a major version).
- Versioning and deprecation: Version schemas semantically in their $id and repository tags. Maintain multiple active major versions when necessary and provide deprecation windows and migration notes.
- Documentation: Render human-friendly documentation from schemas (and OpenAPI) and publish alongside the service.

This decision ensures a single, precise, and reusable contract across services, languages, and runtimes, improving interoperability, validation, and developer experience.

We will use GitHub (GitHub.com organization) as the authoritative source control system for all application, infrastructure, and documentation repositories. All new code will be created under the organization with repository templates enforcing licenses, CODEOWNERS, default branch (main), and security policies. Collaboration will follow a pull-request workflow with required reviews, status checks, and protected branches (no force pushes, required linear history where applicable). Commit signing and branch protection will be enforced; admins are subject to the same policies.

Access will be managed via our SSO/IdP and GitHub Teams for least-privilege, auditable permissions. Default repository visibility is private; projects intended for open source will be public with an approved license and security disclosures. Secrets must not be committed; GitHub secret scanning, Dependabot, and security advisories will be enabled organization-wide.

Large or binary assets are prohibited from repositories unless using Git LFS with prior approval; build artifacts are published to artifact repositories, not GitHub source repos. CI/CD may use GitHub Actions where suitable; other systems will integrate via GitHub Apps with token scopes minimized.

Repositories will be backed up or mirrored per compliance requirements; release tags are immutable. Archived projects remain read-only. Any exceptions (e.g., regulated environments requiring internal mirrors) must be documented and approved. This decision applies to all new work; existing codebases will be migrated to GitHub on a planned schedule.

We will establish a canonical component catalog and decomposition method to identify, name, and manage architecture components across the system.

- Decomposition: Components are defined by business capability and cohesion of responsibilities, not by technology. A component encapsulates its domain logic and exposes well-defined interfaces (API, events, or modules). Cross-cutting concerns (authN/Z, observability, messaging, data platform) are modeled as platform components.

- Granularity: Components must be independently deployable (where applicable), own their data schema, and have stable interfaces. If two parts change together >80% of the time or share persistence models, they are one component; if they have distinct SLAs, scaling, or compliance boundaries, they are separate components.

- Boundaries: Each component owns its contracts, data, and policies. Synchronous calls are allowed only through public APIs; asynchronous integration uses events from a shared schema registry. Direct database access across components is prohibited.

- Documentation: Each component will have a living spec in docs/architecture/components/<component-name>.md including: purpose, responsibilities, interfaces, data ownership, dependencies, quality attributes, SLAs, risks, and runbooks. A C4 Model mapping (System/Container/Component) and sequence diagrams will be maintained.

- Ownership: Each component has an owning team, on-call rotation, and backlog. Ownership and lifecycle state (proposed, active, deprecated) are tracked in the catalog.

- Governance: Changes to components (create/merge/split/deprecate) require an ADR. Dependency rules are enforced via tooling (e.g., module boundaries, import checks, repo policies).

- Traceability: Components map to code repositories/packages, deployment units, and cost centers. Versioned interfaces follow semver with deprecation windows and migration guides.

- Review cadence: Quarterly component reviews validate boundaries, dependencies, and fitness functions (latency, error budgets, cost, reliability).

We will document all significant architectural decisions as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

- Format: Use the MADR 3.0 template (Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives) for clarity and consistency.
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository under docs/adr with sequential numbering (e.g., 0001-title.md) and human-friendly slugs.
- Scope: Record decisions that impact architecture, cross-cutting concerns, critical dependencies, data models, security, scalability, or cost. Minor implementation choices are excluded.
- Process: Create a draft ADR with Status “Proposed” alongside the PR introducing the change. Review and approval happen via the same PR. Merge with Status “Accepted” or “Rejected” and link to related PRs/issues.
- Evolution: Supersede prior ADRs rather than editing historical records. Use the “Supersedes”/“Superseded by” fields to maintain traceability.
- Ownership: The proposer authors the ADR; reviewers include at least one architect and one engineer from an affected domain.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (or compatible scripts) for creation and indexing; enforce presence via CI checks for qualifying PRs.
- Visibility: Summarize the ADR index in the project README and surface critical ADRs in onboarding materials.
- Cadence: Periodically (quarterly) review ADRs for relevance and capture any de facto decisions that were not recorded.

We will build the iOS and Android apps using React Native as a single shared codebase. We will default to the Expo managed workflow to accelerate delivery, OTA updates, and device testing; if we require unsupported native capabilities, we will eject to the bare workflow on a per-need basis. We will enable Hermes and adopt the New Architecture (Fabric/TurboModules) where stable to improve performance and memory usage.

We will write the app in TypeScript, use React Navigation for routing, and prefer cross‑platform React Native components; we will introduce platform-specific native modules only when measurable performance, hardware access, or UX parity require it, and encapsulate them behind typed JS interfaces to preserve portability. Critical performance paths will be benchmarked; if React Native cannot meet targets, we will implement those screens as native components integrated via TurboModules or as platform-specific views.

We will use OTA updates (Expo Updates, or CodePush if on bare) for safe, policy-compliant JS/UI changes, with app-store releases for native changes. CI/CD will build, test, and distribute both platforms from the shared repo.

Chosen option: Adopt the official Cloud Foundry Java Client (org.cloudfoundry:cloudfoundry-client-reactor) for programmatic CF interactions, complemented by CF Env (io.pivotal.cfenv) to consume VCAP_* bindings at runtime.

- Use cloudfoundry-client-reactor for all API operations (app lifecycle, routes, spaces/orgs, service instances/bindings, logs, tasks) instead of shelling out to the cf CLI or hand-rolling REST calls.
- Authenticate via UAA OAuth2 client credentials with least-privilege scopes; load endpoints and credentials from configuration, not from code.
- Encapsulate CF interactions behind a dedicated gateway/service module to centralize auth, timeouts, retries with backoff, and metrics/logging; expose async interfaces aligned with Reactor types used by the client.
- Use CF Env to parse VCAP_SERVICES/VCAP_APPLICATION for runtime bindings; avoid deprecated Spring Cloud Connectors.
- Pin to the latest stable 5.x of cf-java-client and compatible Reactor/Netty versions; manage with dependency constraints to ensure compatibility with our Spring Boot baseline.
- Include contract and integration tests: mock CF API (e.g., WireMock) for unit tests; run smoke tests against a non-prod CF foundation in CI.
- Do not introduce vendor-specific wrappers beyond the official client; reevaluate only if CF API coverage gaps appear.
- Security and compliance: never log tokens; store credentials in secret management; rotate UAA clients; enable TLS verification; validate org/space scoping to prevent cross-tenant actions.
- Operational concerns: instrument with OpenTelemetry, set sensible connection pools and request limits to avoid API throttling, and backpressure large listings with paginated calls.

This decision provides first-class CF API coverage, type-safe models, better reliability than CLI invocation, and reduces maintenance versus custom HTTP integrations, while keeping runtime binding simple and future-proof via CF Env.

We will secure the admin interface exclusively via enterprise Single Sign-On using OpenID Connect (OIDC) with our existing identity provider (e.g., Okta/Azure AD/Keycloak/OpenShift OAuth via Dex) fronted by an auth proxy (e.g., oauth2-proxy) terminating OIDC and injecting verified user identity and group claims to the admin app. Authorization to the admin interface will be granted only to users whose group/role claim contains the designated admin groups (e.g., admin, platform-admin), with a default-deny posture for all others. All authentication must enforce MFA at the IdP, preferring phishing-resistant factors (WebAuthn/PIV) where available. Local application accounts and password-based logins are disabled; no shared accounts are permitted.

Sessions will be short-lived with inactivity timeouts, secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=strict cookies, and refresh token rotation (or no refresh tokens) to minimize risk. Service accounts are blocked from UI access. A single, offline “break-glass” admin account is maintained at the IdP with strong MFA, vaulted credentials, strict use procedures, and mandatory post-use rotation and review.

All authentication and authorization events (logins, denials, group changes, break-glass usage) will be centrally audited and forwarded to the SIEM. Optional IP allowlisting and conditional access policies may be enabled for heightened assurance. CLI/admin API access will use the same IdP via device code or PKCE flows.

## Decision
Adopt an API-first, contract-driven approach using OpenAPI 3.1 as the single source of truth, supported by code generation for server stubs, client SDKs, and documentation. Implement a resource-oriented REST design with consistent naming, plural nouns, and standard HTTP methods and status codes. Use URI-based versioning (/v1) with strict backward-compatibility guarantees for minor updates; deprecate with clear timelines and changelogs.

Architect the service with a hexagonal (ports-and-adapters) pattern: domain logic isolated from transport and infrastructure; controllers thin; business rules testable without I/O. Centralize cross-cutting concerns (authn/z, logging, metrics, tracing, rate limiting) via middleware. Standardize error responses with RFC 7807 (application/problem+json). Provide consistent pagination, filtering, sorting, and sparse fieldsets; default to cursor-based pagination. Enforce idempotency for safe retries on mutating endpoints where applicable.

Adopt OAuth2/OIDC for authentication, JWT access tokens, and scope/role-based authorization; support fine-grained, policy-based access where needed. Require TLS everywhere. Define quotas and rate limits with standardized headers.

Establish a robust CI/CD pipeline that validates the API contract (linting, breaking-change detection), builds artifacts from the spec, runs unit/integration/contract tests, and deploys via infrastructure-as-code. Maintain separate environments (dev, staging, prod) with feature flags and blue/green or canary deployments. Publish live, versioned documentation with an interactive explorer and example payloads.

Instrument the API with structured logging, distributed tracing, RED/USE metrics, and health/readiness probes; expose a standards-based metrics endpoint. Implement comprehensive monitoring and alerting SLAs/SLOs.

Define a formal deprecation policy, semantic versioning for the spec and SDKs, and a migration guide for consumers. Maintain a change review process (ADR + API design review) to govern evolutions and ensure consistency across teams.

We will adopt a message-driven architecture using the framework’s Messenger component as the primary abstraction for in-process dispatch and asynchronous processing.

- Message taxonomy:
  - Commands (intent to change state), Events (facts that happened), Queries (read-only).
  - One handler per Command/Query; Events may have multiple handlers.
  - Messages are immutable, versioned DTOs with explicit schemas.

- Transports:
  - Synchronous (in-memory) transport for Queries and latency-critical Commands.
  - Asynchronous transport via AMQP (RabbitMQ) for Commands/Events requiring decoupling or background processing.
  - Dedicated failure transport (dead-letter queue) for poisoned/expired messages.

- Serialization and schema:
  - JSON serialization with explicit type metadata.
  - Backward-compatible message versioning; handlers support N and N-1.
  - Validation middleware enforces schema before enqueue/handle.

- Reliability and ordering:
  - At-least-once delivery with exponential backoff retries and circuit breaker.
  - Idempotency via message UUID, deduplication store, and idempotent handlers.
  - Partition/route by aggregate ID to preserve per-entity ordering when required.

- Observability and ops:
  - Correlation/causation IDs propagated via stamps/headers.
  - Structured logging, metrics, and distributed tracing middleware.
  - Health checks for consumer liveness and backlog thresholds with autoscaling guidance.

- Security:
  - Allowlist of message classes; signature verification for external ingest.
  - PII minimization; secrets never embedded in messages.

- Development practices:
  - Naming: <BoundedContext>.<Type>.<Action> (e.g., Billing.Command.CapturePayment).
  - Handlers are side-effect free except for their explicit responsibility; no synchronous cross-service calls from handlers.
  - Outbox pattern for publishing domain events within the same transaction as state changes.
  - Feature flags to toggle async vs sync dispatch per message during rollout.

- Configuration and tooling:
  - Declarative routing per message type to transports.
  - Worker processes managed via supervisor/containers; graceful shutdown and drain support.
  - Replay tooling for events with guardrails (no Commands replay).

This standardizes messaging, improves decoupling and resilience, and provides a clear path to scale and evolve processing.

## Decision

We will implement a Community Mirror: a publicly accessible, read-only mirror of vetted product data and APIs, isolated from production. The mirror will be populated via a one-way, scheduled export pipeline that applies irreversible de-identification (PII removal/masking, aggregation where necessary) and schema pruning before publication.

Key elements:
- Isolation: separate cloud account/project, network, and datastore; no inbound connectivity to production; publication via push-only CI/CD.
- Data products: versioned static datasets (CSV/Parquet) in object storage served via CDN, plus a read-only API endpoint that mirrors a subset of production endpoints with synthetic IDs and limited fields. OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas are generated from the same source as production and flagged as “community” profiles.
- Update cadence: daily snapshots with immutable versioning; emergency revocation pipeline for takedowns.
- Tooling: ETL with dbt for transformations and masking, orchestrated by scheduled workflows; integrity and differential checks before publish; signed manifests for datasets.
- Governance: documented data catalog with field-level provenance and sensitivity classifications; usage terms; rate limiting and basic API keys to manage abuse; observability with public status page and internal alerts.
- Sustainability: IaC-managed infrastructure; automated tests to prevent leakage of restricted fields; cost controls via CDN caching and lifecycle policies.

This approach enables community use, reproducibility, and transparency while protecting user privacy and production stability.

We will use Ruby on Rails (Rails 7, API-only mode) as the backend framework to build and expose our application’s HTTP/JSON APIs and domain services. Rails is selected for its mature ecosystem, conventions, security features, and productivity, while allowing us to selectively include only the needed components for lean services.

Key choices within this decision:
- Persistence: PostgreSQL managed via ActiveRecord and migrations.
- Background processing: Sidekiq with Redis for asynchronous and scheduled jobs.
- API design: RESTful, versioned endpoints with consistent JSON serialization; strong input validation and error handling.
- AuthN/Z: Token-based authentication (e.g., JWT) with role/permission checks at controller and policy layers.
- Architecture: Keep domain logic out of controllers/models callbacks; favor service/command objects and clear boundaries to support DDD and event-driven patterns; instrument with Rails notifications.
- Operational posture: 12-factor, containerized deployment, environment-based configuration, structured logging, health checks, and metrics.
- Security and performance: Use Rails security defaults, DB constraints, pagination, N+1 prevention, and caching where appropriate.

We will disable or omit unused Rails components in API-only services to minimize footprint and risk.

Adopt an API-first, contract-driven approach using OpenAPI 3.1 for synchronous REST APIs and AsyncAPI 2.x for event-driven interfaces. All APIs must be designed from the contract, reviewed, linted, and approved before implementation.

Key decisions:
- Style and protocol: Resource-oriented REST over HTTPS with JSON as the canonical wire format; use gRPC internally where latency/typing benefits are material, documenting equivalent contracts via OpenAPI/gRPC-Gateway where external exposure is required.
- Specifications: Maintain machine-readable specs per service in /apis/{service}/{version}/ with versioned OpenAPI/AsyncAPI documents. Enforce a shared API style guide (naming, pagination, filtering, sorting, timestamps, enums).
- Standards: Adopt RFC 7807 for error responses, OAuth2/OIDC for auth, semantic versioning for APIs, URI-based major versioning (/v1) with additive changes only within a major version. Minimum 6-month deprecation policy with sunset headers.
- Documentation: Auto-generate interactive docs (Redocly or Swagger UI) from source specs; publish to a centralized developer portal. Each endpoint/event requires examples, field descriptions, constraints, and business rules. Provide SDKs generated from specs where feasible.
- Governance and quality: Lint specs with Spectral in CI; require design reviews and consumer sign-off for breaking changes. Contract tests must validate implementation vs. spec. Maintain changelogs and migration guides per version.
- Cross-cutting conventions: Standard pagination (cursor-based preferred), consistent idempotency for unsafe methods, correlation IDs via headers, rate-limit headers, and standardized webhooks documented via AsyncAPI.
- Tooling: Use Stoplight Studio or VS Code OpenAPI tools for authoring; Prism for mock servers; Dredd/Postman/Newman for contract testing; Redocly/SwaggerHub for publishing.
- Repository structure: /apis (contracts), /sdks (generated clients), /docs (guides and how-tos), with CI ensuring specs and implementations remain in sync.

This framework ensures consistency, discoverability, and maintainability of APIs and their documentation across the organization.

We will secure the API using Dropwizard’s built-in security features and standard extensions:

- Enforce TLS via Dropwizard’s Jetty HTTPS connectors, with strong cipher suites and HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection; enable mutual TLS in environments requiring service-to-service authentication.
- Implement JWT-based authentication using Dropwizard’s auth framework (AuthDynamicFeature with a custom AuthFilter that validates tokens against our JWKs/issuer), injecting the authenticated Principal via @Auth.
- Apply fine-grained authorization using JSR-250 annotations (@RolesAllowed, @PermitAll, @DenyAll) with RolesAllowedDynamicFeature to enforce role-based access control on resources.
- Configure CORS explicitly for allowed origins, methods, and headers; default to deny-all and open only what’s required per environment.
- Add standard security headers via servlet filters (HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options/Frame-Ancestors, X-XSS-Protection, Referrer-Policy, Content-Security-Policy for any HTML error endpoints).
- Use Dropwizard’s request/response logging, audit logging for authz decisions, and metrics/tracing to monitor authentication/authorization behavior.
- Centralize security configuration in config.yml (TLS, auth keys/JWKs URL, token leeway/clock-skew, required roles per endpoint group) and externalize secrets via environment variables/secret manager.
- Deny by default: all endpoints require authentication unless explicitly annotated as public; admin tasks are isolated behind separate admin connectors and mTLS.
- Validate payloads with Dropwizard’s validation and size limits; set Jetty rate and connection limits; optionally integrate a rate-limiting bundle where needed.
- Provide health checks for key security dependencies (JWKs fetch/rotation, clock skew, mTLS truststore) and fail closed on verifier initialization errors.

## Decision

Adopt Elasticsearch as the primary search and indexing engine for the platform’s full-text, faceted, and relevance-based queries. We will operate a dedicated Elasticsearch cluster (managed service preferred where available) and index denormalized documents sourced from upstream systems of record. Elasticsearch will not be the system of record; it serves read-optimized search and analytics use cases with eventual consistency.

Key implementation choices:
- Use index templates and ILM (Index Lifecycle Management) for schema evolution, rollover, and cost-effective retention.
- Configure language-specific analyzers (e.g., stemming, stopwords) and custom normalizers to support multilingual relevance.
- Employ ingest pipelines (and/or Logstash) for enrichment and field normalization; use bulk APIs for efficient updates.
- Partition data by business domain into separate indices (and aliases) to support independent scaling, zero-downtime reindexing, and controlled access.
- Implement role-based access control and field/document-level security; enable TLS in transit and encryption at rest.
- Standardize on a supported version with tested plugins only; establish blue/green or rolling upgrade procedures.
- Integrate observability (metrics, logs, slow query tracing) and snapshot-based backups to external storage for DR.
- Enforce query guards (timeouts, result window limits) and caching policies to protect cluster health.

This decision centralizes enterprise search capabilities while preserving source-of-truth ownership and enabling scalable, low-latency discovery.

## Decision

We will adopt AWS EC2 Image Builder as the standard mechanism for creating, hardening, testing, and distributing all golden AMIs used across environments (including EC2, ASG launch templates, and EKS node groups). Image Builder pipelines will define versioned recipes and components to apply OS hardening (e.g., CIS-aligned), install baseline agents (SSM, CloudWatch, vulnerability/AV), apply security updates, run validation tests, and perform vulnerability scanning (via Inspector/partner tools) prior to distribution.

AMI distribution will publish to required regions and share to target accounts using a hub-and-spoke model. Produced AMI IDs will be published to SSM Parameter Store for consumption by CloudFormation/Terraform and deployment workflows. We will integrate pipelines with CodePipeline/CodeBuild for change control, approvals, and notifications.

Security and governance controls include least-privilege IAM roles, KMS encryption, mandatory tags, SBOM/artifact provenance where supported, retention/deprecation policies, and immutability of released AMIs. Operationally, we will run monthly patch pipelines plus emergency builds for critical CVEs, maintain at least N previous AMI versions for rollback, and perform blue/green rollouts for ASGs and node groups. Image Builder becomes the primary tool; existing ad hoc/Packer-based builds are deprecated except for documented edge cases.

- Use a managed relational database (PostgreSQL) as the primary OLTP store for strong consistency, transactions, and rich querying.
- Environments:
  - Local: Dockerized Postgres with reproducible seed data.
  - CI: Ephemeral Postgres via Testcontainers for isolated integration tests.
  - Staging/Prod: AWS RDS/Aurora PostgreSQL (provisioned IOPS), multi-AZ.
- Schema and data migrations managed with Flyway; migrations are immutable, forward-only, reviewed, and versioned with application code.
- Data access via ORM for CRUD and type-safety, complemented by hand-written SQL for complex queries and batch operations. Avoid business logic in the database; keep functions/triggers minimal and auditable.
- Identifiers and types:
  - Primary keys: UUID v7 (database-generated where possible).
  - All timestamps stored in UTC with timezone-aware types.
  - Soft deletes via deleted_at; hard deletes only for GDPR/retention workflows.
- Performance and scalability:
  - HikariCP connection pooling at the application layer; optionally PgBouncer on prod.
  - Read replicas for reporting/analytics; route heavy reads off the primary.
  - Sensible indexing policy and automated analysis; add partial/GIN indexes as needed.
  - Consider native partitioning for high-volume tables and time-based data.
- Reliability and recovery:
  - Automated backups with PITR; regular restore drills.
  - Transparent failover (Aurora), with application-side retry and idempotency.
- Security:
  - Private subnets, TLS in-transit, encryption at rest (KMS).
  - Secrets via cloud secret manager; rotate regularly.
  - Prefer IAM-based authentication where supported; least-privilege roles.
  - Row-level security for multi-tenant scenarios if needed.
- Observability:
  - Structured query logging with sampling; slow query log enabled.
  - Metrics on connections, cache hit ratio, replication lag; alerts on SLOs.
- Integration:
  - Change Data Capture (Debezium) for downstream/async needs.
  - Separate analytics warehouse fed via CDC/ETL; no ad-hoc queries on OLTP.
- Capacity management via IaC (Terraform) with parameterized instance classes and storage auto-scaling.

## Decision

We will document architectural choices using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) following Michael Nygard’s lightweight format.

- Repository and location: Store ADRs in version control under docs/adr (one ADR per file, numbered sequentially: 0001-..., immutable once Accepted).
- Template: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered, References. Use concise prose and link related artifacts (RFCs, tickets, designs, PRs).
- Status workflow: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Superseded/Deprecated. Superseding ADRs must link both directions.
- Scope: One significant, user-impacting or cross-cutting decision per ADR (e.g., protocols, persistence choices, service boundaries, SLOs, security posture). Minor implementation details remain in code/PRs.
- Process: Any contributor may propose an ADR via PR. Reviewers include at least one architect/tech lead and relevant domain owners. Decisions are timeboxed and resolved in architecture review meetings or explicitly deferred.
- Change control: Accepted ADRs are never edited for substance; changes require a new ADR that supersedes the old. Typos/formatting may be fixed with a non-substantive PR.
- Discoverability: Maintain an index README in docs/adr with titles, statuses, and tags (e.g., security, data, platform). Link ADRs from service READMEs and system documentation.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (or equivalent) to create and manage ADRs; integrate checks in CI to ensure unique numbering, required sections, and updated index.
- Ownership and cadence: Architecture group curates the backlog, audits ADRs quarterly for relevance, and ensures alignment across teams.

We will not permit application workloads to call the Kubernetes API directly. Only platform components (e.g., GitOps controllers, operators, cluster controllers) may access the API, each via a dedicated ServiceAccount with least-privilege RBAC scoped to required namespaces and resources. External direct API access will remain disabled; the API server is private and reachable only via the bastion using kubectl or automation identities.

Where application behavior requires cluster operations, we will introduce an internal mediation layer (operator/controller or lightweight platform service) that exposes narrowly scoped domain APIs/events and performs cluster mutations on behalf of apps. All delivery automation will prefer declarative GitOps (e.g., Argo CD/Flux) rather than imperative API writes.

Enforcement measures:
- No service account token mounting for application pods (automountServiceAccountToken=false by default).
- NetworkPolicies to block egress to the API server from non-platform namespaces.
- Admission control to restrict creation of RBAC and TokenRequest objects to platform namespaces.
- Short-lived tokens via projected service account tokens for approved components; no static tokens.
- Audit policy to log and alert on unexpected API usage.

This approach minimizes blast radius, improves auditability, and maintains a clean separation between application and platform concerns while still enabling controlled automation paths.

## Decision

Adopt Python as the primary implementation language for application services, CLIs, and supporting tooling. Standardize on CPython 3.12 for production (minimum supported version 3.11), enabling modern language features, improved performance, and comprehensive type hinting. All new code must be fully type-annotated and pass static analysis (pyright/mypy) and style/quality gates (black, ruff). Asynchronous I/O (asyncio) is the default model for network-bound services; multiprocessing or C extensions (cffi, Cython) may be used for CPU-bound workloads when needed. Packaging and dependency management will use a lockfile-based workflow (e.g., Poetry or uv/pip-tools) with reproducible builds; wheels are the default distribution format. Target platforms are Linux (x86_64, aarch64) for production, with developer support on macOS and Windows via containers. Interoperability will be via standard protocols (HTTP/REST, gRPC) and well-supported SDKs. Where runtime isolation is required, services will run under Docker with slim base images (e.g., python:3.12-slim) and explicit OS-level dependencies. Backwards compatibility with Python <3.11 will not be provided except in explicitly designated components.

## Decision

We will adopt CSS Modules as the default mechanism for scoping component styles.

- Each component will have a colocated stylesheet named ComponentName.module.css in the same directory as the component file.
- Class names will be imported and referenced via the generated module map (e.g., import styles from './Button.module.css'; <button className={styles.primary} />).
- The build will be configured to generate locally scoped, hashed class names in non-dev builds and readable names in development.
- Global styles are allowed only for resets, typography foundations, design tokens, and third‑party library overrides, located under a dedicated global.css (or equivalent) and explicitly imported once at the app root.
- Shared, cross-component utilities should be implemented as CSS Modules with composition or via design tokens and CSS variables; avoid ad-hoc globals.
- Theming and dynamic variants should prefer CSS variables and data-attributes over runtime class name concatenation where feasible.
- Type safety for class references may be enabled via typed CSS Modules where supported in the toolchain.

This approach provides deterministic, encapsulated styling, minimizes leakage and naming conflicts, and aligns with tree-shakable, framework-agnostic CSS without introducing a CSS-in-JS runtime.

## Decision

Adopt adr-tools as the primary mechanism for creating, numbering, and maintaining Architectural Decision Records, using a project-specific template to enforce our preferred structure and metadata.

- Use adr-tools (v3+) for standardized filenames (docs/adr/NNNN-title-with-dashes.md), automatic numbering, backlinks, and navigation.
- Store a custom template at docs/adr/.templates/template.md to ensure consistent sections: Title, Date, Status, Context, Decision, Alternatives, Consequences, Implementation, References, and Metadata (Owners, Tags).
- Provide command aliases (e.g., make adr-new, npm run adr:new) that wrap adr-tools with the custom template, title normalization, and default Status=Proposed.
- Enforce template adherence via a pre-commit hook/CI check that validates required sections and filename pattern; reject ADRs missing mandatory fields.
- Generate and version an index (docs/adr/index.md) with adr-log in CI on changes to ADRs.
- Allow template evolution through PRs; changes are versioned and announced, and do not rewrite existing ADR content.
- Keep ADRs co-located with code in the repository (renderable via GitHub’s docs/), ensuring easy discovery and review in pull requests.

Adopt a single, consistent error representation based on RFC 9457 (Problem Details) with content type application/problem+json and an extension property errors for field-level violations. Return:
- 400 Bad Request for schema/format violations detected by request deserialization/json-schema.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity for semantic/business validation failures.

Each entry in errors must include:
- pointer: JSON Pointer to the offending field (e.g., /customer/address/0/postcode). For query/path params use a prefixed namespace (e.g., query.sort, path.orderId).
- code: stable, machine-readable error code (e.g., required, invalid_format, out_of_range, duplicate, unknown_field, conflict).
- messageKey: i18n key for UI mapping, with optional messageParams for interpolation.
- rejectedValue: safely redacted original value when useful.
- severity: error or warning (warnings do not block processing).
- index: for batch/array contexts indicating item position.
- constraint: optional descriptor (min, max, pattern) to aid client-side rendering.

The top-level Problem Details object must include type, title, status, detail (high-level summary), instance (request path), correlationId/traceId, and service-specific metadata. For mixed global errors not tied to a single field, omit pointer.

Define and document the error schema and codes in OpenAPI, including examples. Keep codes backward-compatible and version new ones. Frontend should map messageKey+params for localization; backend messages remain developer-oriented. Log full server-side details; responses must not leak sensitive data.

Adopt Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR) as the standard for documenting architectural decisions across this project.

We will enforce tenant-managed domain policies through a centralized domain-governance component and consistent enforcement at all identity and invitation entry points.

- For each tenant, admins will define managed domains via an allowlist; all other domains are implicitly blocked unless explicitly allowlisted. An optional denylist supports globally disallowed domains (e.g., disposable providers).
- Domain ownership will be verified with a DNS TXT challenge per domain. Successful verification marks the domain as managed for that tenant. Verification must be renewed annually or upon DNS change detection.
- Enforcement points: user self-signup, email change, organization invitations, SCIM provisioning, and SSO Just-In-Time provisioning. Requests with emails not matching a verified managed domain are rejected with actionable error messaging; invitations may be queued as “pending verification” if policy allows.
- All domain comparisons will use strict normalization: lowercasing, Unicode normalization, conversion to punycode (IDNA), and public suffix parsing to prevent subdomain/parent domain spoofing and homograph attacks.
- We will integrate a third-party disposable/temporary email detection service and maintain an internal global denylist for known risky domains, refreshed daily.
- Admin UX will include: add/verify domain flow (DNS TXT), status dashboard, re-verification prompts, downloadable DNS instructions, and audit logs of policy changes and enforcement events.
- A policy API will expose current allow/deny decisions; edge caches (TTL ~15 minutes) will minimize latency with cache-busting on policy changes.
- SSO enforcement: IdP email domain must match a verified managed domain for the tenant; mismatches are rejected unless an admin-approved exception exists.
- We will provide an appeal/override workflow allowing time-bound exceptions recorded with approver, reason, and expiry.
