  - stage: cleaned/typed/validated intermediates.
  - core: conformed, modeled entities (single source of truth).
  - mart: consumer/team-specific denormalized views/tables.
  - meta: lineage/catalog/tests (e.g., dbt artifacts).
  - scratch: ephemeral per-user/project work; auto-purged.
- Governance and constraints:
  - Schemas and objects use lowercase snake_case; fully qualify cross-schema references.
  - Avoid foreign keys across schemas except app -> ref; prefer logical integrity and documented contracts elsewhere.
  - Separate ownership and least-privilege grants per schema; no CREATE privileges in public.
  - Migrations are scoped per schema; forbid circular dependencies across schemas.
  - Backups/retention by schema: audit/raw long-term; scratch short TTL; others per data-classification policy.

We will implement play-frontend-hmrc as a thin, idiomatic Scala/Play wrapper that mirrors hmrc-frontend on a 1:1 basis. This includes aligning component coverage, names, parameters/options, defaults, accessibility behavior, CSS class names, and the generated HTML markup so that consumers can rely on parity with the upstream design system.

Versioning will be kept in lockstep: each play-frontend-hmrc major/minor release will correspond to the matching hmrc-frontend major/minor, with patch releases used only for framework-specific fixes that do not alter the rendered markup or public API. Deprecations and removals will follow upstream timelines and semantics.

We will not introduce bespoke Play-only features, behaviors, or opinionated defaults that diverge from hmrc-frontend. Any enhancements, new components, or parameter additions must be proposed and accepted upstream first; play-frontend-hmrc will implement only what is released in hmrc-frontend. Necessary framework glue (e.g., Twirl helpers, form bindings, i18n hooks) will be added without changing upstream semantics.

Divergence is permitted only for urgent security or accessibility fixes and must be minimized, clearly documented, and upstreamed promptly. This mirroring strategy reduces maintenance risk, simplifies upgrades, and ensures consistent UX and accessibility across HMRC services.

## Decision

We will adopt Quart as the primary HTTP framework for this service.

Quart provides an asyncio-first, ASGI-compliant framework with a Flask-compatible API, allowing us to reuse familiar patterns (blueprints, request/response lifecycle) while enabling native async I/O, WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and HTTP/2. We will run Quart with Hypercorn as the ASGI server.

Key implementation choices:
- Routing and modularity: use Blueprints and async view functions end-to-end.
- Data validation and OpenAPI: use quart-schema (Pydantic v2-based) for request/response validation, schema generation, and interactive docs; fall back to Pydantic directly where needed.
- Error handling: standardize on RFC 7807 Problem Details JSON for all errors; map unhandled exceptions to structured problem responses.
- Middleware: use ASGI middleware for CORS, gzip/br, request ID, and rate limiting; prefer ASGI-native libraries over WSGI/Flask-only extensions.
- Observability: integrate OpenTelemetry (traces/metrics/logs) via ASGI instrumentation; include structured JSON logging with correlation IDs.
- Performance and correctness: prohibit blocking I/O on the event loop; use async clients/drivers (e.g., httpx, async DB drivers). For unavoidable blocking work, offload via thread/process executors or background workers.
- Security: enforce HTTPS termination, HSTS, secure cookies, CSRF (where applicable), and input/output sanitization; validate all external payloads via schema.
- Deployment: containerize and run Hypercorn with multiple workers; optionally place behind a reverse proxy for TLS/offloading and routing.

Where Flask-only extensions are required, we will replace them with ASGI-compatible alternatives or wrap them judiciously.

## Decision

Implement a persistent, global search control in the Application Bar to provide immediate access to SDBM search from any page.

- Add a compact query input with submit and clear actions, plus an overflow menu linking to Advanced Search and Search Help.
- Include an optional “scope” selector (e.g., All, Manuscripts, Sources, People, Places) that maps to existing Blacklight facets/routes; default to All.
- Reuse existing Blacklight/Rails search endpoints; do not create new search APIs. Submissions perform full-page navigations to the results view to preserve URL-driven state and shareability.
- Provide lightweight typeahead suggestions (recent queries and user bookmarks locally; optional server suggestions can be enabled later). Client-side suggestions are debounced and capped to avoid extra Solr load.
- Build as an AngularJS component integrated into the existing header layout; keep it framework-agnostic enough to be replaceable during future frontend upgrades.
- Ensure accessibility: labeled controls, ARIA combobox semantics for suggestions, keyboard shortcuts (e.g., “/” to focus), and high-contrast, responsive design.
- Persist last entered query and scope in session storage to enhance continuity when navigating.
- Track analytics events (focus, submit, scope change) to measure usage and inform refinements; avoid logging PII.
- Defer heavy assets; no additional Solr queries are issued from the App Bar until explicit user action (submit or suggestions enabled).
- Provide feature flags to toggle suggestions and scope selector, enabling staged rollout and A/B validation.
- Maintain security: sanitize inputs, respect existing permissions, and rely on server-side validation already present in search controllers.

We will store build and provenance metadata in container images using OCI-compliant annotations (image labels). Labels will be the authoritative, machine-readable source of image metadata, instead of overloading tags or relying on external registries.

- Standard annotations: adopt org.opencontainers.image.* keys per OCI Image Spec, including at minimum:
  - org.opencontainers.image.title, description, url, documentation, source
  - org.opencontainers.image.version, revision (git SHA), created (RFC3339)
  - org.opencontainers.image.vendor, licenses, authors
- Organization-specific keys: use a reserved namespace (e.g., com.acme.*) for:
  - com.acme.service, component, runtime, platform
  - com.acme.vcs.branch, ci.build-number, ci.pipeline-url
  - com.acme.sbom (OCI artifact reference or URL), com.acme.attestation (provenance ref)
- Labels MUST NOT contain secrets, tokens, PII, or mutable runtime configuration. They are immutable build-time facts only.
- CI/build system will deterministically set labels at image build time (Dockerfile LABEL or build-arg/BuildKit/kaniko equivalents). A shared library/action will standardize population, and CI will fail builds missing required labels.
- Tags remain for human-friendly selection (e.g., v1.2.3, latest), but all automation and audit rely on labels for accuracy and traceability.
- Size and format constraints: keep total label payload small (<4KB) and text-only; store large artifacts (SBOMs, attestations) as OCI artifacts and reference them via label pointers.
- Tooling: image scanners, deployment orchestrators, and inventory tools will read labels to enforce policy (e.g., require SBOM, match commit to deployment, verify build pipeline). Registry metadata sync scripts will prefer labels as source of truth.
- Backward compatibility: do not use deprecated label-schema.org keys; only OCI and com.acme.*.
- Security and compliance: labels support provenance (SLSA) by linking to attestations; supply chain policies can gate promotion based on label presence and values.

This standardizes discoverability and provenance across all images with minimal coupling, improves auditability, and enables consistent automation without embedding environment-specific configuration.

## Decision

Adopt Infrastructure as Code (IaC) as a mandatory, first-class practice for provisioning, updating, and destroying all infrastructure across environments. Use declarative definitions stored in version control with peer-reviewed pull requests as the only path to change.

Standardize on Terraform as the primary IaC tool to enable multi-cloud support and consistent workflows. Allow provider-native templates (e.g., CloudFormation) only by exception when required for a managed service, wrapped or referenced from Terraform where feasible.

Manage Terraform state in a secure remote backend with locking and versioning (e.g., Terraform Cloud or S3 + DynamoDB). Organize code into reusable, versioned modules; separate global, shared, and application-specific stacks; and model environments via workspaces or per-environment stacks as appropriate.

Integrate IaC into CI/CD: enforce fmt/validate, run plan on every PR with human-readable diffs, and apply only from protected branches with approvals. Store secrets outside code using a secret manager (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager/HashiCorp Vault) and pass via variables. Enforce policy-as-code (e.g., OPA/Conftest or Sentinel) for security, compliance, and tagging (cost allocation) before apply.

Require idempotency, immutable patterns (e.g., blue/green where applicable), drift detection, and automated documentation generation of resources and modules. All manual console changes are prohibited and subject to remediation via code.

Use MediaWiki’s ParserCache as the authoritative cache for server‑rendered Termbox output.

- Render Termbox server‑side and embed its HTML (plus minimal serialized data needed for hydration) into ParserOutput as extension data, so it is stored and served via ParserCache/CDN with the page.
- Key and vary via ParserOptions to avoid user personalization: vary on entity revision, content language/interface language (including language variant), and skin; do not vary on user identity or ephemeral preferences.
- Invalidate via normal page purge on term changes (labels/descriptions/aliases) and entity edits; ensure edit actions and term updates trigger ParserCache and CDN purges.
- Use default ParserCache TTLs and eviction; do not introduce a separate cross‑cutting cache for Termbox. For cache misses, SSR on appservers; if SSR fails, fall back to client‑side rendering.
- Do not include user‑specific state in the fragment. Only include data safe for wide caching.
- Monitor cache fragmentation (languages/skins) and adjust vary dimensions if needed.

This leverages existing infra, simplifies invalidation, improves p95 latency and reduces redundant SSR, at the cost of some cache fragmentation across languages/skins.

We will standardize time-based extraction around a single, immutable eventAt field stored in UTC as the canonical timestamp on every record and use [start, end) window semantics. All write paths must populate eventAt at ingestion; any user-supplied local times will be converted to UTC with explicit timezone/offset retained in optional metadata for display purposes.

Query contract:
- All time-based APIs accept start and end in ISO-8601 (UTC) and return results where start ≤ eventAt < end.
- Timezone rendering is applied only at the presentation layer; storage and filtering remain UTC-only.
- Cursor/continuation tokens include eventAt and a stable tiebreaker id to ensure deterministic pagination across boundaries.

Storage and indexing:
- Operational store (e.g., Firestore/OLTP): store eventAt as native timestamp; create composite indexes on (tenantId/siteId, eventAt asc). For common filters add (eventType, eventAt) composites. No string times for filtering.
- Analytical/TSDB/Warehouse: partition by event_date=YYYY-MM-DD derived from eventAt; create time-ordered clustering/primary index on eventAt to enable efficient range scans and rollups.
- Object storage (if used): hive-style partitions (year=YYYY/month=MM/day=DD/) derived from eventAt.

Data modeling and quality:
- eventAt is write-once; corrections require a new record or an audited update path.
- For late/early arrivals, include ingestionAt to differentiate event time vs processing time.
- Backfill/migration will populate eventAt from existing date/time fields with audited timezone assumptions.

Performance safeguards:
- Enforce maximum window sizes per API (configurable), with pagination and server-side limits.
- Provide aggregate endpoints (e.g., hourly/daily buckets) to avoid large raw scans when only summaries are required.

Observability and retention:
- Define retention by partition (warehouse/TSDB) and TTL policies (OLTP) based on eventAt.
- Monitor index selectivity and scan ratios on eventAt queries; adjust composites/partitions as access patterns evolve.

Adopt RFC-compliant UUIDs for all telemetry identifiers. Use UUID version 4 (random) as the default for privacy-preserving, non-guessable IDs (e.g., install_id, device_id, session_id, event_id). Use UUID version 7 (time-ordered) only where stable creation-time ordering materially benefits storage or analytics (e.g., event_id in append-only data stores), and where clock skew risk is acceptable. Do not use non-standard formats (e.g., ULID) for telemetry.

Generation must use platform-standard, cryptographically secure APIs (e.g., uuid4/UUIDv4, UUIDv7 where available or a vetted library compliant with RFC 9562). Do not hand-roll randomness. No semantics may be encoded in UUIDs.

Representation:
- Canonical textual form: lowercase hex with hyphens (8-4-4-4-12).
- Storage: 16-byte binary in databases and columnar stores where supported; otherwise canonical string.
- Transport/logging: canonical string; accept case-insensitive input but normalize on ingest.

Lifecycle:
- Generate server-side for server-created entities; client-generated UUIDs permitted for offline buffering but validated on ingest (version and variant).
- Rotate session_id per session; generate new event_id per event; persist long-lived device/install IDs only with consent and per policy.
- Do not reuse UUIDs across entities or contexts.

Validation and governance:
- Reject malformed/non-RFC UUIDs; record reason.
- Provide shared utility for generation/normalization/validation to avoid divergence.
- Backfill legacy IDs with new UUIDs via mapping, without mutating historical telemetry payloads.

We will adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document architecturally significant decisions.

- Repository and structure:
  - Store ADRs in docs/adr/ as Markdown files.
  - One decision per file; include an index at docs/adr/README.md.
- Naming and identification:
  - File name format: NNNN-short-slug.md with zero-padded sequential numbers (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md).
  - Each ADR includes: Title, Date, Status (Proposed | Accepted | Rejected | Deprecated | Superseded), Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives, References, Links.
- Process:
  - Create an ADR when proposing a significant change affecting architecture, NFRs, interfaces, data models, dependencies, deployment, or security.
  - Submit via PR with reviewers from architecture/owners; acceptance requires at least one architecture approver.
  - Update status through follow-up ADRs; do not edit Accepted content except for typos—use a new ADR to supersede.
  - Cross-link related ADRs and indicate supersession.
- Tooling and compliance:
  - Use a shared ADR template (docs/adr/.template.md) and adr-tools (or equivalent script) to generate IDs and update the index.
  - Add a CI check to validate template compliance, presence of Status, Date, and links.
- Scope and governance:
  - Each team maintains ADRs within its component; cross-cutting decisions live in docs/adr/global/.
  - Keep ADRs concise (<=2 pages) and write them near the time of decision.

We will implement and expose only the Value projection as the canonical read model for all query use cases. All external and internal consumer queries will be served from this single, denormalized projection optimized for retrieval, with no alternate projections (e.g., event, audit, history, or aggregate state projections) maintained for runtime access. The Value projection will encapsulate the required domain calculations and enrichment at projection time, ensuring consumers receive ready-to-use data without additional joins or computation. Any new read requirements will be addressed by evolving the Value projection schema and transformation pipeline rather than introducing parallel projections. Rebuilds will be supported via idempotent re-projection from the event store/source of truth, and the projection will be versioned to allow safe, incremental rollout. Operational metrics, auditing, and investigative needs that require raw or historical detail will rely on the underlying event store or an offline analytics sink, not separate runtime projections. Access patterns, indexing, and caching will be tuned specifically for the Value projection to meet latency and scalability targets.

Adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as the standard mechanism to capture and version-control significant technical and product decisions across the project. Each ADR will be a Markdown file stored in the repository under docs/adr (or adr/), numbered sequentially, and managed via pull requests. We will use a lightweight, consistent template including: Title, Status (Proposed | Accepted | Rejected | Deprecated | Superseded), Context, Decision, Consequences, and References. New ADRs are created when a non-trivial choice is made or reconsidered (e.g., architectural patterns, key libraries, data models, operational practices). ADRs must be linked from relevant code, tickets, and runbooks where appropriate. Changes to previous decisions are recorded by creating a new ADR that supersedes the prior one; existing ADRs are never edited to rewrite history beyond minor corrections. The team will review ADRs during design discussions and code review, and ADR status changes occur via the same process. We will provide a template file (docs/adr/0000-template.md) and a bootstrap ADR (ADR-0001) to formalize conventions. Optionally, we may use adr-tools or a simple script to scaffold records, but no external tooling is required.

## Decision

We will use the Kubernetes in-tree awsElasticBlockStore driver and its in-tree dynamic provisioner (provisioner: kubernetes.io/aws-ebs) for PersistentVolume provisioning on AWS. We will define curated StorageClasses (e.g., gp3 as default for general purpose, io2 for latency-sensitive workloads) and reference them from PVCs for all stateful workloads requiring ReadWriteOnce volumes. Clusters will be pinned to Kubernetes versions that continue to ship the in-tree EBS plugin, and CSIMigrationAWS and related feature gates will remain disabled to ensure consistent in-tree behavior. We will document a forward path to the AWS EBS CSI driver (provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com) and schedule migration as a separate initiative, including StorageClass replacement and controlled PV migration. Until then, snapshot/backup and restore procedures will rely on native EBS capabilities compatible with the in-tree driver, and operational runbooks will reflect the in-tree provisioning model.

We will implement a pluggable TextExtraction service with a stable internal interface that supports multiple backends. The default implementation will use Apache Tika for structured formats (PDF with text layer, Office, HTML, plain text) and fall back to Tesseract OCR for image-based content (images and scanned PDFs). For scanned PDFs, we will first attempt OCR via OCRmyPDF (to produce a text layer), then re-parse with Tika.

Extraction runs asynchronously in a worker queue and is non-blocking for ingestion; failures are recorded and surfaced but do not prevent document availability. Configuration includes: max file size/pages, per-step timeouts, memory/CPU limits, and language packs for OCR (default English, per-tenant override). We will support basic pre-processing (deskew/denoise/binarization) to improve OCR accuracy when enabled.

All parsing/OCR steps execute in a sandboxed environment (container or process isolation) with resource constraints. No document content is sent to external services by default; optional connectors (e.g., cloud OCR) may be added as alternative implementations behind the same interface.

Extracted outputs include normalized plain text, per-page text offsets, and detected metadata (title, author, language). We persist text for indexing and provide digest/hash to avoid redundant re-extraction on identical content. The pipeline is idempotent and retryable with exponential backoff.

This decision balances coverage, accuracy, and operational simplicity by preferring open-source, on-prem components while preserving flexibility via a clear abstraction for future backends.

## Decision

- Use Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for all deployable services, libraries, and public APIs.
- Create immutable release artifacts from the main branch via CI, tagged with the git tag (e.g., 1.4.2), git SHA, and floating tags (1.4, 1, latest for main only). Do not mutate tags.
- Manage releases with git tags; avoid per-release branches. Maintain long-lived support branches only for actively supported minors/majors when needed for hotfixes.
- Use pre-release identifiers for non-final builds: -alpha.N, -beta.N, -rc.N.
- Publish SBOM and provenance for each artifact; sign container images and releases.
- Automate deployments:
  - On merge to main: auto-deploy to development; promote to staging on green checks.
  - Production uses a manual approval with progressive rollout (canary then 25%/50%/100%), with automated health and SLO gates. Support blue/green where applicable.
- Keep deployments backwards compatible across one version (N and N-1) to enable zero-downtime rollouts and quick rollbacks.
- Govern schema and API changes with compatibility-first evolution:
  - Database migrations are forward-compatible; use expand/contract with feature flags.
  - Public API breaking changes require a new MAJOR and deprecation notices; support previous MAJOR for a defined window.
- Externalize configuration; manage secrets via the centralized secrets manager; all infra and deployment configs are versioned as code.
- Maintain a human-readable CHANGELOG per release and release notes in the repository; include upgrade/migration steps.
- Provide a one-click rollback to the last known-good artifact (by version tag) and automated rollback on failed health checks.
- Enforce version policies in CI (tag validation, changelog check, migration lints) and gate promotions on test, security, and compliance checks.

Standardize on New Relic as the single platform to collect, process, and present web analytics for our web properties. We will enable New Relic Browser (RUM) and leverage the Telemetry Data Platform to capture page views, SPA route changes, Core Web Vitals, errors, and performance timings, and to publish product-usage events for key business journeys. Instrumentation will be deployed via a managed browser snippet (preferably through our tag manager/edge inject) and correlated with backend APM traces using distributed tracing headers to provide end-to-end visibility.

We will build curated, version-controlled dashboards for traffic, funnels, SLIs/SLOs, and error budgets, and configure alerting on user-impacting thresholds. Access will be gated via SSO and least-privilege RBAC. Data governance guardrails apply: do not collect or store PII, anonymize IP where feasible, honor consent signals, document data taxonomy, set sampling as needed, and use the EU data region with a defined retention period aligned to policy.

Marketing attribution remains on the existing marketing stack; New Relic focuses on product analytics and performance telemetry without cross-site visitor identification.

Adopt Relay (Relay Modern) as the GraphQL client for the frontend instead of Apollo Client. We will standardize on relay-runtime with the Relay Compiler, TypeScript type generation, and persisted queries. Data access will use the hook-based API (useLazyLoadQuery, useFragment, usePaginationFragment, useRefetchableFragment) with colocated fragments. We will configure the Relay Babel plugin and relay-compiler to emit artifacts during build, enforce query staticness, and enable compile-time validation and types. The Network layer will implement authenticated fetch and (where supported) persisted query IDs for reduced payload size and improved performance. Pagination and mutations will follow Relay’s Connection and mutation patterns to ensure normalized cache consistency at scale.

This choice optimizes for long-term maintainability and performance: Relay’s strictness, compile-time guarantees, and co-location model prevent over-fetching/under-fetching and cache drift, while encouraging modular components and predictable pagination. It also provides first-class support for incremental delivery (stream/defer) and scales reliably in large apps.

We will align our schema with Relay conventions (global object IDs, Node interface, Connection spec). Where necessary, we will add schema adapters/resolvers to satisfy these requirements without disrupting existing server consumers. For edge cases or non-GraphQL interactions, we may use plain fetch, but all GraphQL data flows through Relay.

## Decision

The Publisher application will not use React. Instead, we will build it as a server-rendered, forms-first web app with progressive enhancement:

- Render HTML on the server using our existing template engine.
- Use HTMX for incremental interactivity (inline CRUD, pagination/sorting/filtering, modals) and Turbo-style navigation where beneficial.
- Use Alpine.js (or equivalent lightweight declarative JS) for small, local UI behaviors; no global client-side state management library.
- Integrate specialized, framework-agnostic widgets (e.g., rich text editor, media picker) as isolated vanilla JS modules.
- Rely on standard HTTP semantics (forms, redirects, flash messages) for flow control; no client-side routing.
- Keep build tooling minimal (native ES modules). If needed, use a lightweight bundler (esbuild) only for third-party assets.
- Share components via server-side partials/partials-macros; avoid a client-side component framework.
- Ensure accessibility and keyboard support via semantic HTML and ARIA in server templates.

This approach minimizes bundle size, reduces complexity and maintenance overhead, leverages our server stack, and aligns with Publisher’s primarily CRUD- and workflow-oriented needs without introducing a SPA and React runtime.

We will enforce least-privilege network access to AWS CloudHSM from only explicitly approved Kubernetes namespaces using a layered approach:

- Cluster egress default-deny: Enable cluster-wide default-deny egress via CNI network policy (Cilium) to ensure no namespace can reach CloudHSM by default.
- Namespace allow-lists: Introduce a namespace label (e.g., hsm-access=enabled). Gatekeeper constraints will block HSM-related secrets/configmaps and egress policies in namespaces lacking this label.
- NetworkPolicies: For approved namespaces, define egress NetworkPolicies that only permit TCP to the CloudHSM subnets/ENI IPs on required ports (e.g., 2223/2225/2226) and deny all other external egress.
- Security Groups for Pods (SGP): For EKS workloads that require CloudHSM, attach a dedicated security group to the pods via label selectors. Configure CloudHSM cluster security groups to allow inbound only from this dedicated pod security group, eliminating reliance on broad node or NAT IP ranges.
- Static addressing: Pin CloudHSM endpoints via ENI IPs or managed prefixes and reference them explicitly in policies to avoid wildcard egress.
- Service mesh alignment (if mesh present): Route CloudHSM traffic via a dedicated egress gateway with an allow-list to CloudHSM IPs only; block direct pod egress to the internet for those namespaces.
- Auditing and drift control: Continuously validate policies with Gatekeeper and Cilium Hubble; alert on any egress attempts outside allowed ranges.
- Change control: Access is granted per-namespace via label + SGP binding reviewed through code (PR) and approved by platform security.

This design prevents non-approved namespaces from reaching CloudHSM, limits blast radius, and provides auditable, code-defined access controls at both Kubernetes and VPC layers.

## Decision

Adopt OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect as the sole protocols and implement a unified, cross-platform auth client that wraps well-vetted, platform-native OIDC libraries while enforcing secure defaults and consistent ergonomics.

- Supported flows:
  - Authorization Code + PKCE (default for browsers, mobile, desktop).
  - Client Credentials (service-to-service).
  - Device Authorization Grant (CLI/TV/IoT).
  - Optional: Refresh Token Rotation (with reuse detection) where supported by the IdP.

- Token handling:
  - Access tokens are short-lived; refresh tokens used for silent renewal.
  - Pluggable secure storage: browser (memory or httpOnly cookie via BFF mode), mobile (Keychain/Keystore), desktop (OS keyring), server (in-memory or KMS-backed).
  - Automatic clock skew handling, proactive refresh before expiry, and exponential backoff with jitter.
  - Optional DPoP or mTLS binding when available.
  - JWS validation of ID tokens using OIDC discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and JWKS caching with rotation.

- Security controls:
  - Enforce PKCE, state, nonce, and strict redirect URI validation.
  - CSRF protection for browser flows; CSP guidance and same-site cookies in BFF mode.
  - MFA-ready via OIDC ACR/AMR; propagate required claims.
  - Minimal scopes by default; audience and resource parameter support.

- API design:
  - Small, composable surface: init(config), signIn(), acquireToken(scopes, resource), getUser(), signOut(), onAuthEvent(cb).
  - Evented error model with typed errors; no global singletons.
  - Dependency-light core with adapters per platform; no custom crypto.

- Observability and ops:
  - Structured logs with PII redaction; metrics for token renewals/failures.
  - Feature flags for flow selection and BFF mode.
  - Compliance tests against a reference IdP (e.g., Keycloak/Okta) and conformance suites.

This decision standardizes on proven protocols, secure-by-default flows, and pluggable storage to meet web, mobile, desktop, and service use cases with minimal risk and maximal interoperability.

We will standardize our Nginx configuration around PHP-FPM workloads and ship a canonical include used by all PHP-backed services.

Key elements:
- Route application requests via try_files to index.php; only .php files are executed; no autoindexing.
- Forward .php to PHP-FPM over a Unix socket by default (configurable TCP), with a shared upstream definition per host. Set correct fastcgi_params (SCRIPT_FILENAME, PATH_INFO, PATH_TRANSLATED), include fastcgi.conf, and enable fastcgi_param HTTPS on TLS.
- Align timeouts and buffering with PHP-FPM: fastcgi_connect/read/send_timeout tuned to app SLAs; enable/limit buffering to prevent slowloris; set client_max_body_size to match PHP upload_max_filesize/post_max_size.
- Security hardening: deny execution of PHP in writable/upload directories; block access to hidden files (.git, .env, composer.*); restrict methods to GET/HEAD/POST; sanitize X-Forwarded-*; set real_ip from trusted proxies; add HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, and Referrer-Policy.
- Static asset handling: separate location blocks with long cache-control/immutable, gzip/brotli compression, and etag/last-mod; no PHP for static paths.
- Observability: uniform access/error log formats with request IDs; propagate request ID to upstream; optional slow-request logging via error_log notice/warn.
- TLS: HTTP/2/3 enabled where supported; TLS ciphers per baseline; ACME integration via dedicated location and automated reload.
- Configuration structure: reusable snippets (php.conf, security.conf, gzip.conf); per-app overrides allowed but must not weaken baseline; defaults templatized via infrastructure-as-code.

This decision ensures predictable behavior, security, and performance for PHP-FPM applications while reducing divergence and maintenance cost across environments.

- Run a periodic, idempotent cleanup job that executes cluster‑wide but is single‑active via a distributed lock/lease (e.g., Redis Redlock, Postgres advisory lock, or Kubernetes Lease). Schedule at a safe interval (e.g., every 5–15 minutes).

- Use broker-native retention and dead-lettering:
  - Set per-queue message TTL and max-retry policies.
  - Route messages exceeding retry limits to a dead-letter queue (DLQ).
  - Auto-expire DLQ messages after a configurable retention window.

- Enforce visibility/processing timeouts:
  - Detect and release “stuck” in-flight items whose lease/heartbeat exceeded the visibility timeout back to the ready queue.
  - Mark poison messages that exceed max retries as permanently failed (do not requeue).

- Apply datastore hygiene:
  - Remove completed/succeeded mail jobs older than a retention period.
  - Purge DLQs and associated payload blobs/attachments beyond retention.
  - Clean orphaned reservations/locks with no active worker heartbeat.

- Make cleanup safe and observable:
  - Implement rate limits and batch sizes to avoid broker/database pressure.
  - Expose metrics (counts of requeued, purged, DLQ size, orphaned leases), structured logs, and alerts on anomalies.
  - Provide a dry-run mode and feature flags for incremental rollout.
  - All thresholds (TTLs, retries, retention windows) are configuration-driven per environment.

- The Preservation Object (PO) name will be exactly the FileSet’s primary content digest encoded as lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256, with no prefixes, suffixes, extensions, or additional metadata (length: 64 chars).
- SHA-256 is the canonical algorithm for naming. If absent at ingest, compute it. Additional digests (e.g., MD5) may be stored as metadata but are not used for naming.
- The PO name is stable across re-ingest and independent of source filename, path, MIME type, and timestamps to ensure deterministic addressing and deduplication.
- Path layout may shard the digest into directory segments (e.g., ab/cd/…/abcdef…); however, the terminal object name remains the full digest. Sharding is an implementation detail and not part of the name.
- Collisions: Given SHA-256’s collision resistance, treat identical digests as the same content and do not create a separate PO. If policy requires distinct logical versions, represent them via metadata and references, not by altering the name.
- Backward compatibility: Existing POs with legacy names will be migrated to digest-only names. Maintain lookup aliases/indices from legacy IDs to the digest to avoid breaking references; do not rename the digest once assigned.
- Validation rules: lowercase [a-f0-9]{64} only; reject or recompute if input does not conform. Store the algorithm and any normalization steps (e.g., binary mode) in PO metadata for auditability.
- Future algorithms: If we adopt a new canonical digest, do not rename existing POs. Store additional digests in metadata and only switch naming for newly created POs after a deliberate migration plan.

We will standardize on OpenID Connect (OIDC) and OAuth 2.1 for user and service authentication, federating with a managed enterprise Identity Provider (IdP) as the single source of truth for identities and group membership. All interactive users must authenticate via SSO with MFA enforced by the IdP; privileged/admin actions require step-up MFA. External/partner users will federate through their IdP where possible; otherwise they will onboard to our IdP in a segregated tenant/realm.

Authorization will follow a deny-by-default model using role-based access control (RBAC) with optional attribute-based constraints (ABAC) for tenant/resource scoping. Application roles are mapped from IdP groups/claims and resolved to fine-grained permissions managed in the application. Service-to-service calls will use OAuth 2.0 client credentials with private_key_jwt or mTLS and least-privilege scopes.

Tokens will be short-lived JWT access tokens validated via JWKS with issuer/audience checks; refresh tokens will be rotation-enabled and bound to device/session. Web clients will store tokens in secure, HTTP-only, SameSite=strict cookies; SPAs will use backend-for-frontend (BFF) to avoid exposing tokens to the browser. Session timeout and idle limits will be enforced centrally.

All authn/z events (login, MFA, role/permission changes, failed attempts, privilege escalations) will be auditable. Provisioning and deprovisioning will be automated via SCIM or IdP APIs; local super-admin accounts will not exist. Secrets will be managed by the platform secret store; keys will be rotated regularly. This approach provides consistent, compliant MFA-backed SSO, centralized policy control, least-privilege enforcement, and secure inter-service authentication.

## Decision
- Primary lookup: query Payment by key == notification.merchantReference (our integration sets merchantReference to the commercetools Payment key at payment creation/redirect). This guarantees O(1) unique match.
- Secondary lookup: if merchantReference is missing or not our key, query by transaction.interactionId matching notification.originalReference (for follow-up events) or notification.pspReference (for first event). We search both Authorization and Refund/Chargeback transaction types as applicable.
- Tertiary lookup: if still not found, query by custom field ctPaymentId or interfaceId if we propagated it to Adyen as merchantReference/metadata, and by interfaceInteractions fields where we recorded previous Adyen references.
- On first successful match, persist linkage for future events:
  - Add/update transaction with interactionId = pspReference (or originalReference for follow-ups) and correct type/state.
  - Append interfaceInteraction of type adyen-notification containing full payload, pspReference, originalReference, eventCode, and a computed notificationFingerprint for idempotency.
  - Store adyenMerchantReferenceObserved = merchantReference and lastSeenPspReference(s) in custom fields for fast future matching.
- Idempotency and de-duplication: before mutating, check for existing interfaceInteraction with same notificationFingerprint (hash of [eventCode, success, pspReference, originalReference, amount, currency]) and skip if present.
- Concurrency: use optimistic locking with bounded retries on 409; on conflict, re-fetch and re-evaluate idempotency before applying actions.
- No-match handling: acknowledge to Adyen but route the notification to a reconciliation DLQ with the payload and reason; auto-retry for transient CTP errors (5xx) with exponential backoff.
- Observability: log correlationId = pspReference and include payment.id/key in logs once matched to aid tracing.

## Decision

Expose a single GraphQL endpoint as the primary API for client applications.

- Approach: Schema-first development using SDL, with automated code generation for server and client types (GraphQL Code Generator). Maintain the schema in a registry and enforce schema checks in CI.
- Transport: GraphQL over HTTP. Use persisted queries; serve cacheable queries via GET and mutations via POST. Enable batching.
- Pagination & patterns: Adopt Relay-style connections for pagination. Prefer nullable fields with explicit error signaling via GraphQL errors and extensions codes.
- AuthZ/AuthN: Authenticate via JWT in the Authorization header. Enforce authorization at resolver/field level using custom directives/guards.
- Performance: Use per-request DataLoader for batching and memoization to prevent N+1 queries. Implement query complexity/depth limits, timeouts, and cost-based throttling. Support CDN caching for persisted GET queries and response caching where safe.
- Subscriptions: Support real-time use cases via graphql-ws over WebSocket; fall back to polling where needed.
- Federation: Start with a modular monolith schema. If/when services split, adopt GraphQL Federation with clear ownership boundaries and entity composition.
- Error handling: Return spec-compliant errors with standardized extensions (code, path, correlationId). Avoid leaking internal details.
- Observability: Integrate tracing and metrics (OpenTelemetry) at resolver level; log query signatures, latency, and error rates.
- File uploads: Support multipart requests conforming to the GraphQL multipart request spec.
- Versioning & evolution: Evolve the schema additively, using @deprecated and documented migration timelines. Avoid breaking changes; introduce new fields/types instead.
- Tooling: Provide GraphiQL/Explorer in non-prod, schema docs, examples, and linting.

We will adopt a composable stacked handler (middleware) model, implementing a chain-of-responsibility around request/response processing. All cross‑cutting concerns (auth, tracing/metrics, logging, validation, rate limiting, caching, retries, circuit breaking, content negotiation, transformation) will be expressed as discrete, reusable handlers that can be composed in a deterministic order.

Key aspects:
- Define a minimal Handler interface with next(request) -> response, supporting sync/async, short‑circuiting, and error propagation.
- Provide a standard execution pipeline with well-defined phases and ordering guarantees (e.g., inbound: auth → validation → rate limit → business handler; outbound: transform → metrics/logging).
- Support global, per-service, and per-route stacks via declarative configuration, with sensible defaults and the ability to override/insert/remove handlers.
- Ensure handlers are side-effect free and idempotent where possible; require explicit context passing for shared state; prohibit hidden global mutations.
- Provide structured context (correlation IDs, deadlines/cancellation tokens) and tracing hooks to allow end-to-end observability.
- Establish contract for error types and mapping to responses/status codes to avoid duplicated error handling across handlers.
- Include performance guidelines: minimal allocations, early short-circuit (e.g., cache hit, auth fail), and batched metrics/logging emission.
- Offer testing utilities and golden pipelines for common use cases; publish a curated default stack and a compatibility shim for legacy interceptors/filters.
- Allow feature flags to toggle handlers and gradual rollout, plus telemetry to evaluate impact.

This model standardizes cross-cutting logic, improves reuse and testability, and enables incremental evolution without entangling business handlers.

## Decision
Adopt a canonical on-disk layout using a type-namespace-id directory scheme to ensure predictability, scalability, and cross-platform compatibility:

- Path pattern: {type}/{namespace}/{id}/ with optional versioned subfolders: {type}/{namespace}/{id}/v{semver}/
- Naming rules:
  - type, namespace, id: lowercase kebab-case with optional dots/underscores for namespace: [a-z0-9][a-z0-9\-._]* (no spaces; no trailing dots; case-insensitive uniqueness on case-insensitive filesystems).
  - type is a controlled vocabulary (e.g., service, job, dataset, config, policy, secret, workflow, doc).
  - namespace follows org.project.env style (DNS-like) using dots to preserve the 3-level structure.
  - id is immutable and unique within (type, namespace).
- Directory contents under each id (or version):
  - metadata.yaml (required): name, owner, description, labels, timestamps.
  - spec.(yaml|json): machine-readable definition (schema varies by type).
  - artifacts/ (optional): binaries/assets.
  - refs/ (optional): external references, checksums.
  - logs/ (optional): operational logs/traces.
  - README.md (optional): human docs.
- Versioning:
  - Use semver for subdirectories; create symlink or file alias latest pointing to the highest stable version.
  - Changes requiring breaking semantics must create a new version; patch/minor updates allowed in-place within that version directory.
- Indexing and discovery:
  - Auto-generate index.json at each level listing children and minimal metadata, enabling fast lookup without deep traversal.
- Lifecycle and deprecation:
  - Deprecate by adding DEPRECATED file with rationale and sunset date; archival via archive/ outside primary tree.
- Constraints:
  - No cross-platform forbidden characters; max component length 100 chars; full path length < 260 chars for Windows compatibility.
  - Atomic updates: write to temp and rename; prohibit in-place mutation of metadata without version bump unless explicitly allowed by type policy.

This structure standardizes addressing, enables tooling to resolve resources by fully qualified path, and scales across organizations and environments.

## Decision

Adopt Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR) as the standard for documenting architectural decisions in this project.

- Use the latest stable MADR version (3.x) and include a pinned adr-template.md in-repo.
- Store records under docs/adr/ using sequential numbering (NNNN-title.md), starting at 0001.
- Follow MADR sections: Context and Problem Statement, Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Decision Outcome, Pros and Cons of the Options, Links.
- Maintain statuses (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded). Accepted ADRs are immutable; changes require a new ADR that supersedes or amends the prior one.
- One decision per ADR; keep scope small and specific.
- Submission via pull request with lightweight RFC-style review; at least one architect approval required.
- Maintain an index (docs/adr/README.md) listing all ADRs with status and links.
- Cross-link ADRs and reference related issues/PRs to ensure traceability.
- Provide a helper script or documented steps to scaffold new ADRs consistently.
- Apply this standard across relevant repositories to maximize consistency and knowledge sharing.

## Decision

Adopt Slate.js as the base rich-text editor for timed text, integrated in our React stack, with a custom timing layer to represent per-token timestamps and media sync.

- Editor foundation: Slate.js provides schema-less, JSON-based document modeling, custom elements/marks, robust IME support, and a well-maintained plugin ecosystem suitable for time-coded text interactions (playhead-follow, selection-to-playback, ranged decorations).
- Data model: Canonical transcript stored as an ordered list of tokens {id, text, start, end, speaker?, confidence?}. The editor view materializes these tokens into Slate inline nodes within paragraph blocks (and optional speaker/section blocks). Timing remains attached to tokens; textual edits update or invalidate timing as needed.
- Media sync: Use decorations to highlight the active token range based on the player time; map cursor/selection to time ranges and vice versa. Provide keyboard shortcuts for navigation by word/sentence and snapping to media timecodes.
- Editing rules: Support insert/delete/merge/split with safeguards to preserve token identity where possible; degraded mode for “plain text” edits that drop timing for affected spans with visual indicators and recovery tools (re-align, re-time).
- Import/export: Support WebVTT, SRT, TTML/DFXP, and JSON interchange. Converters maintain timing and speaker metadata when formats permit; fallbacks gracefully degrade.
- Performance: Virtualized rendering for large transcripts, lazy decoration computation, and chunked operations for documents >100k tokens.
- Accessibility/i18n: Full keyboard controls, ARIA roles, screen-reader cues for time boundaries, RTL scripts, and CJK IME correctness.
- Collaboration: Initial single-user local edits; design compatible with operational transform/CRDT backends (e.g., Yjs + Slate) for future real-time co-editing.
- Not chosen: ProseMirror/Draft.js—both viable, but Slate’s simpler data model and decoration ergonomics best fit time-ranged highlights and token-centric logic with lower implementation overhead.

Use deterministic, parameterized AMI resolution instead of ad‑hoc image searches.

- Publish every built AMI to AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with immutable, versioned keys (for example: /images/<family>/<os>/<version>) and a mutable alias key per channel (for example: /images/<family>/<os>/stable -> 2026.01.23, /images/<family>/<os>/latest -> 2026.01.24).
- Infrastructure code (Terraform/CloudFormation) will resolve AMI IDs exclusively via SSM Parameter Store, not via DescribeImages wildcards or “most_recent”.
- Production and other long‑lived environments must pin explicit version parameters (immutable keys). Non‑prod may use the channel alias (“latest”) if desired for faster iteration.
- The image pipeline owns writing/updating SSM parameters, attaching required metadata (build number, git sha, hardening profile) and enforcing uniqueness. It also tags AMIs consistently (Name, Family, Version, Channel, Source, CreatedAt) and shares them across accounts as needed.
- Launch templates and ASGs receive the AMI ID from IaC at deploy time; rollbacks are performed by repointing the channel alias to a previous version (non‑prod) or updating the pinned version (prod) and redeploying.
- Disallow in-repo hardcoded AMI IDs and DescribeImages filters in IaC via linting/policy-as-code; only SSM lookups are permitted.
- Maintain a retention/pruning policy tied to SSM metadata to deregister stale AMIs and clean snapshots once all references are gone.

This approach provides reproducibility (pinned versions), safe promotion (channel aliases), auditable provenance (SSM metadata/tags), and eliminates nondeterministic AMI lookups that cause drift and unpredictable rollouts.

We will express volatile business policies as declarative rules executed by a stateless rule engine, while keeping core workflows and invariants in imperative application code. The rule engine will be used only for decision logic that changes frequently, benefits from transparency, or requires non-technical authoring.

Rules will be stored as versioned, testable artifacts (DSL/JSON/YAML), with clear inputs/outputs and no side effects. The engine will provide deterministic evaluation, conflict resolution (priority/salience), and short-circuiting, and will support explainability via evaluation traces. A dedicated “Decision Service” will encapsulate rule evaluation behind stable application-facing APIs, with adapters to map domain models to rule facts and back.

Operationally, we will add rule authoring and review workflows (linting, unit tests, canary evaluation, and approvals), audit trailing for rule changes, and feature-flagged rollouts. Performance will be addressed via input normalization, memoization/caching of pure decisions, and bounded rule set sizes per decision. Observability (metrics and logs) will be built in to monitor hit rates, latencies, and decision distributions.

We will not migrate all logic into the engine: domain invariants, persistence, and side-effectful actions remain in code. The initial scope targets decisions like eligibility, pricing, routing, and entitlements. If complexity or performance regressions arise, we will fall back to code or split rules into smaller, composable decision points.

- Adopt PostgreSQL (v15+) as the primary relational database for all transactional data.
- Use a managed service for non-local environments (e.g., AWS RDS/Aurora Postgres, GCP Cloud SQL, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL) with single-writer topology; enable automated backups and point-in-time recovery.
- Use Dockerized Postgres for local development and Testcontainers for integration tests in CI.
- Manage schema with versioned, forward- and backward-compatible migrations using Flyway; all migrations must be transactional and idempotent where possible.
- Enforce security: TLS in transit, encryption at rest, least-privilege database roles, and credentials rotated via a secrets manager; disable superuser access in app contexts.
- Use connection pooling and retry logic appropriate to the runtime; set sensible timeouts and statement time limits to protect the database.
- Standardize data conventions: UTC everywhere, timestamptz for temporal data, UUID (v4) or bigint surrogate primary keys, normalized schema, constraints and indexes defined in migrations; use JSONB only when justified.
- Observability: enable pg_stat_statements, slow query logging, and integrate metrics/alerts for replication lag, connections, CPU/IO, storage, and bloat.
- Scale: allow read replicas for read-heavy workloads; avoid cross-service database sharing—each service owns its schema; no cross-database joins.
- Access layer: use parameterized queries or a vetted ORM/SQL library per language; prohibit ad-hoc SQL building to prevent injection.

We will transfer artefact binaries through a centralized, OCI-compliant artifact repository (e.g., Artifactory/Harbor/GHCR/ECR), not via source control, email, or ad‑hoc storage. All pipeline stages publish once and consume by content digest (sha256), ensuring immutability and deduplication.

- Publishing: producers push artefacts with both a semantic tag (e.g., app:1.4.2) and a digest reference. Overwrites are disabled; only new tags may point to existing digests.
- Consumption: consumers pull by digest; tag-to-digest resolution occurs at promotion time to avoid “latest” drift.
- Integrity and provenance: every artefact includes a checksum file and is accompanied by an SBOM and an in-toto/SLSA provenance attestation stored as separate objects in the same repo namespace.
- Security: transfers use TLS 1.2+ with mutual auth where supported. CI/CD authenticates via short‑lived OIDC federated tokens; no long‑lived credentials in pipelines.
- Large files: uploads use multipart/chunked transfer with automatic retry and resume. Clients must support parallel segments to optimize throughput.
- Caching and distribution: a pull‑through cache/CDN is enabled for remote sites to reduce latency; byte‑range requests are supported when available.
- Portability: a thin compatibility layer abstracts the chosen backend so environments may use different providers with identical semantics.
- Retention: artefacts are immutable; lifecycle policies retain promoted digests indefinitely and prune unreferenced snapshots after a defined window.

This approach provides reliable, secure, and reproducible binary transfers across environments and pipelines.

## Decision

Adopt an A/B (dual‑root) operating system layout with a separate persistent data volume.

- Maintain two immutable root partitions (rootfsA, rootfsB). Only one is active at a time; the inactive slot is used for updates.
- Perform OS/application updates by writing the new image to the inactive root, validating integrity/signature, running offline preflight checks, then atomically switching the boot target via bootloader flags. Implement post‑boot health checks with automatic rollback to the previous root on failure.
- Mount the active root read‑only. Use tmpfs for ephemeral paths (e.g., /tmp) and, where necessary, overlayfs for limited writable areas that do not require persistence across reboots.
- Provide a dedicated encrypted data volume (e.g., /data) for all persistent state: application data, configs, secrets, logs, and caches intended to persist. Bind‑mount specific subpaths into application expected locations (e.g., /var/lib/<app>, /etc/<app>) to enforce the write boundary.
- Enforce that no application writes outside /data; CI and runtime policy checks (e.g., AppArmor/SELinux) will gate this.
- Manage data volume schema/versioning with idempotent migrations triggered on first boot after switch; require backward‑compatible migrations or explicit guardrails to prevent downgrade corruption.
- Enable periodic snapshots/backups of /data, quotas where needed, fsck on boot, and metrics/alerts on update health and rollback events.
- Standardize bootloader integration (A/B slot metadata, retry/rollback counters) and image signing to ensure safe, recoverable OTA updates while isolating persistent state from OS churn.

Use two complementary queuing systems with clear responsibility boundaries:

- RabbitMQ (via Bunny) for inter-service messaging, publish–subscribe, and event-driven integration. Use topic/fanout exchanges for domain events, at-least-once delivery semantics, durable queues, and dead-letter exchanges for poison messages. Standardize message envelopes (type, id, correlation_id, occurred_at, schema version), require idempotent consumers, and enforce message size limits (payload by reference if large). Use per-environment virtual hosts, TLS, and authenticated app users. Observability via queue/exchange metrics and consumer lag alerts.

- Redis + Sidekiq for in-process/background job execution within a service (email delivery, webhooks, retries, scheduled jobs, CPU/IO offloading). Leverage Sidekiq’s retries with exponential backoff, unique jobs for de-duplication, and queues by priority. Jobs must be idempotent and store external side effects atomically where possible. Use Redis auth/TLS and set eviction policy to noeviction for reliability.

Do not use RabbitMQ for long-running jobs or Sidekiq for cross-service event distribution. Cross-system bridges are explicit and minimal (e.g., a dedicated consumer that translates a RabbitMQ event into a Sidekiq job when needed). Provision both as managed services where possible; treat them as independent failure domains with circuit breakers and back-pressure. Document routing keys, queue names, and schemas in the integration catalogue.

We will adopt a “docs-as-code” approach so documentation lives with the code, evolves via pull requests, and is validated by CI. All technical docs (READMEs, runbooks, ADRs, API contracts, architecture views) will be stored in the repository as Markdown and diagrams-as-code.

We will generate documentation from executable sources wherever possible:
- APIs: Define OpenAPI contracts first and generate reference docs and client stubs; for JVM services we may use Spring REST Docs if more appropriate.
- Tests: Use BDD/executable specifications (e.g., Gherkin/Cucumber) and illustrative integration tests as living examples, published in the site.
- Contracts: Use consumer-driven contract tests (e.g., Pact) to document and verify service interactions.
- Architecture: Maintain architecture-as-code using Structurizr DSL and/or PlantUML/Mermaid; generate views (C4) in CI.

We will publish a single documentation site (e.g., MkDocs) built on each merge to main and nightly, with versioning tied to releases. The site will include API docs, runbooks, onboarding, ADRs, and architecture views.

We will enforce quality gates in CI: linting, spellcheck, link checking, code/doc sync checks (e.g., fail build on API changes without updated OpenAPI/Changelog), diagram generation, and test status badges. Every code change that alters behavior must update relevant docs; PR templates will require doc impact assessment.

We will assign ownership for each documentation area, define contribution guidelines, and review docs alongside code. We will automate changelog generation and surface key operational metrics/sLOs in the docs. This ensures documentation remains accurate, test-backed, and continuously updated as the system evolves.

Adopt the Spring Framework (via Spring Boot 3.x on Spring Framework 6) as the foundation for the server component. We will build a JVM-based service on Java 21, using Spring’s dependency injection, configuration, and ecosystem for rapid, maintainable development.

Concretely:
- Use Spring Boot starters to standardize dependencies and auto-configuration.
- Prefer Spring MVC (Servlet stack with embedded Tomcat) for synchronous request/response; evaluate Spring WebFlux only for clearly reactive, high-concurrency scenarios.
- Use Spring Data (JPA with Hibernate) for relational persistence; apply Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation) for input validation.
- Secure endpoints with Spring Security (JWT/OAuth2 Resource Server where applicable).
- Provide operational features with Actuator and Micrometer (Prometheus/OTel exporters) for health, metrics, and tracing.
- Externalize configuration via Spring Boot config profiles and environment variables; integrate Spring Cloud Config if central configuration becomes necessary.
- Package as a container using Spring Boot’s layered jars and buildpacks; deploy as a single service (modular monolith or microservice as per system architecture).
- Implement testing with Spring Boot Test (slice tests, testcontainers for integration).

This decision aligns with team expertise, leverages a mature ecosystem, accelerates delivery, and supports production-grade concerns (security, observability, configuration) with minimal boilerplate.

We will support a user-provided relay state across authentication flows and round-trip it unchanged, while enforcing strict validation and security controls. The relay state will be treated as an opaque value and supported for SAML (RelayState) and OAuth2/OIDC (state). Two modes are allowed:
- Opaque reference: a one-time, server-generated nonce that maps to server-side stored return/intention data (preferred).
- Direct intent: a URL/path or small JSON blob describing the desired post-auth action.

Constraints and safeguards:
- Max size 1024 bytes; URL-safe characters only; reject/bucket to opaque mode if exceeded or malformed.
- If conveying a redirect target, only relative paths or URLs on a tenant-specific, allowlisted set of domains; otherwise fall back to a safe default.
- All client-provided relay state is wrapped with a server-generated CSRF/anti-replay token (nonce + timestamp) and HMAC-signed; tampering, expiry, or mismatch results in discard and default post-auth redirect.
- For OIDC, we continue to set our own state for CSRF; user relay state is embedded within and validated server-side. For SAML, we bind RelayState to the auth request ID and session.
- Relay state is single-use; consumed at first successful callback.
- Multi-tenant isolation: relay data is scoped to tenant and client; cross-tenant/state reuse is rejected.
- Logs store only hashed/truncated relay values; PII is not persisted in relay state.
- SDKs and SP integrations expose a uniform parameter (relay_state) and helpers to create opaque references; UI links may include ?relay=… within the above limits.

Failure behavior: on invalid/missing relay state, redirect to the tenant’s default post-auth destination.

Send a single consolidated confirmation email to the submitter and a single consolidated notification to the service team per submission, instead of multiple per-step/per-recipient emails. Use a shared team mailbox or Notify distribution list for the internal notification. Include a concise summary of the submission, key metadata, and links to view/download details in the application rather than attaching files. Suppress intermediate “in-progress” messages; only send on successful submission (and a single failure email if final processing fails). Implement idempotency keys and deduplication to prevent duplicate sends on retries. Configure Sidekiq/queue retries with exponential backoff without generating additional user-visible emails. Enable optional daily digests for non-critical updates instead of immediate notifications.

We will standardize all UK postcode validation, normalization, and lookup (including geocoding to lat/lng, outcode/incode parsing, and administrative area resolution) through the postcodes.io public API. The application will integrate via a lightweight HTTP client library encapsulated in a dedicated PostcodeLookup service, implementing strict timeouts, exponential backoff retries, and short‑lived caching of successful responses to reduce latency and external calls. All requests will use HTTPS and no API key is required. The service will accept raw user input and rely on postcodes.io for normalization (e.g., spacing/casing) and validation, returning a canonical format to the domain layer. Where feasible, batch endpoints will be used for higher‑throughput operations. The solution will be UK‑only; for any future non‑UK needs we will introduce an explicit abstraction to allow alternative providers without changing callers.

We will use React as the primary JavaScript framework for building the web client. The application will be implemented with React 18, using functional components and Hooks as the standard pattern. We will pair React with TypeScript to ensure type safety and maintainability. For application scaffolding, routing, and server-side rendering/SSG, we will adopt Next.js (app router), leveraging its built-in optimizations (code splitting, image optimization, incremental static regeneration) and file-based routing. Styling will be handled with CSS-in-JS or utility-first CSS as appropriate to the product ADRs, but framework choice remains React-centric. This decision standardizes our front-end stack on the React ecosystem, aligns with team expertise, leverages a mature ecosystem and hiring pool, and supports both SPA and SEO-friendly SSR use cases without switching frameworks.

## Decision

We will consolidate our CI/CD on GitLab CI/CD and migrate existing pipelines from Github Actions/CircleCI/Jenkins to .gitlab-ci.yml. GitLab becomes the single source for build, test, security scanning, release, and deployment orchestration.

Key choices:
- Use GitLab Runners: start with shared runners for general workloads; provision autoscaled, self-hosted runners (Docker executor) for privileged jobs (Docker builds, IaC) and cost/control. Tag runners to route jobs appropriately.
- Enforce governance: use protected branches/tags, code owners, and required approvals; restrict pipeline execution on default branches; lock secret usage to protected contexts; leverage environments with deployment approvals.
- Standardize pipelines: create reusable CI templates via include and centralized project templates; adopt multi-project pipelines and downstream triggers for cross-repo workflows; enable merge request pipelines with required green status before merge.
- Integrations: use GitLab Container Registry and Package Registry; integrate SAST/DAST/Dependency/Secret scanning; publish artifacts and SBOMs; push release assets via Release CLI.
- Environments & deployments: define review apps for MRs; stage/prod with manual/approval gates and canary/blue-green where applicable; use deployment variables and protected refs.
- Observability & cost: enable pipeline caching and artifacts retention policies; collect CI metrics; set concurrency limits.

Migration will be phased per repository with parity tests, then deprecate legacy pipelines and enforce GitLab-only CI.

We will reduce support for Internet Explorer 6–8 from “fully supported” to “best-effort, degraded experience” and cease active development and testing for these browsers. Concretely:
- Reclassify IE6–8 as deprecated; no new features or fixes will be implemented specifically for these browsers.
- Remove IE6–8 specific code paths, conditional comments, hacks, and polyfills that materially increase bundle size or complexity (e.g., PNG fixes, HTML5 shims beyond minimal document rendering).
- Set the official browser support baseline to evergreen browsers and IE11+ (or IE9+ where mandated), with build targets and transpilation aligned accordingly; no ES3/IE8-specific transpilation.
- Maintain a minimal, server-rendered, non-JavaScript-dependent fallback that allows core read-only navigation and critical transactions to complete, where feasible.
- Display a lightweight upgrade notice/banner for IE6–8 users with links to supported browsers.
- Update CI/CD to remove IE6–8 jobs; telemetry and error reporting will continue to monitor usage and critical failures only.
- Communicate the change in release notes and customer channels, including an end-of-life timeline if complete removal is planned.

This decision reduces maintenance overhead, bundle size, security exposure, and delivery times while preserving a basic path for legacy users during the transition period.

We will maintain a single, human-curated CHANGELOG.md at the repository root as the authoritative change history. The changelog will follow “Keep a Changelog” conventions and Semantic Versioning, organizing entries under Unreleased and versioned sections with the categories: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, and Security.

We will adopt Changesets to capture human-readable summaries at the time of change. Each PR that changes user-visible behavior must include a changeset with a clear, concise description and the intended semver bump (patch/minor/major). Changesets will be aggregated and transformed into CHANGELOG.md during the release process, preserving contributor-written summaries while ensuring consistent formatting.

Release automation will:
- Validate that user-impacting PRs include a changeset.
- Generate/update CHANGELOG.md and version numbers from accumulated changesets.
- Publish GitHub Releases using the generated notes.

Guidelines:
- Write PR titles and changeset summaries in imperative mood and explain the user impact, not implementation details.
- Group multi-package changes under their respective package sections (if a monorepo).
- Allow maintainers to edit the generated release notes for clarity before publishing.

We will not rely on raw git logs; unlabeled or drive-by commits will not appear without an associated changeset, ensuring the changelog remains readable and useful to humans.

We will standardize RSpec configuration around explicit, file-based organization and autoloading:

- Separate spec_helper (pure Ruby/unit specs) from rails_helper (Rails integration/features). .rspec requires spec_helper by default; Rails specs must require rails_helper.
- Autoload all support code by requiring spec/support/**/*.rb in rails_helper after Rails boots:
  Dir[Rails.root.join('spec/support/**/*.rb')].sort.each { |f| require f }
  Structure support as:
  - spec/support/matchers/**
  - spec/support/shared_examples/**
  - spec/support/helpers/**
  - spec/support/initializers/**
- Use conventional directories and naming:
  - Specs: spec/**/*_spec.rb (RSpec default pattern)
  - Fixtures: spec/fixtures and file fixtures at spec/fixtures/files; set
    config.file_fixture_path = Rails.root.join('spec/fixtures/files').to_s
  - Factories: spec/factories (loaded via FactoryBot railtie; no manual require)
- Enable RSpec Rails conveniences:
  - config.infer_spec_type_from_file_location!
  - config.use_transactional_fixtures = true (override per spec when needed)
- Improve developer workflow and determinism:
  - config.filter_run_when_matching :focus
  - config.example_status_persistence_file_path = 'tmp/rspec_examples.txt'
  - config.order = :random; Kernel.srand config.seed
  - config.mock_with(:rspec) { |m| m.verify_partial_doubles = true }
  - config.shared_context_metadata_behavior = :apply_to_host_groups
- Keep support autoload test-only:
  - Guard any environment-dependent setup inside support files with Rails.env.test?
  - Avoid requiring support files from application code.

This decision enforces predictable file layouts, fast unit runs via spec_helper, full Rails context via rails_helper, and zero-maintenance loading of helpers, matchers, and shared examples through a single, ordered require glob.

## Decision

Adopt MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) as the standard for documenting architectural decisions, using the latest stable 2.x template.

- Location: store ADRs under docs/adr/.
- Template: use the standard MADR sections (Context and Problem Statement, Decision, Status, Consequences, Considered Options, Pros and Cons, Links).
- Naming: one ADR per decision; filename format YYYYMMDD-short-title.md (or incremental numeric prefix); human-readable, lowercase, hyphenated titles.
- Scope: record all significant architectural and cross-cutting decisions (e.g., technology choices, patterns, interfaces, data contracts, infra, security).
- Workflow:
  - Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → (optionally) Deprecated/Superseded.
  - Accepted ADRs are immutable except for metadata; changes require a new ADR that links to and supersedes the prior one.
  - Changes introduced via pull request; review by architecture owners; decisions captured near the time of decision.
- Conventions:
  - Keep entries concise, with explicit assumptions and consequences.
  - Link related ADRs, issues, RFCs, and design docs.
  - Prefer clear rationale over exhaustive detail; capture dissent when relevant.
- Tooling: authors may use adr-tools (or equivalent) for convenience; not mandatory.
- Visibility: reference ADRs in READMEs and change logs; include in onboarding.

We standardize on flattened JSON-LD as the canonical wire format for parsing and emitting self-encoded dialects.

- Parser: Accept flattened JSON-LD (JSON-LD 1.1) as first-class input and resolve nodes by @id from a single top-level @graph. For backward compatibility, expanded JSON-LD is still accepted but is normalized via JSON-LD flattening before model construction. No AMF links are introduced during parsing; graph references remain JSON-LD links.
- Emitter: Emit only flattened JSON-LD by default with a single @graph, one materialization per @id, and JSON-LD references for all relationships. Node ordering is deterministic (sorted by @id) to ensure stable diffs. AMF links/extractToLink are not used in flattened emission.
- Identifiers: Require stable, absolute @id generation for all Linkable elements; emit @base only when needed. Preserve declared node identities across parse/emit cycles.
- Configuration: Provide a feature flag to opt-out (emit expanded for legacy consumers). Advertise via media type profile (application/ld+json; profile="flattened").
- Compatibility: Round-tripping guarantees that flattened->model->flattened is byte-stable except for non-semantic ordering/whitespace; expanded inputs are supported but will be re-emitted as flattened unless explicitly configured otherwise.

## Decision

Adopt OAuth 2.1 with OpenID Connect (OIDC) for user authentication and OAuth 2 for API authorization.

- Use Authorization Code flow with PKCE for all browser-based SPAs, mobile, and traditional web apps; do not use the implicit flow.
- Use Client Credentials flow for service-to-service, non-user interactions.
- Prefer standards-compliant external Identity Provider (IdP)/Authorization Server (e.g., Okta, Azure AD, Login.gov/enterprise) configurable per environment; no custom auth server.
- Issue short-lived JWT access tokens (e.g., 5–15 minutes) signed with asymmetric keys (RS256/ES256) and validate via IdP JWKS; rotate keys per IdP policy.
- Use refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection where supported; for SPAs prefer BFF pattern or use secure, httpOnly, SameSite=strict cookies for tokens; avoid storing tokens in web storage.
- Enforce MFA and PIV/enterprise policies at the IdP; rely on OIDC claims (acr/amr) to assert assurance level.
- Use standard OIDC scopes (openid, profile, email) and least-privilege API scopes; define resource-specific scopes for fine-grained access.
- Require state and nonce; support PKCE for all public clients; enable PAR/DPoP where available.
- Support RP-initiated logout and session revocation via IdP.
- Use standard libraries/SDKs for clients and resource servers; centralize token validation and error handling in middleware.
- Prefer opaque tokens for external exposure if introspection is available; otherwise JWTs with aud/iss checks.

We standardize all serverless functions on a single entrypoint named handler(event, context) with a canonical contract across providers and languages.

- Signature
  - event: a JSON object representing the trigger payload. All provider-specific events (HTTP, queue, cron, storage, pub/sub) are normalized into our CanonicalEvent shape before reaching business code.
  - context: metadata including requestId, deadline/timeout, auth principal (if any), tenant, and tracing fields.

- HTTP functions
  - event.http: { method, path, query, headers, body }
  - Return { statusCode, headers, body } where body is JSON (Content-Type: application/json).
  - Validation via JSON Schema/OpenAPI; 4xx for client/domain errors, 5xx for unexpected failures.

- Non-HTTP triggers
  - event.trigger: { type, id, source, data, attributes }
  - Return { acknowledged: true } or a typed result; retries managed by provider defaults unless overridden.

- Error and logging
  - Throwing/raising bubbles to a 5xx or retry; domain errors returned as structured 4xx with code and message.
  - Structured JSON logging; no stdout prints. Include requestId and correlationId on every log line.

- Tracing and correlation
  - Accept and emit W3C traceparent/tracestate; use X-Request-Id for correlation. Values propagated via headers/attributes and context.

- Configuration
  - Only environment variables for configuration/secrets (injected via provider secret store). No configuration in code.

- Performance and reliability
  - No reliance on global mutable state; optional init() for cold-start optimization only.
  - Enforce idempotency for non-HTTP triggers.
  - Timeouts set per function; long-running tasks delegated to async workers/queues.

- Packaging and layout
  - One entry file per function exporting handler. Shared libraries reside in a common module; no cross-function imports of code by relative paths outside the module.
  - Use our build tooling to generate shims/adapters that map provider-specific events to CanonicalEvent and responses back to provider formats.

This decision yields a uniform developer experience, simplifies testing, and allows portability between AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and GCP by swapping only the thin provider adapter.

## Decision

We will ship a single, canonical configuration file with each release (e.g., config.yaml), containing all supported settings, their defaults, and inline documentation. We will not publish multiple variants (e.g., dev/staging/prod/example) or split configuration across multiple files in release artifacts.

Teams are expected to derive any environment-specific configuration from this canonical file by copying it and adjusting values as needed, or by applying their own templating/overlay mechanisms outside of the release (e.g., CI-generated overlays). The repository and distributed packages will contain only the one reference file and its schema.

The canonical file will:
- Enumerate all keys with sensible defaults and comments.
- Include a schema version to facilitate automated validation and migrations.
- Mark deprecated keys inline and retain backward-compatible mapping where feasible for one deprecation window.

Any config migration tooling we provide will target this single file format. Container images and installers will bundle only the canonical file; no additional per-environment files will be created or maintained by the project.

## Decision

We will deliver the product as an embedded application that runs inside host containers (e.g., enterprise portals, EHRs, device dashboards) using an isolated micro-frontend loaded via iframe/WebView. The embedded app will expose a narrow, versioned integration surface via postMessage-based RPC (and, where supported, a host SDK/JS bridge) to request host capabilities (auth, navigation, file access, print, device features) without direct DOM access to the host. Authentication and authorization will be delegated to the host via OIDC/OAuth tokens passed through a secure out-of-band channel; the embedded app will not store credentials and will operate under the host’s session lifecycle.

The UI will be themable through a constrained contract (CSS variables, design tokens) and scoped via Shadow DOM to prevent style leakage.
