The artifact will be a versioned, static bundle served from our CDN, with cache-busting and integrity (SRI) enabled; hosts integrate by URL. For constrained or air-gapped environments, we will support an optional offline bundle with signed updates.

Communication will be strictly typed, backward compatible, and feature-flagged to allow safe evolution across host versions. Telemetry, auditing, and error reporting will flow to our observability stack with PII controls; host-provided logging endpoints will be supported when required. This approach maximizes distribution flexibility and security isolation, reduces per-host customization, and allows us to maintain a single codebase while meeting varied host constraints.

## Decision

Adopt a trunk-based development model with short-lived branches.

- The default branch is main; all production releases are built from main.
- Create short-lived feature branches from main named feature/<ticket-id>-<slug>.
- Create short-lived fix branches from main named fix/<ticket-id>-<slug>.
- Create release branches only when stabilizing a version: release/<major>.<minor> (kept days, not weeks). Only bug fixes and release metadata changes are allowed here.
- Create hotfix branches from the latest release tag when urgent production fixes are required: hotfix/<ticket-id>-<slug>, then merge back to main and the active release branch (or tag a patch release directly from main if safe).
- Protect main and release/*: require PRs, at least one approval, up-to-date status checks (lint, tests, security), and linear history via squash-merge.
- Use feature flags for incomplete work; no long-running branches.
- Tag releases on main (or release/* during stabilization) with annotated semantic version tags vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (optionally signed). Pre-releases use vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-rc.N.
- Support multiple supported lines with maintenance branches: maintain/<major>.<minor> for backports when needed; patch releases are tagged from these branches and merged forward into main.
- Automate versioning and changelog generation from conventional commits; CI gates publishing on tags.
- Delete merged branches to keep the repo clean.

## Decision

Adopt OpenSearch (managed) as the primary search engine, accessed via a thin domain adapter and queried through our Monocle Query Language (KQL subset per ADR #11). We will denormalize domain entities into dedicated indices (one index per entity type) optimized for relevance, filtering, and aggregations. Index schemas will include keyword, text (with analyzers), numeric, date, and nested fields as needed; we will support synonyms, stemming, highlighting, facets, and typo-tolerant autocomplete via edge n-grams.

Data synchronization will use an eventually consistent pipeline: application emits domain events to an outbox table; a background indexer service reads the outbox (or Debezium CDC when available), transforms records, and performs bulk indexing. Index writes are idempotent and versioned. We use index aliases to enable zero-downtime reindexing and blue/green schema migrations. For scale and cost, we enable index lifecycle policies (rollover/retention) for large/time-based data and tune refresh intervals for write-heavy workloads.

The search adapter abstracts OpenSearch specifics and exposes:
- Query execution (search, aggregations, pagination, sorting, highlighting)
- Autocomplete endpoints
- Relevance configuration (boosts, field weights)
- Index management (create, migrate, reindex, alias switch)
- Health and metrics

Security and multitenancy are enforced with filtered aliases or tenant filters embedded by the adapter. PII fields are excluded or tokenized per policy. Backups rely on managed snapshots. Observability includes slow logs, query traces, and indexer lag metrics.

For constrained deployments, a fallback PostgreSQL FTS implementation (GIN/trigram indexes) is provided behind the same adapter for basic search needs (no facets/typo tolerance). The default and recommended deployment is OpenSearch.

We will consume the shared frontend UI library as a versioned npm package rather than vendoring source or submodules. The library will be published to our private npm registry (e.g., GitHub Packages/Artifactory) and installed via Yarn, declared in package.json with semantic version ranges (caret for non-breaking updates; pin majors). React, React DOM, and TypeScript will be declared as peerDependencies in the library and satisfied in the application to avoid duplicate bundles and ensure compatibility.

We will import components via ES modules to enable tree-shaking, and rely on our bundler’s optimization (e.g., webpack/Vite) to eliminate unused code and CSS. The library will expose a stable public API, typed with TypeScript, and follow semver with CHANGELOG-managed releases. Theming will be provided through design tokens and CSS variables to avoid hard-coded styles; application-specific overrides occur via configuration rather than forking.

Release automation (CI) will handle versioning, changelog generation, and publishing; consumers will receive updates via Renovate/Dependabot PRs. No direct edits to library code within the app are permitted; any changes must be contributed upstream and released as a new version. For SSR contexts, the library must remain isomorphic (no DOM access at import time). Accessibility, i18n hooks, and styling strategy (CSS-in-JS or CSS Modules) will align with our application stack and be documented in the library.

This approach centralizes shared UI, enforces consistency, reduces duplication, and simplifies upgrades while maintaining clear boundaries between application and library.

We will adopt a canonical, opinionated entity model for the Catalog to standardize discovery, ownership, and dependencies across the estate. The core entity kinds and rules are:

- Canonical identifier: entityRef = <kind>:<namespace>/<name>; kind and name are immutable; namespace defaults to default.
- Entity spec versioned via apiVersion; validation via JSON Schema; ingestion via Git-backed YAML and API registration.

Core kinds:
- Domain: top-level business capability; aggregates Systems.
- System: cohesive product area; aggregates Components and APIs; partOf Domain.
- Component: deployable or reusable unit with spec.type ∈ {service, library, website, job, function, datapipeline} and spec.lifecycle ∈ {experimental, production, deprecated}; partOf System; dependsOn {Component|Resource}; providesApis; consumesApis; ownedBy Group|User.
- API: contract artifact with spec.type ∈ {openapi, graphql, asyncapi, protobuf}, lifecycle; providedBy/consumedBy Components; definitionLocation via annotations.
- Resource: infrastructure or external dependency (e.g., database, bucket, topic, secret); provisionedBy; ownedBy.
- Group: team/security group with nesting; owns {Domain|System|Component|API|Resource}; memberOf Group.
- User: person/bot; memberOf Group; owns where applicable.
- Template (optional): software template for scaffolding; produces Components/APIs per rules.

Standard relationships (directed):
- partOf, hasPart
- ownedBy, ownerOf
- dependsOn, dependencyOf
- providesApi, consumedBy
- parentOf, childOf (for Groups)
- provisionedBy (Resource <- Component/Template)

Metadata:
- metadata: {name, namespace, description, tags[], annotations{}}
- spec.owner must reference an existing Group/User entityRef.
- spec.system required for Component; spec.domain required for System.
- Compliance and links via well-known annotations (e.g., runbook, repo, pager, sdlc).

Change control:
- Breaking identifier changes require new entity; soft moves via deprecation annotations and redirect.
- Lifecycle gates enforced via policy (e.g., production requires owner, oncall, repo link, runbook, SLO).

This model will be the single source of truth for cataloged assets and will be extended via kind-specific schemas as needed.

## Decision

Adopt TypeScript as the default language for all new frontend and Node.js backend development. Migrate existing JavaScript codebases incrementally, prioritizing high-churn and high-risk modules first.

- Enable strict typing baseline: "strict": true, noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, and exactOptionalPropertyTypes across all projects.
- Standardize on a shared tsconfig base and project references for multi-package repos; prefer ES modules and target modern runtimes (ES2020+).
- Enforce type quality via ESLint with @typescript-eslint, Prettier for formatting, and strict CI gates (type-check, lint, test).
- Prefer explicit types for public APIs; use inference internally where clear. Disallow use of any, implicit any, and namespace imports; allow unknown with narrowing.
- Model domain contracts with interfaces/types; expose stable public types via .d.ts where needed. Generate types from API schemas (OpenAPI/GraphQL) and share DTOs across services when appropriate.
- Validate untrusted inputs at runtime (e.g., Zod/io-ts) at API boundaries to complement compile-time safety.
- Frontend: use .tsx with React; prefer function components with typed props/state; use React Query/Redux Toolkit with typed hooks; enable strict mode in Vite/Next.
- Backend: use ts-node/tsx for local dev; compile with tsc for production; Jest/Vitest with ts-jest/esbuild for tests.
- Maintain ambient type ownership: track @types dependencies; add shims only as a last resort.
- Provide onboarding guides, examples, and code templates; require TypeScript patterns in code reviews.

## Decision

Adopt a relational SQL schema (PostgreSQL) guided by the following conventions and constraints:

- Modeling: 3NF for core entities; use JSONB only for well-bounded extensible attributes with validation and GIN indexes as needed.
- Keys and identity: surrogate UUIDv4 primary keys (id) on all tables; enforce natural keys with unique constraints where applicable.
- Relationships: explicit foreign keys with ON DELETE/UPDATE behavior specified; junction tables for many-to-many.
- Concurrency and lifecycle: created_at/updated_at (UTC) on all mutable tables; optimistic locking via integer row_version; optional soft delete via nullable deleted_at where business requires recoverability.
- Multitenancy: tenant_id on multi-tenant tables referencing tenants; enable Row-Level Security policies to enforce tenant isolation; composite unique indexes to include tenant_id.
- Enumerations and reference data: dedicated lookup tables with FK constraints (avoid free-text enums); seed via repeatable migrations.
- Naming: snake_case, plural table names, singular column names; FK columns named <referenced>_id; constraints/indexes prefixed by table and purpose (e.g., orders_pkey, orders_customer_id_fkey).
- Indexing: primary, foreign, and unique indexes by default; additional covering/partial indexes based on read patterns; GIN on JSONB; avoid over-indexing writes.
- Partitioning: time- or tenant-based partitioning for high-volume tables when volume thresholds are met; use native declarative partitioning.
- Migrations: manage with versioned and repeatable migrations (Flyway/Liquibase); forward-only in shared envs; include reversible scripts for local; capture DDL in VCS.
- Access control: least-privilege roles (app_rw, app_ro); no object ownership by app user; separate migration role for DDL; audit who/when via session settings.
- Business logic: keep business logic in services; use views/materialized views for read models; stored procedures only for set-based heavy ops with clear ownership.
- Auditing: append-only audit/event tables for critical entities (who, when, before/after); leverage triggers cautiously, prefer application-sourced events when possible.
- Security and compliance: encrypt at rest; column-level encryption for sensitive PII (pgcrypto/KMS-managed); avoid storing secrets; support right-to-erasure via data minimization and segregation.
- Data retention: codify retention per entity; scheduled purges/anonymization.
- Observability: capture slow-query logs; schema-level comments for tables/columns.

This schema draft will be iterated via ADRs as domains evolve; breaking changes require deprecation plans and data migrations.

## Decision

Adopt Go modules and a multi-module monorepo with a go.work workspace at the repository root. Each independently versioned component (domain packages, adapters, applications/CLIs, SDKs) is a distinct Go module with its own go.mod, enabling clear boundaries, separate semantic versioning, and fast, incremental builds.

Project layout conventions:
- cmd/<app>: entry points for binaries (main packages) per application.
- internal/...: implementation details not intended for external use within the same module.
- pkg/...: only for APIs intentionally shared across other modules; prefer internal when in doubt.
- api/: protocol/IDLs (OpenAPI/Protobuf), generated code in api/gen with reproducible generation via tools.
- test/: cross-module integration/e2e tests and testdata where appropriate; unit tests colocated next to code.
- tools/: tool dependencies via a tools.go pattern.
- build/ and scripts/: build, CI, packaging, and dev tooling artifacts.

Module pathing:
- Root workspace managed by go.work (go 1.22+), listing all module directories.
- Module import paths follow VCS pathing: github.com/<org>/<repo>/<module>.
- Major versioning uses module path suffixes (e.g., /v2) when required per Go module semantics.

Dependency and build policies:
- No GOPATH reliance; module-aware builds only.
- Enforce stable, reproducible builds with -mod=readonly and checksum verification in CI.
- Avoid go mod replace in committed code except for local development within the workspace (go.work replaces).
- Discourage vendoring; enable only if mandated by environment, managed centrally per module.
- Prevent cyclic and layer-breaking imports; domain modules cannot import adapters or applications.
- Use build tags for platform-specific code; keep OS/arch-specific files suffixed accordingly.

This layout supports clean architectural boundaries, pluggability, parallel development, and independent release cadence within a single repository.

We will implement strict validation of identity assertions (SAML/OIDC) at the authentication boundary. The service will only accept assertions/tokens that pass all of the following checks:

- Signature: Require signed (and if provided, encrypted) assertions/tokens. Validate XML/JOSE signatures against an allowlisted algorithm set (e.g., RS256/RSASSA-PSS), reject none/weak algorithms, and pin to trusted IdP keys via key IDs and rotating JWKS/metadata.
- Issuer/Audience: Enforce exact match of issuer and audience values to configured identifiers for each environment/tenant.
- Time constraints: Validate exp, iat, nbf (or NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter for SAML) with a minimal, configurable clock skew (default ≤ 2 minutes). Reject expired, not-yet-valid, or long-lived tokens.
- Subject/Confirmation: For SAML, require Bearer subject confirmation with recipient matching the ACS URL; for OIDC, require nonce/state binding for browser flows and PKCE for public clients.
- Claims/Attributes: Enforce presence and format of required claims (sub, email, groups, acr/amr as applicable). Normalize and validate attribute values against schemas and whitelists; ignore unexpected attributes by default.
- Replay protection: Maintain a short-lived cache of assertion IDs/JTI to prevent replay within validity windows.
- Key/Metadata management: Fetch and cache IdP metadata/JWKS with signature validation and automatic rotation; support emergency key pinning and revocation.
- Environment isolation: Separate configuration per environment with distinct client IDs/audiences, issuers, and redirect/ACS endpoints.
- Observability: Emit structured security logs for validation outcomes (without PII) and expose metrics/alerts for validation failures and anomalies.
- Failure handling: Fail closed on any validation error; present generic user-facing errors while preserving detailed diagnostics in logs.
- Testing: Provide conformance test suites and negative tests for each rule; include contract tests with IdP(s).

This validation is enforced in a dedicated auth middleware/library used by all services, centrally configurable, and subject to regular security review.

Adopt ESLint as the single linter for the codebase and use the @typescript-eslint parser and plugin to lint TypeScript. Deprecate and remove TSLint and any duplicate linting pipelines. Standardize on a shared ESLint config that supports both JavaScript and TypeScript, integrates Prettier via eslint-config-prettier and eslint-plugin-prettier, and enforces consistent rules across all packages. Migrate existing TSLint rules to their ESLint equivalents, address or suppress incompatibilities with typed rules where necessary, and enable type-aware linting for projects with a valid TSConfig. Enforce linting in CI and pre-commit via lint-staged, fail builds on lint errors, and provide autofix scripts for developers. Keep the setup current with maintained versions of @typescript-eslint, ESLint, and TypeScript, pinning ranges to avoid known incompatibilities.

We will implement zero-downtime deployments for the E2E environment using a blue-green strategy at the namespace level in Kubernetes, combined with backward-compatible database migrations and strict health gating.

- Maintain two E2E namespaces (e2e-blue, e2e-green). Each deployment creates a fresh, immutable “next” environment (new color) from manifests/Helm with maxUnavailable=0, maxSurge≥1, readiness/liveness/startup probes, preStop hooks, and appropriate terminationGracePeriod.
- Route traffic via Ingress/Service Mesh (e.g., NGINX/Istio) using a stable E2E URL. Initially send 0% to the new color. After deployment, run automated smoke checks and readiness gates; then switch 100% of traffic atomically to the new color. If any gate fails, keep traffic on the old color and abort.
- Use PodDisruptionBudgets and surge/replica policies to ensure capacity during cutover. Disable HPA scale-to-zero and ensure sufficient baseline replicas for both colors during overlap.
- Apply database changes using an expand–migrate–contract (backward-compatible) workflow. Run “expand” migrations (e.g., add columns) before deploying the new app. Run background backfills as jobs. Only after the cutover and verification, perform “contract” migrations (e.g., drop old columns). All migrations must be idempotent and reversible.
- Seed data via snapshot/fixture jobs per environment; isolate test data to avoid cross-run interference.
- CI pipeline: provision new color → run schema expand → deploy services (rolling) → health + smoke → flip traffic → execute E2E suite → if successful, decommission old color; else, instant rollback by reverting traffic to the previous color.

## Decision

- Provide a consistent, discoverable help surface for every API:
  - GET / returns a compact JSON landing document with service name, version, environment, time, and Link headers to rel="help", rel="describedby" (OpenAPI), rel="health", rel="auth", and rel="support".
  - GET /help supports content negotiation: application/json returns machine-readable help (endpoints overview, auth schemes, error model, rate limits, examples); text/html returns human-readable docs.
  - Per-resource OPTIONS responds with allowed methods and Link rel="describedby" to the operation’s section in the OpenAPI document.

- Publish machine-readable documentation:
  - OpenAPI available at /openapi.json and /openapi.yaml (versioned per API version).
  - Include HAL/JSON:API-style links in responses where applicable to improve self-discovery.

- Standardize error help:
  - Use RFC 7807 problem+json; include type, title, detail, instance, and a help link (rel="help") to relevant guidance for that error.
  - Map common error codes to documented remediation steps.

- Standardize headers and metadata:
  - Link headers for help/describedby on all responses.
  - Correlation: X-Request-Id and X-Correlation-Id echoed back.
  - Support Accept-Language for localized help text; default to English.

- Versioning and caching:
  - Help and OpenAPI are version-scoped (e.g., /v1/help, /v1/openapi.json); root links to current stable.
  - Enable ETag and reasonable Cache-Control on help and OpenAPI resources.

- Tooling integration:
  - SDKs and CLI expose a help() method/command that fetches /help.
  - CI validates Link targets and OpenAPI consistency on each release.

We will preserve submission fidelity while protecting downstream integrity by introducing a dual-write pattern on ApplyApplication:

- Add two new fields: raw_payload (JSON) to store the original unvalidated input, and data_quality_status (enum: valid, invalid, corrected) with data_quality_errors (JSON) to capture validation failures.
- Keep existing domain columns constrained (FKs, enums, NOT NULL where business-critical). When a field value is invalid for a constrained column, do not coerce it into the constrained column; instead, store it verbatim in raw_payload and record the error in data_quality_errors. Constrained columns remain NULL/default.
- Gate business workflows: only records with data_quality_status = valid are eligible for processing/export; invalid records are visible in back-office tooling/queues for correction.
- Provide an admin-safe correction path that writes corrected values into constrained columns, preserves the original raw_payload, and transitions status to corrected (with audit trail).
- Relax only non-critical constraints where necessary by moving strictness to the application validation layer; keep primary keys, referential integrity, and invariants that ensure system consistency.
- Add indexes on data_quality_status and created_at for operational queues; add PII/PHI access controls to raw_payload.
- Implement telemetry to track invalid rates by source and schema version to drive upstream fixes.
- Define a migration path to reconcile legacy invalid data via background jobs without downtime.

This approach allows storing “invalid” inputs without corrupting the canonical model and prevents invalid data from contaminating downstream consumers.

## Decision

- Backend
  - Spring Boot 3.x (Java 17 LTS) as the primary backend framework for services (Spring Web MVC, Spring Validation, Actuator).
  - Spring Data JPA (Hibernate) for persistence; Flyway for database migrations.
  - Jackson for JSON serialization; springdoc-openapi for OpenAPI 3 documentation.
  - MapStruct for compile-time DTO/entity mapping; SLF4J + Logback for logging.

- Frontend
  - Next.js (React, TypeScript) as the main frontend framework (SSR/SSG as needed).
  - TanStack Query for server state; Context API for minimal client state.
  - Tailwind CSS for styling; Headless UI where needed for accessibility.

- Testing
  - Spock for backend unit/integration tests (as previously decided).
  - Testcontainers for integration tests against real dependencies (DB, message broker).
  - Jest + React Testing Library for frontend unit tests; Playwright for E2E.

- Build & Tooling
  - Maven for backend build and dependency management.
  - npm for frontend package management and scripts.
  - Docker for containerization; Compose for local orchestration.

- Rationale
  - Maximizes developer familiarity and ecosystem maturity.
  - Balances productivity (auto-configuration, conventions) with flexibility.
  - Ensures strong testing support and reproducible environments.
  - Aligns with prior ADRs (Next.js, Spock) for consistency across the stack.

We will not use React.FC or React.SFC to type functional components. Instead, we will define an explicit Props type and annotate components as standard functions returning JSX.Element (or ReactElement where appropriate). Children will be typed explicitly on Props when needed rather than relying on React.FC’s implicit children. Default props will be expressed via default parameter values or logical defaults, not defaultProps.

For advanced cases:
- Use React.memo and React.forwardRef with explicit generics and inferred return types.
- For components that render null, the return type may be JSX.Element | null.
- For polymorphic/as components, use well-scoped generic Props and utility types rather than FC.

This approach avoids the pitfalls of React.FC/SFC (implicit children, constrained generics, awkward defaultProps behavior, and less precise return typing), improves type inference and readability, and aligns with current React and TypeScript best practices across our codebase.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized format for all custom methods across the codebase and APIs, with a staged migration away from legacy patterns.

- Naming
  - Use lowerCamelCase with action-first verbs (e.g., fetchUser, calculateTotal).
  - Async methods must end with Async (e.g., fetchUserAsync).
  - Boolean predicates start with is/has/can.
  - Event handlers start with on and receive a single event object.
  - Remove legacy prefixes/suffixes (e.g., custom_, do_, _internal).

- Signatures
  - Order parameters as: subject, required inputs, optional options object, rest parameters.
  - Prefer a single Options object when >3 parameters or optional flags are present.
  - Do not accept null; use undefined for optional values.
  - Return explicit types; prefer Result<T, E> for recoverable domain errors over throwing.

- Side effects and purity
  - Methods are pure by default; document side effects in the docstring and name (imperatives like update/write).
  - I/O and stateful methods must be isolated from pure computation.

- Documentation
  - JSDoc/Docstring required: summary, params, returns, errors, side effects.

- Tooling and enforcement
  - Introduce lint rules and CI checks to enforce naming and signature conventions.
  - Provide codemods and examples for migration.

- Migration and compatibility
  - Maintain shims for legacy method names/signatures for two minor versions with deprecation warnings.
  - Apply changes to public APIs in the next major release; internal/private methods migrate immediately.

## Decision

Adopt the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern to provide client-specific APIs per user interface (e.g., Web, Mobile). Each client will have its own lightweight BFF that aggregates, orchestrates, and shapes data from the modular monolith (and future services), exposing a tailored API optimized for that client’s needs.

- The BFFs will handle cross-cutting concerns for their client: authentication/authorization delegation, request shaping, response composition, pagination, caching, rate limiting, feature flags, A/B toggles, and graceful degradation.
- BFFs will primarily expose REST endpoints; GraphQL may be used where client-driven querying and payload shaping are beneficial. API contracts are versioned and validated via schemas to prevent coupling.
- BFFs communicate with the monolith over internal, stable module APIs (HTTP/gRPC) and, when available, subscribe to domain events for cache warming and real-time updates.
- BFFs remain thin and stateless, with shared platform libraries for observability, error handling, and security. They are independently deployable to enable rapid UI iteration without impacting core domain services.
- This pattern isolates client-specific logic from the domain, protects internal models, reduces over/under-fetching, and creates a clear evolution path as we later extract services; BFFs will adapt while backend boundaries harden.

## Decision

Expose human-readable, stable names as the primary identifiers for IAM resources in all external-facing APIs and SDKs; retain UUIDs as internal primary keys and in audit/event streams.

- Identifier model:
  - Names are globally unique within their scope (e.g., tenant/account + resource type).
  - Names are case-insensitive, URL-safe, and immutable by default.
  - Allowed charset: lowercase a–z, 0–9, hyphen (-); length 3–63.
  - Duplicate name attempts return 409 Conflict; invalid names return 400.
  - Soft-deleted resources keep their names reserved for 90 days (configurable).

- API shape:
  - Resource endpoints use names: /users/{name}, /groups/{name}, /roles/{name}, /policies/{name}.
  - List/filter support name, prefix, and exact-match queries.
  - Policy documents and bindings reference principals and resources by name.
  - Provide resolution endpoints for migration and tooling: /resolve/user?id=… -> name and /resolve/user?name=… -> id.

- Mutability:
  - Renames are disallowed by default. A dedicated POST …/rename operation may be enabled per resource type; it atomically updates the name pointer to the same internal ID and emits audit events.

- Backward compatibility:
  - Maintain ID-based endpoints as deprecated for two releases; emit warnings and document migration.
  - SDKs prefer names; ID-based methods remain but are annotated as deprecated.

- Security and correctness:
  - Authorization is enforced on the resolved internal ID.
  - Audit logs and metrics include both name and UUID.
  - Names being guessable is acceptable; access control remains authoritative.

- Errors:
  - 404 when name not found (no existence leakage beyond standard authorization).
  - 409 on conflicts; 422 on rename constraint violations.

We will introduce server-side request classification to identify and count automated traffic and bots separately from human activity. Specifically:
- Add an HTTP middleware that tags each request with an actor label (bot, automated-internal, automated-external, human, unknown) based on: curated/regularly updated known bot user-agents and IP/netblocks; presence of a first-party identification header for our own automation (e.g., X-Client: monitoring|smoke|load-test); request characteristics (HEAD/GET-only, no cookies/JS, high frequency, healthcheck paths); and verification of legitimate crawlers via DNS reverse/forward checks where applicable.
- Emit labeled metrics to our observability stack (e.g., Prometheus counters and histograms with actor label) and structured logs for audit. Forward summarized counts to analytics/warehouse for daily aggregation and reporting.
- Instrument internal automated jobs and monitors to self-identify via a required header and/or OAuth client credentials with a dedicated “automation” audience/scope to ensure precise attribution.
- Provide dashboards separating automated vs human traffic, with alerts on unusual spikes in automated checks.
- Default to detection-only (no blocking) and fail-open if classification is uncertain; classify as unknown and exclude from human metrics.
- Minimize and protect data: do not persist raw IPs; store only hashed/aggregated forms; honor opt-out/DNT where applicable; document the processing in our privacy notice.
- Operationalize maintenance of bot signatures as configuration, version-controlled and redeployable without code changes; review/update quarterly and on incident.

This approach yields reliable counts of bot and automated checks without impacting user experience, while supporting monitoring, capacity planning, and security analytics.

We will require TLS peer verification for all HTTPS/TLS connections across services, tools, and environments. Certificate chain validation and hostname verification must be enabled and cannot be bypassed (e.g., no insecureSkipVerify, curl -k, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0, Requests verify=False). CI/CD will fail builds/tests that attempt to disable verification.

- Server authentication:
  - All public-facing endpoints must present certificates from approved public CAs, with HSTS enabled, TLS 1.2+ (or 1.3 where supported), and weak ciphers disabled.
  - Internal services must use certificates from an approved internal CA (or SPIFFE/SPIRE), with hostname/SAN validation enforced. Mutual TLS is preferred for service-to-service communication.

- Trust management:
  - Use a centrally managed trust store (OS trust store or a curated CA bundle baked into base images). Per-service trust overrides are prohibited unless approved and centrally distributed.
  - For tests and local development, use a test CA and inject its root into the trust store; do not disable verification.

- Operational controls:
  - Automate certificate issuance and rotation (e.g., ACME/internal PKI). Monitor and alert on expiry with thresholds (e.g., 30/14/7 days).
  - Infrastructure code must enforce TLS policies at load balancers, API gateways, and SDK/client configs. Linters/policies will detect and block insecure settings.
  - Health checks, migrations, and background jobs must also verify certificates.

- Exceptions:
  - Temporary exceptions are not allowed in production. For isolated local development only, exceptions require explicit opt-in and must prefer trusting a local CA instead of disabling verification.

## Decision

Adopt a minimal, opinionated configuration surface with a single, human-edited file as the source of truth. The schema will be flat (no deep nesting), strongly typed, and limited to essential, high-impact settings only. Sensible, secure defaults will be provided for all non-critical options; only secrets and environment-specific endpoints must be explicitly set.

We will not support templating, conditionals, includes, inheritance, or computed values in configuration. Advanced tuning, rarely used flags, and feature toggles will remain in code or be controlled via internal feature flags, not exposed as public config. Runtime reload of configuration will not be supported; changes require restart to reduce complexity and failure modes.

Provide a canonical example file and a CLI “init” command to generate validated starter configs. Implement strict validation at startup with clear, actionable error messages and a “dry-run validate” command. Version the schema and apply a documented, conservative deprecation policy (announce, warn, migrate, remove), along with an auto-migration tool for simple changes.

Keep formats simple and ubiquitous (e.g., YAML or TOML), disallowing custom extensions. Configuration keys and semantics will be stable and well-documented, favoring fewer, well-chosen options over flexibility.

## Decision

Introduce an extractToLink emission rule for expanded JSON-LD that, when enabled on a property (via dialect/shape metadata or emitter configuration), emits references as links rather than embedded nodes.

Rules:
- For any value of a property marked extractToLink, if the target node has a stable identifier, emit only a node object with @id (e.g., { "@id": "<iri>" }) at that position.
- Do not include any additional properties (e.g., @type or domain attributes) alongside @id in that position.
- If the target node has no identifier, do not extract: emit the full embedded node. Optionally, allow a separate, explicit setting to mint deterministic blank node identifiers; if not enabled, never mint identifiers just to extract.
- For multi-valued properties, deduplicate by identifier and emit a set of @id link objects.
- Avoid dual representation: when extractToLink applies, never also embed the same node under that property.
- During parsing, treat link objects and embedded nodes as equivalent references: resolve by @id when present; otherwise consume embedded content as-is.
- Ensure global emission remains lossless: the full description of a linked node must still appear elsewhere in the emitted document/graph (e.g., via separate top-level node emission or other occurrences), so no information is dropped solely due to extraction.
- Do not alter source maps beyond the link position; link emission maps only the @id token.

## Decision

Kotlin is adopted as the primary development language for JVM-based services and applications.

- All new production code is written in Kotlin. Existing Java code may remain, but should be incrementally migrated to Kotlin when modified (“touch-and-improve”).
- Use Kotlin coroutines for asynchronous and concurrent code; prefer Flow over Rx in new code. Legacy reactive code may remain until migrated.
- Adopt official Kotlin coding conventions and language features (null-safety, data/sealed classes, extension functions, value classes). Avoid unnecessary inheritance and favor immutability.
- Build with Gradle Kotlin DSL; enable strict compiler settings (treat warnings as errors where feasible) and strict nullability interop (-Xjsr305=strict). Target the current JVM LTS for compilation.
- Standardize on ktlint and detekt for style and static analysis; integrate into CI.
- Prefer Kotlin standard library and kotlinx libraries (coroutines, datetime, serialization where applicable) over third-party Java utilities. Use Java interop only when required.
- For interop: annotate Java APIs with nullability, avoid unchecked platform types, and wrap Java futures/streams with Kotlin equivalents.
- Provide onboarding and code review guidance specific to Kotlin to ensure consistent usage and maintainability.

We will standardize on upstream Dapr LTS releases and pin platform workloads to an exact Dapr minor.patch version per environment. Control plane (dapr-operator, placement, sentry, sidecar-injector) will be deployed via the official Helm charts, version-locked through GitOps (environment-specific HelmRelease/Chart references). Application sidecars will be injected by the Dapr injector and constrained via a namespace-level default and per-deployment override (dapr.io/sidecar-image and dapr.io/enabled annotations), ensuring the sidecar version never drifts from the control plane.

Release cadence:
- Evaluate each upstream LTS within 2 weeks of GA; adopt only after passing our conformance suite.
- Promote versions sequentially: dev → int → stage → prod using canary partitions and workload allowlists.
- Freeze feature flags on promotion; only critical patches allowed mid-cycle.

Compatibility policy:
- Only N-1 control plane to sidecar compatibility supported in production.
- Breaking changes gated behind feature flags; non-default features require explicit opt-in until one full release cycle.

Artifacts and provenance:
- Mirror Dapr images to our registry with immutable digests.
- Record SBOMs and signatures (cosign) for all control plane images.
- Capture Helm chart, values, and image digests in a signed release manifest committed to the ops repo.

Upgrade/rollback:
- Blue/green upgrades of control plane via Helm with health and e2e smoke tests.
- Rollback by reapplying the previous signed manifest; sidecars are pinned, preventing unintended upgrades.
- Data-plane components (state stores, pub/sub) are upgraded separately with provider-specific playbooks.

Observability and SLOs:
- Require zero failed sidecar injections and <0.1% RPS error delta during canary before promotion.
- Publish runbooks and deprecation timelines; unsupported versions are removed one cycle after replacement.

## Decision

We will allow TODO-style annotations only when they are traceable, time-bound, and enforced by automation.

- Allowed tags: TODO (short-term task), FIXME (known defect), HACK (temporary workaround), DEBT (tech debt). Each must include:
  - Reference: issue ID or URL (required)
  - Owner: Git username (required)
  - Date: ISO date added or due (required)
  - Brief intent (<=5 lines)
  - Example: TODO(#1234) @jdoe 2026-02-15: Replace mock with real payment client.

- Before merge, every TODO/FIXME/HACK/DEBT must have a corresponding issue; draft PRs may contain temporary TODOs but they must be resolved or ticketed prior to merge.

- CI will enforce format and traceability and will fail for:
  - Missing/invalid issue link, owner, or date
  - Stale items beyond 30 days (TODO/FIXME/HACK) or past due date (DEBT), unless the linked issue is open and updated within 30 days.

- When closing an issue, related code TODOs must be removed or updated in the same PR; PR descriptions should reference and close the linked issues.

- Keep context minimal in comments; move details to the issue. Prefer refactors/tests over lingering TODOs.

- We will run a monthly grooming job/report to review outstanding items and re-triage or escalate as needed.

## Decision

Assign every Report a single, immutable, globally unique reference (ReportRef) produced by the back end and treated as opaque by clients.

- Identifier scheme: URN with a constrained path
  urn:reports:<tenant>/<source>/<report_type>/<subject>/<period>[@v<version>]
  - tenant: logical owner (e.g. org or environment)
  - source: producing system
  - report_type: canonical type slug
  - subject: natural subject key (e.g. account-id, cohort-id); composite keys joined by “+”
  - period: ISO-8601 interval or date (e.g. 2025, 2025-01, 2025-01-31, 2025-Q1, 2025-01/2025-01-31)
  - version (optional): major schema/content contract version starting at v1
- Encoding rules:
  - Lowercase; ASCII; components slugified; reserved chars percent-encoded
  - No whitespace; max length 512 chars
  - Case-insensitive comparison; store and emit canonical lowercase form
- Generation:
  - Deterministic from natural keys where available; if subject lacks a stable natural key, append “#<uuidv4>”
  - Created by back-end services only; clients must not construct or parse ReportRef
  - Idempotent: same (tenant, source, report_type, subject, period, version) yields same ReportRef
- Stability:
  - Immutable once issued and never re-used
  - Breaking schema/content contract changes bump version (vN); non-breaking revisions do not alter ReportRef and are tracked via separate revision metadata
- Usage:
  - Primary key across storage, APIs, events, and links; included in all report payloads
  - Used as idempotency key for creation and as correlation key in pipelines
- Aliases:
  - Legacy or external IDs may be stored as aliases; APIs must resolve aliases to the canonical ReportRef and return the canonical form in responses

We will containerize all application services using Docker to standardize build, runtime, and deployment. Each service will include a versioned, multi-stage Dockerfile that produces minimal, immutable images, runs as a non-root user, and leverages .dockerignore. Base images will be pinned to specific digests and regularly updated; images will be vulnerability-scanned in CI.

For local development, we will use Docker Compose to orchestrate app services and dependencies, with developer-friendly overrides. Configuration will be provided via environment variables, with secrets injected through Docker/CI secret mechanisms (never baked into images).

CI will build reproducible images (using BuildKit/Buildx for multi-arch when needed), run tests inside containers, tag images by commit and semantic version, and push to a centralized container registry. Production deployments will consume these images via our chosen container platform/orchestrator, ensuring parity across environments.

We will maintain shared base images and templates, document common patterns (health checks, logging to stdout/stderr, graceful shutdown), and enforce resource limits and entrypoint conventions to ensure consistent, secure, and observable containers across all applications.

* Introduce build-time SCSS feature flags by generating a partial _feature-flags.scss during theme compilation from the centralized feature registry (shopware.yaml). Each flag becomes a boolean Sass variable using its full name, e.g. $FEATURE_NEXT_1797: true or false.
* Provide a small SCSS API:
  - function: feature-enabled($flag) -> boolean (unknown flags return false)
  - mixin: feature($flag) { @content } (includes content only if enabled)
  - mixin: feature-disabled($flag) { @content } (optional helper)
* Usage in SCSS:
  - @include feature('FEATURE_NEXT_1797') { /* guarded styles */ }
  - @if feature-enabled('FEATURE_NEXT_1797') { /* guarded styles */ }
* Safe defaults:
  - Unknown or missing flags evaluate to false.
  - The generator emits a warning for unknown references in CI, failing the build in strict mode.
* Source of truth:
  - Flag names and states are read from the same configuration as PHP (shopware.yaml). No duplication in theme configs.
* Lifecycle:
  - When a feature is completed and the flag removed, all guarded SCSS must be unwrapped or deleted in the same merge request that removes the flag elsewhere.
  - Changing a flag requires a theme recompile; runtime toggling without rebuild is not supported.
* Tooling:
  - The storefront build (webpack/sass-loader) prepends _feature-flags.scss via additionalData to every SCSS entry.
  - PostCSS/CSSNano will prune empty rules left after guards.
  - Add a Stylelint custom rule to flag literal FEATURE_* strings not wrapped by the feature mixins/functions.
* Naming:
  - Always use full flag names (FEATURE_XXX_XXX) in SCSS, matching backend usage.
* Documentation:
  - Provide examples and a migration note in the storefront theming guide; require @Since tags on SCSS additions guarded by a new flag in component-level README or code comments.

## Decision

Adopt React Context API to share cross-cutting, app-wide or tree-wide state and services, specifically: authentication/session, theme, localization, feature flags, user preferences, and service singletons (e.g., analytics, API client). Avoid using Context for high-churn, large, or frequently updated collections (lists, form inputs per keystroke); prefer local state or a dedicated state library there.

Implementation guidelines:
- Create narrowly scoped contexts (AuthContext, ThemeContext, I18nContext, FeatureFlagsContext, ServicesContext) rather than a single “global” context to limit unnecessary re-renders.
- Co-locate Providers near the state owner; compose providers at the app root via a Providers component.
- Expose typed custom hooks (e.g., useAuth(), useFeatureFlag()) that throw on missing provider to enforce correct usage.
- Memoize provider values with useMemo; for complex updates use useReducer to keep stable dispatch references.
- For large objects, split value into multiple contexts (state vs. dispatch) or granular contexts to reduce render churn.
- Keep context values serializable where possible; avoid putting non-stable inline functions/objects in value.
- Do not use Context as an event bus; for cross-component events prefer callbacks, local state, or a lightweight pub/sub only where justified.
- Testing: provide test helpers to mount components with minimal providers and sensible defaults.
- SSR: ensure initial values are derivable on server and hydratable on client.

Escalation path:
- If requirements expand to complex, cross-cutting, frequently updated domain state, reevaluate and potentially adopt Redux Toolkit, Zustand, or React Query (for server cache) alongside Context for static services.

We will standardize on Docker Compose V2 (the Docker CLI plugin invoked as `docker compose`) and adopt the Compose Specification for our compose files. We will deprecate and remove reliance on the legacy Python-based `docker-compose` (v1) binaries across local development, CI/CD, and operational scripts.

All compose manifests will be updated to the spec-compliant, versionless format (removing the legacy `version` field), validated against the Compose Specification, and organized into a base compose file plus environment-specific overrides. We will leverage Compose V2 features where beneficial (e.g., profiles, improved `depends_on` semantics, BuildKit integration, `--profiles`, and expanded healthcheck and secrets support). Tooling, Make targets, and documentation will be updated to use `docker compose` commands exclusively.

CI runners and developer environments will be required to use Docker Engine with the Compose V2 plugin enabled; images and pipelines will be adjusted accordingly. Any scripts or third-party actions referencing `docker-compose` will be migrated or replaced with maintained alternatives that support Compose V2.

We will separate the API contract from the implementation into distinct packages/modules, versioned and released independently. The API package is the sole dependency exposed to consumers and contains only stable, technology-agnostic contracts: OpenAPI/Proto/GraphQL schema, service interfaces, request/response DTOs, error model, enums, and client SDKs if generated. The implementation package contains controllers/handlers, business logic, mappers, validation, persistence, and infrastructure; it depends on the API package, never the reverse.

Key rules:
- No implementation types, frameworks, or internal exceptions leak into the API package.
- API package follows semantic versioning; backward-compatible changes are minor, breaking changes require a major version and deprecation period.
- Consumers (internal/external) must reference only the API package; implementation details are internal.
- Mapping between API DTOs and domain models occurs in the implementation package.
- Shared cross-cutting utilities (logging, tracing) live in separate internal libs; not exposed via the API package.
- CI enforces dependency direction (e.g., module boundaries), API compatibility checks (contract tests, schema diff), and generates/publishes the API artifact and SDKs.
- Backward compatibility policies and deprecation annotations are applied in the API package and documented in release notes.
- For monorepos, use separate modules (e.g., :api and :service) with build-time checks; for polyrepos, publish api as its own artifact (e.g., npm, NuGet, Maven).

This separation enables clean architecture, clearer ownership, safer evolution, faster consumer adoption via stable contracts, and independent scaling/deployment of implementation without breaking consumers.

## Decision
We will adopt Lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document all architecturally significant decisions across the project.

- Scope: Record decisions that impact system structure, interfaces, data models, security, scalability, reliability, compliance, technology selection, deployment/runtime topology, and key patterns.
- Format: Each ADR is a standalone Markdown file containing Title, Date, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences. Keep to 1–2 pages, clear prose, with optional bullets for clarity.
- Numbering: Use sequential, zero-padded IDs (e.g., 0001, 0002). Numbers are never reused. New ADRs are append-only.
- Location: Store under version control at docs/adr/adr-<NNNN>-<kebab-title>.md. Changes are tracked via standard review processes (PRs).
- Status lifecycle: proposed → accepted → superseded (by <id>) or deprecated. Superseding ADRs must link both ways.
- Ownership and review: Any contributor may propose an ADR. Acceptance requires review by the architecture owner(s) and relevant stakeholders. High-impact decisions require recorded rationale and alternatives considered.
- Traceability: Reference ADR IDs in code, configuration, runbooks, and RFCs where applicable. Link related tickets and diagrams.
- Change policy: Do not edit accepted ADR narratives substantively; create a new ADR to change course and mark the old one superseded.
- Tooling: Prefer plain Markdown; lightweight generators/indexers are optional. A README index in docs/adr lists ADRs with statuses.
- Adoption: New features and major refactors must include ADRs when they introduce or alter architectural significance. Continuous enforcement via code review checklist.

## Decision

Adopt optimistic concurrency control (OCC) as the default strategy for concurrent updates across persistence, APIs, and messaging.

- Persistence layer (RDBMS): Each mutable aggregate/table will have a version column (BIGINT) or updated_at used as a version token. Updates/Deletes must include the token in the WHERE clause (e.g., WHERE id = ? AND version = ?). On success, increment the version atomically (SET version = version + 1). If zero rows are affected, raise a concurrency conflict.

- REST APIs: Expose an opaque ETag on reads. Require If-Match with the ETag for PUT/PATCH/DELETE. On mismatch, return 412 Precondition Failed and include the latest representation/ETag. For collection writes where ETag is impractical, include a version field in the payload and enforce it server-side.

- GraphQL/command endpoints: Include a required version/etag field in mutation inputs. On mismatch, return a typed CONFLICT error with the latest version.

- Event-sourced streams: Use expectedVersion (or equivalent) on append; reject with WrongExpectedVersion on conflicts.

- Clients: Must handle 412/CONFLICT by reloading the resource, reconciling user intent, and retrying with the new token. Retries should be bounded and surface a clear UX for manual merge if needed.

- Idempotency: For retried unsafe operations, require/support Idempotency-Key to prevent duplicate side effects.

- Exceptions: For rare bulk migrations/backfills or cross-aggregate invariants, allow explicit server-side locks/serializable transactions with approval.

- Observability: Emit metrics/logs for conflict rate, retries, and failure after retries to tune UX and detect contention hotspots.

This standardizes conflict detection without introducing global locks, scales with concurrency, and provides a consistent contract across interfaces.

We will start with a normalized relational data model centered on a small set of core entities and composable relations:

- Adopt UUIDv7 (or ULID) as primary keys for all tables to enable temporal ordering and distributed generation.
- Enforce multi-tenancy by scoping all domain rows with organization_id; avoid cross-tenant FKs.
- Standard columns: created_at, updated_at (UTC), created_by, updated_by, and optional deleted_at for soft-deletes.
- Enforce referential integrity with explicit foreign keys; default ON DELETE RESTRICT, selectively using CASCADE for pure join/link tables.
- Provide optimistic concurrency via row_version (integer) increments.
- Support extensibility using a typed attributes column (e.g., JSONB) per aggregate, constrained by JSON Schema and validated at write-time; keep frequently queried fields as first-class columns.
- Model many-to-many relationships via explicit link tables with composite unique constraints.
- Maintain an outbox table to publish domain events transactionally (outbox pattern) for integrations.
- Store large binaries in object storage; persist immutable metadata and signed URL pointers in the database.
- Use lookup tables (or enum domains) for constrained categorical values to enable referential integrity and evolution.
- Establish naming conventions (snake_case, singular table names), stable identifiers, and consistent index prefixes; create covering and partial indexes for high-frequency queries and uniqueness where applicable.
- Keep read models denormalized in separate materialized views or caches; the write model remains normalized.
- Reserve a migration strategy using idempotent, forward-only migrations with reversible test fixtures.
- Avoid polymorphic FKs; prefer association tables or subtype tables (class table inheritance) where needed.

This model balances integrity, evolvability, and performance while enabling future introduction of specialized projections and columnar analytics without disrupting the core write path.

We will not embed a generic/state-machine framework inside Services to manage entity lifecycle transitions. Instead, Services will expose explicit, intention-revealing commands (e.g., submit, validate, approve, reject) that delegate transition rules to the domain model (aggregates) and persist state changes atomically.

Allowed transitions will be enforced by:
- Guarded domain methods that validate the current status and invariants.
- Transactional persistence with optimistic locking to prevent concurrent illegal transitions.
- Database constraints and enum-based status columns to constrain representable states.
- Contract tests and a documented transition matrix serving as the canonical reference.

For cross-entity or long-running processes, we will use application-level orchestration (sagas/process managers) and domain events rather than an in-service state machine. Events will be published on successful transitions for auditing, observability, and downstream reactions.

This approach keeps Services simple and testable, avoids framework lock-in, and makes transitions explicit and discoverable in code. Where complex, human-centric workflows are unavoidable, we will consider a dedicated workflow/orchestration component at the boundary (not inside Services), with Services remaining thin command handlers over domain invariants.

## Decision

We will accept Base64-encoded file content in JSON requests for controlled use cases:
- small-to-medium files (default hard limit: 5 MB encoded), primarily for service-to-service calls and trusted back-office clients where a single JSON payload simplifies integration.
- synchronous operations where immediate processing is required and multipart or presigned uploads would add undue complexity.

Constraints and requirements:
- Clients must provide: filename, MIME type, Base64 content (standard RFC 4648; no data-URI prefix), and an optional checksum (SHA-256 preferred). If provided, checksum will be verified before persistence.
- Requests must be sent over HTTPS; payload size is limited and enforced server-side to mitigate Base64 overhead (~33%).
- The API will reject malformed Base64 and mismatched MIME types; content sniffing will validate declared type.
- Uploaded content will be streamed to storage after decoding; payloads are not fully buffered in memory where feasible.
- For browser-based uploads and files exceeding the Base64 limit, clients must use multipart/form-data or presigned object storage uploads; SDKs and docs will prioritize these paths.
- Audit fields (uploader identity, source IP, timestamps) are captured consistently across all upload methods.

Operational posture:
- Configuration flags allow per-environment/filetype size limits and enable/disable Base64 uploads.
- Rate limits and WAF rules will protect the endpoint from abuse.
- Telemetry will record success/failure, sizes, and processing time to inform future tuning, with the intent to keep Base64 support narrowly scoped to cases where it materially simplifies integration.

We will establish a Hybrid Tech Radar that combines a curated, company-wide baseline with domain-specific overlays and blends expert judgment with quantitative adoption signals.

- Model
  - Rings: Adopt, Trial, Assess, Hold (with clear entry/exit criteria and timeboxes for Assess/Trial).
  - Quadrants: Languages & Frameworks, Platforms, Techniques, Tools (domains may add one custom quadrant if needed).
  - Entries (“blips”) must include owner, rationale, evidence, links to ADRs/RFCs, date introduced, and next review date.

- Governance
  - Architecture Council owns ring decisions and taxonomy; domain guilds propose blips and ring changes via PRs.
  - Monthly triage of proposals; quarterly publication cycle; emergency updates allowed.
  - Demotion/retirement requires documented rationale; archived items remain discoverable.

- Data and Tooling
  - Source of truth: Git repository with YAML/JSON blip definitions and templates.
  - Rendering: Backstage Tech Radar plugin (or Zalando Tech Radar) generating a static site via CI; embed in developer portal.
  - Signals: Automated enrichment from dependency data (GitHub/org package manifests), cloud inventories, vulnerability scanners, and usage telemetry; signals inform but do not replace curation.

- Process
  - Any team may propose: PR with problem statement, alternatives considered, evaluation, and adoption scope.
  - Required linkage to relevant ADRs; large adoptions must reference an approved RFC.
  - Timeboxed experiments documented as Trials; promotions require success criteria met and at least one production reference.

This approach increases transparency and alignment, preserves domain autonomy, and keeps the radar living, evidence-informed, and actionable.

- Adopt a design token–driven theming system as the single source of truth for all visual primitives (color, typography, spacing, radii, z-index, motion).
- Store tokens in a platform-agnostic format and generate platform artifacts (CSS Custom Properties, TypeScript typings, JSON) via a build tool (e.g., Style Dictionary). Prefer semantic tokens over raw values; map brand tokens to semantic tokens per theme.
- Distribute themes as versioned token packs. Applications select a theme by setting a data-theme attribute on the root (or component host) enabling scoped theming and multi-theme coexistence.
- Components must consume tokens exclusively via CSS Custom Properties and avoid hard-coded values or Sass variables. Sass is allowed only for structure, not for theming.
- Support runtime theme switching (light, dark, high-contrast, brand variants) with zero or minimal JavaScript; honor prefers-color-scheme by default. Provide contrast-safe palettes and enforce WCAG AA for text and UI components.
- Enable per-scope overrides by redefining CSS Custom Properties at container boundaries; allow per-component escape hatches only through documented tokens.
- Ensure SSR compatibility and avoid FOUC by shipping critical theme CSS early; no client-side recomputation required.
- Version the token schema and provide migration guides; treat token removal as breaking change.
- For microfrontends/web components, isolate via shadow DOM with inherited CSS variables and an opt-in fallbacks strategy.

We will standardize on TypeScript v3.4.5 as the project’s baseline compiler and type-checker. The exact version will be pinned in devDependencies (no caret/range), locked via the lockfile, and enforced in CI to ensure deterministic builds across all environments. tsconfig settings will be aligned with 3.4.5 capabilities (e.g., enabling features like const assertions introduced in 3.4), and coding guidelines will restrict usage to language and lib features supported by this version. All application packages and shared libraries in the monorepo will compile under 3.4.5; third-party type definitions that require newer compilers will be replaced, shimmed, or vendored to maintain compatibility. Tooling (ts-node/ts-jest/linters) will be configured with versions compatible with 3.4.5. We will schedule a periodic review (e.g., quarterly) to reassess and plan upgrades, with a controlled migration path and smoke tests before any version change.

We will standardize all entity identifiers as RFC 4151 tag URIs and adopt a strict, organization-wide naming convention:

- Authority: tag:{org-domain},{issued-year}
  - {org-domain} is our reverse-DNS organizational domain (e.g., example.com).
  - {issued-year} is the 4-digit year when the naming authority was established (not the resource creation year).

- Path structure: {tenant}/{bounded-context}/{resource-collection}/{version?}/{business-key}[/{subresource-collection}/{sub-key}...]
  - tenant: mandatory for multi-tenant contexts; omit if single-tenant.
  - bounded-context: DDD-aligned namespace (kebab-case).
  - resource-collection: plural noun (kebab-case).
  - version: optional semantic version prefix (v1, v2) only when identifier semantics must change; avoid for pure representation changes.
  - business-key: immutable, domain-meaningful key; prefer natural keys. If no stable natural key exists, use a deterministic, non-leaking surrogate (e.g., ULID) minted by the domain.
  - Subresources repeat the collection/key pattern as needed.

- Casing and characters:
  - Segments are lowercase, kebab-case for names, do not include spaces.
  - Allowed characters in segments: [a-z0-9-._~]. Any other characters must be percent-encoded.
  - Identifiers are case-sensitive only where the underlying key is case-sensitive; otherwise normalize to lowercase.

- Stability and uniqueness:
  - Chosen business-key attributes MUST be immutable; if a key attribute would change, mint a new URI and maintain explicit mapping.
  - Do not include environment, region, or deployment details in URIs.
  - Do not include PII or secrets in any segment.
  - Collisions are resolved by extending hierarchy (e.g., add issuer namespace) or minting a surrogate key; never by adding ephemeral qualifiers.

- Examples (schematic):
  - tag:example.com,2020:acme/catalog/products/sku-12345
  - tag:example.com,2020:acme/hr/employees/v1/ee-009871

- Governance:
  - Each bounded context documents its resource collections and key schemes.
  - Changes to naming rules require review by the architecture board and a new version segment if semantics of existing identifiers would be affected.

Adopt HTMX as the primary mechanism for front-end interactivity, favoring server-rendered HTML and progressive enhancement over SPA frameworks. Pages and UI fragments will be rendered on the server and exchanged via HTMX (HTML-over-the-wire) using standard HTTP verbs; dynamic regions will be updated via hx-* attributes. We will avoid client-side state management frameworks unless strictly necessary.

Use cases:
- Form submissions, validation, pagination, sorting, filtering, and modal/dialog flows via partial HTML responses.
- Long-running/streaming updates via HTMX extensions (SSE/WebSocket) where applicable.
- Progressive enhancement: all critical flows remain functional without JavaScript; HTMX augments usability.

Complementary tooling:
- Use Alpine.js (or hyperscript) sparingly for lightweight client-side behaviors that do not warrant server round-trips.
- Maintain server-side templates/components as the single source of UI truth to maximize reuse and consistency.

Boundaries:
- For highly interactive, offline-first, or complex real-time UIs with rich client-side state (e.g., canvas-heavy editors), we will evaluate a component framework (React/Vue/Svelte) per feature. Such exceptions require an ADR addendum.

Operational considerations:
- Standardize on partial endpoints returning semantic HTML; include ETags and caching headers where safe.
- Ensure CSRF protection, proper HTTP status codes, and progressive fallbacks.
- Integrate accessibility from templates; preserve focus management and ARIA roles in dynamic updates.
- Use consistent patterns for loading indicators, error handling, and optimistic UI only when justified.
- Instrument with lightweight telemetry for request/response timings to monitor perceived performance.

Testing and maintainability:
- Favor server-side component tests and end-to-end browser tests over brittle DOM-unit tests.
- Document reusable template fragments and hx-* conventions in a UI handbook.

This approach reduces front-end complexity, leverages team familiarity with server frameworks, improves time-to-first-byte and maintainability, and avoids SPA build/runtime overhead while retaining the option to introduce richer client-side frameworks when truly necessary.

## Decision
Adopt a MutableMessageFactory to construct messages efficiently while preserving immutable semantics after handoff.

- Provide a new IMessageFactory implementation (MutableMessageFactory) that:
  - Allocates and populates message fields (headers, attributes, payload) mutably during a construction window.
  - Uses object/buffer pooling to minimize allocations and GC pressure.
  - Exposes a Build/Freeze operation that validates and produces an immutable IMessage snapshot for dispatch.
- Constrain mutability:
  - Factory instances and in-construction messages are not thread-safe; they are scoped per request/operation and must not be shared across threads.
  - After Build/Freeze (or Send/Publish), the returned IMessage is immutable; any further mutation attempts on the builder/factory throw or no-op.
- API surface:
  - Begin()/New() to start construction.
  - SetHeader/SetMetadata/SetKey/SetRouting/SetBody/SetAttributes APIs support incremental assembly.
  - CloneForRetry creates a new mutable builder from an immutable IMessage with copy-on-write semantics.
  - Reset()/Dispose returns pooled resources; using-pattern encouraged to guarantee return to pool.
- Compatibility and defaults:
  - Existing ImmutableMessageFactory remains supported; the mutable factory becomes the default in performance-sensitive paths via DI/config.
  - Wire formats and external contracts remain unchanged.
- Validation and observability:
  - Validation performed at Build; failures are surfaced before dispatch.
  - Correlation/trace IDs and timestamps are bound at Build to ensure immutability of observability data.

We will represent logical truth values explicitly with booleans across all layers and forbid implicit truthiness checks.

- Code: Use the language’s native Boolean type and strict comparisons (e.g., === in JS/TS; explicit bool in Python/Java/C#). Disallow relying on implicit coercion/truthiness of numbers, strings, or collections. Lint rules will flag non‑strict equality and ambiguous conditions.
- APIs: Expose and consume JSON booleans (true/false) only. Do not accept 0/1, "true"/"false" strings, or other aliases at the contract layer.
- Configuration/Env: Parse booleans explicitly; only the canonical tokens true/false (case‑insensitive) are accepted. Anything else is invalid and fails fast.
- Database: Use BOOLEAN columns (NOT NULL with explicit defaults) rather than CHAR/INT 0/1; avoid tri‑state unless required.
- Tri‑state needs: When “unknown” is required, model as an explicit third state (e.g., enum or Optional[bool] with documented semantics), never by overloading False or NULL.
- Serialization: Preserve boolean types end‑to‑end without lossy conversion.

## Decision

We will model “Primary Person” as a single, explicitly designated Person associated to an Account/Household/Case (the “container”) at any time (cardinality 1..1 per container). The Primary Person is required before activation/submission of the container, but may be unset during draft.

Purpose and usage:
- Serves as the default source of contact information (email, phone, mailing address) and notification routing when no field-level override is provided.
- Acts as the default consent/attestation signer and point-of-contact, subject to policy and role-based authorization.
- Does not implicitly acquire data ownership or elevated permissions; access control is orthogonal and enforced via roles/ACLs.

Selection and reassignment rules:
- Default assignment: the person who initiates/creates the container. If ambiguous, choose the highest role priority (e.g., Applicant > Guardian > Member), then adult with legal capacity, then earliest creation timestamp, then lowest stable identifier.
- Authorized users may reassign the Primary Person; every change must be audited (who/when/why), versioned, and emitted as a domain event (PrimaryPersonChanged).
- Reassignment must be non-destructive: no data is migrated; only the reference changes.

Integration and data contracts:
- Expose primaryPersonId on the container; consumers must not infer “head of household” or eligibility from this flag unless explicitly modeled.
- Downstream systems may override routing/consent explicitly; absence of overrides falls back to the Primary Person.
- Reports and analytics must treat Primary Person as a routing/contact convention, not a semantic role, unless specified.

Determinism and validation:
- Enforce exactly one Primary Person per active container.
- Prevent circular or conflicting assignments via validation and consistent tiebreakers.

## Decision

Adopt Taurus (bzt) as the standard framework for defining and executing benchmark and performance tests. All performance scenarios will be authored in Taurus YAML and stored in the repository under tests/performance, with reusable profiles and environment overlays. JMeter will be the default executor; teams may use Locust or Gatling behind Taurus where appropriate, but execution must be orchestrated via Taurus for consistency.

Provide a Dockerized runner and lightweight scripts (e.g., make perf, bzt docker image) to ensure reproducible local and CI execution. Integrate Taurus into CI/CD to run:

- Nightly/weekly baseline benchmarks,
- On-demand comparative runs for release candidates.

Encode SLAs/SLOs as Taurus pass/fail thresholds (response times, error rates, percentiles, throughput) so builds fail on regression. Parameterize tests via environment variables and config overlays; manage secrets via CI secret stores. Require versioning of test data and datasets. Allow extensions, but all benchmark automation must be invoked through Taurus to ensure a uniform developer experience, repeatability, and comparable results across services.

## Decision

- Centralize and version domain types in a dedicated package (types/domain) and separate them from transport DTOs (types/dto) and UI/view models (types/view). No direct coupling between layers; mapping functions are explicit.
- Enable strict typing across the repo: "strict": true, noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, and useUnknownInCatchVariables.
- Replace ambient/global declarations with module-scoped exports; all public types are explicitly exported from index files. No implicit namespace merging.
- Prefer discriminated unions over inheritance for variant modeling; replace enums with const objects + string literal unions for tree-shakeability.
- Introduce branded/nominal types for identifiers and key domain primitives (e.g., UserId, OrderId) to prevent accidental mixing of raw strings.
- Treat API/client types as generated, read-only artifacts (OpenAPI/GraphQL codegen). Domain types are hand-authored. Provide mapping adapters between DTOs and domain.
- Add runtime validation at all external boundaries using Zod (or equivalent). Derive TypeScript types from schemas to ensure drift-free contracts.
- Ban any in application code; allow temporary @ts-expect-error only with a linked ticket. Enforce via ESLint rules (no-explicit-any, consistent-type-imports, no-namespace, no-redeclare).
- Standardize Dates: DTOs use ISO 8601 strings; domain uses Temporal.Instant (or Date until Temporal is available) with mappers handling conversion.
- Adopt project references and path aliases for incremental builds and to prevent circular type dependencies.
- Provide codemods and a migration guide; ship compatibility shims for one minor release and remove in the next. Continuous type coverage metrics are tracked in CI.

We will persist every denied permission request and access-denied decision as immutable audit events.

- Storage: Append-only “permission_denials” audit table in the Authorization service database (PostgreSQL), with CDC to an analytics/event stream (e.g., Kafka topic permission.denied). Events are write-once; no updates.
- Event schema (minimum): event_id (ULID), occurred_at, subject_user_id, actor_id (user/system/policy), client_id, resource_type, resource_id, action, requested_scope, decision=denied, reason_code, reason_message, policy_id/version, correlation_id/trace_id, request_context (ip, ua), jurisdiction/tenant, idempotency_key.
- Integrity and security: At-rest encryption, column-level encryption for PII, tamper-evidence via per-event hash chain and daily anchored digest. Access restricted to Audit/Security roles; subjects may view only their own denials.
- APIs: 
  - Write via internal Authorization component only (no public write). 
  - Read endpoints for: subject self-service history; admin/auditor search with filters and pagination. Export supports redaction.
- Retention: Configurable default 12 months (per tenant), auto lifecycle purge; legal hold overrides purge. Self-service deletion requests honor legal basis; if not deletable, we mask PII for self-views while retaining audit integrity.
- Operations: Idempotent writes (idempotency_key, unique index) to avoid duplicates under retries; rate limiting and sampling guardrails on high-volume systemic denials.
- Observability: Emit PermissionRequestDenied domain event for notifications/workflows; metrics on denial rates by policy/resource; dashboards and alerts on anomalies.
- Performance: Indexes on occurred_at, subject_user_id, resource_id/type, reason_code, policy_id; partition by month and tenant.
- Migration: Create schema, backfill recent denials from gateway logs (if available), and enable CDC stream with versioned event contracts.

## Decision

Decommission Discourse from the DataLab stack and retire all related infrastructure, integrations, and operational processes.

We will expose ingress controllers via a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer backed by the cloud provider’s L4 load balancer (e.g., AWS NLB) and will not use hostNetwork for production clusters.

Implementation details:
- Create two Services per cluster: an external internet-facing LoadBalancer and an internal/private LoadBalancer (separate ingress classes).
- Use cross-zone LBs and health checks; set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client IPs and enable PROXY protocol where required.
- Manage access via cloud-native security groups/firewall rules; disable public exposure by default for internal classes.
- Standardize annotations for LB behavior (idle timeouts, proxy, TLS passthrough as needed) and enforce through IaC/policies.
- Support dual-stack where available; allocate static IPs/Elastic IPs for stable DNS.
- Terminate TLS at the ingress controller with centralized cert management; allow passthrough for specific workloads via class/annotation.
- Scale via multiple replicas per controller and HPA; do not horizontally shard by hostNetwork on nodes.

Exception:
- HostNetwork may be used only in non-production, air-gapped, or bare-metal environments lacking a cloud LoadBalancer, and only behind an external LB (e.g., MetalLB/HAProxy) or for controlled, low-latency use cases with platform approval and node port/iptables hardening.

This decision standardizes ingress exposure, simplifies operations, and maintains portability across clusters while reserving hostNetwork for tightly scoped scenarios.

- Provide a public, read-only SPARQL 1.1 endpoint at /sparql to query published domain data.

- Publish RDF using standard vocabularies (RDF, RDFS, SKOS, Dublin Core/PROV as applicable) plus a versioned, documented custom ontology with stable HTTP IRIs.

- Instrument endpoint with structured query logging, metrics (QPS, latency, timeouts), and dataset provenance exposure (VoID/DCAT).
- Document query examples, ontology, and SLAs; supply a sandbox UI (Fuseki UI) for exploration in non-production.

Implement permissions for record configuration as declarative, tenant-aware policies managed via a dedicated permissions service and enforced in all write/read paths.

- Model: Role-based access control with optional attribute conditions (RBAC + ABAC). Subjects (user, group, role) → Actions (create, read, update, delete, publish) → Resources (record_config, record_type, collection, project) with scope and conditional constraints (e.g., ownership, environment).
- Storage: Authoritative policy store in the application database. Policies versioned and immutable (append-only) with active version pointer; full audit trail (who, when, diff). Soft-delete only.
- Enforcement: Central authorization middleware in the API layer evaluates requests against the active policy set using a policy engine; decisions cached in-memory with short TTL and event-driven invalidation on policy change. All config CRUD endpoints call the enforcer; read paths honor “read” separately from manage.
- APIs/UI: Admin CRUD endpoints for roles, assignments, and policies; batch operations; dry-run “would this be allowed?” endpoint; validation to prevent orphaned roles or conflicting rules. Provide an admin UI for safe edits with previews and rollback to prior versions.
- Safety/Controls: Optimistic locking on config records; guarded operations (delete/publish) require elevated role; optional dual-approval for destructive changes; environment guards (prod vs non-prod).
