- Defaults/Migrations: Secure-by-default roles (Viewer, Editor, Admin) seeded per tenant; backward-compatible default policy grants existing admins equivalent rights. Migration tools to import/export policies.
- Observability: Structured authz logs, metrics on allow/deny, and alerts on repeated denials or missing policies.

This approach provides fine-grained, auditable, and scalable permission management for record configuration with minimal coupling to domain logic.

Adopt a single codebase where test code is co-located with production code in the same repository and module, but ensure strict build-time separation so no test artifacts ship to production. Place test files alongside source files (e.g., Foo.ts with Foo.test.ts), encapsulate shared test utilities in test-only modules, and configure the build toolchain to exclude test sources and dependencies from release artifacts. Avoid conditional compilation or test hooks in production paths; any necessary instrumentation must be guarded behind non-production build profiles. Enforce this separation in CI by failing builds if test code is referenced by production modules, and verify released artifacts are free of test classes, resources, and dev-only dependencies.

We will require all self-hosted CI runners to egress the internet exclusively through a dedicated proxy tier and block all direct outbound internet access at the network boundary.

- Architecture
  - Runners reside in private subnets; security groups allow outbound only to the proxy tier and internal services.
  - Highly available proxy tier (Squid) deployed in at least 2 AZs behind an internal NLB; autoscaled and immutable.
  - No TLS interception. HTTPS CONNECT passthrough with SNI logging for audit.
  - NAT gateway is retained only for proxy health/updates; runners cannot reach NAT directly.

- Policy and controls
  - Default-deny outbound policy; explicit allowlist of destinations and ports (e.g., github.com, api.github.com, ghcr.io, docker.io, registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org, rubygems.org, OS mirrors, time services).
  - Change control for allowlist via IaC PR and approval; time-bounded exceptions supported.
  - Authentication to proxy via mTLS with short-lived client certs issued to runner instances; unauthenticated traffic denied.
  - Full request metadata (timestamp, runner ID, IP, method, SNI/host, port, bytes) logged to a central store with 90-day retention and alerts on anomalies.
  - No bypass: if the proxy is unavailable or a domain is not allowed, jobs fail.

- Runner configuration
  - Standardized environment for proxies (HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY/NO_PROXY), Docker daemon proxy config, and build tool configs (npm/yarn/pip/bundle/git).
  - SSH over proxy via ProxyCommand (CONNECT).
  - Provide a PAC file for local dev parity; CI uses fixed env vars.

- Reliability and operations
  - Autoscaling on CPU/conns; surge buffer for bursty workloads.
  - Health checks, structured logs/metrics, dashboards and alerts (5xx rate, latency, connection pool).
  - Blue/green proxy rollouts via target groups.
  - Disaster scenario runbook; periodic failover tests.

- Rollout
  - Phase 1: non-prod runners.
  - Phase 2: production runners.
  - Phase 3: tighten allowlist to least privilege per workflow.

## Decision

Adopt Lerna to manage package versioning and publishing within our monorepo. We will use Lerna in independent versioning mode so each package evolves at its own cadence, with automatic detection of changed packages. Version increments will be derived from Conventional Commits (feat, fix, chore, perf, refactor with optional BREAKING CHANGE footer), enabling consistent semantic versioning across all packages.

We will enable the following Lerna capabilities:
- lerna version to compute per-package versions, update inter-package dependency ranges, and generate changelogs.
- lerna publish to publish only changed packages to our npm registry, creating Git tags and GitHub Releases.
- Changelog generation via conventional-changelog presets, producing per-package CHANGELOG.md and an aggregated release note.
- Automatic dependency bumping for local cross-dependencies to avoid mismatched ranges.
- Git commit/tag signing as required by repo policy.

CI/CD will run dry-run checks on pull requests and perform versioning/publishing on protected branches after tests pass. Pre-release workflows (alpha/beta/rc) will use dist-tags and Lerna prerelease options. We will enforce commit message format via commitlint and husky to ensure accurate version inference. For packages that must remain aligned, we may optionally group them using Lerna’s versioning configuration.

This approach gives clear, auditable version history per package, minimizes unnecessary publishes, and scales operationally with the monorepo.

- We standardize on Symfony’s EventDispatcher for all events and expose only domain/business events as public extension points. Technical/implementation events remain internal.
- Create custom events only for meaningful domain milestones (e.g., order.placed, payment.captured, shipment.shipped), not for low-level CRUD where entity-written/loaded events already exist.
- Event naming: <bounded-context>.<aggregate|feature>.<past-tense-action> (e.g., checkout.order.placed). If both pre/post are required, use .before and .after suffixes; prefer emitting only one post event when possible.
- Event classes must be immutable: set all properties via constructor, provide typed getters only. Do not expose mutable collections directly.
- Always include Context in the payload. Prefer referencing aggregates by IDs and minimal value objects over passing heavy entities; include snapshots only when necessary.
- Mark events intended for third parties as public and stable; annotate internal/volatile events with @internal and do not document them for public use.
- Implement awareness interfaces as needed (e.g., SalesChannelAware, UserAware, ShopwareEvent) to enable rules/flows and webhooks. Ensure payload is serializable for async handling and webhooks.
- Do not perform business logic in event constructors. Side effects belong to listeners/subscribers. Core flows must not depend on subscriber execution order.
- Error handling: event listeners must not throw unchecked exceptions that break the main transaction. Use compensating actions or dedicated failure channels. Only .before events may veto with documented exceptions.
- Performance: keep payload small; avoid N+1 loading in listeners. Prefer async listeners for slow operations and emit events after transaction commit where consistency matters.
- Versioning: adding new optional fields is allowed; removing/renaming events or fields requires deprecation with @deprecated and a two-release grace period.
- Documentation: every public event must include purpose, payload contract, example usage, and stability guarantees. Add tests asserting emission and payload schema.

We will license the project under a permissive, enterprise-friendly scheme:
- Source code: Apache License 2.0 (with NOTICE file) to provide explicit patent grants and broad reuse.
- Documentation and wiki content: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0).
- Code snippets in docs and examples: CC0 to maximize reuse in external materials.
- Test data and sample datasets: CC0 unless otherwise stated.
- Brand assets (name, logo, trademarks): All rights reserved; not covered by open-source licenses.

We will:
- Adopt SPDX identifiers in file headers and maintain REUSE-compliant metadata (LICENSE, NOTICE, COPYING, and LICENSES/ for third-party texts).
- Only accept third-party dependencies with OSI-approved licenses compatible with Apache-2.0; record their licenses and attributions in NOTICE.
- Preserve original licenses for vendored code and generated files; include their license texts verbatim.
- Require Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) sign-off for all contributions; CLA not required at this time.
- Enforce licensing policy via automated scans in CI and release gates, and publish SBOMs including license info with each release.

We will adopt client-initiated polling as the default integration pattern for external data sources and long-running jobs. Services will poll provider APIs on a configurable schedule rather than relying on inbound webhooks/streams, unless a product requirement demands near‑real‑time (<10s) updates and the provider offers verified, signed, retryable deliveries we can reliably operate.

Implementation guidelines:
- Use conditional requests (ETag/If-Modified-Since) or delta endpoints to minimize payload and cost.
- Apply exponential backoff with jitter, bounded retries, and circuit breaking on failure; honor provider rate limits and Retry-After.
- Support per-tenant, per-endpoint schedules with sane defaults (e.g., 1–5 min for user-facing freshness, 15–60 min for backfills), plus manual re-sync triggers.
- Ensure idempotency and deduplication (content hashing, checkpointing with high-water marks, pagination cursors).
- Parallelize within rate limits; shard workloads; isolate noisy tenants.
- Cache responses where applicable; persist sync checkpoints for exactly-once semantics where feasible.
- Provide observability (metrics for lag, success rate, throughput, cost; logs with correlation IDs; alerts on SLA breaches).
- Implement graceful degradation and resumable progress for large datasets and maintenance windows.
- Document and enforce security (OAuth/API keys management), and data governance for fetched data.

Exceptions to polling require an ADR documenting latency needs, delivery guarantees, security posture, operational readiness, and failure modes, with a tested fallback to polling.

We will scaffold the frontend using Create React App (CRA) and standardize on npm as the sole package manager.

- All dependency management, scripts, and lifecycle commands will use npm (npm install, npm run, npm ci).
- package-lock.json will be committed and treated as the source of truth for deterministic installs; yarn.lock and other lockfiles are prohibited and will be removed/ignored.
- CI/CD pipelines will use npm ci for faster, reproducible builds; local development will use npm install.
- Node and npm versions will be pinned to LTS via engines in package.json and enforced with an .nvmrc/.node-version file.
- Project documentation and onboarding will reference npm-only commands; precommit hooks and tooling will rely on npm scripts.
- CRA defaults will be used (with TypeScript template where applicable); avoid ejecting unless a justified ADR supersedes this decision.
- Environment configuration will use CRA’s built-in mechanisms (REACT_APP_*), and dependency auditing will use npm audit.

This decision aligns the project on a single, widely supported toolchain, reduces contributor friction, and simplifies CI consistency.

Adopt XChart as the standard plotting library for the JVM modules to generate publication-quality static charts (line, bar, scatter, histogram) and export artifacts (PNG, SVG, PDF/EPS) without external runtime dependencies. XChart’s lightweight footprint, simple API, permissive Apache-2.0 license, and solid headless rendering make it a good fit for both server-side batch report generation and optional Swing previews, keeping build size and operational complexity low.

We will wrap XChart behind a PlotService interface to decouple callers from the library and ease future replacement. The service will provide high-level helpers for common chart types, theming, labeling, legends, and file export with deterministic sizing and DPI. Default output formats are SVG for vector reports and PNG for raster previews; PDF/EPS enabled where needed.

Usage guidelines:
- Run in headless mode in servers (java.awt.headless=true); avoid UI components outside desktop tools.
- Validate series sizes and cap point counts for very large datasets; down-sample where necessary.
- Keep rendering off critical paths; generate charts asynchronously and cache results by content hash.
- Standardize a project theme (fonts, colors, margins) for consistency.
- Pin a tested XChart version and monitor updates for security/bug fixes.

Interactive web dashboards are out of scope; for that use case, consider web-native charting separately.

We will not expose individual components as top-level globals. The primary distribution remains ESM/CJS imports. For legacy, non-module consumers we will ship an optional UMD “global” bundle that attaches a single, read-only namespace to window under window.AppComponents (configurable at build-time). All components, utilities, and themes are accessed via that namespace (e.g., window.AppComponents.Button), avoiding per-component globals and name collisions.

To enable safe coexistence of multiple versions, the UMD bundle will publish under a versioned sub-namespace (e.g., window.AppComponents.v1_4_0) and also register the active version as window.AppComponents.latest. The namespace attachment will be idempotent, warn on collision, and never overwrite an existing different version.

The global exposure is opt-in: only the UMD bundle attaches to window; ESM/CJS builds do not. No auto-initialization or DOM side effects occur on attach. The global object is frozen to prevent mutation.

We will document usage and deprecate direct global access in favor of module imports in a future major release, maintaining the UMD global for at least two minor versions before removal consideration.

## Decision

On macOS, we will avoid heavy bind mounts for application source and dependency directories and instead use Docker named volumes to improve filesystem I/O performance. Specifically:
- Use named volumes for write-heavy and churn-prone paths (e.g., node_modules, vendor, build artifacts, database/storage directories) rather than mounting them from the host.
- For source code needed for live reload, prefer a single host bind mount with the :cached or :delegated option (macOS-only) depending on access patterns (read-heavy -> :cached, write-heavy -> :delegated). Exclude dependency directories from this bind mount via volume overrides.
- Provide a “fast” Compose profile for macOS that:
  - Mounts src/ via bind with :cached/:delegated
  - Mounts dependencies and build outputs via named volumes
  - Disables unnecessary file watchers or reduces watch granularity where supported
- Production images will not use host mounts; artifacts and dependencies are copied at build time.
- For projects requiring near-native sync speeds across many files (e.g., large JS/monorepos), we may optionally enable a file sync helper (e.g., Mutagen) behind a separate profile, without changing the default path.

This approach yields faster local dev on macOS while preserving a consistent containerized runtime across environments.

## Decision

We will adopt Google Cloud Storage (GCS) as the primary object storage backend for all binary assets (e.g., images, media, archives, logs, backups).

- Create dedicated buckets per environment (prod, staging, dev) and per product/domain with uniform bucket-level access enabled.
- Use Regional buckets in EU regions by default to satisfy data residency; allow exception-based Multi-Regional buckets for globally distributed, cacheable public assets.
- Enforce IAM least-privilege access via service accounts; grant storage.objectViewer/Uploader per workload and restrict storage.objectAdmin to ops/automation only.
- Expose downloads via signed URLs; use V4 signed POST/PUT for client-direct uploads to avoid backend proxying and reduce egress from app servers.
- Enable object versioning on critical buckets (user content, compliance-related data) and configure lifecycle policies to expire old versions and transient files.
- Apply bucket retention policies (and retention lock when required) for backups and compliance artifacts.
- Use default Google-managed encryption for general assets; enable CMEK via Cloud KMS for sensitive datasets and regulated tenants.
- Serve public assets through Cloud CDN fronted by HTTPS Load Balancer, with cache/key policies set per asset type and object metadata (Cache-Control) managed by pipelines.
- Emit object change notifications via Pub/Sub for downstream processing (e.g., indexing, thumbnails); standardize event schemas.
- Define naming conventions and prefix structure to segment tenants/projects and to optimize listing/parallelism.
- Enable access logs and Audit Logs; monitor storage metrics and costs with budget alerts and per-bucket labels.
- Migrate existing assets using Storage Transfer Service or gsutil with checksum verification and cutover runbook.

## Decision

Introduce first-class support for custom key–value properties on core domain entities via an extensible “properties” map.

- Data model: add a dedicated properties column per supported entity, storing a string→JSON map (e.g., JSON/JSONB or equivalent map type). Supported value types: string, number, boolean, null, and arrays of primitives. No nested objects.
- Namespacing: reserve org/system prefixes (e.g., sys.*, meta.*) and require teams to use reverse-DNS or team prefixes (e.g., teamA.foo). Reject keys outside [a-zA-Z0-9_.-], max 64 chars. Max 50 keys per entity, max 1 KB per value, max 16 KB total.
- API: expose CRUD via PATCH /entities/{id}/properties with partial updates and DELETE for key removal. Reads include properties by default; allow field selection to omit. Enforce optimistic concurrency via ETag/If-Match.
- Validation and governance: server-side schema validates key format, size limits, and value types; optional allow/deny lists per product. Reserve certain keys for platform use. Block secrets/PII by policy tags where applicable.
- Indexing and query: provide opt-in indexed keys registry; for supported stores use path/GIN/secondary indexes. Offer filter/query on registered keys only to avoid unbounded index growth.
- Security and audit: inherit entity ACLs; property mutations audited with actor, keys changed, and diffs.
- SDKs: add typed helpers to get/set/remove properties, with batch operations.
- Backward compatibility: existing entities default to empty map; zero-downtime migration with background backfill and feature flag rollout.

## Decision

We will implement and operate our release workflow in GitLab instead of GitHub. All release orchestration (versioning, tagging, changelog generation, artifact packaging, container image publishing, environment promotions, and release notes) will be defined and executed via .gitlab-ci.yml using GitLab pipelines, environments, and Releases. We will:

- Use GitLab Releases with annotated tags as the system of record, generating release notes from merge requests and conventional commits.
- Publish build artifacts to GitLab’s Package and Container Registries and consume them across stages via needs/artifacts.
- Enforce protected branches/tags, code ownership, and mandatory approvals for release and production deployment jobs.
- Gate promotions with environment-specific approvals, manual actions, and deploy freezes where applicable.
- Leverage GitLab CI variables, scoped and masked, for credentials; and tie pipelines to GitLab security scans for release gating.
- Standardize on reusable pipeline templates and shared runners for consistency and scalability.
- Deprecate GitHub Actions for release activities; any GitHub usage will be limited to repository mirroring and issue/PR sync if needed.
- Adopt GitLab Release CLI (or semantic-release with GitLab plugin) for automated versioning and changelogs.
- Store SBOMs and provenance attestations as release assets to support compliance and auditability.

Adopt a standardized Git workflow and commit convention across all Decentraland repositories:
- Use Conventional Commits v1.0.0 with scopes (e.g., feat(renderer): add PBR support). Allowed types: feat, fix, perf, refactor, chore, docs, style, test, build, ci, revert.
- Commit subject in imperative mood, ≤72 chars; include a detailed body explaining motivation and context; reference issues as “Closes #123”.
- Use BREAKING CHANGE: footer for breaking changes.
- Enforce commit linting via commitlint + husky pre-commit/pre-push hooks; validate with CI.
- Branching: short-lived branches named by type/scope: feature/<slug>, fix/<slug>, chore/<slug>, spike/<slug>, release/<version>.
- Main is protected; require PRs for all changes with green CI, code owners review where applicable, and linked issues.
- Prefer rebase on latest main before merge; use squash-merge to keep a linear history and to ensure a single, well-formed commit message.
- Tag releases semantically (vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH); auto-generate changelogs from commit history; optionally use semantic-release for automation.
- Reverts use revert: <original subject> and link to the reverted commit.
- Multi-repo or monorepo scopes should reflect package or domain (e.g., feat(scene-editor): …).
- Large changes behind feature flags; split into incremental PRs when possible.
- Sign commits (GPG/SSH) and include DCO Signed-off-by where required.

Adopt TypeScript as the primary language for application and library code across the monorepo. All new code must be written in TypeScript; existing JavaScript will be migrated opportunistically when touched. Enable strict type-checking (compilerOptions.strict = true) with noImplicitAny, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, and incremental builds. Use a single root tsconfig with per-package extends for consistent targets (ES2020+ for runtime, ESNext modules where supported) and declaration output for public packages. Enforce type-checking in CI with tsc --noEmit and linting via eslint with @typescript-eslint, integrated with Prettier for formatting. Consume community types via @types; when unavailable, add minimal scoped .d.ts files and progressively refine. Share common domain types in a dedicated types package to avoid duplication and runtime drift. For Node scripts and tooling, prefer tsx/ts-node for local execution; production artifacts are compiled with tsc. Block merges on type errors and lint violations. Document patterns for interop with JS, JSON, and ESM/CJS boundaries, and provide developer onboarding to ensure consistent usage.

## Decision

Adopt MkDocs as the primary tool for maintaining and publishing our documentation site.

- Author content in Markdown under /docs, organized by topic and version.
- Use the Material for MkDocs theme for navigation, search, and consistent UI; configure site navigation via mkdocs.yml.
- Host the generated static site on GitHub Pages (or equivalent static hosting), with an automated CI pipeline to build on every change and deploy on main tags.
- Enable versioning with mike to publish and manage multiple documentation versions aligned with releases.
- Use MkDocs plugins/extensions for improved authoring:
  - mkdocs-material, mkdocs-awesome-pages-plugin (nav from filesystem), mkdocs-redirects (preserve links), mkdocs-minify-plugin.
  - Markdown extensions: admonition, codehilite, toc, pymdown-extensions (including superfences, details, tabbed).
  - Mermaid support for diagrams.
- Keep architectural decisions in ADRs within the repo and surface them in the site navigation.
- Integrate with our code reference strategy:
  - Prefer mkdocstrings for Python/TypeScript reference pages where feasible, or link to Sphinx/RTD if generated elsewhere.
- Treat broken links and build warnings as CI failures to preserve quality.
- Provide local preview via mkdocs serve and a Make/NPM script for a single-entry developer command.
- Enforce docs style and link checks via pre-commit hooks (e.g., markdownlint, prettier) to keep contributions consistent.

Adopt Brakeman as the primary static code analysis tool for our Ruby/Rails codebase. Integrate Brakeman into the CI/CD pipeline to run on every pull request and on merges to main, failing the build on any High severity findings and on Medium severity findings that are not explicitly ignored. Store and publish results in SARIF/JSON for visibility in the pipeline and code scanning dashboards. Provide a standard developer workflow to run Brakeman locally (via bin/brakeman or a make task) prior to commit. Manage legacy noise with a versioned ignore/baseline file committed to the repo and reviewed periodically; all new findings must be addressed or justified via time-bound ignores. Keep the Brakeman rules and gem versions current and schedule at least a weekly scan on default branches. Document configuration, severity thresholds, and remediation guidance, and include Brakeman in the project template for new services.

We will host all containerized applications on Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) as our managed container orchestration platform. We will default to ECS on Fargate for serverless compute and operational simplicity; ECS on EC2 with capacity providers will be used only for workloads requiring specialized instances (e.g., GPUs), daemon-level host integrations, or sustained cost optimizations not achievable with Fargate. We will standardize on one ECS cluster per environment, deploy services behind Application Load Balancers, and use ECS Service autoscaling (CPU/memory/ALB request metrics) with multi‑AZ placement.

Container images will be stored in Amazon ECR. Deployments will use rolling or blue/green (ECS/CodeDeploy) strategies integrated with our CI/CD (e.g., GitHub Actions/CodePipeline). Tasks will run in private subnets with least‑privilege IAM task roles, pull secrets from AWS Secrets Manager/SSM Parameter Store, and emit logs via FireLens/CloudWatch Logs. Metrics, traces, and alarms will be managed through CloudWatch/X-Ray. Where appropriate, we will use AWS Cloud Map for service discovery.

We will enable cost controls via Fargate Spot and EC2 Spot (through capacity providers) for tolerable workloads, enforce tagging and quotas, and apply runtime controls (task size limits, health checks). This approach aligns with our Docker-based workflow, reduces undifferentiated ops, and integrates natively with our AWS networking, security, and monitoring standards.

Adopt a managed e-signature provider (DocuSign) for production and sandbox for non‑production to meet ESIGN/UETA and eIDAS requirements with minimal operational burden.

- Integrate via DocuSign’s REST API using JWT service integration; prefer embedded signing within our app, with remote/email signing as fallback.
- Use provider Templates/Composite Templates; generate documents from server-rendered HTML to PDF, injecting application data and dynamic clauses.
- Default to Advanced Electronic Signature (AdES). Escalate to Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) only where mandated by jurisdiction/policy.
- Authenticate signers through our session (SCA) plus email verification; enable SMS OTP for step‑up on higher‑risk transactions.
- Subscribe to Connect webhooks for envelope lifecycle events; implement idempotent handlers with retries/backoff. Drive downstream workflows (status updates, audit, fulfillment) from completion events.
- Persist minimal data: envelope IDs, status, timestamps, and signer identifiers. Store final signed PDFs and the provider’s certificate of completion; encrypt at rest; apply retention and legal hold policies. Do not store raw PII beyond necessity.
- Ensure accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA) via provider UI; localize templates as needed.
- Choose data residency aligned with regulatory needs (e.g., EU). Rely on provider HA; back up executed documents to S3 with versioning and Object Lock (WORM) for evidentiary integrity.
- Abstract provider behind an interface to allow future vendor substitution with minimal change.

We will adopt Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) across all published artifacts (libraries, services, Docker images, Helm charts) and use API Evolution as the default strategy to maintain backward compatibility.

- Breaking changes:
  - Public APIs (HTTP/GraphQL/gRPC): prefer additive changes. When a breaking change is unavoidable, introduce a new major API version via explicit versioning (e.g., URI prefix /v2 or versioned namespace) while maintaining the previous version for a deprecation window.
  - Libraries/SDKs: bump MAJOR and document migration steps.

- Tagging and releases:
  - Every release is tagged in Git as vX.Y.Z.
  - Docker images are pushed as X.Y.Z and major/minor floating tags (X, X.Y), plus immutable commit-SHA tags.
  - Pre-releases use SemVer prerelease identifiers (e.g., 2.1.0-rc.1).

- Deprecation and support:
  - Announce deprecations at least one minor release in advance; maintain previous major API version for a minimum of 6 months (configurable per product risk).
  - Provide deprecation headers in responses and changelog entries with migration guidance.

- Compatibility guarantees:
  - Minor/patch releases may add optional fields/parameters but must not remove or change semantics of existing ones.
  - Database migrations must be backward/forward compatible during rolling deploys (expand→migrate→contract).

- Documentation and tooling:
  - Auto-generate release notes from conventional commits.
  - Publish OpenAPI/protos per version and host versioned docs.
  - CI enforces version bumps consistent with detected change type.

This policy applies to all environments; deployment pipelines consume immutable version tags to ensure reproducibility and traceability.

Decision

- Represent all machine-interpretable date-time values as timezone-aware instants in UTC.
- Use ISO 8601/RFC 3339 for all external interfaces (APIs, logs): yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss[.SSS]Z or with explicit numeric offset; prefer trailing Z for UTC.
- Distinguish types:
  - Instant (moment in time): field name suffix _at; store as TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE (or equivalent) in databases; serialize as RFC 3339.
  - Date-only (calendar date without time): suffix _on; store as DATE; serialize as yyyy-MM-dd.
  - Time-only or local date-time (rare): only when business meaning is explicitly local; must include an associated timezone identifier field or be confined to UI.
- Never store timezone-naive datetimes in persistence or APIs.
- Normalize inbound timestamps to UTC at system boundaries; preserve original offset only if required by business auditing.
- Precision: milliseconds throughout (SSS). If higher precision is required, consistently use microseconds across storage and APIs.
- Default fields: created_at, updated_at (UTC instants). Use deleted_at for soft deletes (NULL when not deleted).
- Validation: reject ambiguous or non-ISO formats; require offsets when non-UTC; disallow 24:00 and leap seconds in input.
- Do not use epoch integers in public APIs; allowed internally with clear units (ms) and type safety.
- Index frequently queried temporal fields and partition large tables by time where applicable.
- Backfill and migrate existing data to UTC, correcting or annotating records with ambiguous local times.

We will use JWT (RFC 7519) as bearer access tokens for API authorization. Tokens will be signed (not encrypted) using asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) and exposed via a JWKS endpoint for verification and key rotation (kid header required). Access tokens will be short-lived (5–15 minutes) and contain minimal claims: sub, iss, aud, iat, exp, nbf, jti, and scoped authorization (roles/permissions). No PII will be embedded.

Refresh tokens will be opaque, server-managed with rotation on each use; on rotation failure, previously issued tokens are revoked. If a JWT refresh token is required, it will include jti and be rotated with a replay-detection store. Logout and compromise handling will revoke active refresh tokens and mark access token jti values as denied until expiry (bounded TTL).

Validation will enforce alg, signature, exp/nbf with small clock skew, iss/aud match, and scope checks at resource servers. We will reject “none” and disallow symmetric algorithms in multi-service environments.

For browsers, access tokens will be delivered via Authorization: Bearer; refresh tokens (if stored client-side) will be in Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=strict cookies. All issuance and use require TLS. Token size will be limited to fit headers and proxies.

We will integrate with an OAuth 2.1/OpenID Connect-compliant provider where possible; otherwise, we’ll use a well-supported JWT library, implement automated key rotation, metrics/alerts for token errors, and periodic security reviews.

We will place the 0.x line into maintenance mode and begin an explicit deprecation period leading to its end-of-life.

- No new features will be added to 0.x. Only critical bug fixes and security patches will be accepted.
- Backwards-incompatible changes in 0.x will be avoided. If unavoidable, they must be gated behind flags or configuration and accompanied by a deprecation path.
- Any API, CLI, or configuration in 0.x that will not be supported in 1.0 will be marked as deprecated immediately:
  - Annotate code with @deprecated (or equivalent) and include replacement guidance.
  - Surface runtime warnings (one-time per process) and log deprecation messages with stable codes.
  - For HTTP endpoints, emit Deprecation and Sunset headers and link to changelog/migration docs.
- Deprecated elements will remain available for at least two minor releases or 90 days in 0.x (whichever is longer) before removal in 1.0.
- A dedicated release/0.x maintenance branch will be created. Patch releases (0.x.y) will be issued as needed; no further minor versions will be cut unless required for a deprecation window.
- A comprehensive migration guide to 1.0 will be published and kept current, including compatibility shims and codemods where feasible.
- Upon 1.0 GA:
  - 0.x enters limited support for 6 months (security and critical fixes only).
  - After the support window, 0.x becomes EOL with no further releases.
- Communications: deprecation notice in README, release notes, package metadata, and automated advisories to integrators; scheduled reminders before EOL.

This strategy minimizes churn for consumers, provides clear timelines, and focuses investment on the 1.x line.

Build a time-boxed, throwaway prototype to validate key assumptions and de-risk the highest-uncertainty areas. The prototype will:

- Implement a single end-to-end “happy path” covering the core user journey, with minimal UI and only essential logic.
- Stub/mock external integrations and use in-memory or lightweight persistence; avoid full data modeling.
- Prioritize learning over polish: no production-hardening, scalability, performance tuning, or exhaustive test coverage beyond what’s needed to iterate safely.
- Use familiar tools and frameworks to move quickly and reduce setup overhead.
- Include targeted spikes for any high-risk technical areas (e.g., auth flows, critical API integration) to prove feasibility.

Set explicit success criteria: validate user value via stakeholder demos, confirm feasibility of core integrations, capture latency/UX constraints, and surface architectural hotspots. Time-box to 2–3 weeks with a midpoint review; stop when criteria are met or risks are disproven.

Artifacts produced will be a demoable prototype, a list of validated/invalidated assumptions, a refined architecture sketch, and a prioritized backlog. Prototype code is not to be promoted to production without rework; its purpose is to inform design and planning, not to become the foundation of the final system.

Adopt the Argo CD App-of-Apps pattern with a single declarative root per cluster/environment that owns only Argo CD Application/ApplicationSet resources.

- Root applications:
  - One root Application per cluster/environment (e.g., clusters/dev, clusters/stage, clusters/prod).
  - Root points to clusters/<env>/root and syncs only Applications/ApplicationSets (no raw workload manifests).
  - Sync options: automated, prune enabled, self-heal; sync-wave ordering enforced.

- Repository structure:
  - gitops/
    - clusters/
      - <env>/
        - root/ (apps-of-apps definitions, ordering)
        - projects/ (Argo CD Projects: boundaries, destinations, allowed repos)
        - bootstrap/ (CRDs/operators required before apps; separate app with early sync-wave)
    - apps/
      - <domain>/
        - <service>/
          - chart/ or base/ (Helm/Kustomize)
          - overlays/
            - dev|stage|prod (env-specific values/patches)
    - platforms/
      - shared components (ingress controllers, cert-manager, external-dns, logging, monitoring) with env overlays

- Application granularity:
  - One Application per deployable unit per environment overlay (apps/<domain>/<service>/overlays/<env>).
  - Platform components are Applications under platforms/* with controlled sync order.

- Dynamic generation:
  - Use ApplicationSet (git directory or list generator) for domains with many similar services.
  - Enforce naming: <env>-<domain>-<service>; labels: domain, team, tier, env for policy/selectors.

- Ordering and dependencies:
  - Sync waves: 0 bootstrap/CRDs, 1 namespaces/projects, 2 platforms, 3 shared services (db operators, secrets mgmt), 4 application backends, 5 frontends/jobs.
  - Use resource hooks only when necessary; prefer waves.

- Multi-tenancy and security:
  - Use Argo CD Projects per team/domain; restrict destinations, repos, and namespaces.
  - Namespaces per service or per team with network policies; Argo CD service accounts scoped via Projects.

- Promotion strategy:
  - GitOps PRs from lower to higher env overlays; roots pin to branches/tags per env.
  - Image tags managed via image automation or values files; avoid :latest.

- Drift and hygiene:
  - Enable prune and self-heal; soft-delete protections via sync options as needed.
  - Use ignoreDifferences for known noisy fields.
  - Root Application owns only child Applications to avoid accidental cascade.

This structure scales, enforces boundaries, enables automation via ApplicationSet, and keeps environment-specific concerns isolated.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized, configurable middleware for custom HTTP header handling across the API gateway and all edge-facing services with the following principles:

- Allowlist-based propagation: Only explicitly configured custom headers are accepted and forwarded. Support exact names and regex-based prefixes (e.g., X-Company-*, X-Exp-*). Default deny.
- Normalization: Normalize header names to lowercase for internal processing; preserve original value bytes. On outbound, preserve normalized names (HTTP/2/3 compliant).
- Security and privacy:
  - Strip hop-by-hop headers (per RFC 7230/9110) and never forward sensitive headers (Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, Proxy-*), unless explicitly required and isolated.
  - Enforce size limits (per-header and aggregate), max header count, and value charset validation to mitigate abuse.
  - Redact or hash PII-bearing custom headers in logs/metrics; include only approved keys in traces.
- Context mapping: Provide a mapping layer to project approved headers into a typed RequestContext (e.g., correlationId, locale, tenantId, experimentFlags) for downstream consumption; expose via framework DI.
- Observability: Attach approved correlation headers (traceparent, X-Request-Id) to all outbound calls; surface allowlist matches/drops via metrics and debug logs.
- Compatibility: Continue supporting legacy X-* headers via explicit allowlist; publish deprecation timelines and migration guides to standardized names.
- Configuration: Centralized policy managed via configuration (per environment and service), hot-reloadable where supported; versioned in repo with code owners.
- Contracting: Document accepted custom headers in OpenAPI for each endpoint; CI checks ensure only documented headers are referenced.
- Testing and rollout: Ship middleware as a shared library; enforce via gateway first, then services. Provide feature flags for gradual rollout and emergency disable.

## Decision

We will support only Node.js versions that are still receiving security updates per the official Node.js Release Schedule. Concretely:
- The minimum supported Node.js version is the lowest LTS release that is still in “Active LTS” or “Maintenance” with security fixes.
- We will drop support for Node.js versions within 30 days of their EOL date. No compatibility guarantees or patches will be provided for EOL versions.
- The package.json engines field will reflect the current minimum supported LTS (e.g., "node": ">=18.x" as applicable) and we may use “engineStrict” in tooling/CI to enforce it.
- CI will run against: the minimum supported LTS, all currently supported LTS lines, and the latest Current (non-blocking). Release gates will require passing on supported LTS versions.
- When raising the minimum runtime baseline, we will:
  - For libraries: treat as a breaking change and bump the major version, documenting in CHANGELOG and release notes.
  - For applications/services: announce in release notes and deployment docs; coordinate rollout with operations.
- Containers, runtime images, and build environments will be pinned to supported LTS images and updated promptly following Node security releases.

## Decision

We will strip Google Sitelinks Searchbox metadata from saved documents to avoid embedding irrelevant, network-oriented structured data in offline pages.

Specifically:
- Remove JSON-LD scripts (type="application/ld+json") that declare a schema.org WebSite entity with potentialAction of type SearchAction (or equivalent) intended for Sitelinks Searchbox (e.g., target templates with search URLs and query-input definitions).
- Remove matching Microdata/RDFa variants that annotate a WebSite with potentialAction/SearchAction for the same purpose.
- Keep all other structured data intact (e.g., Article, BreadcrumbList, Product, etc.) unless they redundantly or exclusively implement the Sitelinks Searchbox pattern.

Heuristics will be conservative: only content that unambiguously represents the Sitelinks Searchbox will be removed to avoid collateral loss of useful structured data. Where JSON-LD blocks contain mixed content, we will surgically remove only the WebSite/SearchAction nodes, preserving the rest.

This reduces bloat, prevents unintended search integrations, and preserves fidelity of non-related schema metadata.

## Decision

Adopt the Composite pattern for the handler layer to support fan-out, ordering, and policy-driven orchestration of heterogeneous handlers.

- Define a uniform Handler interface:
  - async handle(input, context): Promise<Result>
  - optional lifecycle: init(), shutdown()
- Introduce CompositeHandler implementing the same interface and owning an ordered list of child handlers.
- Execution semantics:
  - Deterministic order (insertion order).
  - Configurable policy:
    - all: run all children; aggregate results; proceed despite individual failures.
    - fail-fast: stop on first failure; bubble error.
    - first-success: stop on first success; report that result.
    - parallel: run concurrently (bounded by configured concurrency); aggregate per above sub-policy.
  - Error isolation: child errors are captured and wrapped with handler id; composite applies policy.
- Configuration:
  - Declarative config (JSON/YAML) with a handler registry for construction by type/id and DI injection of dependencies.
  - Composites can be nested arbitrarily.
  - Defaults: policy=all, concurrency=1, retry=off unless child overrides.
- Observability:
  - Structured logs with handler id, duration, outcome.
  - Metrics per handler (count, error rate, latency) and composite aggregates.
  - Trace propagation via context.
- Safety:
  - Handlers are stateless or explicitly synchronized; execution context is immutable per call.
  - Bounded queues and timeouts for parallel policy; backpressure signaled via rejected promises.
- Lifecycle:
  - Composite delegates init/shutdown to children; guarantees idempotency and ordered teardown (reverse order).
- Extensibility:
  - Leaf handlers focus on IO/side-effects; composites only orchestrate.
  - Policies are pluggable; new policies can be registered without changing existing handlers.

This design enables flexible composition, predictable behavior, and clear observability while minimizing coupling between handlers.

We will interact with the Docker daemon through the official Docker Engine SDK (Docker Client) for our implementation language (e.g., Go/Python/Java), rather than shelling out to the docker CLI. The service will use the SDK to manage images, containers, networks, and volumes via the Docker Engine API over a Unix domain socket (Linux), named pipe (Windows), or TLS-secured TCP (remote/cluster nodes).

We will:
- Pin and negotiate a compatible Docker API version to ensure forward/backward compatibility.
- Require TLS with mutual authentication for any remote daemon access; certificates and keys will be managed via our secret store.
- Encapsulate SDK usage behind an internal interface to enable mocking in tests and to preserve the option to swap implementations (e.g., containerd/Podman shims) with minimal impact.
- Implement resilient connection handling, timeouts, and retries, and surface daemon health in observability.
- Use streaming APIs (logs, events, attach) and typed models provided by the SDK to reduce parsing errors and improve reliability.
- Keep the docker CLI for diagnostics and developer workflows only; it will not be invoked from application code.

This approach provides a stable, secure, and testable integration with Docker while minimizing runtime dependencies and reducing operational risk.

We designate the server-side database as the single source of truth and use a client-side cache for responsiveness and offline support. All authoritative records are stored in the backend (managed relational store), exposed via a versioned REST/GraphQL API. On devices, we persist a normalized cache in IndexedDB via Dexie (per the Storage ADR), seeded at sign-in and incrementally refreshed.

Reads are served from the local cache first, with background revalidation against the server to keep data fresh. Writes use optimistic updates: we immediately update the local cache and enqueue a sync task. A service worker manages the outbound queue, retries with exponential backoff, and processes responses to reconcile local state. Each record includes updatedAt and a version/etag for conflict detection; the server applies last-write-wins by timestamp unless a domain-specific merge strategy is defined. On conflicts, the client marks records as “needs review,” surfaces a non-blocking notification, and retains both versions for user resolution when required.

Real-time coherence is improved via WebSockets/SSE where available; otherwise, periodic background polling runs. Offline-first behavior is default: all create/update/delete operations are stored locally and synchronized when connectivity is restored. Sensitive fields in the client cache are minimized and, where applicable, encrypted at rest. Audit trails and server-side events remain solely on the backend.

- Introduce a centralized feature flag system to control rollout, deprecations, and backward-compatibility toggles across platform layers (PHP, templates, storefront assets, CLI).
- Provide a single source of truth exposed via a Feature service (Feature::isActive(string $flag): bool) available through DI, with framework integrations:
  - PHP: Feature::isActive and Feature::ifActive callbacks.
  - Twig: feature() function and feature tags.
  - JavaScript/SCSS: generate a dump file (e.g., var/config_js_features.json) during build for frontend consumption.
- Configuration hierarchy and evaluation:
  - Flags are defined in configuration (e.g., feature.yaml) with optional metadata (description, owner, removal-by).
  - Environment variables override configuration (e.g., FEATURE_X=1/0).
  - CLI command feature:dump materializes current state for frontend builds and hot reload.
  - Values are cached; changes require cache clear or dump refresh to take effect.
- Naming and semantics:
  - Use uppercase snake_case with product prefix, e.g., FEATURE_NEXT_12345 or FEATURE_FOO_BAR.
  - Flags are strictly boolean; complex strategies must be implemented in code behind the flag, not in the flag value.
  - Default is disabled unless explicitly enabled; tests may opt-in per-suite.
- Lifecycle and governance:
  - Every new breaking/backward-compatibility change must be guarded by a flag.
  - Each flag must have an owner, rationale, and planned removal date.
  - When a flagged path becomes default, flip behavior, announce deprecation, then remove the flag within two minor releases.
  - CI enforces no orphaned flags and fails if removal-by dates are exceeded.
- Observability and safety:
  - Optional logging/metrics hooks for flag evaluations in non-prod.
  - Flags must not gate security-critical checks; use allowlist strategies for risk-sensitive toggles.

We will require individual, per-user SSH key pairs for all interactive access to source code repositories, bastions, and servers. Shared or team SSH keys are prohibited.

- Each engineer must generate their own key pair per device. Use Ed25519 keys by default; RSA 4096 is permitted only for compatibility. All private keys must be protected with a strong passphrase.
- Public keys will be registered to the engineer’s user identity in upstream systems (e.g., GitHub user keys for repo access; authorized_keys or directory-backed sync for server access). Service automation will distribute/revoke public keys as part of onboarding/offboarding.
- Password-based SSH login and shared accounts are disabled. Engineers authenticate with their own user accounts and escalate via sudo as needed. Root login over SSH remains disabled.
- Key rotation is required at least annually and immediately upon suspected compromise or device loss. Revocation is performed by removing the corresponding public key from the centralized sources of truth and configuration.
- For production access, where supported, we will prefer short-lived SSH certificates issued by our SSH CA (or cloud-native equivalents) instead of long-lived static keys; otherwise we fall back to authorized_keys with per-user keys.
- Service and automation access will use narrowly scoped deploy keys or machine identities tied to a single repository or host, not shared human keys.
- Private keys must not be stored or shared via chat, email, or ticketing systems; approved secure storage (e.g., local OS keychain) is required.

We will standardize on AWS-native logging for all workloads. CloudWatch Logs will be the system of record for application, platform, and access logs across Lambda, ECS/EKS, and EC2, with JSON-structured logs and a common correlation schema (trace_id/request_id) to enable cross-service troubleshooting. Log groups will be environment- and service-scoped with KMS encryption, lifecycle policies, and retention tuned per data classification.

Ingestion will use AWS-managed agents: Lambda’s native integration, FireLens/Fluent Bit for ECS/EKS, and the CloudWatch agent or AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (OTel) where applicable. Metric Filters will convert key log patterns to CloudWatch metrics, tied to Alarms and Ops notifications (EventBridge/Slack/PagerDuty). CloudWatch Logs Insights will be the primary query interface for operations, with Contributor Insights enabled for high-cardinality analysis.

For compliance, cost, and analytics, we will stream logs via subscription filters to Kinesis Data Firehose → S3 (partitioned, compressed, encrypted), with optional Athena/Glue catalogs for query, and Glacier for long-term retention. Where required, we will forward a subset to external SIEM via Kinesis or partner integrations.

Access will be controlled with least-privilege IAM and cross-account subscriptions for centralized observability. This approach minimizes undifferentiated heavy-lifting, keeps data resident in AWS, provides consistent developer/ops workflows, and remains extensible via OTel and Kinesis when we need to integrate third-party tools.

## Decision

Adopt a clear, consistent environment taxonomy and naming convention across code, infrastructure, and pipelines.

- Environments: local (developer machine), dev (integration), test/qa (verification), staging/uat (pre‑production), prod (production). Optional: sandbox/demo for ephemeral use.
- Isolation: prod runs in a dedicated cloud account/subscription/project. Non‑prod may share an account but must be logically isolated (resource groups/namespaces). No shared state between environments.
- Identifiers: use lowercase slugs [a‑z0‑9-], e.g., dev, test, staging, prod. Resource names and DNS include the environment suffix/prefix. Environment IDs are immutable and unique per deployment target.
- Configuration: environment is provided as explicit input to apps and tooling (no inference). Use environment-scoped configuration via parameter stores and secret managers; never bake secrets into images. Do not fork code per environment; use configuration and feature flags.
- CI/CD: build once, promote the same artifact through dev → test → staging → prod. Each promotion is gated by automated checks and manual approval for prod. Pipelines require an explicit environment parameter. No direct deploys to prod outside the pipeline.
- Infrastructure as Code: one codebase with per-environment state/workspaces and variables. Drift detection and change reviews per environment.
- Access control: least privilege per environment; production access is tightly controlled and audited. Separate credentials and service principals per environment.
- Backward compatibility: deprecate ambiguous variables (e.g., env, environmentName). Standardize on environment for target tier and account/subscription for cloud boundary, with a documented migration path.

## Decision

Adopt Visual Studio 2017 (v15.9 or later) as the standard Windows IDE for this codebase. All solutions and projects will be upgraded to be compatible with VS2017, including migration to MSBuild 15 and SDK-style projects where applicable. We will standardize on PackageReference for NuGet dependencies, enable C# 7.x language features, and align build and test workflows with VS2017 toolchains. Required workloads include: .NET Desktop Development, ASP.NET and web development, Azure development, and Node.js (where relevant). CI/CD pipelines will use MSBuild 15.x and the corresponding .NET SDKs to ensure parity with local builds. Visual Studio 2015 (and earlier) will be deprecated for this repository; contributors on older versions must upgrade to VS2017 or use the supported CLI toolchain. Configuration will be centralized via solution-level .editorconfig and rulesets to ensure consistent coding standards and analyzers in VS2017. Extensions used by the team must be compatible with VS2017.

## Decision

We will use AWS S3 as the hosting solution for all static website assets and public downloadable artifacts. Buckets will be versioned, encrypted at rest (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), and configured with least-privilege IAM policies. Public access will be served via Amazon CloudFront as the CDN, using Origin Access Control (OAC) to restrict direct S3 access and enforce TLS in transit. Route 53 will manage DNS, and ACM will provide TLS certificates. Where redirects or error documents are required, CloudFront behaviors and functions will be used; S3 static website hosting features will only be used if a website endpoint is strictly necessary.

Content deployment will be automated via CI/CD with atomic updates (upload to versioned prefixes, then update CloudFront behaviors or invalidations). Lifecycle rules will manage storage classes (e.g., transition to Intelligent-Tiering/Glacier for archives) and object expiration for obsolete versions and logs. Access logs will be enabled to S3 and integrated with CloudWatch for monitoring and alerting.

S3 will not host dynamic server-side logic; any dynamic needs will be served through separate managed services (e.g., API Gateway + Lambda) behind the same domain via CloudFront. This approach minimizes operational overhead, improves scalability and performance globally, and aligns with security best practices for static hosting on AWS.

We will standardize a reproducible, single-command local environment for GSP built on containers and profiles:

- Orchestration: Docker Compose v2 as the canonical runtime for all local dependencies (DB, cache, message broker, object storage, mail, reverse proxy). compose.yaml is the source of truth; profiles enable running subsets (api-only, full, e2e).
- Dev container: A .devcontainer/ configuration (Codespaces/VS Code) wraps the same Compose stack to pin toolchains and ensure parity across platforms.
- Bootstrap: make targets (make bootstrap, make up, make down, make logs, make clean) drive common flows; PowerShell scripts are provided for Windows users without Make. No global installers required beyond Docker and Make/PowerShell.
- Configuration: .env.example defines defaults; developers copy to .env. Secrets are never committed and are managed via 1Password/Vault; .env.local is supported for overrides and is gitignored.
- Networking/TLS: Traefik provides local routing and HTTPS; mkcert generates a dev CA and certificates. Stable, documented ports are reserved to avoid collisions.
- Code–container loop: Source is bind-mounted; services run in watch/hot-reload modes for fast feedback. Images are built only when dependencies change.
- Data and migrations: Migrations run on startup; deterministic seed data is provided via idempotent seed scripts. Named volumes persist data; make clean purges them.
- External integrations: LocalStack (AWS), WireMock (HTTP APIs), and MailHog (SMTP) provide offline-compatible mocks toggled via Compose profiles.
- Observability: Optional profile spins up OpenTelemetry Collector, Jaeger/Tempo, and Grafana/Loki for traces/logs/metrics.
- CI parity: The same Dockerfiles and Compose definitions are used in CI; images are tagged consistently to minimize “works on my machine.”
- Tooling/quality: Pre-commit hooks enforce format/lint/type-check; versions are pinned via devcontainer/asdf files.

This setup minimizes host dependencies, accelerates onboarding, and ensures environment parity while remaining flexible for partial stacks and e2e testing.

## Decision

We will document architectural choices using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as described by Michael Nygard. ADRs will be Markdown files committed to the code repository under docs/adr/, numbered sequentially, and tracked through a simple lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded. We will use a lightweight template that captures context, decision, consequences, alternatives, and links to related ADRs. Authors may use adr-tools (or equivalent) to streamline creation and indexing.

Every significant architectural change (principles, platform choices, integrations, cross-cutting concerns, data contracts, SLAs/SLOs, security posture) must be accompanied by an ADR and referenced in the relevant pull requests. ADRs are owned by the proposing team and reviewed asynchronously by designated reviewers (architecture group/tech leads) via standard PR workflow.

ADRs must be concise, source-controlled, immutable once Accepted (only superseded, not edited), and discoverable via an index file (docs/adr/README.md). Teams working across repositories will maintain ADRs in the affected repo(s) and, when cross-cutting, in a central architecture repo with links back to implementation ADRs. Language: clear, implementation-neutral where possible; decision rationale prioritized over exhaustive detail.

## Decision

Adopt Amazon S3 as the primary object storage service for static assets, user-generated content, data exports, and operational logs across all environments.

- Bucket strategy: separate per environment and purpose (e.g., app-{env}-assets, app-{env}-uploads, app-{env}-logs, app-{env}-backups). Enforce Bucket Owner Enforced object ownership and Block Public Access on all buckets.
- Access and delivery: private buckets accessed via VPC endpoints and least-privilege IAM. Public delivery through Amazon CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC); no direct public S3 website hosting.
- Encryption: enforce default encryption (SSE-S3). Use SSE-KMS with customer-managed keys for sensitive data; restrict kms:Decrypt by context and apply key rotation.
- Versioning: enable versioning on critical/config/backups buckets; disable on high-churn uploads/derived-assets to control cost. Configure MFA Delete for break-glass where feasible.
- Lifecycle and retention: 
  - Expire incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days.
  - Transition infrequently accessed objects to Standard-IA at 30 days; to Glacier Instant Retrieval at 90 days; to Glacier Deep Archive at 365 days (per data class).
  - For versioned buckets, expire noncurrent versions after 90 days and cap at 3 noncurrent versions unless stricter retention applies.
  - Use Intelligent-Tiering for unpredictable access patterns.
- Replication: enable Cross-Region Replication (CRR) for compliance-critical buckets to a secondary region with KMS-reencrypted targets; consider Replication Time Control for RPO guarantees.
- Observability and governance: enable S3 server access logs to a dedicated log bucket, CloudTrail data events for sensitive buckets, S3 Storage Lens for org-wide insights, and AWS Config rules for policy drift. Tag all buckets/objects for ownership, environment, data class, and retention.
- Performance and reliability: use multipart uploads by default; presigned URLs for client uploads/downloads; enable S3 Transfer Acceleration only when latency justifies cost. Leverage strong read-after-write consistency.
- Cost management: apply cost allocation tags and budgets/alerts; review Storage Lens and lifecycle reports quarterly.

Constrain Civi to its core competency—a CRM UI for constituent relationship management—and move non-CRM responsibilities into dedicated, domain-owned services. Specifically:
- Identity and access management (authentication, authorization, SSO) will be handled by an Identity Service (OIDC/OAuth2), removing user management from Civi.
- Payments, subscriptions, and invoicing will be owned by a Payments/Billing Service; Civi will no longer initiate or reconcile financial transactions.
- Memberships and entitlements (eligibility, status, benefits) will be owned by a Membership/Entitlements Service; Civi will only display state sourced from this service.
- Messaging (bulk email, transactional notifications) will be handled by a Communications Service; Civi will not send emails directly.
- Event registration workflows and capacity rules move to an Events Service; Civi may surface event data read-only.
- Reporting and analytics move to a Data Platform (ETL/warehouse/BI); Civi will not act as a reporting source of truth.

All integration occurs via a stable API layer and an event bus. We will implement an anti-corruption layer around Civi (adapters + sync processes) to translate between Civi’s data model and canonical domain models. Core domain services are the systems of record; Civi becomes a consumer/producer of events and APIs for operator-facing workflows.

Adopt a strangler-fig migration: freeze new Civi features in the migrated domains, introduce read-only views in Civi where feasible, and retire custom Civi extensions as functions are rehomed. New capabilities must be built in the domain services, not in Civi.

Adopt programmatic, tool-based source formatting as a mandatory, reproducible step across the codebase.

- Use language-appropriate, opinionated formatters (e.g., Prettier for JS/TS/JSON/Markdown/YAML; Black for Python; gofmt for Go; rustfmt for Rust; ktfmt/spotless for Kotlin/Java) and enforce consistent newline/end-of-file conventions via .editorconfig and .gitattributes.
- Provide a single top-level command to format the repository (e.g., make format or npm run format) and a corresponding check command (e.g., make format:check or npm run format:check) that fails on drift.
- Integrate pre-commit automation (e.g., lint-staged + pre-commit hooks) to format only changed files locally; mirror the same commands in CI to gate merges.
- Pin formatter versions and configs in-repo; disallow per-developer overrides that change canonical output.
- Apply a one-time repository-wide formatting baseline commit to minimize ongoing diffs, and document formatter rules in CONTRIBUTING.
- IDE plugins are optional and may invoke the same CLI, but are not the source of truth.

This decision ensures consistent formatting, minimizes review noise, and makes formatting deterministic in local and CI environments.

## Decision

Adopt Spring Boot as the primary backend framework and React with Next.js as the primary frontend framework.

- Backend: Spring Boot
  - Rationale: Mature ecosystem, excellent support for RESTful APIs, security (Spring Security), data access (Spring Data), observability (Actuator), and cloud-native deployment. Strong alignment with team experience in JVM, high performance, and robust tooling (Maven/Gradle).
  - Approach: Modular microservice-ready architecture; standardized dependency management via Spring Boot starters; Kotlin/Java allowed with preference for Kotlin where appropriate; test stack using JUnit 5, Testcontainers, and WireMock.

- Frontend: React + Next.js (TypeScript)
  - Rationale: First-class support for server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), routing, and incremental static regeneration; strong ecosystem, accessibility tooling, and long-term community support. Enables progressive enhancement and good SEO while retaining SPA interactivity.
  - Approach: TypeScript by default; component library alignment (e.g., Radix/Headless UI or internal DS); state management via React Query + minimal local state; form handling with React Hook Form; testing with Jest, Testing Library, and Playwright; styling with CSS Modules or Tailwind CSS, determined per component/library fit.

- Cross-cutting
  - API contract via OpenAPI; generated clients for type safety.
  - CI/CD with containerized builds; Docker images for services; Infrastructure as Code.
  - Security baselines: OWASP Top 10, CSRF protection, input validation, and strict content security policies.
  - Performance budgets and accessibility gates in CI.

This stack optimizes developer productivity, maintainability, and scalability while leveraging the team’s existing skill sets and the strength of established ecosystems.

## Decision

Adopt HashiCorp Nomad as the primary deployment orchestrator for services and batch workloads. We will operate a Nomad cluster with Consul (service discovery/mesh) and Vault (secrets) to provide a lightweight, vendor-neutral platform with lower operational complexity than Kubernetes while retaining robust scheduling, deployment strategies, and multi-environment support.

Key implementation details:
- Workload types: containerized services (Docker driver) and batch/cron jobs; support for non-container workloads where needed.
- Environments: separate Nomad namespaces per env (dev/staging/prod) with per-namespace quotas and ACLs.
- Deployments: rolling and canary updates using Nomad job update stanzas; blue/green via distinct job groups and Consul service tags.
- Networking: Consul service discovery and Connect (service mesh) for mTLS, intentions, and traffic splitting; ingress via Consul API gateway or Traefik integrated with Consul.
- Secrets/config: Vault templates rendered by Nomad; configuration via environment variables and files with strict lease/renewal policies.
- CI/CD: pipeline builds/pushes images, runs policy checks (OPA/Conftest), and submits Nomad jobs (HCL) via Terraform or Nomad Pack; artifact registry is the single source for releases.
- Observability: Nomad/Consul/Vault metrics exported to Prometheus; logs via sidecar/agent to centralized logging; health checks via Consul.
- Capacity: heterogeneous node pools (CPU, memory, GPU) with constraints and affinities; autoscaling via Nomad autoscaler and cloud API; preemption for batch.
- Reliability: multi-az server quorum (3–5 servers), client nodes spread across AZs; periodic snapshots of state; disaster recovery runbooks.

This choice minimizes operational overhead, preserves portability, supports mixed workloads, and aligns with our team’s size and skills while enabling safe, auditable, and repeatable deployments.

Adopt Brakeman as the static application security testing (SAST) tool for all Rails services. Add a CI job in the security stage that runs Brakeman on every pull request and on main. Configure the job to fail the build on any High or Critical findings and to surface Medium findings as warnings; Low/Note findings will not block merges. Publish results to the pipeline artifacts and, where supported, upload SARIF output to the repository’s code scanning for inline annotations.

Provide a bin/brakeman script and document local usage so developers can run scans before opening PRs. Manage false positives via a reviewed brakeman.ignore file with rationale and expiry dates; re-validate ignores in a scheduled weekly scan. Keep Brakeman up to date via Dependabot (Gem or Docker image), pin versions to avoid breaking changes, and review release notes on upgrades.

This decision complements, not replaces, other security practices (dependency scanning, dynamic testing, and code review).

## Decision

Adopt a dedicated Refund Service that orchestrates refunds asynchronously via an event-driven saga, with the following core behaviors:

- Support full and partial refunds, multiple refunds per payment up to the captured amount, and multi-item allocations (line-level attribution).
- Treat charge reversal (pre-settlement void) and refund (post-settlement) as distinct paths; prefer reversal when settlement has not occurred.
- Enforce strict idempotency using a client-supplied idempotency key per payment-provider pair; duplicate requests return the original outcome.
- Normalize payment-provider interactions behind a gateway adapter interface; record provider capabilities (partial allowed, window, fees) and branch logic accordingly.
- Model refunds as a state machine (Requested → Validated → Initiated → Pending → Succeeded | Failed | Expired | Canceled) persisted with immutable audit trails and reason codes.
- Validate business constraints up front (eligibility windows, fraud holds, chargeback state, currency, tax rules, gift card/store credit rules).
- Emit domain events (RefundRequested, RefundInitiated, RefundCompleted, RefundFailed) for fulfillment, inventory, accounting, and customer notifications; publish ledger entries for revenue recognition and tax adjustments.
- Implement retries with exponential backoff for transient provider failures; require manual intervention for hard failures.
- Calculate amounts in minor units with fixed-precision arithmetic; lock exchange rates per original transaction currency.
- Expose synchronous APIs returning immediate acknowledgment plus a refund reference; completion is conveyed via webhooks/events and query APIs.
- Provide configurable policies per merchant/region (refund window, automatic vs manual review, fees, restocking).

## Decision

- Adopt Google-style docstrings for all Python code and require type hints across the public API to ensure consistency and high-quality generated documentation.
- Require docstrings for all public modules, classes, functions, and methods; private members are optional but encouraged when complexity warrants it.
- Generate API documentation from docstrings using MkDocs with mkdocstrings (Python handler) and the Material theme. Store sources under docs/ and publish via CI to the project’s documentation site on every main branch change and tagged release.
- Maintain narrative documentation (getting started, architecture, guides, examples) alongside API reference in docs/, keeping the README as the entry point that links into the docs site.
- Enforce documentation quality in CI:
  - pydocstyle (convention=google) and flake8-docstrings for style conformance.
  - interrogate to measure docstring coverage with a minimum threshold (≥90% for public symbols).
  - mypy to validate type hints referenced in docstrings and examples.
- Provide runnable examples in docstrings and/or docs using code blocks verified by doctest where practical.
- Add a pre-commit hook to run the documentation linters locally.
- Treat documentation as code: changes to public behavior must include updated docstrings and docs in the same PR. Code owners will not approve PRs that reduce doc coverage or break the docs build.

All ViewModels must use constructor injection for their dependencies, with parameters provided by Dagger. A single Dagger-provided ViewModelFactory will be the exclusive mechanism for creating ViewModels, binding each ViewModel into a multibinding map for keyed lookup. Runtime or screen-specific values (e.g., IDs, arguments) must be supplied via assisted injection or SavedStateHandle; do not fetch them from service locators or static singletons. This ensures testable, explicit dependencies, consistent lifecycle-aware creation, and clear module boundaries.

## Decision

Standardize on OpenJDK distributions for all development, CI, and production runtimes. For Arch Linux environments, use the community-maintained openjdk packages (preferably LTS: OpenJDK 11 now, with a planned migration path to 17 LTS). Avoid Oracle JDK due to licensing and redistribution constraints.

Containerized deployments will use vendor-neutral OpenJDK base images (AdoptOpenJDK/Eclipse Temurin when available), pinned by major/minor version and image digest to ensure reproducibility. For minimal footprints, build custom runtime images with jlink where feasible, derived from the same OpenJDK version as development/CI.

Establish a version policy:
- Primary target: Java 11 LTS; secondary compatibility: Java 8 (if required by dependencies) and forward-compat testing on 17 LTS.
- Pin exact package versions in CI and lock Docker image digests; document upgrade procedures and run compatibility suites before promotion.
- Use the same JVM flags and GC settings across environments, with environment-specific overrides via config.

Operational guidelines:
- Enable and validate TLS/cipher providers and timezone data; include common fonts/ICU data for internationalization needs.
- Monitor CVEs for OpenJDK and rebuild images promptly on security releases.
- Record build metadata (JDK vendor, version, commit) in artifacts for traceability.

Tooling:
- CI matrix executes on Arch OpenJDK and container OpenJDK to catch distro-specific regressions.
- Provide a dev bootstrap script to install the correct OpenJDK on Arch and set JAVA_HOME consistently.

This choice reduces licensing risk, improves supply-chain transparency, and aligns dev/prod parity while maintaining a clear, tested upgrade path across LTS versions.

We will manage all GPaas (Cloud Foundry) platform resources with Terraform using the Cloud Foundry provider. Terraform will provision and update orgs/spaces, quotas, user roles, service instances/bindings (e.g., PostgreSQL, Redis, S3-compatible), routes, network policies, and environment variables. Application artifacts will continue to be deployed via the CI/CD pipeline (cf push/zero-downtime strategies), but their platform dependencies and configuration will be declared and reconciled by Terraform to ensure repeatability and drift control.

We will structure the configuration as reusable modules per component, with environment overlays (dev/staging/prod) and Terraform workspaces. State will be kept in a remote backend with locking (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB or equivalent) and separated per environment. CI will run terraform fmt/validate/plan on PRs and gated terraform apply on the default branch with manual approval for production. Credentials for the CF API will be short‑lived or rotated service accounts with least privilege, injected via the pipeline secret store; no secrets will be committed to the repo.

We will implement tagging/labels and consistent naming conventions to support auditability and cost/usage reporting. Changes will be peer‑reviewed and version‑controlled; module versions will be pinned to ensure reproducibility. Where CF provider coverage is incomplete, we will encapsulate necessary cf CLI invocations as Terraform null_resource steps with clear migration paths back to native resources when available.

This decision centralizes infrastructure definitions alongside application code, enables predictable, idempotent provisioning across environments, and provides a single source of truth for platform configuration on GPaas.

We will standardize on MongoDB Change Streams using the Stable API v1 and require MongoDB server 6.0+ with Feature Compatibility Version (FCV) pinned to 6.0 for production. Client drivers must support the Stable API and Change Streams (e.g., MongoDB driver 4.4+ for Node/Java/.NET; equivalent for other runtimes).

Streams must be opened on the narrowest scope required (collection where possible) with:
- readConcern: majority
- fullDocument: updateLookup (and fullDocumentBeforeChange: whenAvailable where supported) to handle updates/deletes robustly
- startAfter using a persisted resumeToken (hex/base64) for exactly-once semantics
- maxAwaitTimeMS and batchSize tuned per workload; retryable reads enabled

We will store one durable resumeToken per stream (partition) in a dedicated, transactional metadata collection with majority writeConcern. Consumers must implement idempotency (dedupe by _id + clusterTime) and honor backpressure. We will detect and alert on invalidate events and resume errors.

Upgrades:
- Patch/minor driver upgrades are allowed freely under API v1.
- Server upgrades follow: set FCV to current, rolling upgrade, then bump FCV, verifying change streams stability in staging; during major upgrades we will dual-run consumers against a shadow stream, validate parity, then cut over by swapping resumeTokens.
- Any change that alters watched namespaces or projections is treated as a breaking change and versioned via consumer group IDs and independent tokens.

We will not use legacy oplog tailing or tailable cursors. If future MongoDB releases introduce Stable API v2 features we will evaluate adopting them behind a feature flag while maintaining compatibility with API v1 until all consumers migrate.

We will introduce a single, cross-platform GPIO base abstraction and migrate all platforms to it.

- Define a minimal, stable GPIOBase with: open/close, get_info (capabilities), configure(mode, pull, drive_strength, debounce), read, write, toggle.
- Split advanced behaviors into narrow extension interfaces: InterruptPin (enable_irq(edge), disable_irq, set_callback), PwmPin (set_duty, set_frequency, enable/disable), and AnalogPin if applicable. Capability discovery is via feature flags returned by get_info.
- Construction is mediated by a PlatformPinProvider/PinFactory that resolves pins by (controller_id, pin_number) and optional logical aliases; it returns an owning PinHandle to guarantee exclusive access (RAII).
- Configuration is applied via immutable config objects (builder pattern) and an atomic apply() to avoid transient states. Reconfiguration validates against capabilities and returns standardized error codes.
- Concurrency model: thread-safe for user-space calls; ISR-safe paths for interrupts. Callbacks are invoked on a dedicated dispatcher; platforms without threads use a pluggable event pump. Async APIs are provided where supported; sync APIs are preserved.
- Establish a unified pin numbering scheme and metadata (name, controller, physical header mapping) for diagnostics and consistent logging.
- Provide a comprehensive Mock/Fake provider for unit tests and a loopback/simulated provider for CI.
