- Deprecate platform-specific GPIO wrappers; provide adapters to the new interfaces with a staged migration plan and shims for backward compatibility where feasible.
- Document timing guarantees (best-effort, not hard real-time) and edge cases (glitches, debounce semantics). Ensure API is ABI-stable for C/C++ consumers and has idiomatic bindings for other languages.

Adopt Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0) across all SDKs. Public API is the documented surface; undocumented/internal packages, classes, and methods are excluded from compatibility guarantees.

- Backward compatibility: patch = bug/security fixes only; minor = backward-compatible features and deprecations; major = breaking changes only.
- Deprecation policy: introduce deprecations in a minor with clear replacements; emit compile-time/runtime warnings where possible; maintain deprecated APIs for at least two subsequent minor releases or 6 months (whichever is longer) before removal in the next major.
- Experimental features: ship behind explicit “experimental” namespaces/flags and pre-release versions (e.g., 1.4.0-beta.1). Experimental APIs may change without compatibility guarantees until first stable release.
- API/Server alignment: SDK major versions track the service API major. An SDK is compatible with the corresponding API major and should remain operational against n and n-1 server minors. Minor SDK releases may require newer server minors only for new features, not for baseline functionality.
- Dependency versioning: avoid exposing transitive dependencies in the public surface. Use conservative version ranges for runtime deps (pessimistic within major); pin build/test deps. Treat dependency major upgrades as potential breaking changes.
- Distribution and tagging: publish signed artifacts to ecosystem registries (npm, PyPI, Maven Central, NuGet, etc.) with immutable git tags (vX.Y.Z). Provide language-appropriate metadata for engines/runtime compatibility.
- Communication: maintain a human-curated CHANGELOG with categorized entries; publish release notes and migration guides for majors; surface deprecation timelines in docs and warnings.
- Support policy: provide fixes on the latest minor of the current major; critical security fixes backported to the latest minor of the previous major for 12 months after new major release.

We will introduce a formal hardware screening program for the OS and gate releases on its results.

- Define two support tiers:
  - Tier 1 (fully supported): maintained images with automated screening on a physical lab; release-blocking.
  - Tier 2 (best-effort): community-tested devices without full automation; non-blocking.

- Establish automated smoke/regression tests per hardware family (boot to onboarding, persistent storage, Supervisor health, networking, update/rollback, add-on start, time sync, USB discovery). Tests run on every release candidate and monthly for stable.

- Maintain a machine-readable hardware manifest (per device SKU) specifying minimal firmware/bootloader, kernel, DT/UEFI requirements, storage, and known quirks. Tests are parametrized from this manifest.

- Introduce release policy:
  - Any Tier 1 failure blocks GA until fixed or device is temporarily disabled.
  - Two consecutive failed cycles or lack of maintenance moves hardware to Tier 2 or deprecates it.
  - New hardware enters as Tier 2 and must pass two consecutive RC cycles to qualify for Tier 1.

- Provide public reporting (dashboard and artifacts) for transparency and reproducibility.

- Require PRs that change boot/kernel/userspace affecting hardware to include updated manifest and screening plan.

This decision prioritizes reliability for commonly used devices while keeping a path for community hardware with clear quality gates and deprecation criteria.

We will standardize on Docker (OCI-compliant) containers to package all runtime applications, background jobs, and CLI utilities. Each service will include a maintained Dockerfile using multi-stage builds to produce minimal, secure images (e.g., distroless or Alpine where appropriate) and run as a non-root user. BuildKit and layer caching will be used to optimize build times; .dockerignore files will be maintained to exclude unnecessary content.

Images will be built reproducibly with pinned base images and explicit dependency versions, producing SBOMs and signed artifacts (e.g., Cosign). Automated vulnerability scanning will be enforced in CI, with policy gates for critical findings. Secrets will never be baked into images; runtime configuration will follow 12-factor practices via environment variables and secret stores.

Images will be published to the organization’s container registry with a consistent naming and tagging strategy: {registry}/{org}/{service}:{semver|git-sha}, with latest only as a convenience tag. Multi-architecture support (amd64/arm64) will be produced via buildx where required.

Entrypoints will be explicit, include graceful shutdown handling, and expose healthcheck endpoints for orchestrators. Common base images and shared build snippets will be curated to reduce duplication and ensure consistency. Local development will use docker-compose for service orchestration; production orchestration is decoupled and may target Kubernetes or a managed container platform without changes to packaging.

This decision ensures reproducible builds, environment parity, platform portability, and a clear supply-chain security posture for all packaged applications.

Adopt automated, opinionated formatting and linting across the codebase to eliminate bikeshedding and ensure consistency.

- Elixir: use mix format with default settings; use Credo for style/lint rules (consistent with our code-analysis ADR).
- JavaScript/TypeScript: use Prettier for formatting and ESLint (with @typescript-eslint where applicable) for linting; start from eslint:recommended and plugin:prettier/recommended with minimal overrides.
- CSS/SCSS: use Stylelint with stylelint-config-standard and Prettier integration.
- JSON, YAML, Markdown: format with Prettier defaults.
- EditorConfig: define global whitespace, newline, and charset rules (.editorconfig) to keep editors consistent.

Principles:
- Prefer tool defaults; avoid project-specific overrides unless a clear, documented rationale exists.
- Any deviation from defaults requires a PR with justification and review from the owning guild.
- Formatting is non-negotiable; linting rules may be tuned for signal-to-noise.

Enforcement:
- Provide shared config packages/presets for each language to ensure uniform adoption.
- Add pre-commit hooks (e.g., lint-staged) to auto-format and run fast linters on changed files.
- CI must run format and lint checks; failures block merges.
- IDE/editor settings and extensions are documented and recommended but not required if hooks/CI pass.

Deliverables:
- Repo-standard configs: .prettierrc, .eslintrc, .stylelintrc, .editorconfig, .credo.exs, and mix format config.
- NPM scripts/mix aliases for format and lint commands, plus a “check” target for CI.

## Decision

We will extract low-level, dependency-light primitives into a dedicated sub-module named core.lowlevel (name may vary per ecosystem: module, package, or crate). This sub-module will host reusable utilities such as byte/bit operations, math and collection helpers, codecs, simple data structures, and platform adapters. Higher-level modules (api, features, plugins) will depend on core.lowlevel, while core.lowlevel will not depend on higher layers to prevent cyclic dependencies and keep the base artifact small and stable.

Public surface area will be curated: low-level APIs are internal by default. Only a small, stable façade will be re-exported from the main module for common use. Symbols moved from the main module will keep backward-compatible shims and deprecation warnings for one minor release, then be removed. Internal visibility modifiers (or naming conventions where unavailable) will be used to signal non-API status.

Build and release changes: core.lowlevel will be a separate artifact built and versioned in lockstep with the main distribution, with strict dependency rules (no heavy/transitive deps). Tests for low-level code will live with the sub-module and run independently. Documentation will reflect the new layering and guide consumers to the supported façade.

We will standardize resource-level lifetime management with explicit, idempotent phases and ownership rules:

- Lifecycle phases: Uninitialized → Initialized → Started → Stopped → Closed. Transitions are monotonic; Close() is terminal and idempotent. Start()/Stop() may be invoked multiple times; Initialize() may be retried until Close().
- API: Initialize(), Start(), Stop(), Close(). Each returns success/failure and is idempotent. Close() must succeed even after partial failures and must release all subordinate resources.
- Ownership: The creator (or injected scope) is the owner and is responsible for Close(). Shared resources use explicit reference management (scope-bound Acquire()/Release() or dependency injection scopes), not implicit singletons.
- Concurrency: Transitions are serialized per resource via an internal lock; long-running work executes outside the lock and observes cancellation tokens. Requests that conflict with an active transition queue and coalesce (e.g., multiple Start() collapse to one).
- Cancellation/timeouts: All transitions accept a cancellation token and timeout. On cancellation or timeout, the resource moves to a safe state (Stopped or Closed) and leaks are prevented via best-effort cleanup.
- Failure semantics: Initialize() or Start() failures must roll back to the previous stable state. After repeated failures, the resource enters a Quarantined state (Stopped) until an explicit Close() or admin action.
- Hierarchies: Parent resources own children; parent transitions propagate: Initialize cascades down, Stop/Close propagates upward first to children then parent. Parents must tolerate child Close() failures and continue best-effort teardown.
- Observability: Every successful transition emits structured telemetry (begin/end, duration, outcome, correlation/owner scope). Repeated failures trigger backoff with jitter and surface health signals.
- Compatibility: Existing components map their current phases to this model; deprecated aliases (e.g., Create/Destroy) remain as thin wrappers until removal.

This decision ensures predictable teardown, prevents deadlocks during reconfiguration, and provides clear, testable contracts for resource reuse and cleanup.

We will adopt a microfrontend architecture organized by business domain, enabling autonomous teams to build, deploy, and scale features independently.

- A lightweight container/shell application will own global concerns: routing, authentication, authorization, global navigation, layout, and cross-cutting observability.
- Feature microfrontends (MFEs) will be delivered as independently deployed artifacts and composed at runtime via Webpack 5 Module Federation (route-based loading). Each MFE exposes a stable entry module and publishes explicit contracts.
- Shared dependencies (e.g., React, router) will be declared as singletons via Module Federation with strict version policies; a versioned design system and utility libraries will be distributed via private NPM packages to ensure UI and behavior consistency.
- Inter-MFE communication will prioritize URL navigation and deep-linking; when needed, use typed, versioned event contracts (CustomEvent) or a lightweight pub/sub bus in the shell. Direct shared state or tight coupling between MFEs is prohibited.
- Styling isolation will be enforced via CSS Modules or Shadow DOM (for Web Components where applicable). Global CSS leakage is disallowed.
- Independent CI/CD pipelines per MFE will produce immutable builds, deploy under dedicated subpaths/subdomains, and register remotes/config in the shell via environment-driven manifests. Backward compatibility and semantic versioning are mandatory.
- Observability will include standardized logging, metrics, tracing, and error boundaries per MFE, with centralized dashboards.
- Security: the shell handles auth flows and token management; MFEs receive only scoped claims/context. No direct token sharing outside defined APIs.
- Performance: apply code splitting, prefetch/preload for critical remotes, CDN caching, and asset budgets; regularly audit bundle sizes.
- Governance: enforce contracts, linting, accessibility, and performance checks via shared tooling and ADRs to manage cross-team evolution.

We will expose a first-class command-line interface (CLI) as the primary user interface for the tool.

The CLI will:
- Be a single entrypoint executable/script with clearly named subcommands and consistent flags.
- Be non-interactive by default, suitable for automation and CI; any prompts will be opt-in.
- Communicate via stdout for normal output, stderr for diagnostics, and well-defined exit codes.
- Provide built-in help (-h/--help) and version (-v/--version) flags, and self-describing usage for each subcommand.
- Support machine-readable output formats (e.g., JSON) via a flag to enable scripting and integration.
- Read configuration from files and environment variables with explicit precedence rules, while allowing full override via flags.
- Maintain backward-compatible CLI contracts; breaking changes will follow semantic versioning and be documented with migration notes.
- Be cross-platform (Linux, macOS, Windows) and distributable as a single binary or lightweight script with minimal runtime dependencies.
- Support localization-ready messages and deterministic behavior (no reliance on terminal state).
- Provide predictable journaling/verbosity controls (-q/--quiet, -v/--verbose, --debug).

Other interfaces (GUI, API/SDK) may be added later and should wrap or reuse the CLI command surface to minimize duplication and preserve consistency.

- Use resource-oriented, noun-based URIs with hierarchical relationships (e.g., /v1/customers/{id}/orders). No verbs in paths.
- Version via URI prefix (e.g., /v1). Backward-compatible changes do not bump version; breaking changes require a new version.
- JSON is the default media type (application/json). Support content negotiation via Accept/Content-Type headers.
- Consistent field naming: camelCase for JSON keys. Use ISO 8601 UTC timestamps, numeric IDs or UUIDs as strings.
- HTTP methods semantics:
  - GET: safe, cacheable; no body required.
  - POST: create or non-idempotent actions; return 201 with Location on create.
  - PUT: full update; idempotent.
  - PATCH (RFC 6902/7386): partial update; idempotent by design of patch document.
  - DELETE: idempotent; return 204 on success.
- Status codes:
  - 200 OK with body, 201 Created with Location, 202 Accepted for async, 204 No Content on empty success.
  - 400 validation errors, 401 auth required, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 412 precondition failed, 415 unsupported media, 422 semantic validation, 429 rate limited, 5xx server errors.
- Unified error format: { code, message, details?, traceId }. Validation errors include per-field issues.
- Pagination: cursor-based preferred (?cursor=...&limit=...). Include paging metadata and next/prev cursors. Sorting (?sort=field,-field) and filtering via explicit query params.
- Concurrency and caching: support ETag/If-Match for updates; ETag/Cache-Control for reads.
- Idempotency-Key header for POST where applicable (e.g., payments).
- Security: OAuth2/OIDC Bearer JWT; TLS required; least-privilege scopes. No sensitive data in URLs.
- Observability: include traceId correlation header; return RateLimit headers when applicable.
- Stability: additive changes only within a version; deprecations announced with Sunset and Deprecation headers.

We will adopt Rook as the storage orchestrator for Kubernetes clusters, standardizing on the Rook-Ceph backend for general-purpose, cloud-agnostic, and on-prem persistent storage. Rook will manage lifecycle, placement, scaling, and healing of Ceph clusters, and expose storage to workloads via CSI with dynamic provisioning of block (RBD), shared filesystem (CephFS), and object (RGW) as needed.

Scope and defaults:
- Default StorageClasses will be provided for RBD (general block) and CephFS (shared read-write-many), with sensible QoS tiers (e.g., gold/silver/bronze) mapped to pool replication, failure domains, and device classes.
- Encryption at rest will be enabled at the pool level; in-transit encryption via Ceph Messenger v2 will be required for multi-node clusters.
- Topology-aware placement will be configured (rack/zone) for failure domain resilience. Monitoring and alerting will be integrated via Prometheus/Grafana.

Operational posture:
- Upgrades will follow Rook/Ceph LTS tracks with blue/green or canary nodes where feasible.
- Backups and DR will leverage snapshots, RBD mirroring/cephfs-journal tools, and off-cluster object replication where required by RTO/RPO.
- Capacity management will use device discovery with admission policies; only vetted device classes (e.g., SSD/NVMe for metadata/WAL, HDD for data) are allowed.

Exceptions:
- Where managed cloud storage (e.g., EBS/EFS/Filestore) materially reduces risk/cost for single-cloud workloads, it may be used; cross-cloud portability or on-prem requirements revert to Rook-Ceph.
- Specialized ultra-low-latency or license-bound storage may be exempt with approval.

This decision provides a unified, portable, and feature-complete storage layer, minimizing vendor lock-in while integrating natively with Kubernetes.

We will implement the client-side using modern JavaScript (ES2020+) as the primary language. We will use native ES modules, strict mode, and browser APIs, targeting evergreen browsers while providing Babel-based transpilation and polyfills (core-js) for any required legacy support. The codebase will be structured with a modular architecture (feature- and domain-based folders), and built with Vite for fast dev feedback and optimized production builds. ESLint (airbnb-base + custom rules) and Prettier will be enforced via pre-commit hooks and CI to maintain code quality and consistency. Unit tests will be written with Vitest/Jest, and end-to-end tests with Playwright. We will adopt a minimal runtime dependency approach, preferring platform features over libraries where feasible, and load third-party scripts via async/defer with Subresource Integrity. Performance budgets (bundle size and TTI) will be monitored, with code-splitting and tree-shaking enabled. Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA), i18n readiness, and security best practices (CSP, Samesite cookies, input sanitization) are mandatory. Documentation will include JSDoc with TypeScript type-checking via // @ts-check for optional static analysis without adopting TypeScript.

## Decision

Standardize on containerized deployments to a managed Kubernetes cluster (AWS EKS) using GitOps. All services will build immutable Docker images in CI, scan for vulnerabilities, and push to Amazon ECR. Environment state (networking, clusters, EKS add‑ons, databases, buckets, queues) is provisioned and versioned with Terraform. Application manifests are defined with Helm charts and reconciled by Argo CD from a dedicated “env” repository per environment (dev, staging, prod).

Deployments use progressive delivery:
- Default: blue/green with automatic health checks and instant rollback via Helm/Argo CD.
- For high‑risk changes: canary releases managed by Flagger with NGINX Ingress (or service mesh where available), using SLO-based metrics (latency, error rate) from Prometheus.

Scalability and resilience:
- Multi‑AZ EKS node groups (on‑demand + spot for non‑prod workloads).
- Horizontal Pod Autoscaling on CPU/RAM and key app metrics.
- PodDisruptionBudgets and Readiness/Liveness probes enforced.

Security and config:
- Secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager injected via CSI driver; no secrets in repos.
- Least‑privilege IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA).
- Image provenance enforced with registry policies and optional Sigstore/attestations.

Release flow:
- Merge to main triggers build/test/scan and image publish.
- Argo CD syncs to staging for manual QA and automated smoke tests.
- Production promotion via signed PR to env repo; database migrations run as pre‑deploy jobs with safe roll‑forward/rollback procedures.

Observability:
- Centralized logs (CloudWatch/OpenSearch), metrics (Prometheus), tracing (OpenTelemetry).
- SLOs and error budgets guide rollout gates.

This approach balances reliability, repeatability, and speed while minimizing operational toil and enabling safe, auditable rollouts.

## Decision

Enable S3 Versioning on all non-ephemeral buckets that store user content, application data, build artifacts, and audit/log data. Do not enable versioning on transient/staging buckets used for intermediate processing or cache, to avoid unnecessary cost.

Enforce versioning configuration via Infrastructure as Code and prevent drift with CI policy checks. In production, lock versioning to “Enabled” (not “Suspended”). For buckets with regulatory or tamper-resistance requirements (e.g., audit logs), additionally enable S3 Object Lock (governance mode with retention and legal hold), subject to compliance approval.

Define lifecycle policies per bucket class:
- Standard data: transition noncurrent versions to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, then Glacier Instant/Flexible Retrieval after 90 days; permanently delete noncurrent versions after 365 days.
- Logs/audit: retain all versions for at least 400 days (or per policy); transition to archival tiers to control cost; do not auto-delete if compliance requires.
- Artifacts: retain latest 10 versions; expire older noncurrent versions after 30–90 days.

Enable cross-region replication (CRR) with version replication to a DR account/bucket for Tier-1 data; use Replication Time Control where RPO/RTO requires. Replicate delete markers but do not replicate permanent deletes unless mandated by policy.

All buckets remain encrypted (SSE-KMS) and block public access. Access policies default to reading the latest version; recovery of prior versions is performed via approved tooling/runbooks with audit logging. Monitor and alert on noncurrent version storage costs and replication failures.

When enabling versioning on existing buckets, communicate that only future objects gain versions; implement a one-time backup/replication where necessary. Document per-bucket lifecycle/retention in the data catalog and review annually.

We will install and lock all package dependencies during the release pipeline, producing deployable artifacts/images that already contain production dependencies. No dependency installation will occur on target environments at deploy time.

- Perform a clean, deterministic install in CI using the project’s lockfile (npm ci or yarn install --frozen-lockfile/pnpm install --frozen-lockfile), respecting engines and reproducible builds.
- Build and package artifacts with compiled output and only production dependencies (exclude devDependencies from runtime). For containers, install in a build stage and copy only production deps into the final image.
- For monorepos, install once at the workspace root and build affected packages, ensuring inter-package references are compiled and resolved.
- Enforce lockfile integrity: releases fail if the lockfile is out-of-sync, modified during build, or missing. Disallow network access during runtime; offline installs (or cached registries) are used only within CI.
- Run vulnerability and license checks during release; block on severity thresholds.
- Cache dependency directories in CI to speed builds, without compromising determinism (cache is optional, not required for correctness).
- Publish SBOM and checksums for the produced artifact/image to enable provenance and repeatability.

This ensures consistent, auditable, and fast deployments by moving dependency resolution from runtime to the controlled release process.

We will standardize on the AWS Load Balancer Controller on EKS to provision and manage Kubernetes ingress and Service LoadBalancers for all edge-facing and internal north-south traffic. The controller will create Application Load Balancers (ALB) for HTTP/HTTPS (including HTTP/2 and gRPC) via Ingress resources and Network Load Balancers (NLB) for TCP/UDP via Service annotations or TargetGroupBinding. TLS will terminate at the ALB using ACM-managed certificates; DNS will be integrated via ExternalDNS. Where required, AWS WAF, Shield, IP allow/deny lists, and security group rules will be attached to the load balancers. We will avoid Classic ELB.

We will codify ingress behavior via Kubernetes manifests and annotations (e.g., path/host routing, stickiness, health checks, cross-zone, deletion protection, access logs). Internet-facing and internal entry points will be separated using dedicated ingresses/load balancers and subnets. For stateful or non-HTTP protocols, we will use NLB with TargetGroupBinding. Weighted target groups will be used to support blue/green and canary releases.

Certificates will be provisioned in ACM per domain and referenced by Ingress; automatic HTTP→HTTPS redirects will be enforced. Logging will be enabled to S3/CloudWatch; metrics and alerts will be sourced from ALB/NLB and controller metrics. IPv6, proxy protocol, and header forwarding (X-Forwarded-For/Proto) will be configured as needed.

This decision centralizes edge traffic policy in Kubernetes, enables least-privilege IAM via IRSA for the controller, and provides a consistent, cloud-native, highly available entry layer for all services.

## Decision

Establish “Search” as an independent bounded context with its own domain model, data storage, and API surface. The Search context will own:
- Index schemas, query DSL, relevance rules, facets, and result shaping (DTOs).
- Its ingestion pipeline (from upstream domains via domain events/CDC), including denormalization and enrichment for indexing.
- Search-specific SLAs/SLOs, scaling policies, and operational dashboards.

Search will expose versioned, query-only APIs (read model) optimized for discoverability and performance, decoupled from transactional systems. It will not be a source of truth; instead, it maintains derived read models (indices) and is rebuildable from upstream events. Consistency is eventual; freshness targets are defined per index.

Integration with other bounded contexts is asynchronous via:
- Domain events (preferred) or change data capture for legacy sources.
- An anti-corruption layer to translate upstream models into search projections.

The Search context will be deployed and scaled independently, with separate repository, CI/CD pipeline, observability, and incident runbooks. It will encapsulate its infrastructure (e.g., indexing, analyzers, synonyms, aggregations) and hide them behind its APIs. Cross-cutting concerns (authZ, rate limiting, PII handling, retention) are enforced within the context.

Teams: a dedicated Search team owns roadmap and operations. Other contexts consume Search APIs; they do not query Search storage directly.

## Decision

We will standardize how “fluxes” (throughput and flow of events/data/work) are measured across all services and pipelines by introducing a Flux Metrics Contract and enforcing its presence and correctness throughout the SDLC.

Key elements:
- Canonical flux metrics: ingress_rate, egress_rate, processing_latency, backlog_depth, saturation/utilization, error_rate, retry/drop counts, and cost-per-unit (where applicable).
- Consistent dimensions/tags: service, env, version, region, tenant (if multi-tenant), workload_type, and source/destination.
- Instrumentation: use OpenTelemetry Metrics SDK in applications; export via OTLP to Datadog. For managed services (e.g., AWS), use CloudWatch → Datadog integrations to capture equivalent flux metrics.
- Validation: each repo includes a flux-metrics.yaml documenting the contract (metric names, units, tags, and SLO targets). CI enforces presence and lints naming/units; unit tests verify metric emission. A /metrics or health endpoint exposure is required for scraping where relevant.
- Release gating: promotion to higher environments requires detected, non-zero, sane flux metrics for a soak period and no critical alerts on flux SLOs.
- Visibility: provide team-ready dashboard and alert templates (Datadog) auto-provisioned from the contract. Default alert thresholds align with SLOs and can be tuned per service.
- Legacy/black-box coverage: where code changes are impractical, deploy sidecars, proxies, or log-derived metrics pipelines to approximate the contract until native instrumentation is added.
- Governance and safety: no PII in metrics/tags; contracts reviewed by the platform observability group; breaking metric changes follow versioned contracts and deprecation windows.

This decision ensures comparable, trustworthy flux measurements across the estate, enabling capacity planning, anomaly detection, and business-level observability with minimal friction.

## Decision

We will implement the application using the Phoenix framework on Elixir/BEAM. Phoenix will provide the core web stack (router, Plug-based middleware, controllers, views) with Ecto for database access (PostgreSQL) and Telemetry for observability. Where appropriate, we will use LiveView for server-rendered interactive UI, and Phoenix Channels/WebSockets for real-time features (e.g., notifications/streaming updates). External interfaces will be exposed as JSON REST APIs (and GraphQL may be considered later if needed). We will structure the code as a standard Phoenix app, adopting an umbrella architecture only if clear domain boundaries emerge. Authentication will use phx.gen.auth with session and token flows as required. We will standardize on Mix for build, ExUnit for tests, Credo and mix format for code quality, and OpenTelemetry for tracing/metrics. The service will be containerized and deployed on BEAM in our target runtime (e.g., Kubernetes), leveraging OTP supervision for fault tolerance and high concurrency.

We will adopt the Excelize (github.com/xuri/excelize) library as the standard package to parse Microsoft Excel XLSX files in our Go services.

Rationale embedded in the decision:
- Excelize is actively maintained, feature-complete for XLSX read/write, and has robust support for sheets, merged cells, styles, shared strings, formulas, data validation, and hyperlinks.
- It provides streaming read APIs (Row/Cell iterators) that allow processing very large workbooks with bounded memory, which aligns with our throughput and footprint targets.
- It is pure Go with no CGO dependencies, easing cross-platform builds and containerization, and is licensed under BSD-3-Clause, compatible with our distribution model.
- Compared to tealeg/xlsx (largely unmaintained) and ad‑hoc CSV exports, Excelize offers better performance, fidelity, and ecosystem support.

Implementation notes included in the decision:
- Standardize on the latest stable v2.x; pin exact minor/patch via Go modules and track upstream security/bugfix releases.
- Use streaming readers by default; disable cell caching where appropriate to control memory; close workbooks and streams promptly.
- Normalize dates/times using the workbook’s 1900/1904 system; coerce cell types explicitly (strings, numbers, booleans, errors).
- Do not rely on Excel formulas for business logic; read values as-is and only invoke Excelize’s calculation engine if explicitly required.
- Validate sheet and named range existence; handle corrupted or password-protected workbooks with explicit error paths and metrics.
- Provide a thin internal wrapper to encapsulate Excelize usage and ease future migration if needed.

## Decision

We will implement a CRUD and search application exposing a versioned, RESTful API for core domain entities, complemented by a flexible query interface for filtering, sorting, and pagination. Create (POST), Read (GET), Update (PUT/PATCH), and Delete (DELETE) operations will follow standard resource semantics with consistent request/response shapes, validation, and error handling.

Search will start with database-backed filtering and full-text capabilities where available. We will abstract search behind a repository/query service to allow seamless evolution to an external search engine (e.g., OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) if relevancy, scalability, or advanced features are required. If/when an external index is introduced, we will use an outbox/event-driven approach to maintain eventual consistency and enable reindexing.

Cross-cutting requirements include:
- Security: role-based access control, field-level authorization where needed, input validation, output encoding, and audit logging for data changes and access.
- Data integrity: optimistic concurrency control (entity version/ETag), soft-deletes for recoverability, and referential integrity checks.
- Performance: pagination defaults and limits, response shaping (select/expand) to reduce payloads, appropriate indexing strategies, and caching of hot list/search queries where safe.
- UX: stable, discoverable queries (documented operators, ranges, partial matches), deterministic sorting, and consistent error codes.
- Observability: structured logging, request IDs, metrics for CRUD/search latencies and result sizes, and trace propagation.

We will define a formal query DSL for search/filter parameters (operators, fields, ranges) and document it alongside the API. DTOs will decouple external contracts from internal models. The design will be testable (unit and contract tests), support backwards-compatible evolution (additive fields, deprecation policy), and be deployable in stages to validate search quality and performance before scaling.

We will distribute the Hamlet Engine as a set of layered OCI/Docker images that separate stable runtime from frequently changing components to optimize pull size, cache reuse, and security posture.

- Compose images in deterministic layer order: base OS (distroless/alpine), language/runtime, engine core, optional plugins/bundles, and a thin entrypoint layer. Frequently updated assets (plugins, rules, templates) will reside in top layers.
- Produce two variants: -slim (distroless, minimal surface) for production and -debug (shell/tooling) for support. Both share identical lower layers for maximum cache hits.
- Use multi-stage builds to ensure clean runtime images and reproducible builds; embed build metadata via OCI labels (org.opencontainers.image.*).
- Publish immutable, content-addressed tags using SemVer (X.Y.Z) with moving aliases (X.Y, X, latest), and nightly/edge channels for pre-release testing.
- Support multi-architecture (amd64, arm64) via OCI manifests with per-arch images built from the same Dockerfile.
- Distribute optional capability sets as separate images that can be referenced directly or used as base images for curated distributions.
- Externalize configuration/secrets via env vars and volumes; provide an optional “config overlay” image for baked, immutable profiles.
- Sign all images (Sigstore cosign) and attach SBOMs (SPDX) and provenance (SLSA/Attestations). Run CVE scans on each layer and maintain a rolling base refresh policy.
- Host on an OCI-compliant registry (e.g., GHCR) with rate-limit friendly mirrors and retention policies.
- Provide docker-compose/Helm references that pin immutable digests while surfacing human-friendly tags for operators.

The Subscription Services product will provide a standardized, API-first capability set focused on end-to-end subscription lifecycle management. Core features include: product catalog and plan management (tiers, billing intervals, regional pricing), checkout and payments (Stripe as primary PSP, tax/VAT via provider), entitlements and access control, trials and coupons/discounts, upgrades/downgrades with proration, pauses/resumes, refunds/cancellations with configurable grace periods, invoicing and receipts, dunning and retry logic, and customer self-serve account management. Operational features include: webhook/eventing for state changes, idempotent APIs, audit logging, SSO integration, role-based admin UI for product/offer management, localization and multi-currency support, and exportable analytics (events to data pipeline) with core dashboards for churn, MRR, activations, and cohorts.

Non-functional commitments: high availability for read operations, eventual consistency guarantees for entitlements within seconds, strict data privacy/GDPR alignment, accessibility compliance, and rate limiting/quotas. PCI scope remains with the payment provider; we will not store raw PAN data. Multi-tenant readiness is supported at the data model and access layers.

Out of scope for initial release: app-store billing (Apple/Google), marketplace/revenue share, complex usage-based/metered billing beyond simple quotas, physical fulfillment/shipping, and multi-PSP orchestration (evaluated in a later phase). Extensibility is enabled via versioned APIs, a pluggable pricing/discount engine, and event hooks to allow future capabilities (metering, alternate PSPs, entitlements sync) without breaking changes.

## Decision

Adopt a “low, predictable specificity” strategy across all styles to ensure easy overrides, theming, and component isolation.

- Prefer single-class selectors for components (e.g., .Button), avoiding ID selectors and tag-qualified selectors (e.g., button.Button).
- Avoid deep nesting; limit to one level for state/variant or child elements (e.g., .Button:hover, .Button__icon). No location-based selectors (e.g., .Sidebar .Button).
- Prohibit !important except in sanctioned escape-hatch utilities (e.g., .u-hidden) documented and limited in scope.
- Encode variants and states via additional classes or component props rather than increasing selector specificity (e.g., .Button--primary, data attributes, or styled-component variants).
- Theming and overrides must be achieved via theme tokens/variables and props, not by crafting more specific selectors.
- Global resets and normalize layers must remain at the lowest specificity and never target component classes.
- For CSS-in-JS (styled-components), avoid selector chaining that targets other components; compose via props and styled(<Component>) with careful rule order. Use transient props to prevent DOM leakage.
- Disallow ID selectors, inline style overrides (except dynamic layout measurements), and compound selectors that mix tags/attributes/classes unnecessarily.
- Establish linting and CI guards: stylelint with selector-max-specificity, no-descending-specificity, and a ban on IDs/important; include a rule to flag deep nesting.
- Document an override contract per component (tokens, props, slots) so consumers never need to rely on specificity wars.

This yields consistent, debuggable styles that remain resilient in varied host apps and support safe theming without regressions.

We will adopt Coveralls.io as the single source of truth for automated test coverage reporting. Coveralls will be integrated into our CI pipeline to collect, aggregate, and publish coverage for all services and packages.

Key aspects:
- Upload coverage from CI using official Coveralls reporters; accept common formats (lcov, Cobertura, JaCoCo, gcov, SimpleCov, Clover).
- Enable parallel builds and monorepo mode to merge coverage across matrix jobs and multiple packages.
- Enforce repository-level minimum coverage thresholds; expose PR status checks and block merges when thresholds regress.
- Post PR annotations/comments highlighting changed-file coverage and uncovered lines.
- Publish a coverage badge in the README; private repositories will use the organization plan with repo-level access controls.
- Store the Coveralls repo token as a CI secret; restrict logs to coverage artifacts only and exclude source where possible.
- Normalize paths (containerized builds), exclude generated/vendor code, and define coverage “flags” per service for trend visibility.
- Run a nightly job to compute baseline coverage and historical trends.

This decision standardizes coverage visibility, supports quality gates in PRs, and provides actionable insights to reduce risk and technical debt.

Use HPACK (RFC 7541) for HTTP/2 header compression across all services and public endpoints that negotiate h2 via ALPN. Rely on the platform/runtime’s built-in HPACK implementation (e.g., Go net/http2, Envoy, gRPC, Netty) rather than custom codecs.

Configuration:
- Dynamic table size: default 4 KB for internet-facing traffic; up to 16 KB for intra-cluster traffic to improve compression efficiency. Respect SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE and advertise limits accordingly.
- Header list size limits: cap to 8 KB (external) and 16 KB (internal) via SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE to mitigate abuse and bound memory usage.
- Disable header compression for explicitly sensitive headers (if runtime supports per-header no-index flags), and use the “never indexed” directive for secrets (Authorization, Set-Cookie) to reduce side-channel risk.
- Enforce canonical header casing/normalization and stable header ordering where applicable to maximize compression ratio.

Interoperability and fallback:
- If HTTP/2 is not negotiated, fall back to HTTP/1.1 without header compression; no alternative (e.g., gzip over headers) will be attempted.
- Do not introduce custom encodings or extensions; remain compliant with RFC 7540/7541.

Operational:
- Expose metrics for header compression ratio, dynamic table evictions, SETTINGS negotiations, and header list size rejections.
- Gate increased table sizes behind configuration flags and document per-environment defaults.

QPACK (HTTP/3) adoption is out of scope and will be addressed in a separate ADR.

We will upgrade the Android app to targetSdkVersion 30 (Android 11) and compileSdkVersion 30 across all modules, keeping minSdkVersion unchanged. As part of the upgrade, we will:

- Replace direct external storage access with scoped storage-compliant approaches (MediaStore and/or Storage Access Framework) and remove requestLegacyExternalStorage.
- Audit and adapt any background location usage to Android 11 requirements (separate user consent flow, foreground service usage, and justification), and declare foregroundServiceType as needed.
- Implement package visibility restrictions by declaring explicit <queries> in the manifest for required package discovery; avoid QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES unless strictly justified and approved.
- Migrate any file:// URI usage to content:// via FileProvider, and review implicit intents and broadcast restrictions for compliance.
- Update Android Gradle Plugin and Gradle to versions compatible with compileSdk 30, and upgrade affected libraries (Play Services, AndroidX, Kotlin, Crash/Analytics, Push) to SDK 30–compatible versions.
- Add automated tests for scoped storage behaviors, media import/export, and permission flows (foreground/background location, camera, microphone).
- Update CI pipelines and lint/static analysis rules to enforce target/compile SDK 30, and block usage of deprecated APIs disallowed by Android 11.
- Provide user-facing migration handling where applicable (e.g., moving legacy files to app-specific directories) and a staged rollout with crash/ANR monitoring.

This change positions the app for Play requirements, security, and privacy improvements while minimizing risk via thorough testing and staged release.

We will deploy the Proxy Node on the GDS Supported Platform (GSP) as containerised workloads on the managed Kubernetes offering. This provides a compliant, supported, multi‑AZ environment with standardized networking, observability, and security controls, reducing undifferentiated operational burden.

Implementation approach:
- Containerisation and images built via CI, pushed to a GSP-supported private registry; supply chain hardened with image signing and vulnerability scanning.
- Infrastructure as Code using GSP-approved Terraform modules for namespaces, network policies, ingress, secrets, and RBAC. Environments (dev/stage/prod) isolated by namespaces and projects.
- Ingress via GSP-managed ingress controller/ALB with WAF, TLS 1.2+, HSTS, and automated certificate management; strict network policies and mTLS for upstream/downstream where required.
- Secrets managed with SOPS + KMS (or GSP secret store), with short-lived credentials and rotation; signing keys protected via KMS/HSM-backed mechanisms as applicable.
- Horizontal Pod Autoscaling and PodDisruptionBudgets for resilience; rolling/canary updates for zero-downtime deploys with health/readiness probes and automatic rollback.
- Centralised logging to the platform stack; metrics via Prometheus/Grafana; SLOs and alerts integrated with incident management.
- Backups/snapshots for stateful components (if any) using platform capabilities; DR tested and documented; UK region residency enforced.
- Compliance and ops: platform guardrails, CIS-aligned baselines, regular penetration testing, and runbooks/playbooks stored with the service repository.

This decision aligns with GDS support, security accreditation pathways, and provides a clear path to scale, operate, and audit the Proxy Node reliably.

We will represent in-memory pixel samples as 64-bit IEEE-754 double-precision arrays within the core processing pipeline to maximize numerical stability, simplify algorithm development, and avoid cumulative rounding errors across multi-stage operations.

- Layout: planar format (one double[] per channel) with row-major ordering and contiguous rows to enable cache-friendly traversal and vectorization. Each plane is 64-bit aligned.
- Value domain: samples are linearized (no gamma) and normalized to [0, 1] for bounded source formats; HDR or wide-gamut sources may exceed 1.0 as needed. NaN denotes missing/invalid data; +/-Inf are disallowed and clamped.
- Color handling: all processing occurs in a defined working color space; conversions happen at the boundaries.
- Boundaries: I/O, GPU kernels, and memory-constrained modes may use alternative representations (e.g., uint8/uint16/float16/float32). Facilities are provided for loss-aware, vectorized conversion to/from double with well-defined rounding.
- Performance: where supported, SIMD paths may internally downcast to float32 for throughput but must meet specified numerical tolerances when compared to the double reference path.
- Configurability: a build/runtime switch allows substituting float32 for doubles in constrained environments; doubles remain the default.
- Memory limits: processing tiles/chunks may be used to cap peak memory while preserving double precision within each tile.

This standardizes on doubles for correctness-first processing while preserving interoperability and practical performance/memory options at the edges.

We will adopt Microsoft Playwright as the standard framework for our functional (end-to-end) web tests. Playwright’s built-in auto-waiting, cross-browser support (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit), parallel execution, and first-class CI tooling (trace viewer, videos, screenshots) provide reliable, maintainable tests with minimal flakiness. Its integrated test runner, fixtures, and network mocking reduce external dependencies and boilerplate.

We will use Playwright Test with TypeScript. For selectors, we will prefer stable data-testids and accessible roles/names. We will apply the Page Object Model for complex flows, and isolate tests with a fresh browser context per test. Authentication will be handled via storageState seeding. Retries will be enabled for known flaky environments, with traces/videos captured on retry/failure.

In CI, pull requests will run a fast smoke suite on headless Chromium; nightly builds will run the full suite sharded across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Artifacts (traces/videos) will be uploaded for failed tests. Docker images provided by Playwright will be used for consistent local/CI execution.

We will deprecate adding new Selenium/WebDriver-based E2E tests, maintaining legacy suites until migrated to Playwright as capacity allows.

We will not use Thread.interrupt (or equivalent low-level thread interruption APIs) as an application-level control-flow or cancellation mechanism. Application code must implement cooperative cancellation using higher-level constructs (e.g., cancellation tokens/contexts, timeouts, futures/promises, async tasks, executor shutdown, reactive/structured concurrency). Business logic must not depend on interrupt delivery/semantics.

Permitted use of interrupts is limited to:
- Framework/runtime managed threads that use interrupts internally to unblock blocking operations during shutdown.
- Propagation: if code catches an InterruptedException, it must promptly restore the interrupt status (Thread.currentThread().interrupt()) and exit or propagate, rather than swallowing it.

Prohibited patterns:
- Interrupting arbitrary threads to forcefully stop work or as a signaling channel.
- Interrupting threads running unknown/third-party code.
- Using interrupt to coordinate state transitions or resource cleanup.

Required patterns:
- Define explicit cancellation APIs on long-running tasks; periodically poll cancellation state and exit quickly.
- Use timeouts on blocking calls and I/O; prefer close/cancel on channels/streams to unblock.
- Use managed executors/thread pools; control lifecycle via shutdown and awaitTermination.
- Ensure cleanup handlers are idempotent and do not rely on interrupts to run.
- Prefer structured concurrency/async frameworks that propagate cancellation via scopes/contexts.

Rationale: avoids nondeterministic behavior, missed signals, fragile coupling, and platform-specific semantics, while improving testability, portability, and graceful shutdown.

Establish a rigorous, automated, and enforceable code quality pipeline integrated into the developer workflow and CI/CD:

- Define and publish coding standards per language, including mandatory automated formatting and linting (e.g., formatter + linter). Formatting is non-negotiable and run both locally (pre-commit hooks) and in CI.
- Introduce static analysis (SAST) and code smells detection with a CI quality gate: zero critical/high issues; new code must not introduce new issues.
- Enforce unit test execution in CI with minimum coverage thresholds: ≥80% overall and ≥70% per component/module on new and changed code; block merges if thresholds are not met.
- Require dependency and container image scanning (SCA) with a policy of no critical/high vulnerabilities on new code and regular remediation of existing findings.
- Enable secret scanning on commits/PRs; auto-revoke and rotate if a secret is detected.
- Protect main branches: require green CI, up-to-date with main, and at least one (preferably two) approving code reviews; mandate small, focused PRs with a template and linked work item.
- Track and manage technical debt explicitly; allow justified waivers with time-bound exceptions recorded in ADRs/tickets.
- Provide dashboards (e.g., coverage, lint, vulnerabilities) visible to the team; review trends in retrospectives.
- Periodically calibrate quality gates to remain pragmatic while preventing regression.

## Decision

We will document architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

- Format: Use the MADR template (Markdown Any Decision Records) with Nygard-style content (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives Considered).
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository under docs/adr/, version-controlled alongside the code.
- Naming and numbering: Sequentially number ADRs (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md). Titles are kebab-case and immutable after merge.
- Lifecycle: Decisions progress through Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Superseded. Superseding ADRs must explicitly reference the prior ADR.
- Scope: One ADR per significant architectural decision (runtime, build, operations, security, data, dependencies, external services). Minor implementation details belong in code comments or design docs, not ADRs.
- Process: New ADRs are introduced via pull request. Reviewers include at least one architect and one representative from the impacted team(s). Approval requires consensus or an explicitly recorded rationale for dissent.
- Traceability: Each ADR links to related issues, RFCs, proofs-of-concept, benchmarks, and affected components. Code changes referencing an ADR must include its ID in commit messages and PR descriptions.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (or adr-tools-npm) to create, list, and supersede ADRs. Rendering to HTML/PDF is optional for publishing to internal portals.
- Visibility: ADR index (README.md in docs/adr/) summarizes decisions and their status, ordered newest-first.
- Compliance: CI will verify presence of an ADR for PRs that introduce major architectural changes (label: architecture-impact).
- Retention: ADRs are permanent historical records; do not delete—supersede when necessary.

## Decision

Define and enforce a uniform, state-managed lifecycle for Channels to ensure predictable operations, safe shutdown, and consistent orchestration across deployments.

States:
- Created → Prepared → Initialized → Started → (Paused | Draining) → Stopped → Closed
- Failed (error state; requires reset to re-enter Prepared)
- Terminal states: Closed (resources released)

Operations (idempotent and validating transitions):
- prepare(), init(), start()
- pause() (halt intake; keep resources allocated), resume()
- drain(timeout) (reject new intake; complete in-flight up to timeout), stop(graceful|immediate)
- close() (final resource release)
- restart(strategy) (e.g., from any non-Closed state → stop → init → start)

Rules and semantics:
- A Channel cannot start unless all dependencies are prepared and initialized.
- pause() is reversible without re-init; stop() requires start() to resume; close() requires init() to rehydrate.
- drain() transitions to Stopped on completion or to Stopped with partial completion on timeout; operators are informed of residual workload.
- Unhandled runtime errors transition to Failed; optional auto-restart policy (max attempts, backoff) is configurable; failure cause is preserved.

Hierarchy and cascading:
- Channels orchestrate child components (consumers, processors, producers); lifecycle operations cascade in order (prepare/init → downstream; stop/close → upstream-aware, reverse order).
- Readiness/health is the aggregation of children.

Observability and control:
- Emit lifecycle events and metrics for each transition; expose health: Started=healthy; Paused/Draining=degraded; Failed=unhealthy.
- Provide synchronous (blocking with timeout) and asynchronous variants of operations.

Compatibility:
- Legacy start/stop map to start()/stop(graceful).
- Default behavior where unsupported: pause→stop(graceful), drain→stop(graceful).

Adopt OpenSearch as the full‑text search engine for indexing and querying application content.

Rationale:
- Open-source (Apache 2.0) with strong community, avoiding Elastic license constraints while remaining API-compatible with Elasticsearch 7.x for mature client ecosystem support.
- Rich search capabilities required by the product: language-specific analyzers, stemming, synonyms, custom tokenizers, relevance scoring (BM25), fuzzy search, highlighting, aggregations, and faceting.
- Operational strengths: horizontal scalability, index lifecycle management, snapshots/restore, security plugins, and availability of managed offerings (e.g., AWS OpenSearch Service) to reduce ops burden.
- Future-ready features: k-NN/vector search and hybrid retrieval to support semantic search use cases.

Implementation outline:
- Operate OpenSearch as a dedicated cluster; treat it as a derived data store (not system of record).
- Define index-per-domain (or per-tenant where needed), with index templates, analyzers, and mappings under version control.
- Use ingestion pipelines for normalization (lowercasing, ASCII-folding), language analyzers, and synonym sets.
- Provide an internal SearchAdapter to abstract engine specifics and enable testability.
- Ensure eventual consistency via async indexing (queue/stream based), with backfill and reindex jobs; use aliases for zero-downtime reindexing.
- Establish relevance evaluation, analyzer tests, and dashboards for monitoring latency, error rates, and cluster health.

Consequences:
- Gains powerful, multilingual search and analytics with scalable performance.
- Accepts added operational complexity (cluster management, mapping/version drift) and ongoing relevance tuning.
- Mitigations include managed service usage, infra-as-code for cluster config, and rigorous indexing/reindexing workflows.

We will enforce business invariants by failing fast with domain-specific exceptions raised at the point of violation in the domain layer (e.g., within aggregates, value objects, and domain services). Instead of returning sentinel values or error codes, operations that would result in an invalid state must throw explicit, typed domain exceptions that clearly describe the violated invariant and relevant identifiers.

Guidelines:
- Define a small, curated hierarchy of domain exceptions (e.g., InvariantViolation, InvalidTransition, InsufficientPermissions) with immutable, structured context.
- Validate commands and state transitions at aggregate boundaries; reject invalid commands before side effects; ensure exceptions trigger transaction rollback.
- Do not use exceptions for normal control flow; use them only for invariant breaches and unrecoverable domain errors.
- Map domain exceptions to application/service-level error contracts (e.g., HTTP 4xx with machine-readable codes) at the boundary; never leak stack traces to clients.
- Log at warning level with correlation IDs; capture metrics to monitor invariant breach rates.
- Ensure exceptions are idempotent-safe (no partial side effects before throw) and compatible with retries/outbox patterns.
- In languages with checked exceptions, declare them explicitly on domain APIs; in others, document and test expected throws.

This approach preserves domain integrity, clarifies intent, and simplifies error handling through a consistent, fail-fast mechanism.

We will not base our containers or build environments on any prebuilt TeX/LaTeX images (e.g., texlive/texlive, blang/latex). Instead, we will start from a minimal, well-maintained base (debian:stable-slim) and install a pinned TeX Live profile that contains only the packages we require.

We will:
- Provision TeX Live via install-tl using a locked TeX Live repository date and a committed profile (texlive.profile) to ensure reproducible builds.
- Use tlmgr to install only the minimal set of packages enumerated in packages.texlive, reviewed and updated as needed.
- Leverage Docker layer caching for the TeX installation step and publish a project-specific image built by our pipeline for CI speed, rather than relying on third-party TeX images.
- For local development, provide a bootstrap script to install the same pinned TeX Live (or TinyTeX) setup outside containers.

This approach reduces image size and attack surface, avoids implicit upgrades and breakages from third-party images, improves supply-chain transparency, and gives us deterministic, auditable builds at the cost of maintaining our package list and initial installation time.

## Decision

Implement a centralized, append-only Service History system that records key lifecycle events and state changes across services for auditability, support, and troubleshooting.

Key elements:
- Event model: Standardized event envelope (event_type, occurred_at, aggregate_type/id, actor, correlation_id, causation_id, tenant, source_service, schema_version, attributes). Events are immutable; corrections are emitted as compensating events.
- Ingestion: Services publish domain events to the event bus (Kafka or SNS/SQS). For legacy systems, backfill and ongoing capture via CDC where feasible. Producers must include idempotency keys to support at-least-once delivery.
- Persistence: Write-optimized append-only store (PostgreSQL partitioned tables) as the source of truth, with an optional searchable index (OpenSearch) for flexible queries. Partition by time and aggregate_type for performance/retention.
- Ordering: Guarantee ordering per aggregate_id; consumers process per-key ordered streams. Global ordering is not required.
- Access: A dedicated History API provides query-by-aggregate, by correlation, and time windows with pagination, filtering, and redaction. A lightweight UI offers timelines for support teams.
- Privacy and compliance: PII kept to a minimum; prefer references over embedding. Field-level encryption for retained PII; redaction events for removals; crypto-shredding keys to satisfy deletion requests while preserving audit structure. Configurable retention by event type and tenant policy.
- Security: Write access only via broker; History service enforces schemas and validation. Read access via scoped roles. All access audited.
- Schemas and governance: Versioned JSON Schemas in a central registry; backward-compatible evolution enforced in CI. Producers must pass contract tests.
- Reliability: Exactly-once effect at sink via upsert-on-idempotency-key. Dead-letter queues and replay tooling for recovery. Health and lag metrics exposed.
- Rollout: Start with high-value domains, backfill critical history, and iterate schema and UI based on support needs.

## Decision

Adopt Kotlin as the primary project language for all new application and library code. Kotlin is selected for its modern language features (null-safety, data classes, sealed hierarchies, coroutines, extension functions), improved developer productivity, and first-class tooling and ecosystem support on the JVM (and Android where applicable). Kotlin’s seamless Java interoperability allows us to integrate with existing Java code and third-party libraries without blocking migration.

Scope and policy:
- All new production and test code is written in Kotlin.
- Existing Java code remains supported; migrate opportunistically when touched for significant changes.
- Avoid Lombok in Kotlin modules; prefer native Kotlin language features. Phase out Lombok in Java modules where feasible.
- Standardize on Kotlin Gradle plugins, JVM target 11+ (or project baseline), and enable strict nullability and opt-in annotations as needed.
- Enforce style and quality via ktlint and detekt; use JUnit 5 with Kotlin test DSLs (e.g., Kotest) where beneficial.

Consequences:
- Positive: Less boilerplate, safer code, easier concurrency with coroutines, faster iteration, and improved readability/maintainability.
- Neutral/Managed: Minor runtime footprint; performance parity with Java for typical workloads.
- Negative/Risks: Team upskilling required; enforce training, code reviews, and a Kotlin style guide. IDE and CI need Kotlin support (IntelliJ, Gradle, static analysis) configured.

Status: Accepted. Effective immediately for new work; migration of legacy Java code is incremental.

Adopt styled-components as the standard approach for component-level styling in React. All new styling will be authored as styled components colocated in the same file as the React component (defined above the component), using ThemeProvider to supply a centralized, typed design theme (tokens for color, spacing, typography, breakpoints). Prefer variant patterns via component props over ad-hoc className composition; compose styles through styled() rather than deep CSS nesting. Use createGlobalStyle only for resets and truly global primitives; avoid additional global CSS and SCSS. For polymorphism, use the “as” prop where appropriate instead of duplicating styled definitions. Name styled elements with a Styled prefix (e.g., StyledButton) and export only the public component by default to minimize style surface area. Enable the babel-plugin-styled-components (or equivalent compiler config) for readable classnames, SSR compatibility, and minimal style duplication. Inline styles are reserved for dynamic, non-CSS properties only. CSS Modules, SASS, and plain CSS are deprecated for new code; legacy styles may remain but should be incrementally migrated when touched.

- Normalize and validate scanned barcodes (UPC-A/E, EAN-8/13, Code128, QR with GS1 AI) into a canonical GTIN using a standards-compliant library; reject/flag invalid checksums and ambiguous encodings.
- Query order of precedence:
  1) Internal catalog/index (authoritative overrides).
  2) GS1 Digital Link resolver and GS1 Registry Platform (authoritative metadata).
  3) Vendor/brand-provided endpoints when whitelisted.
  4) Community/open datasets (e.g., Open Food Facts) as non-authoritative fallback, clearly flagged.
- Return fast, minimal product response from the first hit; trigger asynchronous enrichment to merge additional attributes from lower-precedence sources without blocking the user flow.
- Persist a canonical product document per GTIN with field-level provenance, last-seen timestamps, and confidence scoring; do not overwrite authoritative fields with lower-precedence data.
- Implement lookup caching (positive and negative) with configurable TTLs, ETag/Last-Modified validation where supported, and per-source backoff to respect rate limits; cache warmed by popular GTINs.
- Support offline/poor connectivity by serving from local cache with staleness indicators and queuing enrichment for later.
- Handle errors and throttling with circuit breakers and exponential backoff; degrade gracefully to partial data rather than failing the scan workflow.
- Expose a reconciliation UI/API for admin and trusted partners to correct or pin records; changes write through to the canonical store and invalidate caches.
- Security and privacy: send only GTIN and required AIs to external providers; strip user identifiers; sign requests or use API keys/MTLS where required; log only non-PII telemetry.
- Observability: capture per-source hit rate, latency, error rates, cache effectiveness, and coverage; emit provenance/confidence with responses for downstream consumers.
- Maintain compliance with GS1 standards (AI parsing, Digital Link URI syntax); add unit tests with barcode fixtures covering edge cases (leading zeros, UPC/EAN normalization, variable weight codes).
- Package the querying logic behind a versioned BarcodeResolver service with a stable API to allow swapping providers and tuning precedence without affecting clients.

## Decision

Adopt a globally unique, human-readable, and URL-safe identifier scheme for extension indicators.

Identifier format:
<namespace>.<extension>.<indicator>[:v<major>[.<minor>]]

- namespace: reverse-DNS owner namespace (e.g., com.acme), lowercase a–z, digits, and hyphens; must start with a letter.
- extension: the published extension name, lowercase a–z, digits, and hyphens.
- indicator: the indicator key within the extension, lowercase a–z, digits, underscores, and hyphens.
- version (optional but recommended for breaking changes): v<major>[.<minor>], numeric.

Examples:
- org.example.analytics.page_views:v1
- io.company.search.latency_p95:v2.1
- core.health.alive (implicit v1)

Rules:
- Identifiers are case-insensitive; producers MUST publish and consumers MUST compare using lowercase.
- Max length is 128 characters.
- Identifiers are immutable once published; never repurpose. Deprecate via metadata, do not delete or reassign.
- Version increments: bump major on breaking meaning/units/semantics; minor for additive/backward-compatible refinements.
- The core.* namespace is reserved for platform-defined indicators; third parties MUST NOT use it.
- Temporary/local identifiers MUST use local.* and MUST NOT be published.
- Identifiers MUST be URL-safe; canonical URI form is ext://<identifier> (e.g., ext://org.example.analytics.page_views:v1).
- A central registry enforces uniqueness per identifier (including version) and validates format.
- Collisions are avoided by reverse-DNS ownership; proof of domain control is required to claim a namespace.

Tooling:
- Provide a shared library for generation/validation and a linter for CI to enforce the scheme.

- Implement soft-deletion as the default: resources are marked deleted (tombstone metadata with actor, timestamp, reason, retention-until) and hidden from end-user queries while preserved for recovery, auditing, and legal discovery.
- Enforce restricted delete authorization: only resource owners with the “Deleter” capability or designated admins may request deletion; destructive (hard) deletion requires elevated “Data Steward” role plus a second approver (four-eyes principle) except for automated retention expirations.
- Honor legal/retention constraints: prevent deletion when legal hold, compliance retention, or active litigation flags are present. Configurable retention policies govern when soft-deleted items become eligible for purge.
- Support Right to Erasure (GDPR/CCPA): implement targeted hard-deletion and content scrubbing for personal data with minimal collateral impact; maintain non-identifying audit pointers where lawful.
- Guard referential integrity: deny deletion when live dependencies exist (e.g., child records, foreign keys, search index refs). Provide safe, explicit cascades only when policy allows and impacts are recorded.
- Provide recovery window: allow restore of soft-deleted items within the retention window; restoration requires same or higher authorization as deletion.
- Immutable audit trail: log who/when/what/why for requests, approvals, and executions (including data lineage and downstream purges). Store audits separately with WORM characteristics.
- Operational controls: deletion APIs require explicit intent (idempotent endpoints, confirm tokens), are rate-limited, and are disabled in production except via feature flag and per-tenant policy. Purge executes via scheduled jobs with backpressure and observability.
- Scope of deletion: ensure consistent removal across primary storage, caches, search indexes, replicas, analytics lakes, and backups (via key-based cryptographic erase or time-bounded backup expiry).
- User experience: present clear warnings, impact summaries, and policy reasons when deletion is blocked; require reason codes for approvals.

## Decision

We will expose a public, resource‑oriented REST API over HTTPS using JSON as the canonical wire format.

- Contract and discoverability: Define the API with OpenAPI 3.1, publish interactive docs, and auto-generate SDKs/stubs where useful.
- Versioning: Use URI-based major versions (/v1), with additive, backward-compatible changes only within a major version; formal deprecation policy with minimum 6‑month sunset.
- Authentication/authorization: OAuth2/OIDC with JWT bearer tokens; scopes for least-privilege; service‑to‑service via client credentials.
- Consistency conventions:
  - Resource nouns, plural collections, snake_case fields.
  - Standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
  - Pagination via cursor-based pagination (limit, cursor); sorting and filtering via query params.
  - Idempotency for POST/PUT via Idempotency-Key header.
  - Timestamps in RFC 3339 UTC; monetary values as strings with currency code.
- Error handling: RFC 7807 problem+json with stable error codes and correlation id in X-Correlation-Id.
- Reliability and performance: Enforce rate limits and quotas at the API Gateway; retries with exponential backoff on idempotent operations; timeouts and circuit breakers at clients and gateway.
- Security and privacy: TLS 1.2+; input validation; PII minimization and redaction in logs; audit events for sensitive operations.
- Observability: Structured logging with correlation id propagation, distributed tracing, and metrics per endpoint (latency, error rate, saturation).
- Governance: PR-based contract changes with schema linting and breaking-change detection in CI; contract tests for providers/consumers.
- Deployment: Fronted by API Gateway for routing, auth, WAF, and throttling; blue/green or canary releases.

This standard applies to new APIs; existing ones will converge to it during scheduled revisions.

We will remove Smartdown from the codebase and documentation toolchain and standardize on Markdown (CommonMark) with MDX where interactivity is required.

- Authoring: All new and existing content will be written in .md/.mdx. Smartdown-specific syntax and files (.smartdown) are deprecated immediately and blocked in CI.
- Rendering: The docs site will be built with our SSG’s native Markdown pipeline and MDX, using supported plugins for admonitions, tabs, code highlighting, and diagrams (e.g., Mermaid). Interactive examples will be implemented via MDX components, Web Components, or external embeds (e.g., StackBlitz/CodeSandbox).
- Migration: We will provide a scripted migration path to convert Smartdown constructs to MDX equivalents, plus a checklist for manual edge cases. Converted pages keep canonical slugs; legacy URLs are redirected. A read-only archive of pre-migration Smartdown content will be kept for reference.
- Runtime/Build: Remove Smartdown dependencies, loaders, and custom parsers from build and runtime bundles, reducing complexity and bundle size. Introduce a docs linter to detect disallowed syntax.
- Versioning/Timeline: Deprecation starts now; Smartdown support is removed in the next major release. A feature flag allows temporary fallback during migration and will be deleted before the major release cut.

This decision reduces maintenance burden, eliminates an unmaintained dependency, improves performance and security, and aligns us with widely supported, community-standard tooling.

## Decision

Adopt Selenium WebDriver to automate extraction of Koshvani data where pages require client-side rendering, authenticated navigation, interactive filters, pagination, or file downloads. Implement in Python using headless Chrome (Chrome + ChromeDriver) packaged in a Docker image with pinned versions for deterministic builds. Use requests/BeautifulSoup for static endpoints; default to Selenium only when necessary to minimize overhead and operational risk.

Structure automation with the Page Object Model, resilient CSS/XPath selectors, and explicit waits; add retries with exponential backoff for transient failures. Manage downloads via a controlled headless profile to a mounted workspace, then normalize to a canonical schema and persist to object storage and the warehouse. Ensure idempotency via source checksums, de-duplication, and run checkpoints to support resume on failure.

Run jobs on a scheduler (e.g., Airflow/Cron) with configurable frequency and treasury scope; enforce polite scraping (rate limits, randomized think-times), and comply with Koshvani’s ToS/robots and any published API priorities if available. Secure credentials via a secrets manager; never embed secrets in code. Handle captchas or unexpected auth challenges with a manual-review fallback.

Provide observability: structured logs, metrics, and alerts; capture screenshots and HTML snapshots on failures for diagnosis. Version and health-check the browser/driver pair; include synthetic probes to detect site layout changes. Use network-level capture (e.g., selenium-wire) only if needed and permitted. Implement proxy support and user-agent management where compliant.

We will adopt a multi-project structure, organizing the system into independently versioned projects aligned to clear bounded contexts (e.g., services, UI apps, shared libraries). Each project will have its own repository, CI/CD pipeline, release cadence, and maintainers. Cross-project reuse will occur via published, versioned packages (no source-level imports across projects). Interactions between runtime components will use well-defined, backwards-compatible contracts (REST/gRPC/events) with explicit API versioning.

We will establish:
- Naming and repository conventions, scaffolding templates, and standardized build/test/release workflows.
- A shared dependency and security policy (e.g., approved base images, SBOMs, vulnerability scanning).
- Semantic versioning for all public packages and APIs, with automated contract tests to prevent breakage.
- Clear ownership and CODEOWNERS per project, with RFC/ADR processes for cross-cutting changes.
- A compatibility matrix and integration environment for validating multi-project releases.

Breaking changes require deprecation paths and migration guides. This structure enables parallel work, faster builds, targeted deployments, and safer evolution while preserving a cohesive architecture through enforced standards and contracts.

## Decision

- We will use Jest as the unit/integration test runner, assertion, and mocking framework for JavaScript/TypeScript.
- We will use React Testing Library (RTL) to test React components via user-centric queries and interactions, avoiding implementation details.
- We will use @testing-library/user-event for realistic user interactions; avoid fireEvent except for low-level events.
- We will avoid Enzyme and shallow rendering; prefer RTL’s render with DOM.
- We will minimize snapshot tests to stable, low-variance UI (e.g., SVG/icons). Prefer explicit assertions over broad snapshots.
- For async and networked components, we will use MSW (Mock Service Worker) to mock HTTP interactions at the network layer.
- We will configure Jest with jsdom environment, code coverage thresholds enforced in CI, and watch mode for local development.
- For TypeScript projects, we will use ts-jest or swc-jest for performant transpilation; Babel may be used where already standard.
- We will colocate tests (*.test.ts(x)/.js(x)) with source files and use Testing Library recommended ESLint rules to discourage anti-patterns.
- We will add test utilities (custom render with providers like Router/Store/Theme) to reduce boilerplate and ensure consistent setup.
- We will run tests in CI with jest --ci and generate junit and coverage reports for pipeline visibility.
- We will mock time (jest.useFakeTimers) and modules (jest.mock) where appropriate, preferring behavior-driven tests over heavy mocking.
- We will document common patterns (accessibility-first queries, role/name assertions) and provide examples for contributors.

Adopt a standardized, user-facing error code for all fatal errors and crashes across CLI, UI, and API surfaces. Each fatal error will present:
- A short, human-readable message
- A stable error code (format: E-<domain>-<4digits>, e.g., E-AUTH-1001)
- A correlation/request ID (if available)
- A pointer to documentation (e.g., docs/errors/E-AUTH-1001)

Implementation actions:
- Create a centralized error catalog with ownership, description, likely causes, remediation steps, and severity. Reserve code ranges per domain/service to avoid collisions. Treat codes as immutable once released.
- Introduce an ErrorCode type and helper utilities in all SDKs/services to enforce code presence on fatal paths. Provide wrappers to map exceptions to codes and to attach correlation IDs.
- For APIs: include error.code in JSON bodies and the X-Error-Code response header; keep HTTP status semantics unchanged. For CLI/UI: display message + code; hide stack traces by default behind a verbose flag.
- For logs/telemetry: emit error.code, correlationId, stack, and environment in structured logs; export metrics by error.code for alerting and SLOs.
- Backfill high-incidence fatal errors with codes first; assign codes opportunistically for the rest. Add a lint/check in CI to prevent introducing new fatal errors without a code.
- Documentation: publish a searchable error code directory with troubleshooting and links to known issues; localize user messages while keeping codes language-agnostic.
