This decision improves debuggability, support workflows, and user self-service while keeping internal error details confined to logs and telemetry.

We adopt a concise, machine- and human-friendly branch naming convention to improve traceability, automation, and consistency.

Pattern:
- {type}/{ticket}-{short-slug}
- Example: feature/ABC-123-add-user-search

Rules:
- type: one of feature, bugfix, hotfix, release, refactor, chore, docs, test, ci, spike.
- ticket: required work item ID (e.g., ABC-123). If unavailable, use NO-TICKET (rare, discouraged).
- short-slug: lowercase, hyphen-separated summary; no spaces; ASCII letters/numbers/hyphens only.
- Max length: 80 characters total.
- Use a single slash to separate type from the rest; no additional path segments.
- Avoid special characters (., ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, ], @, \, #). Replace with hyphens.
- Protected branches: main and develop (no direct commits).
- Release branches: release/vX.Y.Z (e.g., release/v1.4.0).
- Hotfix branches: hotfix/vX.Y.Z.
- WIP/personal exploration: spike/{ticket}-{slug} or feature/{ticket}-{slug}; for ad-hoc experiments without a ticket: spike/NO-TICKET-{slug}.
- Automated dependency updates keep their provider prefix: dependabot/{slug} (exempt from ticket requirement).

Rationale:
- Ensures issue auto-linking, easier filtering, and predictable CI/CD rules.
- Clear separation of intent via type.
- Encourages succinct, readable, and portable names.

## Decision
We will organize automated tests into clearly separated suites with deterministic execution and CI-aware selection:

- Unit: Fast, isolated, pure in-process tests run by default on every commit/PR. Target 80% line and 60% branch coverage on domain and business logic. No I/O or network.
- Component/Integration: Verifies integration with databases, message brokers, and external services using ephemeral infrastructure (e.g., Testcontainers) and seeded fixtures. Runs on PR after unit tests and on every merge to main.
- Contract: Consumer-driven contracts (e.g., Pact) for all external HTTP/async integrations. Contracts are verified on PR and enforced on main to prevent breaking changes.
- End-to-End (E2E) and Smoke: Minimal smoke suite runs on PR against ephemeral environment; fuller E2E runs post-merge and nightly against a production-like environment. Retries allowed once for known flaky external dependencies; failures triaged immediately.
- Non-functional: Performance and load tests run on schedule (e.g., nightly/weekly) and before major releases with stable baselines checked into version control.

Conventions:
- Directory and package layout mirrors production code; suites are grouped by type (unit/, integration/, contract/, e2e/).
- Tests are tagged/annotated to enable selective execution (e.g., unit, integration, contract, e2e, perf).
- Test data is owned by tests: immutable fixtures for unit, factory/builders for variability, and idempotent migrations/seeds for integration/E2E.
- All suites are parallelizable by default; shared resources are isolated via namespaces and unique identifiers.
- Flaky tests are quarantined under a dedicated tag and must be fixed before release.
- CI pipeline stages map 1:1 to suites; failures block promotion between stages. Artifacts (reports, coverage, logs, traces) are persisted for diagnostics.

## Decision

We will adopt Lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to document significant architectural decisions.

- Format: Markdown files following Michael Nygard’s template with sections: Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences. Optional sections (Options, Pros/Cons, Risks, References) may be added when useful.
- Location: Version-controlled in the repository at docs/adr (one ADR per file).
- Naming: Sequentially numbered files using kebab-case titles (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md).
- Status lifecycle: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated/Superseded (with backlinks). Only one Accepted ADR should be authoritative for a given topic.
- Scope: “Significant” decisions only (e.g., major tech choices, data model changes, cross-cutting concerns, SLA/SLO shifts, infra/security patterns, removal of capabilities, or explicit non-adoptions).
- Process: ADRs are created and reviewed via Pull Requests. Discussions occur on the PR; key points are summarized into the ADR. Acceptance requires at least one reviewer from architecture/tech leads (or designated delegate).
- Traceability: ADR PRs link to relevant issues/epics; code PRs that implement an ADR must reference its number. Superseding ADRs must link both ways.
- Tooling: Team may use adr-tools or log4brains to scaffold and publish ADRs; not mandatory.
- Governance: A PR checklist item enforces ADR consideration for architectural changes. Quarterly doc hygiene includes pruning and cross-link verification.
- Accessibility: ADRs live with code; optionally indexed on the wiki with links to source for discoverability.

We will support both EOAs and smart contract wallets and enable gasless interactions via meta-transactions.

- Adopt EIP-2771 meta-transactions using a Minimal Forwarder (OpenZeppelin) and EIP-712 typed data for signing. Contracts will integrate Context/MinimalForwarder and use a _msgSender()/_msgData() pattern on all user-facing entry points.
- Operate a relayer service that:
  - Verifies EIP-712 signatures, nonces, and deadlines via the forwarder.
  - Enforces policies: method allowlist, per-user/day rate limits, max gas and calldata size caps, and sponsor budget controls.
  - Falls back gracefully: clients can send direct transactions if relayer is unavailable or policy rejects a request.
- Support smart contract wallets by:
  - Accepting EIP-1271 signatures wherever signatures are validated.
  - Avoiding EOA-only assumptions; authorization derives from _msgSender().
  - Testing with popular wallets (e.g., Safe/Argent) and chain-specific variants.
- Strengthen replay protection and safety:
  - Include chainId in EIP-712 domain; use forwarder-managed nonces per sender.
  - Single trusted forwarder address per chain; upgradable only via governance; ability to pause relaying.
  - Reentrancy guards on meta-tx entry points where state is modified.
- Optimize UX and gas:
  - Prefer EIP-2612/EIP-3009 permit flows to avoid separate approvals.
  - Batch operations where feasible.
- Observability and compliance:
  - Emit events for meta-tx execution and sponsorship.
  - Collect relayer metrics and signed request logs for auditing.
- Future-proofing:
  - Reassess migration path to ERC-4337 account abstraction when mature; keep meta-tx integration modular to swap transport later.

We will adopt Express as the HTTP server framework on Node.js for building our web/API layer. Express provides a stable, minimalist core with a mature, well-supported middleware ecosystem, enabling us to assemble only the features we need (routing, validation, authentication, observability) without imposing heavy architectural constraints. Its unopinionated design supports our preferred libraries and patterns (e.g., TypeScript, dependency injection, OpenAPI tooling) and makes it straightforward to integrate security controls (Helmet, rate limiting, input sanitization) and production concerns (structured logging, metrics, health checks). The widespread community adoption, long-term maintainability, and broad compatibility with existing Node tooling reduce risk and onboarding time. We will standardize common middleware (error handling, request parsing, CORS) and conventions (routing, controllers, DTO validation) to ensure consistency across services, and we will encapsulate framework specifics behind lightweight adapters to keep business logic framework-agnostic. This choice optimizes delivery speed, flexibility, and operational reliability while allowing us to evolve modules independently as requirements change.

## Decision

Adopt a first-class, versioned “data migrations” mechanism distinct from schema migrations, implemented as code in the application repository and executed as one-off jobs during deployments.

Key aspects:
- Definition and storage: Data migrations live in a dedicated directory, are immutable, reviewed, and tagged with a monotonically increasing version and descriptive name. Each migration implements up() and (where feasible) down() or a compensating forward-fix.
- Execution: Migrations run as Kubernetes Jobs (or equivalent one-off tasks) with least-privilege DB credentials, within the app network boundary. CI/CD orchestrates execution: dry-run on integration, auto-run on staging, and gated/manual approval on production.
- Idempotency and safety: Migrations must be idempotent and re-entrant, using checkpoints (e.g., a control table), deterministic filters, and upserts. They run in small batches with configurable throttle, timeouts, and retries to minimize lock contention and production impact.
- Observability: A dedicated “data_migrations” table records version, checksum, parameters, start/finish timestamps, status, row counts, and error details. Logs emit structured events and metrics; alerts trigger on failures or SLA breaches.
- Backward compatibility: Follow expand/contract. Deploy schema and code that can handle both old and new data, backfill via data migration, switch reads, then remove legacy paths in a subsequent release.
- Testing and rehearsal: Provide a local runner and test harness with representative data volumes. All migrations must have unit tests and have been rehearsed on staging with sampled production-like data.
- Operations: Provide a CLI to list, run, resume, and verify migrations. Enforce run windows, concurrency limits, and feature flags. Document a rollback/compensation plan per migration and enforce cleanup of deprecated code after completion.

We will standardize on AWS Application Load Balancer Target Group HTTP(S) health checks hitting a dedicated, side-effect-free endpoint implemented by each service.

- Protocol/path: HTTP or HTTPS to /healthz (configurable per service), supporting both liveness and readiness semantics; readiness governs registration.
- Matcher: 200–399 considered healthy. Services must return 503 to indicate draining/unready so ALB deregisters targets gracefully.
- Timing: interval 10s, timeout 5s, healthy threshold 2, unhealthy threshold 3 (environment overrideable for sensitive workloads).
- Headers: include Host header for virtual hosting; health endpoint must not require auth. No reliance on User-Agent.
- Draining: set deregistration delay to 60s and enable connection draining; services should stop advertising readiness before shutdown and continue serving in-flight until drain completes.
- Deployment safety: enable target group slow_start (30s) for instances behind autoscaling to prevent immediate overload after scale-out or deploy.
- Security: use HTTPS health checks with SNI for internal TLS-terminated services; permit a distinct health check path that does not disclose sensitive info.
- Observability: log health check failures and expose metrics; alarms on consecutive unhealthy counts and high 5xx from health endpoint.
- Infrastructure: manage all target group health check settings via Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform), with per-service overrides for path, port, and protocol; defaults applied via shared module variables.
- Special cases: gRPC services expose an HTTP/2-compatible /healthz (or gRPC health probe via HTTP/2) endpoint; stateful services expose readiness that reflects replication/sync status.

This configuration ensures fast, deterministic fail-out during maintenance or failures, minimizes user-visible errors during deploys, and remains auditable and repeatable across environments.

Adopt a layered malware scanning approach across the platform:

- User uploads: All files are scanned before being accepted. A dedicated scanning service (backed by ClamAV with frequently updated signatures and optional YARA rules) receives files over an internal API, returns a verdict (clean/infected), and attaches scan metadata (engine version, signature version, timestamp, hash). Infected files are rejected and quarantined; the request fails with a 4xx and an incident is logged.

- Object storage: For objects written outside the synchronous path (e.g., bulk imports), trigger an asynchronous scan via event notifications. Until a “clean” tag is applied, objects remain non-distributable. Infected objects are moved to a quarantine location and access is blocked.

- CI/CD and build artifacts: Add a malware scan step for produced artifacts and container layers; any detection fails the pipeline.

- Runtime fleet: Rely on the organization’s standard EDR/anti-malware for hosts; container workloads inherit node-level protections.

- Operations: Signatures auto-update multiple times daily; scanning service scales horizontally with a queue, enforces timeouts, and exposes health metrics. Results and detections are forwarded to the SIEM; high-severity detections page on-call. A time-bound allowlist exists for known benign samples with documented approvals.

This decision ensures all ingress and at-rest content is scanned, detections prevent distribution, and security teams receive actionable telemetry without materially impacting user experience.

Remove database indexes that are redundant, unused, or provide negligible benefit, while preserving those required for primary keys, unique constraints, foreign key enforcement, partitioning, and proven critical query paths. Specifically, drop:
- Indexes with no scans over a representative observation window (e.g., 30–90 days) per engine telemetry (e.g., pg_stat*), unless justified by SLAs or seasonal workloads.
- Duplicates and functional equivalents (prefix/covering overlaps, identical expressions, same sort orders).
- Write-amplifying composite indexes where a narrower alternative suffices.

Execute removals through a versioned migration plan (e.g., concurrent drops where supported) with canary rollout, capturing before/after query plans and key SLOs. Update ORM/schema definitions to prevent regeneration of removed indexes. Document retained rationale and removal criteria.

Provide a fast rollback path: migration scripts to recreate dropped indexes (concurrently), plus query hints/config toggles if needed. Establish ongoing hygiene by adding automated detection of unused/duplicate indexes to CI and periodic reviews.

We will adopt the Serverless Framework’s serverless-offline plugin to emulate API Gateway and AWS Lambda locally for rapid, cost-free development and smoke testing. The service will be runnable with a single command (e.g., npm run dev) that starts serverless-offline alongside other local emulators as needed (e.g., DynamoDB Local or LocalStack for S3/SQS/SNS). We will codify configuration in serverless.yml and standardize local environment variables via .env files, ensuring parity with deployed stages through stage-specific env overlays and seeded test data.

HTTP events will be exercised through serverless-offline; background/asynchronous flows will be supported via companion offline plugins (e.g., serverless-offline-sqs) or LocalStack where practical. For features not faithfully emulated (IAM, VPC networking, identity/authorizers, WAF, X-Ray), we will provide thin mocks or fall back to an ephemeral cloud test stage for integration tests. Local development will rely on hot-reload where supported, and pre-commit hooks will run unit tests against the offline runtime.

CI will execute unit tests with serverless-offline; integration and contract tests will run against a temporary cloud environment to validate cloud-only behaviors. The plugin and local emulators will be pinned to known-compatible versions and validated in CI to prevent drift.

We will integrate with the Kubernetes API as the authoritative interface for container lifecycle, scheduling, networking, and configuration, rather than interacting directly with container runtimes (Docker Engine, containerd) or node-level daemons. Our service will use official Kubernetes client libraries, operate with least-privilege RBAC-scoped service accounts, and rely on declarative resources (Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, Services, Ingress) and watch/informer patterns for event-driven reconciliation.

We will expose a thin, domain-oriented API that translates business operations into Kubernetes primitives, ensuring idempotent, retry-safe requests and consistent status reporting via resource conditions. For platform extensibility we will define CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) where domain concepts do not map cleanly to core K8s resources, and implement controllers/operators to reconcile desired vs. actual state.

Operationally, we will:
- Use Namespaces and labels/annotations for tenancy, policy, and traceability.
- Enforce network, quota, and security policies (NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota, PodSecurity, PSP replacements).
- Leverage readiness/liveness/startup probes and horizontal autoscaling (HPA/KEDA) for resilience.
- Surface metrics, logs, and events through standard Kubernetes observability (Prometheus/OpenTelemetry).
- Manage access via the cluster’s OIDC provider, issuing JWT-bound service accounts for our components.

External consumers will connect through an API gateway/ingress (Envoy/Kong/NGINX) with TLS, rate limiting, and authN/Z, while internal services may use service mesh mTLS where available. This decision provides portability across managed Kubernetes offerings, avoids vendor/runtime lock-in, and aligns with cloud-native best practices.

We will expose a single immutable UiState object per screen from each ViewModel, instead of multiple LiveData/Flow streams. Each ViewModel will hold an internal MutableStateFlow<UiState> (or equivalent) and expose it as a read-only StateFlow/LiveData to the UI. UiState is a data class that aggregates all render-relevant data, loading flags, and error representations required to render the screen in one pass.

State updates will follow unidirectional data flow: the ViewModel receives user/system intents, derives effects (e.g., repository calls), and reduces results into a new UiState via pure reducer functions (copy with). Transient one-off events (navigation, toasts) will be emitted via a separate one-time event channel (SharedFlow/Channel) to avoid embedding them in UiState.

Selectors and derived properties may exist as helper functions or be computed in the UI to keep UiState serializable and minimal. Sub-screens and complex features may compose UiState through nested substates to maintain modularity.

No mutable streams or domain entities will be exposed; mapping to UiState occurs within the ViewModel. Persistence of state across process death will leverage SavedStateHandle where applicable.

Migration strategy: consolidate existing streams into a single UiState per screen, phased by feature. Performance will be monitored; if necessary, we will split large states into memoized selectors or sub-flows internally while maintaining the single public UiState contract.

Decision: Use GNU Make as the single entry point to execute all build tasks across the repository.

- Adopt a top-level Makefile that orchestrates common tasks: help (default), build, test, lint, fmt, clean, dist/package, docker-build, release, ci. Provide component-level Makefiles as needed; the root Makefile delegates via make -C subdir.
- Define all task targets as .PHONY. Use file targets and stamp files where feasible for incremental builds and proper dependency tracking.
- Ensure a self-documenting interface: a help target that lists available targets and descriptions.
- Standardize shell and safety: .SHELL := bash and .SHELLFLAGS for strict mode (e.g., set -euo pipefail -o pipefail). Enforce MAKEFLAGS += --no-builtin-rules --warn-undefined-variables to avoid surprises.
- Enable parallelism with MAKEFLAGS += -j unless explicitly overridden; targets must declare dependencies correctly to be parallel-safe.
- Parameterize tools and versions via variables (e.g., GO, NPM, PYTHON, DOCKER); allow overrides via environment. Pin toolchain versions via asdf/tool-version files or Docker where applicable.
- Support reproducible builds: provide docker-% targets to run tasks inside a standardized container; local tasks should not require Docker but must yield identical outputs.
- Cross-platform guidance: require GNU Make; support Linux/macOS natively and Windows via Git Bash/WSL. Avoid non-POSIX utilities or wrap them.
- Structure Makefiles modularly: include mk/*.mk (e.g., mk/go.mk, mk/js.mk, mk/docker.mk) to keep targets maintainable.
- CI/CD will invoke make ci as the single pipeline entry; local developers use make (help) and the same targets to ensure parity.
- Manage environment via optional include of .env and .env.local; do not commit secrets.

Kyma Eventing will be built on top of Knative Eventing as the core eventing framework.

- Provide Kyma Eventing as a thin abstraction over Knative primitives, aligning with CloudEvents 1.0 for producer/consumer interoperability.
- Ship Knative Eventing components as part of the Kyma stack; lifecycle (install/upgrade) is managed by the Kyma installer.
- Use NATS Streaming (NatssChannel) as the default in-cluster transport for development and standard workloads; offer Kafka Channel as an optional profile for high-throughput, durability, and ordering requirements.
- Expose Kyma CRDs/APIs that map to Knative concepts (e.g., Subscription/Channel or Broker/Trigger), preserving a stable Kyma-facing contract while allowing internal channel pluggability.
- Leverage Knative delivery features (HTTP-based delivery, retries/backoff, dead-letter sinks) as the default reliability model.
- Deprecate and migrate from the legacy Kyma Event Bus to Knative-based Eventing with a guided migration path and compatibility shims where feasible.
- Ensure multi-tenant safety and namespace isolation via Knative constructs and Kyma RBAC/NetworkPolicy defaults.

## Decision

We will adopt Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture significant technical and product architecture decisions.

- Location: ADRs will live in the repository at docs/architecture/decisions/.
- Format: Markdown files following the template: Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives (optional), References (optional).
- Numbering: Sequential IDs (ADR-0001, ADR-0002, …). Filenames will be <id>-<kebab-title>.md.
- Status workflow: Proposed → Accepted → Deprecated → Superseded. Accepted ADRs are immutable except for status changes, links, and minor corrections. Superseding ADRs must explicitly reference the ADR(s) they replace.
- Scope: One decision per ADR. Meaningful, durable decisions only (not routine implementation details).
- Process: Create ADRs via pull request with peer review; discussion occurs in the PR. Decisions become Accepted when approved by the designated maintainers/architecture group.
- Ownership: The team proposing the change owns drafting; maintainers own acceptance and lifecycle stewardship.
- Cross-references: ADRs should link to related ADRs, issues, and design docs.
- Tooling: Use plain Markdown; adr-tools or similar helpers are optional.
- Enforcement: CI will check directory presence and filename pattern; the CODEOWNERS file will require maintainer review for ADR changes.

We will adopt 12‑factor configuration with environment variables as the primary interface, backed by a single typed configuration schema and explicit validation at startup. Configuration precedence will be: compiled-in defaults < environment-specific config file (YAML) if provided < environment variables < CLI flags. Secrets will never be stored in code or config files; they will be sourced from the environment or a cloud secret manager (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager/KMS or Vault) and injected as env vars or mounted files by the runtime (Kubernetes Secrets, Docker secrets). Missing or invalid required values cause a startup fail-fast.

For local development, we will support a .env file (loaded only in non-production) and an optional config.yaml, with .env taking precedence over files. In containerized deployments, non-secret configuration will be delivered via ConfigMaps or environment variables; secrets via Secrets. All configuration will be represented as a single struct with default values, parsed and validated on boot; validation includes type checks, required fields, ranges, and cross-field constraints. Sensitive values will be redacted in logs and any /debug/config endpoint.

Configurations are immutable after startup for initial release; live reload (SIGHUP or file watch) may be added later behind a feature flag. Configuration keys will be kebab/upper snake cased for env vars (e.g., APP_DB_HOST), namespaced per service, and versioned via release notes when breaking changes are introduced.

## Decision

Consolidate the CSSK into a single canonical source of truth managed as a monorepo. The monorepo will contain specifications, reference implementations, shared libraries, schemas, examples, and documentation, all versioned together with clear module boundaries and ownership.

Key elements:
- Repository layout: /specs, /packages/* (independent versioned modules), /examples, /tooling, /docs, /adr, /infra.
- Module isolation: Each /packages/* has its own API surface, tests, CHANGELOG, CODEOWNERS, and semantic versioning; cross-package deps pinned via workspace tooling.
- Unified release process: Automated CI builds, tests, linting, security scans; provenance and SBOMs; release tags per package with a coordinated “CSSK Release” manifest.
- Documentation as code: docs generated from source (schemas, code comments), published to a single site; versioned docs aligned with releases.
- Backwards compatibility policy: public APIs follow SemVer; deprecation windows with warnings; LTS branches for N-1 major versions; compatibility matrix maintained in /docs.
- Governance: mandatory ADRs for breaking changes; code owners enforce reviews; RFC process for new packages; clearly defined support tiers (core, incubating, deprecated).
- Distribution: publish artifacts to official registries; container images signed; example apps updated on release.
- Migration: deprecate satellite repositories; archive with pointers; provide migration guides and shims where feasible.
- Observability: central issue tracker and dashboards; dependency and license auditing enforced in CI.

This decision establishes a single, authoritative, maintainable source for CSSK, reducing drift, improving developer experience, and enabling reliable, auditable releases.

## Decision

We will implement core backend services as independently deployable Kotlin (JDK 21) applications using Spring Boot 3.x (WebFlux) with a hexagonal architecture. Services expose REST (OpenAPI-first) for external clients and gRPC for service-to-service calls. Persistence uses PostgreSQL as the primary relational store (JDBC for OLTP; R2DBC where reactive end-to-end is required). Redis is adopted for caching, ephemeral locks, and short-lived queues. Apache Kafka provides durable event streaming, outbox/inbox patterns, and asynchronous workflows.

All services are containerized (Docker) and orchestrated on Kubernetes. Service networking terminates at an Envoy-based API Gateway/Ingress (rate limiting, auth offload, request shaping). Configuration and secrets are managed via Kubernetes ConfigMaps/Secrets with external secret integration. CI/CD uses GitHub Actions with trunk-based development, automated tests, SCA, SAST, container scanning, and progressive delivery via Helm and Argo Rollouts.

Observability is standardized on OpenTelemetry (traces/metrics/logs) exported to Prometheus + Grafana (metrics), Loki (logs), and Jaeger/Tempo (traces). Structured JSON logging with correlation IDs is enforced. Feature flags are provided via OpenFeature-compatible provider. Authentication and authorization follow OAuth 2.1/OIDC with Keycloak as the IdP; services enforce JWT validation and propagate identity via mTLS between services where required.

Data contracts are versioned via OpenAPI and protobuf with backward-compatible evolution policies and contract tests. Schema migrations are managed by Flyway. Resilience patterns (circuit breakers, retries, timeouts, bulkheads) are applied via Resilience4j. This stack balances developer productivity, operational maturity, and performance, while remaining widely supported and cloud-agnostic.

We will adopt node-vibrant as the standard library to extract representative color palettes from images to drive theme accents and contrast decisions.

Implementation details:
- Use the latest maintained node-vibrant release with TypeScript types, consumed via ESM where available.
- Wrap node-vibrant behind an internal ColorPaletteService interface to enable future replacements without API breakage.
- Configure defaults: 6 swatches, quality set for balanced accuracy/perf, maxDimension capped to limit CPU; allow per-call overrides.
- Run extraction asynchronously and, in browsers, offload to a Web Worker when supported; fallback synchronously otherwise. Add request de-duplication and caching keyed by image URL/bytes.
- Enforce robustness: timeouts, graceful degradation to a deterministic fallback palette, and WCAG contrast validation/adjustment of chosen colors.
- Security and privacy: do not fetch remote URLs internally; operate only on provided Blobs/ArrayBuffers; strip/ignore metadata.
- Cross-runtime support: enable both browser and Node (SSR/precompute) usage via the same wrapper; avoid non-deterministic results between environments.
- Packaging: add node-vibrant as a direct dependency (MIT), ensure tree-shaking, and monitor bundle size. Provide feature flag to disable palette extraction if needed.
- Quality: add snapshot tests for known fixtures and visual regression checks for key UI surfaces.

We will standardize subject viewer selection and options via a single, versioned configuration on the workflow. The workflow will include a subjectViewer block with:
- viewer: a required identifier for the viewer (e.g., singleImage, multiFrame, video, scatter, lightCurve).
- version: optional semver for feature evolution (e.g., multiFrame@1.0.0).
- options: an object with viewer-specific, validated options (e.g., multiFrame.maxFrames, filmstrip.position; video.controls, playbackRate).

Precedence:
1) Explicit workflow configuration (subjectViewer.viewer) is authoritative.
2) If absent, infer from subject media types and counts (e.g., multi-image ⇒ multiFrame; mp4 ⇒ video).
3) Fallback to singleImage.

Validation and defaults:
- Enforce a JSON Schema per viewer type and version; apply defaults where omitted.
- Unknown or invalid options are ignored; emit non-fatal telemetry and fall back to safe defaults.

Runtime integration:
- The classifier reads subjectViewer once per workflow load and supplies options only to the selected viewer.
- Viewers are isolated; no cross-view option leakage.
- Feature flags can gate experimental viewers or options; flags must not change defaults for existing workflows.

Compatibility and migration:
- Legacy keys (e.g., subject_viewer: 'multiFrame', display_all_frames) are supported and mapped to the new shape at load time.
- The API persists and returns subjectViewer as provided; migrations are non-destructive.
- Configuration is part of workflow versioning; changes require a new workflow version.

This approach makes viewer behavior explicit, validated, and evolvable while preserving backward compatibility.

We will implement a dual-mode feedback architecture for routing decisions:

- Synchronous feedback: Every routing attempt returns an immediate, machine-readable acknowledgement that includes a canonical status (accepted, rejected, queued, degraded), a reason code taxonomy (transient, permanent, policy, capacity), optional Retry-After, and a correlation-id. For HTTP, we standardize on 2xx/4xx/5xx with problem+json bodies; for messaging, ACK/NACK with metadata.

- Asynchronous outcome events: Final outcomes (delivered, failed, rerouted, timed-out) and significant state changes are emitted as CloudEvents on the event bus with a versioned FeedbackEvent schema including correlation-id, route-id, target, decision vector, reason codes, retry count, latency, and anonymized feature hashes. PII is excluded or redacted by policy.

- Observability: Aggregate metrics (per-route SLI/SLOs, error budgets, reason-code distributions) are exported to Prometheus and logs to an append-only stream for audit and ML. High-volume events are sampled with dynamic rates; lossless paths exist for audit-critical domains.

- Developer/user feedback: Optional real-time streams (SSE/WebSocket) expose correlated outcomes for consoles and UIs. A /health and /feedback/validate endpoint provide contract linting and schema validation.

- Resilience/backpressure: Feedback encodes retry semantics, idempotency keys, and congestion signals to callers; routing engine consumes failure signals to trigger circuit breakers, load-shedding, and policy fallbacks (e.g., secondary routes, degraded modes).

- Governance: Versioned schemas, schema registry, and compatibility rules; retention policies per data class; access control via scoped tokens. Feature flags enable A/B and shadow routing with outcome tagging to support experimentation and continuous improvement.

We will license the core project under the Apache License 2.0 and require all inbound contributions to be provided under the same terms (inbound=outbound). Contributors must sign off via DCO; a CLA is not required at this time.

We will adopt an allowlist for third‑party dependencies used in shipped artifacts and source: permissive licenses only (Apache-2.0, MIT, BSD-2/3-Clause, ISC, CC0, Unlicense) and weak copyleft MPL-2.0 where transitive obligations are manageable. We will not introduce strong copyleft (GPLv2/v3, AGPLv3, LGPL) in distributed components or transitive runtime dependencies. Dev/test tools may include broader licenses if not shipped, containerized, or linked into release artifacts.

All repositories must:
- Declare the license using an SPDX identifier and include LICENSE and NOTICE (for Apache-2.0).
- Maintain a third‑party attributions file with licenses and copyrights.
- Run automated license scanning in CI on direct and transitive dependencies; releases must pass the policy gate.
- Pin dependencies and record license metadata in lockfiles/manifests.
- Escalate exceptions via architecture review; exceptions are time‑boxed and tracked.

For dual‑ecosystem packages, we will publish SPDX-compliant metadata (e.g., license = "Apache-2.0") and ensure container images, binaries, and docs include required notices.

We will implement the backend as a modular monolith: a single deployable application composed of clearly defined domain modules with strict boundaries. Each module will own its domain model, application services, and persistence layer (separate schema/tables per module within a shared database instance), exposing functionality only via in-process interfaces and domain events. Cross-module communication will occur through explicit interfaces or asynchronous events; direct cross-module data access is prohibited.

We will enforce boundaries via package-level visibility, linting/architecture tests, and module-level ownership. Shared utilities are limited to cross-cutting concerns (e.g., logging, auth, tracing) and will not contain domain logic. Transactional consistency remains within module boundaries; cross-module workflows use eventual consistency where appropriate.

Deployment will be a single artifact to streamline operations, performance, and developer productivity. We will instrument modules with per-module metrics, logs, and feature flags to maintain observability and control.

This structure provides a clear evolutionary path to microservices: any module can be extracted into an independent service with minimal refactoring by preserving contracts (APIs/events), data ownership, and build boundaries from the start.

## Decision
Adopt a consistent, backward-compatible coding convention for all gRPC services and Protobuf schemas:

- Package and file layout:
  - proto files grouped by bounded context/module; one service per file when feasible.
  - package names: company.domain.module.v1 (lowercase, dots); include explicit version suffix.
  - set language-specific options (go_package, java_package, csharp_namespace, ruby_package, objc_class_prefix) consistently.

- Naming:
  - Messages and Services: PascalCase (e.g., GetUserRequest, UserService).
  - RPCs: PascalCase, VerbNoun pattern (GetUser, ListUsers, CreateUser, UpdateUser, DeleteUser, BatchDeleteUsers).
  - Fields: snake_case; enums: UPPER_SNAKE with singular type name; enum values prefixed with type (e.g., USER_STATUS_ACTIVE).
  - Request/Response suffixes for all RPCs.

- Standard request/response shapes:
  - Get/Delete: {name or id}; Response: resource or google.protobuf.Empty.
  - Create: {resource, request_id}; Update: {resource, update_mask}; List: {parent/filter/page_size/page_token/order_by}; Response: {items, next_page_token}.
  - Use google.protobuf.FieldMask for partial updates; use google.protobuf.Empty when no payload.

- Types:
  - Use google.protobuf.Timestamp, Duration, Any, Wrappers; avoid custom datetime/nullable types.
  - IDs as strings; binary data as bytes; use map<k,v> sparingly.

- Compatibility:
  - At-least additive evolution: never reuse or renumber fields; mark removed fields as reserved; prefer new fields/oneof for changes.
  - Default to field presence (proto3 optional where needed).
  - Introduce breaking changes only via new package version (v2, v3).

- Errors and status:
  - Use google.rpc.Status with standard error codes and rich error details; no ad-hoc error fields.

- Pagination and filtering:
  - Consistent page_size/page_token; cap server-side maximums; opaque tokens.
  - filter/order_by as strings with documented syntax.

- Documentation and annotations:
  - Comment every service, RPC, message, field; generate API docs.
  - Use HTTP annotations only in gateway-facing protos.
  - Deprecate using [deprecated = true]; document migration path.

- Linting/CI:
  - Enforce with buf (lint, breaking change checks) and format using buf format; auto-generate code in CI.

We will use a centrally managed network file share (SMB for Windows agents, NFS for Linux agents) as the authoritative storage for large build artifacts, test datasets, and shared tool caches produced by Jenkins pipelines. Builds will run in local agent workspaces; upon successful completion, pipelines will publish outputs to the network path using a dedicated service account and Jenkins credentials binding, via OS-mounted paths or the “Publish Over” family of plugins. The Jenkins controller filesystem will not be used for long‑term artifact retention, and binaries will not be stored in VCS.

Artifacts will be written to immutable, versioned locations following a deterministic scheme (e.g., //<fileserver>/ci/<org>/<project>/<pipeline>/<branch>/<buildNumber>/<artifact>), with checksums and metadata recorded in the build record and alongside artifacts. Agents will mount the share read-only during normal execution; write access is granted only in the publish step to reduce risk. Retention, quotas, and backups (snapshots) are enforced by the storage platform; Jenkins will keep only references and metadata and apply complementary retention on archived links.

To mitigate performance and availability concerns, pipelines will use local caching and only sync deltas to the share (e.g., rsync/robocopy) with retry/backoff. Access control is via per-project directories and ACLs; the service account is rotated and scoped to the required paths. This approach centralizes artifacts across heterogeneous agents, supports MATLAB and other licensed toolchains, integrates with enterprise backup/DR, and avoids the operational overhead of custom artifact servers or cloud object storage at this time.

- Prefer explicit, unidirectional data flow:
  - Parent-to-child: pass data via props.
  - Child-to-parent: pass callbacks via props (onChange/onSelect), or expose a stable dispatch from the parent.
- Avoid prop drilling beyond ~3 levels; when crossed, introduce a narrowly scoped Context at the nearest common ancestor.
  - Use Context for stable, cross-cutting concerns only (e.g., theme, i18n, feature flags, auth/session, routing, ambient config).
  - For mutable shared state via Context, expose a reducer-style API: { state, dispatch } with well-typed actions; avoid exposing raw setters.
- For sibling/peer communication:
  - Lift state to the closest common parent, or introduce a local feature Context if coupling is tight and localized.
- For server state:
  - Treat it as asynchronous, cacheable data; use a dedicated data-fetching/cache library (e.g., React Query) rather than Context for fetching, caching, and synchronization.
- For global client state (rare):
  - Prefer minimal, feature-scoped stores first. Introduce a global store (e.g., Redux Toolkit/Zustand) only when multiple distant areas coordinate frequently or time-travel/devtools are required.
- Use URL/router as the source of truth for navigational state (filters, pagination). Reflect sharable state in query params.
- Encapsulate complex interaction patterns in custom hooks; hooks may internally use Context but expose a simple API.
- Avoid event buses and implicit singletons.
- Ensure providers are colocated with features to limit blast radius; do not put everything at the app root.
- Type all props, actions, and context values; provide stable identities (useCallback/useMemo) to prevent unnecessary re-renders.

## Decision

Adopt a schema-first, headless content model with strict separation of content and presentation. All content will be represented as structured types defined in versioned JSON Schema (or equivalent CMS schema) and exposed via a typed API (GraphQL preferred, REST fallback).

Core content types:
- Page (route-aware, SEO fields, layout composition)
- Article/Post (author, publish schedule, taxonomy)
- Component Blocks (modular, nestable: RichText, MediaGallery, Hero, Callout, CTAs, Table, Code, Embed)
- Taxonomy (Tags, Categories)
- Asset (images, video, documents with renditions/metadata)
- Navigation/Menu (hierarchical)
- Redirect (301/302, regex support)

Rich text will be stored as a structured, portable format (e.g., MDX or CMS-native portable JSON) with embedded references to Assets and Component Blocks; Markdown is allowed but compiled to the portable AST at ingest to preserve structure.

Global requirements:
- Stable identifiers and slugs, with history for redirects
- First-class i18n (per-field localization) and varianting (A/B, market)
- Content lifecycle (draft, review, scheduled publish, archive) with audit/version history
- Reusable blocks and references to eliminate duplication
- Media managed separately with CDNs, responsive renditions, and alt/SEO metadata
- Validation enforced at schema level; editors guided via field constraints
- Composability: Pages are assembled from ordered Blocks with guardrails
- Backwards-compatible migrations via schema versioning and migration scripts

Delivery uses a content API layer that normalizes schemas, enforces access policy, and caches responses at the edge. Rendering systems consume only structured content; no presentational HTML is stored in the CMS.

We will standardize all command handlers to return a structured CommandResult rather than performing console I/O directly.

CommandResult will include:
- outcome: one of OK, INVALID_INPUT, NOT_FOUND, CONFLICT, UNAUTHORIZED, ERROR, CANCELED
- exitCode: integer mapped from outcome (overridable)
- message: user-facing message (and optional i18n key + params)
- payload: optional typed, serializable data for machine consumption
- diagnostics: optional details for debugging (stack traces, validation errors)
- warnings: list of non-fatal issues
- hints: remediation/suggestion strings
- meta: free-form metadata (timings, correlation/trace ids)
- events: optional domain/telemetry events

Rules:
- Handlers must not write to stdout/stderr or decide formatting; they only return CommandResult and use logging for internal traces.
- The command runner translates CommandResult to the selected presentation (human-readable, JSON, YAML), writes to stdout/stderr, and sets the process exit code.
- Exceptions thrown by handlers are caught by the runner and converted into ERROR results with diagnostics (optionally suppressed unless --verbose).
- Validation errors are represented as INVALID_INPUT with field-level details in diagnostics.
- Partial successes should be expressed via OK outcome with warnings, or a domain-specific payload status; not by non-zero exit unless the overall command failed.
- Long-running/streaming operations return a StreamResult variant exposing an async iterator of progress events; the runner renders progress accordingly.
- All results are serializable and stable to enable scripting and testing; the format is versioned.

## Decision

- Adopt react-hook-form (v7+) as the default library for building and editing forms.
- Prefer uncontrolled inputs registered with register for performance; use Controller only for controlled/3rd‑party components (e.g., date pickers, selects).
- Use Zod schemas with @hookform/resolvers/zod for client-side validation; co-locate schemas with form components and align with server validation to reduce drift.
- Initialize forms with defaultValues sourced from fetched entity data; when edit data loads or changes, call reset(newValues, { keepDirty: false }) to sync the form.
- Use FormProvider/useFormContext to avoid prop drilling for nested form components; expose reusable Field components that encapsulate label, help text, error, and registration.
- For collections, use useFieldArray; prefer stable keys (id) when available to minimize re-mounts.
- Handle dynamic logic with watch and setValue; pass shouldValidate/shouldDirty when programmatically updating values.
- On submit, disable inputs/buttons using formState.isSubmitting; map server-side errors into fields with setError; handle non-field errors at the form level.
- Display validation feedback below fields; set aria-invalid and associate errors via aria-describedby for accessibility.
- Optimize renders: avoid wrapping inputs in unnecessary state; memoize field components; prefer resolver-level validation over per-field onChange logic.
- Type-safety: infer form types from Zod schema (z.infer) and use as form generic for accurate field names.
- Exceptions: for trivial, single-input interactions, local component state is acceptable.
- Adoption path: all new/edit forms use react-hook-form; migrate existing forms opportunistically during feature work or substantial refactors.

- Standardize ABCI error semantics across CheckTx and DeliverTx:
  - code: uint32, where 0 means success; non‑zero indicates failure.
  - codespace: short, stable string to namespace codes (e.g., “bank”, “staking”).
  - log: human‑readable, deterministic error message suitable for clients/UI.
  - data: optional machine‑readable, deterministic bytes; applications SHOULD pack a protobuf message for structured details.
  - events: continue to carry structured, deterministic metadata; MUST NOT be used to signal failure.

- Determinism and safety:
  - All error fields in DeliverTx MUST be fully deterministic across replicas.
  - Non‑deterministic diagnostics (e.g., stack traces) are prohibited in DeliverTx; they MAY appear in CheckTx.Info only.
  - Tendermint makes no consensus decisions based on application error content beyond code==0/!=0.

- Namespacing and allocation:
  - Each application/module owns its codespace and code allocation; collisions across codespaces are allowed, within a codespace are not.
  - A global registry (out of scope here) is RECOMMENDED for well‑known modules.

- Backward compatibility and transport:
  - Tendermint transports code, codespace, log, data, events unchanged over ABCI and RPC; no parsing or rewriting.
  - Existing applications that only set code/log remain valid; codespace/data are optional.
  - Clients SHOULD treat non‑zero code as failure and MAY use codespace+code for programmatic handling; log is for display; data for structured decoding.

- Error mapping:
  - Mempool admission (CheckTx) uses the same error model; non‑zero code rejects the tx with surfaced error fields.
  - Block execution (DeliverTx) surfaces the same fields in per‑tx results and aggregate responses.

## Decision

- Use React Context to supply app-wide, stable, low-churn data: theme, locale, feature flags, routing info, and non-sensitive auth/session metadata and user preferences. Prefer explicit props elsewhere to preserve transparency.
- Do not use Context for high-frequency updates, large/volatile objects, or server cache (e.g., lists, search results). For those, use dedicated state tools: React Query/TanStack Query for server state; Redux Toolkit/Zustand/Jotai/Recoil for complex client state.
- Create one context per concern to minimize unnecessary re-renders; avoid “god” contexts. Keep provider trees shallow and colocated near their primary consumers.
- Expose typed custom hooks per context (e.g., useTheme()) that:
  - Enforce presence (throw if used outside a provider).
  - Hide implementation details and default values.
  - Provide stable, well-documented APIs.
- Optimize rendering:
  - Memoize context values with useMemo and avoid changing identities unnecessarily.
  - Split contexts to isolate frequently changing fields.
  - Consider selector patterns (e.g., use-context-selector) if profiling shows re-render pressure.
- Do not pass functions or objects that change identity each render unless memoized; avoid storing transient/derived UI state in context.
- For SSR/streaming, initialize providers with server-derived values at the layout/root, and hydrate consistently on the client.
- Document provider hierarchy in the app shell, and supply lightweight test providers/mocks for unit tests.
- Revisit this decision if prop drilling increases, provider nesting becomes complex, or performance profiling indicates Context-induced re-renders.

## Decision

Adopt platform buildpacks on the PaaS for all production and staging application deployments instead of running custom container images. Buildpacks will be explicitly version-pinned in application manifests; we will restage on security updates and track versions in a changelog. Public container registries will no longer be used for runtime deployments; container images will be retained only for local development and CI tasks that require Docker.

We will align with PaaS-native capabilities for build, run, and release, including managed routing/ingress, TLS termination, logging/metrics, and bindable managed services for configuration and secrets. Secrets will be injected via platform mechanisms (env/credentials bindings) rather than baked into images.

An exception path is defined for workloads that demonstrably require custom runtimes, OS-level dependencies not supported by buildpacks, or advanced networking needs; such exceptions must be approved by the architecture review board and include a compliance plan. If we exit the PaaS or require portability beyond supported buildpacks, we will reassess container-based deployment.

To preserve behavior parity, we will increase integration and smoke testing in PaaS environments, codify buildpack and stack constraints in CI, and automate restage procedures as part of our deployment pipeline. This decision takes effect immediately for new services and will be phased in for existing services during the next release cycle.

## Decision

We will keep Study as a Data Transfer Object (DTO), not a rich domain model. StudyDTO will be a simple, serializable data carrier used to move study data across layers and boundaries (API, services, persistence, messaging) without embedded business logic.

- StudyDTO will be:
  - Immutable where practical (constructor + getters; builders for ergonomics).
  - Flat and serialization-friendly (JSON/Avro/Proto) with explicit types, IDs, and timestamps.
  - Backward/forward compatible via explicit versioning and additive schema changes.
  - Free of domain behavior; no invariants or side-effecting methods.

- Validation and business rules:
  - Syntactic validation (shape/type/range) may occur at DTO boundaries.
  - Semantic validation (domain invariants, workflows) belongs in domain services/use cases/aggregates, not in StudyDTO.

- Mapping:
  - Dedicated mappers/adapters will convert between StudyDTO and internal domain models/entities.
  - Mapping is the only place where field transformations, defaults, and normalization occur.
  - Mapping profiles are tested and versioned alongside DTO schema.

- Persistence:
  - Persistence models (ORM/DAOs) remain separate; no direct coupling of StudyDTO to database schema.
  - Repositories accept/return domain models; translation to/from StudyDTO occurs at service/API boundaries.

- Evolution:
  - Use explicit schema docs and changelogs; deprecate fields before removal.
  - Prefer additive fields over breaking changes; provide fallbacks in mappers.

- Usage boundaries:
  - Inbound: Controllers/handlers accept StudyDTO, validate shape, then map to domain.
  - Outbound: Services return domain models mapped to StudyDTO for transport.
  - Messaging: StudyDTO is the payload contract for events/queues, versioned per topic.

- Testing:
  - Contract tests ensure serialization compatibility.
  - Mapper tests ensure fidelity between DTO and domain models.

This preserves a clean separation of concerns, stabilizes external contracts, and allows the domain model to evolve independently of transport and persistence concerns.

Adopt a single, organization-wide Terraform label module to standardize resource names and tags across all stacks and providers. We will use a thin wrapper around cloudposse/terraform-null-label, vendored in this repo at modules/label, and pin the upstream source to a specific version to ensure reproducibility. All Terraform modules must consume this label module and derive resource names and tags exclusively from it.

The canonical inputs are:
- namespace (org/business unit), environment (e.g., dev, qa, prod), application, component, and attributes (optional list).
- delimiter set to “-”.
- tag_defaults include: Name, Application, Environment, Owner, CostCenter, ManagedBy=Terraform, SourceRepo, and Stack.

The canonical outputs used by modules are:
- id for resource name, id_short (optional truncated), and tags (map) merged into provider-specific tag fields (e.g., aws tags).

Constraints:
- Names are lowercase alphanumeric plus hyphens; attributes are sanitized to this scheme.
- Maximum lengths per provider are enforced by the wrapper (with truncation for id_short when needed); long ids must use id_short.
- No ad-hoc name formatting or hard-coded tags in modules; all naming and tagging must flow from label outputs.
- Changes to naming inputs constitute a breaking change and must follow a migration plan (import/move where applicable).

This decision ensures consistent naming, tagging, discoverability, cost allocation, and simpler policy enforcement across all infrastructure.

We will serve all public static assets (JS, CSS, images, fonts) from a dedicated CDN domain backed by object storage, not from application servers. Build artifacts will be content-addressed with fingerprinted filenames (e.g., app.[hash].js) to enable immutable caching. CDN/browser cache-control: immutable, max-age=1y for fingerprinted assets; max-age=0, no-store for HTML. We will avoid cache-busting query parameters.

The build pipeline will produce:
- Modern ES module bundles with code-splitting and tree-shaking, plus a minimal legacy fallback when required.
- Minified CSS with critical CSS inlined in HTML where applicable.
- Optimized images (AVIF/WebP with JPEG/PNG fallbacks), responsive sizes, and SVG preferred for icons.

Compression: Brotli and gzip precompressed variants uploaded; CDN will negotiate content. HTTP/2/3 and TLS enforced.

Security: Strict Content Security Policy using nonces/hashes, Subresource Integrity for third-party assets, no inline scripts/styles except with CSP nonces, and fonts/images served with correct CORS headers. Source maps will be generated and uploaded privately (not publicly served).

Operationally, CI will build, upload assets to the storage bucket with immutable keys, and update a manifest consumed by the app for deterministic URLs. Because filenames are fingerprinted, CDN purges are generally unnecessary; only HTML/root documents may require targeted invalidations on deploy.

Domain strategy: assets served from a cookieless subdomain (e.g., assets.example.com). For authenticated or personalized files, assets will be proxied via the application and not cached publicly.

This approach reduces app server load, maximizes cache hit ratio and performance, simplifies rollbacks (by referencing previous manifests), and provides a secure, repeatable deployment of static assets.

Adopt Tachyons as the primary utility-first CSS framework for the web UI. We will compose styles via Tachyons classes directly in markup to accelerate development, ensure design consistency, and minimize bespoke CSS. The design system will be expressed through a limited set of tokens (colors, spacing scale, typography) aligned with Tachyons’ scales; any deviations require design review.

Implementation details:
- Install Tachyons via npm and bundle it with the application; pin versions to ensure reproducibility.
- Enable tree-shaking/purging (e.g., PostCSS purge) to remove unused classes and keep CSS payload minimal.
- Prefer functional class composition over custom selectors; author custom CSS only for cross-cutting tokens, rare component-specific edge cases, and third-party overrides.
- Document approved class recipes for common components (buttons, forms, layout grids) to reduce variance and improve readability.
- Use responsive variants and accessibility helpers provided by Tachyons; ensure components meet WCAG AA.
- Co-locate UI code and style recipes in component folders; avoid global CSS leakage.
- Enforce conventions via linting (stylelint) and PR review; add Storybook examples demonstrating sanctioned compositions.

This decision standardizes styling, speeds prototyping, and reduces long-term CSS maintenance while preserving flexibility through documented patterns and minimal overrides.

Adopt AppArmor as the mandatory access control layer for all Linux hosts and container workloads, and use Bane to define and generate per-service AppArmor profiles enforcing least-privilege execution. We will:

- Enable AppArmor on all supported kernels and ensure container runtimes (Docker/Containerd) are configured to load explicit profiles rather than the default.
- Author Bane policy files per service/component in-repo, version-controlled alongside the application, and generate deterministic AppArmor profiles as part of CI.
- Apply profiles at deploy time via runtime flags/annotations, with an initial “complain” mode for new services transitioning to “enforce” after burn-in and alert tuning.
- Maintain a small set of hardened base profiles per workload class (API, worker, cron, migration, one-off admin) to reduce duplication; service profiles will extend these bases.
- Integrate profile verification and drift detection in CI/CD (syntax validation, diff against generated output, and smoke tests under the profile). Builds will fail on missing or overly permissive rules.
- Document and standardize escalation procedures for required capabilities, filesystem access, and network egress; changes must be reviewed by security and tracked via ADRs.
- Provide observability by forwarding AppArmor denials to centralized logging with actionable metadata to support rapid tuning.
- For non-containerized system services, ship curated AppArmor profiles managed by configuration management with the same review and rollout process.

This approach constrains process capabilities and filesystem access by default, reduces blast radius for exploited services, and embeds security policy as code with automated verification and repeatable deployment.

We will support deserialization of text/plain payloads into application domain types via a dedicated PlainTextDeserializer with safe, explicit conventions:

- Encoding: Always treat input as UTF-8; strip optional UTF-8 BOM; normalize CRLF/LF.
- Pass-through: If the target type is String or byte[], deliver the raw body (post-normalization).
- Single-value binding: If the target type exposes one of (String constructor, static valueOf(String), parse*(String)), bind the entire body to that single-argument entrypoint.
- Annotated field binding: If a target type designates a single property via annotation/config (e.g., @TextBody or schema mapping), assign the entire body to that property.
- Key-value mode (optional, disabled by default): If enabled for a specific endpoint/type, parse lines of key=value pairs to populate matching properties (case-sensitive by default; configurable). Lines starting with # are comments; blank lines ignored; escaped delimiters supported.
- Content negotiation: Apply only when Content-Type is text/plain (or no Content-Type and endpoint explicitly opts into plain text).
- Validation and errors: Return 415 for unsupported media type, 400 for malformed key-value content or failed conversions, with field-level error details where applicable.
- Security and limits: Enforce configurable max payload size, reject binary control chars (except TAB/CR/LF), and do not auto-execute expressions.
- Observability: Log parsing mode and conversion failures at debug with redaction; no body content at info/error.
- Configurability: Per-endpoint enablement, max size, key-value mode, delimiter/escape, and property mapping strategy.

We will introduce a new, discriminated-union TypeScript model set for dotcom-rendering (DCR) elements, decoupled from raw CAPI. Each element is a serializable object with:
- _type: string literal discriminator (stable, documented)
- version: semantic version string for the element schema
- props: fully normalized, render-ready data (no functions, no side effects)
- optional meta: accessibility, analytics, and feature flags

Rendering components will accept only these DCR element models and perform minimal logic. Any enrichment, normalization, and legacy shape handling will occur in a dedicated transformation layer that maps CAPI Blocks/Atoms to DCR elements. Text with inline markup may carry sanitized HTML where unavoidable; all other HTML must be constructed by components from structured props.

We will provide:
- Runtime validation via schemas (e.g., zod) and generated JSON Schemas for documentation
- Backwards-compatibility adapters to map legacy Element models to the new DCR models
- A migration path with dual-write/dual-render flags, telemetry on coverage, and per-element rollout
- Strict constraints for SSR/serialization (no Dates/Map/Set; use ISO strings and arrays)
- Accessibility-first defaults encoded in props (e.g., alt, captions, roles)
- Snapshot fixtures and conformance tests ensuring component-model parity

Naming and ownership: elements are namespaced (e.g., dcr.image.v1), reviewed via architectural governance, and versioned per element to allow iterative evolution without breaking changes. Legacy models are deprecated once coverage >95% with an agreed removal date.

We will support project.json as a first‑class input alongside .sb3 archives.

- Interfaces:
  - CLI: add --project-json <path|-> to read a standalone project.json (support stdin with -).
  - API: accept application/json bodies at the same endpoint as .sb3 uploads, gated by a query/field type=project-json.

- Schema:
  - Accept Scratch 3.x project.json schema only. If 2.x is detected, return a clear error with guidance; if the converter module is present, auto‑upgrade and log a notice.

- Asset resolution:
  - When given only project.json, assets referenced by md5ext will be resolved from the configured asset store(s) (e.g., Scratch CDN, local cache) on demand.
  - Allow optional supplementalAssets (CLI: --asset-dir, --asset-map; API: multipart/map) to provide missing assets. Provided assets take precedence over remote.
  - If an asset cannot be resolved, proceed with placeholders where feasible (e.g., transparent image, silent sound) and emit structured warnings; hard‑fail only for operations that require completeness (e.g., lossless repack).

- Outputs:
  - For render/simulate/analyze operations, stream assets as needed; no temporary .sb3 is required.
  - For export/package operations, produce a fully self‑contained .sb3 by bundling resolved and provided assets; fail if any required asset is unavailable unless --allow-missing is set.

- Validation and security:
  - Enforce JSON size limits and depth checks; validate schema before processing.
  - Reject external URL fetches inside JSON; only md5ext asset identifiers are honored.
  - Run resolution with timeouts and cache results; respect offline mode.

- Determinism and caching:
  - Asset fetching and packaging are content‑addressed by md5ext to ensure reproducible builds.
  - Cache successfully resolved assets in the configured cache store for reuse.

- Telemetry and UX:
  - Emit clear diagnostics for each unresolved asset and schema issue.
  - Document examples for CLI and API, including stdin and multipart usage.

This enables lightweight, fast iteration (diffable JSON, smaller uploads), while preserving the ability to produce complete .sb3 artifacts when needed.

We will standardize on GitHub Actions as the CI/CD orchestrator for all provisioning and configuration workflows. Infrastructure and configuration changes will flow through:

- Pull Request: run lint/format (YAML, Ansible, Terraform), security scans, unit tests, and dry-runs (terraform plan/ansible check) with results posted back to the PR.
- Merge to main: automatically provision to a non-prod environment; production requires a protected “environment” with mandatory manual approval and change window controls.
- Credentials: use short‑lived OIDC federated identities to cloud providers; secrets stored in GitHub Environments/Secrets, never hard-coded.
- Idempotency and safety: enable Terraform state locking and plan/application separation; enforce concurrency groups to block overlapping applies; enable automatic drift detection on schedules.
- Reusability and speed: adopt reusable workflows, artifact caching (roles, collections, Packer), and matrix strategies for regions/tenants.
- Auditability and rollback: tag all runs with commit SHAs and change metadata; publish plans and inventories as artifacts; support rollbacks via versioned AMIs/images and Terraform state versioning.
- Observability: centralize logs and metrics from runs; page on failed production deploys; maintain deployment dashboards.

This decision codifies repeatable, auditable, and gated provisioning, integrated with our existing Ansible-based configuration and image-baking pipelines.

We standardize on the suffix “Helper” for small, stateless supporting components that encapsulate cohesive, reusable logic not tied to a specific domain concept or external integration. Examples: DateHelper, QueryStringHelper, MarkdownHelper.

Decision details:
- Scope: “Helper” is reserved for components that are:
  - Stateless/pure or with minimal, isolated side effects
  - Focused on small, cohesive logic (formatting, mapping, parsing, lightweight composition)
  - Free of network, persistence, or framework lifecycle responsibilities
- Avoid “Helper” when the component represents:
  - Domain behavior (use DomainService, Policy, Calculator, Specification)
  - External system access (use Client, Adapter, Gateway)
  - Long-running processes or orchestration (use Service, UseCase, Workflow)
  - Cross-cutting infrastructure (use Logger, Tracer, Metrics)
- Naming conventions:
  - Use PascalCase + Helper (e.g., FooBarHelper)
  - Prefer domain-meaningful stems (e.g., CurrencyHelper over CommonHelper)
  - Test artifacts mirror name (CurrencyHelperTest)
- Packaging:
  - Place under a dedicated helpers folder/package within the owning module/bounded context
  - Keep helpers small; split if responsibilities diverge
- Consistency:
  - Retire/avoid “Util/Utils/Utility/Support” suffixes in new code; migrate opportunistically to “Helper” when touching affected areas
  - Public APIs should expose helpers only when clearly part of the supported surface; otherwise keep internal

This improves discoverability, reduces naming ambiguity, and aligns team vocabulary across repositories and languages.

## Decision

We will store all non-sensitive application and infrastructure configurations in the repository, co-located with the components they configure. Configuration will be declarative (e.g., YAML/JSON/HCL), organized by environment (dev, staging, prod) with shared/base defaults and environment-specific overlays. The repository is the single source of truth for configuration; changes are made via pull requests, reviewed, tested, and versioned alongside code to enable auditability, reproducibility, and straightforward rollbacks.

Secrets will not be committed in plaintext. They must be stored in an approved secrets manager; if repo storage is required, they must be encrypted at rest using organization-standard tooling (e.g., SOPS with KMS) and never exposed in CI logs or artifacts. CI/CD pipelines will consume configuration from the repository at build/deploy time. Local development will rely on checked-in examples (e.g., .env.example) and tooling to fetch real secrets.

Runtime environment-variable overrides are permitted only for ephemeral or host-specific values and must be documented; the repository configuration remains canonical.

## Decision

We will document architectural decisions using Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to create a durable, versioned log of significant choices and their rationale.

- Template: Use the MADR 3.x template (Markdown Any Decision Record) for consistency and clarity.
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository at docs/adr/, committed with the code.
- Numbering: Sequential numbering (e.g., 0001-...), stable filenames with kebab-case titles.
- Status workflow: Proposed → Accepted/Rejected → Deprecated → Superseded. Superseding ADRs must link both ways.
- Scope: One ADR per significant decision impacting architecture, cross-cutting concerns, interfaces, data contracts, reliability, operability, security, or cost. Minor implementation details remain in code or design notes.
- Process: Any change requiring an ADR must be included in its pull request. The ADR is reviewed alongside code and must articulate context, options considered, decision, and consequences.
- Ownership: Tech leads steward ADR quality; all contributors may author ADRs. Disputed ADRs require an architecture review meeting; outcomes are recorded in the ADR.
- Discoverability: Maintain an index at docs/adr/README.md and ensure links from CONTRIBUTING.md and the project README.
- Tooling: Use adr-tools (or adr-tools-python) for generation and linking; optionally render to site via MkDocs.
- Versioning: ADRs live with the code branch; only Accepted ADRs on main reflect the current architecture.

This process ensures transparent decision-making, traceability over time, and shared understanding across teams.

## Decision

Enable GitHub Dependabot Security Alerts and Security Updates across all supported ecosystems in this repository (e.g., npm/Yarn, Maven/Gradle, NuGet, Pip, Cargo, Docker, and GitHub Actions). Configure .github/dependabot.yml to:

- Monitor weekly for security advisories and generate targeted PRs that upgrade only the vulnerable packages (including transitive dependencies).
- Limit concurrent open PRs and group related security updates per ecosystem to reduce PR noise.
- Assign CODEOWNERS as reviewers; require CI, SCA, and policy checks to pass before merge.
- Auto-merge patch-level (and safe minor, where semver guarantees compatibility) security updates for runtime and build-time dependencies; exclude major version bumps from auto-merge.
- Pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs and enable Dependabot updates for actions to mitigate supply-chain risks.
- Ignore pre-releases and allow per-package ignore rules when vendor SLAs or compatibility constraints apply.
- Use private registry credentials (via repository secrets) so Dependabot can resolve all artifacts.
- Notify the security channel via GitHub Alerts integration; triage high/critical alerts within the defined SLO.

This establishes Dependabot as the primary mechanism for detecting and remediating dependency vulnerabilities with minimal manual overhead while preserving build stability.

We will use Amazon Cognito as the system’s primary identity provider.

- Configure a Cognito User Pool for user authentication and profile management; no application passwords or PII will be stored outside Cognito.
- Support multiple client types:
  - Authorization Code with PKCE for web and mobile clients via the Cognito Hosted UI.
  - OIDC-compliant JWTs (RS256) issued by the User Pool for API access.
  - Client Credentials flow for service-to-service calls where applicable.
- Enforce security controls in Cognito: mandatory MFA (TOTP/SMS or WebAuthn where supported), strong password policy, compromised credentials protection, and account recovery via verified email/SMS.
- Use OIDC/SAML federation to external IdPs (e.g., Azure AD) for enterprise SSO. Map IdP groups/roles to Cognito groups and custom claims.
- APIs validate tokens using the User Pool JWKS (issuer, audience, expiry, nonce/at_hash as applicable) and authorize via scopes and role/group claims. No session state is kept server-side.
- For backend/admin operations (e.g., user lifecycle, group membership), use Cognito Admin APIs via AWS SDK with least-privilege IAM roles; no custom authentication logic is implemented in the app.
- Provision all Cognito resources (User Pool, app clients, domains, resource servers/scopes, groups, IdP mappings) via Infrastructure as Code (Terraform), including environment-specific configurations and secrets stored in AWS SSM Parameter Store.
- Centralize audit via CloudWatch: login events, token issuance, admin actions; propagate the Cognito subject (sub) as the canonical user identifier in application logs.
- Where custom UX is strictly required, augment Hosted UI with branded templates; avoid password grants and implicit flow; do not use long-lived refresh tokens on public clients beyond minimums.
- Token lifetimes: access tokens ≤ 1 hour, refresh tokens ≤ 30 days, with rotation enabled; revoke on risk signals via triggers.
- Implement Lambda triggers only where necessary (e.g., Pre-Token to enrich claims, Post-Confirmation for onboarding), keeping custom code minimal to ease maintenance and upgrades.

We establish a single point of ownership for Address readiness. The Prober package is the sole component allowed to determine and persist readiness state transitions (e.g., Ready, NotReady, Unknown) for any Address. All other services must treat readiness as read-only and must not write to readiness flags, status fields, or related audit metadata.

Interactions with readiness occur via:
- Prober APIs to trigger (re)probes or query current status.
- Domain events emitted by Prober on state changes for subscribers.
- Read-only views/tables exposed by Prober for consumption.

We will enforce this boundary by:
- Routing all readiness writes through Prober’s repository/service layer.
- Restricting database permissions so only Prober can update readiness columns/tables.
- Validating incoming requests so readiness updates from non-Prober contexts are rejected.
- Making updates idempotent and timestamped, with reason codes and probe evidence for auditability.

Any future readiness logic or policy changes must be implemented within Prober.

All product work will be captured as user stories following a standard template and workflow:
- Format: “As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <outcome>”.
- Acceptance criteria: mandatory, written in Gherkin (Given/When/Then), testable and unambiguous.
- Sizing: vertical slices that deliver observable value; sized to fit within a single sprint; split if larger.
- Quality gates: must meet Definition of Ready (clear value, ACs, dependencies identified, test implications) before sprint commitment; must meet Definition of Done (implemented, code reviewed, tested, documented, deployed, feature flagged if needed).
- Traceability: each story links to related epics, designs, ADRs, risks, and test cases; code changes reference story IDs.
- Management: tracked in Jira using a shared story template; estimated with story points; prioritized by Product; refined collaboratively.
- Scope boundaries: technical tasks/subtasks may support stories but are not substitutes for value-oriented stories; spikes are time-boxed and produce decision artifacts.

We will provision a new, standalone Salesforce org as the authoritative CRM for contacts, organizations, and engagement, rather than reusing legacy systems or shared orgs. We will adopt standard Salesforce objects and capabilities (Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity, Campaign, Case) with minimal customization, favoring configuration over code and AppExchange packages only when they demonstrably reduce complexity.

All integrations will use well-defined APIs and an integration layer (middleware/event bus) to decouple Salesforce from upstream/downstream systems. Authentication will be federated via SSO (SAML/OIDC) and permissions managed with Permission Sets/Groups aligned to least privilege. We will implement a data governance model (field-level security, record types, sharing rules) and comply with GDPR/PII controls, including data retention, consent tracking, and field history/audit trail.

We will establish an org management strategy: scratch orgs and sandboxes (Dev, QA, UAT) with CI/CD via Salesforce DX, version control as the source of truth, and automated deployments/validations. We will adopt a naming convention and a layered package strategy for metadata to ensure modularity and rollback safety.

Data migration will be phased and scripted, with reconciliation and quality rules enforced in the integration layer and within Salesforce (validations/duplicate rules). Reporting and analytics will use Salesforce reports/dashboards initially, with export to the enterprise BI platform where needed. Custom development will be limited to Apex/Flows/LWC only when standard features cannot meet requirements, with architecture review required for exceptions.

## Decision

Co-locate each component’s styles with the component that owns them to enforce encapsulation and maintainability. Each component must import its own styles from its local folder:
- If using CSS-in-JS, define styled primitives in the component file or a sibling styles file and export only component APIs.
- If using CSS Modules, use a Component.module.css file in the same folder and reference generated class names via import.

No component may import another component’s styles. Shared visual primitives (tokens, mixins, utilities) live in a dedicated design-tokens/theme package and are consumed by components, not copied. Global CSS is limited to a reset, base typography, and CSS variables for tokens; no component-specific rules may live globally.

File organization:
- components/Component/index.tsx (or .tsx)
- components/Component/styles.(ts|tsx) or Component.module.css
- components/Component/index.test.tsx, stories, etc.

Lint/build rules will enforce:
