- No cross-component style imports.
- No global selectors affecting components.
- Use of tokens and theme variables instead of hard-coded values.

Storybook, tests, and SSR must render with only the component’s own styles plus tokens/theme. Theming is applied via ThemeProvider/CSS variables so components remain portable and isolated.

We will standardize on Jasmine as the primary framework for unit testing our JavaScript/TypeScript code. All new unit tests must be written using Jasmine’s BDD-style syntax, matchers, and spies. Where applicable (e.g., Angular), Jasmine will be executed via the project’s conventional runner (e.g., Karma) and integrated with coverage tooling (Istanbul/nyc) to enforce agreed coverage thresholds. Tests must be fast, deterministic, and isolated (no network or persistent I/O), using Jasmine spies/mocks for collaborators. We will incorporate Jasmine test execution into local development workflows (npm scripts) and continuous integration pipelines, failing builds on test or coverage threshold failures. Existing non-Jasmine unit tests may remain temporarily but should be migrated opportunistically to maintain consistency and reduce maintenance overhead.

We will make DNS provisioning in AWS Route 53 optional in our IaC. Introduce a boolean parameter (e.g., CreateRoute53Resources, default: false) and separate inputs for DomainName and HostedZoneId. When enabled, the stack will:

- Prefer using an existing Hosted Zone via HostedZoneId; optionally create/attach a private hosted zone to specified VPCs when CreateHostedZone=true.
- Create environment-scoped records (A/AAAA ALIAS to ALB/NLB/CloudFront, optional CNAMEs) for apex and subdomains, plus TXT records for ACM validation when certificate_dns_validation=true.
- Support split-horizon: optionally create private and/or public records via separate toggles.
- Use safe defaults: TTL 300s (overrideable), UPSERT changes for idempotency, and deterministic record names.
- Tag all Route 53 resources consistently and restrict permissions to least-privilege.
- Emit outputs (FQDNs, HostedZoneId) for downstream consumers and avoid circular dependencies with certificate issuance and load balancer creation via explicit DependsOn or staged apply.
- Provide a no-op path (when disabled) so environments using external DNS or centralized DNS teams can deploy without DNS changes.

This ensures flexible, environment-specific adoption of Route 53 while preventing unintended DNS modifications and accommodating external or pre-existing DNS management practices.

## Decision

Adopt automated, programmatic formatting for all source and definition files across the repository. We will standardize on well-supported formatters per language and file type (e.g., Prettier for JSON/YAML/Markdown, RuboCop/StandardRB for Ruby, gofmt for Go, black for Python, shfmt for shell) and centralize configuration in the repo. Formatting will be:
- Enforced in CI via a dedicated check that fails on drift.
- Executed locally via a pre-commit hook and a single task runner command (e.g., make format or scripts/format).
- Version-pinned via tooling lockfiles or containerized dev environment to ensure deterministic results across machines.

Scope and rules:
- All non-generated files are in scope; generated and vendor directories are excluded.
- Formatter configurations are committed (line length, indentation, quotes, trailing commas) and documented.
- Bulk reformatting will be performed once per tool adoption to create a clean baseline; subsequent PRs should keep formatting changes isolated where reasonable.
- No functional changes may be coupled with formatter configuration changes without explicit approval.

Operational considerations:
- Provide quickstart docs and troubleshooting for local setup.
- Offer a “check” mode for CI and a “write” mode for local development.
- For files lacking a mature formatter, maintain minimal lint rules and revisit periodically.
- In case of formatter bugs or regressions, allow temporary file-level opt-outs via annotations with justification.

This approach guarantees consistent style, reduces review noise, minimizes merge conflicts, and shortens onboarding time while keeping enforcement automated and low-friction.

## Decision

We will implement a layered, declarative validation strategy across the platform:

- Define canonical, versioned schemas for all externally visible payloads and events (JSON Schema v2020-12) and enforce them at service boundaries. Unknown/extra fields will be rejected in strict mode.
- Apply three layers of validation:
  1) Transport/schema validation (shape, types, formats, required/forbidden fields),
  2) Domain validation (invariants, state transitions, cross-field rules),
  3) Referential/business validation (cross-aggregate checks and external lookups), which may be asynchronous when necessary.
- Represent validation failures using field-level error codes and paths, aggregating all schema errors in one response while failing fast on domain violations that make further evaluation meaningless.
- Keep validation logic single-sourced: shared schema packages for clients/SDKs, and domain rules encapsulated in domain services/aggregates to avoid duplication and drift.
- Enforce critical constraints at the database layer (unique, not-null, FK) in addition to application checks for defense-in-depth.
- Treat PATCH and partial updates with dedicated schemas per operation; default missing fields to “not provided” rather than null.
- Localize human-readable messages separately from machine-readable codes; codes remain stable for contract compatibility.
- Version validation rules non-breaking by default; breaking changes require schema version bumps and backward-compat handling.
- Capture validation metrics and samples for observability, and gate rollout of new rules behind feature flags where risk warrants it.
- For streaming/events, validate on produce and consume; invalid events are quarantined with dead-letter routing.

This approach yields consistent, auditable validation, minimizes ambiguity for clients, and balances strictness with evolvability.

We standardize on OpenTelemetry for distributed tracing and will not expose bespoke, per-service “trace” APIs to clients. Services will:

- Propagate W3C Trace Context (traceparent, tracestate) and baggage on all incoming/outgoing HTTP/gRPC calls.
- Export spans to a centralized OpenTelemetry Collector via OTLP (gRPC preferred on :4317; HTTP fallback on :4318). No direct exporter-to-backend configurations are allowed in services.
- Avoid public trace ingestion; the OTLP receiver is internal-only behind the collector. External/consumer access to traces occurs exclusively via the tracing backend UI/API (e.g., Tempo/Jaeger), not through application endpoints.

For operational debugging in non-production only, services may optionally expose a read-only GET /observability/trace endpoint that echoes the current request’s trace IDs and sampling state when invoked with an authenticated request. This endpoint must be disabled in production by default and must perform PII scrubbing.

Sampling policy (default parent-based, traceid-ratio) will be centrally controlled in the collector. Services must not override sampling or redact policies locally. Schema, attribute conventions, and resource attributes follow OpenTelemetry semantic conventions.

This decision ensures consistent propagation, centralized control, and secure ingestion while avoiding fragmented “tracing endpoints” across services.

We will use a managed external search service (Algolia) as the primary search engine for the application. This replaces operating our own search cluster and provides built-in capabilities we require (relevance tuning, typo tolerance, synonyms, facets, sorting, highlighting, analytics, A/B testing) with predictable performance and minimal operational overhead.

Integration will be event-driven and eventually consistent. Domain events (create/update/delete) will be published to a queue; a stateless indexer will transform records, apply denormalization, and upsert to Algolia indices. Real-time indexing is not required; a delay of up to a few minutes is acceptable. A daily full reindex job will be available for recovery and relevance recalibration. Search will be read-only from Algolia; the system of record remains our databases.

We will define index schemas per domain aggregate with explicit attribute types, facets, filterable/sortable attributes, searchable fields, language-specific analyzers, and business rules for ranking. PII will be excluded or minimized; where necessary, we will encrypt or hash sensitive fields. All writes will use API keys with restrictive scopes and per-environment indices. Usage caps, rate limits, and alerting will be configured.

To mitigate vendor lock-in, we will abstract search behind an internal SearchGateway with a minimal query DSL (filters, facets, pagination, sorting, synonyms) and maintain export/import tooling (NDJSON) to support migrations (e.g., to Elastic Cloud/OpenSearch/Meilisearch). We will document SLAs and costs, and implement circuit breakers and graceful degradation (cached popular queries, fallback suggestions) if the provider is unavailable.

Use Cheerio (v1.x) backed by parse5 as the default HTML parser for tests that only need HTML querying/serialization, replacing JSDOM for those cases. Retain JSDOM for tests that require browser APIs (layout, events, canvas, selection, etc.).

Provide a small testing utility that:
- Parses HTML with Cheerio/parse5.
- Normalizes whitespace, attribute ordering, and boolean attributes for stable snapshots.
- Exposes jQuery-like selectors for concise assertions.
- Exports helpers to extract text, HTML, and ARIA-relevant attributes for accessibility assertions.

Update the testing guidelines:
- Prefer Cheerio for component/rendered-markup assertions and snapshot generation.
- Use Testing Library queries over Cheerio when testing user-facing behavior via JSDOM.
- Migrate existing brittle HTML assertions to the Cheerio helpers.

Integrate into the test stack:
- Add a Jest setup module to expose global helpers (loadHtml, $, toCleanHtml).
- Replace ad-hoc string matching with parser-driven assertions.
- Gate usage with a lint rule or codemod to discourage raw string HTML comparisons.

This decision yields faster, more deterministic, and less flaky markup tests while preserving JSDOM where true DOM behavior is required.

We will standardize repository organization to ensure discoverability, maintainability, and consistent automation across projects:

- Required top-level files: README.md, LICENSE, CODEOWNERS, CONTRIBUTING.md, SECURITY.md, CHANGELOG.md, .gitignore, .editorconfig, .gitattributes, and a repository-specific CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md (or org default reference).
- Documentation:
  - /docs for user and operational docs; /docs/adr for Architectural Decision Records.
  - README must include: purpose, architecture overview, quick start, dependencies, how to run/test, release process, support/contacts.
- Source and tests:
  - /src (application code) and /test (integration/e2e). For polyglot or multi-service repos use /services/<service>/ with nested src/test.
  - /cmd for entrypoints (where applicable).
  - /internal or /pkg (language-idiomatic) for shared modules within repo.
- Infrastructure and automation:
  - /infra for IaC (e.g., terraform), with environments under /infra/environments/<env>.
  - /scripts for developer and CI scripts; scripts must be idempotent.
  - Provide Dockerfile and Makefile (or Taskfile) with standard targets: setup, build, test, lint, fmt, run, clean, release.
- Configuration and secrets:
  - No secrets in repo. Use placeholders and .env.example; document secret provisioning.
  - Separate config per environment under /config/<env> (values via secrets manager).
- Branching, releases, and versioning:
  - Trunk-based: feature branches -> PR -> main; protect main with required reviews, status checks, and linear history.
  - Semantic Versioning for libraries; release tagging vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; changelog updated via PR.
- Ownership and access:
  - CODEOWNERS must reflect accountable team(s) and critical paths.
  - Define service ownership in README and add maintainers as repo admins; enforce least-privilege.
- Quality gates:
  - Mandatory CI pipelines for build, test, lint, security scan, license compliance, and IaC validation.
  - Required status checks before merge; no direct pushes to main.
- Issue hygiene:
  - Use standardized labels; provide issue and PR templates; link to roadmap/board if applicable.
- Dependency management:
  - Automate updates (Renovate/Dependabot); lockfiles committed; third-party licenses tracked.
- Archival and deprecation:
  - Mark deprecated repos as read-only with clear notice; archive after migration plan is executed.

We will standardize all application containers on Canonical’s Ubuntu LTS minimal OCI image as the base. Default baseline: ubuntu:24.04 (Noble) minimal, pinned by immutable digest in Dockerfiles to guarantee reproducibility; we will uplift to the latest LTS minimal on a scheduled cadence after security review.

Guidelines:
- Use apt-get with --no-install-recommends and purge build-time packages to keep images small.
- Include only essential runtime deps (e.g., ca-certificates, tzdata if required) and run processes as a non-root user.
- Capture CVE patches via regular rebuilds and base image refresh; automate vulnerability scans in CI.
- Maintain separate build and runtime stages (multi-stage builds) to avoid toolchain leakage.
- For language stacks with official Ubuntu-based images, prefer those only when they track the same LTS and minimal base; otherwise, layer required runtimes on the minimal image.
- Pin locales and timezones explicitly if needed; default to UTC and C.UTF-8.
- Document any package additions in the Dockerfile with justification.

Exceptions:
- Distroless or language-specific slim images may be used where they materially reduce attack surface or size without sacrificing operability; such deviations require an ADR referencing this decision.
- Alpine is not to be used by default due to musl/glibc compatibility considerations unless the runtime is fully compatible and tested.

Image naming and provenance must come from Canonical’s official Docker Hub registry (ubuntu) with digest pins and SBOMs attached during build.

- Adopt AngularJS 1.7.x (last LTS) for the current front-end codebase to stabilize and maintain existing functionality with minimal disruption.
- Standardize on component-based architecture (.component API, introduced in 1.5+), one-way data flow where possible, and controllerAs syntax; avoid using $scope directly except where unavoidable.
- Use ui-router (angular-ui/ui-router) for stateful routing and lazy feature modules; avoid ngRoute.
- Enforce strict dependency injection (ng-strict-di) and use ng-annotate/ts-lib annotations to ensure minification safety.
- Modernize build tooling with Webpack (or Vite via legacy plugin), Babel/TypeScript, ESLint, Prettier, and commit hooks; produce a single versioned bundle with source maps.
- Write unit tests with Karma + Jasmine and component-level tests; add basic e2e coverage (Cypress) for critical flows.
- Limit third-party AngularJS directives; prefer lightweight, framework-agnostic libraries for utilities, and isolate legacy plugin usage behind facades.
- Apply accessibility and i18n practices consistently; avoid custom directives that hinder ARIA or keyboard navigation.
- Freeze introduction of new major features in AngularJS where feasible; new substantial UI capabilities should be implemented as standalone microfrontends or web components integrated into the AngularJS shell.
- Establish a migration strategy away from AngularJS: strangler pattern, building new modules in the target framework and embedding alongside AngularJS; create shared design system and API boundaries to ease replacement.
- Define deprecation timelines and support SLAs for AngularJS features; document coding standards and migration guides to reduce long-term risk.

We will persist all ETL outputs to Azure Blob Storage (Data Lake Storage Gen2) in a dedicated storage account per environment (dev/test/prod), with hierarchical namespace enabled.

Data organization and formats:
- Container per domain/source (e.g., syndication, pomi, curated).
- Partitioned path scheme: container/{schemaVersion}/{yyyy}/{MM}/{dd}/{runId}/
- Primary format: Parquet (snappy) for datasets; CSV (gzip) for interchange where needed; JSON for manifests and metadata.
- Each run writes to a new runId folder with an atomic “_SUCCESS” marker and a manifest including row counts, checksums, schema version, and source lineage.

Reliability and governance:
- Enable blob versioning, soft delete, and time-based immutability for X days to ensure tamper-evidence and rollback.
- Apply lifecycle policies to tier older data to Cool/Archive and purge after retention.
- Replication: use GRS (or RA-GRS for read access) for DR; consider LRS for non-critical dev.

Security and access:
- Enforce Azure AD auth with RBAC; workloads use Managed Identities. No connection strings or account keys in code.
- Private Endpoints and storage firewall restricted to VNets; short-lived User Delegation SAS for external consumers.
- Encryption at rest with Microsoft-managed keys; enable CMK for datasets containing PII.

Operations and integration:
- Emit Event Grid notifications on new manifests for downstream triggers.
- Monitor via Azure Monitor/Activity Logs; set alerts on failures/anomalies.
- Infrastructure and policies defined as code (Bicep/Terraform) with naming, tags, and cost budgets.

We will adopt DfE Sign-in (DSI) as the primary identity and access management provider for all human users of the service (end users, administrators, and support staff). Authentication will integrate with DSI via OpenID Connect using the Authorization Code flow (with PKCE where applicable). Where components cannot support OIDC, we will use SAML via DSI as a fallback.

Application authorization will be derived from DSI-assigned services, organisations, and roles exposed in OIDC/SAML claims. We will maintain a deterministic mapping from DSI roles to application permissions, enforcing least privilege. Role and membership management will occur in DSI; the application will remain stateless with respect to user credentials and will not store passwords.

We will require multi-factor authentication as enforced by DSI policy. Single sign-on will be enabled across all first-party applications integrated with DSI. Elevated operations (admin/support) will be restricted to DSI groups/roles designated for privileged access.

For external or non-DfE users, we will use DSI’s supported federation/guest account mechanisms where available; if not supported, access will not be provided through alternative local accounts.

Programmatic (non-human) access is out of scope for DSI and will use separate service-to-service mechanisms (e.g., OAuth2 client credentials with our platform identity provider), logically isolated from user flows.

Legacy authentication paths will be deprecated and removed following a controlled migration to DSI-backed access.

## Decision

Adopt PostCSS as the standard CSS processing pipeline for the project to enable modern CSS features, consistent cross-browser behavior, and production optimizations while remaining compatible with CSS Modules and styled-jsx.

- Use a single repository-wide postcss.config.js (and per-package overrides if needed) with:
  - postcss-preset-env (stage 3 features) enabling:
    - autoprefixer (driven by our browserslist in package.json)
    - nesting rules
    - custom media queries
    - color functions where safe
    - CSS custom properties with preserve: true (compile-time substitution only when necessary)
  - postcss-import for global stylesheet composition (avoid import loops)
  - cssnano for production builds only
  - postcss-reporter for clear diagnostics in local dev and CI

- Integration:
  - Next.js: rely on built-in PostCSS support; Next will pick up postcss.config.js automatically.
  - Webpack/Vite (where applicable): use postcss-loader / PostCSS plugin with the shared config.
  - Works alongside CSS Modules (scoping preserved) and styled-jsx (affects only their emitted CSS where applicable).

- Guardrails:
  - Prefer spec-aligned plugins; avoid class-renaming or non-deterministic transforms that could conflict with component scoping.
  - Pin plugin major versions and track updates via Renovate/Dependabot.
  - Enforce browserslist centrally to ensure consistent output across apps/packages.
  - Run PostCSS in the build pipeline and in Storybook to ensure parity.

This decision standardizes our styling toolchain, reduces cross-browser defects, and provides a clear, extensible path for future CSS capabilities without committing to a preprocessor.

## Decision

Adopt “Capacity Assignment v2,” moving from static per-cell quotas to a dynamic, policy-driven assignment that optimizes utilization while preserving reliability and multi-tenancy guarantees.

Key elements:
- Scheduling policy: weighted bin-packing across CPU, memory, and ephemeral disk, with memory as the primary packing dimension and CPU as secondary. Prefer least-utilized cells within the same failure domain while ensuring anti-affinity for replicas.
- Headroom: reserve 15% per cell and 30% per cell-group (AZ) for failover and burst. Headroom is not allocatable to tenants and is enforced by the scheduler.
- Quotas and limits: enforce hard per-tenant org/space quotas; apply soft per-app limits that may burst within tenant quota but never cross cell/group headroom. No memory/disk overcommit; allow up to 10% CPU overcommit for best-effort workloads only.
- AZ spread and anti-affinity: require cross-AZ placement for redundant instances; block co-location of identical replicas on the same cell/host.
- Rebalancing: background drain/shift activates when any cell >80% utilization or inter-cell skew >20%. Moves are rate-limited and disruption-aware (respect PDBs/SLAs).
- Autoscaling: expand the cell pool when 95th percentile forecast exceeds 85% for 24h; contract when observed utilization <50% for 7d and rebalance confirms capacity safety.
- Preemption: disabled for guaranteed workloads; allowed only for explicitly marked best-effort jobs.
- Observability and control: expose decisions, utilization, and rebalancing metrics; feature-flag rollout with canary in one cell-group; dry-run for 1 week; instant rollback to v1 static assignment if SLOs degrade.

This approach increases overall utilization, preserves fault tolerance, and reduces hot-spotting without compromising tenant isolation.

## Decision

Enforce explicit program termination and safe fall-through to eliminate “invalid address” faults caused by missing exit instructions.

- Build-time: All binaries must contain an explicit EXIT/HALT on every control-flow path. The verifier/linker will detect missing terminators. In development builds, it auto-injects a final EXIT and emits a warning; in release/production builds, it fails the build.
- Runtime: The VM/JIT will perform strict code-segment bounds checks on instruction fetch. If execution reaches the end of the code segment without encountering EXIT, the runtime will perform an implicit clean termination (EXIT) and emit a telemetry event, never attempting to fetch past bounds.
- Diagnostics: The error reported for premature termination is standardized as ProgramTerminatedWithoutExit (development) with source location, replacing generic “invalid address.” Metrics will track frequency to drive remediation.
- Migration: A deprecation window keeps auto-injection enabled by default; after the window, missing EXIT is a hard error in all build modes. Configuration flags allow projects to opt-in early to hard enforcement.

- Every kata must include a metadata header at the top as a structured comment block: id, title, level (beginner/intermediate/advanced), group (e.g., “Array API”), tags, edition (ESx), status, related (ids), and inDepth (true/false).
- File naming and placement must follow: <edition>/<domain>/<group>/<topic>.js. Examples: es6/language/array-api/from.js, es10/language/object-api/fromEntries-in-depth.js. Use kebabCase for directories and camelCase for filenames where they mirror API names; append “-in-depth” for expert variants; “basics.js” and “the-api.js” are reserved names in API groups.
- Each kata starts with: short purpose, learning goals, constraints, and references (spec links) in the header comment. English only.
- Code formatting and linting must comply with the repo’s shared configuration (ESLint + Prettier). Use const/let (no var), strict equality, explicit returns, no implicit globals.
- Tests must be colocated in a parallel path under test/, mirroring the kata path and filename. Use the standard test runner. Tests use describe/it naming, one focused assertion per it where practical, clear failure messages, and no hidden behavior. Example-based progression from simple to edge cases; edge cases only in in-depth katas.
- Katas must be solvable without network access or external dependencies (beyond the standard test stack). Provide minimal scaffolding and TODO markers where learner code is expected; do not include solutions or hints beyond the stated goals.
- Export/Import style must follow the repository standard (ESM or CommonJS) consistently across kata and tests.
- Each kata includes a minimal README fragment (or header section) for: prerequisites, estimated time, and related katas.
- Accessibility and clarity: avoid ambiguous terminology, prefer small, self-contained exercises, and keep runtime under 2s on CI.
- Any deviations from this format require explicit justification in the kata’s metadata (deviations field).

## Decision

Adopt a single monorepo managed with pnpm workspaces and Turborepo for task orchestration, caching, and incremental builds. Standardize the repository layout as:

- apps/: deployable applications
  - web/, mobile/, api/, admin/, etc.
- packages/: versioned, reusable libraries
  - ui/, utils/, data-access/, config/, eslint-config/, tsconfig/, etc.
- infra/: environment and deployment assets
  - k8s/, terraform/, helm/, scripts/
- docs/: architecture, ADRs, and product documentation
- .github/: CI/CD workflows and shared automation

Conventions:
- All workspaces are first-class packages with their own package.json and semantic versioning where applicable. Internal dependencies use workspace: ranges.
- TypeScript project references are enabled across apps and packages; shared tsconfig presets reside in packages/tsconfig. ESLint/Prettier configs are centralized in packages/eslint-config and consumed via extends.
- Each package builds to dist/ with clean, sideEffect-aware outputs and proper package.json “exports” (module, main, types) to support ESM and CJS as needed.
- Apps import from packages via bare specifiers; no cross-app imports.
- Enforce isolated builds, no implicit imports from src of other packages, and no circular dependencies. Path aliases map to published entry points only.
- CI uses Turborepo to run affected builds/tests/lint with remote caching; reusable composite workflows live in .github/.
- Releases are managed with Changesets: independent versioning for packages, automated changelog generation, and publish to the registry from main. Applications are not published but are version-tagged and deployed via CI.
- Code owners and module boundaries are defined per directory; owners must approve changes to their domains.
- Example naming: @org/ui, @org/utils, @org/config; app names: web, api, mobile. Shared runtime configs live in packages/config; environment-specific values are resolved at build/deploy time via infra.
- Git hooks (lint-staged, commitlint) enforce formatting and Conventional Commits; status checks block merges if boundaries or quality gates fail.

This structure enables modular development, fast feedback via caching, clear ownership, consistent tooling, and scalable CI/CD across all clients, services, and shared libraries.

## Decision

Adopt Node.js (current LTS) as the primary language and build the web application using Express.js with server-side rendering and Nunjucks templating, integrating the GOV.UK Design System (govuk-frontend) for components and styles. Author application code in TypeScript to improve reliability and maintainability.

Key choices:
- Node.js + Express.js for a lightweight, well-supported HTTP framework with broad ecosystem compatibility.
- Nunjucks for accessible, server-rendered templates aligned with GOV.UK patterns and partials/macros.
- GOV.UK Design System as the baseline UI component library.
- TypeScript for static typing; ts-node/tsup (or esbuild) for build tooling.
- Jest and Testing Library for unit/integration tests; Playwright for end-to-end tests.
- ESLint and Prettier for code quality; Commitlint and standard-version (or Changesets) for release hygiene.
- Helmet, CSRF protection, and session management via express-session (or @fastify/secure-session if Fastify is later adopted).
- i18n via i18next (server + middleware) if/when multilingual support is required.
- Feature flags via environment-driven configuration to enable safe, incremental delivery.

This selection prioritizes accessibility, performance, maintainability, and alignment with the GDS Way, enables reuse of shared components across user-facing products, and avoids SPA complexity unless a future need for client-heavy interactivity emerges.

We will adopt a zero‑runtime CSS‑in‑JS approach using vanilla-extract for component-scoped styling and theming. Styles will be authored in TypeScript, compiled to static CSS at build time, and fed through our existing PostCSS pipeline (e.g., autoprefixer) to maintain compatibility and minimize runtime overhead. Design tokens (colors, spacing, typography) and themes will be centralized via vanilla-extract’s tokens/theme APIs and exposed as CSS variables for dynamic theming and runtime overrides where necessary.

We will not use runtime CSS‑in‑JS libraries (e.g., styled-components, Emotion in runtime mode) in application code due to bundle size, runtime cost, and SSR complexity. Exceptions for localized dynamic styling must prefer CSS variables or inline style attributes; introducing a runtime CSS‑in‑JS dependency requires an explicit performance review and ADR.

Global resets and 3rd‑party styles remain as global CSS. Component libraries within the monorepo should follow the same approach to ensure consistency, tree‑shakability, and type safety.

## Decision

Adopt incremental popularity updates driven by event streams rather than periodic full recomputations. Popularity will be updated continuously based on incoming signals (e.g., pageviews, clicks, downloads) aggregated into fixed time buckets (hour/day). We will maintain per-item counters and compute a decayed popularity score (exponential decay with a configurable half-life) to weight recent activity more heavily while preserving historical relevance.

Events will be ingested from the analytics pipeline and queued; workers will apply idempotent, de-duplicated increments to counters and recalculate the score on write. Intermediate aggregates will be stored in a fast, durable key-value store for counters; the materialized popularity score will be propagated to the primary datastore/search index at a controlled cadence (e.g., every few minutes) to bound write amplification. Periodic compaction jobs will fold older buckets into coarser windows to control storage growth.

We will retain a batch backfill/rebuild job for cold start, corruption recovery, and model changes, but day-to-day ranking will rely on the incremental path. Rollout will be feature-flagged with dual-write/dual-read for verification, with observability (lag, error rate, staleness, and drift vs. batch recompute) and alerting. Configuration (signals, weights, decay) will be versioned to allow safe, reversible tuning.

We will implement passwordless authentication via email-based magic links for the frontend using our identity provider’s native passwordless flow. Upon sign-in request, the backend will issue a single-use, short-lived token embedded in a signed link that deep-links to the application. When opened, the frontend posts the token to our backend for verification and exchange for a session established via HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=strict cookies. Links will expire within 10–15 minutes, be bound to the original email address, and be invalidated on first use. A fallback one-time verification code entry path will be supported for users who cannot open deep links.

We will enforce rate limiting, bot protection (CAPTCHA/turnstile), and email domain allow/deny policies as applicable. Emails will use branded templates with clear origin, include an out-of-band “Was this you?” notice, and a one-click report mechanism. We will log all auth events and surface security signals to monitoring.

Admin and privileged roles will continue to require MFA (e.g., WebAuthn or TOTP) after magic-link verification; end users may optionally enroll in WebAuthn for step-up. The flow will support iOS/Android deep links and desktop, and remain WCAG-compliant. Implementation will be IdP-agnostic where feasible, abstracted behind an auth service to permit provider substitution without frontend changes.

## Decision

Adopt Cypress as the primary framework for browser-based integration testing.

- Scope: Validate cross-component user flows within a single browser context (routing, state, network interactions), distinct from unit tests and end-to-end cross-system tests.
- Execution: Run headless in CI across Chromium and Firefox; optional Dashboard recording for parallelization, flake analysis, and artifacts.
- Environments: Default to stubbed network via cy.intercept for third-party and non-critical services to ensure determinism and speed. For critical back-end integration, run against an ephemeral test environment with seeded data.
- Structure: Place specs under cypress/e2e/integration; use data-test attributes and lightweight page objects/selectors. Store fixtures under cypress/fixtures.
- Configuration: Manage baseUrl and env via cypress.config.(ts/js) and CI variables. Enable retries on test and command levels; capture screenshots/videos on failure; emit JUnit reports; upload artifacts in CI.
- Auth: Prefer programmatic login (API token/session seeding) over UI login to reduce flakiness and runtime.
- Stability: Use test isolation, clock control, request waiting with explicit assertions, and network timeouts tuned for CI.
- Accessibility and performance: Optionally integrate cypress-axe for a11y checks and lighthouse CI on deploy previews.
- Maintenance: Review flaky tests weekly, quarantine when necessary, and enforce PR gating on stable integration suite.

## Decision

Implement deep links from search results to PIMS using a centralized URL builder that constructs environment-specific base URLs and the new PIMS route schema. Each result row will render a “View in PIMS” action that opens the PIMS Property Detail page in a new tab (target=_blank with rel="noopener noreferrer"). Where a canonical identifier is available, we will prefer propertyId; if absent, we will fall back to PID/PIN/parcel identifier per PIMS-supported query parameters. If no supported identifier is available, the link will be disabled with an explanatory tooltip and an accessible label.

Links will be conditioned by authorization: only users with PIMS access will see active links; others will see the action hidden or disabled based on product requirements. The URL builder will be configuration-driven (per environment base URL, path templates, and parameter mapping) to avoid hardcoding and to support future PIMS changes. Rollout will be gated behind a feature flag and instrumented with click analytics to validate adoption and detect errors.

We will maintain backward compatibility by supporting the legacy PIMS route for a limited period behind a fallback branch, with warnings logged for telemetry. Comprehensive unit tests will cover URL construction and parameter precedence; end-to-end tests will verify navigation from representative search results.

## Decision

- All endpoints use HTTPS only; canonical base is https://api.example.com.
- API versioning is via the first path segment: /v1/, /v2/; minor/patch changes are backward compatible and not encoded in the URL.
- Resource names are lowercase, plural nouns, kebab-case: /users, /order-items.
- Hierarchy models containment/ownership only: /stores/{storeId}/products/{productId}; avoid deep nesting (>2 levels).
- Use stable opaque IDs (UUIDs) in paths; never expose internal DB keys or composite natural keys.
- No file extensions in URLs (.json, .xml); content negotiated via Accept/Content-Type.
- Trailing slash is not significant; server canonicalizes to no trailing slash (301 redirect).
- Query parameters:
  - Pagination: page, per_page (defaults documented; hard max enforced).
  - Filtering: field operators via dot-notation and simple operators, e.g., status=active, created_at.gte=2024-01-01.
  - Sorting: sort=field or sort=-field for desc; multi-field allowed comma-separated.
  - Sparse fieldsets: fields=field1,field2; for sub-resources: fields[products]=id,name.
  - Search: q=free-text.
- Relationships:
  - Use sub-resources for strong ownership: /orders/{id}/items.
  - Use linking endpoints for associations: /users/{id}/roles; mutations via POST/DELETE on link endpoints.
- Actions that don’t map to CRUD use action sub-resources: /invoices/{id}/send, /reports:generate (POST).
- Multi-tenancy and regions are expressed as first-class segments when applicable: /{tenantId}/v1/... or /{region}/v1/... (one scheme chosen per deployment and kept consistent).
- Reserved characters are percent-encoded; IDs are case-sensitive; all path segments otherwise lowercase.
- Idempotent, safe reads via GET-only; mutations never encoded in query string.
- Stable URLs are maintained; deprecated endpoints respond with 410 after sunset with Link headers to replacements.

We will build the new product pages using Next.js (TypeScript) with React Server Components and the App Router, favoring static site generation (SSG) and incremental static regeneration (ISR) for performance, reliability, and SEO. Pages requiring personalization or frequently changing data will use server-side rendering (SSR) with edge caching where appropriate.

Content will be sourced from a headless CMS via read-only APIs, pulled at build time for SSG or via on-demand revalidation for time-sensitive updates. Rich content will be authored in Markdown/MDX where suitable. This decouples content operations from deployments and supports preview workflows.

We will use our design system components, with Tailwind CSS for utility styling and CSS modules where needed. Accessibility and progressive enhancement are mandatory; pages must remain functional without client-side JavaScript except where interactive components are essential.

The runtime target is Node.js 18+ with deployment on a platform supporting Next.js (e.g., Vercel or an equivalent containerized setup with CDN-level caching). Observability will include web vitals, synthetic monitoring, and error reporting in both server and client contexts.

This stack aligns with team skills, provides strong SEO and performance characteristics, supports rapid iteration, and offers a mature ecosystem and LTS pathway. It also limits operational complexity compared to a bespoke SSR stack, while remaining flexible for future expansion.

## Decision

Adopt CoreTracker and the CoreTrackable interface as the standard tracking APIs across all services and deprecate the Legacy Trackable interface. New features must implement CoreTrackable; no new code may depend on Legacy Trackable. A compatibility adapter will be provided to bridge Legacy Trackable implementations to CoreTrackable during migration, ensuring runtime interoperability and avoiding a flag-day cutover.

We will:
- Publish CoreTracker and CoreTrackable as stable in vNext of the core SDK and mark Legacy Trackable as @Deprecated, to be removed in the next major release.
- Provide a migration guide and code-mod templates to replace Legacy Trackable with CoreTrackable in common scenarios.
- Enforce usage via lint/static analysis rules and CI checks; add an architectural test that forbids new references to Legacy Trackable.
- Maintain feature parity for required capabilities (context propagation, async-safe events, batching, backpressure, PII redaction) in CoreTracker; any new tracking features will only land in CoreTracker.
- Introduce an adapter (LegacyTrackableAdapter) to wrap existing Legacy Trackable implementations behind CoreTrackable until refactoring is complete.
- Update observability pipelines and dashboards to consume CoreTracker event schemas; dual-publish during transition.
- Set a deprecation timeline: code freeze on Legacy Trackable immediately; migration completion within two release cycles; removal in the following major release, with a feature flag fallback if critical issues arise.

This decision standardizes tracking, reduces technical debt, and enables consistent, testable, and privacy-compliant telemetry across the platform.

Split the current monolith into two independently deployable services: Audit Tool and Content Performance Manager (CPM).

- Purpose and scope:
  - Audit Tool: content inventory, quality checks, editorial workflow, remediation tasks.
  - CPM: ingestion, storage, and visualization of performance/engagement metrics.

- Boundaries and ownership:
  - Separate repos, build pipelines, and runtime environments.
  - Separate databases/schemas: Audit owns audit findings and tasks; CPM owns metrics and aggregations. Neither writes to the other’s store.
  - Canonical content metadata continues to come from Publishing API; both services consume it independently.

- Integration:
  - CPM exposes a read-only API for metrics; Audit Tool consumes it.
  - Event-based integration (e.g., domain events via queue) for decoupled updates; HTTP fallback allowed.
  - Shared utilities extracted into versioned libraries/packages (no shared DB).

- Security and access:
  - Shared SSO; distinct RBAC roles per service.
  - Principle of least privilege for data access.

- Deployment and operations:
  - Independent scaling, release cadence, and incident blast radius.
  - Unified observability standards; service-level objectives defined per service.

- Migration:
  - Transitional façade/redirects to preserve URLs and bookmarks.
  - Data backfill and dual-write/feature flags where needed until cutover is complete.

We will migrate external API interactions from the browser to the server, introducing a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) layer that proxies, aggregates, and validates requests on behalf of the client. The server will own authentication/authorization (session or token exchange), secret management, request signing, rate limiting, schema validation, and response shaping. We will leverage server-side caching, retries, circuit breakers, and backoff to improve performance and resilience, and centralize observability (structured logs, metrics, traces) and error handling. CORS and network surface area will be simplified by terminating at our origin only.

Implementation will be phased: new endpoints go via the BFF; existing client calls are wrapped and gradually redirected. We will preserve limited client-initiated channels for real-time features (e.g., WebSocket/SSE) where appropriate, with the server mediating subscriptions/tokens. The BFF will expose stable, UI-oriented contracts, perform data federation where needed, and support SSR/ISR where beneficial; the browser will receive only minimally scoped data.

Non-goals: reinventing downstream services; changing business logic ownership in source systems. Success criteria include reduced client bundle size, fewer CORS/auth issues, improved p95 latency via caching/aggregation, lower error rates via retries/circuit breaking, and clearer security posture through removal of secrets from the client.

We will generate and serve location-aware meta tags on the server for every indexable route and resource. Specifically:
- On initial requests and any URL that changes the canonical content (e.g., map bounds, place detail, language), the server will render canonical, hreflang, og:* and twitter:* tags, plus JSON-LD (schema.org) for location entities; for geocoded resources we will include latitude/longitude via schema.org Place and PostalAddress. We will not use meta refresh.
- Client-side navigation in the SPA will not attempt to “patch” meta for indexable pages; instead, it will trigger a full page load when navigating to a route whose share/SEO metadata must differ, ensuring crawlers and social scrapers receive correct tags.
- For non-indexable ephemeral states (e.g., filters that do not change the canonical resource), we will avoid reloads, update query params for shareability, and exclude from indexing via robots meta and canonical pointing to the base resource.
- We will enforce a single canonical URL per indexable resource and 301-redirect non-canonical variants (e.g., alternate param order, tracking params, legacy paths).
- We will centralize meta generation in a dedicated server module with templates per route type (home, search/map, place detail, collections), including locale-aware titles/descriptions and og:url matching the resolved canonical URL.
- For environments where SSR is not available, we will pre-render static snapshots for crawlers/social scrapers.
- Map viewport and filters will be encoded in URL parameters; reloads preserve state via those parameters rather than client storage.

We will model data with pure, immutable types and provide all behavior as standalone functions. Concretely:
- Define data shapes with TypeScript type aliases or interfaces in types-only modules (e.g., <feature>/types.ts). Avoid classes for domain modeling and avoid embedding methods on data structures.
- Implement operations as pure functions in separate modules (e.g., <feature>/functions.ts), taking typed values as input and returning new values or Results. No implicit mutation.
- Use type-only imports/exports (import type/export type) to prevent accidental runtime dependencies and enable tree-shaking. Do not re-export runtime values from types-only modules.
- Provide barrels that distinguish runtime from types (e.g., index.ts for functions and index.types.ts for types), or co-locate with clear suffixes (*.types.ts).
- Prefer discriminated unions and tagged results over nominal class hierarchies and runtime instanceof checks.
- Keep serialization/deserialization and I/O adapters separate from domain types; map at boundaries.
- Enforce via lint rules: no classes in domain, consistent type-only imports, no mixing types and values in types files, and immutability preferences.

This separation improves testability, composability, and evolution of the domain model, avoids circular dependencies, clarifies what exists at runtime, and reduces bundle size.

Adopt a centralized, standards-based authentication model across all applications using the enterprise Identity Provider (IdP) as the single source of truth.

- Protocols:
  - Primary: OpenID Connect (OIDC) for user authentication.
  - OAuth 2.1 for delegated authorization and API access; Client Credentials for service-to-service.
  - SAML 2.0 supported only for legacy/federated partners; prefer OIDC for new integrations.

- Security controls:
  - Enforce MFA for all users; prefer FIDO2/WebAuthn; allow platform authenticators where supported.
  - Short-lived JWT access tokens (≤15 min), opaque refresh tokens with rotation and reuse detection.
  - Token scoping by audience and least privilege; include tenant, roles, and attributes in claims.
  - JWKS-based signature verification; automatic key rotation.
  - PKCE mandatory for public clients (SPAs/mobile); no implicit flow.

- Application patterns:
  - Web apps: Authorization Code + PKCE via OIDC.
  - SPAs: Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern preferred; if pure SPA, use Authorization Code + PKCE and same-site cookies.
  - Native/mobile: Authorization Code + PKCE.
  - Machine-to-machine: OAuth 2.1 Client Credentials with mTLS or private_key_jwt.
  - Internal service calls: prefer mTLS and token exchange where needed.

- Provisioning and authorization:
  - Centralized user/group/role lifecycle via SCIM from HRIS to IdP; roles/entitlements conveyed via claims.
  - RBAC with optional ABAC using standardized claim names; no app-local credential stores.

- Operational standards:
  - Use approved OIDC/OAuth SDKs and a shared auth middleware; token validation at API gateway and service.
  - Deprecate API keys and basic auth for new development; migrate existing APIs to OAuth/OIDC.
  - Centralized policy enforcement (conditional access, risk-based policies) managed in IdP.

We will use Amazon DynamoDB as the primary data store to exercise and demonstrate real-world Lambda patterns. Specifically:
- Model access patterns with well-defined partition/sort keys and targeted GSIs to reflect production-grade query paths.
- Use On-Demand capacity for elasticity during tests; where predictable load exists, enable Auto Scaling on provisioned capacity.
- Enable DynamoDB Streams (new-image) to drive event-sourced workflows and trigger downstream Lambdas, simulating CDC and fan-out.
- Enforce optimistic concurrency via Condition Expressions and (where needed) transactions to mimic contention and idempotency handling.
- Enable TTL for lifecycle management, and PITR + backups for recovery scenarios.
- Apply least-privilege IAM policies for Lambda-to-DynamoDB access, with per-table/granular action scopes.
- Instrument end-to-end with CloudWatch metrics/alarms, structured logs, and X-Ray traces for latency, throttling, and retry analysis.
- Use item-level retries with exponential backoff and jitter for ProvisionedThroughputExceeded and ConditionalCheckFailedException.
- Support local/dev workflows with DynamoDB Local and SAM/LocalStack for CI.
- Seed representative data volumes and access skews to validate hot partitions, adaptive capacity behavior, and GSI backfills.
- Employ consistent naming, tagging, and CloudFormation for reproducible environments.

This decision ensures our Lambda exercises reflect realistic serverless data access patterns, event-driven triggers, concurrency controls, observability, and cost characteristics common in production.

Chosen option: Accept and safely ignore/preserve unrecognized metadata fields. The system will strictly validate and enforce all known/mandatory fields and constraints, but will not reject payloads solely due to additional, unknown properties.

Implementation details:
- Parsing/validation: Use schema(s) that allow extensibility (e.g., “additionalProperties: true” or equivalent) while keeping strict validation on known fields. Unknown fields must not collide with reserved names or violate type/format constraints of known fields.
- Storage and round‑trip: Unknown fields are preserved verbatim and included in re-serialization to enable forward compatibility and ecosystem extensions. If storage format is normalized, preserve them in an “extensions”/passthrough map.
- Processing: Core logic ignores unknown fields; they have no behavioral effect unless explicitly supported by a feature/extension.
- Security and safety: Apply global limits (size, nesting depth, field count) and content sanitization to mitigate abuse. Unknown fields are subject to the same authorization, PII filtering, and redaction rules as known fields.
- Observability: Emit structured warnings/metrics when unknown fields are encountered (with rate limiting) to aid operability without causing failures.
- Interop modes: Provide a configurable “strict mode” to reject unknown fields in environments requiring exact schemas (e.g., regulatory exports, reproducible builds).
- Documentation and contracts: Publicly document reserved namespaces and extension conventions to avoid collisions and enable vendor/tenant-specific additions.
- Compatibility: Backward/forward compatibility guarantees include pass-through of unknown fields across read-modify-write flows unless explicitly dropped by policy.

This decision balances robustness and extensibility while maintaining strictness where it matters (known fields and invariants).

We designate Microsoft Azure as our primary cloud provider for all new and migrated workloads requiring IaaS, PaaS, or serverless capabilities.

Directives:
- Prefer PaaS/serverless (App Service, AKS only when required, Functions, Logic Apps, Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Storage) over IaaS VMs.
- Use Azure Active Directory (Entra ID) for identity, SSO, and RBAC; adopt managed identities for workload auth; secrets in Key Vault.
- Implement a secure landing zone with hub-spoke networking, Private Link/Endpoints, NSGs/ASGs, and Azure Firewall as needed.
- Enforce Infrastructure as Code using Terraform or Bicep with CI/CD via Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions.
- Enable organization-wide Guardrails: Azure Policy, Blueprints/Definitions, Defender for Cloud, Microsoft Sentinel (as needed).
- Adopt cost management practices: resource tagging standards, budgets/alerts, reservations/savings plans where appropriate; central billing via MCA/EA.
- Observability: Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, Application Insights; centralized dashboards and alerts.
- Reliability: deploy across availability zones; design for region-pair failover and backup/restore objectives aligned to business RPO/RTO; use Azure Backup/ASR where applicable.
- Data residency and compliance: select regions to meet regulatory requirements; enforce encryption in transit and at rest with customer-managed keys where required.

Scope and exceptions:
- Applies to all product teams and shared platforms. Pure SaaS selections are out of scope but should integrate with Azure identity and logging where feasible.
- Any use of non-Azure cloud providers or deviation from these directives requires an explicit ADR with risk, cost, and compliance justification.

Review:
- Reassess this decision in 12 months or upon major strategic/market shifts.

We will decommission Postgres across all environments and remove it as a runtime dependency, consolidating persistence on the JSON/document store (DynamoDB/local JSON) defined in ADR-3. Concretely, we will:

- Disable new writes to Postgres, switch remaining read/write code paths to the document store via our persistence adapter, and remove ORM/repository/migration layers tied to Postgres.
- Decommission the managed Heroku Postgres instances after a read-only stabilization window and final verification.
- Produce and archive final logical dumps (schema + data) and per-environment snapshots with documented restore procedures; retain backups for at least 90 days.
- Preserve a thin persistence abstraction so that reintroducing an RDBMS in the future remains feasible without broad API changes.
- Gate the cutover behind feature flags and environment configuration to allow staged rollout, with a time-boxed rollback path (pointing reads to snapshots and restoring Postgres if required) until the decommission date.
- Update runbooks, CI/CD, and local dev to remove Postgres setup, replacing with local document-store emulation.
- Remove related operational tooling (migrations, seeds, monitoring alerts) and cost centers.

This decision is reversible: if future needs (e.g., ad-hoc relational analytics or strong transactional guarantees) arise, we will evaluate reintroducing an RDBMS behind the existing persistence adapter.

OpenAPI 3.1 will be the canonical, published contract for the Generator API, and OData v4 will be the query protocol and entity model. The API will implement OData-conformant REST endpoints (entity sets, navigation properties, $filter, $select, $expand, $orderby, $top, $skip, $count, delta where applicable), while the exposed contract will be an OpenAPI document generated from the OData EDM at build time and enriched with OData-specific extensions.

We will:
- Implement OData v4 endpoints and $metadata (EDMX) as the source of truth for the data model.
- Generate and publish an OpenAPI 3.1 spec from the EDM, augmenting with x-odata-* extensions and examples to capture OData semantics that OpenAPI cannot fully express.
- Document OAuth2/OpenID Connect security schemes, scopes, error responses (OData error or RFC7807), pagination conventions (server-driven paging, $skiptoken), and rate limits in OpenAPI.
- Enforce guardrails: max page size, $expand depth limits, whitelisted sortable/filterable fields, and request validation aligned with EDM types.
- Provide versioning via URI (/v{n}) and EDM namespace; reflect deprecations in OpenAPI with sunset metadata.
- Support discoverability via service document and $metadata, and publish the OpenAPI spec to the API portal/registry for client generation.
- Generate SDKs from OpenAPI for general consumers; recommend OData-capable clients for advanced query features.
- Use platform-native tooling for generation (e.g., ASP.NET Core OData + Swashbuckle/NSwag or equivalent stack) with CI pipelines to fail builds on drift between EDM and OpenAPI.

This approach gives us rich, standardized querying (OData) while ensuring broad tooling compatibility and governance (OpenAPI), with a single automated source of truth and consistent client generation.

## Decision

Adopt Azure Table Storage as the primary persistence mechanism for operational, key–value style data requiring high availability, low cost, and elastic scale without complex relational queries.

- Data model
  - One table per aggregate/root entity; avoid cross-aggregate joins.
  - PartitionKey chosen to optimize hottest access pattern (e.g., tenantId or entityId), with RowKey as unique, sortable identifier (e.g., ULID/KSUID/timestamp-based) to support efficient range queries.
  - Use additional “index tables” (inverted indexes) for alternate query patterns; denormalize where necessary.
  - Store large/binary payloads in Azure Blob Storage; persist blob URL and metadata in Table entities to keep entities under 1 MB.

- Access patterns and API
  - Use Azure.Data.Tables SDK (or equivalent) with Upsert/InsertOrMerge for idempotent writes.
  - Prefer point queries (PartitionKey + RowKey) and partition-scoped range scans; avoid cross-partition scans.
  - Implement optimistic concurrency with ETags and conditional updates (If-Match).
  - Enable exponential backoff retries for transient failures; ensure operations are idempotent.

- Security and compliance
  - Access via managed identity with RBAC; issue SAS tokens for scoped, time-limited access where needed.
  - Enforce TLS 1.2+ in transit; rely on Azure Storage encryption at rest (Microsoft-managed keys by default; support CMK if required).

- Resilience and lifecycle
  - Choose redundancy per workload (ZRS for zone resilience; GRS/GZRS for geo-DR).
  - Implement periodic export/snapshots to Blob Storage for backup/long-term retention.
  - Add TTL/expiration property and scheduled purge jobs for data lifecycle management.

- Observability
  - Capture request metrics (latency, throttling, retries) and structured audit logs for mutations.

We will implement continuous deployment for all platform Cloud Foundry (CF) applications using per-application Concourse pipelines sourced from each repository’s main branch and CF manifest.

- Pipelines:
  - On merge to main: build, run tests, and deploy automatically to the app’s dev/staging CF org/space.
  - Production promotion requires a signed git tag and a manual approval step; promotion reuses the same artifact/revision.
  - Pipelines and deployment configuration (manifests, vars) are stored in-repo; a shared pipeline template is used for consistency.

- Deployments:
  - Use blue/green deployments (cf blue-green-deploy) to achieve zero-downtime updates.
  - Run smoke tests against the green app before route switch; abort and roll back if checks fail.
  - Retain the previous color for rapid rollback by re-mapping routes; keep last N droplets for recovery.

- Credentials and config:
  - No CF credentials in repos; use Concourse-managed secrets (CredHub/SSM) and per-environment var files.
  - CF org/space, routes, and services are declared via manifest and vars; feature flags/config toggles manage risky changes.

- Quality and safeguards:
  - Pre-deploy unit/integration tests and post-deploy smoke checks are mandatory; health checks are enforced via CF.
  - Observability hooks (logs/metrics/alerts) are validated post-deploy.
  - Only verified (signed) commits/tags are eligible for production deployment.

This standardizes and automates delivery across environments, improves visibility, enables safe rollbacks, and reduces drift by making the repository the single source of truth for CF application deployments.

We will implement a custom save handler in service-front as the single entry point for all client-side persistence operations, replacing ad-hoc or library-default save mechanisms. The handler will:
- Normalize and map UI state to API contracts, including versioning, schema-aware validation, and serialization (e.g., attachments).
- Support optimistic concurrency (ETag/version), idempotency keys, and deterministic retry with backoff; surface conflict-resolution hooks to the UI.
- Provide autosave and manual save flows with debouncing, batching of small mutations, and partial/draft saves.
- Queue operations for offline/poor connectivity with resume and cancellation; ensure ordering guarantees where required.
- Orchestrate multi-step saves (e.g., file upload + metadata) with transactional semantics where possible, and compensations where not.
- Emit structured telemetry (success/failure, latency, payload size, retry counts) and standardize error mapping for consistent UX.
- Enforce feature flags and progressive rollout; support per-form policy overrides (e.g., bypass autosave, require confirmation).
- Offer extension points (pre/post hooks, transformers) for product-specific needs without duplicating core logic.
- Maintain backward compatibility: keep legacy save paths behind a kill switch, migrate screens incrementally, and provide a compatibility adapter for legacy payloads.

Definition of Done: all forms route saves through the handler, conflict handling and retries are verified end-to-end, telemetry dashboards exist, and legacy paths are removable behind feature flags.

We will centralize URL creation in a dedicated, injectable URLBuilder/LinkGenerator service and require all application tiers (controllers, views/templates, background jobs, mailers, workers) to use it instead of ad‑hoc string concatenation or framework helpers directly.

The URLBuilder will:
- Provide typed methods for route names and canonical builders for dynamic paths.
- Enforce canonicalization, encoding, locale/tenant handling, and optional signing.
- Emit structured logs and metrics for every build: route name, base path, redacted params, locale/tenant, build outcome, latency, and correlation/request IDs.
- Integrate with tracing (spans) and our logging facade; PII will be redacted by default.
- Be deterministic and side‑effect‑free (pure function) with adapters for framework-specific helpers; no I/O in core.
- Support configuration of base URLs per environment and product area; feature flags will allow progressive rollout and verbose logging during migration.
- Cache compiled templates for static and high‑volume routes to minimize overhead.

We will deprecate direct URL composition and framework helper usage outside the builder, add linting/code-mods to enforce usage, and provide a thin compatibility wrapper to maintain backward compatibility during migration. Comprehensive unit and contract tests (including golden cases) will be added to validate logging payloads, redaction, encoding, and signature correctness.

Institutionalize continuous domain knowledge crunching as a first-class activity across the product lifecycle.

- Adopt Event Storming (big-picture and process-level) as the primary technique, complemented by domain expert interviews, Example Mapping, and lightweight modeling sessions.
- Maintain a living Ubiquitous Language glossary, domain narratives (user journeys and key scenarios), context maps (bounded contexts with relationships), and core domain model sketches. Store artifacts in the repo (docs/domain/) with versioning and link them to ADRs, epics, and APIs.
- Establish cadence and triggers: inception of a product/epic, before major architectural refactors, when metrics indicate friction (high defect rate, cycle time spikes), after significant regulatory/business changes, and at least quarterly for alignment.
- Define roles: trained facilitator, domain experts (business SMEs), product manager, tech lead, engineers from each affected team, QA, and data representative. Participation is required for contexts they own.
- Make synchronization part of Definition of Ready: stories that change domain behavior must reference updated glossary, context map, and impacted invariants; otherwise they cannot start.
- Treat bounded context boundaries as architectural assets: teams own their contexts, APIs, and contracts; changes go through collaborative modeling and contract testing before implementation.
- Use standard collaboration tools (e.g., Miro/Mural templates, recorded sessions, and issue templates) to ensure repeatability.
- Measure effectiveness via reduced rework, fewer cross-context defects, clearer APIs, and improved lead time; adjust practices accordingly.

We will standardize on Calico (open source) as the Kubernetes CNI for all clusters. Calico provides high‑performance networking with optional eBPF dataplane, first‑class Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement (plus Calico policy extensions), mature IPAM, and broad support across self‑managed and managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE).

Implementation details:
- Install via Tigera Operator/Helm with Calico v3.26+.
- Use Calico IPAM with per‑node CIDRs; enable dual‑stack where clusters are IPv6-capable.
- Dataplane: prefer eBPF mode where supported (sufficient kernel and cloud constraints); otherwise use the standard Linux dataplane.
- Encapsulation: default to VXLAN for simplicity; enable BGP peering only for on‑prem clusters that need routed pod networks or integration with DC fabric.
- Policy: enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy and adopt Calico policy extensions for namespace/default‑deny, DNS egress, and host endpoint protection as needed.
- Encryption: enable WireGuard for node‑to‑node encryption on self‑managed clusters; defer to cloud provider features where managed CNIs conflict.
- Observability: enable Calico Felix metrics and flow logs for network troubleshooting and SLOs.
- Compatibility: integrate with service meshes and Ingress controllers without custom CNI hooks.

This choice balances performance, security, and portability, while minimizing cloud lock‑in and providing a consistent network and policy model across environments.

## Decision

- Upgrade to the new font version and adopt the variable-font build as the default for web and app surfaces, using static-weight fallbacks only where platform support or performance constraints require it.
- Self-host the font via our asset pipeline/CDN with cache-busted, immutable URLs; manage the font as a versioned npm package and lock exact versions to ensure reproducible builds.
- Enable progressive rollout behind a feature flag with canary/prod stages; collect render, CLS, and page weight metrics. Maintain the previous font version in parallel for one stable release window to allow fast rollback.
- Use subsetting and unicode-range for language coverage; ship a minimal Latin subset as critical (preloaded) and lazy-load extended subsets on demand. For apps, bundle only required subsets per locale.
- Set font-display: swap to avoid FOIT; define robust system fallback stacks and ensure consistent metrics via font-metric overrides to minimize layout shift.
- Standardize typography tokens (font family, weights, sizes, line-heights) to the new version; remove deprecated tokens after the deprecation window. Update snapshot tests and visual baselines.
- Align icon fonts/SVGs with the new baseline and adjust hinting/antialiasing if necessary for platform parity.
- Document migration guidance for product teams (token changes, weight mapping, accessibility checks) and require contrast verification. Block adoption in components failing accessibility or performance thresholds.

Adopt a colocated testing strategy with clear layers:
- Unit and component tests live alongside the source they verify (e.g., Foo.ts with Foo.test.ts) to tighten feedback loops and encourage maintenance. Place story-based visual/regression tests next to components as well.
- Shared test utilities, factories, and custom matchers reside in a dedicated test-support package or /test-support directory to avoid duplication across modules.
- Integration tests live within each service/module repository, exercising module boundaries and data access with ephemeral resources (e.g., in-memory or containerized dependencies).
- Consumer-driven contract tests are kept with the consumer; providers verify published pacts in their own repos. Pact artifacts are stored in a shared broker.
- End-to-end tests exist as a separate package within the same monorepo (or a dedicated repo if not in a monorepo) under /e2e to allow independent execution, environment orchestration, and parallelization. They target ephemeral preview environments first, then staging.
- Accessibility and security scanning configurations and scripts are versioned under /ci (or /.github, /pipelines) and executed in CI; findings gate merges and releases.
- Test data, fixtures, and snapshots are versioned under a testdata/ directory per module; sensitive data is never embedded—use generators or sanitized records.
- Test-only endpoints, feature switches, and debug hooks are guarded behind environment flags and never enabled in production builds; ensure test code is excluded by tree-shaking or build-time guards.
- Document directory conventions and naming in CONTRIBUTING.md; enforce via linters and CI to keep structure consistent.

## Decision

Update user- and business-facing summaries and lightweight analytics using locally available data at purchase time, avoiding synchronous calls to external analytics systems.

- Persist the purchase and update denormalized summary tables/counters (e.g., per-customer spend, per-product sales, inventory reserved/remaining, daily revenue) in the same database using atomic UPSERT/merge operations within the purchase transaction or via a transactional outbox + immediate consumer to preserve ordering.
- Emit an idempotent PurchaseRecorded domain event (via outbox/queue) for downstream heavy analytics and the data warehouse; do not block the purchase flow on external processing.
- Make updates idempotent and keyed by purchase_id to safely handle retries and concurrency. Use optimistic locking or versioned aggregates where needed.
- Support compensating changes (refund, cancellation, adjustment) by emitting corresponding events and applying reversible updates to local aggregates.
- Favor eventual consistency for non-critical dashboards; for read-your-write UX (e.g., order confirmation totals), read from transactional data, not aggregates.
- Provide background reconciliation jobs to backfill and repair aggregates from the source of truth, and to reprocess events on demand.
- Maintain schema/versioning for summary tables to enable safe evolution; guard rollout with feature flags and metrics.
- Keep periods immutable once closed (e.g., daily totals) by writing adjustments into the next open period, while preserving auditability.

This approach delivers fast, reliable, and consistent summaries in the request path, while delegating complex analytics to asynchronous pipelines.

## Decision

Define clear logic boundaries so the CDH ETL produces high-quality, reusable datasets while avoiding application-specific concerns:

- ETL responsibilities:
  - Ingest raw sources and land unchanged copies (bronze).
  - Standardize to a canonical model (silver) with schema harmonization, type normalization, code-system mapping, timezone normalization, and units conversion.
  - Apply data quality rules (validation, cleansing, deduplication, survivorship), reference-data enrichment (lookups), and non-domain-specific enrichments (e.g., geocoding).
  - Generate deterministic/surrogate identifiers, handle change data capture and SCD Type 2 history, and maintain lineage, audit, and data contracts.
  - Produce curated, stable, backward-compatible “gold” datasets at entity level (e.g., person, provider, encounter) suitable for broad reuse.
  - Ensure idempotent, re-entrant, and incremental outputs with schema versioning and publish metadata/catalog entries.

- Non-ETL (consumer) responsibilities:
  - Application-specific aggregations, business rules, KPI calculations, ranking/scoring, feature engineering, and presentation shaping (API/view-specific denormalization).
  - Serving-layer concerns such as indexing, caching, query tuning, and authorization policies over data products.

- Versioning and change management:
  - Backward-compatible changes are additive; breaking changes produce versioned datasets/contracts.
  - ETL publishes data quality metrics and release notes; consumers opt into new versions.

This boundary ensures reusable, trustworthy data products from the CDH while preserving flexibility for downstream use cases.

## Decision

- The lifetime of an aggregate is governed exclusively by its Aggregate Root. All lifecycle operations (create, mutate, suspend, close/archive, delete) are executed via the root to preserve invariants.
- Child entities and value objects cannot outlive their aggregate. They may be added/removed only through root-controlled commands; external modules cannot directly mutate children.
- Valid lifecycle states are: Draft (optional), Active, Suspended (optional), Closed/Archived, and Deleted. Transitions are strictly defined and validated by the root; only idempotent transitions are allowed.
- Closing/archiving an aggregate requires all child entities to be in a terminal state as defined by the aggregate’s invariants. The root enforces “no open children on close.” Re-opening after Close is prohibited by default; if business mandates reopen, it must be explicitly modeled with guardrails and event traceability.
- Deletion is soft by default (Archived/Deleted flag) to preserve auditability and references; hard delete is allowed only via privileged maintenance paths and only when referential integrity is guaranteed (e.g., no external references, retention periods elapsed).
- Lifecycle transitions emit domain events (e.g., AggregateCreated, AggregateClosed, AggregateDeleted) to enable projections, integrations, and policy enforcement. Events carry correlation and causation IDs for traceability.
- Concurrency is managed with optimistic concurrency control at the aggregate boundary; lifecycle transitions must include version checks to prevent lost updates.
- Cross-aggregate references are weak (by ID) and must not block lifecycle transitions of the owner aggregate; policies for coordination across aggregates are implemented via sagas/process managers, not by expanding aggregate boundaries.
- Time-based lifecycle policies (TTL, retention, archival schedules) are declaratively configured and enforced via scheduled jobs that invoke root commands, ensuring invariant checks still apply.
- Factories (or named constructors) create aggregates in a valid initial state with immutable identity. Migrations between lifecycle states must be backwards compatible in event-sourced streams and snapshot models.
- Observability: lifecycle transitions are logged and metrified; PII considerations apply when archiving or deleting payloads (redaction/anonymization where required).

## Decision

Adopt a queue-based background job architecture with stateless worker services, orchestrated by Kubernetes. A managed message broker (e.g., AWS SQS with FIFO where ordering is required; alternatively Kafka for high-throughput streams, or Redis for low-latency tasks) will buffer tasks. Application services enqueue jobs via a Job API using the Outbox pattern for reliable handoff. Workers consume jobs with at-least-once delivery, enforcing idempotency via deterministic keys and write guards.

Implement:
- Priority queues and rate-limiting per job type/tenant.
- Concurrency controls and resource quotas per worker pool.
- Retries with exponential backoff, jitter, and circuit breaking; dead-letter queues for exhausted jobs.
- Job lifecycle management: schedule (cron), enqueue, pause/resume, cancel, timeout.
- Payload schema versioning and backward compatibility.
- Observability: distributed tracing, structured logs, metrics (latency, throughput, retries, DLQ), and alerting SLIs/SLOs.
- Security: signed/encrypted payloads where needed; least-privilege IAM for producers/consumers.

Scheduling uses Kubernetes CronJobs for periodic tasks, and a scheduler service for complex calendars. Workers are containerized and autoscaled based on queue depth and lag. Operational tooling includes a web console for inspection/retries and DLQ reprocessing workflows. This design isolates background workloads, ensures reliability and scalability, and minimizes coupling with synchronous request paths.

## Decision

Adopt ECS Fargate as the default host type for running containerized workloads in our ECS clusters. All stateless services, APIs, scheduled tasks, and event-driven workers will be deployed on Fargate to eliminate EC2 cluster management, improve security isolation, and simplify scaling and patching. We will use ECS capacity providers with Fargate (and Fargate Spot where appropriate for fault-tolerant, non-latency-critical workloads) to control cost and resilience.

Workloads requiring host-level access (e.g., privileged containers, custom AMIs, special kernel modules), daemon processes tied to nodes, or highly stateful services with atypical storage needs that exceed Fargate capabilities will remain on ECS with EC2 launch type as exceptions. Such exceptions must be explicitly justified and documented.

Networking will follow awsvpc mode with least-privilege security groups and IAM task roles. Observability will use CloudWatch Logs/metrics, ECS Exec for debugging, and tracing where required. Tasks will be provisioned with right-sized CPU/memory and ephemeral storage; EFS will be used for shared persistent storage when needed and supported. We will standardize on current supported Fargate platform versions and periodically upgrade.

Cost guardrails (Fargate Spot, autoscaling policies, and rightsizing) will be applied, and migration plans will move eligible existing ECS EC2 services to Fargate incrementally.

Use a single, flat ADR catalog under docs/adr with sequential, zero‑padded filenames: docs/adr/NNNN-title-with-dashes.md (e.g., 0001-adopt-adr-format.md). Maintain one ADR per file; never rename or renumber once merged. New decisions always increment the next number.

Include a standard template at docs/adr/_template.md and generate docs/adr/index.md (table of contents) via tooling (e.g., adr-tools/adr-log) as part of CI. Store any images or diagrams in docs/adr/assets, referenced with relative paths.
