Each ADR must contain: Title, Status (Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Deprecated, Superseded), Date (UTC), Context, Decision, Consequences, and Links (Supersedes/Superseded by). Use YAML front matter for metadata (tags, component, authors) to enable filtering/search. Prefer tags over subfolders to keep the sequence global and discoverable.

Lifecycle rules:
- Proposed ADRs may be iterated in draft PRs; once Accepted, content is immutable except for typos and link fixes.
- Changes to an Accepted decision require a new ADR that explicitly supersedes prior ones; do not delete old ADRs.
- IDs are never reused; tombstones remain for auditability.

Process:
- One ADR per pull request; reviewers from affected components must approve.
- Reference relevant ADR(s) from code and PR descriptions when implementing.
- For large monorepos, keep a single global sequence; encode scope via tags (e.g., “platform”, “frontend”) and in the title if useful.

Publishing:
- Ensure ADRs render via GitHub Pages from docs/.
- Enforce structure and linting with a CI check (filename pattern, required sections, status vocabulary).

- The Wikibase extension will maintain a single canonical RELEASE-NOTES.md in the repository, using “Keep a Changelog” style with an “Unreleased” section and categories: Breaking Changes, Deprecations/Removals, Features/Improvements, Bug Fixes, Performance, Security, Docs, and Internal.
- Any user-visible or operator-impacting change must include a release note fragment at merge time under changelog/ (YAML/Markdown snippets). CI will fail merges that modify code without providing either a note fragment or an explicit “no-release-notes” label/marker.
- The release pipeline will aggregate fragments into RELEASE-NOTES.md, roll the Unreleased section into a versioned section at tag time, and start a fresh Unreleased section. The generated notes are committed back to the release branch and included in tarballs and Docker images.
- The pipeline will publish the versioned notes to mediawiki.org (Extension:Wikibase/Release notes) and link them from the GitHub/Gerrit release and releases.wikimedia.org directory index.
- Format conventions: concise imperative entries, link to Phabricator tasks and commits, clearly mark breaking changes and required upgrade actions, and include MediaWiki/Wikibase version compatibility where relevant.
- Emergency/security releases follow the same process with redactions as required until disclosure.

## Decision

Adopt a split-pipeline model: a single, centralized Build pipeline and separate, environment-scoped Deployment pipelines.

- Build pipeline
  - Triggered on merge to main (and tags), runs tests, security scans, and builds immutable artifacts (e.g., OCI images, packages).
  - Produces signed artifacts with SBOM and provenance (e.g., SLSA attestations) and pushes them to an artifact registry.
  - Publishes a version manifest (artifact digest, commit SHA, build metadata) used by deployments.
  - Has access only to source and registry; no deployment credentials.

- Deployment pipelines
  - One per environment (dev, staging, prod, etc.), consuming only published artifacts by digest (“build once, deploy many”).
  - Triggered via promotion (pipeline job, tag, or merge to env-config repo), with required approvals and change controls per environment.
  - Apply environment-specific config via GitOps or infra-as-code (separate config repo), leveraging sealed secrets/variables.
  - Support progressive delivery (canary/blue-green), health checks, and automated rollback to the last known-good artifact.
  - Possess only environment-scoped credentials; no source repo write access.

Implement environment protections, artifact retention, and audit trails in CI/CD (e.g., GitLab Environments). This separation enforces least privilege, improves reproducibility and traceability, decouples release cadence from build frequency, and enables safe, controlled promotions across environments.

Track and store metrics keyed by canonical basepath (URL path) rather than by Content Item (content_id/edition). The basepath will be the primary key for aggregation and reporting, providing continuity across editions, republishes, and content_id changes.

Key points:
- Canonicalisation: normalise URLs by lowercasing host-insensitive parts, stripping fragments and tracking query params, removing trailing slashes (except root), and resolving locale-specific paths per GOV.UK conventions. Maintain a whitelist of params to keep for finder performance where required.
- Redirects: resolve and attribute metrics to the final destination basepath; record redirect events separately to allow analysis of redirect performance without fragmenting core metrics.
- Historical mapping: maintain a mapping table of {content_id, locale} -> basepath with validity intervals to support drill-down from items to metrics and to handle past basepath changes.
- Dimensions: retain content_id, document_type, organisation, locale, and format as secondary dimensions to enable segmentation; basepath remains the aggregation key.
- Backfill and migration: reprocess historical analytics to basepath, deduplicate events across editions, and validate parity against item-based reports for a defined overlap period.
- Edge cases: for content without a stable basepath (e.g., API endpoints, dynamic searches), define synthetic basepaths or specific rules; for attachments/assets, track under the parent page’s basepath where applicable.
- APIs and schemas: update ingestion, warehouse schemas, and downstream queries/dashboards to use basepath_pk; expose compatibility views that map items to basepath for consumers during transition.

This decision improves metric stability, reduces duplication across editions, and aligns reporting with user-facing URLs.

We will treat README.md in the repository root as the canonical, always-up-to-date entry point for project documentation.

- The README will include: project overview, supported versions/status badges, installation/quickstart, minimal usage example, contribution/dev setup link, troubleshooting link, and a table of contents to deeper docs.
- The README will be the single source of truth for high-level information; detailed/living docs (e.g., API reference, architecture deep-dives, tutorials, changelog) will live in /docs and/or the documentation site, linked prominently from the README.
- We will avoid duplicating content between README and /docs. The README will summarize and link; detailed content resides in dedicated docs.
- Any user-facing or breaking change PR must update the README if it affects overview, setup, or quickstart. A PR checklist item will enforce this.
- Keep the README lightweight and fast to render on GitHub, using Markdown only and minimal images; ensure it is readable on both GitHub and package registries (e.g., PyPI/NPM).
- Provide language and platform badges and links to examples/templates.
- The README will include a “What’s next” section that points to versioned docs, ensuring newcomers can orient quickly while experts can dive deeper.

## Decision

We will support multiple sites as first-class, independently deployable applications, managed in a single monorepo to maximize code reuse and operational consistency. Each site will have its own domain/subdomain, environment configuration, CI/CD pipeline, and release cadence, while sharing a common design system, component library, utilities, and backend services where appropriate.

Key decisions:
- Repository and build: Use a monorepo with workspace tooling (e.g., Nx/Turborepo/Yarn Workspaces) to share code and cache builds. Each site is a separate app package; shared libraries are versioned internally.
- Deployment isolation: Each site deploys independently to its own infrastructure targets (e.g., separate buckets, edge configs, containers), enabling selective rollbacks and minimizing blast radius.
- DNS and routing: Dedicated domains/subdomains per site; no runtime path-based multi-tenancy. Edge/CDN configurations are per site.
- Configuration: Strict environment isolation with per-site .env and secrets. No cross-site implicit coupling; shared configuration goes through versioned libraries.
- Theming and branding: Shared design system with theme tokens; sites can override themes without forking components.
- Backend integration: Sites consume shared APIs/services behind stable contracts. Breaking changes are introduced via versioned endpoints or feature flags.
- Observability: Per-site monitoring, logging, and error tracking with shared standards. Cost and traffic are measured per site.
- Content management: Content sourced from a shared CMS space with site-specific content types/entries or separate spaces if needed for isolation.
- Access control: Least-privilege per site (deploy keys, secrets, admin roles), with audited shared ownership of libraries.
- Release management: Conventional commits and automated changelogs per package; canary releases available per site.

This approach balances independence (deploy, scale, compliance) with efficiency (shared code, tooling), reducing duplication while containing risk across multiple sites.

## Decision

We will standardize on AWS SAM CLI for local development, execution, and debugging of our Lambda-based services. All serverless resources (Lambdas, API Gateway, EventBridge, and DynamoDB tables used for local testing) will be defined in a SAM template (template.yaml), built with sam build, and run via sam local start-api (for HTTP APIs) and sam local invoke (for event-driven functions). Developers will use sam sync --watch for rapid inner-loop iteration and sam logs for function log streaming. Docker is required to provide Lambda-compatible runtimes locally.

Environment variables and test events will be managed via SAM parameter overrides, env.json files, and event payload fixtures committed to the repo. Where feasible, we will use SAM’s native emulation; for AWS service integrations that cannot be emulated sufficiently, we will target a sandbox AWS account with least-privilege IAM and isolated resources provisioned by SAM stacks. This decision aligns local behavior closely with production CloudFormation, reduces drift, simplifies onboarding, and provides a consistent, scriptable developer workflow across platforms and languages.

We will support wrapperless usage as a first-class path by distributing a single, cross-platform executable per target OS and a language-native entry point, eliminating the need for shell/batch wrapper scripts. Concretely:
- Provide platform-specific, self-contained artifacts (e.g., statically bundled binary or fat/uber package with entry point) that can be placed on PATH and invoked directly.
- Publish a native entry point via the ecosystem’s standard mechanism (e.g., console_scripts for Python, executable JAR or native-image for JVM, npx/CLI bin for Node), ensuring consistent invocation across environments.
- Offer an official container image for hermetic execution without host dependencies.
- Encode runtime defaults via config files and environment variables, not wrapper logic; include discovery order and overrides in documentation.
- Introduce versioned install channels (package managers where feasible) and checksum-signed releases; avoid per-OS wrapper glue.
- Deprecate existing wrapper scripts with a migration guide and a grace period, retaining only thin shims that delegate to the new executable where removal is not yet possible.

This approach reduces operational fragility, simplifies support across shells/OSes, and provides a predictable, documented invocation surface.

We will standardize on Terraform to provision and manage infrastructure across all AWS accounts using account-scoped root modules and environment-specific directories (no workspaces for env separation). Each account will maintain its own remote state in an account-local S3 bucket with DynamoDB for state locking, with strict separation of state per account, region, and environment.

Authentication and authorization will rely on short-lived credentials via AWS SSO and IAM role assumption (assume_role) for local development, and GitHub Actions/OIDC (or equivalent CI OIDC) to assume per-account deploy roles in CI/CD. Production applies will require manual approval.

Providers will be configured per account/region via explicit provider blocks and aliases where needed; cross-account access will only occur through clearly defined data sources and assume_role boundaries. Reusable infrastructure will be encapsulated as versioned Terraform modules in a shared registry, with uniform tagging, naming, and guardrails enforced via tflint, checkov, and policy-as-code.

Plans and applies will be executed from the corresponding account/env directories; only plans are allowed on feature branches, with applies restricted to protected branches. Secrets will be handled via SSM Parameter Store/Secrets Manager references, never in state or code. This approach ensures clear account boundaries, auditable changes, and scalable multi-account governance.

We will standardize on a hub-and-spoke VPC design with segregated Public and Private subnets across a minimum of two Availability Zones (preferably three) to achieve high availability and least-privilege network exposure.

- Public subnets: Internet-facing Application/Network Load Balancers, NAT Gateways (one per AZ), and no compute other than an exceptional, time-bounded bastion if absolutely required.
- Private subnets: All application services, ECS/EKS/EC2 workloads, data tiers, and internal ALBs. No public IPs assigned. Egress to the internet only via the AZ-local NAT Gateway; ingress only through ALBs/NLBs and VPC endpoints.

Key configurations:
- Per-AZ route tables ensuring zonal NAT egress (no cross-AZ NAT).
- VPC Interface Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for control-plane and API services; Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to keep traffic on the AWS backbone and reduce NAT costs.
- Prefer AWS Systems Manager Session Manager over bastion hosts for administrative access; if a bastion is used, restrict by IP, time-box, and require MFA.
- Enable VPC DNS hostnames/support and Route 53 Private Hosted Zones for service discovery.
- Security Groups as primary controls; Network ACLs left mostly default/deny-hardened where appropriate.
- Enable VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch Logs with log retention and guardrail alerts.
- Dual-stack readiness: IPv4 primary; optionally enable IPv6 with an Egress-Only Internet Gateway for private subnets.
- Deterministic IP plan: VPC /16, per-AZ /20, per-tier /24 (or larger as needed), with reserved ranges for future growth.
- Standard tagging and IAM boundaries for network resources; infrastructure codified and versioned.

We will introduce a dedicated Common Records layer as a standalone, versioned module that contains immutable, logic-free data contracts shared across components and services. This layer will host canonical record types such as IDs, value objects, enums, error codes, request/response DTOs, and event schemas. It will be the single source of truth for cross-cutting data shapes and serialization metadata.

The Common Records module will:
- Expose records as immutable types (e.g., language “record”/data classes) with validation constrained to invariants intrinsic to the data shape.
- Contain no business logic, persistence, or integration code; only types, simple mappers, and serialization configuration.
- Be published as a read-only dependency via our artifact repository and versioned with strict SemVer; changes favor backward-compatible, additive evolution.
- Provide schema definitions (e.g., OpenAPI/JSON Schema/Avro/Protobuf as applicable) and generate code where feasible to reduce drift.
- Enforce dependency direction: domains and services may depend on Common Records, but the Common Records layer must not depend on any domain/service.
- Include compatibility tests (wire/contract tests) to guard against breaking changes and ensure stable interop.

This decision standardizes shared data models, reduces duplication and drift, and enables consistent, governed contracts across the system.

## Decision

We will standardize prop conventions across Primer React Components to ensure consistency, accessibility, and safe extensibility:

- Naming
  - Use variant, size, and align for stylistic variants; use tone for semantic intent.
  - Boolean flags are prefixed with is/has (e.g., isLoading, hasShadow).
  - Use leadingVisual/trailingVisual for decorative slots; icon for a single icon prop.
  - Use id, className, style for DOM identity; prefer sx for system styling overrides.

- Polymorphism and refs
  - Components may be polymorphic via an as prop with proper type constraints; refs are forwarded and typed to the rendered element.
  - Interactive components default to button semantics unless as overrides to a semantic equivalent; enforce required props (e.g., href for as="a").

- Controlled vs uncontrolled
  - Support value/onChange and defaultValue (and checked/defaultChecked) pairs where applicable; do not mix both in runtime.
  - Fire onChange with synthetic event or well-typed payload consistently.

- Accessibility
  - Accept role, aria-*, and data-* pass-through; expose key a11y props explicitly (aria-label, aria-describedby, aria-expanded, disabled).
  - Do not render invalid ARIA for given roles; warn in development when misused.

- Prop pass-through and safety
  - Allow a curated set of native props to pass to the DOM; never blindly spread unvalidated rest onto DOM nodes (except aria-* and data-*).
  - Omit undefined props from DOM; map props to attributes explicitly.

- Types and defaults
  - Prefer discriminated unions/enums over free-form strings; document defaults in props and Storybook.
  - Deprecate props via codemods and DEV-only warnings; maintain one minor with shims before removal.

- Events
  - Use on<Event> naming; no handle* props. Events are stable and do not re-fire on identical values.

- Backwards compatibility
  - Avoid breaking prop renames; add aliases during deprecation windows.

We will build the desktop application using Electron to deliver a single cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux) client that wraps our existing web UI and shared TypeScript code. We will adopt Electron (v29+ or current LTS) with a security-first configuration: nodeIntegration disabled, contextIsolation enabled, sandboxed renderers, strict Content Security Policy, and a minimal, audited preload layer exposing only whitelisted APIs via contextBridge. All main–renderer communication will use typed IPC channels with runtime validation.

We will package and distribute using Electron Builder, producing signed installers (MSIX for Windows, notarized DMG/PKG for macOS, AppImage/Deb/RPM for Linux) and enable differential auto-updates via electron-updater, backed by our release pipeline. We will implement single-instance locking, deep-link handling, native menus/tray, and OS-level integrations as needed (protocol handlers, notifications, file associations). Crash reporting and telemetry will be wired via a privacy-compliant provider with opt-in where required.

We will encapsulate any native functionality behind well-defined modules to keep platform-specific code isolated and testable, preferring pure web APIs or Rust/Node-API bindings only when necessary. GPU acceleration will be configurable to mitigate driver issues. We will enforce code signing, integrity checks for downloaded updates, and supply chain controls (frozen lockfiles, dependency scanning).

Should Electron’s footprint or native performance constraints become unacceptable for specific features, we will reassess those features for alternative implementations (e.g., native helpers) while retaining Electron as the primary shell.

- Standardize on TypeScript across frontend and backend for type safety and shared models.
- Frontend: React with Next.js for SSR/SSG/ISR, routing, and performance; styling with Tailwind CSS and component library based on our design system; state via React Query and minimal Redux only when necessary.
- Backend: Node.js LTS with NestJS for modular architecture, DI, validation, and testing ergonomics; lightweight Express services permitted for simple adapters.
- APIs: REST/JSON as default with OpenAPI 3 contracts and codegen; Webhooks for event notifications; consider GraphQL only for complex client aggregation use cases.
- Data: PostgreSQL as the primary relational datastore; Prisma as the TypeScript ORM; Redis for caching, ephemeral data, and rate limiting; S3-compatible object storage for files and media.
- Messaging and async: Use RabbitMQ for reliable work queues and pub/sub; scheduled jobs via NestJS schedule/Quartz-like library; idempotency enforced at handler level.
- AuthN/Z: OpenID Connect (OIDC) and OAuth2.1 with JWT access tokens; RBAC enforced via NestJS guards and policy layer; secrets managed via environment vault/KMS.
- Observability: OpenTelemetry for traces/metrics/logs; Prometheus + Grafana for metrics; structured JSON logging; Sentry for error monitoring.
- Security: OWASP ASVS-aligned controls, input validation (class-validator), output encoding, CSRF protection, dependency scanning, and container image scanning; HTTPS everywhere.
- Packaging & runtime: Docker containers; Kubernetes for deployment, autoscaling, and blue/green rollouts; Helm charts for manifests.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions with PR checks (lint, type-check, tests), SAST/DAST, SBOM generation, and automated deployments using GitOps.
- Testing: Jest (unit), Supertest (integration), Playwright (E2E); contract tests against OpenAPI; test data via factories.
- Tooling: pnpm for package management; ESLint + Prettier for code quality; commit hooks with lint-staged.
- Accessibility and i18n: WCAG 2.1 AA compliance; i18n support via industry-standard libraries in the UI.
- Performance: CDN fronting Next.js; server-side caching headers; Redis caching layer; database indices and query budgets.

We will standardize on RSpec request specs as the primary way to verify controller behavior and routing, and deprecate legacy controller specs. All new HTTP-facing behavior must be covered by request specs that exercise the full Rails stack (routing, middleware, filters), validating status codes, headers, redirects, response payloads, and observable side effects (DB changes, jobs enqueued, audits).

Implementation notes:
- Add request-spec helpers: authentication (Devise::Test::IntegrationHelpers or Warden), JSON parsing (json_response), header builders (auth, content-type, accept), and shared contexts for common scenarios (authorized/unauthorized, pagination).
- Prefer black‑box testing via public endpoints over stubbing controller internals; do not rely on assigns or render_template.
- For HTML flows, use follow_redirect! and verify final rendered content; for APIs, assert contract with parsed JSON and (where applicable) schema matchers.
- Use system specs for browser/UI interactions; keep domain logic in model/service specs with unit tests.
- Establish a migration path: convert controller specs opportunistically (touching code) and for high‑value endpoints first; block addition of new controller specs in CI.

This decision aligns tests with Rails/RSpec guidance, increases fidelity by running through the full request lifecycle, and produces more maintainable, behavior-focused tests.

We will compute grant-wise expenditure via an automated, idempotent ETL pipeline that aggregates transaction-level vouchers to grants using a centrally-governed Grant Master and a mapping table from chart-of-accounts/fund/function/scheme codes to grant_id. The pipeline will:

- Ingest daily incremental transactions with late-arrival handling (watermarks) and maintain a full audit trail.
- Apply deterministic grant attribution using effective-dated mappings; unresolved or conflicting mappings are quarantined for stewardship.
- Record reversals/adjustments and reclassifications using effective-dated entries; recompute affected aggregates via change data capture.
- Persist a normalized fact table (fact_expenditure) keyed by grant_id, txn_id, date, amount, and dimensions (department, scheme, function, fund, geography), plus a snapshot-aggregates mart (daily/MTD/QTD/YTD).
- Enforce data quality checks (sum-to-source reconciliation, duplicate detection, negative/zero validation, posting period bounds) and publish reconciliation metrics.
- Provide consistent outputs through a materialized view and an API endpoint parameterized by grant_id, date range, and dimensions; all results are versioned with dataset_run_id for reproducibility.
- Schedule daily runs with backfill capability; changes to mappings follow a governed workflow and trigger targeted re-aggregation.
- Document methodology, mapping lineage, and reconciliation results with each extract; where mappings are incomplete, mark amounts as “unattributed” until resolved (never silently drop).

This decision delivers reliable, auditable, and timely grant-wise expenditure suitable for reporting and downstream analysis.

## Decision

The seed template will remain unopinionated with respect to a specific state management framework.

- Default: Use the platform’s native primitives (e.g., component/local state) and a minimal, optional example of app-wide state using Context + reducer to demonstrate composition, testability, and separation of concerns.
- Extension points: Provide a clear “state/” module structure, an interface-first pattern (actions/selectors/effects), and guidance for async data (fetch/cache/invalidation) without coupling to any library.
- Optional add-ons: Offer official, opt-in integrations via template flags (or separate packages) for popular solutions (e.g., Redux Toolkit, Zustand, MobX, or RxJS), each with a pre-wired example, tests, and docs.
- Consistency: Define shared conventions (naming, file layout, action/effect patterns, error handling) that apply regardless of the chosen library to ease migration and contribute examples.
- Testing: Include framework-agnostic testing utilities and examples focused on state contracts (selectors, effects) rather than implementation details.
- Documentation: Provide a comparison guide (trade-offs, when to choose what), migration tips, and performance considerations.
- Governance: Reevaluate annually based on ecosystem maturity and internal adoption; promote an add-on to “recommended” if strong consensus emerges.

This approach minimizes lock-in and template bloat while enabling teams to adopt the most suitable solution with a smooth path and consistent patterns.

Use the median as the representative value when discretizing gamma values. Specifically:
- For each bin/window/segment, compute the 50th percentile (median) of the gamma samples/observations assigned to it, rather than the arithmetic mean.
- For even cardinalities, define the median as the average of the two central ordered values; ensure deterministic ordering and stable tie-breaking.
- For streaming or large datasets, employ a quantile estimator (e.g., t-digest or GK) with a target error ≤1% for the 0.5 quantile to keep memory and latency bounded.
- Update all downstream components (bucketization, lookups, thresholds, and reports) to read the median-based representative; keep mean-based summaries only for auxiliary reporting, not discretization.
- Make the representative statistic configurable, but set “median” as the default in all environments and documentation.
- Recompute existing artifacts (caches, model priors, reference tables) that depend on prior mean-based discretization and add tests validating robustness against outliers and skew.

We will defer committing to a solution until the context, forces, and success criteria are explicitly captured. Concretely:
- We will author a complete Context for ADR-000 that defines scope, drivers, constraints, assumptions, non-goals, stakeholders, and measurable success metrics.
- We will enumerate at least three viable options (including “do nothing”), with pros/cons, risks, costs, dependencies, and impact on UX, operations, security, and data.
- We will run timeboxed technical spikes where needed to validate feasibility and performance assumptions.
- We will establish decision criteria (e.g., user value, time-to-market, total cost of ownership, interoperability, maintainability) and score options transparently.
- We will assign an owner, reviewers, and an approval path; target a decision within one iteration, or explicitly reframe the problem if criteria cannot be met.
- We will document the chosen option, rationale, and roll-out plan (phased milestones, telemetry, rollback), and update this ADR’s Status accordingly (Proposed → Accepted/Rejected/Superseded).
- Until then, we will avoid irreversible work; any exploratory implementation must be behind feature flags and isolated from production data.

We will standardize on PHP 7.2 (64-bit) as the minimum and only supported runtime across all environments (local, CI, staging, production). All builds, images, and deployment targets must use a 64-bit PHP 7.2 distribution. Support for PHP <7.2 and any 32-bit builds is discontinued.

We will:
- Pin Composer platform to php=7.2.0 and fail builds when the runtime does not meet this requirement.
- Update base images and runtime AMIs/containers to 64-bit PHP 7.2 variants, and validate architecture in CI.
- Align all required extensions and their versions with PHP 7.2, removing compatibility shims for older versions.
- Adopt language features available in 7.2 (e.g., improved type hints, object type, libsodium) and allow code modernization assuming 7.2.
- Remove test matrix entries for older PHP versions and enforce the requirement via preflight checks and documentation.

This decision simplifies maintenance, improves security posture, and enables consistent behavior across platforms.

## Decision

Adopt Continuous Delivery as the default release practice across all services. Every commit to the main branch triggers a standardized Concourse pipeline that: builds and tests the code, runs security and compliance checks, produces an immutable, versioned artifact, and automatically deploys to non-production environments. Promotion to production is automated via the same pipeline using environment-specific configuration stored in Git, with guarded controls (e.g., lightweight approval, change record automation) where required by policy. Deployments use progressive delivery strategies (blue/green or canary) and feature flags to enable safe, incremental releases and fast rollbacks by promoting a previously known-good artifact. No manual changes are permitted in environments; all changes flow through pipelines and Infrastructure-as-Code. Pipelines are per-service, declaratively defined in-repo, and include automated smoke checks and health gates post-deploy. Trunk-based development is the default (short-lived branches, frequent merges), ensuring the main branch is always releasable. Release metadata (build provenance, SBOM, signatures) is generated and verified in the pipeline. Operational metrics and deployment status are exposed to teams via the CD tooling to support rapid feedback and continuous improvement.

## Decision

Adopt Semantic Versioning (SemVer 2.0.0) as the standard versioning scheme across all deployable artifacts and libraries.

- Version format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-PRERELEASE][+BUILD].
- Increment rules:
  - MAJOR: any backward-incompatible change to public APIs, contracts, database schemas (without automated migration), or infrastructure interfaces.
  - MINOR: backward-compatible feature additions, deprecations, or performance improvements.
  - PATCH: backward-compatible bug fixes and dependency updates that do not change behavior or public contracts.
- Pre-releases: use -alpha, -beta, -rc.N for unstable or staged releases; only release candidates (-rc) may progress to GA without changes except version tag.
- Tagging: every release is tagged in Git as vX.Y.Z; pre-releases as vX.Y.Z-qualifier.
- Changelog: auto-generate release notes from Conventional Commits; CI validates commit messages and calculates the next version (fail build on ambiguity).
- Deprecations: announce in MINOR with clear migration notes; removal happens in the next MAJOR.
- Multi-component repos: apply independent versioning per package/service (or per published artifact); shared contracts/schemas versioned separately.
- Tooling: enforce via CI/CD (e.g., semantic-release or equivalent) to compute versions, create Git tags, publish artifacts/images, and create releases.
- Branching: only main/master produces release versions; feature branches may publish pre-releases.
- Rollbacks: re-deploy prior tag; never reuse or mutate published versions.

All domain objects shall have an immutable, globally unique, opaque identifier (ID) assigned at creation and used as the primary key and external reference.

- Format: UUID version 7 as defined in RFC 9562. Canonical external representation is lowercase hex with hyphens (36 characters). Internal storage SHOULD use 16-byte binary where supported; otherwise canonical string.
- Generation: IDs are generated client-side by the creating service using a UUIDv7 library with monotonicity support to minimize clock skew issues and improve index locality. No auto-increment or database-sequenced IDs are permitted.
- Semantics: IDs must not encode business meaning, tenancy, or routing information. They are opaque tokens and immutable for the lifetime of the object.
- Exposure: IDs are stable across APIs, events, and logs. They must be URL-safe as-is; no additional encoding required. When compact representations are required (e.g., QR), Base32 Crockford without separators MAY be used as an alternative view, but the canonical value remains the hyphenated UUIDv7.
- Validation: Services validate format and version (accept v7; v4 remains supported for legacy records). New records MUST use v7. Cross-service references must not assume ordering beyond “roughly time-ordered” properties of v7.
- Indexing: Datastores should index IDs as primary clustered keys where possible to leverage v7’s temporal ordering for write locality.
- Migration: Existing v4 IDs remain valid; no rekeying. Systems must handle both v4 and v7 during the transition window; telemetry should track adoption until ≥95% of new IDs are v7.
- Security: IDs are not secrets; do not rely on them for access control. Apply authorization based on object ownership and scope, not ID entropy.

External parameters required by Presenters and Routers (e.g., IDs, feature flags, deep-link data, environment/config values, locale, and experiment assignments) will be provided explicitly as constructor/initialization arguments at creation time. These components will not read from globals, singletons, service locators, process environment, storage, or platform primitives (e.g., Intent/Bundle/UserDefaults) directly.

Parameters will be encapsulated in immutable, strongly-typed value objects specific to each feature’s boundary (e.g., ScreenArgs, RouterArgs). Parsing, validation, and defaulting of raw inputs occur at the composition root (app entry/deeplink handler/navigation builder), which is responsible for constructing these argument objects. If parsing fails, the composition root handles fallback/redirect; Presenters/Routers assume already-validated inputs.

Where late-arriving parameters are unavoidable (e.g., async feature flags), they will be injected via explicit method parameters or dedicated input streams/observers rather than internal lookups. Optional parameters must be modeled explicitly (nullable/Optional) to avoid hidden coupling.

Dependency injection frameworks (e.g., Dagger/Hilt/Koin/Swinject) will wire Presenters/Routers with both their service dependencies and their argument objects. No Presenter/Router will fetch arguments from DI containers at runtime.

Public APIs of Presenters/Routers will reflect only domain-relevant arguments; platform-specific details remain outside. This makes Presenters/Routers deterministic, easier to unit test (arguments can be freely constructed/mocked), safer to reason about, and simpler to evolve.

We will standardize on Terraform as our primary Infrastructure-as-Code tool for provisioning and managing all cloud resources. We will:

- Pin Terraform and provider versions (required_version and provider constraints) and commit the .terraform.lock.hcl file.
- Isolate state per stack/environment using a remote backend with locking (e.g., S3 + DynamoDB or Terraform Cloud), prohibiting local state for shared environments.
- Use a modular architecture: small, reusable versioned modules; thin root modules per stack; publish internal modules via a private registry when practical.
- Enforce changes via CI: plan on pull requests, apply only from main on approved changes; prohibit direct applies to production from local machines.
- Manage environment configuration via tfvars and remote state data sources where necessary; never commit secrets—load sensitive values from a secret manager or CI-provided variables.
- Adopt naming/tagging conventions for traceability (app, env, owner, cost center, compliance).
- Validate consistently with terraform fmt, validate, and tflint; run security checks (e.g., tfsec/checkov) in CI.
- Use workspaces only when appropriate; prefer explicit state separation over workspaces for strong isolation.
- Document state locations, module interfaces, and expected inputs/outputs; record breaking changes in module CHANGELOGs.
- Prefer immutable changes and blue/green patterns where feasible; use terraform import for adoption of existing resources with review of state drift.

We will deploy Pact Broker as a containerized service on AWS ECS Fargate within private subnets, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) with ACM-managed TLS and Route53 DNS. PostgreSQL will be provided via Amazon RDS (multi-AZ) as the persistent data store. Service configuration and credentials (database URL, secrets, webhook tokens) will be managed in AWS Secrets Manager and injected via task definitions. Logs will be shipped to CloudWatch Logs with metric filters and alarms; ALB access logs will be enabled to S3. Backups will rely on RDS automated snapshots plus daily snapshots and S3 exports; cross-region snapshot copies will be enabled for DR.

Infrastructure will be provisioned via AWS CloudFormation to align with our AWS-first standard and enable repeatable, versioned deployments. Networking will use an existing VPC with private subnets, NAT gateways, and VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and CloudWatch; security groups will restrict ALB-to-service and service-to-RDS traffic. The service will run at least two Fargate tasks across AZs for high availability and use ECS Service Auto Scaling based on CPU/Memory and ALB target metrics.

Authentication will be integrated via OAuth/OIDC (e.g., AWS Cognito or enterprise IdP) with fine-grained Pact Broker RBAC enforced in-app. Blue/green deployments will be performed using ECS and ALB weighted target groups. This approach minimizes operational overhead, provides managed scalability and resilience, and keeps cost predictable while meeting security and compliance requirements.

We will provision a dedicated VPC for OPG Metrics in each environment (dev, staging, production), rather than deploying into a shared or centralized VPC. This VPC will have:

- Unique, non-overlapping CIDR blocks managed via IPAM.
- Per-AZ public and private subnets; workloads reside in private subnets without public IPs.
- Ingress via ALB/NLB as required; egress via NAT Gateways in each AZ.
- VPC endpoints (Gateway/Interface) for access to AWS services without traversing the public Internet.
- Centralized egress control using NAT + egress VPC/Firewalls (where available) or route table policies.
- Connectivity to core/platform services via Transit Gateway peering; direct VPC peering only if TGW is unavailable.
- DNS integrated with Route 53 (private hosted zones) and corporate resolvers via Route 53 Resolver rules.
- Strict security boundaries using security groups and NACLs; no default SG usage.
- Centralized logging: VPC Flow Logs and ALB/NLB logs to a dedicated logging account/bucket; CloudTrail and Config enabled per org standards.
- SSM for access and management (no direct SSH), with Session Manager and SSM Agent.
- Standardized tagging, guardrails, SCPs, and IAM least-privilege policies aligned with org controls.
- Baseline high availability: multi-AZ subnets, multiple NATs, and ALB/NLB across AZs.

We will not colocate OPG Metrics with other products or in a shared PaaS VPC. Any required third-party integrations will traverse TGW or approved egress controls. Future changes (e.g., migration to shared network fabric or service mesh) may be evaluated if they preserve isolation guarantees and operational autonomy.

Deprecate and remove the chi-squared test option from our analytics/feature-selection APIs, CLI, and UI. The option will be disabled by default immediately and produce a clear deprecation error with guidance; it will be fully removed in the next major release. Workflows requiring categorical association testing must migrate to:
- Fisher’s exact test for small samples or sparse contingency tables
- Likelihood-ratio (G-test) for large samples
For supervised feature selection:
- Use ANOVA F-test for continuous features vs. categorical targets
- Use mutual information for categorical features/targets

Configuration keys (e.g., test: chi2 or selector: chi2) will be rejected with a descriptive error. Pipelines referencing chi-squared in saved configurations will not execute; the migration tool will auto-rewrite to recommended alternatives based on data schemas and provide a diff. UI elements exposing chi-squared will be removed. Documentation, examples, and training materials will be updated to reflect replacements and limitations. Telemetry will track remaining usage to assist teams with migration. Versioning: soft deprecation in the current minor release; hard removal with a breaking change note in the next major version.

## Decision

Adopt a centralized, policy-driven authorization model combining RBAC with resource-scoped ABAC.

- Identity and authentication: All human and service actors authenticate via OIDC/OAuth2 (enterprise IdP for users; workload identities for services). Tokens include subject, tenant, groups, and device/assurance claims.
- Authorization: A dedicated Authorization Service (backed by a policy engine) evaluates access decisions. Policies are versioned, reviewed, and deployed via CI/CD. Deny rules explicitly override allow rules. Decisions are exposed via a low-latency API/sidecar with short-lived caching.
- Permission model:
  - Actors: end-user, org admin, project admin, maintainer, contributor, reader; integration/service accounts with scoped roles.
  - Resources: organization, project, dataset, artifact, secret, job/run, environment.
  - Actions: administer, manage, write, read, execute, share/grant.
  - Hierarchy: inheritance flows org → project → resource; supports explicit exceptions at any level.
  - ABAC: constraints on tenant, environment, data classification, time, network, and ownership.
- Multitenancy: Every resource and decision is tenant-scoped; cross-tenant access is disabled by default and requires explicit, auditable grants. Datastores enforce row-level security by tenant and project.
- Administration: A dedicated UI allows org/project admins to grant/revoke roles and time-bound permissions; just-in-time elevation requires approval. Service accounts are keyless where possible and limited by audience, scope, and TTL.
- Observability and safety: All authorization decisions, grants, and escalations are audit-logged and exportable. Break-glass roles are isolated, require MFA and approval, and trigger alerts.
- Defaults: Private-by-default, least privilege, minimal token lifetime, mutual TLS for service-to-service calls.

We will implement Redux as the single source of truth for client-side state, using Redux Toolkit (RTK) as the standard approach. The store will be configured via RTK’s configureStore with React-Redux hooks (useSelector/useDispatch), DevTools enabled in development, and the default middleware including redux-thunk. State will be organized into feature-based slices (createSlice), co-locating reducers, action creators, and selectors per domain. Where appropriate, we will normalize collections using RTK’s createEntityAdapter to keep state flat and enable efficient updates.

We will use TypeScript for strong typing (RootState, AppDispatch) and provide typed hooks (useAppDispatch/useAppSelector). Cross-slice interactions will occur through dispatched actions and selectors rather than direct coupling. Side effects and async flows will use createAsyncThunk; long-running or cross-cutting behaviors can be encapsulated as custom middleware if needed. We will gate dev-only middleware (immutableCheck, serializableCheck, logger) behind environment flags to minimize runtime overhead in production.

For API data, we will either integrate RTK Query for declarative data fetching/caching or, if requirements remain simple, continue with thunks and dedicated API services; selection will be revisited per feature. We will define a minimal persisted state surface (if persistence is required) via redux-persist, explicitly whitelisting slices. Feature teams will expose selectors for read access and keep state updates isolated to slice reducers. Testing will target reducers and thunks in isolation, with component tests relying on a test store. Continuous monitoring will leverage Redux DevTools in development and structured action/state logs where appropriate in non-production environments.

## Decision

Adopt a canonical-identifier-first model with a managed alias layer:

- Canonical IDs are the only persistent primary keys; aliases are optional, many-to-one labels that resolve to a canonical ID.
- Aliases must be unique within a defined scope (e.g., tenant/project/environment/resource-type). Cross-scope duplication is allowed; scope is always part of resolution.
- Resolution order: exact alias match (within scope) → exact canonical ID → normalized alias match (case-insensitive, whitespace/punctuation collapsed). Ambiguous matches fail fast with a diagnostic listing candidates.
- Aliases cannot collide with any canonical ID within the same scope. Canonical IDs are immutable; aliases are mutable with audit.
- Store aliases in a dedicated metadata store with fields: alias, canonical_id, scope, resource_type, status (active/deprecated), created_by, created_at, expires_at (optional).
- Provide RBAC-protected CRUD for aliases; updates are versioned and fully audited. Bulk import/export is supported for migrations.
- Enforce normalization rules: case-insensitive comparison, NFC Unicode normalization, trim surrounding whitespace, collapse internal whitespace to single spaces. Display preserves user-entered casing.
- Deprecation workflow: mark alias deprecated → emit warnings/telemetry for a grace period → optionally set expiry → removal. Provide automated suggestions for replacements.
- Prevent creation of aliases that shadow reserved words, CLI subcommands, or environment names. Validate in CI for configuration repos.
- Client behavior:
  - APIs accept alias or canonical ID; responses include both (id, aliases[]) with the canonical ID preferred for automation.
  - CLI accepts --id and --alias; outputs show canonical ID prominently with resolved alias used for human readability.
  - SDKs expose resolveAlias(scope, name) and listAliases(id) utilities.
- Caching: in-memory LRU per scope with short TTL; cache is invalidated on alias CRUD events via pub/sub.
- Error handling: all “not found”/ambiguity errors include nearest matches (Levenshtein) and the active scope.
- Telemetry: record alias usage, deprecation hits, and ambiguities to guide cleanup and naming conventions.

This decision ensures stable references, human-friendly names, safe evolution, and predictable resolution across environments.

We will standardize on Luxon as the sole date/time library across frontend and backend. All domain logic will use Luxon’s DateTime, Duration, and Interval types. Default computation will occur in UTC; user-facing display will use the user’s timezone and locale via Intl. For persistence: APIs will exchange ISO 8601 UTC strings (e.g., 2026-01-24T13:45:00Z); databases that support native timestamp types will continue to store native timestamps. No direct Date arithmetic is allowed; all parsing, formatting, math, and timezone handling must use Luxon.

Implementation notes:
- Import via ESM (import { DateTime, Duration, Interval } from 'luxon') to enable tree-shaking.
- Provide a small date-utils wrapper (parseISO, toISO, nowUTC, fromMillis, withZone, diff, startOfDayUTC, etc.) to encapsulate common operations and centralize conventions.
- Migrate existing moment/date-fns usages incrementally; forbid new usages via lint rules.
- For environments lacking full Intl support, include the minimal necessary polyfills.
- Establish test fixtures for timezone-sensitive cases (DST transitions, leap years) using Luxon’s setZone.
- Store and compare only normalized UTC values in business logic; never persist localized display strings.
- Version-pin Luxon and document upgrade steps; align APIs to accept/emit ISO 8601.

This decision unifies timezone handling, reduces bundle size versus Moment, improves immutability/type safety, and prepares for a smooth future path toward Temporal if/when adopted.

Adopt a controlled WebView-based embedding strategy for rendering external content in the native app.

- Use a single, sandboxed WebView component to load content only from an explicit allowlist of origins (e.g., app.example.com), enforced by native URL interception and a strict Content Security Policy.
- Disable risky WebView capabilities by default (file:// access, arbitrary downloads, eval, mixed content, third‑party cookies); enable JavaScript only when required. Prevent navigation to non-allowlisted domains and open external links via the system browser.
- Establish a typed bi-directional bridge (postMessage on web side, native handler on app side) for minimal interactions: close view, share, open-deeplink, telemetry events, and authentication state updates. Version messages with a stable schema and reject unknown messages.
- Support offline/low-connectivity via a versioned content manifest and cache: prefetch critical content on app update; fall back to server when online. Content is immutable and addressed by hash; update by publishing a new manifest.
- Use short-lived, user-scoped signed URLs or token injection for authenticated content; tokens never exposed to query parameters and are rotated per session.
- Provide a feature flag (embed_content_enabled) and server-driven kill switch; log feature exposure and failures for rollback.
- Isolate embedded content per screen (separate WebView instances or profiles) to avoid state leakage; clear storage on logout and on domain changes.
- Ensure accessibility parity: propagate native accessibility settings (font scale, contrast) to the WebView via CSS variables or meta viewport.
- Instrument performance (TTI, memory, crashes) and enforce budgets; block content that exceeds defined thresholds.
- Document an embedding contract (allowed origins, message schema, lifecycle hooks) and include automated tests (origin enforcement, bridge compatibility, offline fallback) in CI.

We will officially support “frontend-only” deployments and workflows. The product can be delivered as a standalone SPA/MPA hosted on static infrastructure (e.g., CDN-backed object storage) and consume APIs owned by other teams or third parties. Our scope of support explicitly covers client-side code, build pipelines, asset optimization, and edge/CDN configuration; API availability and backend changes are out of scope and treated as external dependencies.

To enable this mode:
- The frontend will integrate with APIs via HTTPS using contract-first schemas (OpenAPI/GraphQL SDL) and strict versioning.
- Authentication is browser-native (OIDC/OAuth2 with PKCE) without client secrets; tokens are stored using best-practice patterns to mitigate XSS/CSRF.
- CORS, rate limits, and error contracts must be defined by API providers; the frontend will implement resilient retries, timeouts, and graceful degradation.
- Local development uses mock servers and generated clients from contracts; end-to-end tests run against staging endpoints where available.
- Observability includes client-side telemetry (performance, errors, user events) and synthetic checks of critical user journeys from the edge.
- Deployments are immutable and atomic with rollbacks; environment configuration is injected at runtime where possible to avoid rebuilds per environment.
- Feature flags and remote configuration are used to decouple releases from backend availability and to enable progressive delivery.

Support policy: we provide SLAs for the build/deploy pipeline, static hosting, and client behavior; upstream API incidents are escalated but not remediated by the frontend team. Coordination with API owners follows documented contracts and change-management gates.

## Decision

We will adopt Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as our primary infrastructure platform for running Kubernetes workloads. We will use regional, autopilot or standard clusters (standard for advanced controls, autopilot for low-ops workloads) with private, VPC-native networking, multiple node pools, and cluster autoscaling. Control plane will be fully managed by GKE to reduce operational overhead, while we retain portability by using upstream Kubernetes APIs and avoiding GKE-only features where feasible.

Infrastructure will be provisioned via Terraform, with configuration stored in version control and promoted through environments. Workload authentication will use Workload Identity to map Kubernetes service accounts to Google service accounts. We will use Google-managed Container/Artifact Registry for images, Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring for observability, Cloud KMS for key management, and Cloud Load Balancing with managed SSL. Network Policies and Pod Security Standards will be enforced; Binary Authorization and Admission Controllers will be enabled for supply-chain controls.

We will deploy across multiple regions/projects as needed for availability and blast-radius reduction, and implement backup/restore for stateful components (e.g., GCS/PubSub snapshots, managed databases). To mitigate vendor lock-in, we will keep cluster-agnostic manifests/Helm charts and maintain IaC modules compatible with alternative Kubernetes providers.

We will not provide a dedicated ingress controller by default for each team/namespace. The platform will offer a shared, hardened ingress controller fleet as the baseline. Dedicated ingress controllers will be provisioned only by exception, when one or more of the following are required:
- Custom WAF/modsecurity policies that cannot be scoped per‑Ingress
- Layer 7 features or timeouts incompatible with the shared baseline
- Per‑service DDoS/waf isolation or strict blast‑radius/latency isolation SLOs
- Regulatory or tenancy constraints requiring network segregation

When approved, dedicated controllers will be:
- Deployed via a standardized, automated module (IngressClass, Helm chart, Flux/Argo) with opinionated defaults
- Backed by an NLB with enforced quotas per VPC/AZ and SG rule budgets
- Cost-allocated to the requesting team, including NLB, IPs, data processing
- Observed with shared dashboards/alerts and SLOs; teams own run/support
- Security-hardened (TLS policy, cipher suites, security headers) consistent with platform baselines

Capacity controls:
- A per-environment cap on dedicated controllers; requests require justification and review
- Periodic revalidation; idle or noncompliant controllers will be reclaimed
- Load/perf tests required before adding additional dedicated capacity

Teams must use the shared controllers unless an exception is approved; all Ingress resources must reference an allowed IngressClass managed by the platform.

Adopt a Jenkins Pipeline strategy that provisions assets-frontend per version using Service Manager as a build matrix, rather than starting all versions on a single node. Each matrix leg pins a specific supported version (via Service Manager profiles/tags) on an ephemeral agent, performs health checks, runs the relevant test suite, and then performs a guaranteed teardown. Parallel execution is enabled to reduce end-to-end duration, with per-leg timeouts and retries to improve resilience. Version coverage is driven by a centrally managed AF_VERSIONS list (e.g., majors and LTS), allowing quick updates without pipeline code changes.

We will:
- Use Service Manager to start the targeted assets-frontend version with isolated ports/workspaces.
- Gate test execution on readiness probes and fail fast on startup errors.
- Archive per-version logs and diagnostics for triage.
- Cache dependencies where possible to reduce startup time; no persistent services are left running on Jenkins agents.
- Treat each version as an independent pass/fail signal; overall build fails if any required version fails.

This decision ensures deterministic, reproducible environment setup for each supported version, avoids resource contention from co-locating multiple versions, and simplifies scaling and maintenance across Jenkins agents.

## Decisions

Adopt a single, versioned API root across all public surfaces to ensure consistency, discoverability, and forward-compatibility:

- HTTP: Standardize on /api/v1 as the canonical prefix for all public endpoints (e.g., /api/v1/messaging, /api/v1/pubsub, /api/v1/secrets, /api/v1/state, /api/v1/actors, /api/v1/config, /api/v1/health).
- gRPC: Use a unified package namespace dapr.api.v1.* mirroring HTTP resources and operations.
- WebSocket/Streaming: When applicable, mount under /api/v1/streams/*.

Scope and separation:
- Reserve /internal/* and dapr.internal.v1.* for non-public/unstable and control-plane APIs.
- Reserve /admin/v1 for operator/management endpoints that require elevated privileges.
- Optional multi-tenancy: enable a gated prefix /api/v1/tenants/{tenantId}/... for tenant-scoped APIs; default off.

Versioning and compatibility:
- Freeze the prefix per major version (e.g., /api/v1) and introduce breaking changes only under a new prefix (/api/v2).
- Provide compatibility shims and HTTP 308 redirects from legacy paths for two minor releases; document deprecation timelines.

Namespacing and resource taxonomy:
- Align resource nouns and verbs across protocols; prefer nouns for collections and POST/GET/PATCH/DELETE semantics.
- Ensure uniform error models and pagination/query conventions across all endpoints under the prefix.

Security and policy:
- Enforce authentication/authorization uniformly at the prefix boundary with consistent scopes/claims.
- Support per-prefix rate limits, quotas, and audit logging for operational consistency.

We will handle all response-driven navigation and state transitions on the client. Backend endpoints will return data (and structured error metadata) rather than HTML pages or server-initiated redirects. A centralized HTTP client wrapper with request/response interceptors will normalize responses and translate them into client-side navigation and UI states.

Key behaviors:
- Authentication: On 401/419, attempt silent token refresh; on failure, redirect to Sign-in with returnTo. On 403, route to Access Denied.
- Resource routing: On 404, navigate to Not Found. On 409, surface conflict UI with retry guidance. On 422, map validation errors to form fields. On 5xx, show a resilient error page with retry and log telemetry.
- Redirect hints: Prefer application-level next field in JSON payloads over server 3xx; fall back to Location header if present and safe. The client router will resolve and navigate accordingly.
- Guards: Implement route guards for auth and authorization, fed by normalized user/session state. Pre-fetch critical data during navigation where feasible; cancel stale requests on route change.
- Consistency: Define a canonical response envelope { data, error: { code, message, details }, next } across services. Treat non-2xx as exceptions only after normalization to preserve partial data when provided.
- UX: Centralized loading and error toasts; inline form feedback for 4xx; optimistic updates with rollback on failure and idempotency keys for retriable mutations.
- Observability: Emit structured logs and metrics for response categories, retries, and navigations; capture correlation IDs from response headers and propagate in subsequent requests.
- Security: Never trust client for authorization; server enforces permissions and returns 403 with codes. The client only interprets and routes. Strip sensitive fields from logs/UI.
- Progressive enhancement: If JavaScript is unavailable, server provides minimal fallback entry points for critical flows; primary UX remains SPA-driven.
- Extensibility: Response-to-route mappings are declared in a single module to enable product-specific overrides and A/B tests without backend changes.

This decision removes server-rendered redirects and HTML error pages from APIs, standardizes response shapes, and centralizes navigation logic in the client to improve UX consistency, performance, and cross-service interoperability.

## Decision

When a release branch is cut, the CI/CD system will automatically create and publish a coherent set of release-candidate (RC) artifacts for all deliverables from the branch tip. These artifacts will be built once, signed, and tagged with semantic prerelease versions (e.g., vX.Y.Z-rc.0) and the source commit SHA, then published to the prerelease channel in our artifact registries. Subsequent commits to the release branch will increment the RC iteration (rc.1, rc.2, …) and produce a new full set, ensuring the RC set always reflects an internally consistent build of the branch.

Promotion to GA will not rebuild; it will re-tag and promote the selected RC artifacts (immutability preserved) after release approval and verification gates pass. Only security or must-fix issues will trigger a new RC iteration. Nightly builds on the release branch are disabled to avoid diverging artifacts—only explicit merges or hotfix commits trigger RC regeneration.

Branch protection and versioning rules will enforce:
- Automatic version bumping to prerelease on branch cut.
- Unique, immutable artifacts per rc.n iteration.
- Mandatory metadata: commit SHA, build manifest, SBOM, signatures, provenance.

This decision ensures testable, reproducible, and promotable release sets with clear traceability and minimal manual intervention.

## Decision

Adopt short‑lived, federated credentials as the only supported mechanism for human and machine access to AWS.

- Human access: Use AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS SSO) with enforced MFA and device trust where available. Users are assigned to least‑privilege permission sets that map to assumable roles in target accounts (via AWS Organizations). Session durations are time‑boxed; no long‑lived IAM user access keys are issued.
- Automation/CI/CD: Use OIDC federation from approved providers (e.g., GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps) to assume narrowly scoped roles without storing secrets. Workloads running in AWS (EKS, ECS, Lambda) assume roles via native mechanisms (IRSA/task roles/execution roles); no static credentials in code or images.
- Governance: Block creation and use of IAM user access keys via SCPs and AWS Config rules; alert on violations. Maintain a single break‑glass IAM user with MFA and hardware token, stored in a secure vault with dual control and audited access.
- Security hygiene: Enforce least privilege via permission boundaries and scoped policies; standardize session durations; require MFA for sensitive role assumptions; rotate any exceptional credentials automatically with short TTLs.
- Observability: Audit all access via CloudTrail/CloudWatch/Lake; regularly review role usage and tighten scopes. Centralize role/permission set definitions in IaC with mandatory peer review and change history.

## Decision

All official release tarballs produced by the Wikibase release pipeline will be hosted on releases.wikimedia.org as the single canonical distribution channel. Tarballs will be published under the established Wikimedia directory structure (for example, mediawiki/extensions/Wikibase/<version>/), use deterministic, versioned filenames, and include accompanying SHA256 checksums and detached GPG signatures. Documentation, release notes, and announcements will link to these URLs exclusively; no tarballs will be attached to GitHub/Gerrit releases or distributed via alternative package registries. Non-release artifacts (nightly builds, CI outputs) may be stored elsewhere but will not be advertised as official releases. Retention and mirroring will follow Wikimedia operations policies for releases.wikimedia.org.

## Decision

We will prioritize using tools, frameworks, and services that are already familiar to the team and widely adopted in our organization and industry. “Familiar” means: demonstrable team experience, strong community support, mature documentation, and proven operational reliability. New or niche tools may be introduced only when they deliver clear, material benefits (e.g., order-of-magnitude improvements in performance, cost, or developer productivity) that outweigh adoption, training, and operational risks. Any proposal to adopt unfamiliar tools requires an ADR/RFC outlining rationale, alternatives considered, risk mitigation, support/exit strategy, and a limited-scope pilot. We will prefer managed/hosted offerings where available to reduce operational burden. Tool choices will be revisited periodically to avoid stagnation and retire legacy where appropriate. This approach optimizes delivery speed, maintainability, onboarding efficiency, and incident response while balancing innovation with risk.

## Decision

We will make repositories open by default when the code is broadly reusable, non-sensitive, and free of customer- or environment-specific configuration or business logic. Repos meeting these criteria must be licensed under Apache-2.0 (unless otherwise mandated), include README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, and CHANGELOG files, and define CODEOWNERS for stewardship.

Before opening:
- Security: pass secret scanning, dependency vulnerability checks, SAST; remove credentials, endpoints, and infra details; validate SBOM availability.
- Legal/IP: verify third-party licenses, export controls, and trademark usage; add NOTICE as required.
- Product/Privacy: ensure no customer data samples, logs, or proprietary domain logic are present; split or refactor if necessary.
- Operational: ensure CI/CD does not expose internal systems; use public-safe pipelines and artifact publishing.

Process:
1) Triage repo against an “Open Checklist” (security, legal, product).
2) Refactor/split into open-core if needed; move private parts to configuration-only or solution-specific repos.
3) Approve via lightweight review (security + legal + owning team).
4) Publish under the designated public organization; enable Discussions and Issues; tag with topics; add release cadence and support policy.
5) Set branch protections, required reviews, and mandatory status checks; enable Dependabot and secret scanning.
6) Define governance: maintainers, contribution workflow, and vulnerability disclosure channel.
7) If a repo cannot be opened, document rationale and revisit quarterly; consider public mirror of a sanitized package or extracted module.

All new greenfield components should be designed for openness from inception; exceptions require a documented risk and business justification.

We will include the project wiki as a dedicated git submodule within the main repository under docs/wiki. The wiki will remain its own repository with its own maintainers and release cadence; the application repository will pin a specific wiki commit to ensure reproducible documentation with each code release.

Contribution workflow:
- Content changes are made via pull requests to the wiki repository.
- The main repository updates the submodule reference in a separate commit when pulling in approved wiki changes.
- CI will fetch submodules, validate links/structure, and (where applicable) build/publish static documentation snapshots aligned to tagged releases.

Operational details:
- Developers must initialize and update submodules (git submodule update --init --recursive).
- The submodule will be read/write for contributors with wiki access; others will propose changes via PRs to the wiki repo.
- No direct edits to the submodule contents in the main repo; all edits occur in the wiki repo to avoid divergence.

This approach keeps documentation decoupled yet co-located, enables version pinning with code, and supports offline/local browsing and review.

We will standardize on a clear, stable, and tree-shakeable module export structure:

- Use named exports exclusively across the codebase; no default exports.
- Define the public API surface via package-level barrel files (index.ts) at feature/package boundaries only. Avoid nested barrels to reduce cycles; internal files are not re-exported unless part of the public API.
- Prohibit deep imports into internal paths. Consumers must import from the top-level entry or documented subpath entries only.
- Declare explicit subpath entry points through package.json “exports” with conditions: { import, require, types }. Provide stable, documented subpaths (e.g., ".", "./react", "./node") for intentional surface areas.
- Ship dual builds: ESM as the primary artifact with CJS compatibility via conditional exports. Include type definitions per entry point using “types” conditions.
- Ensure modules are side-effect-free; set "sideEffects": false in package.json, whitelisting any files that must run side effects.
- Preserve symbol names across re-exports to enable refactoring tools and avoid aliasing unless necessary for deprecation or compatibility.
- Group platform-specific or optional integrations behind dedicated subpaths (e.g., ./react) instead of mixing into the root API.
- Mark any deprecated exports in root as re-exports with deprecation notices and a migration path to new subpaths; remove in the next major release per semver.
- For internal consumption between packages in a monorepo, use the same public entry points to avoid accidental reliance on private internals.

This structure provides a minimal, stable import surface, improves tree-shaking and DX, and enforces API boundaries through the exports map.

We will implement “special pages” via a registry-based router that maps a page slug to either:
- a generic CMS-driven PageTemplate (default), or
- a bespoke, code-defined React component (for pages requiring custom logic/UX).

Details:
- Routing: slugs (e.g., /about, /team, /campaigns/foo) are resolved through a registry. Unknown slugs fall back to the CMS template; missing entries render 404.
- CMS pages: PageTemplate fetches content by slug from Contentful, supports localized content, hero/media, SEO fields (title, description, OpenGraph), and simple component blocks (rich text, images, embeds). Draft preview is available behind an auth-gated “preview” mode.
- Bespoke pages: Implement as lazy-loaded React components registered by slug for advanced behavior (data fetching, experiments). Keep them thin and reusable; prefer composing shared UI primitives.
- Performance: lazy-load bespoke pages, cache CMS responses (HTTP caching + client memoization), and prefetch on likely nav paths.
- Governance: new special pages default to CMS; bespoke pages require an ADR or tech lead approval. Slug collisions prefer bespoke only if explicitly configured.
- Observability: consistent analytics and error boundaries; 404/500 are bespoke pages.
- Accessibility/SEO: enforce shared metatags and a11y checks in both paths.

We will standardize all date and time representations to ISO 8601. Concretely:
- For API payloads, logs, and any text storage, use ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 extended format.
- Datetime values must include a timezone: prefer UTC with a trailing “Z” (e.g., 2026-01-24T15:04:05Z). If a local time is required, include the numeric offset (e.g., 2026-01-24T15:04:05-05:00).
- Date-only values use YYYY-MM-DD (e.g., 2026-01-24). Time-only values (rare) use HH:mm:ss with optional fractional seconds and must not assume a timezone.
- Fractional seconds are optional; when present, use up to 3 decimal places for milliseconds (e.g., 2026-01-24T15:04:05.123Z). Do not exceed milliseconds unless explicitly required.
- All back-end persistence should use native timestamp types in UTC where supported; when only strings are possible, store ISO 8601 UTC strings.
- Prohibit locale-specific or ambiguous formats (e.g., 01/02/2026), day/month names, and two-digit years.
- Serialization/deserialization libraries must be configured to emit/parse ISO 8601 strictly, rejecting invalid or non-normalized inputs.
- Lexicographic sorting of ISO 8601 strings is relied upon; therefore, always zero-pad components and include the timezone for datetimes.
- Documentation and contracts will specify the exact expected format per field (date-only vs datetime) and whether fractional seconds are permitted.

## Decision

Adopt progressive delivery with automated canary deployments for production releases, using AWS Lambda aliases and AWS CodeDeploy traffic shifting, with Terraform managing all infrastructure and deployment policies.

Key elements:
- For serverless APIs (Chalice → Lambda + API Gateway): publish versioned Lambda artifacts to S3; Terraform creates Lambda versions and alias (prod) managed by CodeDeploy with linear canary (e.g., 10% every 5 minutes). CloudWatch alarms (latency, 5XX rate, error rate, DLQ age) gate promotion and trigger automatic rollback on breach. Pre/post-traffic hooks perform smoke checks and schema validation.
- For non-production: rolling full-shift (no canary) to speed feedback; production only uses canary.
- Backward/forward compatibility: database and contract changes follow expand-and-contract; deployments enforce ordered migrations and feature flags to decouple code rollout from feature exposure.
- Rollback: fully automated via CodeDeploy on alarm breach; manual override supported via alias reset in Terraform. All releases are immutable and reproducible from versioned artifacts.
- Environments: isolated dev, stage, prod accounts; promotion by artifact promotion, not rebuild. Route 53/API Gateway remain stable; only alias weights change.
- Observability: mandatory dashboards, SLOs, and alarms defined in Terraform per service; deployment health evaluated on real user metrics and error budgets.
- Release cadence: trunk-based development with short-lived branches; CI builds, tests, and signs artifacts; CD promotes through environments via approval gates on stage→prod.

This strategy minimizes user impact during releases, enables rapid, safe rollouts with automated rollback, and remains fully IaC-driven and auditable.

We will model domain lifecycle explicitly using a finite-state machine with a single canonical state field persisted in the primary data store. Allowed states and transitions will be enumerated and versioned in code, with all state mutations executed via validated transition commands that enforce preconditions and emit domain events for auditing and downstream consumers. Ad-hoc boolean/status fields will be deprecated in favor of deriving behavior from the canonical state. APIs will expose state as a first-class attribute; write operations that imply a state change must specify the intended transition and will be idempotent. Background workers and integrations must consume domain events to react to state changes rather than directly mutating state. Migration will include mapping legacy flags to canonical states and introducing guardrails to prevent invalid states.

## Decision

- Implement a fail-fast startup sequence that validates configuration, secrets, and mandatory downstream dependencies before accepting traffic. On validation failure, the process exits with a non-zero code to be cleanly restarted by the orchestrator.
- Gate traffic with explicit liveness and readiness probes. Sprout will bind its port early but will not register as “ready” (discovery, load balancer, gateway) until all critical dependencies are reachable and initialization (schema/caches/migrations) has completed successfully.
- Classify dependencies as mandatory vs. optional. Mandatory ones are required for readiness; optional ones are warmed up asynchronously and do not block liveness. Readiness flips only when mandatory checks pass.
- Configure bounded startup retries with exponential backoff for dependency connections to avoid hot crash loops; rely on orchestrator backoff (e.g., Kubernetes restartPolicy/backoffLimit) to throttle repeated failures.
- At the edge, ensure the gateway/load balancer respects readiness and returns 503 for unroutable targets; enable circuit breaking and jittered retry policies to prevent retry storms during start or partial outages.
- Reduce cold-start risk by persisting and preloading essential caches where feasible, and feature-flag heavy, non-critical initializations to defer them post-readiness.
- Enhance observability: structured logs for each startup phase, metrics for init durations and failure causes, and distinct exit codes to differentiate configuration errors from transient dependency failures; add alerts tied to repeated startup failures and prolonged unready states.
- Provide an operational runbook covering expected startup timelines, known failure modes, and remediation steps.

- Rebuild the threebot-deployer flist on the updated Ubuntu 20.04 base with zinit as the init system.
- Pin and install the required Python toolchain (python3.8, pip) and Poetry at a vetted version; install dependencies strictly from the lockfile; remove build tooling post-install to minimize the runtime surface.
- Externalize configuration via environment variables and config files; mount persistent volumes for:
  - /var/lib/threebot (state)
  - /var/log/threebot (logs)
  - /var/cache/pip and /var/cache/poetry (optional caches)
  - /mnt/secrets (TLS keys, API tokens)
- Run processes as a non-root user; adjust file/dir permissions accordingly.
- Provide zinit services for API, worker/scheduler, and a healthcheck script; expose a readiness/health endpoint and graceful shutdown.
- Harden image: apply security updates, strip dev packages, clean apt caches, and lock down permissions; enable TLS configuration.
- Add basic observability: structured logs to stdout/stderr and optional Prometheus metrics endpoint.
- Optimize size: prune docs/tests, compile bytecode, and vendor wheels where possible.
- Define a deterministic, idempotent build pipeline; sign and publish the flist to hub with semantic versioning, immutable digest, and a “latest” alias.
- Supply migration notes and a helper script to move existing deployments to the new volume paths and service names without downtime.

- Adopt explicit major-versioned base paths for all public APIs and assets (e.g., /v1/...); do not expose an unversioned root.  
- Store release artifacts and static content in versioned directories: bucket/service/{major}.{minor}.{patch}/…; expose read-only aliases:
  - bucket/service/major/ -> latest patch of that major (atomic pointer update)
  - bucket/service/latest/ -> latest stable release (internal use only; not public URL)
