  - Fully specified in OpenAPI; JSON Schema used for field-level validation where applicable to keep parity with other interfaces.
  - Backward compatible evolution through additive changes and new rulesVersion values.
- Non-goals:
  - No file storage or import; no implicit correction of data.

We will secure all externally accessible prototype deployments with HTTP Basic Authentication. Protection will be enforced at the edge/web server or hosting layer (e.g., NGINX auth_basic, Apache .htpasswd, platform-provided basic-auth, or reverse-proxy), not within the app, to block unauthenticated requests and assets (HTML, APIs, static files).

A single, non-personal set of credentials will be provisioned per environment (e.g., prototype, review apps), stored in the organization’s secrets manager and injected via CI/CD. Credentials will be distributed to approved stakeholders via the team password manager and rotated at least every 90 days or on personnel changes.

This mechanism is explicitly for low-risk prototypes and usability testing content; it will not be used for production or sensitive data. For sessions, we rely on the browser’s basic-auth caching; users will be instructed to close the tab/window to clear it.

Additional safeguards:
- Disallow indexing via 401 on root, robots.txt disallow, and X-Robots-Tag: noindex.
- Do not collect analytics by default on prototype domains.
- Log access attempts without recording credentials.
- Apply rate limiting at the proxy where available.

If stronger access control is required, we will switch to SSO/OIDC-based protection.

We will add the Citerus repository as a Git submodule pinned to an explicit commit to ensure reproducible builds. The submodule will live under third_party/citerus and be referenced read-only from the upstream origin. We will not modify Citerus code in-place; any required changes will be proposed upstream, and until accepted we will apply minimal patch files in our repo or temporarily point the submodule to a maintained fork. Updates to the submodule will be done via dedicated pull requests that bump the submodule SHA, include a changelog summary, and trigger full CI. All developers and CI must use recursive clone and submodule init/update in workflows; we will add pre-commit and CI checks to verify the submodule is initialized and clean. Branch policy: track the upstream stable branch (or annotated tags) but always pin to a commit rather than floating refs. Access will use HTTPS with read tokens as needed; for air-gapped builds we will vendor a tarball mirror per release. The build system will reference headers and libs from third_party/citerus without copying artifacts. Licensing notices from Citerus will be included in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES and surfaced in distribution packages.

We will consolidate our environment provisioning into a single root CloudFormation stack per environment, packaged and deployed as one artifact through CI/CD. The root template will orchestrate modular components as nested stacks (e.g., networking, security, data, compute, observability) to preserve maintainability while providing a single point of deployment, drift detection, and rollback.

Key conventions:
- One root stack per environment/account/region with a minimal, stable parameter set; opinionated defaults codified in the templates.
- Nested stacks for logical domains to avoid template-size/limit issues and enable targeted updates.
- Standardized tagging, IAM boundaries, and guardrails applied at the root and inherited by nested stacks.
- Cross-resource wiring handled via nested stack outputs; avoid cross-stack exports between independent roots.
- Shared/runtime values stored in SSM Parameter Store and passed as parameters.
- Use Change Sets, Stack Policies, and automatic stack drift detection in CI/CD gates.
- For multi-account rollouts, use StackSets to deploy the same root stack pattern.

This approach yields a single source of truth and consistent promotion flow, while retaining modularity and scale via nested stacks.

## Decision

We will treat data freshness as a first-class attribute in the cold-chain monitoring platform and enforce strict handling for delayed readings.

- All sensor payloads must include device timestamp, monotonic sequence number, and firmware clock skew metadata. Devices must sync time via NTP on boot and at least every 6 hours.
- The ingestion layer will apply a broker/topic-level TTL; messages older than 10 minutes at arrival are tagged stale. Anything older than 60 minutes is rejected for operational workflows but archived for audit.
- The processing pipeline will compute freshness = now() − device_timestamp and propagate it as a field. Records are classified as:
  - Fresh (≤5 minutes): eligible for alerts, dashboards, and controls.
  - Late (5–60 minutes): excluded from real-time alerts, included in dashboards with “stale” badge.
  - Stale (>60 minutes): quarantined; not surfaced to users except in audit views.
- Alerting is driven by device timestamps, not arrival time, with guardrails to prevent retroactive alerts from late data. Health alerts trigger if no fresh reading is received within 10 minutes (heartbeat missing).
- Backfill jobs can reprocess late data for analytics-only aggregates but will not trigger historical operational alerts.
- Data contracts and validation will reject payloads with non-monotonic sequence, excessive clock skew (>2 minutes), or missing timestamps.
- Observability will include per-device freshness SLOs, last-seen times, and stale-rate KPIs; devices breaching SLOs will auto-create support tickets.

Adopt Code Climate Quality and Test Coverage as mandatory checks in the CI pipeline for all repositories in scope. Configure a .codeclimate.yml at repo root to enable relevant engines (e.g., duplication, complexity/cognitive complexity, rubocop/eslint/markdownlint where applicable) and define path filters to exclude generated code, vendor deps, and binaries. Upload test coverage from CI using the Code Climate Test Reporter; require a minimum coverage threshold of 80% to pass, with a ratcheting rule to only increase the threshold over time.

Integrate Code Climate as required GitHub/GitLab status checks on pull requests: maintainability issues above severity “major,” new code duplication above 5%, or coverage drops on changed lines will fail the check and block merges. Display project badges (Maintainability, Test Coverage) in README.

Pin the Code Climate reporter version and engines, manage the CC_TEST_REPORTER_ID via CI secrets, and run the reporter in after-success steps to ensure parallelized test coverage is correctly aggregated. For monorepos, configure per-package channels and aggregate reports before upload.

Establish a baseline by whitelisting existing issues on main; new or worsened issues must be addressed or waived with a documented rationale. Generate weekly Quality snapshots for the team, and track remediation work as technical debt tasks. Reassess rulesets quarterly to tune noise vs signal and keep engines current.

Adopt Pydantic v2 BaseModel as the canonical SkyPy Model abstraction.

- All domain entities are defined as frozen (immutable) Pydantic models with strict type checking, explicit field aliases, and constrained types. Extra fields are forbidden; defaults are explicit.
- Validation occurs at system boundaries (I/O, API, persistence) and when constructing/updating models. Internally, models are treated as already valid to minimize overhead.
- Mutations use purely functional copy-on-write semantics (model = model.model_copy(update={...})) and domain behaviors are exposed as pure methods/functions that return new model instances.
- Serialization uses model_dump/model_dump_json with a versioned schema (__schema_version__) and JSON Schema generation for interoperability. Back/forward compatibility is handled via migration functions keyed by schema version.
- Numerical and scientific data interop:
  - NumPy arrays supported via pydantic-numpy types (or custom validators) with shape/dtype constraints.
  - Astropy Quantity, Time, and SkyCoord supported via custom pydantic validators/encoders.
  - Large arrays are referenced via memory-efficient containers (e.g., dask/array-like protocols) with lazy loading adapters where applicable.
- Extensibility:
  - Generic models (e.g., Model[T]) for reusable containers.
  - Protocols/ABCs define behavior contracts; repositories, services, and adapters are separate from models.
  - Plugin registry for custom field types and validators.
- Performance:
  - Use Pydantic compiled validators; defer expensive validations behind smart constructors where needed.
  - Batch construction utilities for vectorized scenarios.
- Concurrency and safety:
  - Models are hashable when fields permit; safe for caching.
  - Thread/async safe due to immutability.
- Configuration:
  - Strict mode on, arbitrary_types_allowed only for vetted scientific types.
  - Uniform time/units policy (UTC, SI by default) enforced via validators.
- Tooling:
  - Auto-generated docs from model schema.
  - Linting and tests enforce stability of public fields and schema versions.

We explicitly avoid coupling models to persistence (no ORM mixins), runtime mutation, and framework-specific base classes beyond Pydantic. This yields type-safe, validated, interoperable, and evolvable domain models suitable for scientific workflows.

## Decision

Adopt a centralized DNS strategy using Amazon Route 53:

- Maintain a single public hosted zone per root domain in the shared “Network/Shared Services” account.
- Delegate environment/application subdomains (e.g., dev.example.com, prod.example.com) to child hosted zones in workload accounts via NS records.
- Use private hosted zones only when required for intra-VPC resolution; associate them explicitly to target VPCs and avoid overlapping/cascading private zones.
- All DNS zones and records are managed via Infrastructure as Code (e.g., Terraform) with change reviews; workloads receive the hosted zone ID or delegated subdomain as inputs and must not create root hosted zones.
- Cross-account record management is performed via delegation where possible; direct cross-account writes require an approved IAM role and narrow permissions.
- Wildcard records are permitted only for specific use cases (e.g., dynamic app routing) and must not shadow critical records.
- For ephemeral/preview environments, create and destroy delegated subdomain hosted zones automatically under a designated parent subdomain (e.g., *.preview.example.com).
- Enable DNSSEC signing on public hosted zones where supported; enforce HTTPS via ACM certificates matching hosted zone/domain structure.
- Implement health checks and failover/latency-based routing where applicable; default to simple routing otherwise.
- Audit hosted zones and records continuously; prohibit manual console edits except for break-glass scenarios.

## Decision

We will enforce validation at two layers: contract validation at system boundaries and domain validation within the core.

- Contract validation: All external inputs and outputs (HTTP requests/responses, messages/events) will be validated against a single-source API contract defined in OpenAPI 3.1 using JSON Schema (draft 2020-12). Validation is applied via framework middleware at the edge of each service. Unknown fields are rejected (fail-closed), formats/enums are enforced, and payload sizes and nesting depth are bounded to mitigate resource exhaustion. Responses are also validated in non-production and in production for critical paths and during deployments.

- Domain validation: Business invariants are enforced within the domain model (entities/value objects/aggregates) independent of transport schemas to protect against bypass and to keep rules close to the business logic. Persistence constraints (unique, not-null, FK, check constraints) provide an additional safety net.

- Source of truth and generation: The OpenAPI contract is versioned and reviewed. DTOs, validators, and client/server stubs are generated from the contract to minimize drift. Backward-compatible changes follow semantic versioning; breaking changes require a new versioned endpoint/topic.

- Error handling: Validation failures return RFC 7807 problem+json with a stable error code, message, and per-field details. IDs and sensitive values are never echoed.

- Observability and performance: Validation metrics (rate, field, schema version) and sampled payload hashes are emitted. Hot paths use compiled validators and short-circuit evaluation.

This approach provides clear contracts, early failure, and defense-in-depth while keeping business rules encapsulated within the domain.

We will produce a single, self-contained HTML file as the primary build/export artifact.

- Inline all CSS and JS into the document via <style> and <script> tags, with minification enabled.
- Embed images, icons, and other binary assets as data: URLs (base64). Apply a configurable inlining threshold (default 250KB per asset) to control size; assets exceeding the threshold will be compressed before embedding. The build will fail with a clear error if the final HTML exceeds a configurable max size.
- Bundle fonts as WOFF2 data: URLs when licensing permits; otherwise, omit and fall back to system fonts.
- Embed runtime data/state needed for offline use as a JSON block within a non-executing <script type="application/json"> tag.
- Generate deterministic output (stable ordering of assets, pinned versions) to improve reproducibility; include build metadata and content hash in an HTML comment.
- Provide a --single-file (default on) and a --multi-file (debug) build mode to aid local development and reduce iteration time.
- Enforce security best practices: sanitize any user-generated content before embedding; include a CSP allowing only 'self' and data: for images/fonts; use nonce or hash-based policies for inline scripts/styles.
- Ensure accessibility and performance: preserve semantic markup, precompute critical CSS, defer non-critical scripts, and include basic preload hints as appropriate for single-file context.
- Publish the file with a .html extension and UTF-8 encoding, requiring no external network access to function.

## Decision

We will integrate with Microsoft 365 mailboxes using Microsoft Graph API (v1.0) as the single interface for email send, read, sync, and eventing.

- Authentication/authorization: Use Azure AD OAuth 2.0 with MSAL. Employ application permissions for backend/daemon workflows and delegated permissions for user-initiated actions. Enforce least-privilege scopes and tenant admin consent where required. Store tokens securely and use managed identities where available.
- Sending email: Use /sendMail with clientMessageId for idempotency, support HTML/plain bodies, and handle attachments including large files via upload sessions. Enforce per-tenant and per-user send limits and surface delivery errors.
- Reading/sync: Use delta queries (/messages/delta) for efficient mailbox synchronization and pagination. Normalize message payloads, handle soft-deletes, and preserve Graph IDs for referential integrity.
- Eventing: Use Graph change notifications (subscriptions + webhooks) for new/updated messages and mailbox events; fall back to periodic delta sync if subscriptions lapse. Validate notifications and renew subscriptions proactively.
- Mailbox access: Target /users/{id}/... endpoints for specific mailboxes; support multi-tenant operation with verified domains. Do not use EWS or IMAP/POP.
- Reliability and scale: Implement retries with exponential backoff honoring 429/Retry-After, use request batching where appropriate, and respect service throttling guidance. Apply circuit breakers and queue-based processing for bursts.
- Security and compliance: Do not log message content or PII; redact headers when needed. Ensure data residency alignment, retention policies, and DLP are honored by deferring to tenant policies.
- Observability: Capture request IDs, latency, and quota metrics; emit structured telemetry for auditing and support.
- Backward compatibility: Feature-flag SMTP as a temporary fallback only if Graph is unavailable, with a plan to deprecate.

Adopt Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) to specify and verify user-facing behaviors using Gherkin feature files as living documentation. Author Feature files (Given-When-Then) in plain language, version them alongside the code, and review them with product and delivery stakeholders. Limit BDD to externally observable behaviors (critical user journeys, business rules, acceptance criteria); do not use BDD for low-level unit tests.

For UI and end-to-end tests, implement scenarios with Cypress using cucumber-js via the @badeball/cypress-cucumber-preprocessor. Store features under tests/e2e/features and step definitions under tests/e2e/steps with reusable, declarative steps. For API/service behaviors, use cucumber-js integrated with our Node.js test stack (e.g., supertest/axios) under tests/api/features and tests/api/steps.

Standardize on tags for suite selection (e.g., @smoke, @regression, @accessibility, @wip) and require each scenario to map to a tracked requirement or user story ID. Enforce linting and style guides for Gherkin, keep scenarios independent and deterministic, and prefer high-level steps that hide UI mechanics.

Integrate BDD execution into CI/CD: run smoke-tagged scenarios on each PR, full regression nightly, and publish readable reports and artifacts. Treat failing BDD scenarios as release blockers.

Standardize the application file-system layout to separate code, configuration, stateful data, caches, and logs, using OS-appropriate conventions and an abstraction layer:

- Application binaries and static assets: read-only under /opt/<app> (Linux) or Program Files\<App> (Windows).
- Configuration: /etc/<app> (Linux/macOS via XDG_CONFIG_DIRS) and %ProgramData%\<App>\config (Windows); support per-user overrides via ~/.config/<app> and %AppData%\<App>.
- Persistent data: /var/lib/<app> (Linux), ~/Library/Application Support/<App> (macOS), and %ProgramData%\<App>\data (Windows).
- Cache: /var/cache/<app> (Linux), ~/Library/Caches/<App> (macOS), and %LocalAppData%\<App>\Cache (Windows).
- Logs: /var/log/<app> (Linux), ~/Library/Logs/<App> (macOS), and %ProgramData%\<App>\logs (Windows), with structured JSON logs to stdout/stderr in containers.
- Temp files: OS temp directories only; no runtime writes alongside binaries or source.

Introduce a path-resolution library to compute these locations at runtime based on XDG Base Directory spec on Unix-like systems and known folders on Windows. Default to environment overrides (e.g., APP_CONFIG_DIR, APP_DATA_DIR) for testing and single-binary deployments. In containers, mount /config, /data, and /cache explicitly and keep /app read-only.

Maintain backward compatibility by reading from legacy paths first-run, migrating data atomically to the new locations, and leaving compatibility symlinks for one release cycle. Enforce least-privilege file permissions, rotate logs, and document the layout for operators and developers. This decision eliminates ad-hoc paths, improves portability, and simplifies backups and security hardening.

Adopt “device(s)” as the canonical domain term, replacing “asset(s)” across product, code, APIs, events, UI, documentation, and data models.

Scope
- Code and domain: rename classes, modules, services, and configuration keys from asset* to device*.
- Data model: migrate table/collection names and fields (e.g., assets → devices) with reversible, zero-downtime migrations and views/aliases for compatibility.
- APIs: introduce v2 endpoints using device terminology; keep v1 endpoints with asset terminology deprecated for two minor releases; map v1→v2 at the edge where feasible.
- Events/streams: publish “device.*” events; emit dual events (“asset.*” as aliases) during the deprecation window.
- UI/UX and copy: update all labels, help text, and error messages to “device(s)”.
- RBAC/permissions: rename scopes/claims (asset:read → device:read), maintain backward-compatible synonyms during deprecation.
- Observability: update metrics, logs, and alerts to device terminology with metric aliasing/shims where supported.
- Docs/SDKs: update references and code samples; provide a migration guide and changelog.

Compatibility and migration
- Provide read/write aliases (DB views/synonyms) and translation middleware for API requests to avoid breaking clients during the deprecation window.
- Maintain id stability; no changes to primary keys or identifiers beyond naming.
- Versioning: bump minor for clients adding device terminology; major for removing asset terms.
- Communicate deprecation timelines and provide automated lint/upgrade scripts for SDK consumers.

Acceptance criteria
- No downtime; existing clients using asset terminology continue to function during the window.
- All user-facing surfaces and new integrations use device terminology exclusively.
- Telemetry parity maintained (no metric loss).
- Data migration validated with backfill and checksum; rollback plan documented.

Timeline
- Phase 1: Introduce device terminology (v2), add aliases, update docs.
- Phase 2: Switch defaults, emit deprecation warnings.
- Phase 3: Remove asset terminology after agreed deprecation period.

We will continue to use the Flutter stable channel for all production builds and customer-facing releases, and adopt the Flutter beta channel only for R&D, upcoming-platform validation, and pre-integration testing.

- Scope of beta usage:
  - Create a dedicated “beta-integration” branch that tracks the latest Flutter beta.
  - Use beta for evaluating new SDK features (e.g., Material 3 updates, Impeller, new iOS/Android SDK requirements), upcoming OS releases, and breaking-change discovery across our packages/plugins.
  - Internal QA-only builds may be produced from beta; no public releases from beta.

- Version pinning and tooling:
  - Pin Flutter versions per branch using fvm (fvm_config.json) and in CI (explicit flutter --version).
  - Lock plugin and Dart dependencies via pubspec.lock committed on the beta branch to ensure reproducible builds.
  - Maintain a per-upgrade CHANGELOG and compatibility matrix for first-party plugins and critical third-party packages.

- Upgrade cadence and gates:
  - Auto-check for new beta weekly; upgrade only if:
    - All apps compile for Android and iOS,
    - Core E2E smoke tests pass,
    - No P0 regressions in performance or app startup are detected.
  - If failures occur, revert the beta bump and file issues upstream as needed.

- CI/CD and branching:
  - Add a parallel CI workflow “beta-verify” running analyze, test, build IPA/AAB, and selected integration tests on the beta branch.
  - Block merges from beta into main unless stable has caught up, or the change is source-compatible with stable.

- Release policy and rollback:
  - Only stable channel builds are shipped to users.
  - If a critical platform deadline (e.g., new Play/iOS requirements) is only met by beta, we will wait for the corresponding stable release or adopt a Google-endorsed release candidate flagged as stable; otherwise, file an exception with explicit risk acceptance.
  - Maintain a documented rollback to the last known-good stable Flutter version.

This approach gives early visibility into breaking changes and platform shifts while preserving production stability and predictable releases.

## Decision

We will standardize on a single, organization-approved primary cloud provider for all new workloads and migrate existing workloads to it in phases. This consolidation enables unified security and compliance controls, consistent platform tooling, streamlined operations, stronger vendor leverage, and optimized cost management.

Key elements:
- Establish a centrally managed landing zone with baseline guardrails (identity and access management, network segmentation, encryption, logging/monitoring, backup/DR, artifact registries).
- Adopt a multi-account/project structure per product/team with standardized CI/CD, infrastructure-as-code, and observability.
- Provide a curated platform toolkit (e.g., Kubernetes/PaaS, managed databases, messaging, secrets management) and a golden-path service catalog.
- Implement FinOps practices (budgeting, tagging, chargeback/showback, rightsizing) across all environments.
- Maintain pragmatic portability to reduce lock-in where feasible (Terraform/IaC, containers/Kubernetes, OpenAPI/GRPC, data export processes), without compromising delivery speed.
- Define an exceptions process for secondary cloud/services where required by regulatory, data-residency, latency, or unique capability needs; all exceptions must document risk, exit plans, and costs.
- Enforce “primary-by-default” for all new workloads; prioritize migration of high-cost/high-risk legacy workloads; set milestones and success metrics.
- Create a dedicated Platform Engineering function to operate the cloud foundation and enable teams.
- Review the provider choice and portability posture annually, or upon material changes in business, compliance, or market conditions.

- Standardize on Kubernetes as the container orchestration platform for all environments.
- Prefer managed Kubernetes in cloud (GKE/EKS/AKS) for production; use kind/k3d for local development and a single managed provider per region to meet data residency requirements.
- Use upstream Kubernetes APIs and portable tooling to avoid vendor lock-in; no provider-specific CRDs unless encapsulated.
- Adopt GitOps with Argo CD for declarative deployments, version-controlled manifests, and drift detection.
- Package and release applications with Helm charts; maintain a shared chart library for common patterns and values; environment-specific values live alongside app code.
- Use Kubernetes Deployments with rolling updates as default; enable canary/blue/green via Argo Rollouts where needed.
- Enforce multi-tenancy via namespaces per product/team, RBAC, resource quotas, and network policies; default to containerd runtime.
- Autoscaling: enable Cluster Autoscaler; use HPA (CPU/memory/custom metrics) and selectively VPA for non-latency-sensitive workloads.
- Networking: use managed CNI; standardize on NGINX Ingress Controller (or cloud LB integrations where native) with TLS via cert-manager.
- Storage: use CSI drivers with dynamic provisioning; select storage classes per workload characteristics (RWO/RWX, SSD/HDD).
- Secrets: adopt External Secrets Operator integrated with cloud KMS/Secret Manager; encrypt at rest and in transit.
- Observability: ship metrics via Prometheus and OpenTelemetry Collector, logs to centralized backend, traces via OpenTelemetry; expose /healthz and /readyz.
- Security: apply Kubernetes Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted), image signing and scanning, admission policies via OPA Gatekeeper, and minimal base images.
- Disaster recovery: back up cluster state (where applicable) and persistent volumes; define cluster bootstrap via Infrastructure as Code.

We will use GitHub as the single system of record for the Architecture Decision Log (ADL) and all Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

- ADRs will live in the project repository under docs/adr/ as sequentially numbered Markdown files (e.g., ADR-0001-title.md), with an index at docs/adr/README.md.
- All changes to ADRs will be made via Pull Requests. Proposed decisions start as “Proposed” ADRs, reviewed by CODEOWNERS, and merged when accepted. Superseded ADRs will be updated with a “Superseded by” link.
- We will use a GitHub Issue template for ADR proposals and a PR template to enforce required sections (Status, Context, Decision, Consequences) and consistent titling/numbering.
- Branch protection rules will require at least one architecture reviewer approval for ADR changes. ADR files are protected by CODEOWNERS.
- Labels (adr, proposed, accepted, superseded) will be used to track lifecycle; GitHub Projects/Boards may be used to visualize ADR workflow.
- GitHub Actions will validate numbering, generate/update the ADR index, and optionally publish ADRs via GitHub Pages for easy browsing.
- Releases will snapshot the ADR state corresponding to product versions; ADR changes will be included in release notes.
- For multi-repo setups, a central “architecture” repo will host cross-cutting ADRs, with repository-level ADRs kept locally and cross-linked.

This approach ensures versioned, reviewable, discoverable, and auditable ADRs integrated into our normal development workflow.

We will use Sidekiq with Redis to handle all outbound email delivery asynchronously. Application code will enqueue idempotent mailer jobs to Sidekiq instead of sending synchronously; Redis will serve as the durable job store. We will use Sidekiq’s built-in concurrency, retries with exponential backoff, and dead-set handling to improve deliverability and resilience under provider/network failures. We will define specific Sidekiq queues (e.g., mailers, mailers_low) with priority and dedicated concurrency, and apply rate limiting to respect provider throughput constraints. Jobs will include stable deduplication keys to avoid duplicate sends, and will be designed to be idempotent at the provider level when possible (e.g., provider message IDs).

We will prefer direct Sidekiq integration over generic ActiveJob to leverage Sidekiq’s monitoring, middleware, and scheduling capabilities. Operationally, we will provision a dedicated Redis instance/namespace for Sidekiq to isolate from cache usage, set appropriate persistence (AOF) and connection limits, and enable Sidekiq Web for observability and alerting (queue latency, retries, dead). Sensitive payload data will not be stored in jobs; instead, jobs will reference secure records. Timeouts and circuit breakers will protect against slow/broken providers, with categorized retries (transient vs permanent) and a dead-letter workflow for manual inspection or automated reprocessing. Environments will use the same mechanism (with lower concurrency) to ensure parity.

## Decision

We will adopt the ORID (Objective–Reflective–Interpretive–Decisional) framework as the standard facilitation structure for architecture reviews, incident/postmortem debriefs, roadmap prioritization, and quarterly retrospectives.

- Scope: ORID will be used to structure agendas, notes, and outcomes for the above meeting types; ad‑hoc use is encouraged elsewhere.
- Templates: Meeting and ADR templates will include ORID sections; the ADR Context maps to Objective/Reflective/Interpretive and the ADR Decision maps to Decisional.
- Facilitation: The meeting owner is responsible for enforcing the ORID flow and timeboxes; a facilitator may be delegated.
- Artifacts: Outcomes must include a documented Decisional section with explicit options considered, decision, owners, and next steps.
- Tooling: Confluence/Docs templates and ticket forms will be updated to include ORID prompts; bots/checklists will nudge adherence.
- Training: A 30‑minute enablement session plus a quick reference guide will be provided to all leads and facilitators.
- Compliance: ORID use is required for decisions impacting APIs, data contracts, security, SLOs, or multi‑team dependencies; otherwise recommended.
- Review: After two sprints, we will assess adoption, meeting efficiency, and decision clarity; adjustments will be proposed via ADR if needed.

This decision aims to improve psychological safety, reduce bias, separate observations from judgments, and produce clearer, actionable decisions with traceability.

Non-leaf keys MUST NOT carry values and arrays MUST be dense (no holes). Concretely:
- A key that has children is a pure container; it SHALL NOT have a value (only metadata allowed). If input provides both value and children, the operation MUST fail or be normalized by dropping the value according to policy.
- Arrays are represented with strictly consecutive indices starting from #0 without gaps. Missing indices (holes) are invalid and MUST be rejected or automatically compacted to a dense form before commit.
- Storage, import/export, merge, and transformation plugins MUST preserve these invariants and either normalize or fail fast on violations.
- Lookup and iteration MAY rely on these guarantees (no need to handle mixed value/container nodes or sparse arrays), simplifying client logic and ensuring consistent semantics across backends.

We standardize the API repository as a single-service repo with a consistent, navigable layout, clean architecture boundaries, and clear separation of app code, tests, contracts, deployment, and automation.

Top-level layout:
- src/ — production code
  - Api/ — ASP.NET Core host (controllers, DI, pipeline)
  - Application/ — use-cases (feature folders with MediatR requests/handlers, validators)
  - Domain/ — entities, value objects, domain services, events (no external deps)
  - Infrastructure/ — persistence, external services, EF Core, implementations
- tests/ — mirrors src structure (Api.Tests, Application.Tests, Domain.Tests, Infrastructure.Tests)
- contracts/ — OpenAPI specs, JSON schemas, or proto files (source of truth; versioned)
- deploy/ — IaC (e.g., Terraform), Helm/k8s manifests, environment overlays (non-secret)
- scripts/ — developer tooling, build/release scripts
- docs/ — ADRs, runbooks, architecture diagrams
- .github/ — CI/CD workflows, issue/PR templates
- .config/ — editorconfig, dotnet-tools.json, analyzers settings

Conventions:
- One solution file at repo root includes all projects and tests.
- Enforce reference rules: Api -> Application; Application -> Domain; Infrastructure -> Application/Domain only via abstractions; Api never references Infrastructure directly (composition root wires interfaces to implementations).
- Feature-by-folder in Application: Features/<Feature>/{Commands,Queries}/ with request/handler pairs and validators; controllers remain thin.
- Contracts drive implementation (contract-first); breaking changes require versioned specs and backward compatibility plan.
- No secrets or environment-specific config in repo; use secret stores. Configuration-as-code lives under deploy/.
- Naming: PascalCase for project names, kebab-case for folders; consistent namespace = Company.Product.Api|Application|Domain|Infrastructure.
- Mandatory CI: build, test, lint, SCA, SBOM; artifacts published per project; release pipelines consume deploy/.
- Optional: samples/ for usage examples; tools/ for local dev containers.

This structure improves discoverability, testability, and modularity, and enables repeatable builds and deployments while keeping business logic isolated and portable.

We will adopt an OpenAPI 3.1, contract-first approach as the single source of truth for documenting the API. The specification will be maintained in version-controlled YAML within the repository, reviewed via pull requests, and validated in CI using Spectral (linting) and oasdiff (breaking-change detection). We will generate and publish interactive documentation (Redoc as primary, Swagger UI as fallback) at a stable, versioned URL (e.g., /docs and /docs/v{major}). The spec will include comprehensive schemas, reusable components, tagged operations, request/response examples, standardized error models (problem+json), authentication flows, pagination/filtering/sorting conventions, rate limit headers, and deprecation metadata.

We will implement semantic versioning, produce and host a spec per API version, and maintain a human-readable changelog aligned with spec changes. Client SDKs and server stubs may be generated from the spec where appropriate, with manual curation for developer ergonomics. We will publish a generated Postman collection and example workflows from the spec. Documentation builds will be reproducible via Docker and integrated into release pipelines. The latest spec will be accessible as machine-readable JSON at a canonical endpoint (e.g., /openapi.json) and optionally published to an API catalog/portal. All new or changed endpoints must include updated spec segments, examples, and tests before merge, ensuring documentation remains accurate and discoverable.

## Decision

We will adopt MUI (Material-UI) v5 as the primary React component framework for building our web UI.

- Use @mui/material v5 with the default @emotion styling engine (no styled-components).
- Establish a single, shared theme (light and dark variants) defining color tokens, typography scale, spacing, shape, and component overrides; consume via the sx prop and theme augmentation.
- Prefer MUI’s composed components for standard UI (buttons, forms, navigation, dialogs) to ensure consistency, accessibility (WCAG/ARIA), and faster delivery; use @mui/base for highly bespoke interactions when design requires minimal styling.
- Optimize bundle size via component-level imports, tree-shaking, and icon subset selection (@mui/icons-material with explicit imports).
- Enable SSR compatibility and performance in Next.js (CacheProvider, createEmotionCache) and use CSS injection order best practices.
- Follow MUI’s theming/customization patterns instead of ad-hoc CSS; disallow global CSS that conflicts with MUI baselines.
- Use MUI X components (e.g., Data Grid) where advanced data presentation is needed; evaluate license (Pro/Premium) per feature needs.
- Create a small internal library of shared components built atop MUI to codify our design system and reduce duplication.
- Document accessibility and testing guidelines (React Testing Library) for MUI components and enforce via linting and Storybook.

We will propagate domain events using a broadcast (publish/subscribe) pattern rather than direct point-to-point invocation. Domain events will be emitted as immutable messages to topic-based channels and fanned out to any interested subscribers within or across bounded contexts.

Events will be wrapped in a standard envelope containing: event_id (UUID), event_type (versioned), occurred_at, aggregate_type/id, tenant, correlation_id, causation_id, and schema_version. Producers persist events in an Outbox within the same transaction as the aggregate change; a dispatcher broadcasts from the Outbox to the message bus, ensuring at-least-once delivery. Consumers must be idempotent and maintain their own offsets/checkpoints.

Transport selection: in-process broadcasts use an in-memory bus for tests and local dev; inter-process broadcasts use the configured message broker (e.g., Redis Streams/NATS/Kafka) with topic conventions <bounded-context>.<aggregate>.<event>. No synchronous request/response over broadcasts; commands remain separate.

Event schemas are contract-tested and backward compatible (additive changes); deprecations are versioned and announced. Security and tenancy metadata flow with the envelope; PII is avoided in payloads or encrypted when necessary. Observability is provided via tracing (propagating correlation/causation), metrics (publish/consume rates, lag), and structured logs.

This decision enables loose coupling, fan-out to multiple modules (e.g., projections, integrations, real-time UI), and independent evolution of consumers while preserving reliability through the Outbox and idempotent handlers.

Consolidate the separate api-redis instance into the existing backend-redis by running a single managed Redis cluster. Use distinct Redis users/ACLs, key prefixes (e.g., api:* and backend:*), and, where supported, separate logical databases only for non-shared features to avoid key collisions and enable access scoping. Right-size the cluster capacity (memory, throughput, connections) based on combined load plus headroom, and enable eviction/TTL policies appropriate to each namespace. Update clients to use namespace-specific credentials and prefixes; migrate existing keys with a one-time copy and validation. Establish dashboards and alerts segmented by namespace to detect contention or latency regressions. If sustained resource contention or SLO impact occurs, be prepared to re-split into dedicated Redis instances for the API and backend. This consolidation reduces operational overhead and cost while preserving isolation via ACLs and conventions.

We will extract domain models and health functionality from the Android app into independent Gradle modules with clear contracts and optional implementations.

- Create a pure-Kotlin domain module (:domain-models) containing immutable domain entities, value objects, and use-case contracts, with no Android dependencies.
- Introduce a health API module (:health-api) defining the public interfaces (e.g., HealthRepository, PermissionsManager, Metrics, Sync contract) and data contracts used by the app and features.
- Provide pluggable health implementations as separate modules (e.g., :health-healthconnect, :health-googlefit), depending on :health-api and the respective platform SDKs. These modules must not depend on the app.
- Isolate persistence and platform concerns: keep Room entities and DAOs in :data-persistence (Android-only), and map to/from :domain-models via mappers in :data-mappers. Health implementations may use these via dedicated ports if needed.
- The app module depends only on :domain-models and :health-api. Health implementation selection is wired via DI (Hilt bindings) and/or build flavors; default binding is provided in the app to avoid hard dependencies in libraries.
- Apply semantic versioning to :domain-models and :health-api; introduce API surface checks (metalava/binary-compatibility-validator) and enforce package visibility boundaries.
- Publish library modules as AAR/Maven artifacts for reuse (internal registry), with CI pipelines building, testing, and versioning each module independently.
- Enforce dependency inversion: platform SDKs, Google Fit/Health Connect, analytics, and UI must not leak into :domain-models or :health-api. No module may reference the app package.
- Provide migration facades and deprecation shims to move existing code incrementally; add compile-time lint to prevent app-layer imports in libraries.
- Testing: unit tests reside in each module; instrumented tests only where Android APIs are required. Contract tests validate :health-impl-* against :health-api.

This separation yields a thinner app, faster builds, reusable libraries, and safer evolution of domain and health contracts while keeping platform-specific code optional and replaceable.

## Decision

We will adopt Lightweight Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture all significant architectural decisions.

- Format: Michael Nygard’s lightweight ADR structure (Title, Status, Context, Decision, Consequences, Alternatives). Keep each ADR concise and focused on one decision.
- Location: Store ADRs in the repository under doc/adr (or docs/adr). Each ADR is a numbered Markdown file (e.g., 0001-record-architecture-decisions.md).
- Tooling: Prefer Nat Pryce’s adr-tools (or adr-tools-python) to create and manage ADRs; otherwise, use the provided template in doc/adr/0000-template.md.
- Scope: Record only “significant” decisions (e.g., changes to architecture, cross-cutting concerns, data model, infrastructure, SLAs/SLOs, external integrations, security posture, resilience patterns, cost-impacting choices).
- Process: Create a draft ADR during design, iterate via Pull Request discussion, and mark as Accepted upon consensus. Supersede prior ADRs rather than editing history; reference superseded IDs.
- Ownership: The author of the change initiates the ADR; all reviewers are responsible for clarity and completeness. Tech Lead (or designated architect) arbitrates unresolved disputes.
- Conventions: Use clear, testable language; capture rationale, trade-offs, and rejected alternatives. Link to related issues, RFCs, and diagrams.
- Governance: Review ADRs in Architecture Review meetings; validate alignment with principles and non-functional requirements.
- Automation: CI enforces presence of an ADR for qualifying changes (labels or paths), checks template compliance, and maintains an index (README.md) in doc/adr.

We will standardize on AMaps (Gaode) as the primary map engine across all clients and services, integrating its SDKs (iOS/Android/JS) behind a provider-agnostic MapCore adapter. All map features (rendering, markers/overlays, geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, POI search, geofencing) must call MapCore interfaces; direct SDK calls are disallowed.

Provider selection will be dynamic by region and capability: AMaps is default for Mainland China (GCJ‑02), with fallback providers (e.g., Mapbox/Google) selectable via config/feature flags for RoW and when specific features or SLAs require them. Coordinate system conversion utilities (WGS‑84 ⇄ GCJ‑02) are included in MapCore to ensure positional accuracy.

We will pin SDK versions, wrap breaking changes in the adapter, and publish the MapCore library as a semver artifact. API keys will be centrally managed with rotation, per‑env quotas, and telemetry. Tile/data caching, exponential backoff, request coalescing, and client‑side rate limiting will be implemented in the adapter.

Compliance and privacy (GDPR/CCPA/China data residency) will be enforced at the adapter boundary with redaction and opt‑in consent flows. We will migrate existing direct Google/Leaflet usages to MapCore via shims, deprecating direct references on a phased schedule with contract tests and mock providers to ensure parity.

We will adopt a test automation strategy based on the Test Pyramid: fast, deterministic unit tests as the foundation; focused integration/contract tests for service boundaries; and a minimal set of high-value end-to-end journeys. Concretely:
- Unit tests: use language-appropriate frameworks (e.g., Jest/Mocha for JS/TS, pytest for Python, JUnit for Java) with Testing Library for UI components; prefer pure functions, deterministic seeds, and mocks only at external boundaries.
- Integration tests: use Testcontainers or equivalent to run real dependencies (DB, message broker) in ephemeral environments; API tests include schema validation and happy/pathological paths.
- Contract tests: use Pact (or equivalent) for consumer-provider verification.
- End-to-end: use Cypress (or Playwright) for a small set of critical user flows; run in parallel with isolated test data.
- Non-functional: smoke tests post-deploy; performance and resilience tests per release.

Quality gates: all tests run in CI on every PR; unit and integration tests must pass to merge; e2e runs on PRs affecting UI and nightly. Minimum coverage thresholds: 80% lines/branches overall and 90% on critical modules; coverage is informative for e2e. Flaky tests are quarantined within 24 hours and fixed or removed within one sprint. Results are surfaced in CI with trend reporting; failures block releases.

## Decision

Adopt a standardized, lightweight ADR template and workflow for all architectural decisions.

Template:
- Title: Short, descriptive noun phrase
- Date
- Status: Proposed | Accepted | Rejected | Deprecated | Superseded (with links)
- Context: Forces, constraints, assumptions, risks
- Decision: The choice and rationale
- Consequences: Positive, negative, and neutral outcomes
- Alternatives (optional): Considered options and why not chosen
- References (optional): Links to issues, docs, PRs, and related ADRs

Conventions:
- Author ADRs in Markdown, one decision per file, concise (≤1–2 pages).
- File location: docs/adr/
- Filename: YYYY-MM-DD-kebab-case-title.md
- Immutability: Do not rewrite history; only update Status and add supersession links; fix typos via PRs without altering intent.
- Cross-link related ADRs and record decision drivers and trade-offs.

Workflow:
- Create ADR as Proposed via pull request.
- Review by architecture owners and relevant stakeholders.
- Decide and set Status; merge when Accepted/Rejected.
- Supersede via a new ADR; mark old as Superseded and link both ways.

Tooling:
- Provide docs/adr/_template.md with this structure.
- Optionally use adr-tools or repo snippets to scaffold new ADRs.

## Decision

Rename the utils-demo package to migrations to accurately reflect its purpose as the home for database/content/application migration tooling and scripts.

Actions:
- Change package name from utils-demo to migrations (e.g., @ourorg/migrations), update package.json (name, bin, description), and rename the repository folder accordingly.
- Update all internal references, imports, CI workflows, release pipelines, and documentation to point to migrations.
- Publish a final utils-demo version that depends on and re-exports migrations (CLI and library) to provide a painless upgrade path for one minor release cycle; mark utils-demo as deprecated on the registry with guidance to migrate.
- Preserve semantic versioning continuity by starting migrations at the next minor version matching utils-demo’s current line.
- Update distribution artifacts (CLI name, Docker image tags if any) to migrations; provide alias shims in the compatibility release.
- Communicate the rename in the changelog, migration guide, and release notes; notify stakeholders and update onboarding templates and examples.
- Enforce the rename via CI by blocking new releases of utils-demo after the compatibility window and adding a linter rule to prevent new imports.

We will introduce a minimal, stable Player interface that decouples domain behavior from input, UI, and networking concerns. The Player will be modeled as a controllable Entity composed with a pluggable CommandSource (human input, AI, script, or network), following ports-and-adapters.

Key decisions:
- Define IPlayer as a domain port with:
  - identity: id()
  - state accessors: snapshot()/queryCapabilities()
  - action intake: submit(Command cmd) returning Result/Events
  - lifecycle: tick(GameTime), onEvent(DomainEvent)
  - controller management: setCommandSource(CommandSource), getCommandSource()
- Commands are immutable DTOs validated against capabilities; execution yields domain events. No UI types, input devices, or rendering primitives appear in the interface.
- Use composition over inheritance: Player wraps a core Entity model and a CommandProcessor; capabilities are discovered via queryCapabilities() to keep the interface stable as abilities evolve.
- Asynchronous operations (e.g., pathfinding, network latency) are supported via Promise/Future-returning submit and an event stream (Observer interface) to avoid blocking the game loop.
- Provide adapters: InputCommandSource (keyboard/mouse/controller), AICommandSource, ScriptedCommandSource, and NetCommandSource. Swapping controllers requires no changes to Player.
- Version the interface (IPlayer v1) and keep a narrow surface to minimize churn; extend via new Commands/Events, not new methods.
- Error handling returns typed failures (e.g., NotPermitted, InvalidState, CooldownActive) rather than throwing.
- Serialization uses explicit PlayerSnapshot DTOs for save/load and deterministic replays (event log-driven).

Non-goals: tying Player to rendering, physics engine specifics, or UI widgets; embedding inventory/skills API in the interface (access via capabilities).

This structure maximizes testability, enables human/AI/network control with the same pipeline, and keeps domain logic independent of delivery mechanisms.

## Decision

We will standardize on Sentry as the centralized exception monitoring platform for all applications (backend services, web frontends, and mobile), using Sentry Cloud (SaaS).

- Integrate official Sentry SDKs for each runtime/framework and initialize as early as possible to capture unhandled exceptions, crashes, and breadcrumbs. Wrap request/job boundaries to capture handled failures.
- Configure projects and environments (prod, staging, dev) with environment and release tagging. Publish release versions from CI/CD and upload source maps/symbols for accurate stack traces.
- Adopt structured context: add tags for service, subsystem, version, region, tenant/account, and correlation/trace IDs. Exclude health checks and expected noise.
- Enable performance tracing with conservative sampling (server- and client-side), aligning with our OpenTelemetry setup where available. Adjust sample rates per environment and apply inbound rate limits to control cost.
- Enforce privacy-by-default: enable server-side PII scrubbing, URL and header sanitization, and explicit allowlists. Do not send secrets or sensitive payloads. Anonymize user identifiers where required by policy/GDPR.
- Define alerting and workflows: route P1/P2 alerts to on-call via PagerDuty; send lower-severity notifications to Slack; auto-create/link Jira issues for regressions. Use issue grouping rules and ignore lists for known business exceptions.
- Manage DSNs and auth tokens via secret management. Restrict access with SSO and role-based permissions. Set data retention per compliance needs and periodically review sampling, filters, and alert noise.

## Decision

We will implement method-level authorization, row-level filtering, and field redaction using datashield4j. Enforcement will be annotation-driven on service/application-layer methods, with runtime interception via AOP proxies. The library will integrate with our SecurityContext, deriving subject attributes (roles, permissions, scopes, tenant, data ownership) from JWT/OIDC claims and request context.

Policies will be centrally defined in a DataShieldPolicyRegistry loaded from configuration and version-controlled. We will use:
- @Allow/@Require (roles, permissions, scopes, attributes) for authorization
- @RowFilter(expression or predicate) for attribute-based, tenant/ownership filters
- @Redact(fields, strategy) and @Mask(strategy) for selective field-level protection
- @Deny for explicit blocks
Default posture is deny-by-default unless explicitly allowed.

Enforcement is fail-closed: if policy evaluation or policy store access fails, access is denied. All decisions (allow/deny, filter, redact) are auditable with structured logs and correlation IDs. We will enable a report-only (dry-run) mode in initial rollout to surface violations without blocking, then switch to enforce per service.

Performance: cache compiled policies; prefer pushdown filters to repositories/queries where supported; apply filtering before pagination; short-circuit evaluation on first decisive rule. We will add a build-time annotation processor to fail builds on unknown or malformed policies.

Scope: method-level protection augments (does not replace) transport-level authentication and gateway authorization. We will provide contract tests and policy unit tests to validate expected access, filtering, and redaction across roles and tenants.

Adopt a canonical, typed “map of objects” data model to drive Terraform configuration across environments. All deployable units (e.g., services, databases, buckets) will be described in per-environment YAML files (one file per env), loaded via yamldecode(file(...)) into a single input variable, validated with explicit object types, and normalized in locals. Modules will consume this normalized data using for_each (not count) to ensure stable addressing. Optional attributes will be modeled with nullable types and sensible defaults in locals. No module will read arbitrary files directly; all data flows through a single, versioned schema variable. Schema versions will be embedded and validated at plan time, with migration notes documented on changes. Mixed-type collections are disallowed; keys must be deterministic and human-readable. Environment overrides live only in env/*.tfvars or YAML, not sprinkled across .tf files. Remote-state lookups are confined to a dedicated composition layer to keep modules pure. This approach enables repeatable plans, clear diffs, safer refactors, and simpler reviews while decoupling data shape from module internals.

We will use a managed JSON document database (e.g., MongoDB Atlas/Azure Cosmos DB/AWS DocumentDB) as the aggregate data repository for read-heavy, denormalized views across services.

- Data model: One aggregate per document, keyed by aggregateId (and tenantId where applicable). Embed closely related sub-entities; reference only when cardinality/volatility dictates. Target document size within platform limits (preferably < 1 MB).
- Access patterns: Repository is read-optimized. Only projection/updater jobs write; application clients read only. Updaters perform idempotent upserts.
- Consistency: Eventual consistency is acceptable. Track version, source watermark, and lastUpdated for each document. Use optimistic concurrency (version check) to avoid lost updates.
- Ingestion: Materialize aggregates from upstream events/CDC/ETL. Maintain replayable pipelines and a dead-letter queue for poison messages. Support backfills and replays.
- Indexing: Unique index on (tenantId, aggregateId). Add compound indexes to cover top queries; avoid unbounded regex scans. Periodically review index health and cardinality.
- Schema governance: Enforce JSON Schema validation with a schemaVersion field. Support additive changes first; provide migration scripts for breaking changes. Maintain backward-compatible readers during transitions.
- Scaling and partitioning: Shard by tenantId (preferred) or aggregateId to balance load and enable tenant isolation. Use pagination and server-side limits. Monitor hot partitions.
- Operations: Enable backups, PITR, encryption at rest/in transit, auditing, and least-privilege access. Classify and minimize PII; apply field-level encryption where required.
- Observability: Emit change events/metrics; use change streams for cache invalidation. Establish SLOs for freshness and query latency; alert on staleness and projection lag.

This choice prioritizes developer velocity, flexible schemas, and scalable read performance for aggregate views.

## Decision

We will package all Kyma component Helm charts into the Kyma Installer container image and make the image the single, versioned, immutable artifact for installation and upgrade.

Key aspects:
- Embed pinned Helm charts (as tgz or rendered manifests) in the installer image at build time; the image tag defines the Kyma version. A lockfile records exact chart SHAs to guarantee reproducibility.
- Use Helm v3 libraries (tillerless) from the installer to install/upgrade components in a deterministic, dependency-aware order, with retry and resume-on-failure semantics.
- Drive installation via a Kubernetes Installation CRD that declares the desired Kyma version, enabled components, and profile. Component values are supplied via Override ConfigMaps/Secrets; precedence is well-defined.
- Provide profiles (e.g., evaluation, production) as curated component/values sets bundled in the image; allow selective component enablement for constrained environments.
- Support air‑gapped and offline scenarios by removing runtime dependency on external chart repositories or the public internet.
- Upgrades are performed by updating the installer Deployment to a new image; the controller detects the version change and executes chart upgrades with 3‑way merge, hooks, and health checks. Rollback is supported by redeploying the previous image.
- Expose dry-run/plan, progress status, and per-component conditions via CR status for observability and automation.
- For development, allow an optional “dev mode” to source charts from a remote repo or local mounts; releases default to embedded charts only.

This approach ensures consistent, auditable installs and upgrades, simplifies version skew management, and enables secure, air‑gapped deployments while preserving developer flexibility.

Adopt Helix Extensions as the single, first-class mechanism for platform extensibility. All new integrations, customizations, and domain-specific features must be implemented as Helix Extensions conforming to the Helix SDK and manifest schema; existing ad-hoc plugins will be migrated to this model.

- Scope: data sources/sinks, pipeline steps, UI actions, webhooks, and automation hooks must be delivered as extensions.
- Packaging & Versioning: extensions are packaged as versioned modules with semantic versioning aligned to the Helix SDK compatibility matrix. Breaking changes require a major bump and deprecation window.
- Distribution: extensions are published to the internal registry and resolved via an allowlisted catalog. Only signed, reviewed artifacts are loadable in production.
- Runtime & Isolation: extensions run sandboxed with capability-based permissions, resource quotas, and well-defined contracts (IPC/HTTP/gRPC as provided by Helix). No direct access to host internals outside declared capabilities.
- Configuration: each extension declares a manifest (name, version, capabilities, configs, permissions). Instance configuration is declarative and environment-overridable. Feature flags control rollout.
- Observability: extensions must emit standardized logs, metrics, and traces with correlation IDs and health endpoints; usage is tracked via the catalog.
- Security: mandatory code signing, SCA scanning, static checks, and manual review for elevated permissions. Least-privilege by default with periodic permission audits.
- Testing & Quality: contract tests against the SDK stubs are required; CI validates compatibility across supported SDK versions. Backward compatibility tests are maintained for LTS windows.
- Operations: progressive delivery (canary/percent rollout), safe rollback, and kill-switch support are required. Extensions declare upgrade notes and migration hooks where applicable.
- Naming & Ownership: extensions use a namespaced convention (e.g., org.helix.<domain>.<name>) and have documented ownership and support SLAs.
- Documentation: every extension provides README, manifest docs, configuration examples, and operational runbooks.

This decision standardizes extensibility, reduces integration risk, and enables secure, observable, and governable evolution of platform capabilities.

We will implement the liveness probe for the Registry-Buddy container as an exec probe that runs curl against a local health endpoint, avoiding external DNS/network dependencies and enabling richer, in-process health validation.

- Use an exec probe: /bin/sh -c 'curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:${HEALTH_PORT:-8080}/healthz || exit 1'
- Ensure the image includes a minimal HTTP client (curl preferred; fall back to wget -qO-).
- Expose a lightweight HTTP health endpoint on localhost that returns 200 only when the process is healthy and its critical dependencies (e.g., credentials, registry connectivity if required) are verified.
- Configure probes:
  - startupProbe (exec with same curl command): periodSeconds=2, failureThreshold=30, timeoutSeconds=2
  - livenessProbe (exec): initialDelaySeconds=10, periodSeconds=10, failureThreshold=3, timeoutSeconds=2
  - readinessProbe may use the same endpoint/command with periodSeconds=5 and failureThreshold=3
- Bind the health server to 127.0.0.1 to avoid exposure and reduce attack surface.
- Ensure the command works under the container’s user (non-root) and shell availability; if using distroless, provide a small sidecar or static curl binary.
- Return non-200 for degraded states requiring restart only in liveness; use readiness to reflect transient issues without restart.

We will standardize on Ansible as our primary configuration management and application provisioning tool. Ansible will manage OS/user packages, system services, application runtime configuration, deploy artifacts, and orchestrate post-provision steps across Linux hosts via agentless SSH. We will structure code as reusable roles with clear defaults/vars, employ inventories per environment, and manage secrets with Ansible Vault (and/or cloud KMS/SSM integration). Infrastructure resource creation will remain with Terraform; Ansible will configure on top of provisioned resources. Playbooks and roles will be versioned in Git, validated with ansible-lint, and tested via Molecule (including containerized and cloud drivers). CI/CD will run idempotent playbooks for drift correction and deployments, with dry-run (check mode) and diff where feasible. We will prefer official/community-supported modules over ad-hoc shell tasks, codify minimal host facts gathering for speed, and leverage dynamic inventories for cloud environments. Access will use SSH keys with least privilege and optional sudo, rotating credentials via platform mechanisms. Rollbacks will be supported with tagged tasks and reversible handlers where practical; blue/green or canary patterns will be orchestrated via playbooks when needed. Documentation and examples will accompany each role, and a small set of approved Galaxy dependencies will be curated to reduce supply-chain risk.

Adopt a de-versioned V8 code base. Remove version numbers from source directories, namespaces, and package identifiers, consolidating to a single canonical code path. Manage versioning exclusively through Git tags, release branches, and artifact semver; do not duplicate code per version in-tree.

Enforce a rolling-release model with clear deprecation policies: breaking changes require a deprecation window and/or compatibility shims/feature flags, with removals happening only at tagged releases. Consumers must pin to a release tag or commit SHA; mixing multiple V8 versions within the same repository is disallowed.

Update build, packaging, and distribution to emit semver-tagged artifacts (e.g., vX.Y.Z) while the source remains unversioned. Provide an LTS branch policy for downstreams needing stability, and publish migration notes for any breaking API/runtime changes.

Add CI guardrails to prevent introduction of versioned directories and to detect duplicated APIs. Provide tooling to surface deprecated APIs and guide migrations. This simplifies the codebase, eliminates drift between versioned trees, reduces maintenance overhead, and centralizes compatibility management while retaining explicit, tag-based versioning for releases and consumption.

Adopt a single, unified WASM-based Ribosome as the sole execution environment for all zomes. All application code MUST compile to wasm32-unknown-unknown and interact with the host exclusively through a versioned, stable host API provided by the HDK. We will retire and remove all alternative ribosome variants and non-WASM execution paths.

Use one WASM engine backend across all platforms/builds, pinned to a specific version to ensure deterministic behavior. The conductor will load and cache compiled modules, instantiate per-call execution contexts, and enforce sandboxing with resource limits (memory, fuel/instruction metering, and execution timeouts).

The host function surface is explicitly defined and semver-versioned; changes to host capabilities require a new API version and compatibility shims as needed. Native extensions are not permitted; all logic must reside in WASM zomes or host functions approved in the HDK.

Provide a migration path for existing zomes to recompile to the unified target and map any deprecated host calls to their versioned equivalents. Update build tooling, CI, and release artifacts to assume a single WASM ribosome and to run conformance tests against the pinned engine.

We will adopt standardized pull request templates to improve review quality, consistency, and release readiness. Templates will be stored in .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/ and selected by authors from multiple options (e.g., feature.md, bugfix.md, chore.md, security.md, docs.md). A default.md will be applied when no specific template is chosen. For org-wide repos, fallback templates may be provided in the organization’s .github repository.

Each template will include:
- Summary and motivation
- Linked issues (Closes #…)
- Type of change (bug fix, feature, breaking change, docs, chore)
- Implementation notes
- Tests added/updated and coverage impact
- Backward compatibility and migration/breaking changes
- Security/privacy considerations
- Performance and observability (metrics, logs, alerts)
- Documentation updates (user/dev)
- Screenshots or demos (when applicable)
- Release notes entry (imperative, user-facing)
- Checklist for labels, reviewers, and CI status

We will enforce template usage via:
- Branch protection requiring status checks that validate presence of required sections/checkboxes
- PR label and title checks aligning with our changelog conventions
- CODEOWNERS for mandatory reviews on sensitive areas

Templates will be reviewed quarterly and evolve with team feedback. Exceptions (e.g., trivial CI/config changes) may use the chore template but must still include a minimal summary and validation.

We will standardize on Nginx for simple HTTPS reverse proxying and TLS termination. Nginx will front small services with minimal routing logic (path- or host-based) and forward to a single upstream per virtual host. We will ship a hardened baseline config: HTTP→HTTPS redirect, TLS 1.2/1.3 with curated ciphers, HSTS, OCSP stapling, sane proxy timeouts, gzip/brotli where appropriate, request size limits, and basic rate limiting toggles. Observability is via structured access/error logs and optional Prometheus exporter sidecar.

Provisioning will use the official nginx stable image with a templated server config and environment-driven upstream/hostname variables. Certificates will be managed via ACME (Let’s Encrypt) using an external controller (e.g., cert-manager on Kubernetes) or certbot + shared volume in standalone deployments. For Kubernetes, we will prefer the Nginx Ingress Controller for multi-host scenarios; for single-service or edge nodes, a dedicated Nginx pod/VM is acceptable.

Scope is intentionally narrow: no complex auth, content rewriting, or L7 policy—those belong in upstream gateways/service meshes. HTTP/2 will be enabled; HTTP/3/QUIC can be toggled where supported. Any need for dynamic discovery, weighted routing, canarying, or mTLS will use Envoy/Traefik or the platform’s ingress. This keeps the proxy layer lean, secure, and easy to operate.

We will integrate with Workday using productized interfaces first, following a “Workday-first” design. Priority order: (1) Public REST APIs and SOAP WWS, (2) EIB and RaaS for bulk extracts/imports, (3) Workday Studio only when necessary for complex orchestration not achievable by standard means.

All integrations will be mediated via the enterprise integration layer (iPaaS/message bus) using a canonical HR data model, with transformations and routing outside Workday. We will prefer asynchronous patterns using Workday Business Events/webhooks where available; otherwise, scheduled, incremental pulls using effective-dated queries and change detection.

Keys and identity: use immutable Workday IDs (e.g., Worker, Position, Org) as system-of-record identifiers; map to local surrogate keys via canonical model. Enforce idempotency, exactly-once delivery semantics where possible, and support pagination, throttling, and exponential backoff to respect Workday rate limits.

Security and compliance: use OAuth2/OIDC or certificate-based auth per Workday best practice; encrypt in transit and at rest; apply least privilege via Workday security groups; minimize PII; mask in non-prod; honor data residency and GDPR/retention requirements; log access for audit.

Reliability and operations: implement retries with dead-letter queues, compensation where side effects occur, and end-to-end correlation IDs. Monitor with synthetic checks, functional alerts, and contract tests. Use Workday Sandbox/Preview for integration testing; promote via CI/CD with configuration migration control. Version APIs and mappings; document SLAs and maintenance windows aligned to Workday release cycles.

We will standardize on active HTTP health checks in HAProxy that validate application readiness, not just port availability.

- Each application must expose a readiness endpoint that returns 200 only when the app and its critical dependencies are ready (e.g., /healthz or /_healthcheck_<app>). It must be fast (<100ms) and unauthenticated.
- HAProxy backends will use option httpchk GET <health_path> with an explicit Host header matching the app’s vhost to ensure the correct virtual host is exercised.
- Health check parameters will be standardized: inter=2s, rise=3, fall=2, timeout check=1s. These may be tuned per app with documented overrides.
- For TLS-terminating frontends, health checks run over HTTP to the upstream (or HTTPS with check-ssl verify none if the backend requires TLS). For TLS passthrough backends, we will use tcp-check rules to send an HTTP GET with SNI (ssl_fc_sni where applicable) and expect a 200 response.
- During deployments and autoscaling, servers will be added in maintenance mode (disabled/no traffic) and only enabled after they pass health checks (first pass + rise). Draining will be used before stopping instances to avoid 5xx during rollout.
- Default behavior routes traffic only to healthy servers; unhealthy servers are automatically removed from rotation and re-added after rise consecutive successes.
- Configuration will be templated in our HAProxy config management (e.g., Puppet/Ansible) with per-app variables: health_path, host_header, tls_check, and custom thresholds.
- Metrics and logs from HAProxy (httpchk status, rise/fall events) will be exported to our observability stack for alerting on backend health and elevated failure rates.

This approach ensures that traffic is only sent to instances that are genuinely ready, reducing 5xxs during deploys and node replacements.

We will run all visual regression tests inside a pinned Docker image on Jenkins to ensure a fully reproducible runtime. The image will be owned by the team and versioned; it will include a fixed OS base, Node.js, test runner (e.g., Playwright), a specific headless browser build (Chromium/Firefox/WebKit), and a curated, versioned font set (e.g., Noto/DejaVu). Jenkins pipelines will execute tests on Linux agents using this image only.

Determinism settings will be enforced by the pipeline:
- Fixed viewport and deviceScaleFactor=1; disable GPU; headless mode.
- Set environment variables: TZ=UTC, LANG=C.UTF-8, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0 (using image-bundled browsers).
- Install and use only bundled fonts; disable remote font loading; provide CSS to prefer-reduced-motion and disable animations/transitions.
- Freeze network and time: mock dates, random seeds, and network responses; block nondeterministic endpoints; pre-seed data.
- Normalize rendering: turn off subpixel AA where possible and standardize color profile.

Baselines will be stored in the repository (or a versioned artifact store) tied to the Docker image tag. The pipeline will:
- Generate diffs with a consistent threshold (e.g., pixelmatch with anti-aliasing handling).
- Fail on unexpected diffs and publish artifacts (actual, expected, diff) for review.
- Provide a controlled “approve/update baselines” job that runs in the same image after human review, updating baselines on an approval branch/PR.

Any changes to tools, fonts, or browsers require building a new image tag and updating baselines in a dedicated maintenance PR, ensuring changes are explicit and auditable.

- Target Python versions: support 3.10–3.12; develop and deploy on 3.12 by default.
- Version management: use pyenv (or asdf) to install/switch Python versions; .python-version committed per repo.
- Dependency and environment management: use Poetry for packaging, dependency resolution, and virtualenvs; commit poetry.lock; use semantic version ranges for libs and exact pins for tooling; publish with PEP 517/518 (pyproject.toml only).
- Multi-version testing: use tox to run test, lint, and type-check environments across supported Python versions; CI mirrors tox envs.
- Linting and formatting: use Ruff for linting and import/order checks and as the formatter (ruff format) to avoid tool overlap; no Black or isort.
- Type checking: use mypy with strict incremental settings; type: ignore and Any usage must be justified with comments.
- Testing: use pytest with pytest-cov; enforce unit tests co-located with code and integration tests under tests/integration; minimum coverage thresholds in CI.
- Pre-commit: enforce ruff (lint+format), mypy (fast mode), detect-secrets, end-of-file-fixer, trailing-whitespace; pre-commit autoupdate monthly.
- Configuration: centralize tool config in pyproject.toml; include .editorconfig; provide .env.example and load via python-dotenv or pydantic-settings; never commit .env.
- Reproducibility: lockfiles are required; use Poetry groups (main/dev/optional) and extras; renovate/dependabot configured for weekly bumps; pinned CI base image.
- Developer UX: Makefile (or taskfile) with targets: bootstrap, install, fmt, lint, typecheck, test, tox, clean.
- Containers: optional devcontainer/Docker for parity; image builds from poetry export --without dev + wheels; CI uses the same Dockerfile for build/test when containerized.
- Commit the minimal scaffolding: pyproject.toml, poetry.lock, tox.ini, .pre-commit-config.yaml, .editorconfig, .python-version, .env.example, Makefile, CI workflow.

This standardizes tooling, enforces quality gates pre-commit and in CI, and provides reproducible, multi-version Python development across local and CI environments.

## Decision

- Custom field labels shown in the storefront must be resolved server-side using the SalesChannelContext language. Resolution order:
  1) label in current language (from custom_field.config.label[locale] or translation)
  2) parent language
  3) system default language
  4) technical name as last fallback
- Label loading must happen via a dedicated CustomFieldLabelProvider service, injected into Page/PageletLoaders. Controllers must not query repositories directly.
- The provider loads labels in batches per CustomFieldSet to minimize queries, based on the entity/sets relevant to the page (e.g., product, category, customer, order). It returns a structure mapping customField technical names to resolved, localized labels.
- Only custom fields marked for storefront visibility are exposed. Fields flagged inactive, private, or admin-only are not rendered in storefront.
- Storefront renders localized labels received from the Page/PageletLoader; no client-side (AJAX) label lookups. For headless clients, an equivalent Store-API route exposes localized labels for requested sets.
- Caching:
  - Provider results are cached per sales channel, language, and set combination (PSR-6/Redis) and pages with labels are HTTP-cached when safe.
  - Cache invalidation is triggered on CustomField, CustomFieldSet, and their Translation write events.
- Accessibility and formatting:
  - Where a label is missing and a technical name is used, it must be humanized (e.g., snake_case → “Snake case”) for display.
  - Labels are plain text; HTML is not rendered from custom field config.
- Template usage must consume the provider’s prepared map; templates must not read or parse config directly.
- Backward compatibility: existing pages that render customFields values continue to do so; they must adopt the provider to display labels.

We will keep build-time transformations to a strict minimum and never mutate source files in place. The build may perform only deterministic, reproducible, and idempotent steps such as:
- Formatting and static analysis that fail the build on violations (auto-fix is allowed locally but not during CI).
- Resource filtering and version/commit metadata injection into non-source assets.
- Code generation executed in dedicated phases/locations that output to target/generated-sources (per ADR-002), not overwriting hand-written code.
