- Primary key: effective (Period end, else dateTime; earlier first). If only start present, use start; if only date, use start-of-day; configurable policy.
- Secondary keys (for tie-breaking, in order):
  - issued (earlier first),
  - subject (reference string),
  - code (system+code),
  - category (lexicographically on canonical codes),
  - id (stable final tie-breaker).
- Null handling: missing effective sorts after present; missing issued sorts after present.
- Stable, locale-independent, total ordering guaranteed.

Implementation notes
- Provide implementations in core domain module, language-idiomatic (e.g., Comparator in Java/TS).
- Expose functional variants and builders for policy tweaks (time tolerance, unit converters).
- Comprehensive unit tests with fixtures covering unit conversions, component reordering, nulls, and edge temporal cases.
- Document performance characteristics; comparators are allocation-light and suitable for large collections.

## Decision

Adopt a pull-request (PR)–centric workflow for all code changes.

- All changes must be made on short-lived feature branches and merged via PR; direct pushes to protected branches (main/release) are disallowed.
- Every PR requires at least one approval (two for security-/prod-critical code); CODEOWNERS will route required reviewers.
- CI must be green (build, tests, linters, security checks) before merge; status checks are enforced.
- Prefer small, focused PRs with clear, actionable scope; large PRs should be split or staged behind feature flags.
- Use draft PRs early to enable iterative feedback; convert to “ready for review” when complete.
- PRs must link to the originating work item/issue and include: intent/motivation, summary of changes, testing approach/results, risk/rollback plan; include screenshots/video for UI changes.
- Use a standard PR template; maintainers may request updates to meet the template before review.
- Default to squash-merge to maintain a linear, readable history with meaningful merged titles/descriptions; require branches to be up-to-date (rebase/merge) before merging.
- Enable automerge when approvals and checks are satisfied; require signed commits in repos where applicable.
- Hotfixes follow the same PR process with expedited reviews; emergency changes still require a PR post-facto if a temporary bypass is invoked.
- No long-lived divergent branches; regularly rebase with main to minimize drift.
- Discussions and design rationale happen in the PR thread and are considered part of the permanent record.

Decision

We will propagate compute launch changes using AWS Auto Scaling Groups backed by Launch Templates and the ASG Instance Refresh feature. The delivery pipeline will:

- Build a new AMI (or configure changes), create a new immutable Launch Template version, tag it, update the ASG to point to that version, and trigger an Instance Refresh.
- Use rolling replacements with health-aware pacing: 20–30% max in-flight, 90% min healthy, ELB/target-group health checks, and instance warm-up aligned to app readiness.
- Employ lifecycle hooks for graceful drain/termination (deregister from target groups, drain connections/queues), with SSM or a termination handler to finalize shutdown.
- Gate progress with CloudWatch alarms; auto-pause/rollback on alarm breach. Rollback = switch ASG to previous LT version and trigger a refresh (or fail back traffic for blue/green).
- For high-risk changes (kernel/OS, major runtime), use blue/green: stand up a new ASG with the new LT, attach to weighted target groups, shift traffic gradually, then decommission the old.
- Manage via IaC (Terraform): model LT versions immutably, trigger instance_refresh with configurable strategy, ignore_changes for LT default_version to avoid churn, and expose safe defaults.
- Record deployed LT version and AMI ID in release metadata for traceability.

This approach yields predictable, zero-/low-downtime rollouts, fast and reversible change propagation, and minimal manual effort, while deprecating legacy Launch Configurations in favor of Launch Templates.

## Decision

- Katas are named using a zero-padded numeric prefix and a short, descriptive kebab-case slug: NN-topic[-qualifier], e.g., 01-reflect-basics, 12-async-await, 27-generics-advanced.
- Use two-digit padding up to 99; if more are needed, extend to three digits consistently across all katas.
- Slugs:
  - lowercase only, kebab-case, ASCII characters.
  - concise (ideally ≤3 words), avoid abbreviations unless widely recognized (e.g., api, io, sql).
  - reflect the primary concept taught; optional qualifier clarifies scope or level (e.g., -intro, -advanced).
- Series or sequels use an additional numeric stage suffix: NN-topic-01, NN-topic-02 (not letters), where NN groups the series in the overall order.
- Breaking down a kata into parts within the same folder is discouraged; prefer distinct katas with their own NN-topic-XX entries.
- Directory and file layout per kata:
  - /NN-slug/
    - README.md (kata description and instructions)
    - src/ (starter code)
    - test/ (tests; filenames kebab-case with .spec.[js|ts])
  - No spaces in any path; no trailing punctuation; no emojis.
- Test suite top-level describe matches the kata slug converted to a sentence-cased title (e.g., "Reflect basics").
- Do not rename existing katas; future renames require creating a new NN-slug and deprecating the old one via README note.
- Reserve numbers by PR to avoid collisions; once merged, numbers are immutable.
- Tags for indexing (difficulty, topics) live in README front matter; they do not alter the slug.

- Status: accepted
- Decision: Monitoring data forwarders will be storage independent by design. We will deploy stateless forwarders that do not require Kubernetes PersistentVolumes or any specific storage class to operate.
- Implementation:
  - Use OpenTelemetry Collector for metrics and traces, and Fluent Bit or Promtail for logs.
  - Run forwarders as DaemonSets (node-local) with outputs streaming directly to remote backends over the network (e.g., Prometheus remote_write/OTLP, Loki, Elasticsearch, Kafka), avoiding durable cluster storage.
  - Use bounded, best-effort buffering and checkpoints on node-local ephemeral locations (hostPath to /var/log and /var/lib/<agent>) or in-memory buffers to survive pod restarts without introducing PV dependencies.
  - Enable at-least-once delivery with retries/backoff, backpressure, and rate limits; drop policies and health alerts protect cluster stability when backends are unavailable.
  - Externalize configuration via ConfigMaps and credentials via Secrets; outputs are pluggable to switch destinations without redeploying agents or changing storage.
  - High availability is achieved through per-node isolation (DaemonSet), multiple replicas for gateway/aggregator collectors, and load-balanced endpoints.
- Constraints:
  - No PersistentVolumeClaims or CSI dependencies for forwarders.
  - Node-local disk usage is strictly bounded and monitored; forwarders fail fast rather than blocking nodes when limits are reached.
- Rationale:
  - Eliminates coupling to any storage provider, simplifies multi-cloud and on-prem deployments, reduces operational toil, and ensures consistent behavior across environments.

We will standardize Java container images on a multi-stage build using Eclipse Temurin Java 21 (LTS):

- Builder stage: eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-jammy (or :21-jdk-jammy-alpine only if musl compatibility is proven). Build with Maven/Gradle wrapper; no build tools in the final image.
- Runtime stage (default): eclipse-temurin:21-jre-jammy (slim). No Alpine for runtime due to glibc/musl issues and TLS/JNI nuances. For heightened hardening needs, teams may opt into gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian12 as an approved alternative.

Security and portability:
- Pin base images by digest; manage updates via Dependabot/Renovate rules. Only use vendor-signed images (Eclipse Temurin/Adoptium, Distroless).
- Run as non-root (UID 10001), read-only filesystem, drop Linux capabilities, set a non-writable workdir (/app), and expose only required ports.
- Include SBOM and image attestations at build time; scan images in CI.
- Multi-arch builds (amd64/arm64) published via Buildx.

Runtime defaults:
- ENTRYPOINT uses exec form to run the fat jar: ["java","-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75","-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError","-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError","-Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom","-jar","/app/app.jar"]
- HEALTHCHECK via a lightweight HTTP endpoint.
- Only CA certificates and timezone data included; no shell or curl in runtime images (distroless has none by design).

Operational guidance:
- Prefer layered caching: copy build descriptors first, then sources.
- Store configuration in env/Secrets Manager; no baked secrets.
- Image labels follow OCI (org.opencontainers.image.*) with git SHA, version, commit time, and source URL.

This composition yields consistent, secure, and efficient Java containers while allowing an approved hardened variant when required.

## Decision

- Provide a reusable Generic Startup Library to orchestrate application/service initialization across platforms and modules.
- Expose a minimal API:
  - StartupTask: id, dependencies, execute(), rollback()/onFailure (optional), isCritical flag.
  - StartupOrchestrator: register(task), registerAll(tasks), run(mode = Cold|Warm), shutdown(), status(), onProgress callbacks.
- Enforce deterministic, dependency-ordered execution using a DAG; detect cycles at registration time.
- Support async and parallel execution where dependencies allow; configurable concurrency, timeouts, and retry policies.
- Require tasks to be idempotent and side-effect-safe; orchestrator guarantees at-most-once execution per run.
- Provide failure policies: fail-fast for critical tasks; continue/skip for non-critical with aggregated error reporting.
- Integrate observability: structured logs, timing/metrics per task, tracing hooks.
- Configuration via code and dependency injection; no runtime reflection required to remain compatible with restricted platforms.
- Offer platform bindings:
  - JVM/Server: invoked in main or DI container bootstrap.
  - Android: Application.onCreate and ProcessLifecycle for cold/warm starts.
  - iOS: AppDelegate/SceneDelegate hooks.
  - CLI/tools: simple main wrapper.
- Packaging: internal library published to our artifact repository with semantic versioning; zero external heavy dependencies.
- Provide reference tasks (config load, logging, telemetry, feature flags, remote config sync) and scaffolding for app-specific tasks.
- Include comprehensive tests (unit for DAG/order/failure, integration per platform) and sample apps for adoption.

## Decision

Adopt a production runtime posture that depends only on Google Cloud Platform services and private network paths. All synchronous, in-path runtime dependencies must be GCP-native (e.g., GKE/Cloud Run, Cloud Load Balancing, Cloud SQL/Spanner, GCS, Pub/Sub, Memorystore, Secret Manager, KMS, Cloud Logging/Monitoring, Artifact Registry). Third-party SaaS and non-GCP endpoints are prohibited on the critical request path; integrations must be asynchronous, optional, and resilient (e.g., via Pub/Sub subscriptions, export jobs, or webhooks with queues, retries, and circuit breakers).

Guidelines:
- Prefer managed GCP services over self-managed software; if self-managed is required, run it within GCP (GKE/GCE) with private IPs and managed backups.
- Enforce private connectivity (VPC, Private Service Connect, Serverless VPC Access) and, where applicable, VPC Service Controls for data exfiltration protection.
- Centralize secrets in Secret Manager; key operations via Cloud KMS; artifacts in Artifact Registry; observability in Cloud Logging/Monitoring/Trace.
- Regionalize deployments and data to meet latency and residency requirements; use multi-region or DR patterns as needed.
- Provide abstraction interfaces for portability (e.g., storage, queue, secrets) and document a migration path; avoid service-specific leakage across domain boundaries.
- Staging/preprod mirror this policy to ensure parity.
- Any exception (hard runtime dependency on non-GCP) requires an approved ADR/RFC specifying SLO impact, rollback/exit plan, security review, and cost analysis.

This reduces operational risk, simplifies IAM/compliance, and improves reliability while keeping a practical path to portability.

We will not use mutable global configuration or implicit singletons. All configuration must be supplied explicitly to components via dependency injection or passed as function parameters. Each module receives a typed, immutable configuration object limited to its scope; cross-cutting settings are provided through scoped providers (e.g., request/job context) rather than process-wide globals.

Configuration is loaded and validated once at application startup, normalized into strongly typed objects, and then distributed through the composition root. Runtime mutation of configuration is prohibited; changes require restart or a controlled hot-reload mechanism confined to the configuration layer.

The only exception is a minimal, read-only constants module for compile-time, non-environmental values (e.g., feature flags defaults, version info).

Existing global configuration will be deprecated, wrapped behind injectable interfaces, and phased out incrementally with tests ensuring no component implicitly reads process-wide state.

We will model phosphorylation and dephosphorylation using linear mass-action kinetics as the default reaction formalism. Specifically:
- Phosphorylation: S + K -> S_p with rate kf · [S] · [K]
- Dephosphorylation: S_p + P -> S with rate kr · [S_p] · [P]

By default, enzymes (K, P) can be treated in pseudo-first-order when present in excess or assumed constant, collapsing to kapp · [S] and kapp · [S_p] to improve numerical stability and performance for large networks. An option will allow explicit enzyme species and conservation when needed.

Multi-site phosphorylation will be represented as independent states (e.g., S0, S1, …, Sn) with linear transitions between adjacent states, each with its own forward/reverse rate constants. We will avoid combinatorial explosion by generating only reachable states and disallowing cross-site coupling in the default model. Users may override with custom topologies if required.

We will not include saturation, cooperativity, or allostery (e.g., Michaelis–Menten/Hill) in the default; a pluggable kinetics layer will allow opting into those forms per reaction when data justify it.

Rate constants and units will be enforced as:
- Second-order (explicit enzyme): M^-1·s^-1
- First-order (pseudo-first-order): s^-1
Unit checks and automatic conversion will be provided.

The ODE solver will use deterministic continuous-time integration with support for stiff solvers. We will include validation tests (single-step, reversible pair, and linear cascades) against analytical solutions to ensure mass conservation (for explicit enzymes) and substrate conservation across phosphorylation states.

This decision prioritizes simplicity, identifiability, and performance while preserving an escape hatch for richer kinetics where necessary.

## Decision

Adopt snapshot testing to assert stable, human-reviewable outputs where structure and presentation are more important than specific values.

- Scope:
  - Frontend: Use snapshots for presentational components (markup/DOM trees), styles, and serialized props where output is deterministic.
  - Backend/CLIs/codegen: Use “golden file” snapshots for serialized data (JSON/YAML/text) and generated artifacts.
  - Do not use snapshots for core business logic, complex algorithms, or large/volatile payloads; prefer explicit assertions there.

- Tooling:
  - Web: Jest snapshot tests for JS/TS.
  - Other stacks: language-appropriate snapshot libraries (e.g., golden files) producing human-readable diffs.
  - Store snapshots alongside tests in VCS with small, well-scoped files.

- Determinism:
  - Normalize and mask nondeterministic fields (timestamps, IDs, UUIDs, floats ordering).
  - Mock time, randomness, and network; sort keys; seed RNGs.

- Review & updates:
  - Updating snapshots requires explicit developer action and code review.
  - PRs must justify snapshot changes and avoid “accept all” without understanding diffs.
  - CI blocks on unexpected diffs; no auto-approve of snapshot updates.

- Maintenance & size:
  - Keep snapshots minimal and focused; avoid megabyte-scale files or binary formats.
  - Periodically prune obsolete snapshots and refactor overly broad ones.
  - Prefer inline snapshots for small outputs; external files for larger artifacts.

- Integration:
  - Run snapshot tests in CI on all branches; protect main with passing snapshot suite.
  - Combine with accessibility, unit, and integration tests; snapshots do not replace them.

## Decision

We will establish a two-tier benchmarking approach for APS: microbenchmarks for core algorithms and end-to-end benchmarks for scenario-level performance.

- Microbenchmarks: Use JMH to measure core scheduling/optimization hotspots (heuristics, constraint evaluation, search operators). Configure warmup/measurement iterations, forked runs, fixed JVM flags, and GC logging. Version and pin JDK and dependencies to ensure comparability.

- End-to-end: Use Gatling-driven workloads (or k6 if JS-based teams prefer) to exercise APIs with representative APS scenarios. KPIs include solve time, throughput, schedule stability, deadline adherence, optimality gap, CPU/memory footprint, and p95/p99 latencies.

- Datasets: Curate a canonical corpus of real and synthetic APS scenarios with documented characteristics (size, constraints, variability). Provide synthetic data generators with fixed seeds for repeatability.

- Environment: Containerize the benchmark runner and SUT; use CPU pinning, fixed resource quotas, and isolated nodes. Collect system metrics via Prometheus + Grafana; capture GC, heap, and async-profiler flamegraphs for regressions.

- Reporting: Persist raw results as JSON/CSV artifacts; publish trend dashboards and regression gates in CI (baseline comparisons, +/- thresholds). Benchmarks run nightly and on performance-sensitive changes; microbenchmarks run in PRs with shortened profiles.

This framework becomes the single source for performance claims, capacity planning, and regression detection in APS.

## Decision

Adopt TypeScript as the default language for all new application code (frontend and Node.js services) and migrate existing JavaScript code incrementally. Use strict typing across the codebase (compilerOptions: { strict: true, noImplicitAny: true, strictNullChecks: true, noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true }). Maintain a shared base tsconfig and project references for multi-package repos. Standardize on ESM with NodeNext module resolution, target ES2020+, and emit type declarations for publishable libraries.

Integrate type-checking into CI (tsc --noEmit) and enforce consistent style with ESLint (typescript-eslint) and Prettier. For dev UX, use ts-node/tsx or framework-native tooling (e.g., Vite, Next.js) and fast builds with tsup/esbuild where applicable; production builds use tsc or framework build pipelines.

Manage third‑party types via @types packages; prefer unknown over any, avoid non-null assertions, and wrap untyped integrations with typed adapters. Publish and reuse shared types (DTOs, API schemas) from a common package, deriving types from schemas (e.g., zod/io-ts/OpenAPI) where possible to ensure runtime validation.

Document typing conventions and patterns (React props, Redux/Zustand stores, API clients), and require type coverage gates on critical modules. This standardization aims to improve correctness, maintainability, and developer experience while controlling migration risk.

We will adopt GA4GH Variation Representation Specification (VRS) types as the canonical model for representing genomic variation across APIs, storage, and inter-service messaging.

- Use Allele as the default type for sequence-level variants (SNVs, MNVs, small indels), represented with SequenceLocation (inter-residue coordinates) and SequenceState.
- Use Haplotype for phased combinations of Alleles on the same molecule; use Genotype for zygosity/unphased counts of Alleles/Haplotypes.
- Use CopyNumber and CopyNumberChange for CNVs and aneuploid events; use Range/DefiniteRange for imprecise CN assignments.
- Use VariationSet only to package multiple variations without implying phase.
- Locations must use reference-accessioned sequences with explicit species/genome build semantics handled upstream; no implicit coordinate systems.
- All variation objects must be normalized per VRS normalization rules (trim/left-shift to inter-residue canonical form). Legacy HGVS/VCF inputs must be converted and normalized to VRS.
- Serialization will be VRS JSON with ga4gh CURIE identifiers (e.g., ga4gh:VA…, VSL…, VCN…) and computed digests as primary keys where feasible. No ad-hoc or partially conformant types are permitted in persisted or published interfaces.
- Client-facing descriptors (labels, annotations, external IDs) will be carried outside core VRS objects via a VariationDescriptor wrapper; internal logic must not rely on human-readable fields for identity.
- Backward compatibility: existing internal variant types will be mapped to VRS through a translation layer; external APIs that previously emitted legacy formats will continue to do so only where contractually required, sourced from the VRS canonical model.
- Validation: all inputs and outputs will be validated against the VRS JSON Schema; non-conformant payloads are rejected with actionable errors.
- Versioning: pin to a specific VRS minor version (initially VRS 1.x); any upgrade requires a compatibility review and regeneration of digests where semantics change.

This decision establishes a single, interoperable, and loss-minimizing representation for variation, enabling consistent normalization, deduplication, and exchange with external GA4GH-compliant systems.

Deprecate DynamicServiceLocator and schedule removal in the next major release.

- Status: Accepted
- Scope: Deprecate the DynamicServiceLocator component, its public interfaces, factory methods, and configuration keys. New features will not target this mechanism.
- Rationale: The dynamic resolution pattern introduces runtime ambiguity, hampers observability, complicates dependency analysis, and overlaps with supported DI/container-based service resolution and explicit ServiceRegistry patterns. It increases cold-start latency and makes behavior environment-dependent, reducing testability and reproducibility.
- Timeline:
  - Current minor release: Mark APIs as @Deprecated; emit structured runtime warnings when used; add docs with migration guidance.
  - Next minor release: Maintain backward compatibility only; no new enhancements.
  - Next major release: Remove APIs, configuration, and code paths.
- Migration:
  - Prefer explicit wiring via the supported DI container (e.g., Spring/Guice) or the project ServiceRegistry/ServiceFactory abstraction.
  - For dynamic needs, use a registry-backed ServiceResolver with explicit, versioned descriptors rather than name-based or reflection-based lookups.
  - Provide a compatibility adapter: a thin resolver that maps legacy dynamic identifiers to registry entries; ship as an optional module to ease incremental migration.
- Operational guidance:
  - Add metrics/logging to inventory remaining usages.
  - Provide a config linter to flag deprecated keys in CI.
  - Document equivalent configuration snippets and code examples for common DynamicServiceLocator patterns.
- Risk mitigations:
  - Keep binary stubs (throwing/forwarding) for one minor to reduce breakage.
  - Validate performance and startup improvements via benchmarks and publish results.
- Success Criteria: Zero runtime warnings in default distributions; no production usage detected for one minor before removal; simplified startup and clearer service graphs.
